meaning: “Good God!” / “Holy God!” (an exclamation of surprise, anger, disgust, etc.).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection (often with “Oh”): “Dio santo!” It expresses strong emotion (shock, frustration, disgust, disbelief). In many contexts it can be considered blasphemous or rude, so it’s common in informal speech but best avoided in polite/formal situations.
target_language_example: Dio santo, che confusione qui dentro!
native_language_example: Good God, what a mess in here!

meaning: "Sky People" / "people from the sky" (a named group).
additional_notes: Usually capitalized because it’s used like a proper name for a specific group (often in stories: outsiders, invaders, aliens, etc.). Grammatically it’s "gente" (people) + "del" (= di + il, "of the") + "cielo" (sky/heaven).
target_language_example: Dicono che la Gente del Cielo tornerà presto.
native_language_example: They say the Sky People will return soon.

meaning: “divine warrior”; a holy/legendary warrior (often a title).
additional_notes: Usually a capitalized title or role in stories, games, or mythology. With the indefinite article it’s “un Guerriero Divino” (a Divine Warrior); with the definite article it’s “il Guerriero Divino” (the Divine Warrior). Agreement changes with gender/number: “Guerriera Divina” (female), “Guerrieri Divini” (plural).
target_language_example: Dicono che il Guerriero Divino protegga il regno.
native_language_example: They say the Divine Warrior protects the kingdom.

meaning: 'on vacation' (used as a nickname/label, typically in usernames, tags, or captions).
additional_notes: Although the natural Italian is usually written without hyphens ("in vacanza"), the hyphenated form "In-Vacanza" is common as part of a handle, tag, or stylized label (e.g., "Alex-In-Vacanza" = "Alex-on-vacation"). In standard prose you’d normally write: "Sono in vacanza."
target_language_example: Non credo di aver conosciuto questo Alex-In-Vacanza.
native_language_example: I don’t think I’ve met this Alex-on-vacation.

meaning: "Pearl of the Spirit" (a poetic/religious expression, sometimes used as a title or name).
additional_notes: Literally "perla" = "pearl" and "dello Spirito" = "of the Spirit" (di + lo). It’s not a common everyday phrase in Italian; you’re more likely to see it in spiritual/religious writing or as a proper name (e.g., a book, prayer group, or initiative).
target_language_example: Ho letto un libro intitolato "Perla dello Spirito".
native_language_example: I read a book titled "Pearl of the Spirit."

meaning: "Fourth Lady" / "Fourth Madam" (a respectful title used to address the 4th lady/wife in a household).
additional_notes: Used like a title or form of address: you can say it by itself when calling someone or speaking to them (e.g., bringing tea). It literally means “fourth + lady,” so it implies there are several “Signore” ranked/numbered in the same family or household (common in historical/drama contexts rather than everyday modern Italian). Often written with capitals as a title.
target_language_example: Quarta Signora, la cena è pronta.
native_language_example: Fourth Lady, dinner is ready.

additional_notes: Formal Catholic title for the Pope. In Italian it’s usually capitalized (Santo Padre). You can use it with an article when talking about him: "il Santo Padre" (the Pope), "dal Santo Padre" (from the Pope), "del Santo Padre" (of/about the Pope). When addressing him directly, it can be used without an article, like a title: "Santo Padre, ..."
target_language_example: Ho avuto un’udienza con il Santo Padre.
native_language_example: I had an audience with the Holy Father (the Pope).

additional_notes: Usually used as a title/nickname (often capitalized) for someone who secretly controls people or events “from behind the scenes.” It can also be a codename or the name of a specific character/target in a story.
target_language_example: Dicono che il Signore dei Burattini controlli tutto nell’ombra.
native_language_example: They say the Puppet Master controls everything from the shadows.

meaning: “Your Majesty” (a respectful way to address a king/queen).
additional_notes: Used when speaking directly to, or about, a monarch. It’s a very formal honorific; in Italian it’s usually written with capital letters (Sua Maestà). The verb normally agrees with the real person (often 3rd person singular: “Sua Maestà pensa…”).
target_language_example: Sua Maestà desidera parlare con voi.
native_language_example: Your Majesty wishes to speak with you.

additional_notes: Used in Italian just like in English. In speech you may also hear the feminine form "una t-shirt"; plural is often "le t-shirt" (invariable), though some people write "t-shirts". Common in shopping contexts when choosing sizes, colors, or materials (e.g., di cotone = cotton).
target_language_example: Vorrei una T-shirt nera, taglia M.
native_language_example: I’d like a black T-shirt, size M.

meaning: “Third Lady/Madam”: a respectful title for the third wife or the third high-ranking woman in a household.
additional_notes: Used like a formal address or reference (often in historical/aristocratic or fiction settings): the ordinal number (prima/seconda/terza…) shows her rank/order among the wives or ladies. It’s usually capitalized as a title and can be used with prepositions: dalla Terza Signora (“to/at the Third Lady’s place”), il figlio della Terza Signora (“the Third Lady’s son”).
target_language_example: Devo parlare con la Terza Signora prima di partire.
native_language_example: I have to speak with the Third Lady before leaving.

meaning: 'Your Majesty' (formal way to address a king or queen).
additional_notes: Very formal honorific used when speaking directly to a monarch (often capitalized in writing). It usually goes with third-person singular verbs: "Come sta Vostra Maestà?" = "How is Your Majesty?"
target_language_example: Mi perdoni, Vostra Maestà, non volevo interromperla.
native_language_example: Forgive me, Your Majesty, I didn’t mean to interrupt you.

meaning: “Your Honor.” (a formal way to address a judge)
additional_notes: Used in court or in legal settings to speak directly to the judge. It’s very formal and usually capitalized. You can use it alone (“Sì, Vostro Onore.”) or in a sentence (“Mi scusi, Vostro Onore…”). In everyday life Italians don’t use it unless they’re in a courtroom or talking to a judge in an official context.
target_language_example: Vostro Onore, posso fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Your Honor, may I ask a question?

meaning: A nickname or friendly form of address (like “buddy/dude”), used when talking to someone.
additional_notes: Used like a person’s name in direct address (often with commas), to get someone’s attention or to encourage/reassure them. It’s not standard Italian; it’s more like a specific nickname/slang term, so the meaning depends on who’s speaking and to whom.
target_language_example: Dai, Ya-sho, ce la fai!
native_language_example: Come on, buddy, you can do it!

meaning: to dance (after a verb, e.g., “to go/learn/start to dance”).
additional_notes: "A" + infinitive is common in Italian after certain verbs (e.g., andare a…, imparare a…, iniziare a…, insegnare a…, portare qualcuno a…). It introduces the action you’re going to do: "andare a ballare" = to go out dancing; "imparare a ballare" = to learn to dance. As an infinitive, it doesn’t change for person/number.
target_language_example: Stasera vogliamo andare a ballare.
native_language_example: Tonight we want to go dancing.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "giocare" or "essere bravo/brava" to talk about playing baseball or being good at it. "A" here means "at" (a sport/game).
target_language_example: Mio fratello gioca a baseball ogni sabato.
native_language_example: My brother plays baseball every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "giocare" (to play) to say which sport someone plays: "giocare a + sport". Here "basket" is a common short form of "pallacanestro" (basketball).
target_language_example: Giochi a basket il sabato?
native_language_example: Do you play basketball on Saturdays?

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "a" + infinitive after many verbs to express an action/purpose, e.g. "andare a bere" (go to drink / go out for a drink), "ricominciare a bere" (start drinking again). Often implies drinking alcohol in context, but it can also be coffee/water depending on what follows.
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro andiamo a bere qualcosa?
native_language_example: After work, shall we go have a drink?

meaning: to go have something to drink; to go for a drink.
additional_notes: Used after verbs of going out/movement (e.g., andare/uscire/passare) to suggest a casual drink (often at a bar). It can imply an informal social meet-up, similar to “grab a drink” in English.
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, vuoi venire a bere qualcosa?
native_language_example: After work, do you want to come grab a drink?

meaning: on board (on/in a vehicle or boat).
additional_notes: Used for being on a means of transport (ship, plane, train, bus, etc.). Common in welcomes/announcements ("Benvenuti a bordo!") and invitations/commands ("Vieni a bordo"). It can also mean someone has joined or is ready to start/participate ("Quando sei a bordo, partiamo").
target_language_example: Quando tutti sono a bordo, possiamo partire.
native_language_example: When everyone is on board, we can leave.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is inside and traveling on a ship. Pattern: "a bordo di" + means of transport (a bordo del treno, a bordo dell’aereo). "Della nave" = "di + la nave" (of the ship).
target_language_example: Siamo già a bordo della nave e stiamo aspettando la partenza.
native_language_example: We’re already on board the ship and we’re waiting for the departure.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside and traveling on a means of transport. It’s often followed by a noun like "treno", "aereo", "traghetto", "autobus". In everyday Italian you’ll also hear "a bordo di" without the article when the noun is plural (e.g., "a bordo di due autobus") or with other articles (e.g., "a bordo di una nave").
target_language_example: Siamo a bordo di un aereo diretto a Roma.
native_language_example: We are on board a plane headed to Rome.

additional_notes: Used to say something will happen in a short time, often with the future tense or with "tra poco" as a close synonym. Common in announcements and everyday speech: "sarà pronto a breve", "arriverà a breve".
target_language_example: Ti richiamo a breve.
native_language_example: I'll call you back soon.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "essere" to describe something’s price ("È a buon mercato" = it’s cheap), or with buying verbs to mean buying/getting something for a low price ("comprare a buon mercato"). It can also mean "cheap-looking" or "of low quality" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho trovato questa giacca a buon mercato.
native_language_example: I found this jacket cheap.

meaning: (vulgar) “with kicks in the ass”; used to threaten/force someone physically or to say you’ll make them do something.
additional_notes: Very vulgar/impolite. Often used with verbs like "prendere (qualcuno) a calci in culo" (= to kick someone in the ass) or to mean "I’ll make you go/do it by force" ("Sì che ci vai, e a calci in culo!"). Not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Muoviti, o ti ci porto a calci in culo.
native_language_example: Move, or I’ll drag you there with kicks in the ass.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "giocare" to mean the sport of soccer: "giocare a calcio" = "to play soccer". In Italian, "calcio" usually refers to soccer (not American football).
target_language_example: Mio fratello gioca a calcio ogni sabato.
native_language_example: My brother plays soccer every Saturday.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "giocare" to talk about playing soccer after school. "A calcio" means "soccer/football" (literally "to football"), and "dopo la scuola" means "after school". You can change the verb tense (gioco/giocavo/giocherò/giocheremo) to fit when it happens.
target_language_example: Oggi giochiamo a calcio dopo la scuola.
native_language_example: Today we’re playing soccer after school.

additional_notes: Often follows verbs like riuscire (to manage), iniziare (to start), imparare (to learn), provare (to try): verb + a + infinitive. With avere problemi a..., it means “to have trouble (doing something)”.
target_language_example: Sto imparando a camminare con le stampelle.
native_language_example: I’m learning to walk with crutches.

additional_notes: “A” + infinitive is used after many verbs to mean “to do (something)”, especially with verbs like cominciare/iniziare (to start), riuscire (to manage), insegnare (to teach someone), forzare (to force someone), and similar. Here, “a cantare” means “to sing” as the action that follows.
target_language_example: Non sono riuscito a cantare perché ero senza voce.
native_language_example: I couldn’t manage to sing because I had no voice.

additional_notes: Used with verbs that take an infinitive introduced by “a” (e.g., forzare/costringere qualcuno a + infinitive): “Mi hanno forzato/a a cantare una canzone” = “They forced me to sing a song.” The “a” here means “to” (not “at”). Agreement: for a woman, “forzata”; for a man, “forzato.”
target_language_example: Non voglio essere costretto a cantare una canzone davanti a tutti.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be forced to sing a song in front of everyone.

meaning: 'to understand' / 'to figure out' (used before an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used as “a + infinitive” after many nouns/adjectives to mean “to …”, especially with difficulty/speed/ability: “difficile a capire” (hard to understand), “lento a capire” (slow to understand), “capace a capire” (able to understand). It can also follow verbs like “cominciare” in the pattern “cominciare a + infinitive” (to start to …).
target_language_example: È difficile a capire senza un esempio.
native_language_example: It's hard to understand without an example.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition “a” + infinitive (“capire”) to express an aim/effort/result, often after verbs like “provare” (to try), “riuscire” (to manage), or “aiutare” (to help): “Sto provando a capire il francese.”
target_language_example: Sto provando a capire il francese, ma è difficile.
native_language_example: I’m trying to understand French, but it’s difficult.

meaning: at the head; in charge (also: new line/paragraph in “punto, a capo”).
additional_notes: Most common meaning is “in charge / leading,” usually in the pattern **essere a capo di + [group/thing]** (“to be in charge of...”) or **mettere qualcuno a capo di...** (“to put someone in charge of...”). In writing/dictation, **punto, a capo** means “period, new line” (start a new paragraph). In the fixed phrase **a capo coperto**, it literally means “with the head covered.”
target_language_example: Domani Laura sarà a capo del progetto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow Laura will be in charge of the project.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like aiutare (to help), andare (to go), or verbs of wanting/hoping, to express the action someone helps with or is going to do. Structure: aiutare + [person] + a + infinitive. Here, caricare = to load; il camion = the truck.
target_language_example: Puoi venire ad aiutarmi a caricare il camion?
native_language_example: Can you come help me load the truck?

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "giocare" (giocare a carte = to play cards). In "una partita a carte", it means a game/round of cards. Often implies playing a card game in general, not a specific one (like poker or scopa) unless named.
target_language_example: Dopo cena giochiamo a carte con gli amici.
native_language_example: After dinner we play cards with friends.

meaning: (in giocare a carte con) “to play cards with (someone).”
additional_notes: Used after the verb "giocare": "giocare a carte" = to play cards; add "con + person" to say who you play with (e.g., "con Roy"). Common past forms in the examples: "giocò" (simple past) and "ha giocato" (present perfect).
target_language_example: Stasera gioco a carte con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m playing cards with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to mean "home" (andare a casa = to go home, tornare a casa = to come back home). With verbs that describe being or staying somewhere, it means "at home". Italian usually uses casa without an article in this expression when talking about someone's home.
target_language_example: Stasera resto a casa.
native_language_example: I'm staying home tonight.

additional_notes: This is a common pattern: **a casa** (“at home/home”) followed by another **a** that introduces (1) a place (**a casa a Boston** = “at home in Boston / home to Boston”), (2) a time (**a casa a ottobre** = “at home in October”), or (3) a purpose with an infinitive (**andare a casa a pranzare** = “go home to have lunch”). With verbs like *mandare/portare*, it means sending/bringing someone home.
target_language_example: Siamo a casa a Milano per le vacanze.
native_language_example: We’re at home in Milan for the holidays.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially "andare") to say you go back home walking, not by car/bus/etc. "a casa" = (to) home; "a piedi" = on foot. Word order is commonly "andare a casa a piedi".
target_language_example: Oggi torno a casa a piedi perché è una bella giornata.
native_language_example: Today I’m walking home because it’s a nice day.

additional_notes: Used to say you are going home immediately or that something/someone needs to be taken home right away. Often follows verbs like andare (to go) or portare (to bring/take).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo tornare a casa adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to go home now.

meaning: 'home at' (used to say what time someone gets/comes home).
additional_notes: Used with a time after it: "a casa alle + ora". Common with verbs like "venire" (to come) or "tornare" (to return): "Vengo/Torno a casa alle cinque" = "I come/get home at five". "Alle" is the contraction of "a + le" and is used with plural time expressions (most clock times).
target_language_example: Torno a casa alle sette e un quarto.
native_language_example: I get home at a quarter past seven.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was staying at home together with another person. Often used with verbs like "essere" (to be) and "restare/rimanere" (to stay).
target_language_example: Stasera resto a casa con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm staying at home with my friends.

additional_notes: Used with **da** to show where you’re coming from when you go/are back home (**a casa da Boston** = “home from Boston”). It can also indicate staying home instead of going somewhere, especially work/school (**sto a casa da lavoro** = “I’m staying home from work / I’m off work”). With people (**a casa da voi / da Maria**) it means “to your/Maria’s place (home)”.
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa da scuola.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying home from school.

meaning: at home from school / home from school.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is (already) at home after leaving school, or has come/arrived home from school. Common with verbs like essere (to be), venire (to come), and arrivare (to arrive): “È a casa da scuola” (He/She is home from school), “È venuto/a a casa da scuola” (He/She came home from school).
target_language_example: Quando torno a casa da scuola, faccio i compiti.
native_language_example: When I get home from school, I do my homework.

meaning: at home alone; (go) home by herself.
additional_notes: Used for a female speaker/subject (sola). For a male, say a casa da solo. With verbs like essere/restare it often means “(to be/stay) home alone”; with andare/tornare it often means “(to go/come back) home alone,” i.e., without company.
target_language_example: Stasera sono a casa da sola.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m home alone.

meaning: at home alone; home by yourself.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is alone at home, or goes/comes home without anyone else. "A casa" = at home/home, and "da solo" = alone/by yourself (for a woman: "a casa da sola"; plural: "a casa da soli / da sole").
target_language_example: Stasera resto a casa da solo.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm staying home alone.

meaning: 'home and…' / 'at home and…' (used to link to the next action).
additional_notes: "A casa" can mean "home" in two common ways: (1) with movement verbs like andare/tornare/correre/arrivare, it means "(go/come) home"; (2) with state verbs like stare/restare, it means "(stay) at home." "E" simply means "and" to continue the sentence with another action.
target_language_example: Sono andato a casa e ho fatto una doccia.
native_language_example: I went home and took a shower.

additional_notes: Used to say you will arrive home no later than midnight. “A casa” = “(at) home,” and “entro” means “by / within” a deadline (not “between”). You can swap the time: “a casa entro le 10”, “a casa entro domani”, etc.
target_language_example: Devo essere a casa entro mezzanotte.
native_language_example: I have to be home by midnight.

additional_notes: Used with "essere" to say where someone was the previous evening. "A casa" means "at home" (often without an article), and "ieri sera" means "last night / yesterday evening." In the passato prossimo with "essere," the past participle agrees: "siamo stati" (mixed/masc. plural) vs "siamo state" (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ero a casa ieri sera, non sono uscito.
native_language_example: I was at home last night; I didn’t go out.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/returning (e.g., tornare, ritornare, andare) to mean “(go/return) home” and then specify where that home is. With countries you typically use "in" (in Egitto, in Nigeria, in Australia). You can also say just "a casa" when the place is obvious, or "a casa mia" = “to my home/at my place.”
target_language_example: Dopo l’università, è tornata a casa in Canada.
native_language_example: After university, she went back home to Canada.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/returning (andare, tornare) to say you travel to/return home using the bus. Common word order: (verb) + a casa + in autobus (e.g., "Vado a casa in autobus").
target_language_example: Oggi torno a casa in autobus perché piove.
native_language_example: Today I'm going home by bus because it's raining.

additional_notes: “a casa” means “at home,” and “la domenica” means “on Sundays” (the definite article is commonly used in Italian to talk about something that happens regularly, like days of the week). Used to describe a usual habit or routine.
target_language_example: Sono spesso a casa la domenica perché lavoro dal lunedì al sabato.
native_language_example: I’m often at home on Sundays because I work from Monday to Saturday.

meaning: (She) went home sick / went home feeling ill.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like andare/tornare: "andare a casa malato/a" = to go home sick. The adjective agrees with the person who is sick: malato (male), malata (female). In natural Italian you’d usually say "è andata a casa malata" or simply "è andata a casa perché stava male".
target_language_example: Oggi Lucia è andata a casa malata dopo pranzo.
native_language_example: Today Lucia went home sick after lunch.

meaning: at my house; to my place.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is at your home or comes to your home. Often implies your personal space/territory, especially in questions like “Che ci fai a casa mia?” (“What are you doing in my house?”). You can swap the possessive: a casa tua (your place), a casa sua (his/her place, formal your place).
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a casa mia dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place after dinner?

meaning: at our house; to our place.
additional_notes: Used to talk about being/going to the speaker’s home (shared with others). Often interchangeable with "da noi". It can mean location ("at our house") or direction ("to our place") depending on the verb (e.g., "essere" vs. "venire/andare").
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a cena a casa nostra stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to come over to our place for dinner tonight?

additional_notes: Used to indicate two possible places/contexts (home vs. workplace). Common in questions like where you are, where you do something, or whether something is allowed/needed in one place or the other (e.g., rules, internet access, routines).
target_language_example: Usi più spesso il computer a casa o al lavoro?
native_language_example: Do you use the computer more often at home or at work?

additional_notes: Uses the time word “ora” (now) with “a casa” (home). With verbs of motion like “portare/andare,” “a casa” often means “(to) home” (destination): “portarti a casa ora” = “take you home now.” With “essere,” it means “at home”: “essere a casa ora” = “be at home now.” With “chiamare,” it means “call home” (the home/household).
target_language_example: Sono a casa ora, possiamo parlare.
native_language_example: I’m at home now; we can talk.

meaning: at home for (an occasion/reason); (go/come) home for.
additional_notes: Used with an occasion or purpose introduced by "per" (e.g., "per Natale" = for Christmas, "per riposarmi" = to rest). With verbs of movement like "andare/venire/tornare", it often means going/coming back home for that occasion; without a movement verb it can simply describe being/staying at home for that reason.
target_language_example: Torno a casa per le vacanze.
native_language_example: I'm going back home for the holidays.

meaning: (stay) at home so I can rest.
additional_notes: Used to explain the purpose of staying at home: “a casa” = “at home,” and “per potermi + infinitive” means “so that I can / in order to be able to …” (here: “riposare” = “rest”). The verb “restare/rimanere/stare a casa” can be used depending on context; “potermi” agrees with the subject (“-mi” = me).
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa per potermi riposare.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying home so I can rest.

a casa per tutto il giorno

target_language_multi_word_term: a casa per tutto il giorno
additional_notes: Used to say someone stays/was/will be at home for the entire day. Often follows verbs like "essere" (to be), "stare" (to stay/be), and "restare" (to remain). You can swap the subject and change the verb tense as needed.
target_language_example: Oggi sono a casa per tutto il giorno perché lavoro da remoto.
native_language_example: Today I’m at home all day because I work remotely.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stayed home due to rain. Often follows verbs like "restare" or "rimanere" (to stay): sono rimasto (male), sono rimasta (female). "Pioveva" is the imperfect tense of "piovere" (it was raining), describing ongoing background weather.
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a casa perché pioveva tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: We stayed at home because it was raining all day.

meaning: at home because it was raining.
additional_notes: Used to explain a reason for staying/being at home: "a casa" = "at home" and "perché" = "because". "stava piovendo" is the imperfect progressive (literally "it was raining"). In the examples, "siamo restati/rimasti" (masc./mixed group) and "siamo restate/rimaste" (fem. group) mean "we stayed"; "restare" and "rimanere" are both common for "to stay/remain" and the past participle agrees with the subject when using "essere".
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a casa perché stava piovendo.
native_language_example: We stayed home because it was raining.

additional_notes: Used to say someone goes/comes back/arrives home earlier than usual or earlier than expected. Common with verbs like andare (to go), tornare (to return), arrivare (to arrive), venire (to come).
target_language_example: Stasera voglio essere a casa presto.
native_language_example: Tonight I want to be home early.

a casa prima che faccia buio

target_language_multi_word_term: a casa prima che faccia buio
additional_notes: Used to say you should arrive home before nightfall. "prima che" (“before”) is followed by the subjunctive, so you often see "faccia" (from "fare"), meaning “it gets (dark)”. You can use it after commands ("Siate..."), advice ("Provi..."), or statements about your plan ("Tornerò...").
target_language_example: Dobbiamo essere a casa prima che faccia buio.
native_language_example: We have to be home before it gets dark.

meaning: at his/her place; to his/her place (home).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is at another person’s home (location) or is going there (destination), depending on the verb. "Sua" agrees with the person whose home it is (his/her/your formal). With names you can clarify: "a casa sua, a Boston" = at his/her place in Boston. For other people: "a casa mia" (my place), "a casa tua" (your place, informal), "a casa loro" (their place).
target_language_example: Stasera ceniamo a casa sua.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re having dinner at his/her place.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like arrivare/tornare to say you reached home late. Often combined with time expressions like ieri sera (“last night”) or alla sera (“in the evening”).
target_language_example: Siamo tornati a casa tardi dopo il concerto.
native_language_example: We got home late after the concert.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/comes/goes to the other person's home. Often with verbs like andare/venire/arrivare/essere: “Andiamo a casa tua” (let’s go to your place), “Verrò a casa tua” (I’ll come to your place). In “Sentiti a casa tua”, it means “Make yourself at home.” Variants: a casa mia (my place), a casa sua (his/her/your formal place), a casa nostra (our place), a casa loro (their place).
target_language_example: Stasera ceniamo a casa tua?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner at your place tonight?

additional_notes: Used to say you stayed at home for the whole day. Common with verbs like rimanere (to stay/remain) and restare (to stay). You can change the time phrase: tutto il giorno (all day), tutta la giornata (the whole day), tutta la notte (all night).
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa tutto il giorno perché non sto bene.
native_language_example: Today I'm staying home all day because I don't feel well.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done without a specific reason, plan, or selection criteria (e.g., scegliere/prendere/comprare/fare qualcosa a caso). As a question ("A caso?") it can mean "Randomly?" or "Just like that?"
target_language_example: Ho scelto un ristorante a caso e alla fine era buonissimo.
native_language_example: I picked a restaurant at random, and in the end it was really good.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something (often with a negative cause). It’s commonly followed by “di” + noun/pronoun: “a causa del traffico” (because of the traffic), “a causa mia” (because of me / my fault). Similar to “per via di”.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in ritardo a causa del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, usually followed by a noun: a causa del traffico (because of the traffic). It’s made of a causa di + the definite article (di + il = del). It can be negative or neutral in tone.
target_language_example: Abbiamo cancellato il viaggio a causa del maltempo.
native_language_example: We canceled the trip because of the bad weather.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something, usually with a negative or problematic cause. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (della = di + la). Variations: a causa del (masc. sing.), a causa dei/degli (masc. plural), a causa delle (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Abbiamo perso il volo a causa della nebbia.
native_language_example: We missed the flight because of the fog.

additional_notes: Used to give the reason for something (often with a negative cause). It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: a causa di + il traffico / a causa di lui / a causa di quel virus. For a verb clause, Italian often uses "perché" instead (e.g., "Sono in ritardo perché ho perso il treno"). Note: when followed by a definite article, it stays "a causa di" (not combined), e.g., "a causa di + il" → "a causa di il" is usually avoided by rephrasing; in practice you’ll most often see it with no article or with a demonstrative/possessive ("a causa di quel...", "a causa di questo...").
target_language_example: Il volo è stato cancellato a causa di un forte temporale.
native_language_example: The flight was canceled due to a severe storm.

additional_notes: Used to describe being on a horse or traveling by riding a horse. Very common with the verb "andare": "andare a cavallo" = "to go horseback riding / to ride a horse". You can also use it with nouns: "passeggiate a cavallo" = "horseback rides".
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a cavallo in campagna.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going horseback riding in the countryside.

meaning: to dinner; for dinner (out to eat in the evening).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like invitare (to invite), andare (to go), uscire (to go out) to mean going out for an evening meal. With "invitare a cena" it usually implies being invited to someone’s place or being treated, but it can also be a dinner invitation to a restaurant (context makes it clear).
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a cena con noi stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to dinner with us tonight?

meaning: to look for; to search for.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like *andare* (to go), *mettersi* (to start), *cominciare* (to begin): **andare a cercare** = “go and look for,” **mettersi a cercare / cominciare a cercare** = “start looking for.” It’s usually followed by what you’re searching for (often with *un/una*, or *dei/delle*).
target_language_example: Vado a cercare le chiavi.
native_language_example: I'm going to look for the keys.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "a" + infinitive ("cercare") to express purpose/going to do something, often after verbs of movement or starting an action (e.g., "andare a...", "venire a...", "mettersi a..."). Literally "to/at look for the book" → natural English: "to look for the book" / "in order to look for the book."
target_language_example: Vado in biblioteca a cercare il libro.
native_language_example: I'm going to the library to look for the book.

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time when something happens. Very common in questions about schedules and routines (work, meals, opening/closing times). Often placed at the beginning of the question, but it can also come after the subject: “Tu a che ora…?”
target_language_example: A che ora comincia la lezione?
native_language_example: What time does the lesson start?

additional_notes: Used to ask the opening time of a place (shop, bank, museum, etc.). You can add the place after it (A che ora apre la banca?) or say it alone when the place is clear (A che ora apre?). More formal with “Sa…?” and informal with “Sai…?”.
target_language_example: Scusi, a che ora apre il museo domani?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does the museum open tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to ask the closing time of a place (restaurant, shop, etc.). You can add the place after the verb: “A che ora chiude il negozio?” If it’s clear from context, you can just say “A che ora chiude?” (“What time does it close?”). “Chiude” is 3rd person singular of “chiudere” (to close), referring to the place.
target_language_example: Scusi, a che ora chiude la farmacia?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does the pharmacy close?

additional_notes: Used to ask about a store/place’s closing time. Often followed by a noun (supermercato, negozio, ristorante): “A che ora chiude quel supermercato?” In conversation it can be embedded after “Lo sai/Lo sa/Lo sapete…?” (“Do you know…?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, a che ora chiude quel negozio?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does that shop close?

additional_notes: Used to ask the starting time of an event (concert, game, school, meeting, etc.). You can say it by itself if the context is clear (“A che ora comincia?”). It can also be used inside a longer sentence after “voglio sapere…” (“I want to know…”).
target_language_example: Scusa, a che ora comincia il film?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does the movie start?

additional_notes: Used to ask the start time of an event or activity. Follow it with a feminine singular noun (la riunione, la lezione, la pausa). For masculine nouns use: “A che ora inizia il …?” (e.g., il film). You can swap “inizia” with “comincia” with similar meaning.
target_language_example: A che ora inizia la cena?
native_language_example: What time does dinner start?

additional_notes: Used to ask departure time for a masculine singular means of transport. It’s typically followed by a noun like il treno (train), il volo (flight), il pullman (coach/bus). For feminine nouns, use: "A che ora parte la ...?" (e.g., la nave).
target_language_example: A che ora parte il treno per Milano?
native_language_example: What time does the train to Milan leave?

meaning: 'What time are you leaving?' / 'What time do you leave?'
additional_notes: Used to ask the time someone leaves (departs). Present tense (parti) is often used for scheduled or near-future plans; you can add a day (domani) or a starting place with "da" (e.g., "da qui", "da Roma").
target_language_example: A che ora parti domani da Milano?
native_language_example: What time are you leaving Milan tomorrow?

meaning: "what time did you (…)?" / "at what time were you (…)?"
additional_notes: Used to ask the time when something happened, especially with verbs that use essere in the past tense (passato prossimo), e.g. "sei andato/a" (you went), "sei entrato/a" (you came in). It often introduces a longer verb phrase: "A che ora sei andato/a a letto?" = "What time did you go to bed?"
target_language_example: A che ora sei arrivato/a a casa ieri?
native_language_example: What time did you get home yesterday?

meaning: "what time are you (plural)" (asking about the time something happened).
additional_notes: Used to ask at what time someone did something. Literally "at what hour are you"; in real use it’s often followed by a past participle in the passato prossimo (e.g., siete arrivati/entrati/andate a letto). Use "siete" for you-plural (or formal singular "Lei"); for singular informal use "A che ora sei…?".
target_language_example: A che ora siete arrivati alla stazione?
native_language_example: What time did you arrive at the station?

meaning: "at what time is" / "what time is" (asking when something happens).
additional_notes: Used to ask for the time of an event or schedule. Often followed by a noun (il treno, la cena) or by a time expression. With a person it can mean “by/at what time is (someone) at home?” or “at what time was (someone) born?”. You’ll also see it without è: "A che ora" + verb (e.g., "A che ora vai a letto?").
target_language_example: A che ora è l'appuntamento?
native_language_example: What time is the appointment?

meaning: "At what time is the ...?" (asking when something happens).
additional_notes: Used to ask the time of an event, usually followed by a noun: "A che ora è il treno/il concerto/il volo?". You can change the article to match the noun: "a che ora è la...", "a che ora sono i/le...". Often written with a question mark: "A che ora è il...?"
target_language_example: A che ora è il concerto stasera?
native_language_example: What time is the concert tonight?

meaning: “how far along / what stage (are you) at?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about progress or the current status of something. Very common with "essere": "A che punto sei?" (to one person), "A che punto siete?" (to more than one person / formal). You can add what you’re working on with "con": "A che punto sei con il progetto?"
target_language_example: Scusa, a che punto sei con la relazione?
native_language_example: Sorry, how far along are you with the report?

meaning: to do with; to deal with.
additional_notes: Used with "avere" ("avere a che fare") to mean either (1) having a connection/relationship to something: "ha a che fare con..." = "it has to do with...", or (2) dealing with a person/thing, often in warnings: "Non sai con chi hai a che fare" = "You don’t know who you’re dealing with." It commonly appears in questions like "Con chi credi di avere a che fare?".
target_language_example: Questo problema ha a che fare con la sicurezza.
native_language_example: This problem has to do with safety.

meaning: to have to do with; to deal with.
additional_notes: Used to show a connection/relation (often with "avere": "Che cosa ha a che fare con...?" = "What does that have to do with...?") or to say you deal with a person/thing/situation ("Ho a che fare con..." = "I have to deal with..."). Often appears as "avere molto a che fare con" = "to have a lot to do with".
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che fare con te.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with you.

meaning: to do with it; to be related to it.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere": "avere a che fare con ..." = “to have to do with / to be connected with ...”. Very common in negatives: "non ha nulla/niente a che fare con ..." = “it has nothing to do with ...”. "Essa" is a formal pronoun meaning “it” (feminine); in everyday speech you’ll often hear "con questo", "con ciò", or "con quella cosa" instead.
target_language_example: Questo problema non ha nulla a che fare con essa.
native_language_example: This problem has nothing to do with it.

meaning: to do with / related to (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used in the common expression "avere a che fare con" meaning "to have to do with" or "to deal with." "La" is the feminine singular article, so it’s followed by a feminine noun (e.g., "la scuola"). Often used in negatives: "Non ha niente a che fare con..." = "It has nothing to do with..."
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che fare con la scuola.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with school.

a che fare con la questione

target_language_multi_word_term: a che fare con la questione
meaning: to have to do with the issue/matter.
additional_notes: Built on the very common expression “avere a che fare con …” = “to have to do with … / to be related to …”. Here, “la questione” means “the issue/matter” (not a literal “question” in the sense of something you ask). Often used in negatives: “Non ha niente a che fare con la questione.”
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che fare con la questione.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with the issue.

meaning: to do with her; to deal with her.
additional_notes: Used after (usually) the verb "avere": "avere a che fare con lei" = "to have dealings with her / to have to deal with her". It can mean (1) being connected/related to her, or (2) having interaction/business with her. "Lei" is the polite/formal "you" or "she/her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non voglio avere più a che fare con lei.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have anything to do with her anymore.

a che fare con lo scandalo

target_language_multi_word_term: a che fare con lo scandalo
meaning: to have something to do with the scandal; to be involved/connected with the scandal.
additional_notes: Used mainly in negatives (non ho nulla/niente a che fare con...) to deny any connection, responsibility, or involvement. The core phrase is “avere a che fare con + [something]” = “to have to do with / to deal with / to be connected to.” You can swap “lo scandalo” with another noun (e.g., il problema, questa storia).
target_language_example: Io non ho nulla a che fare con lo scandalo.
native_language_example: I have nothing to do with the scandal.

meaning: 'to do with this' / 'to have to do with this'.
additional_notes: Used to say something is related to this topic/situation. Often appears in questions or negatives: "Che c'entra?" / "Non ha niente a che fare con questo" (= it has nothing to do with this). The core expression is "avere a che fare con" (to have to do with / to deal with).
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che fare con questo problema.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with this problem.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "avere": "avere a che vedere con" = "to have to do with / to be connected with". Very common in negatives: "non ha (niente) a che vedere con..." = "it has nothing to do with...". It can also introduce what something concerns: "Che c’entra? / Cosa c’entra?" is a related expression meaning "what does it have to do with?".
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che vedere con il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with my job.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask who is the indirect object (the person something is owed/given/said to). Often with verbs like dovere (owe), dare (give), dire/scrivere (say/write). You may also see it after expressions like "tocca a..." (it’s ...’s turn): "A chi tocca...?" = “Whose turn is it...?”
target_language_example: A chi hai mandato l’email?
native_language_example: Who did you send the email to?

meaning: “who does it belong to?” / “whose is it?”
additional_notes: Used to ask who the owner is. Literally “to whom it belongs.” Often followed by a noun/pronoun: “A chi appartiene questo?” (= Who does this belong to?) You can also omit “questo” if it’s clear what you’re talking about.
target_language_example: Scusi, a chi appartiene questa valigia?
native_language_example: Excuse me, who does this suitcase belong to?

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t important, often as a rhetorical question. Common patterns: "A chi importa?" (Who cares?) and "A chi importa se..." (Who cares if...). Can sound dismissive or impolite depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: A chi importa se arriviamo con cinque minuti di ritardo?
native_language_example: Who cares if we arrive five minutes late?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like chiudere/essere (chiuso) to say something is locked using a key (i.e., not just closed). Common patterns: "Chiuso a chiave?" (Is it locked?), "È chiuso a chiave" (It’s locked), "Chiudere ... a chiave" (to lock ...).
target_language_example: Hai chiuso la macchina a chiave?
native_language_example: Did you lock the car?

meaning: (as written) ‘with a key the…’ — not a standard standalone phrase; typically appears as part of a larger sentence like “a chiave la porta”. The usual idiomatic expression is “a chiave” in “chiudere a chiave (la porta)” = “to lock (the door)”.
additional_notes: “A chiave la” by itself is incomplete in Italian (it expects a noun after “la”, e.g., “a chiave la porta”). In normal usage you’d say “Ho chiuso la porta a chiave.” or “Chiudi la porta a chiave.” If you specifically need the exact string “a chiave la” in a sentence, it can be forced by placing the object right after it (e.g., “a chiave la porta”).
target_language_example: Ho chiuso a chiave la porta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I locked the door with a key before going out.

meaning: 'the door' (when used with chiudere a chiave: 'to lock the door').
additional_notes: Used with the verb "chiudere" (or "chiudere a chiave") to mean locking a door with a key: "Chiudi a chiave la porta" = "Lock the door." Word order can vary; you’ll often see "Chiudi la porta a chiave" too. Not to be confused with just "chiudere la porta" (to close the door, not necessarily lock it).
target_language_example: Prima di uscire, chiudi a chiave la porta.
native_language_example: Before going out, lock the door.

additional_notes: This isn’t a complete phrase on its own; it normally appears with a verb like mettere a chiave (“to lock away”) or chiudere a chiave (“to lock”). La sua means “his/hers” (formal “yours”), referring to a feminine noun (e.g., la bici, la valigia, la porta).
target_language_example: Ho messo a chiave la sua valigia.
native_language_example: I locked his/her suitcase away.

meaning: “with a key” in the sense of locking (as in: *chiudere a chiave la sua porta* = “to lock his/her door”).
additional_notes: In Italian this sequence is normally part of the fixed expression **chiudere a chiave** (“to lock”, literally “to close with a key”). The possessive can change: *la mia porta* (my door), *la tua porta* (your door), *la sua porta* (his/her door), etc. The standalone string *a chiave la sua porta* sounds incomplete without the verb; it is most natural after *chiudere* (or in some contexts *serrare*).
target_language_example: Ha chiuso a chiave la sua porta.
native_language_example: He/She locked his/her door.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific thing or idea, often after verbs like "stare attento" (be careful), "pensare" (think), "prestare attenzione" (pay attention), or "tenere a" (care about). It matches English "to what/that which" and introduces a clause or noun phrase describing the thing.
target_language_example: Fai attenzione a ciò che firmi.
native_language_example: Pay attention to what you sign.

meaning: (Be careful) how you speak / what you say; mind your language.
additional_notes: Used after a warning like "Attento/a!" or "Stai/Sta' attento/a!" to tell someone to watch their tone, words, or respect when speaking (often a reprimand). "A" here means "about/as for" + "come" (how) + "parli" (you speak). You can change it for formality/person: "a come parla" (he/she speaks), "a come parlate" (you all speak).
target_language_example: Stai attento a come parli con mia sorella.
native_language_example: Watch how you talk to my sister.

a comprare uno dei suoi dipinti

target_language_multi_word_term: a comprare uno dei suoi dipinti
meaning: to buy one of his/her paintings.
additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that are followed by “a + infinitive,” such as “essere interessato/a a …” (to be interested in …). “Suo/suoi” refers to the owner (his/her/their), and “dipinto/i” means “painting(s).”
target_language_example: Siamo interessati a comprare uno dei suoi dipinti.
native_language_example: We’re interested in buying one of his/her paintings.

additional_notes: Introduces a condition that must be met for something to happen. It’s often used after statements like "Accetterò..." (I’ll accept...) or "Lo farò..." (I’ll do it...). In Italian it’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., "a condizione che tu mi aiuti").
target_language_example: Te lo presto, a condizione che tu me lo restituisca domani.
native_language_example: I’ll lend it to you, provided that you give it back to me tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used with **essere a conoscenza di** (“to be aware of / to know about”) and **venire a conoscenza (di)** (“to find out / to learn about”). Often appears with **ne** to mean “of it/of that” (e.g., *ne sono a conoscenza* = “I’m aware of it”).
target_language_example: Non ero a conoscenza del cambiamento.
native_language_example: I wasn’t aware of the change.

additional_notes: "A" + infinitive means "to" do something, often after verbs like andare (to go), provare (to try), imparare (to learn), or avere problemi (to have trouble). With controllare, it can mean either "to check/inspect" (Vado a controllare…) or "to control/manage" emotions, passions, a dog, etc. Note: it looks like English "to control," but Italian controllare is very commonly used for "to check."
target_language_example: Vado a controllare la porta.
native_language_example: I’m going to check the door.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition + infinitive pattern: "a" + infinitive often follows verbs like riuscire a (to manage to), provare a (to try to), imparare a (to learn to). "La sua rabbia" means "his anger" (literally "his anger"), but "sua" can also mean "her/your" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non riesce a controllare la sua rabbia quando guida.
native_language_example: He can’t control his anger when he drives.

additional_notes: Used after many verbs (especially ones meaning “start/begin,” “manage,” “go,” “put oneself”) to introduce the action of running: *iniziare/cominciare a correre* (to start running), *riuscire/ce la fare a correre* (to manage to run), *andare a correre* (to go running). It can also be figurative: *la mente ha iniziato a correre* (“my mind started racing”). In the phrase *un rischio che sono disposto a correre*, *correre* means “to take (a risk)”—not literal running.
target_language_example: Domani mattina vado a correre al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning I'm going to go running in the park.

additional_notes: Used with a noun to say you don’t have enough of something (money, staff, time, ideas, etc.). Common with: contanti/soldi/fondi (“cash/money/funds”), personale (“staff”), tempo (“time”). In expressions like “a corto di parole,” it means “at a loss for words.”
target_language_example: Siamo a corto di tempo, quindi dobbiamo finire subito.
native_language_example: We’re short on time, so we have to finish right away.

meaning: “What is it for?” / “What is it used for?”
additional_notes: Used to ask the purpose or function of something. Often followed by a noun: “A cosa serve questa cosa?” (= What is this thing for?). It comes from the verb “servire” (to be used for / to be useful). You can also add “E” to link to a previous topic: “E a cosa serve?” (= And what is it for?).
target_language_example: Scusa, a cosa serve questo pulsante?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what is this button for?

meaning: even if it means; even at the cost of (doing).
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something no matter the consequences or sacrifice involved. It’s followed by an infinitive (a costo di ripetermi, ammalarsi, morire, farsi ammazzare) or sometimes by a noun (a costo di tutto = no matter what). Often translates as “even if I have to… / even at the risk of…”.
target_language_example: Lo farò a costo di restare sveglio tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I’ll do it even if it means staying up all night.

additional_notes: Often used after forms of **andare** (e.g., *va, vanno*) as **andare a + infinitive** to say someone is going somewhere in order to do something: *Va a costruire negozi in Australia* = “He/She is going to build shops in Australia.” You can change the place after **in** (countries, regions, big areas).
target_language_example: Domani vanno a costruire negozi in Italia.
native_language_example: Tomorrow they’re going to build shops in Italy.

additional_notes: Used when the verb is in the infinitive and is followed by a clause introduced by che. Common after expressions like cominciare a… (to start to…), continuare a… (to keep…), or sbagliare a… (to be wrong to…). After che, you conjugate the verb normally: a credere che + (loro) siano / (io) abbia, etc.
target_language_example: Sto iniziando a credere che abbia ragione.
native_language_example: I’m starting to believe that he/she is right.

additional_notes: “A + infinitive” often means “to + verb” in English. You see it after certain verbs and expressions like aiutare (to help): “aiutare qualcuno a cucinare” = “to help someone cook”, and essere bravo/a a (to be good at): “bravo a cucinare” = “good at cooking.”
target_language_example: Mi aiuti a cucinare stasera?
native_language_example: Will you help me cook tonight?

additional_notes: Used in relative clauses after the preposition "a" to refer back to a person or thing mentioned earlier. Common with verbs/adjectives that take "a", e.g. "rispondere a" (to answer), "dare a" (to give to), "tenere a" (to care about), "essere interessato a" (to be interested in). It can refer to people or things: "la persona a cui..." / "la cosa a cui...".
target_language_example: Questo è il numero a cui devi chiamare.
native_language_example: This is the number you need to call.

additional_notes: Usually used in set phrases: **stare a cuore (a qualcuno)** = “to be important/dear to someone” (*Mi sta a cuore* = “I really care about it”); **avere a cuore (qualcosa/qualcuno)** = “to have someone’s best interests at heart / to care about”; **prendere a cuore (qualcosa)** = “to take something to heart; to take something very seriously.” Often intensified with **molto/tanto** (e.g., *mi sta molto a cuore*).
target_language_example: Mi sta a cuore che tu stia bene.
native_language_example: I really care that you’re doing well.

a dare un passaggio a casa

target_language_multi_word_term: a dare un passaggio a casa
meaning: to give someone a ride home.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or a noun to specify who you’re giving the ride to: "a dare *a Maria* un passaggio a casa" / "a darti un passaggio a casa". Common with verbs like "andare" or "venire" (e.g., "Vado a dare un passaggio a casa a..."), referring to taking someone home by car (or another vehicle). Note: "passaggio" here means “ride/lift,” not “passage,” which can mislead English speakers (false cognate).
target_language_example: Vado a dare un passaggio a casa a Luca dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I'm going to give Luca a ride home after work.

meaning: to the right; on the right.
additional_notes: Used for directions and locations. Common with verbs like "voltare" (to turn), "girare" (to turn), and "essere" (to be): "volta/gira a destra" = "turn right"; "è a destra" = "it’s on the right".
target_language_example: Il bagno è a destra, vicino alla porta.
native_language_example: The bathroom is on the right, near the door.

additional_notes: Used to compare two people/things and highlight a contrast. It’s followed by a noun or pronoun: "a differenza di lei" (unlike her), "a differenza di tutti voi" (unlike all of you). It can also be used with a clause via "a differenza di quanto..." meaning "contrary to what..." (e.g., "a differenza di quanto si dice" = contrary to what people say).
target_language_example: A differenza di ieri, oggi ho tempo per uscire.
native_language_example: Unlike yesterday, today I have time to go out.

additional_notes: Used with verbs/adjectives that take “a + infinitive” (similar to English “to + verb”), e.g. essere disposto a dire (to be willing to say), stare attento/a a dire (to be careful about saying), riuscire a dire (to manage to say). It’s not usually a standalone phrase; it’s part of a larger structure.
target_language_example: Non riesco a dire niente in italiano quando sono nervoso.
native_language_example: I can’t manage to say anything in Italian when I’m nervous.

meaning: to tell the truth; actually (to be honest).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a more honest, accurate, or slightly correcting statement—often like “actually…” or “to be honest…” at the start or end of a sentence. It can soften disagreement or add a clarifying detail.
target_language_example: A dire il vero, non mi va di uscire stasera.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used as a discourse marker to introduce a frank or sincere opinion, often at the start of a sentence (like “to be honest,” “truthfully”). It can also appear in other forms such as “dire la verità” (“tell the truth”) after verbs like convincere (“to convince”) or vergognarsi di (“to be ashamed to”).
target_language_example: A dire la verità, non ho molta voglia di uscire stasera.
native_language_example: To be honest, I don’t really feel like going out tonight.

meaning: "to come and tell me (it) in my …" (usually: in my room).
additional_notes: Used after a verb of motion like **vieni/venite/venga** (“come”) to mean “come and tell me.” **dirmelo** = “tell it to me” (dire + mi + lo). **nella mia** means “in my …” and normally needs a noun right after it, e.g. **nella mia stanza / nella mia camera** (“in my room/bedroom”).
target_language_example: Vieni a dirmelo nella mia stanza, per favore.
native_language_example: Come and tell me in my room, please.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "sentirsi" (to feel) or "sembrare" (to seem) to say someone feels socially uncomfortable, awkward, or not relaxed in a situation (not usually physical pain). Can also be used with an object: "far sentire qualcuno a disagio" = "to make someone feel uncomfortable."
target_language_example: Mi sento a disagio quando parlo in pubblico.
native_language_example: I feel uncomfortable when I speak in public.

additional_notes: Used to say something is available/ready to be used (tempo a disposizione = time available). With a person it often appears as “tenersi/mettersi a disposizione (di qualcuno)” meaning “to make yourself available” or “to be at someone’s disposal.” Common in formal/polite contexts (e.g., dealing with police, work).
target_language_example: Se ha domande, sono a disposizione.
native_language_example: If you have questions, I'm available.

additional_notes: Used (1) with "di" to mean "after/with a gap of" a certain amount of time: "a distanza di settimane/anni" = "weeks/years apart"; and (2) with verbs like "stare/tenersi/tenere" to mean keeping physical or figurative distance: "State/Stia a distanza" (instruction: "Keep your distance"); "tenere qualcuno a distanza" = keep someone at arm’s length.
target_language_example: Per favore, stia a distanza di un metro.
native_language_example: Please keep a distance of one meter.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "imparare" (to learn) or "riuscire" (to manage) to express an ability or skill: "imparare a distinguere" = learn to distinguish, "riuscire a distinguere X da Y" = manage to tell X from Y. Often used when two things/people are similar (e.g., twins).
target_language_example: Non riesco a distinguere Marco da Luca: si assomigliano troppo.
native_language_example: I can’t tell Marco and Luca apart: they look too similar.

a distinguere il giusto dallo sbagliato

target_language_multi_word_term: a distinguere il giusto dallo sbagliato
additional_notes: Used with verbs like imparare/aiutare/insegnare ("to learn/help/teach") to talk about understanding what is morally or practically correct vs. incorrect. Literally: "to distinguish the right from the wrong."
target_language_example: I genitori dovrebbero aiutare i figli a distinguere il giusto dallo sbagliato.
native_language_example: Parents should help their children distinguish right from wrong.

a distinguere un ermellino e una donnola

target_language_multi_word_term: a distinguere un ermellino e una donnola
meaning: to tell an ermine and a weasel apart; to distinguish between them.
additional_notes:
Used as an infinitive phrase, often after another verb (e.g., *imparare a...* = “to learn to...”, *riuscire a...* = “to manage to...”): *Non riesco a distinguere...*.
Note: In Italian, it’s also very common to say **distinguere X da Y** (“to distinguish X from Y”): *distinguere un ermellino da una donnola*. The version with **e** (“and”) is understandable but slightly less standard in this specific structure.
target_language_example: Non riesco a distinguere un ermellino e una donnola.
native_language_example: I can’t tell an ermine and a weasel apart.

additional_notes: Common goodbye meaning you’ll meet/talk again tomorrow. Often said alone or with a filler like “allora” (“A domani allora”). Can also literally mean “until tomorrow.” Note: in proverbs like “Non rimandare a domani…” it means “until tomorrow”/“to tomorrow” (don’t postpone).
target_language_example: Va bene, ci sentiamo dopo: a domani!
native_language_example: Alright, we’ll talk later: see you tomorrow!

meaning: to your home; home delivery (to an address).
additional_notes: Used with services brought to someone’s home/address. Very common with delivery: "consegna a domicilio" / "consegne a domicilio" (home delivery) and "servizio a domicilio" (at-home service, e.g., a doctor/hairdresser coming to your house). Often asked as a question in shops/restaurants: "Avete/Fate la consegna a domicilio?".
target_language_example: Vorrei una pizza con consegna a domicilio, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a pizza with home delivery, please.

meaning: See you later. / Talk to you later.
additional_notes: A very common, informal-friendly goodbye meaning you’ll see or speak again later the same day (or soon). Often used on its own (“A dopo!”) or with a name/title (“A dopo, Manuela.” / “A dopo, signor Wenger.”). Similar to “a più tardi.”
target_language_example: Devo andare adesso: a dopo!
native_language_example: I have to go now: see you later!

additional_notes: Used as "a" + infinitive to express an action you are going to do or trying to do. Common after verbs like andare (vado a dormire = I’m going to sleep/bed), tornare (torna a dormire = go back to sleep), and provare (ha provato a dormire = he tried to sleep). Often translates as "to sleep" or, with "andare", as "go to bed" in natural English.
target_language_example: Sono stanco: vado a dormire presto.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed early.

meaning: 'two' (used with a measure: two km, two blocks, etc.).
additional_notes: Used to express a distance/quantity when a number is followed by a unit of measure (chilometri, isolati, minuti, metri, ecc.). Often appears as "a due + [unit]" or "a due + [unit] da" to mean "two [units] away from" someone/something.
target_language_example: La fermata dell'autobus è a due minuti da qui.
native_language_example: The bus stop is two minutes from here.

additional_notes: a + fare is often used before the infinitive after another verb, adjective, or noun. In English it often becomes just 'to do/make' or, after andare, 'go and do': essere l'unico a fare = 'be the only one to do'; andare a fare = 'go and do'.
target_language_example: Vado a fare la spesa.
native_language_example: I'm going grocery shopping.

meaning: to go shopping; to do some shopping.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/coming (andare, uscire, venire) to mean you go somewhere in order to shop. Often followed by a place with “in/a” (e.g., in centro, al supermercato). Similar to “fare shopping,” but this is the more neutral/common phrasing.
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a fare acquisti in centro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going shopping downtown.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/movement (andare, uscire, venire) to say you’re going out to shop: “andare/uscire a fare compere”. Often implies shopping for various items (not necessarily groceries). Similar to “fare shopping”, but “fare compere” sounds more neutral/standard.
target_language_example: Dopo lavoro vado a fare compere con un’amica.
native_language_example: After work I’m going shopping with a friend.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like aiutare, rifiutarsi, volere, etc. to mean “to do homework.” It’s the preposition a + infinitive fare (“to do/make”) + i compiti (“the homework”). Often implies school homework; in context it can also mean “to do the chores/tasks” but “homework” is the most common meaning.
target_language_example: Devo andare a casa a fare i compiti.
native_language_example: I have to go home to do my homework.

meaning: to do his/her homework (after a verb like “help”).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose after certain verbs, especially with "aiutare": "aiutare qualcuno a fare..." = "to help someone (to) do...". "i suoi compiti" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context; you can change the possessive: "i miei compiti" (my homework), "i tuoi compiti" (your homework), "i loro compiti" (their homework).
target_language_example: Ho aiutato Tom a fare i suoi compiti.
native_language_example: I helped Tom do his homework.

meaning: to go/start to do (the)…; to go and be/work as (a)…
additional_notes: Used after verbs like **andare** (to go) or **mettersi** (to start) to introduce an activity or role: **andare a fare il sugo** = go make the sauce; **andare a fare il frate / il militare** = go become a monk / do military service; **mettersi a fare il moralista** = start acting like a moralist (often with a critical tone). The noun after **il** changes depending on what you’re doing/being.
target_language_example: Stasera vado a fare il barbecue.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going to do the barbecue.

meaning: to go on doing / to do (in the sense of ‘to act like / play at being’), used after another verb (often continuare, passare la vita, andare) + a fare la + role/label.
additional_notes: Structure: [verb] + a fare la + noun/role. With roles/labels it often carries a critical or ironic tone, meaning “to act like / play the…”: continuare a fare la vittima = “keep playing the victim”, passare la vita a fare la snob = “spend your life acting like a snob”. With tasks/activities it can be more literal: andare a fare la marmellata = “go make jam”. The article agrees with gender: a fare la cassiera (f.), a fare il cassiere (m.).
target_language_example: Continuare a fare la vittima non aiuta nessuno, soprattutto te stesso.
native_language_example: Continuing to play the victim doesn’t help anyone, especially you.

additional_notes: Uses “a” + infinitive to mean “to (do something)”, especially after verbs like insegnare (to teach), imparare (to learn), and provare (to try). Example patterns: “imparare a…” = “to learn to…”, “insegnare a…” = “to teach (someone) to…”, “provare a…” = “to try to…”.
target_language_example: Sto imparando a fare la pizza a casa.
native_language_example: I’m learning to make pizza at home.

meaning: to go grocery shopping; to do the shopping (for food and household items).
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like andare/venire (e.g., "vado a fare la spesa" = "I’m going grocery shopping"). "La spesa" refers to the groceries/shopping, and "fare la spesa" is the common everyday phrase for buying food and basic household items.
target_language_example: Stasera vado a fare la spesa prima di tornare a casa.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going grocery shopping before going back home.

meaning: “to do anything to/for (someone/something)” (often: “willing/ready to do anything to/for…”).
additional_notes: Used after expressions like "essere disposto/a" (to be willing) or "essere pronto/a" (to be ready): "Sono disposto a fare qualunque cosa per...". It introduces the goal or person you’re doing it for. Often implies strong determination (sometimes desperation).
target_language_example: Sono disposto a fare qualunque cosa per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I’m willing to do anything to help you.

meaning: to do this / at doing this.
additional_notes: Uses "a" + infinitive (fare) to express doing an action. Common after verbs/adjectives like "tornare" (to go back to), "essere pronto/a" (to be ready to), or "essere bravo/a" (to be good at). Often translates as "to do this" or, with "bravo", "at doing this".
target_language_example: Non sono pronto a fare questo da solo.
native_language_example: I’m not ready to do this alone.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (andare, venire) to express the purpose: “to go do some shopping.” Often appears as “andare a fare shopping” (to go shopping). It uses the English loanword “shopping,” common in everyday Italian.
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a fare shopping in centro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going shopping downtown.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like andare (“to go”) to say you’re going to do an activity. Structure: andare + a fare + activity (often with sports). In the past you’ll see: è/sono andato/a/i/e a fare surf.
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a fare surf al mattino.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going surfing in the morning.

meaning: to do/make a (…); to go and do a (…).
additional_notes: "A" + infinitive is often used to show purpose or what someone is sent/forced/invited to do. Common after verbs like mandare (to send), obbligare (to force), andare/venire (to go/come): "mi hanno mandato a fare un servizio" = "they sent me to do a job/assignment". With "ci vuole a…" it means "how hard is it to…? / what does it take to…?"
target_language_example: Mi hanno chiamato a fare un controllo dei documenti.
native_language_example: They called me to do a document check.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of going/movement (especially "andare"): "andare a fare un picnic" = to go out to have a picnic. Often followed by a place ("al parco", "sulla collina") or with someone ("con lei", "assieme").
target_language_example: Domenica andiamo a fare un picnic al parco.
native_language_example: On Sunday we’re going to have a picnic in the park.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like "andare" (to go) or "portare" (to take/bring someone) to mean doing the activity: "andare a fare una nuotata" = go for a swim; "portare qualcuno a fare una nuotata" = take someone for a swim. "Una nuotata" means one swimming session (a swim).
target_language_example: Dopo pranzo andiamo a fare una nuotata al mare.
native_language_example: After lunch, we’re going for a swim at the sea.

additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like andare/venire/uscire/portare to express going out for a walk (often for leisure, exercise, or to walk the dog). Common patterns: "andare a fare una passeggiata" (go for a walk), "uscire a fare una passeggiata" (go out for a walk), "portare il cane a fare una passeggiata" (take the dog for a walk). Literally "to do a walk," but the natural English is "go for a walk."
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a fare una passeggiata dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to come for a walk after dinner?

a fare una passeggiata con me

target_language_multi_word_term: a fare una passeggiata con me
meaning: for a walk with me; to go for a walk with me.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "andare" (to go) or as an invitation: "Vuoi venire a fare una passeggiata con me?" Literally it’s like “to go do a walk with me,” but the natural English meaning is “to go for a walk with me.”
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a fare una passeggiata con me dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a walk with me after dinner?

a fare una passeggiata dopo la colazione

target_language_multi_word_term: a fare una passeggiata dopo la colazione
meaning: to go for a walk after breakfast.
additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement like andare or uscire (e.g., "andare/uscire a...") to say you go somewhere in order to do an activity. "Fare una passeggiata" is a common way to say "go for a walk," and "dopo la colazione" means "after breakfast."
target_language_example: Domani mattina andiamo a fare una passeggiata dopo la colazione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow morning we’re going to go for a walk after breakfast.

additional_notes: Used when referring back to an action already known from context. It’s made of: "a" + infinitive "fare" (to do/make) + direct object pronoun "lo" (it). Common after verbs/adjectives like "essere disposto/a" (be willing), "essere preparato/a" (be ready), "acconsentire" (agree), "aiutare" (help), etc. The pronoun can change depending on what “it” is (e.g., a farla, a farli, a farle).
target_language_example: Non sono sicuro di riuscire a farlo oggi.
native_language_example: I’m not sure I can manage to do it today.

additional_notes: A highly offensive insult used to tell someone to go away or express strong contempt. It’s not appropriate in polite conversation and can easily start a fight. You may also hear it after “vai” (“vai a farti fottere”).
target_language_example: Se non ti sta bene, vai a farti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, go fuck yourself.

additional_notes: Used to express support/approval for a person, idea, proposal, or side in a debate or vote. Common with verbs like essere (to be), votare (to vote), schierarsi (to side), and with nouns like opinione (opinion) or decisione (decision). Opposite: "contro" (against).
target_language_example: Sono a favore di questa proposta.
native_language_example: I’m in favor of this proposal.

additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like "tagliare" (to cut) or "fare" (to make): "tagliare a fette" = to slice, "fare a fette" = to cut into slices/pieces. Often followed by an adjective to say the thickness: "a fette spesse" (thick slices), "a fette sottili" (thin slices).
target_language_example: Puoi tagliare il pomodoro a fette sottili?
native_language_example: Can you slice the tomato into thin slices?

meaning: to finish; (with andare/va a finire) to end up / to end.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive after many verbs (especially motion or ability), e.g. "andare a finire" = "to go and finish" / "to end up" depending on context. Very common patterns: "Ce la fai a finire?" = "Can you manage to finish?"; "Dove andremo a finire?" = "Where will we end up?"; "Va a finire che + [clause]" = "It’ll end up that..." / "It’ll probably happen that...".
target_language_example: Non so come andrà a finire.
native_language_example: I don’t know how it will end up / how it will end.

meaning: on the surface of; just beneath/at the edge of (about to come out).
additional_notes: Used mostly in set expressions followed by a noun, especially: “a fior di pelle” (just beneath the surface, barely held back—often with emotions), “a fior di labbra” (on the tip of one’s tongue/lips, about to be said), and “a fior d’acqua” (at the water’s surface). It suggests something is very close to appearing or being expressed.
target_language_example: Avevo le lacrime a fior di pelle.
native_language_example: I was on the verge of tears.

additional_notes: Used mainly after a noun to describe something decorated with flowers (especially clothes, fabric, wallpaper): "un vestito a fiori" (a floral dress), "una camicia a fiori" (a floral shirt).
target_language_example: Mi piace questa camicia a fiori.
native_language_example: I like this floral shirt.

additional_notes: Used to say you want to understand, discuss, or examine something deeply and completely. Common with verbs like parlare (talk), conoscere/capire (know/understand), studiare/analizzare (study/analyze), and also with actions like pulire (clean) meaning “thoroughly”.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo analizzare il problema a fondo prima di decidere.
native_language_example: We need to analyze the problem in depth before deciding.

meaning: shaped like; in the shape of.
additional_notes: Used to describe what something looks like (its shape). It’s followed by a noun: "a forma di cuore" (heart-shaped), "a forma di cubo" (cube-shaped). Often corresponds to English “-shaped” or “in the shape of …”.
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei biscotti a forma di stella.
native_language_example: I bought star-shaped cookies.

meaning: by doing something repeatedly / from doing something so much.
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive (a forza di + verb) to say that repeating an action many times causes a result (often tiredness, change, or learning). It can mean “by dint of” or “from” doing something so much.
target_language_example: A forza di studiare ogni giorno, alla fine ho capito tutto.
native_language_example: By studying every day, I finally understood everything.

meaning: 'in exchange for' / 'in return for' (given a cost, condition, or benefit).
