additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". With verbs of motion (andare, venire, tornare) it often means "to the supermarket" (Andiamo al supermercato). With verbs describing location or actions happening there (essere, comprare, lavorare), it means "at the supermarket" (Sono/Compro al supermercato). You can add an adjective or specify which one: "al supermercato asiatico", "al supermercato dove vado".
target_language_example: Devo andare al supermercato dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to go to the supermarket after work.

meaning: at the table; (with motion) to the table.
additional_notes: "Al" = "a" + "il". Used to say someone/something is positioned at a table (often sitting and eating/working): "Sono seduto al tavolo." With verbs of movement like "tornare/andare", it can mean "to the table": "Torna al tavolo." Often interchangeable with "al tavolo" vs "a tavola" ("a tavola" focuses more on mealtime: "Siamo a tavola").
target_language_example: Puoi venire al tavolo? La cena è pronta.
native_language_example: Can you come to the table? Dinner is ready.

additional_notes: Used to say you are speaking via a telephone call (essere/parlare al telefono = to be/talk on the phone). With verbs like rispondere, it means “to answer the phone” (rispondere al telefono). It can also describe spending time using the phone in general (passare tempo al telefono).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare adesso: sono al telefono.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now: I’m on the phone.

additional_notes: Used to say where something is in a building (rooms, offices, etc.). "al" = "a + il" and can mean "on the" (location) or "to the" (direction) depending on the verb: "La mia camera è al terzo piano" (is on), "Vada al terzo piano" (go to). Note: in Italy, the ground floor is often "piano terra"; "primo piano" is typically one level above the ground floor.
target_language_example: L’ufficio del dottore è al terzo piano.
native_language_example: The doctor’s office is on the third floor.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "il tuo". Used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., "al tuo lavoro" = "to/at your job"). The exact meaning depends on the verb: with movement/aim it’s often “to your …” (e.g., "tornare al tuo villaggio"), and with location/occasion it can be “at your …” (e.g., "al tuo matrimonio").
target_language_example: Puoi venire al tuo appuntamento alle tre?
native_language_example: Can you come to your appointment at three?

meaning: in your place; if I were you.
additional_notes: Used either literally (someone replaces you in a role/seat/job: “io al tuo posto”) or figuratively to give advice/opinion: “Al tuo posto, farei…” (= If I were you, I’d…). In commands it can mean “stay in your place / stay in your lane”: “Stai al tuo posto.”
target_language_example: Al tuo posto, parlerei con il capo domani.
native_language_example: If I were you, I’d talk to the boss tomorrow.

additional_notes: Common idiom used with “essere” (e.g., “sono al verde”) to say you have no money left. It’s fairly informal. Note: in other contexts, “al verde” can also literally mean “to green” (e.g., a traffic light changing “dal rosso al verde”).
target_language_example: Dopo aver pagato l'affitto, sono al verde.
native_language_example: After paying the rent, I'm broke.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is driving (in control of the car). Common in warnings and rules: “Non bere al volante” = “Don’t drink and drive.” You can also use it to comment on someone’s driving ability: “Sei bravo/pessimo al volante.”
target_language_example: Non usare il telefono al volante.
native_language_example: Don’t use your phone while driving.

meaning: quickly; on the fly; in a flash.
additional_notes: Used to say something is done very fast or with no preparation. Common with verbs like fare/prendere/andare/salire/saltare “al volo” (= quickly, at the last second). In “furti al volo” it means quick grab-and-run thefts (snatch theft). In “prendere la palla al volo” it can mean literally “catch the ball in mid-air,” and also figuratively “pick up an opportunity/idea immediately.”
target_language_example: Te lo spiego al volo e poi andiamo.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you quickly and then we’ll go.

meaning: "to your" / "at your" (addressing more than one person, or formal "your").
additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: **al vostro + noun** (e.g., *al vostro capo* = to your boss). It’s made of **a + il = al** plus **vostro**. The exact meaning can be “to your” or “at your” depending on the verb/context. Related forms: **alla vostra** (feminine singular), **ai vostri** (masculine plural), **alle vostre** (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Posso parlare al vostro medico?
native_language_example: Can I speak to your doctor?

additional_notes: Used for the decorated tree people put up during Christmas. With an indefinite article it’s “un albero di Natale”; with a possessive it’s “il mio/suo albero di Natale”.
target_language_example: Quest'anno compriamo un albero di Natale vero.
native_language_example: This year we’re buying a real Christmas tree.

meaning: “any place to” (in negative sentences: “no place to”).
additional_notes: Used with a following infinitive (e.g., dormire, nascondersi) to mean “a place where/in which to do something.” It’s very common in negative phrases like “non ho alcun posto in cui…” = “I don’t have anywhere to…”. Similar alternatives: “nessun posto dove…”, “non ho un posto dove…”.
target_language_example: Non abbiamo alcun posto in cui sederci.
native_language_example: We don’t have anywhere to sit.

additional_notes: Used almost always in negative statements (often with “non”) to say something is meaningless or doesn’t make sense: “non ha alcun senso” = “it makes no sense / there’s no point.” “Alcun” is like “any” and is common in negatives; in positive sentences you usually use “qualche” instead.
target_language_example: Questa regola non ha alcun senso.
native_language_example: This rule makes no sense.

additional_notes: Plural phrase using the feminine plural of “alcuno/a” + “cose.” Used when you refer to an unspecified number of things. Often followed by “di” + noun (“alcune cose della vita” = “some things in life”) or by a relative clause (“alcune cose che posso fare…” = “some things I can do…”).
target_language_example: Vorrei dirti alcune cose importanti.
native_language_example: I’d like to tell you some important things.

additional_notes: Used when you mean an unspecified number of questions (more than one). Often appears with verbs like fare (to ask) or rispondere a (to answer): fare alcune domande = to ask some questions; rispondere ad alcune domande = to answer some questions.
target_language_example: Vorrei fare alcune domande prima di iniziare.
native_language_example: I’d like to ask a few questions before we start.

meaning: some people (a certain number, not all).
additional_notes: Used to talk generally about an unspecified group of people. Often followed by a verb in the plural (e.g., credono, vogliono). You can change gender/number: "alcuni" (some, masculine/mixed) + "persone" (people) stays feminine plural; e.g., "alcune persone" is always feminine because "persone" is feminine.
target_language_example: Alcune persone preferiscono lavorare da sole.
native_language_example: Some people prefer to work alone.

meaning: at the library; to the library.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at + the). Use it with verbs of going/moving (andare, tornare) to mean "to the library" and with location/stay verbs (essere, lavorare, conoscere qualcuno) to mean "at the library."
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla biblioteca domani pomeriggio.
native_language_example: See you at the library tomorrow afternoon.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going or coming (andare/venire) to mean “to the party,” and with verbs describing what happens there (divertirsi, ballare, parlare) to mean “at the party.” It’s the contraction of a + la (to/at + the) + festa.
target_language_example: Vieni alla festa sabato sera?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party on Saturday night?

meaning: "to my question" / "to my request" (i.e., as a reply to what I asked).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "rispondere" (to answer): "rispondere alla mia domanda" = "to answer my question." "Alla" is the combination of "a" + "la" and here means "to" (to the question). You can change "mia" to match who asked: "alla tua domanda" (to your question), "alla sua domanda" (to his/her question).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla mia domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

meaning: to the mosque; at the mosque.
additional_notes: Means “a + la moschea” (to/at the mosque). With movement verbs like andare/portare it usually means “to the mosque” (going/taking someone there). With essere/stare it can mean “at the mosque” (being there): “Sono alla moschea.”
target_language_example: Domani vado alla moschea con un amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the mosque with a friend.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a" + "la" + "sua". Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "alla sua famiglia" = to his/her family, "alla sua chiamata" = to his/her call). "Sua" can mean either "his" or "her"—the context tells you which. With masculine singular you’d use "al suo"; with feminine plural "alle sue"; with masculine plural "ai suoi".
target_language_example: Ho risposto alla sua email subito.
native_language_example: I replied to his/her email right away.

additional_notes: Means “to the party” (motion: inviting/going) or “at the party” (location: being/having fun), depending on the verb and context. The structure is a + la = alla (“to/at the”), sua = “his/her” (possessive), festa = “party.” Often the gender of the owner is understood from context; if needed you can clarify with “la sua festa” (her) vs “la sua festa” (his) still looks the same, or use a name: “alla festa di Maria.”
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla sua festa sabato sera.
native_language_example: See you at his/her party Saturday night.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at their desk (often at work) or does something there. "alla" = "a" + "la" (at the). "sua" agrees with the desk (scrivania, feminine), and can change depending on the person: alla mia scrivania (at my desk), alla tua scrivania (at your desk), alla loro scrivania (at their desk). Sometimes you may also hear "alla scrivania" without the possessive if it’s clear whose desk it is.
target_language_example: Sono alla sua scrivania e sto finendo il rapporto.
native_language_example: I'm at his/her desk and I'm finishing the report.

meaning: to the library; at the library.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at the). Use it with verbs of going/returning (and sometimes access) to indicate destination ("to the library") or location ("at the library"), depending on context.
target_language_example: Domani vado alla biblioteca per studiare.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the library to study.

additional_notes: A place phrase. "alla" = "a" + "la" and can mean "to the" (movement: invitate/i... alla...) or "at the" (location: si sono incontrati... alla...). "della" = "di" + "la" meaning "of the" (the library belonging to the mosque).
target_language_example: Domani ci vediamo alla biblioteca della moschea alle cinque.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’ll meet at the mosque’s library at five.

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + la". Commonly used with verbs like "rispondere" (to answer): "rispondere alla domanda" = "to answer the question". Also used to refer to a specific question already mentioned (e.g., on a form, website, or in a conversation).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer the question, please?

additional_notes: As an interjection, “Alla faccia!” expresses surprise, admiration, or sometimes sarcasm (tone and context matter). In other contexts it can be literal, meaning something happened or was done to someone’s face: “Che ti è successo alla faccia?” = “What happened to your face?” You may also hear “Alla faccia sua!” as an exclamation directed at someone (often meaning “Yeah, right—look at him/her!” or “Well, would you look at that!” depending on tone).
target_language_example: Alla faccia, che bella macchina!
native_language_example: Wow, what a nice car!

additional_notes: Means either location ("at the party") or direction ("to the party"), depending on the verb: e.g. essere/stare "alla festa" = at the party; andare/venire "alla festa" = to the party. "Alla" is the contraction of "a + la".
target_language_example: Vieni alla festa con noi?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party with us?

additional_notes: Used (1) with "di" + time period to mean "at the end of" something: "alla fine di maggio" = "at the end of May"; and (2) on its own to summarize the final outcome or what happened after all: "Alla fine ci sei riuscito!" = "You managed it in the end!" It can also be used in conversation like "so/anyway, in the end..." when concluding.
target_language_example: Alla fine abbiamo deciso di restare a casa.
native_language_example: In the end we decided to stay home.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the end point of a time period or event (alla fine del mese/discorso) or the end of a place/route (alla fine del corridoio). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun introduced by “del” (= di + il). For feminine singular you use “alla fine della…”, and for plural “alla fine dei/degli/delle…”.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla fine del corso.
native_language_example: See you at the end of the course.

meaning: at the ends of the earth; in a very remote place.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a place is extremely far away or hard to reach (often exaggerating). It can be literal (a very remote location) or figurative (“in the middle of nowhere”). Often used with verbs like andare/essere (to go/be).
target_language_example: Il ristorante è buonissimo, ma è proprio alla fine del mondo.
native_language_example: The restaurant is amazing, but it’s really in the middle of nowhere.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens when something finishes. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la giornata, la discussione, la riunione). With masculine nouns you use "alla fine del" (e.g., alla fine del film).
target_language_example: Alla fine della lezione facciamo un ripasso veloce.
native_language_example: At the end of the lesson we do a quick review.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of position or movement: “essere/stare alla finestra” = to be at the window; “andare/correre alla finestra” = to go to the window. In requests you’ll often see “vicino alla finestra” (“near the window”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un tavolo vicino alla finestra?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a table near the window?

additional_notes: Formed by **a + la = alla** plus **gente** (“people”). Used to show who something is directed to (an indirect object): *parlare alla gente* (“to talk to people”), *insegnare ... alla gente* (“to teach ... to people”). With words like **davanti**, it can mean “in front of people” (*davanti alla gente*).
target_language_example: Non dire queste cose alla gente.
native_language_example: Don’t say these things to people.

meaning: really well; great; in a big way.
additional_notes: Used to say something is going very well or will turn out great (often like “great!” / “awesome!”). It can also mean doing something on a grand scale or making a strong, impressive exit (e.g., “leave in style”). Common in spoken Italian.
target_language_example: L’esame è andato alla grande!
native_language_example: The exam went really well!

meaning: literally; word for word; exactly (to the letter).
additional_notes: Used when something is understood in the most literal sense or followed very precisely: *prendere alla lettera* (to take literally), *seguire/rispettare alla lettera* (to follow exactly). In some contexts *alla lettera* can also simply mean “to the letter” in the non-idiomatic sense (e.g., *rispondere alla lettera* = “to reply to the letter”).
target_language_example: Segui le istruzioni alla lettera.
native_language_example: Follow the instructions exactly.

meaning: “to my / at my” (used with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Contraction of “a + la” (= “to/at the”) + “mia” (= “my”). You’ll see it before feminine singular nouns: alla mia festa (to/at my party), alla mia casa (to my house). In phrases like “alla mia portata” it means “within my reach/ability.”
target_language_example: Stasera puoi venire alla mia casa?
native_language_example: Can you come to my house tonight?

additional_notes: Used mainly after verbs like rispondere (to answer): rispondere alla mia domanda = “to answer my question.” The preposition “a” + “la” becomes “alla.” “Domanda” is usually a question (not “demand” in the English sense).
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alla mia domanda, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer my question, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe people, clothes, objects, or ideas that follow current trends. Often with verbs like essere (è alla moda), tornare (tornare alla moda = to come back into fashion), or restare (restare alla moda = to stay fashionable). Can also be used sarcastically to criticize something as “trendy.”
target_language_example: Quel ristorante è molto alla moda, ma è caro.
native_language_example: That restaurant is very fashionable, but it’s expensive.

additional_notes: Usually means someone is led/sent toward dying (often figuratively or dramatically): *condurre alla morte* “to lead to death,” *mandare alla morte* “to send to their death.” With *pensare a*, it can also mean “to think about death” (*pensare alla morte*).
target_language_example: Non voglio mandarti alla morte per una causa persa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to send you to your death for a lost cause.

meaning: to the mosque; at the mosque.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" and is used with feminine singular places. With motion verbs (andare/venire/ritornare) it usually means "to the mosque"; with stative context it can mean "at the mosque."
target_language_example: Domani vado alla moschea con un amico.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to the mosque with a friend.

additional_notes: Combination of **a** (“to/at”) + **la** (“the”) + **nostra** (“our”, feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun: **alla nostra casa** (to our house), **alla nostra età** (at our age), **alla nostra tavola** (at our table). The same pattern exists with other forms: **al nostro** (to our, masculine singular), **ai nostri / alle nostre** (to our, plural).
target_language_example: Non avvicinarti alla nostra macchina!
native_language_example: Don’t come near our car!

additional_notes: Used to talk about the worst-case scenario, often to reassure someone that there’s a fallback plan. It’s similar in meaning to "nel peggiore dei casi" (more formal). You’ll often see it with a verb like "andare" (to go): "Alla peggio, andiamo a casa".
target_language_example: Alla peggio, prendiamo un taxi.
native_language_example: At worst, we’ll take a taxi.

additional_notes: Used as an adverbial phrase to say something works/goes extremely well, with no problems (common with verbs like funzionare, andare). In "La ripetizione porta alla perfezione", it means "to perfection" (practice leads to perfection).
target_language_example: Il test è andato alla perfezione, non c’erano errori.
native_language_example: The test went perfectly; there were no mistakes.

meaning: at the door; to the door.
additional_notes: Used with feminine singular nouns: a + la = alla. Very common in phrases like "bussare alla porta" (to knock on the door) and with motion/delivery verbs like "andare/portare alla porta" (to go/bring to the door). Often followed by a specification: "alla porta della camera" (at the bedroom door).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato il pacco alla porta.
native_language_example: I left the package at the door.

meaning: on the radio; on the radio station (heard/broadcast via radio).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sentire (to hear), ascoltare (to listen), dire (to say), passare/trasmettere (to play/broadcast) to indicate something was heard or broadcast via radio. Literally 'at the radio', but in English it’s usually 'on the radio'.
target_language_example: L'ho ascoltata alla radio stamattina.
native_language_example: I heard it on the radio this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is/was/will be present at a meeting. It’s made of a + la (“to/at the” + feminine singular), and riunione means “meeting” (a gathering). Often goes with essere/stare (“to be”) and presente (“present”).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla riunione di domani.
native_language_example: See you at tomorrow’s meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done or oriented in the opposite direction/way than normal. Common with verbs like leggere (to read), scrivere (to write), fare (to do), mettere (to put), and can refer both to physical orientation (upside down) and to a process/order done in reverse.
target_language_example: Hai messo la maglietta alla rovescia.
native_language_example: You put your T-shirt on inside out/backwards.

meaning: “Cheers!” (a toast) / “to (your) health”; also “to health” in general.
additional_notes: Used in two main ways: (1) as a toast when clinking glasses: “Alla salute!” or “Alla salute di tutti” (“To everyone’s health”). (2) In phrases like “fa bene/male alla salute” meaning “is good/bad for your health.” Often includes a possessive: “alla tua/vostra salute” (“to your health”).
target_language_example: Allora, alla salute!
native_language_example: So, cheers!

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency or how often something happens within a week (often with numbers: “una volta alla settimana”, “tre volte alla settimana”). It’s also used to say how many regular activities you have each week: “quattro lezioni alla settimana”.
target_language_example: Vado in palestra due volte alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym twice a week.

additional_notes: Used especially with verbs like "cogliere" (to catch) or "prendere" (to take) to mean someone is surprised and not ready to react ("cogliere/prendere qualcuno alla sprovvista" = to catch someone off guard). Often follows the verb: "mi ha colto alla sprovvista". Agreement note: "colto" (male) / "colta" (female) agrees with the person being caught off guard.
target_language_example: La domanda mi ha preso alla sprovvista.
native_language_example: The question caught me off guard.

meaning: at the train station; to the train station.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to/at + the). With places, it can mean either being there (at) or going there (to), depending on the verb and context: "Ci vediamo alla stazione" (meet at) vs. "Come arrivare alla stazione?" (how to get to). Often used with "vicino alla stazione" = "near the station."
target_language_example: Andiamo alla stazione a prendere il treno.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the station to catch the train.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a destination or location. It combines the preposition + article "a" + "la" → "alla" ("to the/at the"), with "stazione degli autobus" (bus station). Often used with verbs of movement like "andare" (to go).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla stazione degli autobus alle otto.
native_language_example: See you at the bus station at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say you are at (or arrived at) a specific train/metro station. It’s a + la = alla, and it’s typically followed by the station name: alla stazione di Osaka, alla stazione di Shibuya. Common with verbs like essere (to be), arrivare (to arrive), andare (to go), incontrare/imbattersi (to meet/run into).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla stazione di Milano Centrale alle 8.
native_language_example: See you at Milan Central Station at 8.

additional_notes: Combination of the preposition+article “a + la” → “alla” (“to the”) + the possessive “sua” (“his/her/its”). It’s used before a feminine singular noun: “alla sua dieta” = “to his/her diet”, “alla sua condizione” = “to his condition” (condizione is feminine in Italian). The possessive agrees with the thing owned (sua/sue vs suo/suoi), not with the owner.
target_language_example: Non dare ascolto alla sua storia.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to his/her story.

additional_notes: Means going/being/participating at someone else’s party. It’s made of: a + la = alla (“to the/at the”) + sua (“his/her”) + festa (“party”). Note: sua can mean “his” or “her” (the owner is understood from context), while festa is feminine, so it stays sua (not suo). Common with verbs like andare (to go), essere (to be), invitare (to invite), partecipare (to participate), divertirsi (to have fun).
target_language_example: Non posso venire alla sua festa stasera.
native_language_example: I can’t come to his/her party tonight.

additional_notes: Uses "a" + "la" → "alla" to mean being at a place. "Sua" agrees with "scrivania" (feminine singular) and can mean either his or her depending on context. Often used for where someone is working, studying, eating, etc., typically at a desk (home or office).
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno di lui, è alla sua scrivania.
native_language_example: If you need him, he's at his desk.

additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian to urge someone to do something immediately (“E alla svelta!” = “And make it quick!”). It can also describe doing something quickly (e.g., falling asleep). Often overlaps with "presto" and "in fretta".
target_language_example: Finisci i compiti alla svelta, poi usciamo.
native_language_example: Finish your homework quickly, then we’ll go out.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + la tua**. It’s used before a **feminine singular noun**: *alla tua casa* (to your house), *alla tua destra* (to your right), *alla tua auto* (at/to your car). In a different context, **Alla tua!** can also be a toast meaning “To you!/Cheers!”, short for *alla tua salute*.
target_language_example: Puoi lasciare il pacco alla tua porta?
native_language_example: Can you leave the package at your door?

meaning: 'at the sight of' (when seeing something triggers a reaction).
additional_notes: Used with a noun (often with a reaction like being scared, shouting, crying, etc.). It’s a fixed expression meaning “upon seeing” or “as soon as (someone) saw”. The article changes with the noun: alla vista del (di + il), alla vista dello (di + lo), alla vista della (di + la), alla vista dei/degli/delle.
target_language_example: Alla vista del sangue, mi sono sentito male.
native_language_example: At the sight of blood, I felt sick.

meaning: at a time; one by one.
additional_notes: Used to say you should do something in separate turns or small batches, often with numbers (e.g., "tre alla volta" = three at a time) or with "uno" ("uno alla volta" = one at a time / one by one). Common for instructions like entering, speaking, taking items, or increasing something gradually.
target_language_example: Parlate uno alla volta, per favore.
native_language_example: Speak one at a time, please.

meaning: toward; on the way to; headed for.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement (especially "andare", "partire", "mettersi") to say you are setting off in the direction of a place. Common in writing and news-style Italian; in everyday speech you can often say "verso" instead.
target_language_example: Siamo partiti alla volta di Firenze alle sette.
native_language_example: We left for Florence at seven.

meaning: at the party; to the party.
additional_notes: “Alla” = “a + la” and can mean either “to the” (movement/direction: andare/venire/essere diretto) or “at the” (location: essere/incontrarsi). “Festa” means “party,” and you’ll also often specify whose party: “alla festa di Mary” = “to/at Mary’s party.”
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alla festa stasera?
native_language_example: See you at the party tonight?

additional_notes: Contraction of "a + la mia". Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., "alla mia macchina" = "to my car", "alla mia salute" = "to my health" in a toast). It can express direction/relationship ("to"), adaptation/connection ("to"), or be used in set phrases like toasts.
target_language_example: Non toccare alla mia borsa!
native_language_example: Don’t touch my bag!

additional_notes: Used after verbs of going/coming/inviting (e.g., venire/andare/invitare) to say someone should come/go to your party. "Alla" = "a" + "la" (to the), and it agrees with the feminine noun "festa". Formal invitation: "Venga alla mia festa" (Lei form).
target_language_example: Ti va di venire alla mia festa sabato sera?
native_language_example: Do you feel like coming to my party on Saturday evening?

additional_notes: Used after verbs like consegnare (hand over/turn in), denunciare (report), portare (take/bring) to indicate that someone/something is handed over, reported, or taken to the police. It can also refer to going to the police station (e.g., “alla polizia più vicina”).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo andare alla polizia per denunciare il furto.
native_language_example: We have to go to the police to report the theft.

meaning: at the station; to the station.
additional_notes: "Alla" = "a" (to/at) + "la" (the). With motion verbs like "portare" (to take/bring), "accompagnare" (to accompany), "andare" (to go), it usually means "to the station" (destination). In other contexts it can mean "at the station" (location), e.g., something happened there.
target_language_example: Possiamo incontrarci alla stazione alle otto?
native_language_example: Can we meet at the station at eight?

meaning: to/at his or her (feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (or an implied one): alla sua professoressa = “to/in front of his/her teacher”; alla sua partenza = “at his/her departure.” It’s the combination a + la (“to the/at the”) + sua (“his/her”). Note: in very formal Italian, Sua (capital S) can mean “Your” (formal), e.g., alla Sua attenzione.
target_language_example: Non ho potuto partecipare alla sua festa.
native_language_example: I couldn’t attend his/her party.

additional_notes: Contraction of **a + la tua** (“to/at the your”, feminine singular). Used before a feminine singular noun: **alla tua festa** = “at your party”, **alla tua mamma** = “to your mom”. For masculine singular you usually use **al tuo** (a + il tuo).
target_language_example: Puoi dirlo alla tua amica?
native_language_example: Can you tell it to your friend?

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. It’s the preposition “a” + the plural article “le” (for ore, “hours”): “alle” = “at the”. Common with verbs like partire (to leave) and essere (to be).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle otto davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: See you at eight in front of the movie theater.

additional_notes: Used to say the exact time something happens. "Alle" = "a" + "le" (at the + plural), used with most clock times: alle due, alle sette, alle 9. With 1 o’clock you usually say "all’una" (singular). You can add parts of the day like "domattina" (tomorrow morning) or "di sera" (in the evening).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the preposition “a” + the plural article “le” because “ore” (hours) is understood: “alle sette (ore)”. For 1 o’clock you usually say “all’una” (not *alle una*).
target_language_example: Il treno parte alle sette e dieci.
native_language_example: The train leaves at 7:10.

meaning: in high school (during your high school years).
additional_notes: Short for "alle scuole superiori" (Italy’s upper secondary school). Used to talk about a time in your life: meeting someone, what you were like, what happened back then. Often with verbs like "essere" or "conoscere": "Ero... alle superiori", "L’ho conosciuto alle superiori".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti alle superiori.
native_language_example: We met in high school.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s the preposition "a" + the feminine plural article "le" (because "ore" = hours is feminine), so you say "alle" for most clock times: "alle cinque", "alle sei". For a time range, you can use "dalle ... alle ..." (from ... to ...).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

meaning: in high school (attending upper secondary school).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere/andare/fare to say someone is/was in high school. It refers to the school level (le scuole superiori) and is common when talking about a period in someone’s life. Often used in the past: "Quando ero alle superiori..."
target_language_example: Quando ero alle superiori, studiavo inglese tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: When I was in high school, I studied English every day.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. It’s made of a (to/at) + le (the, plural) → alle + dieci (ten). It can refer to 10:00 in the morning or at night; the context (e.g., going to bed) makes it clear.
target_language_example: L’appuntamento è alle dieci.
native_language_example: The appointment is at ten o’clock.

additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns (e.g., figlie, labbra, aspettative). It’s the preposition + article + possessive: a + le + mie = alle mie. Often translates naturally as “to my” or “at my,” depending on the verb (e.g., piacere: “to my daughters”).
target_language_example: Non dare retta alle mie amiche, stanno scherzando.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to my (female) friends; they’re joking.

additional_notes: Means "to my questions" (a + le = alle). Often used with verbs like: rispondere alle mie domande (to answer my questions), non rispondere alle mie domande (not to answer my questions). Note: domande means "questions" (not "demands").
target_language_example: Puoi rispondere alle mie domande, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you answer my questions, please?

additional_notes: Used to say what time something happens. With most clock times in Italian you use "alle" + the hour (e.g., alle due, alle nove). For 1 o’clock, Italian usually uses the singular: "all’una".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle nove davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at nine in front of the station.

meaning: "at the gates/door"; imminent or just outside/nearby.
additional_notes: Used literally for being at/near an entrance (alle porte di servizio = at the service doors). Very commonly used figuratively with events or situations to mean they’re about to happen soon: "L’autunno è alle porte" = autumn is just around the corner. Can also suggest a threat is very close: "Il nemico è alle porte".
target_language_example: Gli esami sono alle porte, devo studiare di più.
native_language_example: The exams are just around the corner, I need to study more.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. "Alle" = "a" (at) + "le" (the, feminine plural), because "ore" (hours) is implied: "alle (ore) sei". For 1 o’clock you usually say "all’una" (singular), not *alle uno*.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sei davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at six in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say the time something happens. With clock times, Italian uses "a" + the plural article ("le") for most hours: "alle" + hour (alle due, alle sette). For 1 o’clock, it’s singular: "all’una". You can use it with or without "a casa" depending on context ("tornerà alle sette" = he/she will be back at seven).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sette davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: See you at seven in front of the movie theater.

meaning: behind (someone); left behind; off (someone else’s support).
additional_notes: Literally “at the shoulders,” used as a common idiom. (1) Physical position: "dietro" someone (e.g., "qualcuno alle spalle" = someone behind you). (2) Figurative: "lasciare ... alle spalle" = to put something behind you / leave it in the past. (3) With "campare/vivere alle spalle di qualcuno" = to live off someone else (depend on them financially or for support), often with a negative tone.
target_language_example: Dai, lasciamoci questo periodo difficile alle spalle.
native_language_example: Come on, let’s put this difficult period behind us.

meaning: to the stars; sky-high (very high, soaring).
additional_notes: Literally “to the stars.” Used with verbs like “mirare” (to aim) for ambition (“aim high”), and very commonly with “salire” (to rise) to say prices/costs have skyrocketed: “I prezzi sono saliti alle stelle.” Can be used figuratively for anything that becomes extremely high.
target_language_example: Dopo l’estate, gli affitti sono saliti alle stelle.
native_language_example: After the summer, rents skyrocketed.

meaning: in high school; to/at high school.
additional_notes: Short for "alle scuole superiori" (upper secondary school). Common with verbs like "andare alle superiori" (to go to high school) and "insegnare alle superiori" (to teach in high school). It can also mean "back in high school" when talking about the past: "alle superiori odiavo..." = "in/during high school I hated...".
target_language_example: Ci siamo conosciuti alle superiori.
native_language_example: We met in high school.

additional_notes: Used to say the time when something happens. With hours, Italian uses the preposition "a" + the definite article: "alle" (a + le) for most hours (e.g., alle undici, alle due). For 1 o’clock it’s "all’una". In ranges you’ll often see "dalle ... alle ..." (from ... to ...).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle undici davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at eleven in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has an allergy to something. It agrees with the noun that follows: allergico/a (masc./fem. sing.), allergici/he (masc./fem. pl.). “Alle” = “a + le” and is used before feminine plural nouns (e.g., le noci, le fragole). Often used with foods, animals, medicines, etc.
target_language_example: Sono allergico alle noci.
native_language_example: I’m allergic to nuts.

meaning: at the zoo; to the zoo (depending on the verb).
additional_notes: "Allo" = "a + lo" and is used before masculine singular nouns starting with z, s+consonant, gn, ps, x, y (like "zoo"). With "essere/stare" it usually means location ("at the zoo"); with "andare" it means destination ("to the zoo").
target_language_example: Andiamo allo zoo domenica mattina.
native_language_example: Let’s go to the zoo on Sunday morning.

additional_notes: Used when referring to a specific chef and then adding a description with a relative clause. "allo" = "a" + "lo" (to the). "che era" means "who/that was" and introduces more information about the chef. It usually needs something after it (e.g., "allo chef che era in cucina" = "to the chef who was in the kitchen").
target_language_example: Ho parlato allo chef che era in cucina.
native_language_example: I spoke to the chef who was in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is looking at themselves or seeing their reflection. Very common with reflexive verbs like guardarsi (to look at oneself), vedersi (to see oneself), and studiarsi (to study oneself): guardati allo specchio! = “look at yourself in the mirror!”
target_language_example: Non mi piace come sto oggi: non voglio guardarmi allo specchio.
native_language_example: I don’t like how I look today: I don’t want to look at myself in the mirror.

additional_notes: Used mainly for cooking meat: "pollo/maiale allo spiedo" (rotisserie chicken/spit-roasted pig). In a figurative (often threatening) sense, "mettere qualcuno allo spiedo" can mean to torture someone or put them through a harsh interrogation/ordeal. The phrase itself is neutral, but it can appear in very aggressive or vulgar sentences depending on context.
target_language_example: Stasera prendiamo un pollo allo spiedo.
native_language_example: Tonight we’ll get a rotisserie chicken.

meaning: at the same (point/level/place); in the same situation.
additional_notes:
Usually followed by a noun, especially in set phrases like: 
- "allo stesso punto" = at the same point / no further along 
- "allo stesso livello" = at the same level 
It’s "a" (to/at) + "lo" (the) + "stesso" (same), and often corresponds to English "at the same ...".
target_language_example: Dopo due ore di discussione, siamo ancora allo stesso punto.
native_language_example: After two hours of discussion, we’re still at the same point.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens or is done similarly to something else. It can refer to actions/behavior (“fare/guardare allo stesso modo”) or to sharing the same opinion/feeling (“pensarla/sentirsi allo stesso modo”). Often placed at the beginning of a sentence to mean “likewise,” in a formal/neutral tone.
target_language_example: Anche io la vedo allo stesso modo.
native_language_example: I see it the same way too.

meaning: at the same time; at once.
additional_notes: Used to say two things happen simultaneously, or that two qualities/ideas are true together ("both... and..."). Common in contrasts like "... ma allo stesso tempo ..." ("...but at the same time...").
target_language_example: Vorrei aiutarti, ma allo stesso tempo devo finire questo lavoro.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but at the same time I have to finish this work.

meaning: in/to the stomach; (with symptoms) in the stomach area.
additional_notes:
Used mainly with health/pain/discomfort to say where you feel something: 
- avere qualcosa allo stomaco = to have something on your stomach / something bothering your stomach
- avere/male allo stomaco = to have a stomachache
Also used for diseases affecting the stomach (e.g., cancro allo stomaco = stomach cancer).
target_language_example: Dopo aver mangiato, ho avuto un peso allo stomaco.
native_language_example: After eating, I had a heavy feeling in my stomach.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like dedicare/dare (to dedicate/give) to say someone dedicates time, energy, or their life to studying a particular field. Grammar: a + lo studio = allo; della is di + la and changes with the noun that follows (del, dello, dei, delle): allo studio del diritto, allo studio delle lingue.
target_language_example: Sto dedicando molto tempo allo studio della lingua italiana.
native_language_example: I’m dedicating a lot of time to studying the Italian language.

additional_notes: "Allo" = "a" + "lo" and means "to/at the" before a masculine singular noun that starts with z (like "zoo"). Use it for going there (andare allo zoo) or being there (essere allo zoo).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo allo zoo con i bambini.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the zoo with the kids.

additional_notes: Used to say you went/are going to the zoo together with someone. **Allo** = **a + lo** (“to the”), used before masculine singular nouns like **zoo**. **Con** means “with.” Often appears with **andare** (“to go”): *andare allo zoo con…*. In the past with **essere** (*sono andato/andata*), the ending can agree with the subject (e.g., *sono andata* = female speaker).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo allo zoo con i bambini.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the zoo with the kids.

additional_notes: Old-fashioned, literary variant of "quando" or "nel momento in cui". You’ll mostly see it in poetry, songs, or older texts rather than everyday conversation.
target_language_example: Allor che arrivò la notte, la città si fece silenziosa.
native_language_example: When night fell, the city became quiet.

meaning: “So, what…?” / “So, how about…?” (used to prompt an answer or decision).
additional_notes: Used in conversation to start a question after a pause or to push things forward (often impatiently or insistently). It commonly introduces questions like “che facciamo?” (what do we do?), “che succede?” (what’s happening?), “che hai saputo?” (what did you find out?).
target_language_example: Allora, che decidiamo per stasera?
native_language_example: So, what are we deciding for tonight?

additional_notes: Common conversation opener to check in or move things forward (often after a pause or when changing topic). It’s typically followed by a question: "Allora, come va?" / "Allora, come andiamo?" Note: Italian "come" means "how," not English "come".
target_language_example: Allora, come è andata la giornata?
native_language_example: So, how did your day go?

additional_notes: Used as a conversational lead-in before a question, often to move things along, prompt an answer, or introduce a new topic. Common with questions like “cosa ne pensi?” (what do you think?) or “cosa vi porta qui?” (what brings you here?). Tone depends on context; it can sound casual, or slightly insistent like “Well then…?”.
target_language_example: Allora, cosa facciamo adesso?
native_language_example: So, what are we doing now?

additional_notes: Used to set a minimum frequency or minimum number of times. Very common with time expressions: "almeno una volta alla settimana" (at least once a week), "al mese" (a month), "al giorno" (a day). You can change the number: "almeno due volte" (at least twice).
target_language_example: Devi provarlo almeno una volta.
native_language_example: You have to try it at least once.

additional_notes: Used to compare height: "X è alta come Y" = "X is as tall as Y". With "non" it means "not as tall as". "Alta" agrees with the person being described (female); for a male subject you usually say "alto come".
target_language_example: Mia sorella è alta come me, ma mio fratello non è alto come noi.
native_language_example: My sister is as tall as me, but my brother isn’t as tall as us.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s height to their mother’s. "Alta" is feminine singular (for a woman/girl); for a man/boy you’d say "alto come sua madre". "Come" means "like/as" in comparisons. You can change the possessive: "mia madre" (my mother), "tua madre" (your mother), etc.
target_language_example: Mia sorella è alta come sua madre.
native_language_example: My sister is as tall as her mother.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is spoken or read so others can hear it. Common with verbs like “leggere” (to read) and “dire” (to say): “leggere ad alta voce” = “to read aloud”. Often written as “ad alta voce”.
target_language_example: Puoi leggere questo messaggio ad alta voce, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you read this message out loud, please?

meaning: ups and downs; highs and lows.
additional_notes: Used to talk about periods of good and bad moments in life, a relationship, health, mood, work, or business results. Often used with verbs like "avere" (to have) or "passare" (to go through): "Abbiamo avuto tanti alti e bassi".
target_language_example: In questo periodo ho molti alti e bassi.
native_language_example: These days I have a lot of ups and downs.

meaning: ups and downs (good and bad times; fluctuations).
additional_notes: Used to talk about the natural changes in life, moods, relationships, work, health, or success—periods of improvement (“alti”) and difficulty (“bassi”). Common with verbs like avere (“to have”), vivere (“to live through”), attraversare/affrontare (“to go through/face”). Often plural: i miei/ i suoi alti e bassi.
target_language_example: In ogni relazione ci sono alti e bassi, ma l’importante è parlarne.
native_language_example: In every relationship there are ups and downs, but what matters is talking about it.

additional_notes: A comparison using **come** (“like/as”). **Alto** agrees with the person described (masc. **alto**, fem. **alta**). **Suo padre** means “his father” (literally “his father”); often used after a verb like **essere**: *È alto come suo padre.*
target_language_example: È alto come suo padre, ma molto più giovane.
native_language_example: He’s as tall as his father, but much younger.

additional_notes: Used in comparisons like “più di qualunque/qualsiasi altra cosa” = “more than anything else.” With an article it often introduces an extra point: “Un’altra cosa!” = “Another thing!” (also written with apostrophe: “un’altra cosa”).
target_language_example: Prima di andare via, un'altra cosa: chiamami quando arrivi.
native_language_example: Before you leave, one more thing: call me when you arrive.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different part of something (“un’altra parte”) or the opposite side (“dall’altra parte” = on the other side). Often appears with prepositions: “da/dall’altra parte” (on the other side), “all’altra parte” (to the other side), “nell’altra parte” (in the other part). Agreement changes with gender/number: “altro/altre parti”.
target_language_example: Il bagno è dall’altra parte del corridoio.
native_language_example: The bathroom is on the other side of the hallway.

additional_notes: Often used with negation to mean “no other choice,” especially in the set phrase: “non avere altra scelta” = “to have no other choice.” Also common as “Non c’è altra scelta” (“There’s no other choice”).
target_language_example: Non ho altra scelta: devo partire subito.
native_language_example: I have no other choice: I have to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used with a negative (usually "non") to say there is only one possible option. Pattern: "non avere altra scelta che" + infinitive (or "non avere altra scelta se non" + infinitive). Example: "Non ho altra scelta che andare" = "I have no choice but to go."
target_language_example: Non avevamo altra scelta che annullare il viaggio.
native_language_example: We had no choice but to cancel the trip.

additional_notes: Often used as (un’)altra volta to mean “another time” (in the future) or “again/once more” (repeat an action). Common in polite refusals or postponing: “Magari un’altra volta” = “Maybe another time.”
target_language_example: Possiamo parlarne un'altra volta.
native_language_example: We can talk about it another time.

additional_notes: Used to talk about additional matters beyond what’s already mentioned. Very common in phrases like “avere altre cose in mente / per la testa” (to have other things on your mind) and with “da fare” (to do): “molte altre cose da fare” = “many other things to do.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso venire: ho altre cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have other things to do today.

additional_notes: Literally “other questions.” Used to ask if there are additional questions (common in meetings, interviews, classes, or court: “Altre domande?”). Also used to say you have more questions: “Ho altre domande.” You may also hear it with “Ci sono” or “Avete”: “Ci sono altre domande?” / “Avete altre domande?”
target_language_example: Se avete altre domande, scrivetemi pure.
native_language_example: If you have any other questions, feel free to write to me.

meaning: another ten minutes / ten more minutes.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or grant additional time beyond what was already expected or agreed. Common with verbs like aspettare (to wait), dormire (to sleep), and concedere (to grant). It agrees in number with the noun: altri (plural) + minuti (plural).
target_language_example: Possiamo restare qui per altri dieci minuti?
native_language_example: Can we stay here for another ten minutes?

additional_notes: Usually used with an article: **un altro modo** (“another way”). Common in problem-solving or suggesting alternatives: **Deve esserci un altro modo** (“There must be another way”). It often takes **per + infinitive** to say “another way to do something”: **un altro modo per farlo**.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo un altro modo per risolvere questo problema.
native_language_example: Let’s look for another way to solve this problem.

additional_notes: Used to say something is completely different from what you’re used to, or far better/worse than something else. Often with essere/sembrere: “È un altro pianeta” = “It’s a whole different world.” You can also specify compared to something: “Rispetto a prima, è un altro pianeta.”
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è un altro pianeta rispetto a quello di ieri.
native_language_example: This restaurant is a whole different league compared to yesterday’s one.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a different location from the one being discussed or expected. Very common with an article: “un altro posto” (another place), and with prepositions like “in/da/a un altro posto” (in/from/to another place).
target_language_example: Non c’è parcheggio qui: cerchiamo un altro posto.
native_language_example: There’s no parking here: let’s look for another place.

additional_notes: Used when asking for a refill or ordering one more glass of wine. Often said with an article and/or politeness phrase, e.g. "Un altro bicchiere di vino, per favore" or "Vorrei un altro bicchiere di vino".
target_language_example: Un altro bicchiere di vino, per favore.
native_language_example: Another glass of wine, please.

meaning: another world; (figuratively) out of this world.
additional_notes: Literally “other world.” Often used with an article ("un altro mondo") or in the expression "di un altro mondo" to describe something that feels completely different, unusual, or amazingly good/strange (similar to English “out of this world”).
target_language_example: Quel posto sembra di un altro mondo.
native_language_example: That place seems like it’s from another world.

meaning: “nothing but / only” (in negatives), or “far from! / more like…!” (as an exclamation).
additional_notes: Common patterns: **non … ad altro che + noun/pronoun** = “think of nothing but …” (e.g., *Non pensa ad altro che a se stesso*). **non fare altro che + infinitive** = “do nothing but …” (often a complaint: *Non fai altro che lamentarti*). Used alone or with a noun as an emphatic reaction (**Altro che controllo!**) meaning “yeah right / far from it / more like the opposite”.
target_language_example: Oggi non faccio altro che studiare.
native_language_example: Today I’m doing nothing but studying.

meaning: to stand up; to make someone stand up.
additional_notes: Used for getting (yourself) to your feet or asking/telling someone to do so. Very common with the causative construction "fare + infinitive" ("fare alzare in piedi" = "make someone stand up"). In everyday speech you’ll also often see the reflexive form "alzarsi in piedi" = "stand up".
target_language_example: John ha fatto alzare in piedi Maria.
native_language_example: John made Maria stand up.

meaning: to raise your hands; (figuratively) to give up / surrender.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: physically lift your hands (e.g., in class, at a concert, or when told by police). Figurative meaning: admit you can’t do anything more and stop trying ("I give up"). Often used as "alzare le mani" or with "in segno di resa" (in surrender).
target_language_example: Ci ho provato in tutti i modi, ma alla fine ho dovuto alzare le mani.
native_language_example: I tried everything, but in the end I had to give up.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/hanno alzato la mano". Often refers to raising your hand to ask a question, volunteer, or get attention (e.g., in class or a meeting). Gender/number agreement is usually not shown because "alzato" stays the same with "avere" (you can also hear "ha alzato la mano" for both men and women).
target_language_example: Ho alzato la mano per fare una domanda.
native_language_example: I raised my hand to ask a question.

meaning: (being) up until late; stayed up late.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "rimanere" (or "stare") to say someone didn’t go to bed early: "Sono rimasto alzato fino a tardi" = "I stayed up late." It agrees with the subject: "rimasto alzato" (male/singular), "rimasta alzata" (female/singular), "rimasti alzati" (male/mixed plural), "rimaste alzate" (female plural).
target_language_example: La notte scorsa lui è rimasto alzato fino a tardi a lavorare.
native_language_example: Last night he stayed up late working.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "alzare la mano". It literally means to lift/raise the hand, and it’s used for gestures like raising your hand to ask a question in class/meetings, or raising your hand to reach/grab something. In everyday conversation you’ll often hear the passato prossimo instead: "ha alzato la mano".
target_language_example: Durante la riunione, alzò la mano per chiedere una cosa.
native_language_example: During the meeting, he/she raised his/her hand to ask something.

meaning: “(he/she) loves the …” (used before a plural noun).
additional_notes: From the verb *amare* (“to love”). *Ama* is the present tense for “he/she loves” (also the formal *Lei* form: “you love”), and *i* is the masculine plural definite article (“the”). Used with masculine plural nouns (e.g., *i treni*, *i cani*). With feminine plural, you’d use *ama le* (e.g., *le montagne*).
target_language_example: Mio fratello ama i film d’azione.
native_language_example: My brother loves action movies.

meaning: "(he/she) loves the" (often also "(he/she) really likes the").
additional_notes: Third-person singular present of *amare* ("to love"). Used with **il** + a masculine singular noun (e.g., *il gelato*, *il lavoro*). In Italian, *amare* can sound strong like "love," but it’s also commonly used to mean "really like" for things/activities.
target_language_example: Ama il caffè la mattina.
native_language_example: He/She loves coffee in the morning.

additional_notes: "Amano" is the 3rd person plural present of "amare" (to love), used for "loro" (they) or any plural subject (e.g., "Sami e sua moglie"). Italian often uses "la" before general nouns like "musica"; in English you usually just say "music" (not "the music") unless you mean specific music.
target_language_example: I miei genitori amano la musica classica.
native_language_example: My parents love classical music.

meaning: "love only because..." (plural command), introducing the reason for loving.
additional_notes: This is a fragment that usually needs more words after it: "amate solo perché + [reason]". "amate" is the imperative (command) form for "you all love" (or a formal/older-style "you love"), used when telling a group what to do. "solo" = "only", and "perché" = "because".
target_language_example: Amate solo perché vi fa stare bene, non per abitudine.
native_language_example: Love only because it makes you feel good, not out of habit.

additional_notes: This is a full clause, not a set phrase. Here "ami" is the present subjunctive of "amare" (to love), commonly used after expressions like "Pensi che…?" / "Pensa che…?" (Do you think that…?). "ancora" = still, "le mie lettere" = my letters. It can refer to "tu" (you, informal), "lui" (he), or "lei" (she/you formal) depending on context.
target_language_example: Pensi che lui ami ancora le mie lettere?
native_language_example: Do you think he still loves my letters?

additional_notes: Used to describe a friend’s place of residence. It’s usually followed by a city/country: “un amico che vive a Roma / a Londra”. You’ll often see it after “Ho” (I have) or “Un mio” (a friend of mine): “Ho un amico che vive a…”.
target_language_example: Ho un amico che vive a Milano.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Milan.

additional_notes: Someone you regularly write to (traditionally by letters, but also by email/messages). Often used with "avere" (to have) or "essere" (to be): "Ho un amico di penna" / "Vorrei essere il tuo amico di penna".
target_language_example: Da bambino avevo un amico di penna in Spagna.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I had a pen pal in Spain.

meaning: “my friend” (a friendly way to address someone).
additional_notes: Used as a form of address, often at the end of a sentence, to sound warm, familiar, or sometimes slightly dramatic/ironic depending on tone. Literal word order is “friend my,” but in English you translate it as “my friend.” Can also be used to show sympathy (e.g., “Povero amico mio” = “My poor friend”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, amico mio: andrà tutto bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, my friend: everything will be fine.

meaning: to kill time; to pass the time while waiting.
additional_notes: Common, everyday expression used when you’re waiting or have nothing to do and you do some activity just to make the time go by (e.g., browsing, taking a walk, reading). It’s often used with verbs like “fare qualcosa per ammazzare il tempo” (to do something to kill time).
target_language_example: Mentre aspettiamo il treno, facciamo una passeggiata per ammazzare il tempo.
native_language_example: While we’re waiting for the train, let’s take a walk to kill time.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition or a doubt (“even if that’s true…”). It often implies skepticism: “assuming they even want to…”. Typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., “ammesso che sia vero…”). Don’t confuse it with the verb phrase “(ho/hanno) ammesso che…”, which means “(I/they) admitted that…” (examples 4–6).
target_language_example: Ammesso che lui venga, dove lo ospitiamo?
native_language_example: Assuming he comes, where will we host him?

meaning: CEO; managing director (the top executive of a company).
additional_notes: Used as a formal job title in companies. Often abbreviated as “A.D.” in Italian business contexts. It agrees for gender and number: amministratore delegato (m.), amministratrice delegata (f.), amministratori delegati (pl.). You may also see “delegato” meaning “appointed/delegated” to run the company.
target_language_example: Qual è il nome del nostro amministratore delegato?
native_language_example: What is the name of our CEO?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a confession/admission, followed by information about someone’s state or identity (often with an adjective or noun): “ammise che era stanco/sposata/divorziata…”. Note: “ammise” is passato remoto (common in books and storytelling); in everyday conversation you’ll often hear “ha ammesso che era…”. “Era” agrees with the subject implied by context (“che era…” = “that (he/she) was…”).
target_language_example: Alla fine ammise che era in torto.
native_language_example: In the end, he admitted that he was wrong.

additional_notes: Ammisero is the passato remoto (remote past) of ammettere (“to admit”). It’s used especially in written narratives, news, and in some regions when talking about the distant past; in everyday speech you often hear hanno ammesso instead. che introduces what they admitted, and erano is the imperfect of essere (“to be”) used to describe a state (e.g., guilty, scared, worried) at that time.
target_language_example: Alla fine ammisero che erano nervosi prima dell’esame.
native_language_example: In the end they admitted that they were nervous before the exam.

meaning: "I love" + a masculine plural noun ("I love the …").
additional_notes: "Amo" is the 1st-person singular of "amare" (to love). "I" is the masculine plural definite article (the). Use it before masculine plural nouns: "i broccoli", "i colori", "i panda". For feminine plural nouns, use "le" instead: "Amo le fragole" (I love strawberries). In everyday Italian, people often use "mi piace/mi piacciono" for "I like" instead of "amo".
target_language_example: Amo i film italiani.
native_language_example: I love Italian movies.

additional_notes: Amo is the first-person singular of amare ('to love'). Il is the masculine singular definite article ('the') used before many nouns starting with a consonant. Italian often uses il in places where English would not use 'the', for example amo il karaoke = 'I love karaoke'.
target_language_example: Amo il mare d'estate.
native_language_example: I love the sea in summer.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun with a possessive: amo il mio + noun (e.g., amo il mio appartamento). If the noun is feminine, you’d say “amo la mia …” (amo la mia casa). The verb is “amare” (to love) in the 1st person singular present: “amo” = “I love.”
target_language_example: Amo il mio lavoro, ma voglio più tempo libero.
native_language_example: I love my job, but I want more free time.

meaning: "I love the" (used before feminine singular nouns).
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking/love for something feminine singular. "Amo" is the 1st person singular of *amare* (to love). "La" is the feminine singular form of "the". With a masculine singular noun you’d use "amo il" (or "amo lo" in some cases).
target_language_example: Amo la cucina italiana.
native_language_example: I love Italian food.

meaning: "I love" (talking about things you really like), with feminine plural nouns ("the").
additional_notes: Used to express strong liking. "Amo" is the 1st-person singular of "amare" (to love). "Le" is the feminine plural definite article (“the”), used before feminine plural nouns (e.g., le arti, le scimmie). For masculine plural nouns, you’d use "amo i" or "amo gli" instead.
target_language_example: Amo le pizze!
native_language_example: I love pizzas!

additional_notes: "Amo" is the 1st-person singular of "amare" (to love). "Le lingue" means "languages" (plural). You can use it to talk about loving languages in general, or specify which kind: "Amo le lingue straniere" (I love foreign languages), "Amo le lingue artificiali" (I love constructed languages).
target_language_example: Amo le lingue, soprattutto l'italiano e lo spagnolo.
native_language_example: I love languages, especially Italian and Spanish.

additional_notes: Used to say two people fell in love immediately when they first met (or first saw each other). Often appears with forms of essere or essere + stato (“è/era/fu amore a prima vista”, “è stato amore a prima vista”).
target_language_example: Per loro è stato amore a prima vista.
native_language_example: For them it was love at first sight.

additional_notes: An affectionate way to address a partner (and sometimes a child). Often used on its own as a form of address (like “Honey.” / “Yes, darling.”). Word order is commonly noun + possessive (amore mio = “love mine” → “my love”).
target_language_example: Buonanotte, amore mio.
native_language_example: Good night, my love.

additional_notes: Used to say the same thing applies to you too. Common with verbs like piacere: “Anche a me piace…” = “I like it too.” It can also stand alone as a short reply (“Anche a me.”). Word order can vary (e.g., “a me anche”), but “anche a me” is the most common.
target_language_example: È successo anche a me ieri.
native_language_example: It happened to me too yesterday.

meaning: “I like it too” / “me too, I like it.”
additional_notes: Used to agree with someone who has said they like something. It literally means “also to me it is pleasing.” Use it with a verb (piace + infinitive) or a singular noun: “Anche a me piace ballare / la torta.” For plural things, use “Anche a me piacciono …” (e.g., “Anche a me piacciono i film”).
target_language_example: Anche a me piace questa canzone.
native_language_example: I like this song too.

additional_notes: Used to say something applies to the other person as well, or to return a wish/greeting. Often comes after the thing being wished: "Buon Natale anche a te" = “Merry Christmas to you too.” You can change the pronoun: "anche a me" (me too), "anche a lei" (you too, formal), "anche a voi" (you all too).
target_language_example: Buona giornata anche a te!
native_language_example: Have a nice day to you too!

additional_notes: Used to add an extra item/group to a list or point. "Anche" = "also/too" and "i" is the masculine plural form of "the" (used before masculine plural nouns like "i quadri" = "the paintings"). It often corresponds to English "also" or "too" and can come before the noun phrase: "anche i miei amici" = "my friends too / also my friends".
target_language_example: Porta anche i documenti, per favore.
native_language_example: Bring the documents too, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you feel the same way or did the same thing as someone else. Often used as a short reply by itself: "Anche io." ("Me too."). Word order can change for emphasis (e.g., "io anche"), but "anche io" is very common at the start of a sentence.
target_language_example: —Sono stanco. —Anche io.
native_language_example: —I'm tired. —Me too.

meaning: “also the keyboard shortcut” (you can also use the keyboard shortcut).
additional_notes: Used in instructions to add an alternative method: besides clicking/menu options, you can use a keyboard shortcut. "Scorciatoia da tastiera" = keyboard shortcut; "anche" = also/too. Often followed by the key combination (e.g., Ctrl+Alt+R).
target_language_example: Se preferisci, puoi usare anche la scorciatoia da tastiera Ctrl+S.
native_language_example: If you prefer, you can also use the keyboard shortcut Ctrl+S.

additional_notes: Used to include a woman in addition to someone else (“also she/her”). In questions it often means “you too?” when speaking formally/politely to a woman (lei = formal ‘you’ for a woman). Position can vary: “anche lei lo sa” = “she/you too know it.”
target_language_example: Vuole un caffè anche lei?
native_language_example: Would you like a coffee too (ma’am)?

additional_notes: Used to include yourself/your group in what was just said (agreement or adding your group to an action/condition). With verbs like "siamo" it usually means "we too" (subject). In other contexts it can mean "us too" (object), similar to English: "Vengono anche loro" = "They’re coming too"; "Vogliono interrogare anche noi" = "They want to question us too."
target_language_example: Se andate voi, veniamo anche noi.
native_language_example: If you go, we’ll come too.

additional_notes: Used to agree or add yourself to what was just said. Common in orders and preferences ("also for me") and in feelings/opinions ("it was the same for me too"). Often used alone as a short reply: "Anche per me."
target_language_example: Un caffè, per favore—anche per me.
native_language_example: A coffee, please—me too (one for me as well).

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or concession: something is true/will happen despite another fact. With a real/known situation it often takes the indicative (Anche se è stanco...). With a hypothetical/uncertain situation it commonly takes the subjunctive (Anche se fosse vero...).
target_language_example: Vengo anche se piove.
native_language_example: I’m coming even if it rains.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or condition where something is true despite the fact that it isn’t the case (or might not be the case). Typically followed by a verb: “Anche se non + verb…”. Often used like English “even if I don’t…”, “even though you’re not…”.
target_language_example: Anche se non ho tempo, ti chiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: Even if I don’t have time, I’ll call you later.

meaning: “even if it rains” / “even though it’s raining.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’ll do something despite the rain. Commonly follows the main clause: “Vado/andrò… anche se piove.” You can intensify it with expressions like “anche se piove a catinelle” (“even if it’s pouring”).
target_language_example: Andiamo al parco anche se piove.
native_language_example: We’re going to the park even if it rains.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a contrast or concession: something happens despite a condition being true. "È" is the 3rd person singular of *essere* (he/she/it is). Often followed by an adjective or noun phrase: *anche se è stanco/giovane/doloroso*; with a person it can mean "even though he/she is" or "even if he/she is" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ti aiuto anche se è tardi.
native_language_example: I’ll help you even though it’s late.

additional_notes: Used to include the person being spoken to in addition to someone else already mentioned or understood. It's often used for emphasis at the start of a sentence, but the idea can also appear later in the sentence depending on word order.
target_language_example: Anche tu vieni con noi?
native_language_example: Are you coming with us too?

additional_notes: Used to include the person you’re speaking to in the same statement as someone else (like “me too” but with the verb “to be”). Word order is typically: Anche + tu + sei + adjective/noun (e.g., "Anche tu sei stanco"). In questions, it’s the same words with a question mark/intonation: "Anche tu sei nuova?" (“Are you new too?”).
target_language_example: Anche tu sei italiano, vero?
native_language_example: You’re Italian too, right?

meaning: “you too / you as well” (plural or formal “you”).
additional_notes: Used to include the listener(s) in addition to someone else ("also you"). "Voi" can be plural “you all” or formal “you” in some contexts. Common in questions ("Did you also…?") and invitations/encouragements ("Come on, you say something too").
target_language_example: Venite anche voi alla festa?
native_language_example: Are you coming to the party too?

additional_notes:
Used with the preposition **a** in several common patterns:
- **ancora a + place** = “still in/at” a place: *Vivono ancora a Tokyo.*
- **ancora a + infinitive** = “still (doing) / (starting) again to”: *Cominciate ancora a litigare…*
- With verbs that naturally take **a** (like **giocare a**, **pensare a**, **somigliare a**), **ancora** adds the idea of “still”: *Giocate ancora a hockey?* / *Penso ancora a Tom.* / *Somiglia ancora a…*
target_language_example: Siete ancora a casa o siete già usciti?
native_language_example: Are you still at home, or have you already gone out?

additional_notes: Used to say someone continues to feel angry toward a person. It’s followed by a person (or pronoun): ancora arrabbiato con me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro. Change the adjective for gender/number: ancora arrabbiata (f.), ancora arrabbiati (m. pl.), ancora arrabbiate (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Sei ancora arrabbiato con me?
native_language_example: Are you still angry with me?

additional_notes: Used to say someone continues to need assistance. Often appears with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho ancora bisogno di aiuto" = "I still need help." You can also turn it into a question: "Hai ancora bisogno di aiuto?"
target_language_example: Hai ancora bisogno di aiuto con i compiti?
native_language_example: Do you still need help with your homework?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (e.g., "Ho ancora dei sentimenti per..." / "Hai ancora dei sentimenti per...?") to say you still have emotional—often romantic—feelings for a person. "Ancora" = "still"; "dei sentimenti" = "some feelings"; "per" introduces the person you feel them for ("per lui/lei").
target_language_example: Pensi di avere ancora dei sentimenti per lui?
native_language_example: Do you think you still have feelings for him?

additional_notes: Used to say you remain uncertain after an explanation or discussion. Often appears with the verb "avere": "Ho ancora dei dubbi" (I still have doubts) or as a question: "Ha ancora dei dubbi?" (Do you still have doubts / Are you still unsure?). "Ancora" = still; "dei dubbi" = some doubts.
target_language_example: Se hai ancora dei dubbi, posso spiegartelo di nuovo.
native_language_example: If you still have doubts, I can explain it to you again.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is continuing to be/stay/live in a place. Very common with verbs like essere (to be), vivere/abitare (to live), restare (to stay): e.g., "Sei ancora in Italia?" = "Are you still in Italy?". "Ancora" usually comes before the verb ("è ancora in...") or right after it for emphasis.
target_language_example: Siamo ancora in ufficio.
native_language_example: We’re still in the office.

additional_notes: Used with a verb like "andare" (to go) or "venire" (to come): "Vai ancora in chiesa ogni domenica?". "Ancora" means "still" (as in continuing to do something). "In chiesa" here means "to church" (going there), and "ogni domenica" means "every Sunday".
target_language_example: Andiamo ancora in chiesa ogni domenica, anche d’estate.
native_language_example: We still go to church every Sunday, even in the summer.

meaning: still in touch with; still in contact with.
additional_notes: Used to say a relationship or communication continues. Often with verbs like "essere" (to be) or "rimanere" (to stay): "Sono ancora in contatto con..." / "Rimango ancora in contatto con...". Followed by a person or group ("con Maria", "con i miei ex colleghi").
target_language_example: Sono ancora in contatto con i miei amici del liceo.
native_language_example: I'm still in touch with my high school friends.

additional_notes: Used to say someone continues to work (often right now/in this period). Common with "stare" to form the present continuous: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno ancora lavorando" = "(we/you/they) are still working". With "con" it means working with someone; with "per" it means working for someone.
target_language_example: Siamo ancora lavorando al progetto.
native_language_example: We’re still working on the project.

additional_notes: Used to say an activity is continuing at the present time. Often followed by a person, team, company, client, or tool you’re collaborating with (e.g., "ancora lavorando con il team", "ancora lavorando con questo cliente"). In a full sentence you’ll usually add a subject and the verb "essere" (e.g., "Sto ancora lavorando con...").
target_language_example: Sto ancora lavorando con Marco su quel progetto.
native_language_example: I’m still working with Marco on that project.

additional_notes: Used to say you continue to be employed by someone (or doing work for them). Very often you’ll see it with "stare" to form the present continuous: "Sto ancora lavorando per..." (I’m still working for...). You can also refer to a past time with "ero": "Ero ancora lavorando per..." (I was still working for...).
target_language_example: Sto ancora lavorando per la stessa azienda.
native_language_example: I'm still working for the same company.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone continues to have/keep your letters (often with the verb "tenere": "tenere ancora le mie lettere" = “to still have/keep my letters”). "Ancora" means “still/yet,” and "le mie lettere" means “my letters.”
target_language_example: Pensi che lui tenga ancora le mie lettere?
native_language_example: Do you think he still has/keeps my letters?

additional_notes: Used to say there are tasks remaining (often implying you’re not finished yet). Common with verbs like “c’è/ci sono” (there is/are), “restano” or “rimangono” (there remain). Word-by-word: ancora (still) + molte cose (many things) + da fare (to do).
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: ho ancora molte cose da fare.
native_language_example: I can’t go out: I still have many things to do.

meaning: “still a lot to …” (used before an infinitive).
