native_language_example: The apartment has two bedrooms and a living room.

additional_notes: Used for a (male) person who has won a world championship title in a sport or competition. Feminine form: "campionessa del mondo". You can specify how many times with numbers: "tre volte campione del mondo" (three-time world champion), "sette volte campione del mondo" (seven-time world champion).
target_language_example: È difficile capire cosa significa essere un campione del mondo.
native_language_example: It’s hard to understand what it means to be a world champion.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the area where people play golf. Often with possessives/articles: il/un campo da golf; il mio campo da golf. In commands you might hear: Vada via/Se ne vada dal campo da golf! (“Go away/Leave the golf course!”).
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo a golf in un campo da golf vicino alla città.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing golf at a golf course near the city.

additional_notes: Used literally for an area with landmines, and very commonly as a metaphor for a situation full of hidden dangers where one wrong move can cause big problems (e.g., relationships, politics, a tense conversation). Often appears with verbs like "essere in" (to be in), "sembrare" (to seem), or "camminare in/su" (to walk in/on) a minefield.
target_language_example: Parlare di soldi con loro è un campo minato.
native_language_example: Talking about money with them is a minefield.

additional_notes: Used to specify a group of Canadians based on where they live. The verb "vivono" is 3rd person plural ("they live"), and it’s followed by a place (in + country/city): "che vivono in Australia" = "who live in Australia". "che" here means "who/that" and introduces a describing clause.
target_language_example: Ci sono molti canadesi che vivono in Italia.
native_language_example: There are many Canadians who live in Italy.

additional_notes: Medical term. Often used with the article: “il cancro ai polmoni”. Common verbs: “avere il cancro ai polmoni” (to have lung cancer), “diagnosticare un cancro ai polmoni” (to diagnose lung cancer). You may also hear “tumore ai polmoni” with a similar meaning.
target_language_example: Gli hanno diagnosticato un cancro ai polmoni.
native_language_example: They diagnosed him with lung cancer.

additional_notes: Medical term for cancer located in the stomach. Often used with verbs like avere (to have), soffrire di (to suffer from), or medicine/cure for it (medicine per/contro il cancro allo stomaco).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, mio zio ha un cancro allo stomaco.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, my uncle has stomach cancer.

meaning: Not a natural/standard Italian phrase; sounds like a mistaken attempt at “dog, sit” / “sit (down), dog”.
additional_notes: "Cane di sedersi" is grammatically odd and not something Italians would normally say. To command a dog to sit, Italians typically say "Seduto!" (common dog command) or "Siediti!" (informal singular: “Sit down!”). If you need to include "cane" explicitly, more natural options are "Cane, seduto!" or "Seduto, cane!".
target_language_example: Ho sentito qualcuno dire "cane di sedersi", ma in italiano suona strano; meglio "Cane, seduto!".
native_language_example: I heard someone say “cane di sedersi,” but in Italian it sounds strange; “Dog, sit!” is better.

additional_notes: Used to say that a dog (cane) bit you (mi = me). It’s usually said with a possessive before cane (il tuo/il suo/il vostro cane = your/his/her/your-plural dog) and you can add the body part: mi ha morso la mano = it bit my hand. Word order is flexible: Mi ha morso il cane is also common.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma il tuo cane mi ha morso.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but your dog bit me.

additional_notes: “Cane” means “dog” (masculine singular). “È” is the 3rd-person singular of “essere” (to be): it matches singular subjects like “il cane” (the dog) or “questo cane” (this dog). Often you’ll see it with an article or a demonstrative: “il cane è… / questo cane è…”.
target_language_example: Il cane è molto tranquillo.
native_language_example: The dog is very calm.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone can/knows how to sing a specific song. Often appears with verbs like "potere" (can/be able to) or "sapere" (know how to). You can swap in another song: "cantare quella canzone" (that song) or add a title: "cantare la canzone '…'".
target_language_example: Sai cantare questa canzone in italiano?
native_language_example: Do you know how to sing this song in Italian?

additional_notes: Used for the action of singing a (specific or unspecified) song. Very common with verbs like "lasciare" (let) and "potere" (can), and can be followed by "per" to mean singing for someone/audience: "cantare una canzone per tutti" = "sing a song for everyone."
target_language_example: Vuoi cantare una canzone con me?
native_language_example: Do you want to sing a song with me?

additional_notes: Used to say someone has the ability (or the courage) to do something. Very often followed by an infinitive: "capace di + verb" (e.g., "capace di guidare"). It can also be followed by a noun: "capace di complimenti" (capable of giving compliments). In the negative, "non sono capace di..." often means "I can’t / I’m not able to..." or "I’m not good at...". Adjective agreement: capace (sing.), capaci (pl.).
target_language_example: Non sono capace di parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: I’m not able to speak in public.

additional_notes: A common way to describe someone’s appearance. Often used with the verb "avere": "Ha i capelli biondi" = "She/He has blond hair." You can also use it with "con" (with): "una ragazza con i capelli biondi" = "a girl with blond hair." Note the plural: "capelli" (hair) is usually plural in Italian.
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha i capelli biondi.
native_language_example: My brother has blond hair.

additional_notes: This phrase is understandable, but in everyday Italian you more commonly say **capelli rossi** (“red hair”) or **capelli di colore rosso** (“red-colored hair”). Using **di + color** can describe someone’s hair color, especially if you want to emphasize the shade or a dyed color.
target_language_example: Si è tinta i capelli di rosso.
native_language_example: She dyed her hair red.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is “long hair.” Used to describe someone’s hairstyle: *Ho i capelli lunghi* (“I have long hair”) or *Porta i capelli lunghi* (“He/She wears long hair”). Plural agreement: *capelli* (hair) + *lunghi* (masc. plural). Singular for one hair: *un capello lungo*.
target_language_example: Lei ha i capelli lunghi e castani.
native_language_example: She has long, brown hair.

additional_notes:
Commonly used to describe someone by hair color. You’ll often see it with articles and prepositions: 
- i capelli rossi = red hair (someone has red hair)
- con i capelli rossi = with red hair
- coi capelli rossi = with red hair (contracted form of “con i”)
Used like an adjective phrase after the noun: capelli rossi (not *rossi capelli*).
target_language_example: Lei è quella con i capelli rossi.
native_language_example: She’s the one with red hair.

additional_notes: Used to talk about comprehension of the French language (spoken or written). Often appears with verbs like "riuscire a" (manage to/can) or "sapere" (know how to). You can replace "il francese" with other languages (e.g., "capire l’italiano").
target_language_example: Non riesco a capire il francese quando parlano troppo velocemente.
native_language_example: I can’t understand French when they speak too fast.

additional_notes: Used to check/confirm something the speaker believes is true. “Giusto?” works like an English tag question (“right?” / “isn’t that so?”). You can swap “il francese” with another language or subject (e.g., “capire l’italiano, giusto?”). Often said with “riuscire a” (“to manage to / be able to”): “Riesci a capire…?”
target_language_example: Riesci a capire il francese, giusto?
native_language_example: You can understand French, right?

meaning: “capital of the” (used before a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to name the capital city of a country/region/area when the following noun is feminine singular (e.g., la Francia, la Toscana). For masculine singular nouns, use “capitale del” (del = di + il). Often followed by a proper noun: “La capitale della Francia è Parigi.”
target_language_example: La capitale della Francia è Parigi.
native_language_example: The capital of France is Paris.

additional_notes: Used to introduce which team someone is the captain of (sports, school teams, etc.). Often followed by a team name or organization: “capitano della squadra di calcio” (captain of the soccer team) or “capitano della squadra di Milano” (captain of Milan’s team). You may also see “il capitano della squadra” when the team is already clear.
target_language_example: Lei è la capitano della squadra di pallavolo della scuola.
native_language_example: She is the captain of the school volleyball team.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *capitare* (“to happen/occur”), most often as **è capitato qualcosa di + adjective** (e.g., *strano, bello, grave*). Very commonly you add the person it happened to with an indirect pronoun: **mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi è capitato qualcosa di…** = “something … happened to me/you/him/her/us/you all.”
target_language_example: Mi è capitato qualcosa di strano ieri sera.
native_language_example: Something strange happened to me last night.

additional_notes: Commonly refers to a military tank. It’s masculine: il carro armato; plural: i carri armati. Used with typical verbs like avere (to have), mettere in (to put into), tornare con (to return with/by).
target_language_example: Durante la parata militare abbiamo visto un carro armato enorme.
native_language_example: During the military parade we saw a huge tank.

additional_notes: Used when a vehicle has broken down, is stuck, or needs to be removed. Often appears with verbs like chiamare (to call), aspettare (to wait for), and avere bisogno di (to need). Commonly used with the definite article: il carro attrezzi.
target_language_example: La macchina non parte: ho chiamato il carro attrezzi.
native_language_example: The car won’t start: I called the tow truck.

additional_notes: Used when paying, booking, or giving card details. Agreement: una carta di credito / le carte di credito. Possessives change with formality: la mia (my), la tua (your—informal singular), la vostra (your—formal singular or plural).
target_language_example: Posso pagare con la carta di credito?
native_language_example: Can I pay with a credit card?

additional_notes: Common everyday item for the bathroom. Often used with quantity words like "un rotolo" (a roll), "una scorta" (a supply/stock), or with "avere/comprare/usare" (to have/buy/use).
target_language_example: Scusi, dov'è la carta igienica?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where is the toilet paper?

additional_notes: Plural of "carta di credito". Used when asking if a place accepts card payments (often with "accettare" or "prendere": "Accettate/Prendete carte di credito?"). In Italy you may also hear "carta" (card) or "bancomat" (debit card).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non accettiamo carte di credito.
native_language_example: Sorry, we don’t accept credit cards.

additional_notes: Used for an animated movie or TV show (a cartoon). Often preceded by an article: un/il cartone animato; plural: cartoni animati. Literally refers to something like “animated drawing,” not typically translated word-for-word in English.
target_language_example: Da bambino guardavo sempre un cartone animato dopo scuola.
native_language_example: As a kid I always watched a cartoon after school.

additional_notes: Used for animated TV shows or movies, often for kids but also for adults. Usually plural: "i cartoni animati". In speech you may also hear "cartone animato" (singular) for one cartoon/show/film.
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo i cartoni animati in TV.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re watching cartoons on TV.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/returning (andare/venire/tornare) to say you go home by walking: “andare/tornare a casa a piedi”. Word order is usually “a casa a piedi”.
target_language_example: Oggi torno a casa a piedi.
native_language_example: Today I'm walking home.

meaning: 'home from school' / 'at home (having come) from school'.
additional_notes: This isn’t a very standard standalone phrase in Italian. You’ll more often see it used with a verb of coming/going, e.g. "tornare a casa da scuola" (to come back home from school) or "andare a casa da scuola" (to go home from school). On its own, it may sound incomplete.
target_language_example: Sono tornato a casa da scuola alle tre.
native_language_example: I came home from school at three.

additional_notes: Usually used with the preposition **a**: **a casa da solo** (male speaker) or **a casa da sola** (female speaker). You can also say **a casa da soli** for a group. Means being at home without other people.
target_language_example: Stasera resto a casa da solo.
native_language_example: Tonight I'm staying home alone.

meaning: nursing home; care home (a facility where people receive care).
additional_notes: Used for a residential facility where people (often elderly, but not only) live and receive ongoing medical or personal care. Depending on context it can also refer to a clinic/rehabilitation facility where someone stays to recover.
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, mio nonno è rimasto per due settimane in una casa di cura.
native_language_example: After the operation, my grandfather stayed in a nursing home for two weeks.

additional_notes: Refers to the company that publishes books (and sometimes magazines, etc.). Often used with prepositions like in/da/presso: “lavorare presso una casa editrice” (to work at a publishing house), “ordinare un libro dalla casa editrice” (to order a book from the publisher).
target_language_example: Mia sorella lavora in una casa editrice a Milano.
native_language_example: My sister works at a publishing house in Milan.

additional_notes: Used to set a deadline for arriving home. Often appears with a verb like "essere" (to be) or "tornare" (to come back): "Devo essere casa entro mezzanotte" = "I have to be home by midnight." "Entro" means "by" (no later than).
target_language_example: Devo tornare a casa entro mezzanotte.
native_language_example: I have to be back home by midnight.

meaning: “a big house and two …” (two of something).
additional_notes: This looks like an incomplete fragment you might see in spoken Italian or in listings/notes, where “e due …” is followed by what there are two of (e.g., “due camere” = two bedrooms, “due bagni” = two bathrooms). By itself, it usually needs a noun after “due” to be fully clear.
target_language_example: Vorrei una casa grande e due camere da letto.
native_language_example: I’d like a big house and two bedrooms.

additional_notes: As written, it’s missing the preposition **a** in normal Italian. Most often you say **a casa ieri sera** (“at home last night”). Used to say where someone was the previous evening: **Ero a casa ieri sera**. **Ieri sera** means “last night / yesterday evening” (the evening of yesterday).
target_language_example: Ero a casa ieri sera.
native_language_example: I was at home last night.

meaning: '(at) home on Sundays' / '(at) home on Sunday'.
additional_notes: This is understood as “(a) casa la domenica” = “at home on Sunday/Sundays.” In Italian you usually include the preposition: **a casa la domenica** (at home on Sundays). For a specific Sunday, you can say **a casa domenica** or **a casa questa domenica** (at home this Sunday).
target_language_example: Di solito sono a casa la domenica.
native_language_example: I’m usually at home on Sundays.

additional_notes: Means someone’s own home/house. Often used in welcoming expressions like “casa mia è casa tua” (“my home is your home”). In standard word order you’ll also hear “la mia casa” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a casa mia dopo le lezioni?
native_language_example: Do you want to come to my place after class?

meaning: "at home or at work" (talking about being in either place).
additional_notes: In full, you’ll very often hear this as **a casa o al lavoro** (“at home or at work”). **casa** means “home,” and **al lavoro** = **a + il lavoro** (“at work”). Used to describe where someone is, or where something can be done/found.
target_language_example: Puoi lavorare a casa o al lavoro, come preferisci.
native_language_example: You can work at home or at work, however you prefer.

additional_notes: A purpose phrase: "per" + infinitive means "in order to". "potermi" = "to be able (for me)" + verb (here "riposare", to rest). Often used after verbs like "andare/tornare" (to go/return): "Vado a casa per potermi riposare."
target_language_example: Torno a casa per potermi riposare un po'.
native_language_example: I'm going back home so I can rest a bit.

meaning: at home for the whole day; home all day.
additional_notes: In real Italian you will usually say **a casa per tutto il giorno** (“at home all day”). **Casa** means “home/house”; in this expression it normally refers to being/staying at home. Often used with verbs like **stare** (to stay) or **restare** (to remain).
target_language_example: Oggi resto a casa per tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Today I'm staying home all day.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment. In a full sentence you’ll often see it with a verb before it (e.g., “sono tornato/a a casa perché stava piovendo” = “I went back home because it was raining”). Often you need the preposition “a” before casa: “a casa” = “(at) home / to home.” “Stava piovendo” is the imperfect/progressive meaning “it was raining” (ongoing in the background).
target_language_example: Sono tornato a casa perché stava piovendo.
native_language_example: I went back home because it was raining.

additional_notes: Typically used with verbs of going/returning: "andare/venire/tor­nare a casa presto" = to go/come/get home early. In Italian you normally say "a casa" (with the preposition "a"); "casa" alone can appear in some contexts, but "a casa presto" is the common beginner-friendly pattern.
target_language_example: Oggi devo tornare a casa presto.
native_language_example: Today I have to get home early.

additional_notes: Used to say you should get/ be home before nightfall. Very often you’ll hear it as **a casa prima che faccia buio** (“(go/be) home…”). After **prima che** (“before”), Italian normally uses the **subjunctive**: **faccia** is the subjunctive of **fare** in the expression **fare buio** (“to get dark”).
target_language_example: Devo essere a casa prima che faccia buio.
native_language_example: I have to be home before it gets dark.

additional_notes: Means “his/her home/house.” In Italian, possessive adjectives often come after the noun: casa sua = “his/her house” (sua agrees with casa, which is feminine). The context usually tells you whether it’s “his” or “her.” Often used with vicino a / nei paraggi di (“near”).
target_language_example: Abita non lontano da casa sua.
native_language_example: He/She lives not far from his/her home.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s home. Like English, Italian often uses “casa” for both “house” and “home” depending on context. It can also appear with motion verbs: “andare a casa tua” = “to go to your place/home.” In commands it can sound brusque depending on tone: “Vai a casa tua!” = “Go home!”
target_language_example: Stasera ceniamo a casa tua?
native_language_example: Are we having dinner at your place tonight?

additional_notes: In real Italian you’ll most often hear/see it with the preposition **a**: **a casa tutto il giorno** (“at home all day”), especially after verbs like **stare** (to stay) or **restare** (to remain): *Sto a casa tutto il giorno.* Without **a**, it can sound incomplete unless it’s part of a longer phrase.
target_language_example: Oggi sto a casa tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: Today I’m staying at home all day.

additional_notes: Common phrase for unpleasant or negative information. Often used with verbs like ricevere (to receive), dare (to give), avere (to have), or sentire (to hear): Ho una cattiva notizia / Ho delle cattive notizie. You can also say Brutte notizie with a very similar meaning.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ho delle cattive notizie.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but I have some bad news.

meaning: a bad smell; a foul odor.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) for things that smell bad: "X ha un cattivo odore". You can also use it with "venire da" (to come from) to say where the smell is coming from: "Il cattivo odore viene da...". Often used with "un" (singular) even if the object is plural.
target_language_example: C'è un cattivo odore in cucina.
native_language_example: There’s a bad smell in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels grumpy/irritable or is not in a good mood. Often with verbs like essere/avere: "Sono di cattivo umore" (I’m in a bad mood). Note: "umore" means "mood" (not "humor").
target_language_example: Oggi sono di cattivo umore, scusa se rispondo male.
native_language_example: Today I’m in a bad mood, sorry if I answer rudely.

meaning: 'the cause of the' / 'the case (lawsuit) of the'.
additional_notes: Most commonly it means the reason for something: "la causa della morte" = "the cause of death". In legal contexts, "causa" can also mean a court case/lawsuit (e.g., "la causa della Corona" = "the Crown’s case"; often also seen as "causa contro [someone]" = "case against [someone]"). It’s the phrase "causa di" + the feminine singular article ("della" = "of the").
target_language_example: Non conosciamo ancora la causa della scomparsa.
native_language_example: We still don’t know the cause of the disappearance.

additional_notes: Literally “black horse” (cavallo = horse, nero = black). Used to describe the color of a horse; “nero” agrees with the masculine singular noun “cavallo.”
target_language_example: Il cavallo nero corre nel prato.
native_language_example: The black horse runs in the field.

additional_notes: Very vulgar/insulting. Used before a noun to emphasize anger, annoyance, contempt, or frustration (similar to English “fucking” in “the fucking door / do your fucking job”). Often appears with an article (il/la/lo/un/una) before it: “la cazzo di porta”, “il tuo cazzo di lavoro”. Avoid in polite or neutral situations.
target_language_example: Spegni quel cazzo di telefono.
native_language_example: Turn off that fucking phone.

additional_notes: Extremely rude/vulgar. Used to insult someone’s mouth when telling them to stop talking, especially in the fixed phrase **Chiudi quella/quel cazzo di bocca!** (“Shut your fucking mouth!”). **cazzo di + noun** works as a harsh intensifier (“fucking/damn + noun”) and changes for gender/number: **quel cazzo di…** (masc.), **quella cazzo di…** (fem.), etc.
target_language_example: Chiudi quella cazzo di bocca e ascoltami.
native_language_example: Shut your fucking mouth and listen to me.

additional_notes: Used to express shock, anger, or frustration. Often appears in questions like “Che/ Cosa cazzo sta succedendo?” or “Che cazzo succede?” It’s vulgar (literally “dick”) and not appropriate in polite/company settings; use “Che cosa sta succedendo?” for a neutral version.
target_language_example: Che cazzo sta succedendo? Nessuno mi sta dicendo niente.
native_language_example: What the fuck is happening? Nobody is telling me anything.

meaning: pronoun combination used in expressions like “ce la fare” = “to manage / to succeed (to do it)”.
additional_notes: “Ce” and “la” are clitic pronouns that often appear together before a verb. Very commonly, “ce la fare” means “to make it / to be able to do it” (e.g., “Ce la faccio” = “I can do it”; “Ce la fai?” = “Can you manage?”; “Non ce la farai” = “You won’t make it”). The “la” doesn’t refer to a specific feminine noun here; it’s part of the fixed expression. In other verbs it can be more literal (depending on context), but in beginner Italian you’ll most often meet it with “fare” in this sense.
target_language_example: Dai, ce la fai ancora per dieci minuti!
native_language_example: Come on, you can manage for another ten minutes!

additional_notes: Used to say that something exists/is available in some quantity. It combines ci/ce (“there”) + ne (“of it/them”) + sono (“are”), often answering an implied question like “Do you have any?” or “Are there any?” Common with words like ancora (“still/left”) and with di + adjective to describe them: "Ce ne sono di meravigliose" = “There are some wonderful ones.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ce ne sono ancora.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: there are still some (left).

meaning: it (as an object pronoun, used in set expressions)
additional_notes: Combination of pronouns (ce = ci, ‘to us/it’; la = ‘it’, feminine) that appears in many common expressions. In your example, it’s part of the idiom «bersela» (literally “to drink it”), meaning “to believe it / to buy it” in a skeptical sense: «E credi che ce la beviamo?» = “And you think we’ll believe that?”
target_language_example: Non ce la beviamo: non è vero.
native_language_example: We don’t buy it: it’s not true.

meaning: “We’ll manage / we’ll get through it / we’ll make it.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **cavarsela** (“to manage, to cope”). **Ce la** are fixed pronouns used with *cavarsela*; they don’t translate word-for-word, but refer generally to “it/this situation.” **Caveremo** is the 1st person plural future (“we will”). Often used to reassure someone or express confidence in a difficult situation.
target_language_example: Non sarà facile, ma ce la caveremo insieme.
native_language_example: It won’t be easy, but we’ll get through it together.

meaning: "we can do it / we’ll manage" (we’re able to succeed).
additional_notes: From the verb phrase «farcela» = to manage, to succeed, to make it. «Ce la facciamo?» is used to ask if something is possible/achievable; «Non ce la facciamo» means “we can’t do it / we won’t make it.” Very common with «più»: «Non ce la facciamo più» = “we can’t take it anymore / we can’t keep going.” Other persons: «ce la faccio» (I can), «ce la fai» (you can), «ce la fanno» (they can).
target_language_example: Dai, ce la facciamo se lavoriamo insieme.
native_language_example: Come on, we can do it if we work together.

meaning: "I can do it" / "I can manage" / "I can make it."
additional_notes: Used to say you’re able to do something or to cope with a situation, often after difficulty: "Non ce la faccio" = "I can’t do it / I can’t manage (anymore)." It commonly appears with additions like "da solo" (by myself) or "più" (anymore): "Non ce la faccio più."
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo: sono stanco, ma ce la faccio.
native_language_example: Wait a moment: I’m tired, but I can do it.

meaning: (Usually in the negative) “I can’t do it anymore / I can’t take it anymore.”
additional_notes: Most often you’ll hear it as **“Non ce la faccio più”** to say you’ve reached your limit (too tired, stressed, fed up) or you can’t manage to continue. It’s based on the idiomatic verb **farcela** (“to manage, to make it”). With **più**, it means “anymore / any longer.”
target_language_example: Non ce la faccio più, sono esausto.
native_language_example: I can’t take it anymore, I’m exhausted.

additional_notes:
From the verb phrase **farcela** = “to manage / to succeed (in doing something)”. Very common in spoken Italian.
- **Ce la fai?** = “Can you do it?” / “Are you able to?”
- Often followed by **a + infinitive**: **Ce la fai a correre?** = “Can you manage to run?”
- Can also be encouraging or challenging: **Dai, ce la fai!** = “Come on, you can do it!”
target_language_example: Dai, ce la fai a finire i compiti oggi?
native_language_example: Come on, can you manage to finish your homework today?

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "farcela" (to manage, succeed, get through something). "Ce la farai" is used to encourage someone or to ask if they will manage to do something difficult (an exam, a trip, a hard moment). "Ce" and "la" don’t translate separately here; they refer generally to “it/that task/situation.”
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: ce la farai anche stavolta.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you’ll make it this time too.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "farcela" = to manage/succeed. "Ce" and "la" are pronouns that don’t translate literally here; together they refer to “it/that” (the goal or situation). Used to encourage someone ("Ce la faremo!") or to express doubt as a question ("Ce la faremo?").
target_language_example: Non sarà facile, ma ce la faremo.
native_language_example: It won’t be easy, but we’ll make it.

meaning: "Will he/she ever manage it?" / "Will he/she ever make it?"
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **farcela** = “to manage (to do something), to succeed.” **Ce la farà mai?** is often a rhetorical question expressing doubt or impatience. You can change the subject: **ce la farò mai?** (will I ever manage?), **ce la farai mai?** (will you ever manage?).
target_language_example: Con tutto questo lavoro, ce la farà mai a finire in tempo?
native_language_example: With all this work, will he ever manage to finish on time?

meaning: “I’ll make it / I’ll manage / I’ll be able to do it.”
additional_notes: From the idiom **farcela** (“to manage, to succeed, to make it”). **Ce la farò** is the future tense (“I will manage”). Often used to reassure someone (**Ce la farò, non temere**) or to express doubt (**Non so se ce la farò**). Very common with **a + infinitive**: **Non ce la farò a finire in tempo** (“I won’t manage to finish in time”). In negatives: **Non ce la farò**.
target_language_example: Tranquillo: ce la farò a finire il lavoro oggi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ll manage to finish the work today.

meaning: “You can do it / you can make it.”
additional_notes: From the verb **farcela** = “to manage; to succeed; to make it.” **Ce** and **la** are fixed pronouns used with *farcela* and don’t translate word-for-word. Common as encouragement (*Forza, ce la puoi fare!*) or to say someone is capable of succeeding in something difficult. Also possible: *non ce la puoi fare* (“you can’t do it”), *ce l’hai fatta* (“you did it / you made it”).
target_language_example: Dai, ce la puoi fare: manca solo un chilometro!
native_language_example: Come on, you can do it: there’s only one kilometer left!

meaning: “it to us” / “him to us” (combined object pronouns).
additional_notes: Used before the verb (or attached to an infinitive/imperative) to replace two objects at once: **ce** = “to us” (sometimes “for us”), and **lo** = “it / him” (masculine singular direct object). Common with verbs like **dire** (to tell), **dare** (to give), **spiegare** (to explain), **garantire** (to guarantee), **prendere** (to take). In English you usually translate it as “it” or “him” + “to us”: *Ce lo disse* = “He told it to us.”
target_language_example: Ce lo puoi spiegare, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to us, please?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs of leaving/moving away, especially in expressions like **andarsene** (“to leave/go away”): **ce ne andiamo** = “we’re leaving.” It’s made of two little pronouns (**ce** + **ne**) and doesn’t translate word-for-word into English; think of it as adding the idea of “away/from here/from there.” You’ll also see it with **stare** to emphasize the action in progress: **ce ne stiamo andando** = “we’re leaving / we’re on our way out.”
target_language_example: È tardi: ce ne andiamo subito.
native_language_example: It’s late: we’re leaving right away.

additional_notes: From the verb "andarsene" = "to leave / go away". "Ce" and "ne" are pronoun particles that are part of the verb; you commonly see them with different people: "me ne vado" (I’m leaving), "te ne vai" (you’re leaving), "se ne va" (he/she leaves), "ce ne andiamo" (we’re leaving). Often used to announce departure or to say someone wants/asks you to leave ("vuole che ce ne andiamo?").
target_language_example: È tardi: ce ne andiamo adesso.
native_language_example: It’s late: we’re leaving now.

additional_notes: From the verb **andarsene** (“to leave, to go away”). **Ce** and **ne** are pronouns that are commonly used with *andarsene* and usually stay with the verb (often written separately): *me ne vado, te ne vai, se ne va, ce ne andiamo/andremo*. It’s frequently used with **via** (“away”) or with a place: **da qui/di qui** (“from here”). With negation: **non ce ne andremo** (“we won’t leave”).
target_language_example: È tardi: ce ne andremo dopo cena.
native_language_example: It’s late: we’ll leave after dinner.

meaning: "we ... it" / "we ... from there" (pronouns used with a verb in the past: *we have ...*).
additional_notes: This is a common clitic pronoun cluster: **ce** (here often = “ci”, “to it/there”) + **ne** (“of it/from it/from there”) + **siamo** (“we are/have” used with *essere* in the passato prossimo). The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows. Examples: **ce ne siamo accorti** = “we noticed it” (with *accorgersi di* = to notice/realize); **ce ne siamo andati / ce ne siamo dovuti andare** = “we left / we had to leave” (with *andarsene* = to go away/leave). With *dovere*, agreement can appear: **dovuti** (mixed/masc. plural) / **dovute** (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Non ce ne siamo resi conto subito.
native_language_example: We didn’t realize it right away.

additional_notes: Used to say that some exist/are present, referring back to something already mentioned. Common with quantities: "ce ne sono due/tre/tanti" = "there are two/three/many (of them)." Often appears in conditional phrases like "se ce ne sono" = "if there are any."
target_language_example: Se ce ne sono ancora, prendiamone due.
native_language_example: If there are any left, let's take two (of them).

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number (in the hundreds) of things or units of time. It’s followed by a plural noun: centinaia di libri (hundreds of books), centinaia di anni (hundreds of years). You can also say diverse centinaia di to mean “several hundred.”
target_language_example: Ci sono centinaia di persone in piazza.
native_language_example: There are hundreds of people in the square.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an amount of money in dollars. "Cento" = 100, and "dollari" is plural (used for amounts other than 1). You’ll often see it after verbs like "dare" (to give), "perdere" (to lose), "risparmiare" (to save), or with "una banconota da cento dollari" = “a 100-dollar bill.”
target_language_example: Mi devi cento dollari.
native_language_example: You owe me one hundred dollars.

additional_notes: A common place-name phrase for a large building/area with many stores (often also restaurants and a supermarket). Used with common verbs like andare al/nel centro commerciale (to go to the mall) and aprire (to open).
target_language_example: Andiamo al centro commerciale sabato pomeriggio?
native_language_example: Shall we go to the mall Saturday afternoon?

additional_notes: "Centro commerciale" means "shopping mall" in everyday Italian. "Con" means "with" and introduces the person you go with: "al centro commerciale con Tom" = "to the mall with Tom". The phrase often appears after verbs of going (andare, venire) and can be preceded by "al" (= a + il, "to the").
target_language_example: Vado al centro commerciale con mia sorella.
native_language_example: I’m going to the shopping mall with my sister.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive: cerca di + verb (e.g., cerca di capire = try to understand). It can be a suggestion/command (Cerca di… = Try to…).
target_language_example: Cerca di parlare più lentamente, per favore.
native_language_example: Try to speak more slowly, please.

meaning: "try not to" (used to tell someone to avoid doing something).
additional_notes: Common in advice and requests, often as an imperative: "Cerca di non..." + infinitive. The negation "non" goes right before the infinitive (e.g., "non fare", "non preoccuparti"). It can sound like a gentle instruction rather than a strict order.
target_language_example: Cerca di non dimenticare il passaporto.
native_language_example: Try not to forget your passport.

additional_notes: "Cercai" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "cercare" for "io". It’s common in stories, historical writing, and in some regions; in everyday conversation many speakers use "ho cercato di" instead. It is followed by an infinitive: "cercai di + verbo" (e.g., "cercai di parlare").
target_language_example: Cercai di chiamarti, ma non avevo campo.
native_language_example: I tried to call you, but I had no signal.

additional_notes: Formed from the verb "cercare" + "di" + infinitive: "cercando di + verb". It often implies an attempt/effort that may or may not succeed. Common with verbs like trovare, capire, aiutare, salvare, sopravvivere.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: I'm trying to learn Italian.

additional_notes: Uses the gerund (cercando) + di + infinitive (fare) to describe an ongoing effort or attempt. Often followed by another verb: cercando di capire (trying to understand), cercando di aiutare (trying to help). You can add an object after fare: cercando di fare la spesa (trying to do the grocery shopping).
target_language_example: Sto cercando di fare tutto in tempo.
native_language_example: I'm trying to do everything on time.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun: cercando un + [noun]. Very common with the present/past continuous: stare + cercando (e.g., state cercando… = “are you looking…?”, stava cercando… = “was looking…”). For feminine nouns you usually use "cercando una".
target_language_example: Sto cercando un ristorante vicino.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a restaurant nearby.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to express making an effort or attempt to do something. Without di, cercare usually means "to look for" something.
target_language_example: Dovremmo cercare di aiutarle.
native_language_example: We should try to help them.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people attempted to hide a feeling or state (often followed by a noun like ansia “anxiety”, paura “fear”, confusione “confusion”). Note: "cercarono" is passato remoto (a narrative past common in books/stories), equivalent in meaning to "hanno cercato" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Cercarono di nascondere la loro preoccupazione durante la riunione.
native_language_example: They tried to hide their worry during the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction or advice to a group of people. "Cercate" is the plural formal/informal command of "cercare" (to try), followed by "di" + infinitive; adding "non" makes it negative (try not to do something). You can also use singular: "cerca di non..." (you), and polite singular: "cerchi di non...".
target_language_example: Cercate di non fare troppo rumore in biblioteca.
native_language_example: Try not to make too much noise in the library.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary "avere" ("ho/hai/ha... cercato di") + an infinitive to say someone made an attempt to do something. Literally "cercare" means "to look for", but "cercare di + infinitive" means "to try to".
target_language_example: Ho cercato di chiamarti ieri, ma non avevi campo.
native_language_example: I tried to call you yesterday, but you had no signal.

meaning: “(have/has) tried to hide the …” (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment you’ll usually see as part of a full sentence, most commonly after an auxiliary verb: **ho/ha/hanno cercato di…** (“I/he/they tried to…”). **Nascondere** means “to hide” and normally takes a direct object. **La** is “the” for a singular feminine noun (e.g., **la verità**, **la chiave**, **la foto**).
target_language_example: Ho cercato di nascondere la verità.
native_language_example: I tried to hide the truth.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "cercare di" + infinitive (e.g., "cerchi di ricordare" = "try to remember"). "Cerchi" is the formal (Lei) form, often used to give polite instructions or advice. In informal speech to a friend you’d more often say "cerca di...".
target_language_example: Cerchi di arrivare in orario, per favore.
native_language_example: Please try to arrive on time.

additional_notes: From the verb *cercare* (“to try/attempt” in this structure) + *di* + infinitive: **Cerco di + verb**. Used to talk about making an effort or attempting something (sometimes repeatedly or over time). Other persons: *cerchi di* (you try), *cerca di* (he/she tries), *cerchiamo di* (we try), *cercate di* (you all try), *cercano di* (they try).
target_language_example: Cerco di parlare italiano ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I try to speak Italian every day.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of "cercare di" + infinitive, common in written stories and narration. In everyday speech, you’ll often hear the passato prossimo instead: "ha cercato di" = “(he/she) tried to”.
target_language_example: Cercò di aprire la porta, ma era bloccata.
native_language_example: He tried to open the door, but it was stuck.

additional_notes: Used before a noun for an emotion or feeling (e.g., ansia, confusione, preoccupazione, rabbia). "Cercò" is the passato remoto (common in narratives and in some regions); in everyday speech you often hear "ha cercato di nascondere la sua".
target_language_example: Cercò di nascondere la sua paura, ma tremava.
native_language_example: He/She tried to hide his/her fear, but was trembling.

additional_notes: Used to refer to particular things without naming them, often because they’re vague, sensitive, or obvious from context. Common in phrases like “su certe cose” (about certain things) and “per certe cose” (for certain things).
target_language_example: Con te posso parlare di tutto, ma non di certe cose.
native_language_example: I can talk to you about anything, but not about certain things.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the preposition **a**: **a un certo punto** = “at a certain point / at some point,” especially when telling a story or describing how a situation changed. You can also hear it in discussions to mean “beyond a certain point” (e.g., **oltre un certo punto**).
target_language_example: A un certo punto ho capito che era meglio andare via.
native_language_example: At some point I realized it was better to leave.

meaning: a certain sense; in a way.
additional_notes: Most often used in the full expression "in un certo senso" (= "in a certain sense / in a way") to soften or qualify what you’re saying. It introduces a partial agreement or a limited point of view: you mean it’s true, but not completely or not in every respect.
target_language_example: In un certo senso, hai ragione, ma non del tutto.
native_language_example: In a way, you’re right, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm or emphasize what you’re saying, often in answer to a question or to agree/insist: "Certo che lo siamo" = "Of course we are." It’s usually followed by a full clause with "che" (che + subject + verb). Similar in tone to "ma certo" (of course!).
target_language_example: Certo che vengo con te!
native_language_example: Of course I’m coming with you!

additional_notes: Used to strongly confirm something. "Certo che" introduces a clause meaning “of course/sure,” and "lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” (referring to something already known from context). Often said with emphasis, sometimes as a strong reply.
target_language_example: Certo che lo capisco.
native_language_example: Of course I understand it.

additional_notes: Used mainly in questions to ask if there is anything more (another option, more information, etc.). Often followed by a verb: "Che altro sai?" (= What else do you know?). It can also be used more generally to mean "what other (thing/things)", but the natural English translation is usually "what else".
target_language_example: Che altro possiamo fare adesso?
native_language_example: What else can we do now?

meaning: “What does it look like?” / “What does it look like (right now)?”
additional_notes: Used to ask about the appearance of something or someone. Often followed by the subject: “Che aspetto ha la città?” = “What does the city look like?” You can also say it on its own (“Che aspetto ha?”) when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Che aspetto ha questa stanza dopo i lavori?
native_language_example: What does this room look like after the work?

meaning: 'what a nice/beautiful…!' (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Used as an exclamation to praise or admire something. It’s the shortened form of "che bello" before a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant: "che bel fiore!". For masculine nouns starting with a vowel, use "che bell'..." (e.g., "che bell'idea!"); for feminine nouns, use "che bella" (e.g., "che bella casa!").
target_language_example: Che bel posto!
native_language_example: What a nice place!

additional_notes: An exclamation used to react with admiration or enthusiasm, often before a feminine singular noun: Che bella sorpresa! Che bella fotografia! With masculine nouns: che bello; plural: che belli/che belle. Often used with Guarda… / Senti… / Cavolo… for emphasis.
target_language_example: Che bella giornata oggi!
native_language_example: What a beautiful day today!

additional_notes: An exclamation used to show pleasure, excitement, or approval about a situation (“How nice!” / “That’s great!”). Often followed by a clause with che: “Che bello che sei qui” = “How nice that you’re here.” You can also use it alone as a reaction: “Che bello!”
target_language_example: Che bello! Domani non lavoro.
native_language_example: Great! I’m not working tomorrow.

meaning: "what the heck" / "what the hell" (mild rude emphasis).
additional_notes: Used to show annoyance, surprise, or impatience, especially in questions (Che cavolo fai? = What the heck are you doing?). It can also be exclaimed on its own (Che cavolo!) or said to someone like a reproach (Chris, che cavolo.). Informal; a softer alternative to stronger swear versions like "che cazzo".
target_language_example: Ma che cavolo stai facendo?
native_language_example: What the heck are you doing?

additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive. Used to express anger, shock, or strong frustration, usually in questions. Common patterns: “Che cazzo hai fatto?” = “What the fuck did you do?” and “Che cazzo di + noun …?” to mean “What the fuck kind of …?” (e.g., “Che cazzo di idea è?”). Avoid in polite situations; use milder options like “che diavolo…?” or “che cavolo…?” if you want to be less offensive.
target_language_example: Che cazzo stai dicendo?
native_language_example: What the fuck are you saying?

meaning: "what the fuck…" / a very rude way to say "what a…" or "what…" (to complain or show anger).
additional_notes: A vulgar intensifier used before a noun ("che cazzo di caldo" = "what fucking heat") or in questions ("che cazzo di problemi hai?" = "what the fuck is your problem?/what fucking problems do you have?"). Very offensive; avoid in polite situations. Often sounds like "che cazzo" + "di" + noun.
target_language_example: Che cazzo di film era quello?
native_language_example: What the fuck kind of movie was that?

meaning: “What the fuck are you doing?” (very vulgar).
additional_notes: A very strong, aggressive way to ask what someone is doing, often showing anger, shock, or impatience. It’s the profanity version of “Che fai?” / “Che cosa fai?” Avoid in polite situations; it can easily start a fight. You may also hear similar forms like “Che cazzo stai facendo?” (same meaning).
target_language_example: Ehi, che cazzo fai? Lascia stare la mia roba!
native_language_example: Hey, what the fuck are you doing? Leave my stuff alone!

meaning: “What the hell are you doing?” (very rude/vulgar).
additional_notes: Used to angrily or incredulously question what someone is doing. Literally “what dick are you doing,” but it functions like “what the fuck/what the hell are you doing?” It’s highly offensive and not appropriate in polite conversation; use "Che stai facendo?" or "Cosa stai facendo?" for a neutral version.
target_language_example: Ehi, che cazzo stai facendo con il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Hey, what the hell are you doing with my phone?

meaning: "What the fuck is happening?" / "What the hell is going on?"
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar (uses *cazzo*). Used to show shock, anger, or strong confusion. Common patterns: **Che cazzo succede qui?** (…here?), **Che cazzo succede a tutti?** (…to everyone?). Safer alternatives: **Che succede?** / **Che sta succedendo?** / **Che diavolo succede?** (less vulgar).
target_language_example: Che cazzo succede qui? Ho sentito un botto!
native_language_example: What the fuck is happening here? I heard a bang!

additional_notes: Used to ask about the color of something (Che colore ha...?). You can also use it to ask someone’s preference (Che colore preferisci?/Che colore le piace? more formal). With an exclamation, it can express a reaction to a color: Che colore terribile!
target_language_example: Scusi, che colore preferisce per la maglietta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what color do you prefer for the T-shirt?

additional_notes: Used to ask the color of something. Often followed by the thing you’re asking about: "Che colore è la macchina?" or "Che colore è questa maglietta?" You can also hear "Di che colore è...?" (same meaning).
target_language_example: Che colore è questa borsa?
native_language_example: What color is this bag?

additional_notes: Used to ask the color of something masculine singular: **Che colore è il + noun?** (e.g., *il libro, il telefono*). Change the article to match the noun: **Che colore è la…?** (feminine singular), **Che colore sono i…?** (masculine plural), **Che colore sono le…?** (feminine plural). Often followed by an object: *Che colore è il tuo zaino?*
target_language_example: Che colore è il tuo zaino?
native_language_example: What color is your backpack?

additional_notes: Common question phrase used to ask for information about a thing, action, or situation. It is often interchangeable with cosa or che, and can sound a bit more full or neutral than just che on its own.
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi fare domani?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tomorrow?

meaning: "what ... with it/there" (often: "what can I/you do about it?").
additional_notes: This is the start of a question: **che cosa** = “what,” and **ci** is a pronoun that often means “there” or “with/about it/them” depending on the verb. Very common in patterns like **Che cosa ci posso fare?** (“What can I do about it?”) and **Che cosa ci vedi in lui?** (“What do you see in him?”). The full meaning depends on the verb that follows (e.g., *succedere* = happen, *fare* = do, *vedere* = see).
target_language_example: Ho sbagliato, ma che cosa ci posso fare adesso?
native_language_example: I made a mistake, but what can I do about it now?

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or guidance. "Dovrei" is the conditional of "dovere" ("must/to have to") and often sounds polite or uncertain, like asking what the best course of action is. You can add details after it: "Che cosa dovrei fare riguardo a..." ("What should I do about...") or "Che cosa dovrei fare senza..." ("What would I do without...").
target_language_example: Non so che cosa dovrei fare adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t know what I should do now.

additional_notes: Used to ask for advice or the best course of action. Literally “what thing should we do”; *dovremmo* is the conditional of *dovere* (“must/should”), making it sound like “should we…?” It can take extra details: *Che cosa dovremmo fare oggi/qui/con loro/riguardo a…?*
target_language_example: Non abbiamo molto tempo: che cosa dovremmo fare?
native_language_example: We don’t have much time: what should we do?

additional_notes: Question used to ask either (1) what someone does in general (often their job: "Che cosa fa sua moglie?" = "What does your wife do?") or (2) what someone is doing right now, especially with a time word like "adesso" ("Che cosa fa tua sorella adesso?" = "What is your sister doing now?"). Often shortened in speech to "Cosa fa...?" or "Che fa...?".
target_language_example: Scusi, che cosa fa lei nella vita?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you do for a living?

meaning: “what are you doing?” / “what do you do?”
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing (right now or at a certain time: Che cosa fai domenica?/ora?) or what they do in general (work/role), often with context (Che cosa fai in Giappone? = what are you doing there?). In the exclamation “Che cosa fai!”, it can sound like a reprimand or surprise (“What are you doing!?”). Also commonly said as “Cosa fai?” or “Che fai?” (more casual).
target_language_example: Che cosa fai stasera?
native_language_example: What are you doing tonight?

additional_notes: A question using the future tense (farete = “you all will do”). Used when speaking to more than one person (voi). Often followed by a time word like oggi (“today”) or domani (“tomorrow”). In everyday speech you may also hear: Cosa farete? or Che farete?
target_language_example: Allora, che cosa farete dopo la cena?
native_language_example: So, what will you do after dinner?

meaning: 'What are you (plural) doing?' / 'What do you (plural) do?'.
additional_notes: Uses the plural 'voi' form: fate (from fare). It can ask about what someone is doing right now or what they plan to do, depending on context (e.g., with a time like questa estate). Often shortened in speech to 'Che fate?' or 'Cosa fate?'.
target_language_example: Che cosa fate dopo la lezione?
native_language_example: What are you (all) doing after the lesson?

meaning: "what ... to him?" / "what ... to him/them?" (in a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask a question where the action is directed to someone via the indirect object pronoun gli (“to him”; also often used colloquially for “to them”). It commonly appears before verbs like dire (to say/tell), comprare (to buy), succedere (to happen): Che cosa gli hai detto? = “What did you tell him?”
target_language_example: Che cosa gli vuoi dire?
native_language_example: What do you want to tell him?

meaning: "what have you ...?" (used to ask what someone has done).
additional_notes: Used to start a question, usually followed by a past participle in the passato prossimo: "Che cosa hai fatto/detto/visto?". In everyday speech it’s often shortened to "Che hai...?" or you may hear "Cosa hai...?".
target_language_example: Che cosa hai fatto ieri sera?
native_language_example: What did you do last night?

meaning: "What did you do?" / "What have you done?"
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (hai fatto). It can be a neutral question about someone’s actions (often with a time expression: ieri, ieri sera), or it can express surprise/shock or a reproach depending on tone (e.g., “Mio Dio, che cosa hai fatto?”). You can also add what it’s about: “Che cosa hai fatto al dito?” (“What did you do to your finger?”).
target_language_example: Che cosa hai fatto oggi dopo il lavoro?
native_language_example: What did you do today after work?

additional_notes: Used to ask what you did (often with surprise, worry, or defensiveness). You can add details like "di male" (“wrong/bad”) or "io" for emphasis: "E che cosa ho fatto io?" = “And what did I do (then)?”
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa ho fatto?
native_language_example: Sorry, what have I done?

additional_notes: Used to ask “what” while referring to someone with the indirect object pronoun **le** (“to you” in the polite **Lei** form, or “to her”). It often appears in questions like **Che cosa le piace…?** (“What do you like…?”), **Che cosa le hanno rubato?** (“What did they steal from her/you?”), or **Che cosa le devo?** (“What do I owe you?”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, che cosa le serve?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you need?

meaning: “what … me/to me …?” (used to start a question).
additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening/what someone is doing or saying to you, or what you will receive/what is left for you. “Che cosa” = “what,” and “mi” is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to me” (or sometimes “me,” depending on the verb). It’s normally followed by a verb: “Che cosa mi dici?” (What are you telling me?).
target_language_example: Che cosa mi consigli di fare?
native_language_example: What do you recommend that I do?

meaning: "what ... of it/them/him/her"; often in "Che cosa ne sarà di..." = "what will become of..."
additional_notes:
"Ne" is a pronoun meaning “of it/of them/about it,” referring to something already known from context. 
- With the future of "essere" (sarà/saranno) + "di" + person/thing: "Che cosa ne sarà di..." = “What will become of...?” (expresses worry/uncertainty).
- With "fare": "Che cosa ne hai fatto?" = “What did you do with it/them?”
The "di" part can refer to a person (di lui/lei/me/te/noi/voi) or a thing/place (del Giappone).
target_language_example: Che cosa ne sarà di noi senza questo lavoro?
native_language_example: What will become of us without this job?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. Very common in polite conversation, especially with Lei (e.g., Che cosa ne pensa? = What do you think?). The pronoun “ne” refers back to something already mentioned, often introduced with di/del/della/di quel…: Che cosa ne pensa di…? = What do you think about…?
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensa di questa proposta?
native_language_example: What do you think about this proposal?

meaning: "What do you think (about it)?" (asking a group).
additional_notes: Used to ask for people’s opinions. It’s the plural form (you all): pensate = “you (plural) think.” The pronoun “ne” refers to what you’re talking about (“about it/of it”), often followed by “di + [topic]”: Che cosa ne pensate di questo piano? You can also say “Cosa ne pensate…?” (more common in speech) or “Che ne pensate…?” (shorter).
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensate di questo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you think about this restaurant?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s opinion. Often followed by "di/del/della..." to specify the topic: "Che cosa ne pensi del film?". The "ne" refers back to something already mentioned (roughly “about it/about that”). You can also say "Che ne pensi?" (more common) or "Cosa ne pensi?" (more informal).
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensi di questa idea?
native_language_example: What do you think of this idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone’s opinion about something. It’s often followed by a noun: “Che cosa ne pensi del film?” (“What do you think of the movie?”). The little word “ne” refers back to “about it/of it” (the topic you’re asking about). In speech, you’ll also hear “Cosa ne pensi del …?” or “Che ne pensi del …?”
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensi del mio piano?
native_language_example: What do you think of my plan?

additional_notes: Used to ask what action is possible or what you should do next. Common in offers of help (Che cosa posso fare per te? = “What can I do for you?”) and when you’re unsure what to do (Non so che cosa posso fare = “I don’t know what I can do”). Often interchangeable with “Cosa posso fare?” and more formal than “Che posso fare?”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, che cosa posso fare per aiutarti?
native_language_example: I’m sorry—what can I do to help you?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the identity/meaning of things in the plural: Che cosa sono questi numeri? = “What are these numbers?” It’s the plural form of “che cosa è?” (what is it?). Often followed by a noun with a demonstrative (questi/queste/quelli/quelle). In casual speech it may be shortened to “cosa sono…?” or “che sono…?”.
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa sono questi simboli?
native_language_example: Sorry, what are these symbols?

additional_notes: Interrogative phrase using the present continuous structure stare + gerund: sta facendo = "is doing." It refers to a third-person singular subject (lui/lei). Variants by person: che cosa stai facendo? (you), che cosa sto facendo? (I), che cosa stanno facendo? (they). Often used with context like lì (there), con... (with...), or in... (in/at...) to specify what/where.
target_language_example: Che cosa sta facendo lì?
native_language_example: What is he/she doing there?

meaning: "what are you ... (doing)?" (introduces a question with the present continuous).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now, followed by the verb "stare" + a gerund: "Che cosa stai + verb-ando/-endo?" (e.g., aspettando, bevendo, leggendo). You can also hear "Cosa stai..." (more common and slightly more informal) or "Che cosa stai facendo?" = "What are you doing?".
target_language_example: Che cosa stai cercando?
native_language_example: What are you looking for?

additional_notes: A common way to ask what someone is doing right now. It uses the present progressive: “stai” (you are) + “facendo” (doing). Often said simply as “Che stai facendo?” or “Cosa stai facendo?”. In strong/emotional contexts it can sound like “What on earth are you doing?”.
target_language_example: Ehi, che cosa stai facendo con il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Hey, what are you doing with my phone?

meaning: "what are they" (starting a question in the present continuous).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone is doing right now. It’s typically followed by a present participle (gerundio), e.g., "che cosa stanno facendo/ dicendo/ scrivendo?" You can also use "cosa stanno..." (more common in speech) or "che cosa state..." for "what are you (plural) ...".
target_language_example: Che cosa stanno facendo i bambini?
native_language_example: What are the kids doing?

additional_notes: Used to ask what a group of people is doing/saying/pointing at/etc. It’s typically followed by a gerund (stare + -ando/-endo) to form the present continuous: “Che cosa state facendo?” = “What are you doing (you all)?” The verb “state” is 2nd person plural (voi) of “stare.”
target_language_example: Che cosa state facendo qui?
native_language_example: What are you all doing here?

additional_notes: Used to ask what is happening now or what will happen next. Often followed by a time word (adesso = now) or a situation (e.g., dopo la morte = after death). You can also say "Che succede?" (more casual) or "Cosa succede?".
target_language_example: Che cosa succede se perdiamo il treno?
native_language_example: What happens if we miss the train?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the result or consequence of a possible situation. Often followed by a verb in the present tense (e.g., “se la polizia ci chiede…”), even when talking about the future. You can also hear the shorter “cosa succede se…”.
target_language_example: Che cosa succede se perdiamo l’ultimo treno?
native_language_example: What happens if we miss the last train?

meaning: "what ... (to) you?" (used to start a question addressed to 'you').
additional_notes: Used at the beginning of questions. "Che cosa" means "what" and "ti" is the unstressed pronoun for "to you" (or sometimes "you" with certain verbs). It often appears with verbs like dire (Che cosa ti ha detto...? = What did he/she tell you?), rubare (Che cosa ti hanno rubato? = What did they steal from you?), venire in mente (Che cosa ti viene in mente? = What comes to mind for you?). In everyday speech you may also hear "Cosa ti..." instead of "Che cosa ti...".
target_language_example: Che cosa ti serve per la ricetta?
native_language_example: What do you need for the recipe?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone what they like (in general) or what they like about a specific person/thing. Often followed by “di + [noun/pronoun]” to mean “What do you like about…?” (e.g., Che cosa ti piace di me?). You can also hear the shorter version “Cosa ti piace?” in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Che cosa ti piace di questo ristorante?
native_language_example: What do you like about this restaurant?

additional_notes: "Che cosa" means "what" and "vi" is "you" in the sense of "to you" or "you all" (also used as a formal/polite "you"). It’s used to start questions like: "Che cosa vi motiva?" (What motivates you?), "Che cosa vi è successo?" (What happened to you?), or "Che cosa vi consiglio?" (What do I recommend to you?).
target_language_example: Che cosa vi serve per oggi?
native_language_example: What do you need for today?

meaning: “what do you want?” / “what would you like?”
additional_notes: Direct question using che cosa (“what”) + vuoi (2nd-person singular of volere, “to want”). Common in everyday speech; you can soften it with “Scusa, che cosa vuoi?” or “Che cosa vuoi sapere?” (“What do you want to know?”). Similar to “cosa vuoi?” (more casual) and “che cosa desideri?” (more formal).
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa vuoi ordinare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what would you like to order?

additional_notes: A common question asking about someone’s plans or intentions. Often shortened to “Cosa vuoi fare?” You can add time/context words: “adesso” (now), “stasera” (tonight), “da grande” (when you grow up). You can also add “E tu…?” to mean “And you, what do you want to do?”
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi fare dopo pranzo?
native_language_example: What do you want to do after lunch?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the meaning of a word, phrase, symbol, or message. Often followed by the thing you’re asking about (e.g., Che cosa vuol dire questa parola?). You can add “esattamente” (exactly) for emphasis or “in + language” (e.g., in arabo). With formal “Lei,” it becomes “Che cosa vuol dire?” or “Sa che cosa vuol dire?” (= “Do you know what it means?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, che cosa vuol dire “scontrino”?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what does “receipt” mean?

additional_notes: Used to ask what something is or what’s going on. In everyday Italian it’s often contracted to **che cos’è** (or **cos’è**), but **che cosa è** is also correct and a bit more explicit/formal.
target_language_example: Che cosa è questa storia?
native_language_example: What’s this all about? / What’s this story?

additional_notes: Used to ask what happened in a situation (often when something unexpected occurred). In speech it’s often shortened to “Che è successo?” or “Cos’è successo?”. Note: Italian “successo” means “happened” here (not “success” in English).
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa è successo qui?
native_language_example: Sorry, what happened here?

additional_notes: Common way to ask “what?” in questions. Often interchangeable with just “cosa?” (more casual) or “che?” (very common in speech). It can also introduce an embedded question after verbs like sapere/capire/dire: “Sai che cosa voglio” = “You know what I want.”
target_language_example: Che cosa vuoi fare stasera?
native_language_example: What do you want to do tonight?

meaning: “what do you want?” (to more than one person, or formal “you”).
additional_notes: Used to ask what someone wants/needs. With **da** + person: “What do you want from her/him?” With **di più**: “What more do you want?” With **dopo**: “What do you want next/afterwards?” Often sounds direct; you can soften it with *Scusate, che cosa volete?* or *Che cosa desiderate?*.
target_language_example: Scusate, che cosa volete ordinare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what would you like to order?

additional_notes: Direct question using "che cosa" (“what”) + "vuoi" (2nd person singular of volere, “you want”). Often used alone (“Che cosa vuoi?”) or followed by an infinitive to ask what someone wants to do/buy (“Che cosa vuoi comprare?”). With "da" it asks what someone wants from a person (“Che cosa vuoi da lui/da me?”). Can also appear inside a longer sentence: “Non so che cosa vuoi…” = “I don’t know what you want…”.
target_language_example: Scusa, che cosa vuoi che faccia adesso?
native_language_example: Sorry, what do you want me to do now?

additional_notes: Common question used to ask what someone wants/needs. "vuole" is the formal (Lei) form, so it can mean "what do you want?" when speaking politely to one person. You’ll often see it followed by "da" + someone to mean "what do you want from ...?" (e.g., "Che cosa vuole da lei?"). Less formal: "Che cosa vuoi?" / "Cosa vuoi?"
target_language_example: Scusi, che cosa vuole da me?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what do you want from me?

additional_notes: Used to show strong surprise, annoyance, or disbelief, often in questions: Che diavolo dici? (“What the hell are you saying?”). It’s informal and can sound rude, so use with friends or when you want to emphasize frustration. You can also hear it with di (“Di che diavolo…?” = “What the hell… about/are you talking about?”).
target_language_example: Che diavolo succede qui?
native_language_example: What the hell is going on here?

meaning: “What difference does it make?” / “What does it matter?”
additional_notes: Used to say that something isn’t important or won’t change the outcome. Often said as a rhetorical question, sometimes with emphasis like “Ma…” (But…) or “Ormai…” (At this point…). You can also use it about someone else: “Per te/lei che differenza fa?” = “What difference does it make to you/her?”
target_language_example: Scegli tu: per me che differenza fa?
native_language_example: You choose: what difference does it make to me?

additional_notes: Used to ask about someone or something that has disappeared, is missing, or is no longer around/available. It often implies surprise or concern. You can use it with a name or noun (Che fine ha fatto Blue? / Che fine ha fatto il resto dei soldi?) or on its own (Che fine ha fatto?). Literally it’s “what end did it make?”, but it’s said like “what became of…?”
target_language_example: Che fine ha fatto il mio telefono? L’avevo qui un minuto fa.
native_language_example: What happened to my phone? I had it here a minute ago.

meaning: "What happened to...?/Where did ... go?" (referring to a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to ask what became of someone/something, often implying it has disappeared, been forgotten, or changed. It’s commonly used as: “Che fine ha fatto X?” (“What happened to X?”). The article changes with the noun: “che fine ha fatto il libro?”, “che fine ha fatto la chiave?”, “che fine hanno fatto le chiavi?” (plural uses “hanno fatto”).
target_language_example: Scusa, che fine ha fatto il mio zaino?
native_language_example: Sorry, what happened to my backpack?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the type/category of something (often followed by a noun). In questions it can stand alone ("Che genere di?") or be followed by the thing you’re asking about ("Che genere di domande?"). Note: "genere" can also mean "genre" (books/movies), but in this expression it usually means "kind/type."
target_language_example: Che genere di musica ti piace?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you like?

meaning: 'which search engine' (asking what search engine someone uses).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which search engine someone uses. Often followed by a verb like "usate" (do you use) or the more formal "utilizzate" (do you use). Adding "voi" can emphasize the subject (“you all/you”) or make the question sound a bit more direct.
target_language_example: Scusa, che motore di ricerca usi di solito?
native_language_example: Sorry, which search engine do you usually use?

additional_notes: Used to ask about the time. Often followed by a form of "essere": "Che ora è?" (What time is it?), "Che ora era?" (What time was it?), "Che ora sarà?" (What time will it be?). You’ll also see it in longer questions like "Da che ora a che ora...?" (From what time to what time…?/What are the hours…?) and "Che ora ti va bene?" (What time works for you?).
target_language_example: Scusa, che ora è adesso?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it now?

meaning: “what time does it close?” / “what time it closes”.
additional_notes: Used to ask about a store/place’s closing time. Very often you’ll hear it as a full question with **A**: **A che ora chiude?** (“What time does it close?”). The subject is often implied (e.g., the shop/restaurant). You can also specify it: **A che ora chiude il supermercato?**
target_language_example: Scusi, a che ora chiude oggi?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time does it close today?

additional_notes: Usually used as part of a full question with a noun after it, often with “A” at the start: “A che ora chiude quel negozio/quel bar/quel museo?” Here “quel” = “that” (masculine singular), and it must agree with the noun that follows. For feminine nouns you use “quella” (e.g., “quella farmacia”).
target_language_example: A che ora chiude quel supermercato?
native_language_example: What time does that supermarket close?

additional_notes: Usually used as a question: **A che ora comincia?** (More natural than *Che ora comincia?*). You can add what is starting: **A che ora comincia il film / la lezione / la partita?**. The verb **cominciare** means “to start / to begin.”
target_language_example: A che ora comincia il film?
native_language_example: What time does the movie start?

meaning: 'what time does the … start' (often with A: 'A che ora inizia la …?').
additional_notes: Used to ask about the start time of an event with a feminine singular noun after it (la lezione, la riunione, la partita, la conferenza, etc.). In natural Italian, you usually say: “A che ora inizia la …?” Without “a” it can sound incomplete or less natural in a direct question.
target_language_example: A che ora inizia la lezione?
native_language_example: What time does the lesson start?

meaning: "what time does the … leave" (asking a departure time).
additional_notes: Used in questions about schedules, especially with a masculine singular noun introduced by **il** (e.g., **il treno**, **il bus**, **il volo**). Very commonly you’ll hear it with **A** at the beginning: **A che ora parte il treno?** = “What time does the train leave?”
target_language_example: A che ora parte il treno per Roma?
native_language_example: What time does the train for Rome leave?

additional_notes: Common question to ask for the current time. Often used on its own (Che ora è?) or with a location/time reference: Che ora è a Londra? You can make it more polite with “Mi scusi, che ora è?” or more emphatic/surprised with “Ma che ora è?”
target_language_example: Scusa, che ora è?
native_language_example: Sorry, what time is it?

meaning: 'What time is the…?' (asking the time of a specific event/thing).
additional_notes: Used when you’re about to name a masculine singular noun/event: "Che ora è il concerto?" = What time is the concert? For the general question "What time is it?", say "Che ora è?". With feminine singular nouns, use "Che ora è la…?".
target_language_example: Che ora è il concerto?
native_language_example: What time is the concert?

additional_notes: Common way to ask the current time. You can add "adesso" (now) for emphasis: "Che ore sono adesso?" For a more polite/formal request, use "Mi scusi, che ore sono?" or "Può dirmi che ore sono?" In indirect speech it stays the same: "Mi deve dire che ore sono" (You have to tell me what time it is).
target_language_example: Scusi, che ore sono?
native_language_example: Excuse me, what time is it?

additional_notes: Very informal and mildly vulgar (literally refers to "balls"). Used as an exclamation to show annoyance, impatience, or boredom—similar to "Ugh" or "This sucks". You can say it by itself ("Che palle!") or with a clause ("Che palle che..." / "...se no sai che palle"). Avoid in polite/formal situations.
target_language_example: Che palle, dobbiamo rifare tutto da capo.
native_language_example: What a pain, we have to redo everything from scratch.

additional_notes: Used in questions to ask where within a place something/someone is from or located (often with prepositions: di che parte... = 'from which part...', in che parte... = 'in which part...'). It can also mean 'which side' in a debate/team sense, or 'what role/part do I play?' (e.g., in a game, group, or activity).
target_language_example: Di che parte d'Italia sei?
native_language_example: Which part of Italy are you from?

meaning: "what kind/sort of" (often expressing criticism or surprise).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to ask or exclaim about the type of something: "Che razza di madre..." = "What kind of mother...". Frequently has a negative, judgmental tone in exclamations (similar to "what the hell kind of..."). In questions it can be more neutral, depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Che razza di posto è questo?
native_language_example: What kind of place is this?

meaning: 'What is that?' / 'What kind of thing is that?' (often with surprise, disapproval, or amazement).
additional_notes: Uses *roba* (“stuff/thing(s)”) in a very general way to comment on something you see or don’t understand. Tone depends on context: it can sound critical (*Che roba ti sei messa addosso?* = “What are you wearing?”) or impressed (*Che roba!* = “Wow, that’s something!”). Common in spoken Italian and usually informal; in polite/formal situations you can use *Che cos’è?* or *Che cosa è?*.
target_language_example: Che roba hai comprato al mercato?
native_language_example: What on earth did you buy at the market?

meaning: "What’s the point?" / "What sense does it make?"
additional_notes: Used to question the meaning, purpose, or logic of something. Often rhetorical, showing confusion, criticism, or frustration. It can be followed by a noun or infinitive (e.g., “Che senso ha vivere così?”) or used alone (“Che senso ha?”).
target_language_example: Che senso ha discutere ancora, se non vogliamo ascoltarci?
native_language_example: What’s the point of arguing again if we don’t want to listen to each other?

additional_notes: Used either (1) as a question about someone/something’s type or category: “Che tipo (di musica) ti piace?” = “What kind (of music) do you like?”; you may also see it with “di”: “Di che tipo?” = “What kind?” or “Che tipo è?” = “What kind of person is he?” (2) as a comment/exclamation about a person, often with a judgmental tone: “Che tipo strano!” = “What a strange/weird guy!”
target_language_example: Quel nuovo collega, che tipo è?
native_language_example: That new coworker—what kind of person is he?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a category or description of something. It’s typically followed by a noun: "Che tipo di + nome?" (e.g., "Che tipo di musica ti piace?"). In casual speech you may also hear "Che tipo" without "di" when the noun is understood.
target_language_example: Che tipo di musica ascolti di solito?
native_language_example: What kind of music do you usually listen to?
