native_language_example: Could you hand me the pencil, please?

meaning: to resign (to hand in your resignation).
additional_notes: Used when someone quits a job or an official position. Commonly used with a subject + "dare" + "le dimissioni" (often in the infinitive after verbs like "decidere di" or modals like "dovere/potere"). Note: "dimissioni" may look like English "dismissal," but it means resigning (quitting), not being fired.
target_language_example: Dovrei dare le dimissioni perché ho trovato un altro lavoro.
native_language_example: I should resign because I found another job.

meaning: to assume; to take/consider (someone or something) as.
additional_notes: Used with a past participle, adjective, or noun to say you consider something to be true or someone to be in a certain state (often without being sure). Common patterns: "dare per scontato" (to take for granted), "dare per perso" (to consider lost), "dare per morto" (to assume dead). Usually followed by the thing/state you assume: "dare per + participle/adjective/noun".
target_language_example: Non dare per scontato che lui venga alla festa.
native_language_example: Don’t take it for granted that he’ll come to the party.

meaning: to take for granted; to assume (as obvious/true).
additional_notes: Used when you assume something is certain or obvious without checking. Often followed by a clause with "che": "Do per scontato che..." (I assume that...). Can sound a bit critical if the assumption was wrong.
target_language_example: Non dare per scontato che io sia libero stasera.
native_language_example: Don’t take it for granted that I’m free tonight.

meaning: to listen to; to pay attention to; to heed (someone/something).
additional_notes: Usually used with "a": "dare retta a qualcuno/qualcosa". Common in everyday speech, often in the negative or as an imperative: "Non dare retta" = "Don’t listen/pay attention". Similar to "ascoltare" but with the idea of taking someone’s words seriously or following advice.
target_language_example: Non dare retta a quello che dice: non è vero.
native_language_example: Don’t listen to what he says: it’s not true.

meaning: to get on someone’s nerves; to annoy someone.
additional_notes: Commonly used with an indirect object pronoun: "Mi dai sui nervi" (You’re getting on my nerves), "Gli dai sui nervi" (You annoy him). Colloquial and can sound blunt or irritated depending on tone.
target_language_example: Il rumore del trapano mi dà sui nervi: smettila, per favore.
native_language_example: The sound of the drill gets on my nerves: please stop.

additional_notes: dare means "to give," and un is the masculine singular article "a/an." Use it before a masculine singular noun: dare un nome = "give a name." In many common expressions, English may use a different verb, depending on the noun. With feminine nouns, use dare una instead, as in dare una mano = "lend a hand / help."
target_language_example: Ti posso dare un consiglio?
native_language_example: Can I give you a piece of advice?

meaning: to give a hit/blow; to knock (once).
additional_notes: Literally “to give a blow.” Used for a single strike or knock: dare un colpo alla porta (knock on the door), dare un colpo a qualcuno/qualcosa (hit someone/something). Often expands with “di” to specify the type: dare un colpo di telefono (give someone a quick call), dare un colpo d’occhio (take a quick look).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di dare un colpo alla porta, ma nessuno ha risposto.
native_language_example: I decided to knock on the door, but nobody answered.

meaning: to give someone a ride home.
additional_notes: Usato quando offri o chiedi a qualcuno di accompagnarti a casa in macchina (o in generale con un mezzo). Spesso compare con un pronome indiretto: “Mi riesci a dare un passaggio a casa?” / “Gli/le riesci a dare un passaggio a casa?”. Puoi anche dire “dare un passaggio a qualcuno” senza “a casa” se la destinazione è già chiara dal contesto.
target_language_example: Mi riesci a dare un passaggio a casa dopo il lavoro?
native_language_example: Can you give me a ride home after work?

meaning: to give (someone) a ride from (someone’s place).
additional_notes: "Dare un passaggio" means to give someone a lift/ride (usually by car). With "da" + person/pronoun (da lui/da lei/da loro), it indicates who is giving the ride and often implies it starts from that person’s place/where they are. Common pattern: "(Mi) sono fatto/a dare un passaggio da ..." = "I got ... to give me a ride" (male: fatto, female: fatta).
target_language_example: Mi sono fatta dare un passaggio da Marco fino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I got Marco to give me a ride to the station.

meaning: to take a quick look; to have a look.
additional_notes: Common, everyday way to say you’ll look at something briefly (a message, a document, a place, a product, etc.). Often used with "a" or "al/alla": "Dai un'occhiata a questo" (Take a look at this), "Dai un'occhiata al menu" (Have a look at the menu).
target_language_example: Puoi dare un'occhiata a questa email prima che la mandi?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this email before I send it?

meaning: to give a lesson; (also) to teach someone a lesson.
additional_notes: Used literally for teaching (giving a class/lesson): e.g., "dare una lezione di matematica" = "to give a math lesson." It can also be used figuratively to mean "teach someone a lesson" (make someone learn from a mistake or as a punishment), often in contexts of warning or revenge. In the figurative sense, alternatives like "dare una lezione a qualcuno" or "dare una bella lezione" are common.
target_language_example: Se continui a copiare, il professore ti farà dare una lezione.
native_language_example: If you keep cheating, the teacher will have you given a lesson.

meaning: to help; to lend a hand.
additional_notes: Common, everyday way to offer or ask for help. Often used with a + infinitive ("dare una mano a fare...") or with a person ("dare una mano a Tom"). It can sound friendly and cooperative, like "give me a hand" in English.
target_language_example: Mi devi dare una mano a portare queste borse.
native_language_example: You have to give me a hand carrying these bags.

meaning: to give away; to get rid of (by giving/selling).
additional_notes: Used when you stop keeping something and pass it on to someone else (often by donating, handing it over, or sometimes selling it off). Common with objects you no longer need: "dare via dei vestiti", "dare via dei libri". Note: "dare il via" is a different expression meaning "to start / to give the go-ahead".
target_language_example: Voglio dare via i vestiti che non uso più.
native_language_example: I want to give away the clothes I don’t use anymore.

meaning: to give life to; to bring into existence (create/found).
additional_notes: Usually used with "a" + a noun: "dare vita a un progetto/azienda/idea" = create or found it; "dare vita a un personaggio" = bring a character to life. Note that Italian "dare" means "to give" (not English "to dare").
target_language_example: Vogliamo dare vita a un nuovo progetto quest'anno.
native_language_example: We want to bring a new project to life this year.

meaning: 'to give me a hand' (to help me).
additional_notes: Common way to ask for help. It can be made more formal/polite by changing the verb form (e.g., Può darmi una mano...? / Potrebbe darmi una mano...?) and adding “per favore”. You can also specify what you need help with using “con” + noun (e.g., con questa scatola) or “a” + infinitive (e.g., a spostare questo tavolo).
target_language_example: Potresti darmi una mano a portare queste borse, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you give me a hand carrying these bags, please?

additional_notes: Used in official/personal information contexts (forms, ID, registrations, appointments). Typically asked with: "Qual è la sua data di nascita?" (formal) or "Qual è la tua data di nascita?" (informal).
target_language_example: Per aprire il conto, mi serve la sua data di nascita.
native_language_example: To open the account, I need your date of birth.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "dare" + "mi" (to me): "date" (you plural / formal) + "mi" → "datemi". Use it to ask for something, often with "per favore" or "per piacere". It can be addressed to more than one person ("you all") or used as a polite/formal command/request (instead of informal singular "dammi").
target_language_example: Datemi un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore.
native_language_example: Give me a glass of water, please.

additional_notes: From the expression "dare da mangiare a" = "to feed" (literally, "to give [someone] something to eat"). "Dato" is the past participle of "dare" (given), and "al" = "a" + "il" (to the). It’s used when the person/animal being fed is masculine singular (e.g., al cane, al bambino). For feminine singular you’ll see "alla" (alla bambina).
target_language_example: Ho dato da mangiare al cane prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I fed the dog before going out.

meaning: (having) fed the dog; given the dog something to eat.
additional_notes: Built from the very common expression **dare da mangiare a [someone/animal]** = “to feed [someone/animal]”. In the past tense you’ll usually use it with **avere**: **Ho dato da mangiare al cane** = “I fed the dog / I gave the dog something to eat.” You can change **al cane** to **al gatto**, **ai bambini**, etc.
target_language_example: Ho già dato da mangiare al cane.
native_language_example: I’ve already fed the dog.

meaning: 'given the' / 'was given the' (past participle of dare + il).
additional_notes: Used with **dare** (“to give”). In the **passive**, you’ll often see it with **essere**: *fu dato il Premio* / *è stato dato il Premio* = “the prize was given.” In the **active**, it can appear as *ha dato il…* = “(he/she) gave the…”. Note: *si è dato il caso che…* is a fixed expression meaning “it happened that…,” but that’s a separate idiom.
target_language_example: Mi è stato dato il numero di telefono.
native_language_example: I was given the phone number.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has been granted authorization to do something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., “dato il permesso di entrare” = “given permission to enter”). Often appears in passive or formal contexts, similar to “avere il permesso di” (“to have permission to”).
target_language_example: Mi hanno dato il permesso di entrare in anticipo.
native_language_example: They gave me permission to go in early.

meaning: 'given his number' / 'having been given his number'.
additional_notes: "Dato" is the past participle of "dare" (to give). This phrase is often used in writing to introduce a reason or situation (similar to "given that...") and it frequently appears with more detail, e.g. "dato il suo numero di telefono" (given his phone number).
target_language_example: Dato il suo numero di telefono, l’ho chiamato subito.
native_language_example: Given his phone number, I called him right away.

meaning: “(I) gave my word” → “I promised / I gave my word.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb *dare* (“to give”): *dare la mia parola* = to give your word (make a promise). *Dato* is the past participle, used with *avere* (e.g., *ho dato* = “I gave”). Often said to emphasize you will keep a promise.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ti ho dato la mia parola.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I gave you my word.

additional_notes: Past participle of the phrase "dare le dimissioni" (used with avere: "ha/hanno dato le dimissioni"). It means to quit a job or position. Often followed by what you resign from: "ha dato le dimissioni da direttore". More formal alternative: "presentare le dimissioni".
target_language_example: Ho dato le dimissioni perché ho trovato un altro lavoro.
native_language_example: I resigned because I found another job.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason or context before stating a conclusion. It’s typically followed by a clause (often with "è" or "hai" etc.), e.g. "Dato tutto quello che è successo, ...". Slightly formal; in everyday speech you may also hear "visto tutto quello che…" (same idea: "given/seeing all that...").
target_language_example: Dato tutto quello che è successo, è meglio rimandare.
native_language_example: Given everything that happened, it's better to postpone.

additional_notes: Used with forms of *avere* (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) to talk about giving something in the past: *ho dato un regalo* = “I gave / I’ve given a gift.” Very common with objects: *dato un ordine* (gave an order), *dato un pugno* (gave a punch), *dato un nome* (gave a name). Word order: auxiliary + *dato* + *un* + noun.
target_language_example: Ti ho dato un consiglio ieri.
native_language_example: I gave you some advice yesterday.

additional_notes: This is a past participle phrase ("dato" = "given") and is usually used with an auxiliary verb like "ho" (I have) or "avevo" (I had): "Ho dato un regalo natalizio...". In everyday Italian you more often say "(un) regalo di Natale" than "regalo natalizio".
target_language_example: Le ho dato un regalo natalizio.
native_language_example: I gave her a Christmas present.

additional_notes: Past participle of "dare" (to give), used with "avere": "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/hanno dato". It’s followed by a feminine singular noun: "una scelta" (a choice), "una multa" (a fine), "una bicicletta" (a bike), "una (buona/bellissima) idea" (an idea), "una missione" (a mission), "una mancia" (a tip). With an indirect object it often uses "a" or a pronoun: "gli/le ho dato una…" (I gave him/her a…).
target_language_example: Le ho dato una risposta chiara.
native_language_example: I gave her a clear answer.

additional_notes: Introduces the reason or cause for something (similar to "perché" or "siccome"). It’s common at the start of a sentence, but can also appear before a request: "Dato che sei qui…" = “Since you’re here…”.
target_language_example: Dato che non ho contanti, posso pagare con la carta?
native_language_example: Since I don’t have cash, can I pay by card?

additional_notes: Informal, sometimes a bit sharp. It’s the (tu) imperative of the reflexive verb phrase “darsi una calmata” (literally “give yourself a calming”). Used to tell someone to relax/stop overreacting.
target_language_example: Datti una calmata e ascoltami un attimo.
native_language_example: Calm down and listen to me for a moment.

additional_notes: Imperative phrase using the informal 'tu' form (datti = 'give yourself'). Used to push someone to act faster; tone ranges from playful/teasing to impatient. It can easily become rude, especially with insults (e.g., 'stronzo'). You can soften it with 'dai' or 'per favore' (e.g., 'Dai, datti una mossa, per favore').
target_language_example: Dai, datti una mossa: stiamo per perdere il treno!
native_language_example: Come on, hurry up: we’re about to miss the train!

meaning: 'in front of' (before/preceding something in space or time).
additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement in front of someone/something: "sedere davanti a", "passare davanti a". It can also mean "in someone’s presence" (e.g., "davanti a lui" = in front of him / with him watching). Less commonly, it can indicate something that comes earlier in time or order ("davanti a un periodo" = before a period/era). Often pairs with pronouns: davanti a me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro; and with reflexive "davanti a sé" = in front of himself/herself/yourself.
target_language_example: Non parlare di questo davanti ai bambini.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about this in front of the children.

meaning: in front of me; right before my eyes.
additional_notes: Means physically in front of the speaker (position), or figuratively meaning something happens in the speaker’s presence (“in front of me / before my eyes”). Often used with verbs like essere/stare (“to be/stay”), mettere (“to put”), vedere (“to see”), litigare (“to argue”).
target_language_example: Non parlare così davanti a me.
native_language_example: Don’t talk like that in front of me.

meaning: in front of us; ahead of us.
additional_notes: Used for physical position (something is directly in front of your eyes) and for things coming up in the future (work, challenges, time ahead). Often with verbs like vedere (to see), essere (to be), avere (to have): “È davanti a noi”, “Abbiamo molto lavoro davanti a noi”.
target_language_example: C'è una lunga strada davanti a noi.
native_language_example: There’s a long road ahead of us.

meaning: in front of everyone; in public.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens while everyone is watching or can hear. Often implies doing something publicly (sometimes awkward/embarrassing), e.g., "non facciamo una scena davanti a tutti" = “let’s not make a scene in public.”
target_language_example: Non voglio parlarne davanti a tutti.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about it in front of everyone.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or doing something in the presence of someone/something. It’s the combination of davanti a + la → alla, so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., la porta, la clinica, la squadra, la gente). For masculine singular you use davanti al; for plural davanti ai / alle.
target_language_example: Aspettami davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: Wait for me in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize necessity. It’s made of: davvero (“really”) + bisogno di (“need of / need to”). Follow it with a noun ("bisogno di una macchina") or with an infinitive verb ("bisogno di fare..."). Word order can vary: "Ho davvero bisogno di..." is very common.
target_language_example: Ho davvero bisogno di dormire un po'.
native_language_example: I really need to sleep a bit.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is truly the case, introducing a clause with che. Very common with verbs like credere/pensare: "Credi davvero che…?" = "Do you really think that…?" Often you can also hear just "davvero" without "che" when the clause is clear.
target_language_example: Credi davvero che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Do you really think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: "Decise" is the third-person singular past form of decidere: "he/she decided." It is followed by an infinitive. This form is common in written stories and formal narration; in everyday speech, Italians more often say "ha deciso di".
target_language_example: Alla fine, decise di partire subito.
native_language_example: In the end, he/she decided to leave right away.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of the verb phrase “decidere di” + infinitive. It’s common in written storytelling or formal narration; in everyday speech people often use “ha deciso di non andare” (passato prossimo). The subject is implied by context (lui/lei), or can be stated (e.g., “Tom decise…”).
target_language_example: Alla fine, decise di non andare al concerto.
native_language_example: In the end, he decided not to go to the concert.

meaning: "I decided to" (simple past: I made the decision to do something).
additional_notes: "Decisi" is the passato remoto of "decidere" ("to decide"), used especially in written narratives and in some regions to talk about a completed action in the past. It’s followed by "di" + infinitive: "decisi di chiamare" (I decided to call). In everyday speech, many learners will more often hear "ho deciso di" for "I decided to".
target_language_example: Dopo un attimo di esitazione, decisi di andare via.
native_language_example: After a moment of hesitation, I decided to leave.

additional_notes: Used after forms of the verb "decidere" to introduce what someone has chosen to do: "ho deciso di + infinitive" (I decided to + verb), "abbiamo deciso di..." (we decided to...). It normally refers to a deliberate choice or plan.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: I decided to stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "decidere" + "di" + infinitive to say someone has made a decision to do something. It changes with the subject/tense: "ho deciso di andare" (I decided), "hai deciso di andare" (you decided), "ha deciso di andare" (he/she decided). In questions, it often follows "Dove..." (Where...?): "Dove hai deciso di andare?"
target_language_example: Alla fine abbiamo deciso di andare a casa.
native_language_example: In the end we decided to go home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone made a decision to go somewhere. The preposition **in** is often used with **countries, regions, and some places** (e.g., *in Italia, in Toscana, in ufficio*). Depending on context, it can mean “to” (destination) or “into” (entering a place). You’ll often see it after a subject: *Ho deciso di andare in…* / *Abbiamo deciso di andare in…*.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di andare in Italia quest’estate.
native_language_example: I decided to go to Italy this summer.

meaning: "decided not to" (made the decision to not do something).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "decidere" to say someone has chosen not to do an action. Structure: (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) deciso di non + infinitive. Example: "Ho deciso di non andare" = "I decided not to go."
target_language_example: Ho deciso di non uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I decided not to go out tonight.

meaning: "(I/you/he/she/they) decided not to go to (a place)."
additional_notes: Used with a form of "decidere" (e.g., ho/hai/ha deciso) + "di" + infinitive. "Andare in" is used before many places, especially countries/regions (in Italia, in Francia, in Toscana) and some common destinations (in ufficio, in banca). Often followed by a place name or noun.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di non andare in ufficio oggi.
native_language_example: I decided not to go to the office today.

additional_notes: Usually used after the verb "decidere" in the passato prossimo: "Ho deciso di studiare" = "I decided to study" / "I’ve decided to study." You can also say "Sono deciso a studiare" to mean "I’m determined to study" (slightly different structure and meaning).
target_language_example: Ho deciso di studiare italiano ogni sera.
native_language_example: I decided to study Italian every evening.

meaning: “(I/you/he/she/they) decided to sell the …” (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: after **la** you must add a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la macchina*, *la casa*). In full sentences you often see it with **ho/hai/ha/hanno deciso di vendere la…** (“(someone) has/have decided to sell the…”). You can also use **il/lo/i/gli/le** depending on the noun’s gender and number.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di vendere la macchina.
native_language_example: I decided to sell the car.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say a song is for someone (often as a tribute or romantic gesture). The verb is dedicare (io dedico = I dedicate). The person comes after a: a lei (to her, formal), a te (to you, informal singular), a voi (to you, plural).
target_language_example: Dedico questa canzone a mia madre.
native_language_example: I dedicate this song to my mother.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of "dedicare": dedicò = "devoted" (often in stories, biographies, history; in everyday speech you often hear "ha dedicato"). Usually followed by "a" + infinitive (a combattere, ad aiutare) or "a/alla/allo" + noun (alla medicina, allo studio). "Sua" changes with the person: "dedicai la mia vita" (I devoted my life), "ha dedicato la sua vita" (he/she has devoted his/her life).
target_language_example: Marie Curie dedicò la sua vita alla ricerca scientifica.
native_language_example: Marie Curie devoted her life to scientific research.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the partitive/indefinite plural article used before a masculine plural noun starting with a vowel (amici). It often corresponds to English "some" or is simply omitted in English: "Hai degli amici?" = "Do you have any friends?" It’s also used after verbs like "considerare" to mean "as (some) friends": "Considero Tom e Mary degli amici" = "I consider Tom and Mary (to be) friends."
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto degli amici italiani in vacanza.
native_language_example: I met some Italian friends on vacation.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the partitive article (di + gli) used to talk about an indefinite quantity of a plural noun. It’s common with food: "Ho cucinato degli spaghetti" = you made some spaghetti, not a specific portion. You can also say "spaghetti" without "degli" in many contexts, especially when speaking generally.
target_language_example: Vuoi degli spaghetti?
native_language_example: Do you want some spaghetti?

additional_notes: "Degli" is a partitive article meaning “some” (not a specific amount). "Per cena" means “for dinner.” You can swap the food: "del riso per cena" (some rice for dinner), "della pizza per cena" (some pizza for dinner).
target_language_example: Stasera faccio degli spaghetti per cena.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m making some spaghetti for dinner.

meaning: “of the men / of humans”; “of Men” (as a group).
additional_notes: "Degli" is the contraction of "di" + "gli" and means "of the" with a masculine plural noun. "Uomini" is the plural of "uomo". In fantasy or historical contexts, "gli Uomini" can mean “Men” as a people/species (often capitalized in Italian translations), e.g., opposed to elves, dwarves, etc.
target_language_example: È una legge degli Uomini.
native_language_example: It’s a law of Men (humans).

additional_notes: "Degli" is the contraction of "di" + "gli" ("of the"). It’s used to talk about other people in general, often after expressions that take "di" (e.g., "avere paura di..." = "to be afraid of...", "prendersi gioco di..." = "to make fun of...").
target_language_example: Non parlare male degli altri.
native_language_example: Don’t speak badly of others.

meaning: "of the guests" (plural); also used in set phrases like "guest room" and "guest book".
additional_notes: "Degli" is a contraction of "di" + "gli" and often means "of the" with masculine plural nouns. Common collocations: "lista degli ospiti" (guest list), "stanza degli ospiti" (guest room), "libro degli ospiti" (guest book / visitors' book).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere gli asciugamani nella stanza degli ospiti?
native_language_example: Can you put the towels in the guest room?

meaning: “of the men”; also used in comparisons as “than men.”
additional_notes:
It’s the contraction of **di + gli**.
- **degli uomini** = “of the men” (partitive/possessive: *le leggi degli uomini* = “the laws of men/people”).
- In comparisons after **meglio/peggio/più/meno**, **degli uomini** means **“than men”**: *meglio degli uomini* = “better than men.”
Often **uomini** can mean “men” or more generally “human beings/people,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Le regole degli uomini non valgono sempre in natura.
native_language_example: People’s rules don’t always apply in nature.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the plural partitive/indefinite article (di + gli). It’s used before masculine plural nouns like "alberi" to mean an unspecified quantity: "some" or simply plural "a/an" in English. Often omitted in English (e.g., "Ha piantato degli alberi" = "He planted trees"), but common in Italian.
target_language_example: Vorrei piantare degli alberi davanti a casa.
native_language_example: I’d like to plant some trees in front of the house.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the plural partitive/indefinite article (di + gli) used before a masculine plural noun like "amici". It often means "some" (Ho degli amici a Roma = I have some friends in Rome) and can also simply introduce an indefinite plural idea in sentences like "Ha degli amici?" (= Do you have friends?/any friends?). In "farsi degli amici" it means "to make some friends."
target_language_example: Vorrei farmi degli amici qui.
native_language_example: I’d like to make some friends here.

additional_notes: "Degli" is the plural partitive article (di + gli). It’s used with masculine plural nouns like "animali" to talk about an unspecified quantity: "some" in affirmative sentences (Vedo degli animali = I see some animals) and often "any" in questions/negatives (Ha degli animali? = Do you have any animals?). Literally it looks like "of the animals," but in everyday Italian it usually means "some/any."
target_language_example: Nel parco ho visto degli animali molto strani.
native_language_example: In the park I saw some very strange animals.

additional_notes: "Degli" is a partitive article meaning "some" (plural masculine). Here it refers to an unspecified number of mistakes/errors. Often used in questions and statements when you don’t mean specific, known mistakes.
target_language_example: Credo che ci siano degli errori in questo documento.
native_language_example: I think there are some errors in this document.

additional_notes: "Occhiali da sole" means "sunglasses." "Degli" is a partitive article meaning "some" (masculine plural) and is often used when you’re talking about an unspecified pair of sunglasses, especially in questions like "Ti/Le/Vi servono...?" (Do you need...?). In everyday English you usually just say "sunglasses" without "some."
target_language_example: Ho comprato degli occhiali da sole nuovi.
native_language_example: I bought some new sunglasses.

additional_notes: "Degli" is a partitive article (di + gli) used to mean “some” with masculine plural nouns like "spaghetti". It’s used when you don’t specify an exact quantity. In questions it can express surprise/confirmation ("Are these really spaghetti?").
target_language_example: Per cena facciamo degli spaghetti al pomodoro.
native_language_example: For dinner we’re making some spaghetti with tomato sauce.

additional_notes: "Degli" can be (1) a partitive article meaning "some" with plural nouns: "degli studenti stranieri" = "some foreign students"; or (2) the preposition "di" + "gli" meaning "of the": "la lingua degli studenti stranieri" = "the language of the foreign students". Which one it is depends on the sentence.
target_language_example: Nella mia classe ci sono degli studenti stranieri.
native_language_example: In my class there are some foreign students.

meaning: "of his/her" (referring to a masculine plural noun); also used as "than his/her" in comparisons.
additional_notes: Formed by di + i suoi (“of the his/its”). Used before masculine plural nouns: dei suoi cani = “of his dogs”, dei suoi istinti = “of his instincts”. With comparisons (più/meno…): più soldi dei suoi genitori = “more money than his parents”. The feminine plural is delle sue; masculine singular is del suo; feminine singular is della sua.
target_language_example: Parla spesso dei suoi amici di scuola.
native_language_example: He often talks about his school friends.

additional_notes: Used to show possession/relationship with the preposition "di" (“of”). "dei" = "di" + "i" ("of the") and is used before a plural noun. "suoi" agrees with the noun possessed ("figli" = masculine plural), and can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Parla spesso dei suoi figli.
native_language_example: He/She often talks about his/her children.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean an indefinite amount/number: "some" + adjective. It’s the plural form of "un bel" (a nice/beautiful). "Bei" is a special form of "belli" used before many consonants (e.g., bei posti, bei capelli, bei libri).
target_language_example: Abbiamo visto dei bei panorami in montagna.
native_language_example: We saw some beautiful views in the mountains.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine plural noun to mean “some (good) …”. It’s made of the partitive article "dei" (= some) + the adjective "buoni" (= good). Often you’ll see it as "dei buoni" + noun: "dei buoni genitori" (good parents), "dei buoni voti" (good grades), "dei buoni ristoranti" (some good restaurants).
target_language_example: Cerco dei buoni libri in italiano.
native_language_example: I’m looking for some good books in Italian.

additional_notes: "Dei" is the partitive plural (di + i), often used to mean “some” with plural nouns. "Consigli" means “pieces of advice / tips” (Italian treats it as countable, unlike English “advice”). Very common with verbs like chiedere (to ask) or andare/rivolgersi a qualcuno per (to go/turn to someone for) advice.
target_language_example: Posso chiederti dei consigli su questo esercizio?
native_language_example: Can I ask you for some advice on this exercise?

additional_notes: "Dei" is the partitive article (di + i) and often means “some” with a plural noun. In questions it can mean “any”: "Ha dei figli?" = “Do you have children?” Often you can translate it simply as “children” without “some.” With the verb "avere": "avere dei figli" = “to have children.”
target_language_example: Vorrei avere dei figli un giorno.
native_language_example: I’d like to have children one day.

additional_notes: "Dei" is a partitive article meaning “some” with masculine plural nouns. "Dei fiori" is used when you mean an unspecified quantity (not “the flowers” = "i fiori"). Common with verbs like "comprare" (to buy), "portare" (to bring), "raccogliere" (to pick/collect).
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori per mia madre.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for my mother.

meaning: “some flowers to (someone)” (i.e., flowers for a recipient).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like dare (to give) and comprare (to buy) to show who will receive the flowers. Here, dei is a partitive article meaning “some” (not specific), and a introduces the indirect object (the person). In speech you’ll often hear it as "Ho comprato dei fiori a Maria" = “I bought Maria some flowers.”
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei fiori a mia madre per il suo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought some flowers for my mother for her birthday.

additional_notes: Used when you’re buying, bringing, or picking flowers as a gift for a person. "dei" is a partitive meaning “some,” and "per" means “for” (the recipient): "dei fiori per mia madre". You can change it to "dei fiori per + name/pronoun" (e.g., "per lei") or replace "dei" with a number: "due fiori per...".
target_language_example: Ho preso dei fiori per te.
native_language_example: I got some flowers for you.

additional_notes: Used to say you intend or expect something important/good (or ambitious) for someone’s future. It often appears with a pronoun after per: per te (for you, informal singular), per voi (for you, plural or formal). You can change tense (abbiamo/avevano) and subject without changing the expression.
target_language_example: Ho dei grandi piani per questa estate.
native_language_example: I have big plans for this summer.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive plural article "dei" (= "some") before a masculine plural noun like "libri". Common in questions and statements when you mean “any/some books” rather than specific ones. (Note: "libro" = book; "libreria" = bookstore; "biblioteca" = library.)
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare dei libri in italiano.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy some books in Italian.

additional_notes: `dei` is a partitive article meaning “some” (plural, masculine). `pancake` is commonly used in Italian as a borrowed word; you may also see `frittelle` in some contexts. `per colazione` means “for breakfast” (what you eat at breakfast).
target_language_example: Domani voglio dei pancake per colazione.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I want some pancakes for breakfast.

additional_notes: Plural of "un piano" meaning a plan/arrangement. Very common with verbs like "avere" (to have plans) and "fare" (to make plans). "Hai già dei piani?" often means "Do you already have plans?" (e.g., for tonight/weekend). Note: it looks like English "pianos" but here it means "plans," not the musical instrument.
target_language_example: Stasera non posso: ho già dei piani.
native_language_example: I can’t tonight: I already have plans.

additional_notes: Used with avere: avere dei piani per + time/event = to already have something arranged/decided. Very common in questions to ask if someone is free (e.g., Hai dei piani per stasera?). Often implies you might be inviting them or suggesting something.
target_language_example: Non posso venire: ho dei piani per domani.
native_language_example: I can’t come: I have plans for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used (often in a question) to ask if someone has anything scheduled for tomorrow. "dei" is a partitive article here, like “some/any” in English: "Hai dei piani...?" = “Do you have any plans...?” You can add a time: "per domani sera" = “for tomorrow evening.”
target_language_example: Non ho dei piani per domani, sei libero?
native_language_example: I don’t have any plans for tomorrow—are you free?

additional_notes: "Dei" is a partitive article meaning "some" with masculine plural nouns (here: popcorn). It’s commonly used when offering, giving, or asking for an unspecified quantity: "Mi dai dei popcorn?" You can also say "i popcorn" for popcorn in general or a specific portion already known in context.
target_language_example: Mi dai dei popcorn, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me some popcorn, please?

additional_notes: "Dei" is the plural partitive article (di + i) and often means "some" with plural nouns. "Avere dei problemi" = "to have problems" (general/unspecified problems). Common patterns: "avere dei problemi con" (to have problems with), "avere dei problemi a + infinitive" (to have trouble doing something), and "causare dei problemi" (to cause problems).
target_language_example: Ho dei problemi a capire questo esercizio.
native_language_example: I'm having trouble understanding this exercise.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "avere": "avere dei problemi a + infinitive" = "to have trouble / difficulty doing something". Often translated as "I can’t manage to..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho dei problemi a capire questa lezione.
native_language_example: I’m having trouble understanding this lesson.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere dei problemi a dormire" = to have difficulty sleeping. It can refer to occasional trouble or an ongoing issue; the tense changes ("ho/avevo/aveva/avete") depending on who and when.
target_language_example: Ultimamente ho dei problemi a dormire.
native_language_example: Lately I’ve been having trouble sleeping.

additional_notes: Used with forms of "avere" (ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno) to say you’re having trouble, difficulties, or conflict with something or someone. It can refer to practical issues (e.g., a device or situation), relationships ("con Tom"), or health ("con i polmoni" = with your lungs). In questions like "Avete dei problemi con quello?" it means "Are you having problems with that?"
target_language_example: Ho dei problemi con la connessione internet.
native_language_example: I’m having problems with the internet connection.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "avere": "avere dei sentimenti per qualcuno". It means you have emotional (often romantic) feelings toward a person. You can add words like "ancora" (still) to ask if the feelings remain: "Hai ancora dei sentimenti per...".
target_language_example: Penso di avere dei sentimenti per te.
native_language_example: I think I have feelings for you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" ("to have"): "avere dei sentimenti per lei" = "to have feelings for her." "Dei" here means "some" (an indefinite amount), but in English you usually just say "feelings for her." You can change the person: "per lui" (for him), "per te" (for you), "per me" (for me).
target_language_example: Credo di avere ancora dei sentimenti per lei.
native_language_example: I think I still have feelings for her.

meaning: "(romantic) feelings for him" / "feel something for him."
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere dei sentimenti per lui" = to have feelings for him, usually romantic or emotional attachment. "Ancora" adds the meaning "still": "hai ancora dei sentimenti per lui?" = "do you still have feelings for him?"
target_language_example: Credo di avere ancora dei sentimenti per lui, ma non lo so con certezza.
native_language_example: I think I still have feelings for him, but I'm not sure.

additional_notes: "Dei" is a partitive/indefinite article meaning “some” with plural nouns. So "dei soldi" often means “some money” in general, especially when you’re not specifying an amount. With verbs like "dare" (to give), "prestare" (to lend), and "donare" (to donate), it commonly refers to giving/lending/donating money. Note: "dovere dei soldi" means “to owe money.”
target_language_example: Mi puoi prestare dei soldi fino a domani?
native_language_example: Can you lend me some money until tomorrow?

additional_notes: “Dei” is a partitive article meaning “some” with masculine plural nouns. “Vestiti” means “clothes” (literally “items of clothing/outfits”). Used when you mean an unspecified quantity: comprare dei vestiti (to buy some clothes), mettersi dei vestiti (to put some clothes on). Often in everyday speech it can simply mean “clothes” without stressing the exact amount.
target_language_example: Devo comprare dei vestiti per l’inverno.
native_language_example: I have to buy some clothes for the winter.

additional_notes:
“Dei” is usually the contraction of “di + i” (= “of the”). It’s used in many common patterns: 
- talking about a topic: “Cosa sai dei cani?” = “What do you know about dogs?”
- comparisons: “più … dei cani” = “more/less … than dogs”
- with “nessuno/alcuno/uno”: “nessuno dei cani” = “none of the dogs”.
Note: “dei” can also mean “some” in other contexts (partitive plural), but in these examples it means “of the” / “than”.
target_language_example: Nessuno dei cani voleva uscire sotto la pioggia.
native_language_example: None of the dogs wanted to go out in the rain.

additional_notes: Used when talking about two people/things and you’re comparing or choosing between them. Common after a superlative: “il più alto dei due” (“the taller of the two”). In a question, “Chi dei due?” means “Which of the two (people)?”.
target_language_example: Tra Marco e Luca, chi dei due è il più giovane?
native_language_example: Between Marco and Luca, which of the two is younger?

meaning: "of my" / "of mine" (masculine plural), often "one/some of my".
additional_notes: Uses the preposition+article "dei" (di + i) with the possessive "miei". It commonly appears in partitive structures like "uno dei miei..." (one of my...), "alcuni dei miei..." (some of my...), or after nouns like "la donna dei miei sogni" (the woman of my dreams). "miei" is masculine plural; compare: "dei miei amici" (my male friends / my friends), "delle mie amiche" (my female friends), "dei miei anni" (my years/age).
target_language_example: Posso invitare uno dei miei amici alla festa?
native_language_example: Can I invite one of my friends to the party?

meaning: (very vulgar) “my ass / my balls!”, used to insult or show contempt (like “so-called” or “fucking”).
additional_notes: A crude, vulgar expression added after a noun to dismiss it or insult someone: “X dei miei coglioni!” ≈ “X my ass!” / “fucking X!” / “so-called X!”. It’s offensive and not appropriate in polite conversation.
target_language_example: Che riunione dei miei coglioni!
native_language_example: What a fucking meeting!

meaning: “about my plans, as soon as …” (likely a sentence fragment).
additional_notes: This isn’t a common fixed phrase on its own; it looks like two parts that often appear together in a full sentence: **dei miei piani** = “about my plans” (di + i → dei; “of/about the”), and **appena** = “as soon as / just.” Typically you’ll see it as: **(parlare/dire) dei miei piani appena + [something happens]**.
target_language_example: Ti parlerò dei miei piani appena arrivo a casa.
native_language_example: I’ll tell you about my plans as soon as I get home.

additional_notes: This is the contraction of **di + i nostri**. It’s used before a **masculine plural** noun: *dei nostri vestiti* = “some of our clothes” / “our clothes.” It can also appear after verbs that take **di** (e.g., *lamentarsi di* = “to complain about”): *ci lamentiamo dei nostri vicini* = “we complain about our neighbors.” For feminine plural, use **delle nostre**.
target_language_example: Ho parlato con alcuni dei nostri amici ieri sera.
native_language_example: I talked with some of our friends last night.

meaning: one of us; part of our group/side.
additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to your group (friends, team, organization, "our side"). Often after the verb essere: "Sei dei nostri" = "You’re one of us" / "You’re with us". It can also be used after a number/quantifier: "due/quanti dei nostri" = "two/how many of our people". Tone is fairly informal and group-focused.
target_language_example: Dai, vieni con noi: sei dei nostri!
native_language_example: Come on, come with us—you’re one of us!

additional_notes: "Dei" is the plural partitive article (di + i) and often means "some" or "any" with a plural noun. So "dei segni" usually refers to an unspecified number of signs/marks (e.g., marks on something, warning signs, clues). In some contexts it can be closer to "signs" in general rather than a specific set.
target_language_example: Ci sono dei segni sul muro.
native_language_example: There are some marks on the wall.

meaning: "of his" / "of her" (referring to his/her things or people).
additional_notes: Used when the noun is plural masculine: "dei" = "di" + "i" (of the), and "suoi" = "his/her" (plural masculine). It often means "some of his/her..." or "about his/her..." depending on context (e.g., "le storie dei suoi viaggi" = "the stories of his/her travels"). For plural feminine, you’ll see "delle sue".
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare dei suoi problemi adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t want to talk about his/her problems right now.

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article **dei** (“some”) + **suoi** (“his”) + **dipinti** (“paintings”). Depending on context, it can mean **some of his paintings** (when talking about an unspecified number) or simply **of his paintings** after certain verbs/expressions (e.g., “to talk about,” “to know,” “to see some of”).
target_language_example: Al museo abbiamo visto dei suoi dipinti.
native_language_example: At the museum we saw some of his paintings.

additional_notes: Used with masculine plural nouns to mean “some of your …” or “of your …,” often after words like un paio (a couple), alcuni (some), quali (which). It’s the combination di + i (of the) + tuoi (your, masc. plural). For feminine plural you’ll see delle tue; for singular del tuo/della tua.
target_language_example: Ho visto alcuni dei tuoi amici ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw some of your friends last night.

additional_notes: Used when you mean an indefinite quantity of flowers (not specific ones). It’s made of the partitive article “dei” + “fiori” (flowers), and is common with verbs like lasciare (to leave), portare (to bring), disegnare (to draw), or volere (to want).
target_language_example: Possiamo comprare dei fiori per la cena?
native_language_example: Can we buy some flowers for dinner?

additional_notes: "Dei" is the plural partitive/indefinite article (di + i). Most often it means an unspecified quantity: "I bought dei libri" = "I bought some books." In certain contexts it can also be literal "of the books" (e.g., "la copertina dei libri" = "the cover of the books").
target_language_example: Ho comprato dei libri per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: I bought some books to learn Italian.

additional_notes: "Dei" is a partitive article meaning "some" (plural, masculine). So "dei problemi" is a common way to say you’re having difficulties with something: "avere dei problemi a + infinitive" = "to have trouble (doing something)". You’ll also hear it with "ci sono" (there are): "Ci sono dei problemi" = "There are some problems."
target_language_example: Ho avuto dei problemi a trovare l'indirizzo.
native_language_example: I had some trouble finding the address.

additional_notes: "Dei" is a partitive article meaning "some" (plural). "Dei rischi" is used to talk about unspecified risks in general, often with verbs like "correre" (to take/run risks): "correre dei rischi" = "to take some risks". If the risks are specific/known, Italian often uses "i rischi" (the risks).
target_language_example: In quel lavoro ci sono sempre dei rischi.
native_language_example: In that job there are always some risks.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article "dei" (roughly “some”) + plural noun "soldi" (“money”). Common after verbs like "volere" (to want), "chiedere" (to ask for), "prestare" (to lend), and "dovere" when it means “to owe (someone) money” (e.g., "Ti devo dei soldi" = “I owe you some money”). Often implies an unspecified amount rather than a specific sum.
target_language_example: Mi servono dei soldi per il biglietto.
native_language_example: I need some money for the ticket.

additional_notes: "del" is the contraction of "di + il". With "suo", it is used before a masculine singular noun: for example, "del suo partito" = "of his party". Depending on the verb or adjective, "di" can also be understood as "about" or "with regard to," as in "felice del suo nuovo impiego".
target_language_example: Parlano spesso del suo lavoro.
native_language_example: They often talk about his/her work.

meaning: about his/her work; of his/her work.
additional_notes: “Del” = “di + il” and is used after many verbs/adjectives to mean “about/of.” “Suo” can mean “his” or “her” depending on who it refers to. Common with verbs like parlare/discutere (“to talk/discuss about”) and adjectives like fiero/orgoglioso/stufo (“proud/tired of”).
target_language_example: Non parla mai del suo lavoro a casa.
native_language_example: He/She never talks about his/her work at home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare: “fare del suo meglio” = “to do one’s best.” The possessive changes with the person: del mio meglio (my), del tuo meglio (your), del nostro/vostro meglio (our/your pl.), del loro meglio (their). Often implies putting in maximum effort, even if the result isn’t perfect.
target_language_example: Penso che Tom farà del suo meglio.
native_language_example: I think Tom will do his best.

meaning: “his/her best to …” (typically used with *fare*: “to do his/her best to …”).
additional_notes: Most often appears in the structure **fare del suo meglio per + infinitive**. *Suo* can refer to either “his” or “her” depending on context. The possessive can vary (e.g., **del mio/tuo/suo/nostro/vostro/loro meglio per**), but this entry focuses on **del suo meglio per**.
target_language_example: Ha fatto del suo meglio per aiutarmi.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her best to help me.

additional_notes: "Del" is the partitive (di + il) and is used when you mean an indefinite quantity of something uncountable, like coffee: "del caffè" = "some coffee". In everyday English you might also just say "coffee". Often used with verbs like bere (to drink), preparare/fare (to make), offrire (to offer), volere (to want).
target_language_example: Vuoi del caffè o del tè?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee or some tea?

additional_notes: Partitive article: "del" = "di" + "il" and is used with uncountable masculine singular nouns like "cibo" to mean an unspecified amount (“some/any”). In many contexts English omits “some”: "Ho comprato del cibo" = “I bought food.” For feminine nouns you’ll often see "della" (e.g., "della pasta").
target_language_example: Ho preso del cibo da asporto.
native_language_example: I got some takeout food.

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) used to mean an unspecified amount of something uncountable or plural. So "mangiare del gelato" = “to eat some (ice cream)” (not a specific portion). You can also hear "mangiare il gelato" when talking about the ice cream in general or a specific one.
target_language_example: Vorrei del gelato, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some ice cream, please.

meaning: some milk (an unspecified amount of milk).
additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + il = del) with an uncountable noun: *latte*. Very common for talking about an indefinite quantity, especially with verbs like *bere* (to drink) and *versare* (to pour). In English it often translates as “some” or is omitted (“Tom drinks milk”). Literally it’s “of the milk,” but the meaning is “some milk.”
target_language_example: Vorrei del latte, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some milk, please.

meaning: "some bread" (partitive: an unspecified amount of bread).
additional_notes: Del = di + il. With uncountable nouns like pane (“bread”), it’s commonly used to mean “some” in general: comprare del pane = “to buy some bread.” In other contexts it can also literally mean “of the bread” (referring to a specific bread).
target_language_example: Per favore, prendi del pane mentre torni a casa.
native_language_example: Please pick up some bread on your way home.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (di + il = del) to mean an unspecified amount: “some” or “any” tea, especially when talking about drinking, pouring, or serving. With an amount you’d usually use a measure instead (e.g., “una tazza di tè” = “a cup of tea”).
target_language_example: Vuoi del tè caldo?
native_language_example: Do you want some hot tea?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like bere (to drink), ordinare (to order), portare (to bring), rovesciare (to spill) to mean an unspecified amount of wine. It’s a common partitive form: di + il → del. If you mean a specific wine, you’d typically use il vino (the wine) or un vino (a wine).
target_language_example: Vuoi del vino o dell’acqua?
native_language_example: Do you want some wine or some water?

meaning: "of the forest/woods" (used to describe where someone/something is from or associated with).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of "di + il" → "del" plus "bosco" (forest/woods). Very common in titles, names, and roles: "la Strega del Bosco" = "the Witch of the Woods"; "gli Elfi del Bosco" = "the Forest Elves." Often capitalized when it’s part of a name or title.
target_language_example: Ho incontrato un lupo del Bosco durante la passeggiata.
native_language_example: I met a wolf from the woods during the walk.

additional_notes: Combination of "di" + "il" → "del". Used to specify that something belongs to or refers to the whole world, very common in set phrases like "la mappa del mondo" (the world map).
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una mappa del mondo.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a world map.

additional_notes: Uses the contraction **del** (= **di** + **il**) before a masculine singular noun. Often seen in names and titles (e.g., **Via del Sole**, **Tempio del Sole**). **Sole** is often capitalized in names, but it can also be lowercase (**del sole**) in normal text.
target_language_example: Abitiamo in Via del Sole.
native_language_example: We live on Via del Sole (Sun Street).

meaning: “about the case” / “of the case” (referring to a specific investigation or matter).
additional_notes: Used with a specific case name or identifier (e.g., “del caso Fuller”) to mean information, details, documents, or archives related to that case. Grammatically it’s the contraction of “di + il” → “del” (“of the”).
target_language_example: Ho letto tutti i rapporti del caso Bianchi.
native_language_example: I read all the reports about the Bianchi case.

meaning: fucking / shitty / damn (a vulgar insult or negative emphasis).
additional_notes: Very vulgar slang. Used after a noun to show annoyance, contempt, or that something/someone is worthless or irritating (e.g., "traffico del cazzo" = "fucking traffic"). It can also appear in fixed insults like "(un) duro del cazzo" meaning something like "a tough-guy asshole" (not literal). Avoid in polite situations.
target_language_example: Ho perso di nuovo questo cellulare del cazzo.
native_language_example: I lost this fucking phone again.

meaning: "of the body" (sometimes "of the corpse/body" depending on context).
additional_notes: It’s the contraction of **di + il** → **del**. Used to talk about body parts or anything related to the body: **parti del corpo** (parts of the body), **la salute del corpo** (the health of the body). In **guardia del corpo / guardie del corpo**, it means **bodyguard(s)** (literally “guard(s) of the body”). In some contexts **corpo** can also mean a **dead body** (“corpse”), e.g. **Che ne hai fatto del corpo?** = “What did you do with the body?”
target_language_example: La salute del corpo è importante.
native_language_example: The health of the body is important.

meaning: "of the heart" (literal), or "dear/close" in set phrases.
additional_notes: Literally "di + il cuore" = "of the heart." Used both in a physical/anatomical sense (e.g., "più in alto del cuore" = "higher than the heart") and in common expressions about feelings and closeness: "amici del cuore" = very close friends; "dal (più profondo) del cuore" = from the (very) bottom of my heart / sincerely.
target_language_example: Grazie dal profondo del cuore per il tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: Thank you from the bottom of my heart for your help.

additional_notes: “Del” is the contraction of “di + il” and is used before a masculine singular noun (il film). You’ll see it after verbs and expressions that take “di” (e.g., pensare/parlare di: “Cosa ne pensi del film?” = “What do you think about the film?”) and with nouns that describe something related to the film (e.g., la durata del film = the film’s duration, il manifesto del film = the film poster).
target_language_example: Parliamo del film dopo cena.
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the film after dinner.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something of the same type/kind as what’s being talked about. Often follows a noun: "un errore del genere" (= an error like that / of that kind). Very common with "qualcosa": "qualcosa del genere" (= something like that).
target_language_example: Non dire una cosa del genere!
native_language_example: Don’t say something like that!

additional_notes: Used to link something to the government (ownership, responsibility, or connection): e.g. "istituzioni del governo" (government institutions), "propaganda del governo" (government propaganda). It’s the contraction of "di" + "il" → "del". Similar forms: "dello" (di + lo), "della" (di + la), "dei" (di + i), "degli" (di + gli), "delle" (di + le).
target_language_example: Non mi fido delle promesse del governo.
native_language_example: I don’t trust the government’s promises.

del lavoro che ho scelto da

target_language_multi_word_term: del lavoro che ho scelto da sola / da solo
meaning: “of the job/work that I chose on my own” (emphasizes you made the choice independently, without help or influence).
additional_notes: Used to stress personal independence in choosing a job/path. It agrees with the speaker’s gender: **da sola** (female speaker), **da solo** (male speaker). It commonly appears after a past participle like **ho scelto**: *del lavoro che ho scelto da sola/da solo*.
target_language_example: Sono molto fiera del lavoro che ho scelto da sola.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of the job that I chose on my own.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di + il" ("of/about the"). Used to specify something related to a book (e.g., the title, a copy, your opinion). Often follows questions/verbs like "che ne pensi del..." = "what do you think about the...?"
target_language_example: Non ricordo il nome dell’autore del libro.
native_language_example: I don’t remember the name of the author of the book.

additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "fare": "fare del male (a qualcuno)" = to hurt someone / to harm someone (physically or emotionally). With "a" to name who is harmed: "fare del male a una mosca" is an idiom meaning someone is very gentle and wouldn’t hurt even a fly.
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male.
native_language_example: I don't want to hurt you.

additional_notes: A fragment rather than a complete expression by itself. It is the contraction of di + il mio, and it is used before a masculine singular noun: del mio libro, del mio problema, del mio cavallo. Depending on the verb or adjective, it can correspond to 'of my', 'about my', or sometimes natural English uses like 'with my' (e.g. contento del mio lavoro = happy with my work).
target_language_example: Non voglio parlare del mio problema.
native_language_example: I don't want to talk about my problem.

additional_notes: Used especially after expressions that require the preposition "di", most commonly "avere bisogno di" (to need). "del" is the contraction of "di + il". So "Hai bisogno del mio aiuto?" literally means "Do you have need of my help?" and naturally translates as "Do you need my help?"
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del mio aiuto, chiamami.
native_language_example: If you need my help, call me.

meaning: my best (as well as I can).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "fare": "Fare del mio meglio" = "to do my best". It can also appear after verbs like "cercare" (to try) to mean you’re making your best effort. Often used to reassure or promise effort: "Farò del mio meglio."
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in orario.
native_language_example: I'll do my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Usually used after the verb "fare": "fare del mio meglio per + infinitive" = "to do my best to + verb". You can change "mio" to match the subject: "del tuo meglio" (your best), "del suo meglio" (his/her best), "del nostro meglio" (our best).
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Most often used after a superlative to mean “in the world”: il più X del mondo = “the most X in the world” (migliore/più bello/più profondo, etc.). It can also be used more generally to sound emphatic or dramatic: la fine del mondo (“the end of the world”), il re del mondo (“king of the world”).
target_language_example: Questo è il gelato più buono del mondo.
native_language_example: This is the best ice cream in the world.

additional_notes: Contraction of "di" + "il nostro" (= "of our"). Used to show possession or connection to something: "le date del nostro viaggio" (the dates of our trip), "in segno del nostro apprezzamento" (as a sign of our appreciation). In the common expression "fare del nostro meglio", it means "to do our best" (literally "to do of our best").
target_language_example: Faremo del nostro meglio per arrivare in tempo.
native_language_example: We’ll do our best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: “Del” = “di + il” (“of the”), used here to introduce what someone needs. With “avere bisogno di” (to need), Italian typically says “avere bisogno del nostro aiuto” (literally “to have need of our help”). You can also use it after “ho bisogno…” / “hai bisogno…” etc.
target_language_example: Se hai bisogno del nostro aiuto, chiamaci.
native_language_example: If you need our help, call us.

meaning: anyway; besides / for that matter (also: “of the rest”).
additional_notes: Often used as a sentence add-on to comment on what you just said, meaning “besides/anyway/for that matter” (e.g., listing another example: “O Glenn Gould, del resto.”). In more literal contexts with "il resto" it can mean “of the rest,” as in "Per non parlare del resto" = “not to mention the rest.”
target_language_example: Non mi sorprende, del resto: lo conosci bene.
native_language_example: It doesn’t surprise me, anyway: you know him well.

additional_notes: Used before a man’s surname to show possession or reference: il figlio del signor Rossi = “Mr. Rossi’s son”; i film del signor Bianchi = “Mr. Bianchi’s films.” It’s a contraction of di + il + signor. Often used in more formal contexts; in writing you may also see Signor abbreviated as Sig.
target_language_example: Potrei parlare con la segretaria del signor Conti?
native_language_example: Could I speak with Mr. Conti’s secretary?

additional_notes: Used to specify something related to the sun (e.g., raggi del sole = sunrays, luce del sole = sunlight, dio del sole = sun god). It’s the contraction of di + il, and it changes with the noun: della luna (of the moon), dell’acqua (of the water), dei raggi (of the rays).
target_language_example: Non uscire senza crema: i raggi del sole sono forti oggi.
native_language_example: Don’t go out without sunscreen: the sun’s rays are strong today.

additional_notes: Used after a comparative (often with più/meno or prima/dopo) to compare something to what normally happens: prima del solito (earlier than usual), più felice del solito (happier than usual). Very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Oggi ho finito il lavoro più tardi del solito.
native_language_example: Today I finished work later than usual.

additional_notes: Usually followed by a masculine singular noun, as in del suo lavoro. del is the contraction of di + il, and suo can mean his, her, its, or your (formal), depending on context. In sentences, di can mean things like 'of' or 'about'.
target_language_example: Abbiamo parlato del suo progetto ieri.
native_language_example: We talked about his/her project yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally "of your help". It commonly follows expressions like "avere bisogno di" (to need): "Ho bisogno del suo aiuto" = "I need your help" (formal) or "I need his/her help," depending on context. "suo" can refer to a formal "you" (Lei) or to "he/she."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ho bisogno del suo aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need your help with this form.

meaning: "of his/her mistake"; "about his/her mistake" (after some verbs).
additional_notes: "Del" = di + il, and it’s used here to mean "of the" (often after verbs like ridere di = "to laugh at/about"). "Suo" means "his/her/its" and agrees with the noun (errore is masculine singular, so suo). The gender of the person isn’t specified—Italian uses suo for both "his" and "her".
target_language_example: Non parlare del suo errore adesso.
native_language_example: Don’t talk about his/her mistake now.

additional_notes: Formed by **di + il → del** + **suo** (his/her/its) + **lavoro** (job/work). It’s used after verbs/adjectives that take **di** (e.g., *parlare di* “to talk about”, *essere fiero di* “to be proud of”, *essere stufo di* “to be fed up with”). **Suo** agrees with *lavoro* (masculine singular), so *del suo lavoro* can refer to either “his” or “her” job—context tells you which.
target_language_example: Sono orgoglioso del suo lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m proud of his/her work.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb “fare”: “fare del suo meglio” = “to do one’s best.” “Suo” refers to a third person (his/her/its). For other persons, it changes to “del mio/tuo/nostro/vostro/loro meglio” (e.g., “del mio meglio” = “my best”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: farà del suo meglio.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he/she will do his/her best.

meaning: “his/her best to …” (typically used with *fare*: “to do his/her best to …”).
additional_notes: Most often appears in the structure **fare del suo meglio per + infinitive**. *Suo* can refer to either “his” or “her” depending on context. The possessive can vary (e.g., **del mio/tuo/suo/nostro/vostro/loro meglio per**), but this entry focuses on **del suo meglio per**.
target_language_example: Ha fatto del suo meglio per aiutarmi.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her best to help me.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/adjectives that take **di** (e.g., *essere sicuro/certo di...* “to be sure/certain of...”, *vantarsi di...* “to boast about...”). **Del** = *di* + *il* (“of the”). **Suo** can mean “his”, “her”, “its”, or “your” (formal), depending on context.
target_language_example: Non dubito del suo successo.
native_language_example: I don’t doubt his/her success.

additional_notes: Used after verbs/expressions like "pensare di" (to think about) or "che cosa ne pensa..." (what do you think of...) to refer to someone’s suggestion. "del" = "di + il". "suo" is the formal "your" (Lei); in informal speech you’d often say "del tuo suggerimento".
target_language_example: Che cosa ne pensa del suo suggerimento?
native_language_example: What do you think of your suggestion?

meaning: about his/her trip; about your trip (formal).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like **parlare di** (to talk about) and **dire di** (to tell/say about). **del** = **di + il** (“about/of the”), and **suo** can mean **his**, **her**, or **your** (formal **Lei**). In many contexts it translates best as “about.”
target_language_example: Vorrei sapere di più del suo viaggio.
native_language_example: I’d like to know more about your trip.

additional_notes: Del = di + il (“of the”). With tempo it can mean (1) “of time” in a general or sci‑fi/historical sense (confini dello spazio e del tempo; corridoio del tempo; del tempo di Luigi…), and (2) “about the weather” especially after verbs like parlare/discutere: “Parliamo del tempo” = “Let’s talk about the weather.”
target_language_example: Parliamo del tempo: domani piove?
native_language_example: Let’s talk about the weather: will it rain tomorrow?

additional_notes: Contraction of "di + il tuo". Used before a masculine singular noun to mean "of your" (possession/connection) or, with verbs like "parlare/dire", "about your". It changes with gender/number: "della tua" (fem. sing.), "dei tuoi" (masc. pl.), "delle tue" (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Parlami del tuo lavoro.
native_language_example: Tell me about your job.

additional_notes: Common after expressions like "avere bisogno di" (to need): "Abbiamo bisogno del tuo aiuto" = "We need your help." "del" is the contraction of "di" + "il" (of the). "tuo" agrees with the noun: "aiuto" is masculine singular, so "tuo".
target_language_example: Ho bisogno del tuo aiuto con questo esercizio.
native_language_example: I need your help with this exercise.

additional_notes: Used with fare: fare del tuo meglio = “to do your best.” It can be advice/encouragement (Fai del tuo meglio!), a reminder (Devi fare del tuo meglio), or recognition after the fact (Hai fatto del tuo meglio). Also common with possessives: del mio meglio, del suo meglio, del nostro meglio, etc.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: fai del tuo meglio e andrà bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: do your best and it will be fine.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a statement, meaning “completely/fully.” Very common with negatives: "non del tutto" = “not completely / not entirely.” It can also appear with agreement/disagreement: "del tutto in disaccordo" = “completely disagree.”
target_language_example: Non sono del tutto sicuro di aver capito.
native_language_example: I’m not entirely sure I understood.

meaning: of the village; from the village.
additional_notes: "Del" = "di + il" and shows possession/association ("the village's...") or origin ("someone from the village"). It’s used before a singular masculine noun (villaggio). Often translates as "of the village" or "in the village" depending on context (e.g., "la gente del villaggio" = "the village people / the people in the village").
target_language_example: Il bar del villaggio è chiuso oggi.
native_language_example: The village bar is closed today.

additional_notes: "Del" is the contraction of "di + il" ("of the"). With "vostro" it means "of your" (your = plural "you" or polite/formal). It’s used with masculine singular nouns: "del vostro viaggio" (of your trip), "del vostro tempo" (of your time). In requests it can sound like "some of your": "un sorso del vostro vino" (a sip of your wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei sapere di più del vostro progetto.
native_language_example: I’d like to know more about your project.

additional_notes: Used after expressions like “avere bisogno di …” (“to need …”): “Ho/Abbiamo bisogno del vostro aiuto” = “I/We need your help.” “Vostro” is the plural “your” (addressing more than one person) and can also be a formal singular “your” (Lei-form). It comes from “di + il” → “del” + “vostro aiuto”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno del vostro aiuto per finire oggi.
native_language_example: We need your help to finish today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare: fare del vostro meglio = “to do your best” when speaking to more than one person or using the formal/plural “you” (voi). It can also be used after other verbs like provare a (“try to”) + fare del vostro meglio.
target_language_example: Fate del vostro meglio e non preoccupatevi troppo.
native_language_example: Do your best and don’t worry too much.

additional_notes: Used with the partitive article (del = di + il) to mean an unspecified amount of coffee. In questions it often corresponds to “any coffee?” in English (e.g., “Vuoi del caffè?” = “Do you want some/any coffee?”).
target_language_example: Vuoi del caffè dopo pranzo?
native_language_example: Do you want some coffee after lunch?

additional_notes: Used when offering or choosing between two drinks. "Del" is the partitive article (di + il) and often means “some” with uncountable nouns like caffè and tè. In questions, it’s a polite way to ask what someone would like.
target_language_example: Per colazione preferisci del caffè o del tè?
native_language_example: For breakfast, do you prefer coffee or tea?

additional_notes: Used when talking about mixing or serving food. "del" and "della" mean "some" (an unspecified amount): "del" + masculine noun (chilli), "della" + feminine noun (senape).
target_language_example: Mi piace mangiare del chilli con della senape sui panini.
native_language_example: I like to eat some chili with mustard on sandwiches.

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) used to mean “some” with uncountable nouns like cibo (“food”). In English you often just say “food” without “some.” It can also literally mean “of the food” in certain contexts, but in everyday sentences like the examples it usually means “some food.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato del cibo per il viaggio.
native_language_example: We bought some food for the trip.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article **del** (= “some”) with **cibo** (“food”). **Halal** is an invariable adjective/loanword, so it stays the same (not *halala/halali*). Often used when asking for or ordering food that follows Islamic dietary rules.
target_language_example: Avete del cibo halal nel menù?
native_language_example: Do you have any halal food on the menu?

additional_notes: “Del” = “di + il” and is used as a partitive article to mean “some” with an uncountable noun (food). Common in offers, orders, and requests: “Vuoi del couscous?” / “Ho ordinato del couscous.” You can also see “del” change with gender/number: “della pasta”, “dei biscotti”, “dell’acqua”.
target_language_example: Per cena prendiamo del couscous e delle verdure.
native_language_example: For dinner let’s have some couscous and some vegetables.

additional_notes: Partitive form (di + il = del) used when you mean an unspecified amount of money. Common with verbs like dare (to give) and dovere (to owe): “dare del denaro” = to give someone some money; “dovere del denaro (a qualcuno)” = to owe someone money.
target_language_example: Non ho del denaro da prestarti oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t have any money to lend you today.

additional_notes: `del` is the partitive article (di + il) and is used to talk about an unspecified amount of something you can’t easily count (like ice cream, water, bread). It often translates as “some” or is left untranslated in English: *Vuoi del gelato?* = “Do you want (some) ice cream?” You can also hear *del* used in questions meaning “any”: *Vende del gelato qua?* = “Do they sell ice cream here?”
target_language_example: Prendiamo del gelato dopo cena.
native_language_example: Let’s get some ice cream after dinner.

additional_notes: "Del" is the partitive article (di + il). With uncountable nouns like latte, it often means “some” (an unspecified amount) and is very common when talking about buying, drinking, pouring, etc. In English you may simply say “milk” rather than “some milk,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Vorrei del latte nel caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like some milk in my coffee, please.

additional_notes:
Common pattern with two contractions:
- **del** = *di + il*: partitive article meaning “some” (used with uncountable nouns like *latte*).
- **nel** = *in + il*: “in the”.
Used when saying you put/have some milk **in** something: *del latte nel caffè* (“some milk in the coffee”). With other nouns it changes (e.g., *dello zucchero nel tè*, *dell’acqua nel bicchiere*).
target_language_example: Vuoi del latte nel tè?
native_language_example: Do you want some milk in your tea?

additional_notes: Used to say you have tasks to complete. "del" is a partitive article meaning “some” (un po’ di), and "da fare" means “to do/to be done.” In everyday speech you may also hear it without "del": "Ho lavoro da fare."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso uscire: ho del lavoro da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out: I have some work to do.

additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase “fare del male (a qualcuno)” = “to harm/hurt (someone)”. It commonly appears with indirect object pronouns: “farmi del male” (hurt me), “farti del male” (hurt you), “gli/le fare del male” (hurt him/her), “farvi del male” (hurt you all/you formal).
target_language_example: Non voglio farti del male.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt you.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb fare: fare del male a qualcuno = to hurt/harm someone (physically or emotionally). With a pronoun: fare del male a me/te/lui/lei/ci/vi/loro. In Italian, male means “bad/evil” or “pain,” not “male” (man).
target_language_example: Non voglio fare del male a nessuno.
native_language_example: I don’t want to hurt anyone.

additional_notes: Uses the partitive article (del = di + il) to mean an unspecified quantity of an uncountable noun: “some bread / (any) bread.” Common with food and drink. In questions it often means “any”: “Hai del pane?” = “Do you have any bread?” With a specific bread already mentioned, “del” can also be closer to “of the bread,” but most beginner uses are simply “some.”
target_language_example: Vorrei del pane, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like some bread, please.

additional_notes: "Del" is a partitive article (di + il) meaning “some” or “any” with a masculine singular mass noun. Used when talking about an unspecified quantity of fish (e.g., buying, selling, eating, cooking). Often paired with alternatives like "carne o pesce?"
target_language_example: Prendo del pesce e un po' di verdure.
native_language_example: I’ll have some fish and some vegetables.

additional_notes: "Del" is partitive: di + il = del. It’s used to talk about an unspecified quantity of something uncountable or plural (like rice). In English you often just say “rice,” or “some rice.” Used with verbs like mangiare (to eat), comprare (to buy), fare (to make/cook).
