additional_notes: Most often appears in set expressions: **fare di testa tua** = “to do it your way / be headstrong” (ignoring advice or rules): *Ha fatto di testa sua.* Also **uscire di testa** = “to go crazy / lose your mind,” and **far uscire di testa (qualcuno)** = “to drive (someone) crazy.” Colloquial, not usually used alone outside these phrases.
target_language_example: Non fare di testa tua: aspetta e parliamone prima.
native_language_example: Don’t do it your way: wait and let’s talk about it first.

meaning: "to go back home / to return home" (as an infinitive after another verb).
additional_notes: Used with the preposition "di" + infinitive when the action "tornare a casa" depends on another verb or expression (e.g., "dire a qualcuno di..." = to tell someone to..., "permettere di..." = to allow to..., "aspettare di..." = to wait to..., "essere contento/a di..." = to be happy to...). "A casa" means "home" (toward home).
target_language_example: Non vedo l’ora di tornare a casa dopo il lavoro.
native_language_example: I can’t wait to go back home after work.

meaning: away; out of the way (often: “off my back”).
additional_notes: Used mainly with verbs like "togliere" or "levare" ("togliersi di torno", "levare qualcuno di torno") to tell someone to go away or to remove/get rid of someone/something. It can sound annoyed or rude depending on tone and context. Also appears in fixed sayings like "levare il medico di torno" (= keep the doctor away).
target_language_example: Puoi toglierti di torno per favore? Sto lavorando.
native_language_example: Can you get out of the way, please? I’m working.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it lasts three years ("un contratto di tre anni"), or to say someone/something is three years old ("un bambino di tre anni"). In time expressions you’ll also see it with other structures, e.g. "Sono più di tre anni che..." / "Sono più di tre anni da quando..." = “It’s been more than three years since...”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo un abbonamento di tre anni.
native_language_example: We have a three-year subscription.

additional_notes: Used after certain verbs that take "di" + infinitive (especially pensare di = "to think about/plan to", sperare di = "to hope to"). In English this often becomes "to" + verb ("to find a job"), not "of finding a job."
target_language_example: Sto sperando di trovare un lavoro a Milano.
native_language_example: I’m hoping to find a job in Milan.

meaning: "of your mother" / "your mother's" (used to refer to something belonging to your mother).
additional_notes: Used after a noun to specify relation/possession: e.g., "il numero di telefono di tua madre" = "your mother's phone number". In some contexts it can also be used as a vulgar insult tag in phrases like "[insult] di tua madre!"—this is offensive and should be avoided.
target_language_example: Qual è il cognome di tua madre?
native_language_example: What is your mother's last name?

meaning: 'of your father' / 'your father's' (possession, origin, or relation).
additional_notes: Used to indicate that something belongs to, comes from, or is related to the person addressed’s father. Common after a noun (e.g., la coppa di tuo padre = your father's cup) and in comparisons (quella di tuo padre = the one belonging to your father). Often translates as English possessive 'your father's' rather than a literal 'of your father.'
target_language_example: Questo libro è di tuo padre?
native_language_example: Is this book your father's?

additional_notes: Used to compare or rank something against a whole group of feminine plural nouns (often followed by a noun or by “altre” = “others”): “più/meno … di tutte le altre” = “more/less … than all the others.” It can also mean “of all the + [plural noun]” without a comparison: “di tutte le scelte” = “of all the choices.”
target_language_example: Questo è il migliore di tutte le soluzioni.
native_language_example: This is the best of all the solutions.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun (usually with a following descriptor like tipi, colori, generi) to mean “of all kinds/sorts.” Often forms set phrases like di tutti i tipi (“of all kinds”) and di tutti i colori (“in every color”). With beni, it means “all goods” (i beni = goods/products).
target_language_example: Al mercato trovi frutta di tutti i tipi.
native_language_example: At the market you can find all kinds of fruit.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to describe something as part of normal routine or ordinary life (e.g., vita di tutti i giorni = everyday life; problemi di tutti i giorni = day-to-day problems). Often carries a contrast with something special/extraordinary, and can be used with negative feelings like boredom or frustration (sono stufo della… = I’m fed up with…).
target_language_example: Non mi piace la routine di tutti i giorni.
native_language_example: I don’t like the everyday routine.

additional_notes: Used after a superlative or ranking to mean across all history/time, not just “right now”: il migliore/peggiore di tutti i tempi; uno dei più grandi di tutti i tempi (“one of the greatest of all time”). Often in questions with Chi è…? (“Who is…?”).
target_language_example: È il film più bello di tutti i tempi, secondo me.
native_language_example: It’s the best movie of all time, in my opinion.

meaning: from all over the world; in the whole world.
additional_notes: Used after a noun to mean it comes from everywhere worldwide ("persone di tutto il mondo" = people from all over the world). With superlatives it often means “in the whole world” ("la più bella di tutto il mondo" = the most beautiful in the world).
target_language_example: Abbiamo amici di tutto il mondo.
native_language_example: We have friends from all over the world.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to an entire situation, set of facts, or things just mentioned or understood from context. Often follows verbs and expressions that take di (e.g., occuparsi di “to deal with/take care of,” essere responsabile di “to be responsible for,” parlare di “to talk about”). Depending on the verb, English may use “of,” “about,” or sometimes “for” (“Thanks for taking care of all this”).
target_language_example: Sono responsabile di tutto questo, lo riconosco.
native_language_example: I’m responsible for all this, I admit it.

additional_notes: Composed of di + un. It is usually used before a masculine singular noun and often corresponds literally to 'of a'. In context, di can express possession, relation, description, or material, so English may sometimes sound more natural with other phrasing.
target_language_example: Ho sentito la voce di un bambino.
native_language_example: I heard the voice of a child.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate a different person/thing/place: *di un altro Paese* = “from another country.” It changes with gender/number: *di un’altra* (fem. sing.), *di altri* (masc. plural), *di altre* (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Sono di un altro quartiere.
native_language_example: I’m from another neighborhood.

meaning: (of) a ride home / a lift home.
additional_notes: Usually used after verbs like "avere bisogno" (to need) or "chiedere" (to ask for): "Ho bisogno di un passaggio a casa" = "I need a ride home." You can also say "dare un passaggio a casa (a qualcuno)" = "to give someone a ride home."
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un passaggio a casa: puoi accompagnarmi?
native_language_example: I need a ride home—can you take me?

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "di" + indefinite article "un" + "uomo" (man). Most often it expresses possession or a description ("la vita di un uomo" = "a man’s life"), or what something is connected to/concerns (depending on the noun before it).
target_language_example: Non so niente di un uomo con quel nome.
native_language_example: I don’t know anything about a man with that name.

meaning: 'of a woman' / 'by a woman' (depending on context).
additional_notes: Uses the preposition "di" + "una donna" to specify possession/origin ("the promise of a woman"), responsibility/cause ("because of a woman" = "per colpa di una donna"), or authorship/characteristic ("looks like a woman's handwriting"). "Di" is very common and often corresponds to English "of"; the exact translation can shift with the whole phrase.
target_language_example: È il profumo di una donna che non dimenticherò mai.
native_language_example: It’s the perfume of a woman I’ll never forget.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like chiedere (to ask), invitare (to invite), o pregare (to request) to express what you want someone to do: “ask (someone) to join us.” Unirsi is a reflexive verb meaning “to join,” and a noi means “to us.” Common variants include di unirti a noi (you, informal singular), di unirvi a noi (you all), di unirsi a me (to join me), di unirsi a loro (to join them).
target_language_example: Chieda loro di unirsi a noi.
native_language_example: Ask them to join us.

additional_notes: This is a fragment that usually depends on a previous verb or expression that requires "di" (like "avere bisogno di" = "to need to"). It introduces an infinitive action ("usare" = "to use") followed by a masculine singular noun with "il" (e.g., "il telefono", "il computer"). If the noun is feminine, you’ll use "di usare la" instead.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di usare il telefono.
native_language_example: I need to use the phone.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition di + infinitive (usare) to say what someone is free/allowed to do, often after essere libero/a (e.g., Sei libero/a di...). Il mio means 'my' (masculine singular), and yacht is masculine in Italian: lo yacht / il mio yacht.
target_language_example: Sei libero di usare il mio yacht quando vuoi.
native_language_example: You’re free to use my yacht whenever you want.

meaning: 'to go out' / 'to leave (a place)' (used as an infinitive after another verb).
additional_notes: You often use **di + infinitive** after certain verbs/expressions, e.g. **chiedere di uscire** (“to ask [someone] to go out”), **avere voglia di uscire / mi va di uscire** (“to feel like going out”). With places you can add **di**: **uscire di casa** (“to leave the house”).
target_language_example: Non ho voglia di uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I don't feel like going out tonight.

meaning: to see her (or: to see you, formal, feminine).
additional_notes: Used as “di + infinitive” after many verbs/adjectives to express what someone feels/thinks/decides (e.g., essere felice/sorpreso di…, sperare di…, rifiutarsi di…). “Vederla” = vedere + la, where “la” is an object pronoun attached to the infinitive.
target_language_example: Sono felice di vederla di nuovo.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see her again.

additional_notes: Used after verbs or expressions that take "di" + infinitive (e.g., "pensare di", "decidere di", "parlare di"). "Vendere" = "to sell". "La sua" is a feminine singular possessive pronoun meaning "his/hers" and usually refers to a feminine noun already known from context (often repeated earlier), e.g., "la casa" (house), "la macchina" (car), "la bici" (bike). If the noun is stated, you’ll often see: "vendere la sua + [noun]".
target_language_example: Marco vuole tenere la sua bici, ma Luca sta pensando di vendere la sua.
native_language_example: Marco wants to keep his bike, but Luca is thinking of selling his.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive verb follows another verb that takes "di" (common with verbs like dire "to tell" and pensare "to think/plan"). In English you usually just say "to come"; Italian often requires "di" + infinitive: "dire a qualcuno di venire" = "to tell someone to come", "pensare di venire" = "to think/plan to come".
target_language_example: Ti ho chiesto di venire alle otto.
native_language_example: I asked you to come at eight.

additional_notes: Used when an infinitive is introduced by **di** (often after verbs/expressions like *capitare di*, *succedere di*, *avere voglia di*, etc.) and **venire** takes **a** to show destination: *venire a Roma* = “come to Rome.” Note: *venire* is “come” (toward the speaker or the situation), while *andare* is “go.”
target_language_example: Mi capita spesso di venire a Milano per lavoro.
native_language_example: I often happen to come to Milan for work.

additional_notes: Used with a verb before it (often a request, invitation, advice, etc.). The preposition “di” introduces the infinitive: e.g. “Ti chiedo di venire a casa” = “I’m asking you to come home.” “Venire a casa” means “to come (to my/our/your) home,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ti chiedo di venire a casa entro le otto.
native_language_example: I’m asking you to come home by eight.

meaning: 'to come and see me' / 'to come see me'.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like dire/chiedere (to tell/ask) to report an instruction: "dire a qualcuno di + infinitive" = "to tell someone to + verb". "A vedermi" means "to see me" (purpose of coming). "Vedermi" = "see me" (vedere + mi).
target_language_example: Puoi dirgli di venire a vedermi domani?
native_language_example: Can you tell him to come see me tomorrow?

meaning: to come here (infinitive phrase, often after another verb).
additional_notes: Used with verbs/expressions that are followed by an infinitive introduced by "di", such as dire a qualcuno di... (to tell someone to...), proporre di... (to suggest/propose to...), or essere contento di... (to be happy to...). The pronouns can change: Dille/Ditegli/Ditele di venire qui = tell her/him/you(pl. formal her) to come here.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di venire qui domani.
native_language_example: He/She asked me to come here tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally “of wine.” Common after quantities/containers: una bottiglia di vino (a bottle of wine), un bicchiere di vino (a glass of wine). It can also describe something flavored/scented of wine: sa di vino = “it tastes/smells like wine.”
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of wine, please.

meaning: "of wine in his/hers" (a fragment, not a fixed phrase).
additional_notes:
This isn’t a standard standalone expression; it’s a sequence you might see inside a longer sentence. 
- **di vino** = “of wine” (often used to specify what something contains: *una bottiglia di vino* = “a bottle of wine”).
- **nella** = “in the” (in + la).
- **sua** = “his/her/its” (feminine singular, used before a feminine noun like *borsa*, *casa*, *auto*). You normally need the noun after *sua* (e.g., *nella sua borsa*).
target_language_example: C’è una bottiglia di vino nella sua borsa.
native_language_example: There’s a bottle of wine in his/her bag.

additional_notes: Used after a quantity or a noun to specify that something is red wine (e.g., "un bicchiere di vino rosso" = "a glass of red wine"). You’ll often see it in orders at a bar/restaurant or in recipes.
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Used with nouns like “problemi di vista” (= vision problems) and in the common expression “perdere di vista (qualcuno/qualcosa)” (= to lose sight of someone/something, not see them anymore, often in a crowd or from far away). Also: “tenere d’occhio” is the opposite idea (keep an eye on).
target_language_example: Nel buio ho perso di vista la strada.
native_language_example: In the dark I lost sight of the road.

additional_notes: Literally di + voi. It often means "of you" with plural voi, as in qualcuno di voi = "some of you." After certain verbs and expressions, English may translate it more naturally as just "you" or "about you," for example fidarsi di voi = "trust you" and ricordarsi di voi = "remember you."
target_language_example: Molti di voi parlano già un po' di italiano.
native_language_example: Many of you already speak a little Italian.

meaning: of your father; about your father.
additional_notes: Uses the preposition **di** + possessive (**vostro**, used with **voi** = “you (plural)”) + a family member (**padre**). Common after nouns/adjectives like **conoscenza di...** (“acquaintance with...”), **fiero/orgoglioso di...** (“proud of...”), and to show possession: **la casa di vostro padre** (“your father’s house”).
target_language_example: Siete fieri di vostro padre?
native_language_example: Are you proud of your father?

meaning: "of sugar in my coffee" / "(some) sugar in my coffee."
additional_notes: Used to specify that you want sugar added to your coffee. It often appears after quantities: due cucchiaini di zucchero nel mio caffè (“two teaspoons of sugar in my coffee”), una zolletta di zucchero nel mio caffè (“a sugar cube in my coffee”). With commands/requests you’ll often hear: Per favore/Per piacere, metta… (formal) or metti… (informal) = “please, put/add…”.
target_language_example: Per favore, metta un po’ di zucchero nel mio caffè.
native_language_example: Please, put a bit of sugar in my coffee.

meaning: (formal) “let him/her do his/her part” / “may he/she contribute”.
additional_notes: From the verb *dare* (“to give”) + *il suo* (“his/hers”). Used in formal, polite contexts (Lei form) to encourage someone to contribute or do their share, often implying “do your best” or “make your contribution.” You may also hear it in longer phrases like *dia il suo contributo* (“make your contribution”).
target_language_example: Per favore, dia il suo contributo e risponda al questionario.
native_language_example: Please, contribute by answering the questionnaire.

additional_notes: Used with the formal command form (Lei) of **dare**: **dia** = “give” (polite/formal). It’s usually followed by an infinitive to say what the thing is for, e.g. **da mangiare** (to eat), **da bere** (to drink), **da leggere** (to read). Often appears with an object pronoun: **Mi/ci dia qualcosa da…** = “Give me/us something to…”.
target_language_example: Mi dia qualcosa da bere, per favore.
native_language_example: Please give me something to drink.

additional_notes: From the verb dare (to give). Dia is the formal imperative (Lei form) and is also used after words like che/lascia che (“let…”) to mean “(that you) give…”. It’s often used with an indirect object pronoun: Gli dia un consiglio. = “Give him some advice.”
target_language_example: Per favore, dia un bicchiere d’acqua a mia madre.
native_language_example: Please give a glass of water to my mother.

meaning: (that) he/she gives a hand; (that) he/she helps.
additional_notes: From the verb phrase **dare una mano** = “to give a hand / to help.” **Dia** is the **subjunctive** form (often after *vuoi che…*, *vogliono che…*) and can also be used as the **formal (Lei) command**: *Mi dia una mano* = “Help me, please.” With pronouns: *ti/mi/le/gli dia una mano* = “help you/me/her/him.”
target_language_example: Mi dia una mano, per favore.
native_language_example: Please give me a hand / Please help me.

additional_notes: This is the polite/Lei command form of dire (“to say/tell”), used for giving instructions or requests in a formal or respectful way. It’s typically followed by a person: dica a Maria…, dica a Tom… (“tell Maria…, tell Tom…”). If the direct object is a pronoun, it can come before: Lo dica a Tom. (“Tell it to Tom.”).
target_language_example: Mi scusi, dica al professore che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Excuse me, tell the professor that I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: “Dica” is the formal command (Lei) form of *dire* (“to say/tell”). With “che” it introduces what you want someone to report: *Dica che sono occupato* (“Tell them I’m busy”). In negatives like *Non mi dica che…*, it often means “Don’t tell me that…” / “You can’t be telling me that…”. The informal equivalent is usually *di’ che* (tu).
target_language_example: Per favore, dica che richiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: Please tell them I’ll call back later.

additional_notes: “Dica” is the formal (Lei) command/subjunctive form of dire (“to say/tell”). “Dica di …” is used to ask someone politely/formally to tell something about a topic/person (“Mi dica di suo figlio” = “Tell me about your son”) or to report what someone should do/say (“Le dica di non parlare” = “Tell her not to talk”). With sì/no: “dica di sì/no” = “say yes/no.”
target_language_example: Mi dica di che cosa ha bisogno.
native_language_example: Tell me what you need.

additional_notes: Uses the formal imperative of dire (Lei form): dica. You say it to someone you address with Lei (a stranger, older person, customer, etc.). With friends/family (tu), you’d usually say: Di' la verità. In statements or hopes (not a command), it can also appear as the present subjunctive after verbs like sperare: Spero che ... dica la verità.
target_language_example: Signora, per favore, dica la verità.
native_language_example: Ma’am, please tell the truth.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (Lei) of the verb dire: dica = “tell/say” (to you, formal). It’s followed by loro (“to them”) and di + infinitive to give an instruction (e.g., dica loro di aspettare = “tell them to wait”). Common in polite requests, instructions, or official situations.
target_language_example: Dica loro di aspettarmi qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Please tell them to wait for me here.

additional_notes: Uses the formal (Lei) imperative of dire (“dica” = “tell/say”). It’s usually followed by another verb to complete the idea: “Dica quello che vuole/pensa/sa” = “Say what you want/think/know.” In English you often translate it as “Tell me what…” or “Say whatever…”, depending on context.
target_language_example: Dica quello che pensa, per favore.
native_language_example: Please tell me what you think.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says or claims. Dice is the 3rd-person singular form of dire ('to say'), so it can mean 'he says', 'she says', or 'says' with a named subject before it, as in 'Mary dice che...'. In English, 'that' is often optional.
target_language_example: Luca dice che oggi non viene.
native_language_example: Luca says that he isn't coming today.

meaning: "she says that she likes" (literally: "she says that it pleases her").
additional_notes: Used to report what a woman says she likes. In Italian, "piacere" is structured as "something is pleasing to someone": "A lei piace X" = "She likes X". "A lei" adds emphasis/contrast (e.g., 'she likes it' as opposed to someone else). Often followed by an infinitive for activities ("piace farlo / insegnare") or a noun for things ("piace il cibo cinese").
target_language_example: Dice che a lei piace viaggiare da sola.
native_language_example: She says that she likes traveling alone.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says they are required to do. The subject is often understood from context and can be added (e.g., “Lui/Lei dice che deve…”). “Che” = “that,” and “deve” (from *dovere*) expresses obligation (“has to/must”).
target_language_example: Lei dice che deve lavorare stasera.
native_language_example: She says she has to work tonight.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says they like. With piacere, Italian often says "it is pleasing to him": "gli" = "to him" (for "to her" you usually use "le"). The thing liked can be a verb ("gli piace vivere...") or a place/thing ("gli piace qui/qua a Boston").
target_language_example: Marco dice che gli piace questa città.
native_language_example: Marco says that he likes this city.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce what someone claims or reports. The subject is often understood from context ("dice" = he/she says), but you can also add it: "Tom dice che ha...". It’s followed by something someone says they have (a need, an illness, time, money, a plan, etc.).
target_language_example: Lei dice che ha fame, ma ha già mangiato.
native_language_example: She says she’s hungry, but she already ate.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone/something says. "dice" = "(he/she/it) says" (from *dire*), "che" = "that" (introduces a clause). "la" is often the feminine singular article "the" before a noun (e.g., *la verdura*, *la parete*, *la crisi*), but in some contexts it can also be the object pronoun "her/it"—the meaning depends on what follows.
target_language_example: Marco dice che la lezione oggi finisce alle cinque.
native_language_example: Marco says that the class ends at five today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says: **dice che...** = “(he/she) says that…”. **le piace** literally means “it pleases her” and is the common way to say “she likes it.” What is liked can come after (**le piace la musica**) or be implied (**le piace qui** = “she likes it here”). You can change **le** depending on who likes it: **mi piace** (I like), **ti piace** (you like), **gli piace** (he likes), **ci piace** (we like), etc.
target_language_example: Giulia dice che le piace questo ristorante.
native_language_example: Giulia says she likes this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says in indirect speech. "dice" = "he/she says" (also used for "you say" in formal address). "che" means "that" and introduces the clause; "non" negates the verb that follows ("non sa" = "doesn’t know", "non muore" = "doesn’t die"). Often followed by another verb: "dice che non + verbo".
target_language_example: Dice che non può venire oggi.
native_language_example: He/She says (that) he/she can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims. "Dice" = "(he/she) says", "che" = "that", "non ha" = "doesn’t have". In conversation you can replace the subject with a name (e.g., "Mary dice...") or use "Lui/Lei dice che non ha...". Often followed by a noun phrase: "rimpianti" (regrets), "altra scelta" (another choice), "idea" (an idea), "vizi" (vices).
target_language_example: Lei dice che non ha tempo oggi.
native_language_example: She says she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims they are able to do. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., Mary dice che può… = “Mary says she can…”). "che" introduces the subordinate clause, and "può" is the present tense of "potere" (can / be able to). You can change tense/person: "dicono che possono" (they say they can), "ha detto che poteva" (he/she said he/she could).
target_language_example: Dice che può venire più tardi.
native_language_example: He/She says he/she can come later.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says about their physical or emotional state. "si sente" is from "sentirsi" (to feel), and the subject is understood from context (lui/lei). You can add an adjective or phrase after it: "dice che si sente meglio" (feels better), "dice che si sente dispiaciuta" (feels sorry).
target_language_example: Marco dice che si sente stanco oggi.
native_language_example: Marco says he feels tired today.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone claims or states they want to do. The subject is often implied from context (lui/lei, Maria, Tom, etc.). Note: Italian **dice** means “says/tells” and can be confused with English “dice” (the game pieces).
target_language_example: Mio fratello dice che vuole cambiare lavoro.
native_language_example: My brother says he wants to change jobs.

meaning: "(He/She) says he/she wants to speak with…"
additional_notes: Used to report what someone says (indirect speech): **dice che + [verb]**. **Vuole parlare con + [person]** means “wants to talk/speak with [someone].” The subject (lui/lei) is often implied by context; you can change the verb for different subjects (e.g., *dico che voglio parlare con…*, *dicono che vogliono parlare con…*).
target_language_example: Dice che vuole parlare con il responsabile.
native_language_example: He says he wants to speak with the manager.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says: **dire** (to say) in the present (**dice**) + **che** (that) + **è** (is). Often introduces an opinion, description, or claim. If you need the subject, you can add it: **Lui/Lei dice che è…**; for “they say” (people in general), you can use **La gente dice che è…**.
target_language_example: Lui dice che è troppo caro, ma a me piace lo stesso.
native_language_example: He says it’s too expensive, but I like it anyway.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive. dice is the he/she/it form of dire. When the subject stays the same, it often means 'says that...' in natural English: dice di sapere = 'says that he/she knows'. If there is an indirect object pronoun (mi, ti, gli, le, ci, vi), it can mean 'tell someone to...': le dice di fare = 'tells her to do'.
target_language_example: Luca dice di essere pronto.
native_language_example: Luca says he's ready.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone says they need. It’s built from: dice = “(he/she) says”, di avere bisogno di = “to need”. After bisogno di you can use a noun (di aiuto, di una vacanza) or an infinitive verb (di parlare, di farlo). You can change dice to dico/dici/dicono, etc., depending on who is speaking.
target_language_example: Lui dice di avere bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: He says he needs more time.

additional_notes: Common reporting structure: **dire + di + infinitive**. Here **non avere** = “not to have.” The subject is the person speaking (lui/lei) and is often clear from context: *Tom dice di non avere…* = “Tom says he doesn’t have…”. Usually followed by what is lacking (e.g., *scelta* = choice, *tempo* = time, *rimpianti* = regrets).
target_language_example: Dice di non avere tempo oggi.
native_language_example: He/She says (that) he/she doesn’t have time today.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone is telling the truth. It’s the present tense of "dire" (to say/tell): "dice" can mean "he/she says" or "he/she tells". You can change the subject: "Dico la verità" (I tell the truth), "Dici la verità" (you tell the truth), "Dicono la verità" (they tell the truth).
target_language_example: Credo che dice la verità.
native_language_example: I think he/she is telling the truth.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech or an explanation of what someone said. Often follows a verb of speaking/calling/apologizing: “mi ha chiamato… dicendo che…”. With “ti sto dicendo che…”, it’s a common way to emphasize or clarify a point (“I’m telling you that…”).
target_language_example: Ti sto dicendo che non devi preoccuparti.
native_language_example: I'm telling you that you don't have to worry.

additional_notes: Gerund of "dire" (to say/tell). Often used with "stare" to talk about an action in progress: "Mi stai dicendo la verità?" = "Are you telling me the truth?" You can also use it after verbs like "pensare" or "sapere" to report what someone was doing: "pensavo che stesse dicendo la verità".
target_language_example: Non credo che tu stia dicendo la verità.
native_language_example: I don't think you're telling the truth.

meaning: "he/she was saying that" / "he/she used to say that".
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, thought, or claimed. "Diceva" is the imperfect tense of *dire* (to say), so it often suggests something ongoing in the past (was saying) or repeated/habitual (used to say), depending on context. The subject (he/she) is usually understood from context: *Lui/lei diceva che...*.
target_language_example: Quando ero piccolo, mia nonna diceva che dovevo mangiare più verdura.
native_language_example: When I was little, my grandma used to say that I had to eat more vegetables.

meaning: 'what do you say about...?' / 'how about...?' or 'you say/claim to...'.
additional_notes: Used mainly with questions like “Che/Cosa (ne) dici di…?” to ask someone’s opinion or to make a suggestion (“How about…?”). It can also be used with an infinitive to report a claim: “dici di essere…” = “you say you are…”. Often paired with “che/cosa” and sometimes “ne” (a small pronoun meaning roughly “about it”).
target_language_example: Che dici di prendere un caffè insieme?
native_language_example: How about having a coffee together?

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you’re not joking and what you’re saying is true. Often said with emphasis or as an exclamation (e.g., “No, dico sul serio!”). You can also hear it as “ti dico sul serio” (“I’m telling you seriously”).
target_language_example: Dico sul serio: non ho più soldi.
native_language_example: I’m serious: I don’t have any money left.

additional_notes: Used to report what others say (hearsay/rumor) or to introduce reported speech. Literally “they say that.” It’s the present tense of dire (“to say”): dicono = “they say,” followed by che = “that.” After che, Italian may use the indicative (facts/neutral reporting) or the subjunctive (often with opinions/uncertainty), depending on context.
target_language_example: Dicono che questo ristorante sia molto buono.
native_language_example: They say this restaurant is very good.

additional_notes: Used to report what other people claim or say. **Dicono** = “they say” (3rd person plural), and **che** introduces the following clause. Often followed by an infinitive (e.g., *venire*, *parlare*, *lasciare*) to express what they want to do.
target_language_example: Dicono che vogliono cambiare lavoro.
native_language_example: They say they want to change jobs.

additional_notes: Used to talk about duration (per/da dieci anni = for ten years), age (ha dieci anni = is ten years old), and comparisons (dieci anni più giovane = ten years younger). Also common in time expressions like sono passati dieci anni = ten years have passed.
target_language_example: Lavoro qui da dieci anni.
native_language_example: I’ve worked here for ten years.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened 10 years before now (or before the time you’re talking about). Commonly placed at the end of the sentence (e.g., “È successo dieci anni fa.”). You can swap the number: “due anni fa” (two years ago), “venti anni fa” (twenty years ago).
target_language_example: Abbiamo comprato questa casa dieci anni fa.
native_language_example: We bought this house ten years ago.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money in dollars, often after "per" (for) to say the price ("per dieci dollari" = for ten dollars), or with verbs like "dare" (to give) and "scommettere" (to bet).
target_language_example: Te lo vendo per dieci dollari.
native_language_example: I’ll sell it to you for ten dollars.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration or a time offset. Common patterns: “tra/fra dieci minuti” = “in ten minutes” (from now); “in dieci minuti” = “in ten minutes” (time it takes); “(essere) indietro/avanti di dieci minuti” = “(to be) ten minutes slow/fast” (about clocks).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: See you in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a very short amount of time or a countdown (e.g., “you have ten seconds left”). Often appears with verbs like "restare" (to be left): "Ti restano dieci secondi" = "You have ten seconds left."
target_language_example: Aspetta dieci secondi, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait ten seconds, please.

meaning: “(He/She) fed the …” / “(He/She) gave food to the …”.
additional_notes: Past historic/remote past of the phrase “dare da mangiare a” = “to feed” (literally “to give to eat”). Used especially in written stories or in some regions for past actions. “al” = “a + il” (“to the”). You can also say “ha dato da mangiare al …” (more common in everyday speech).
target_language_example: Diede da mangiare al gatto prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He/She fed the cat before going out.

additional_notes: “Diede” is the passato remoto (simple past) of dare (“to give”), used often in books, stories, and in some regions (especially in the South) for completed past actions. It’s commonly followed by a direct object with an article (“un premio/un regalo/un libro”) and often an indirect object with a/alle or a pronoun: “diede un premio a John”, “le diede un regalo”. It can also be used in set phrases like “diede un morso” = “took a bite”.
target_language_example: Ieri Maria diede un consiglio a Luca.
native_language_example: Yesterday Maria gave Luca some advice.

additional_notes: "Diede" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "dare" (to give), used especially in stories, books, and in some regions (more common in the South) to talk about completed actions in the past. In everyday conversation, you’ll often hear "ha dato un bel regalo" instead. "Un bel" means "a nice" ("bello" becomes "bel" before a consonant like r in "regalo").
target_language_example: Per il suo compleanno, diede un bel regalo a sua sorella.
native_language_example: For her birthday, he/she gave his/her sister a nice gift.

additional_notes: “Diede” is the passato remoto (simple past) of dare (“to give”), common in storytelling and in some regions of Italy; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear “ha dato un regalo” instead. The receiver can be shown with “a + person” (Diede un regalo a Tom) or with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi diede un regalo).
target_language_example: Ieri mi diede un regalo per il compleanno.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she gave me a birthday present.

additional_notes: From the verb "dare" (to give). "Diede" is the passato remoto (a narrative/literary past tense, common in books and historical storytelling; in everyday speech many regions prefer "ha dato"). "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article, so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., "una bambola", "una spinta"). Often used with "a" to mark the recipient: "diede una collana a Maria".
target_language_example: Il re diede una risposta al messaggero.
native_language_example: The king gave an answer to the messenger.

meaning: “I gave my half” / “I gave my share.”
additional_notes: "Diedi" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "dare" (to give), often used in stories or in some regions instead of "ho dato". "La mia metà" means “my half/my share” of something (money, food, a bill, etc.). You can add an indirect object: "a Tom" (to Tom), "a loro" (to them), or use pronouns: "gli diedi" (I gave him), "le diedi" (I gave her), "gli diedi" (I gave them).
target_language_example: Quando abbiamo diviso la pizza, diedi la mia metà a mia sorella.
native_language_example: When we split the pizza, I gave my half to my sister.

additional_notes: Means you promised/swear you will do something (a serious commitment). "Diedi" is the passato remoto of "dare" (to give), common in literature/storytelling or in some regions for past events; in everyday speech you’ll often hear "ho dato la mia parola". You can add an indirect object pronoun to say who you promised: "Gli diedi la mia parola" (I gave him my word), "Le diedi la mia parola" (…to her), "Vi diedi la mia parola" (…to you all).
target_language_example: Ti diedi la mia parola che sarei tornato.
native_language_example: I gave you my word that I would come back.

additional_notes: Used to indicate position or movement to the back of something: *dietro la casa* (behind the house), *dietro la scrivania* (behind the desk). It’s made of *dietro* + the feminine singular definite article *la*; with other nouns you’ll see *dietro il / lo / i / gli / le*. In expressions like *avere gli occhi dietro la testa*, it’s figurative: “to be very watchful / to notice everything.”
target_language_example: Il gatto è dietro la porta.
native_language_example: The cat is behind the door.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a position/location on the other side of a door (often partially hidden). Common in instructions like “Controlla dietro la porta” (“Check behind the door”) or “Mettiti dietro la porta” (“Get behind the door”). In phrases like “(La porta) si chiuda dietro la porta”, it refers to closing the door behind you (i.e., after you pass through).
target_language_example: Ho trovato le chiavi dietro la porta.
native_language_example: I found the keys behind the door.

additional_notes: Used literally for physical position (hands/objects behind the back). It can also be used figuratively ("alle spalle/di nascosto"), but in these examples it’s physical: "Metti le mani dietro la schiena" = put your hands behind your back.
target_language_example: Tieni lo zaino dietro la schiena mentre attraversi la strada.
native_language_example: Keep the backpack behind your back while you cross the street.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something physically located behind something else (e.g., dietro le montagne, dietro le mura) or figuratively what is hidden/underlying (dietro le parole = “behind the words”). It must be followed by a feminine plural noun; compare: dietro il/lo (masc. singular), dietro i/gli (masc. plural), dietro la (fem. singular).
target_language_example: C'è un parcheggio dietro le case.
native_language_example: There’s a parking lot behind the houses.

meaning: behind the scenes; out of the spotlight.
additional_notes: Literally “behind the curtains” (theater). Used for work that happens privately or in the background, or for someone who prefers not to be seen/featured publicly (stare/lavorare dietro le quinte).
target_language_example: Lei organizza tutto dietro le quinte, ma non vuole apparire.
native_language_example: She organizes everything behind the scenes, but she doesn’t want to appear in public.

additional_notes: Used to mean someone is in prison/jail. Common with verbs like essere/restare (“to be/stay”) or mettere (“to put”): "mettere qualcuno dietro le sbarre" = to send someone to jail. Often used figuratively, but it refers to real imprisonment.
target_language_example: Se continui così, finirai dietro le sbarre.
native_language_example: If you keep this up, you’ll end up behind bars.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "dietro" to say someone/something is positioned or hides behind a tree. Often appears with verbs like "essere" (to be), "nascondersi" (to hide), "andare" (to go), and in phrases like "da dietro un albero" (= from behind a tree).
target_language_example: Il cane si è nascosto dietro un albero.
native_language_example: The dog hid behind a tree.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is located behind a person or object. It’s commonly followed by a stressed pronoun: dietro di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro (e.g., "Dietro di te"). You can also hear "dietro" alone (e.g., "sono dietro" = "I’m behind/in the back"), but "dietro di" is typical right before pronouns.
target_language_example: C'è un gatto dietro di noi.
native_language_example: There’s a cat behind us.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is positioned at your back (physically behind you). Often used with verbs like essere/stare: “È dietro di me?” = “Is it behind me?” You can swap “me” for other pronouns: dietro di te (behind you), dietro di lui/lei (behind him/her), dietro di noi (behind us).
target_language_example: Scusa, puoi passare? Sei dietro di me.
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you get by? You're behind me.

additional_notes: Used to indicate the position of someone/something behind the person you’re speaking to. Very common as a warning ("Attento!", "Guarda!") or to say where you are sitting/standing. In sentences it can be used with verbs like "essere" (to be), "stare" (to be/stand), "sedersi" (to sit), or "camminare" (to walk) to describe location.
target_language_example: C'è una macchina dietro di te, spostati un attimo.
native_language_example: There’s a car behind you—move over for a moment.

additional_notes: Uses the common pattern “la differenza tra X e Y” (“the difference between X and Y”). Here, “argento” = silver and “stagno” = tin (a metal). Note: “stagno” can also mean “pond” in other contexts, but with metals it means tin.
target_language_example: Qual è la differenza tra argento e stagno?
native_language_example: What’s the difference between silver and tin?

additional_notes: Used to say something is hard to do: difficile da + infinitive (imparare, pronunciare, rispondere, fare, capire, trovare, ecc.). The subject can be a thing/person: Questa lingua è difficile da imparare. Note: in everyday Italian you also often hear “difficile da + infinitive” where more formal grammar might prefer “difficile + infinitive” (e.g., È difficile capirlo).
target_language_example: Questo numero è difficile da ricordare.
native_language_example: This number is hard to remember.

additional_notes: Used to say that written text is not easy to read (because of messy handwriting, small print, poor quality, or because it’s in a language you don’t know well). Pattern: "è difficile da + infinitive" = "it’s hard to + verb" (e.g., difficile da capire = hard to understand).
target_language_example: Questa scritta è troppo piccola: è difficile da leggere.
native_language_example: This writing is too small: it’s hard to read.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for a particular person or group. It’s often followed by a pronoun (me, you, him/her, us, them): difficile per me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro. It can also be used with an infinitive: È difficile per Tom farlo. Agreement: difficile becomes difficile/difficili and can match what’s difficult (un momento difficile; delle decisioni difficili).
target_language_example: È stato difficile per me imparare l’italiano all’inizio.
native_language_example: It was hard for me to learn Italian at the beginning.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is hard for you personally. Often appears as "È/era/è stato difficile per me..." + infinitive (e.g., "dire", "fare", "capire") or with "troppo" to mean "too difficult for me".
target_language_example: È difficile per me capire questo esercizio.
native_language_example: It’s difficult for me to understand this exercise.

additional_notes: Used with a plural subject: **difficili da + infinitive**. With a singular subject, you’ll see **difficile da** (e.g., *È difficile da capire* = “It’s hard to understand”). The verb after **da** stays in the infinitive (*capire, fare, comprendere*).
target_language_example: Questi esercizi sono difficili da capire.
native_language_example: These exercises are hard to understand.

additional_notes: Used to report a message to a third person: **di'** (imperative of *dire*, “to say/tell”) + **gli** (“to him”) + **che** (“that”). You usually follow it with a complete clause: *Digli che arrivo presto.* It can also mean “tell them that…” in some contexts, but the most common beginner meaning is “tell him that…”.
target_language_example: Per favore, digli che sono in ritardo.
native_language_example: Please tell him that I'm late.

additional_notes: Used to give an instruction to a third person (him): **Digli di + infinitive**. It’s the imperative **di’** (tell) + indirect object pronoun **gli** (to him). Variants: **dille di…** (tell her to…), **ditegli di…** (tell him, plural/formal), **digli che…** is used with a full clause instead of an infinitive.
target_language_example: Digli di chiamarmi appena arriva.
native_language_example: Tell him to call me as soon as he arrives.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone to pass a message to a woman/girl. It’s the informal imperative of "dire" ("dì") + the indirect object pronoun "le" (to her) + "che" (that). In formal Italian you’d say: "Le dica che…" (tell her that…).
target_language_example: Dille che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Tell her that I’ll be there in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dimenticare" (often as the past participle "dimenticato") + "di". Use it with an infinitive to mean "forgot to do" (e.g., "Ho dimenticato di chiudere la porta" = "I forgot to close the door"). Use it with a person/thing to mean "forgot about" (e.g., "Mi sono dimenticato di Tom" = "I forgot about Tom"). Often appears in the reflexive form "(mi/ti/si) sono dimenticato/a di" in the past.
target_language_example: Mi sono dimenticato di comprare il latte.
native_language_example: I forgot to buy milk.

dimenticato di chiudere a chiave la

target_language_multi_word_term: dimenticato di chiudere a chiave la
meaning: 'forgot to lock the …' (with a feminine noun, e.g. 'la porta').
additional_notes: Used to say you forgot to lock something with a key. It must be followed by a feminine noun (la porta = the door, la macchina = the car). For a masculine noun, use: "dimenticato di chiudere a chiave il" (e.g. "il cancello"). Common structure: "Ho dimenticato di + [verb]" = "I forgot to + [verb]".
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato di chiudere a chiave la porta.
native_language_example: I forgot to lock the door.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pattern "dimenticare di + infinitive" to say you forgot to do something (here: to buy). In the past, you’ll often see it as "ho/hai/ha dimenticato di comprare…" (with avere) or "mi/ti/si è dimenticato/a di comprare…" (common alternative, especially in spoken Italian).
target_language_example: Mi sono dimenticato di comprare il latte.
native_language_example: I forgot to buy milk.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "dimenticare" (to forget) + a masculine singular noun: "dimenticato il + noun" (e.g., "Ho dimenticato il libro" = "I forgot the book"). In everyday Italian you may also hear "(si) è dimenticato di + noun" (e.g., "Mi sono dimenticato del compleanno"). Word order changes with questions and other sentence structures, but the idea stays the same: forgetting something specific introduced by "il".
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il biglietto a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot the ticket at home.

additional_notes: Fragment often used when the thing that was forgotten is understood from context. In Italian, possessives usually take the definite article: “il suo” = “his/hers/its” (masculine singular). Common in sentences like “Ha dimenticato il suo + noun” (e.g., “il suo telefono”).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio biglietto, e lui ha dimenticato il suo.
native_language_example: I forgot my ticket, and he forgot his.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with avere to say someone forgot their umbrella (e.g., ha/aveva dimenticato il suo ombrello). You can change the possessive depending on the person: il mio (my), il tuo (your), il suo (his/her), il nostro (our), il vostro (your plural), il loro (their). In many contexts Italians also say: si è dimenticato/a il suo ombrello (reflexive).
target_language_example: Tom aveva dimenticato il suo ombrello, così gli ho prestato uno dei miei.
native_language_example: Tom had forgotten his umbrella, so I lent him one of mine.

meaning: “forgot to” (simple past: he/she forgot to do something).
additional_notes: “Dimenticò di” is the passato remoto (remote past) of “dimenticare di” and is common in storytelling, books, and some regions of Italy. In everyday conversation many speakers use the passato prossimo instead: “ha dimenticato di…”. You’ll also often see the reflexive version “si dimenticò di…”. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamare, firmare, dire).
target_language_example: Dimenticò di spegnere le luci prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He/She forgot to turn off the lights before going out.

additional_notes: "Dimenticò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of "dimenticare" (to forget), often used in stories or in some regions in place of "ha dimenticato." "Chiudere a chiave" means "to lock" (literally, "to close with a key"). It’s followed by what you forgot to lock: "la porta", "casa", "l’auto".
target_language_example: Ieri dimenticò di chiudere a chiave l’ufficio.
native_language_example: Yesterday he forgot to lock the office.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is determined by (or varies according to) a person, thing, or situation. The structure is usually: [something] dipende da + noun/pronoun (dipende da te = it depends on you) or da + clause/idea (dipende da quello che fai = it depends on what you do). Note the combined forms with articles: da + il = dal, da + lo = dallo, da + la = dalla, da + i = dai, da + gli = dagli, da + le = dalle.
target_language_example: La risposta dipende da come ti senti oggi.
native_language_example: The answer depends on how you feel today.

additional_notes: Used to say the result or answer changes based on a factor: Dipende dal + noun. It’s the contraction of di + il (“of/from the”). Use dipende dalla for feminine singular (dalla situazione), dipende dai for masculine plural (dai dettagli), and dipende dalle for feminine plural (dalle circostanze).
target_language_example: Dipende dal prezzo: se è troppo alto, non lo compro.
native_language_example: It depends on the price: if it’s too high, I won’t buy it.

additional_notes: Used when you mention the person who receives the message: dire a qualcuno = to say/tell something to someone. It is often followed by di + infinitive to mean telling someone to do something: dire a qualcuno di venire = to tell someone to come.
target_language_example: Devo dire a Marco che siamo in ritardo.
native_language_example: I have to tell Marco that we're late.

meaning: to tell them; to say it to them.
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object introduced by **a** (“to”). In everyday Italian, **a loro** is often used for emphasis/clarity; it’s also very common to replace it with an indirect object pronoun: **dire a loro** → **dirgli** (“to tell them”), e.g. **Glielo devo dire** = “I have to tell them (it).”.
target_language_example: Devo dire a loro la verità.
native_language_example: I have to tell them the truth.

meaning: to say goodbye; to bid farewell.
additional_notes: Used for taking leave from a person or (more figuratively) from something like memories, a place, or a phase of life. Often sounds more emotional or final than just saying "ciao" or "arrivederci." You can say "dire addio a qualcuno/qualcosa" (to say goodbye to someone/something).
target_language_example: Devo dire addio a questa città domani.
native_language_example: I have to say goodbye to this city tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a full clause after reporting, explaining, or clarifying something. In phrases like «vuoi dire che...?» or «volevo dire che...», it often means «do you mean that...? / I meant that...». After negative expressions such as «non posso dire che...», the following verb is often in the subjunctive.
target_language_example: Volevo dire che mi dispiace per il ritardo.
native_language_example: I meant to say that I'm sorry for the delay.

additional_notes: Used to express refusal or to set a boundary. Often followed by what you’re refusing (e.g., “dire di no a qualcosa/qualcuno” = “to say no to something/someone”). You can also use gestures with it: “scuotere la testa per dire di no” = “to shake your head to say no.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, devo dire di no alla tua proposta.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I have to say no to your proposal.

additional_notes: Used to ask for more information, especially about a person. It’s most commonly followed by a stressed pronoun after "di" ("su di lui/lei/loro") or a name ("su di Maria"). With things, Italian often drops "di" and uses "su" + noun ("su questo argomento"), but the version with "su di" is required with pronouns. Polite forms include "Mi può…" / "Mi riesce a…"; informal is "Mi puoi…".
target_language_example: Mi puoi dire di più su di lei?
native_language_example: Can you tell me more about her?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest clarification, correction, or slightly contrasting point. Often appears as "A dire il vero, ..." ("To tell the truth, ...") or "Per dire il vero, ...". Neutral in tone (not slang).
target_language_example: A dire il vero, non ho molta voglia di uscire stasera.
native_language_example: To tell the truth, I don’t really feel like going out tonight.

additional_notes: Used when someone speaks honestly instead of lying or hiding something. Often appears with modal verbs (dovere/potere/volere) or in phrases like “a dire la verità …” = “to tell you the truth … / honestly …”.
target_language_example: È difficile, ma devo dire la verità.
native_language_example: It’s hard, but I have to tell the truth.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object introduced by a (a Tom, a Mary). Often appears with verbs like dovere (must/have to) or potere/dovrebbe (should) when talking about honesty or confessing something.
target_language_example: È meglio dire la verità a tua madre.
native_language_example: It’s better to tell the truth to your mother.

additional_notes: Often used with "non" to mean “don’t say anything / don’t say a word”: "Non dire niente." You’ll also hear it after another verb with "di" + infinitive: "Mi ha detto di non dire niente" = “He/she told me not to say anything.”
target_language_example: Per favore, non dire niente a nessuno.
native_language_example: Please, don’t tell anyone anything.

meaning: to say nothing / not say anything.
additional_notes: Very common with the negation: **non dire nulla** = “don’t say anything / say nothing.” It can be used as an order (**Non dire nulla!**) or to mean you can’t reveal or comment on something (**Per ora non posso dire nulla** = “For now I can’t say anything.”). Often followed by a clause specifying what you avoid saying: **non dire nulla che...** = “not say anything that...”.
target_language_example: Non dire nulla a nessuno, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone anything, please.

additional_notes: Used when you need to speak up or communicate a message. Often followed by the person you’re speaking to: "dire qualcosa a + person" (e.g., "Devo dire qualcosa a Tom"). With pronouns, the person can come before the verb: "ti/le/gli devo dire qualcosa" = "I have to tell you/her/him something."
target_language_example: Scusa, devo dire qualcosa a tutti prima di andare via.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to tell everyone something before leaving.

additional_notes: Used when someone isn’t able/willing to speak, or to stress that there are no limits on what can be said. Often after expressions like "prima che" (before), "troppo ... per" (too ... to), or verbs like "avere paura di" (to be afraid to). It can also mean "to say whatever" depending on context.
target_language_example: Non ho avuto il tempo di dire qualsiasi cosa.
native_language_example: I didn’t have time to say anything.

meaning: to say anything; to say anything at all.
additional_notes: Means saying anything at all, often in contexts of hesitation, fear, or reluctance to speak. With "puoi" it can emphasize that there are no restrictions on what may be said (e.g., "Puoi dire qualunque cosa"). Close variants: "dire qualsiasi cosa" (same meaning), "dire qualcosa" (to say something), "non dire nulla" (to say nothing).
target_language_example: Tom aveva paura di dire qualunque cosa.
native_language_example: Tom was afraid to say anything.

additional_notes: Used when talking about expressing certain statements/remarks, often with emphasis or disapproval depending on context (e.g., “How can you say such things?”). In speech, Italian often moves object pronouns before the verb and can repeat the noun for emphasis: “Me le devi dire, queste cose” = “You have to tell me these things.”
target_language_example: Non puoi dire queste cose a tua madre.
native_language_example: You can’t say these things to your mother.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say something (introducing a statement) or when reacting to what someone said, often with a modifier: “dire una cosa del genere” (say something like that), “così ridicola/crudele” (so ridiculous/cruel). Common in questions or negatives: “Come puoi…?” “Non dire…”.
target_language_example: Posso dire una cosa?
native_language_example: Can I say something?

additional_notes: Often used in the negative as a firm instruction: “Non dire una parola!” = “Don’t say a word!” It can also mean “without saying anything” in phrases like “senza (nemmeno) dire una parola” = “without (even) saying a word.”
target_language_example: Ti prego, non dire una parola finché non arriviamo a casa.
native_language_example: Please, don’t say a word until we get home.

additional_notes: Used with movement verbs (andare, venire, tornare) to say you go home without stopping anywhere else first. Often placed after the verb phrase: “Sono andato direttamente a casa.”
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro sono andata direttamente a casa.
native_language_example: After work I went straight home.

additional_notes: "Dirgli" = "dire" (to tell) + "gli" (to him). Used when you want to say you should/must be honest with a man or boy. You can swap the pronoun: dirle la verità (tell her the truth), dirvi la verità (tell you the truth), dirci la verità (tell us the truth).
target_language_example: È meglio dirgli la verità adesso.
native_language_example: It’s better to tell him the truth now.

additional_notes: Used in formal or neutral contexts (news, law, politics) to talk about basic rights and freedoms everyone should have. Commonly appears with verbs/nouns like: rispettare (to respect), violare (to violate), difendere (to defend), una violazione dei diritti umani (a human-rights violation), un avvocato per i diritti umani (a human-rights lawyer).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo difendere i diritti umani di tutti.
native_language_example: We must defend everyone’s human rights.

meaning: 'the right to' (to be allowed/entitled to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to talk about someone’s entitlement or permission to do something: avere diritto di... = “to have the right to...”. Common intensifiers: tutto il diritto di (“every right to”), alcun diritto di (“any right to” in negatives), ogni diritto di (“every right to”). Often appears in negatives to say someone is not entitled: Non hai/avete diritto di... (“You don’t have the right to...”).
target_language_example: Hai diritto di chiedere una spiegazione.
native_language_example: You have the right to ask for an explanation.

additional_notes: Uses the indirect object pronoun **le** (= “to her”) attached to the infinitive **dire** (“to tell/say”). Often used with modal/conditional forms like **dovrei/avrei dovuto** (“I should / I should have”) or in phrases like **Se devo dirle la verità...** (“If I have to tell you the truth...”); with a different person, change **le** (e.g., **dirti la verità** = to tell you the truth).
target_language_example: Devo dirle la verità: ho perso il biglietto.
native_language_example: I have to tell her the truth: I lost the ticket.

additional_notes: Used when you want to say/tell “it” (lo = “it”) to someone: dire + lo + a + person. Often follows another verb (e.g., assicurarsi di…, avere paura di…, dimenticare di…): “di dirlo a lui” = “to tell it to him.” In everyday Italian this is frequently merged with the indirect object pronoun: “dirlo a lui” → “dirglielo” (to tell it to him), “dirlo a Tom” → “dirglielo” (if Tom is “him”).
target_language_example: Devo dirlo a Maria prima di cena.
native_language_example: I have to tell it to Maria before dinner.

additional_notes: "Dirlo" = "dire" (to say/tell) + "lo" (it). "A lei" means "to her" (formal or simply "to her" when referring to a woman/girl). Used when you’re talking about telling some piece of information to a female person; with questions/commands like "Vuole/Può/Vada/Si assicuri di dirlo a lei".
target_language_example: Devo dirlo a lei prima di sera.
native_language_example: I have to tell it to her before evening.

additional_notes: "Dirlo" = "to say/tell it" (dire + lo). "A loro" = "to them" (emphasized; often used instead of just "gli" / "a loro" can clarify who you mean). Common in questions and instructions: "Hai paura di dirlo a loro?" / "Assicurati di dirlo a loro."
target_language_example: Puoi dirlo a loro, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you tell it to them, please?

meaning: to tell it to anyone (used with negation: “to tell nobody/no one”).
additional_notes: Made of: dire (to say/tell) + lo (it) + a nessuno (to nobody/anyone). It’s most commonly used with a negative (non, non puoi, non voleva, non ha voluto), where Italian uses “nessuno” to mean “anyone” in a negative sentence: Non puoi dirlo a nessuno = “You can’t tell anyone” / “Tell no one.” You can swap “lo” for another object pronoun: dirla a nessuno (it, feminine), dirgli a nessuno isn’t correct because “gli” already means “to him” (different structure).
target_language_example: Per favore, non dirlo a nessuno: è un segreto.
native_language_example: Please don’t tell anyone: it’s a secret.

meaning: “tell me how to get (there)” / “give me directions (to).”
additional_notes: Used to politely ask for directions. It’s built from dire (“to tell”) + mi (“to me”) + come (“how”) + arrivare (“to arrive/get”). Often followed by a place with a (“to”) or da qui/da qua (“from here”). You’ll commonly see it with polite forms like Potresti…? (informal you) / Potreste…? (formal or plural you) or Puoi…?
target_language_example: Scusi, può dirmi come arrivare al museo da qui?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can you tell me how to get to the museum from here?

additional_notes: Used to ask for more information about a person/thing. It’s built from: dire (to say/tell) + mi (to me) + di più (more) + su di (about). Often followed by a pronoun like lui (him) / lei (her) or a noun: “Puoi dirmi di più su di Marco?” You can change the person: “dirmi” → “dirci” (tell us), “dirle” (tell you formal/sir/ma’am), etc.
target_language_example: Puoi dirmi di più su di questo corso?
native_language_example: Can you tell me more about this course?

additional_notes: Used when introducing something you want to say to someone (often important, personal, or a bit delicate). It commonly appears with verbs like devo/volevo/voglio (“I have to / I wanted to / I want to”) and can be followed by però (“though/but”) to signal a reservation or add a twist.
target_language_example: Ehi, posso dirti una cosa?
native_language_example: Hey, can I tell you something?

meaning: "nightclub all night (long)" / "going to a nightclub for the whole night."
additional_notes: Literally “nightclub for the whole night.” In real Italian you’ll more often hear it as part of a longer sentence, e.g. **andare in discoteca tutta la notte** (“to go clubbing all night”) or **stare in discoteca tutta la notte** (“to stay at the nightclub all night”). **Per tutta la notte** means “all night (long).”
target_language_example: Siamo andati in discoteca per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: We went clubbing all night long.

meaning: “sorry for having … (done something to you)” (usually: “Mi dispiace di averti …”).
additional_notes: This is not a complete sentence on its own: you normally say **Mi dispiace di averti + past participle** (e.g., svegliato/a, disturbato/a, fatto aspettare). **averti** = “to have you” (informal singular “you”), used to build the past infinitive: “to have + done.” Make the past participle agree in gender/number when needed (e.g., **averti disturbata** to a woman).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace di averti disturbato ieri sera.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for disturbing you last night.

meaning: "(to be) sorry about/for" (used to express regret or sympathy).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **Mi dispiace per...** (“I’m sorry about/for...”), to react to bad news or to apologize for a situation. You can follow it with a noun (e.g., *il ritardo*, *la tua perdita*) or a person/thing you feel sorry for.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per il ritardo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry about the delay.

meaning: “Do you mind if…?” / “Would it bother you if…?”
additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission or check if something is okay. The structure is typically (Non) ti/gli/le dispiace se + verb (present) to mean “(Don’t) you/he/she mind if…”. Often appears in questions with "Non" to sound softer: "Non ti dispiace se…?" ≈ “You don’t mind if…?”.
target_language_example: Ti dispiace se apro la finestra?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

meaning: "Do you mind if I sit down?"
additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission before sitting. Very common as a question: "Ti dispiace se mi siedo?" (to a friend) or more formal "Le dispiace se mi siedo?" (to a stranger/older person). You can also say "Posso sedermi?" for a simpler "Can I sit down?".
target_language_example: Le dispiace se mi siedo qui?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I sit here?

meaning: 'I'm very sorry' / 'it really bothers (me)' (often in apologies).
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **Mi dispiace tanto** (“I’m very sorry”). With pronouns it can mean “it bothers + someone a lot”: **Mi/ti/le/gli dispiace tanto**. Often followed by **per** + noun/verb: **Mi dispiace tanto per il ritardo** (“I’m very sorry about the delay”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace tanto per quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I’m very sorry about what happened.

additional_notes: Used to express sympathy for a man (“lui”). Often appears with verbs like sentirsi (“to feel”) or essere (“to be”): "mi sento dispiaciuta per lui". Dispiaciuta is feminine; a male speaker would usually say "dispiaciuto per lui". "Dispiaciuto" means “sorry” (not “displeased”).
target_language_example: Mi sento dispiaciuta per lui, ma non posso aiutarlo.
native_language_example: I feel sorry for him, but I can’t help him.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form (used with a woman or a feminine noun). It’s followed by an infinitive verb. The masculine form is "disposto a" (or "disposto ad" before a vowel). Common for offering, agreeing, or being open to doing something: "Sono disposta ad aiutarti" = "I’m willing to help you."
target_language_example: Se serve, sono disposta ad aspettare qualche minuto.
native_language_example: If needed, I’m willing to wait a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state that a woman/girl is willing to help someone. "Disposta" agrees with a female subject; for a male subject use "disposto ad aiutare". Often used with "essere" (e.g., "Sei disposta ad aiutare...?", "È disposta ad aiutare...?").
target_language_example: Sei disposta ad aiutare Tom domani?
native_language_example: Are you willing to help Tom tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is willing/ready to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive verb (disposto ad + verb), e.g. disposto ad aiutare. It agrees with the person: disposto (male), disposta (female), disposti/disposte (plural). Often appears with conditional forms (sarei disposto/a...) to sound more polite or hypothetical: “I would be willing to…”.
target_language_example: Sarei disposto ad aiutarti, ma oggi non posso.
native_language_example: I would be willing to help you, but I can't today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is ready/agreeable to help (often implying they choose to do it, not that they are forced). With a specific person, add the direct object: "disposto ad aiutare Tom". Agreement: "disposto" (male) / "disposta" (female). After the preposition, use "ad" before a vowel: "ad aiutare" (vs. "a" before most consonants).
target_language_example: Sono disposto ad aiutare, ma ho bisogno di istruzioni chiare.
native_language_example: I'm willing to help, but I need clear instructions.

additional_notes: Past historic (passato remoto) of *dire a* (“to say/tell to”). It introduces who the message is addressed to: *disse a Maria…* = “he/she told Maria…”. Common in stories and writing; in everyday conversation you’ll more often hear *ha detto a* (“said/told to”).
target_language_example: Il poliziotto disse a Luca di restare calmo.
native_language_example: The police officer told Luca to stay calm.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato remoto) of dire (“to say/tell”), common in stories and written narration. Used to report what someone told everyone. After che era you add an adjective/noun phrase: interessata/o (interested), sola/o (alone), stanca/o (tired), nervosa/o (nervous). Era agrees with the subject being described, and the adjective also changes for gender/number (stanco/stanca; interessato/interessata).
target_language_example: Disse a tutti che era felice di essere lì.
native_language_example: He/She told everyone that he/she was happy to be there.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the passato remoto form of dire ("to say"). It is common in books, stories, and historical narration; in everyday spoken Italian, "ha detto che" is usually more common. "Che" introduces reported speech and often corresponds to English "that," which is sometimes omitted in English.
target_language_example: Luca disse che non aveva fame.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wasn't hungry.

additional_notes: Used in reported/indirect speech in the past. Italian often uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”) with an indirect object: a lui piaceva = “he liked it” (literally “it was pleasing to him”). You can add what was liked after it (e.g., il film, la pizza) or use a pronoun (gli piaceva).
target_language_example: Marco disse che a lui piaceva il film, ma a me non piaceva.
native_language_example: Marco said that he liked the movie, but I didn’t like it.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech. disse is the passato remoto of dire, so it is common in writing, stories, and more formal narration; in everyday speech, ha detto che aveva is more common. Italian usually leaves out the subject pronoun, so aveva can refer to he, she, or formal you from context. Also, avere is used in many expressions where English does not use 'have', such as aveva fame = 'was hungry' and aveva paura = 'was afraid'.
target_language_example: Paolo disse che aveva perso il portafoglio.
native_language_example: Paolo said that he had lost his wallet.

additional_notes: Past tense reporting: **disse** = “(he/she) said” (passato remoto, common in writing and storytelling); **che** = “that”; **aveva bisogno di** = “(he/she) needed” / literally “had need of.” The person and number are 3rd person singular; change it for other subjects (e.g., *ho bisogno di* = I need, *avevano bisogno di* = they needed). After **bisogno di**, you typically use a noun or an infinitive: *aveva bisogno di soldi* (needed money), *aveva bisogno di dormire* (needed to sleep).
target_language_example: Disse che aveva bisogno di aiuto subito.
native_language_example: He said that he needed help right away.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech. "disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (common in storytelling, books, and in some regions for past events). "che" introduces the clause (“that”). "aveva paura" literally “had fear,” meaning “was afraid” (imperfect: an ongoing state in the past).
target_language_example: Maria disse che aveva paura del buio.
native_language_example: Maria said that she was afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to introduce what someone said in the past. "disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (common in writing/storytelling), "che" means "that", and "aveva" is the imperfect of "avere" (often used for background information or a state in the past). It’s usually followed by a noun: "un" (a, masculine singular) or "una" (a, feminine singular).
target_language_example: Disse che aveva un problema e che sarebbe arrivato tardi.
native_language_example: He said he had a problem and that he would arrive late.

meaning: "(he/she) said that (he/she) had to / was supposed to."
additional_notes: Used in reported speech: *disse* is the simple past (passato remoto) of **dire** (“said”), common in narratives and writing (in everyday speech you often hear **ha detto che doveva**). After **disse che...**, Italian typically uses **doveva** (imperfetto) to show a “backshift” in time (sequence of tenses): someone reported an obligation from that moment in the past.
target_language_example: Mi disse che doveva partire subito.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she had to leave right away.

additional_notes: A reported-speech phrase used to tell what someone said in the past. "Disse" is a narrative/literary past form of dire, so you will see it often in books and stories; in everyday spoken Italian, "ha detto che era" is more common. "Era" can mean he/she/it was, and the context or the following adjective usually makes it clear.
target_language_example: Disse che era stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said that he was tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Used in storytelling and reported speech, usually in the past (disse = “said”). "Che" introduces what was said (“that”), "era" = “was”, and "davvero" intensifies the adjective that follows (“really”). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context and not stated.
target_language_example: Disse che era davvero stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said he was really tired after the trip.

additional_notes: "Disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (to say/tell), often used in narratives and in some regions for past actions. The subject is often implied (he/she). "Che" introduces reported speech, and "era" is the imperfect of "essere" (was). You can add details after "felice" (e.g., "di farlo" = to do it, "qui/qua" = here).
target_language_example: Disse che era felice di essere con noi.
native_language_example: He said he was happy to be with us.

meaning: "he/she said that he/she was in…" (reported speech; usually followed by a place/situation).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "Disse" is the remote past (passato remoto) of "dire" (to say), common in narratives and in some regions; in everyday conversation many people use "ha detto" instead. "era" is imperfect of "essere" (was), and "in" is followed by a place or situation (e.g., "in ufficio", "in Italia", "in ritardo").
target_language_example: Disse che era in ufficio.
native_language_example: He said he was in the office.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about themselves or someone else. "disse" is the passato remoto of "dire" (said/told), common in narratives and written Italian; in conversation you’ll often hear "ha detto" instead. "che" = "that" introduces reported speech. "era" (imperfect of "essere") sets the description in the past. You usually add an adjective after "molto" (e.g., "molto stanco", "molto felice").
target_language_example: Disse che era molto stanco dopo il viaggio.
native_language_example: He said that he was very tired after the trip.

additional_notes: Uses the reporting verb “disse” (passato remoto of *dire*, common in stories/writing; in conversation you often hear *ha detto*). The subject is often implied from context (e.g., *Tom disse…*). After *che*, Italian commonly uses the imperfect (*era*) to describe the situation at that time in the past.
target_language_example: Luca disse che era molto felice di vederti.
native_language_example: Luca said that he was very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used in reported/indirect speech. **Disse** is the past historic (passato remoto) of *dire* (“to say”), common in narratives and in some regions; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear **ha detto** instead. **Era pronta** is the imperfect of *essere* + *pronta* (“ready”); the subject “she” is understood from context.
target_language_example: Disse che era pronta a partire.
native_language_example: She said that she was ready to leave.

additional_notes: Disse is the passato remoto of dire (“to say”), common in narratives, news reports, and especially in the South; in everyday conversation many speakers prefer ha detto. Che introduces an indirect statement (“that...”). Era pronto means “was ready” (pronto = ready, not “prompt”).
