additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "avere un incidente" = "to have an accident." "Ha" can refer to a person or something like a car/company depending on context. Often followed by where/when it happened: "sul lavoro" (at work), "mentre stava lavorando" (while he/she was working).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: Marco ha avuto un incidente ieri.
native_language_example: I'm sorry: Marco had an accident yesterday.

meaning: "(he/she) had a" / "has had a" (past of "avere" + feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of "avere" (to have): "ha" + past participle "avuto". Used to talk about past experiences or events someone had (e.g., a surprise, a bad day, a conversation, a discussion). The article "una" is used because the following noun is feminine singular (una sorpresa, una conversazione, una discussione, una giornata).
target_language_example: Ieri ha avuto una giornata molto impegnativa.
native_language_example: Yesterday she had a very busy day.

additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of baciare (“to kiss”): ha + baciato. Used for a completed action in the recent or relevant past. The subject is often understood from context (lui/lei has kissed). With an object: Ha baciato Mary. With a pronoun: Mi ha baciato… (“He/She kissed me…”). You can add where: in fronte (“on the forehead”), la mano (“[on] the hand”).
target_language_example: Ieri mi ha baciato sulla guancia.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she kissed me on the cheek.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of **battere** with **avere**. Meaning depends on what comes after it: **ha battuto qualcuno (a un gioco/sport)** = beat/defeat someone; **ha battuto (alla porta)** = knocked (on the door); **ha battuto gli occhi** = blinked; it can also mean “beat someone to it / got there first” in contexts like **Qualcuno ci ha battuto** (“Someone beat us to it”).
target_language_example: Mi ha battuto a calcio, ma poi mi ha battuto anche alla porta per salutarmi.
native_language_example: He beat me at soccer, but then he also knocked on the door to say goodbye.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of bere (to drink): avere (ha) + past participle (bevuto). Used to say someone drank/has drunk something. With quantities you often see "ha bevuto due bicchieri di..." or with partitives like "ha bevuto del latte" (= some milk).
target_language_example: Marco ha bevuto solo acqua oggi.
native_language_example: Marco drank only water today.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: **ha bevuto** is the passato prossimo of *bere* (to drink) for *lui/lei* (he/she), using the auxiliary **avere**. **del** is the partitive article (*di* + *il*) meaning “some (of the)” and is typically used before an uncountable noun (e.g., *del vino*, *del latte*). In a question or with emphasis you may also see *ne*: *Ne ha bevuto?* (“Did he/she drink any?”).
target_language_example: Ha bevuto del vino a cena.
native_language_example: He drank some wine at dinner.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo (present perfect) of cambiare for lui/lei/Lei: avere (ha) + past participle (cambiato). Used for a completed change in the past with a present result. Often takes a direct object (Ha cambiato idea. = He/She changed their mind.) and can also mean “switched” in contexts like Ha cambiato lavoro. = He/She changed jobs.
target_language_example: Da allora, ha cambiato idea.
native_language_example: Since then, he/she has changed their mind.

additional_notes: Used with a third-person subject (lui/lei, a name, etc.) to say someone decided differently than before. You can add details like "a riguardo" (about it) or "su" + topic (about/on). For other persons: "ho cambiato idea" (I changed my mind), "hai cambiato idea" (you changed your mind), "abbiamo cambiato idea" (we changed our mind).
target_language_example: Scusa, ha cambiato idea e non viene più.
native_language_example: Sorry, he changed his mind and he’s not coming anymore.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun that follows (e.g., *il suo stato, il suo approccio*). It means someone has changed something that belongs to them. *Suo* refers to the owner (his/her/its), and it agrees in gender/number with the thing owned: *il suo* (m. sg.), *la sua* (f. sg.), *i suoi* (m. pl.), *le sue* (f. pl.). In speech you often add the noun: *Ha cambiato il suo numero / il suo olio / il suo testamento.*
target_language_example: Ha cambiato il suo numero di telefono ieri.
native_language_example: He/She changed his/her phone number yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of cambiare: “ha cambiato” = “has changed/changed.” Often used with an object pronoun to say whose life changed: mi ha cambiato la vita (changed my life), ti ha cambiato la vita (changed your life), gli/le ha cambiato la vita (changed his/her life). You can also specify the person: ha cambiato la vita di Marco = “it changed Marco’s life.”
target_language_example: Quell’esperienza mi ha cambiato la vita.
native_language_example: That experience changed my life.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *cantare* (to sing): **ha** (present of *avere*) + **cantato** (past participle). The subject is often implied by context: *ha cantato* can mean “he sang” or “she sang.” Used for completed past actions, often with a specific time (*ieri*, *quando*, etc.). In questions you can keep the same order: *Quando ha cantato?* = “When did he/she sing?”
target_language_example: Ieri sera ha cantato al karaoke.
native_language_example: Last night he/she sang at karaoke.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *capire* (“to understand”). It literally means “has understood.” In a question (*Ha capito?*, *Ha capito tutto?*), it often addresses **Lei** (formal “you”), e.g. to check understanding (“Did you understand?”). It can also describe someone else: *Ha capito una frase* (“He/She understood a sentence”). Common in authority/police contexts: *Maresciallo, ha capito?* = “Marshal, did you understand?”
target_language_example: Scusi, ha capito come funziona?
native_language_example: Excuse me, did you understand how it works?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "cercare di" + infinitive. It usually means “he/she tried to …” (subject depends on context). Note: "cercare" can also mean “to look for/search,” but with "di" + infinitive it commonly means “to try to.”
target_language_example: Ha cercato di chiamarmi, ma non avevo campo.
native_language_example: He/She tried to call me, but I had no signal.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: it needs a noun after **la** (feminine singular “the”), e.g. *la verità* (the truth), *la chiave* (the key). **Ha cercato di + infinitive** is a common way to say “tried to …” (literally “has tried to …”) in the **passato prossimo**. The subject (lui/lei) is often omitted in Italian.
target_language_example: Ha cercato di nascondere la verità.
native_language_example: He/She tried to hide the truth.

additional_notes: Present perfect form of chiamare for lui/lei/Lei. It can mean someone called or phoned, and with a direct object it can also mean someone named or called a person or thing something.
target_language_example: Maria ha chiamato ieri sera.
native_language_example: Maria called last night.

meaning: "he/she called his/hers" (i.e., called their own one).
additional_notes: "Il suo" is a possessive pronoun meaning "his/hers/its" used on its own, standing in for a noun already understood from context (e.g., "his taxi", "her doctor"). So "ha chiamato il suo" means the person called their own one (taxi, doctor, etc.), without repeating the noun.
target_language_example: Io ho chiamato il mio taxi e lei ha chiamato il suo.
native_language_example: I called my taxi and she called hers.

additional_notes: “Ha chiamato” is the passato prossimo of chiamare (“to call”), used for a completed action: “he/she called”. “La” is “the” (feminine singular), so it’s followed by a feminine singular noun: la madre (the mother), la scuola (the school), la moschea (the mosque). You can also add a possessive: “ha chiamato la sua madre” (“called his/her mother”), though in everyday Italian you often hear “ha chiamato sua madre” (without “la”).
target_language_example: Ha chiamato la segreteria della scuola ieri.
native_language_example: He/She called the school office yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “chiamare la polizia” = “to call the police.” The subject is often omitted in Italian: “Ha chiamato la polizia” can mean “He called the police” or “She called the police,” depending on context. You can also say “Ho chiamato la polizia” (I called) / “Abbiamo chiamato la polizia” (we called).
target_language_example: Ha chiamato la polizia perché c'era un ladro.
native_language_example: He/She called the police because there was a thief.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of chiamare (to call). The subject is often implied from context (ha chiamato = he/she called). It can also mean “arranged a taxi (for someone)”: Ha chiamato un taxi per lui = He called a taxi for him; Mi ha chiamato un taxi = He called/arranged a taxi for me.
target_language_example: Lui ha trovato un telefono pubblico e ha chiamato un taxi.
native_language_example: He found a public phone and called a taxi.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of chiedere. It usually means he/she asked or has asked, and can also refer to formal you depending on context. It is used both for asking a question and for asking for/requesting something.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aiutarlo.
native_language_example: He asked me to help him.

additional_notes: Forma al passato prossimo del verbo "chiedere": "ha chiesto" = "he/she asked". Si usa con "a" per introdurre la persona a cui si fa una domanda o una richiesta. Strutture comuni: "ha chiesto a [persona] di + infinito" (asked [someone] to do something), "ha chiesto a [persona] se..." (asked [someone] if...), "ha chiesto a [persona] che.../chi.../cosa..." (asked [someone] what/who...). Per altre persone cambia l’ausiliare: "ho chiesto a" (I asked), "hai chiesto a" (you asked), ecc.
target_language_example: Tom ha chiesto a Mary di passargli la bottiglia.
native_language_example: Tom asked Mary to pass him the bottle.

additional_notes: Past tense of "chiedere" in the passato prossimo (ha chiesto = "has asked" / "asked"). Very often followed by "di" + infinitive to say what someone asked to do: "Mi ha chiesto di aiutarlo" = "He asked me to help him." It can also mean "asked about" a topic/person: "Ha chiesto di mia madre" = "He asked about my mother." (In this use, you can also see "chiedere di + [someone/something]" meaning to ask for news/about them.)
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aspettarlo fuori.
native_language_example: He asked me to wait for him outside.

meaning: "he/she asked to come" (or "has asked to come").
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of *chiedere* (ha chiesto = asked/has asked) + *di* + infinitive to say that someone requested permission or wanted to do something: *chiedere di + infinitive* = “to ask to + verb.” The subject (he/she) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Marco ha chiesto di venire con noi alla festa.
native_language_example: Marco asked to come with us to the party.

additional_notes: Used to report a yes/no question indirectly. "Ha chiesto" is the passato prossimo of "chiedere" (to ask), and "se" introduces the embedded question (“if/whether”). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto se avevo tempo domani.
native_language_example: He/She asked me if I had time tomorrow.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "chiudere" with the auxiliary "avere". Used for something someone closed/shut (a door, eyes, windows, etc.). Common fixed expression: "non ha chiuso occhio" = "he/she didn’t sleep a wink" (literally “didn’t close an eye”).
target_language_example: Marco ha chiuso la finestra perché faceva freddo.
native_language_example: Marco closed the window because it was cold.

meaning: (he/she) locked (it) with a key; locked up.
additional_notes: Passato prossimo (past tense) of "chiudere a chiave" = to lock (with a key). Uses "avere" + past participle "chiuso". Often followed by what was locked: "ha chiuso a chiave la porta/la macchina". It can also mean locking someone/something inside a place (e.g., "ha chiuso a chiave il cane nel bagno" = locked the dog in the bathroom).
target_language_example: Ha chiuso a chiave la porta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He/She locked the door before going out.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **chiudere a chiave** (“to lock (with a key)”). **Ha chiuso** is the *passato prossimo* (past tense) and the subject is often omitted in Italian (it can mean “he locked…” or “she locked…”). **La** must be followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., *la porta*, *la macchina*).
target_language_example: Ha chiuso a chiave la porta.
native_language_example: She locked the door.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "chiudere" (to close). "Ha" is the auxiliary (to have) and "chiuso" is the past participle. The subject is often implied in Italian, so it can mean "he" or "she" depending on context. You can change the object: "ha chiuso la finestra" (closed the window), or add a place: "ha chiuso la porta della stanza" (the room door).
target_language_example: Ha chiuso la porta prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He/She closed the door before going out.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *colpire* with *avere*: *ha colpito* = “has hit/struck.” It can be literal (physical hitting: *Ha colpito il cane.*) or figurative (something that “struck” you emotionally or caught your attention: *Mi ha colpito il tuo messaggio.*). Often used with object pronouns: *mi/ti/lo/la/ci/vi/li/le ha colpito*.
target_language_example: Mi ha colpito la tua gentilezza.
native_language_example: Your kindness really struck me.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of cominciare: avere (ha) + past participle (cominciato). The subject can be “he,” “she,” or “it” and is often understood from context. Often followed by “a” + infinitive: “ha cominciato a capire” = “(he) started to understand.”
target_language_example: Ha cominciato a lavorare alle otto.
native_language_example: He/She started working at eight.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo), 3rd person singular: “he/she started to …”. It’s made with avere + cominciato + a + infinitive (e.g., “ha cominciato a leggere” = “started to read”). You can replace the subject: “ho cominciato a” (I started to), “abbiamo cominciato a” (we started to), etc.
target_language_example: Ha cominciato a lavorare qui la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: He/She started working here last week.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "cominciare a lavorare". "Ha" + past participle "cominciato" is used for completed actions in the past. The subject is often understood from context (lui/lei). Commonly followed by a place or job: "qui" (here), "da" + store/company (e.g., "da Walmart" = at Walmart), "in" + place ("in centro", "in una palestra", "in un bar"), or a schedule like "part-time".
target_language_example: Ha cominciato a lavorare in un ristorante la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: He/She started working in a restaurant last week.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "cominciare a" + infinitive. It describes the moment someone begins to shout or scream. With "a voce alta" it emphasizes loudly; with "alla vista di..." it means "upon seeing...".
target_language_example: Appena ha visto il ragno, ha cominciato a urlare.
native_language_example: As soon as she saw the spider, she started screaming.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of comprare with a singular subject: it means 'he/she has bought' or, in many contexts, simply 'he/she bought.' You also use it with names or singular nouns, like Tom ha comprato...
target_language_example: Maria ha comprato un libro ieri.
native_language_example: Maria bought a book yesterday.

additional_notes: "Ha comprato" is passato prossimo of "comprare" (to buy) with the auxiliary "avere". The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean “he bought” or “she bought” depending on context. "Dei fiori" means “some flowers” (plural, indefinite). You can add the recipient with a + person (to someone): "a sua madre", "ad Anna", "alla sua fidanzata"; or use "per" to mean “for” someone: "per Layla".
target_language_example: Ha comprato dei fiori per il compleanno di sua madre.
native_language_example: He/She bought some flowers for his/her mother's birthday.

meaning: “(he/she) bought something for …” / “(he/she) has bought something for …”.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone bought an item/gift for another person. Structure: **ha comprato** (has bought/bought) + **qualcosa** (something) + **per** (for) + a person/pronoun (e.g., *per Tom, per loro, per me*). Often used in questions with intonation: *Ha comprato qualcosa per Tom?* You can change subject/tense as needed (e.g., *Ho comprato qualcosa per…*, *Aveva comprato qualcosa per…*).
target_language_example: Ha comprato qualcosa per loro?
native_language_example: Did he/she buy something for them?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of comprare (to buy): ha (from avere) + comprato (past participle) + questo (this). The subject is often implied in Italian, so it can mean “he bought this,” “she bought this,” or even “you (formal) bought this,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha comprato questo ieri al mercato.
native_language_example: He/She bought this yesterday at the market.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone (usually “he/she”) bought something. It’s the passato prossimo of comprare: ha (auxiliary) + comprato (past participle). “Un” is the masculine singular article; use “ha comprato una …” for a feminine noun (e.g., una casa).
target_language_example: Ha comprato un biglietto per il concerto.
native_language_example: He/She bought a ticket for the concert.

additional_notes: Past tense with passato prossimo: "ha comprato" = "has bought/bought" (auxiliary "avere" + past participle "comprato"). The subject (he/she/it) is often implied in Italian. Used for a completed action in the past; in a question, raise intonation: "Ha comprato un cane?"
target_language_example: Ha comprato un cane ieri.
native_language_example: He/She bought a dog yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: **ha comprato** = “bought/has bought” (auxiliary **avere** + past participle). The subject (**lui/lei**) is often omitted in Italian and understood from context.
target_language_example: Ha comprato un dizionario per studiare italiano.
native_language_example: He/She bought a dictionary to study Italian.

additional_notes: “Ha comprato” is the passato prossimo of comprare (“to buy”) with the auxiliary avere, used for completed past actions. The subject is not stated here: “ha” can mean “he has” or “she has” depending on context (e.g., Lui/Lei ha comprato un libro). You can add details with prepositions: in/da + place (in una libreria “in a bookstore”), per + person (“for her/him”), su + topic (“about…”).
target_language_example: Lei ha comprato un libro per suo fratello.
native_language_example: She bought a book for her brother.

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of comprare: ha comprato = “(he/she) bought / has bought”. You normally add a masculine singular noun after nuovo (e.g., un nuovo computer). For a feminine noun, use una nuova (e.g., ha comprato una nuova macchina). You can also use ho/hai/abbiamo/avete/hanno comprato depending on who did the buying.
target_language_example: Ha comprato un nuovo telefono ieri.
native_language_example: He/She bought a new phone yesterday.

meaning: 'he/she bought a couple of' / 'he/she bought a pair of'.
additional_notes: Common pattern: **comprare + un paio di + noun**. **Un paio di** can mean either **a pair** (two items that go together, e.g. shoes, socks) or more generally **a couple of** (a small number). **Ha comprato** is the passato prossimo for **lui/lei** (“he/she bought/has bought”); you can change the subject: *ho comprato* (I bought), *abbiamo comprato* (we bought), etc.
target_language_example: Ha comprato un paio di scarpe nuove.
native_language_example: He/She bought a pair of new shoes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone bought a present for another person. "Ha comprato" is the passato prossimo of "comprare" (he/she has bought → he/she bought). "Un regalo" = a gift/present, and "per" introduces the recipient (for + person). You can replace the recipient with a name or with a possessive + family member (e.g., "per sua madre", "per il suo amico").
target_language_example: Ha comprato un regalo per me.
native_language_example: He/She bought a gift for me.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (una + noun). You usually add the item right after: “ha comprato una macchina / una collana / una rosa”. If the subject is specified, it can come before: “Tom ha comprato una …”.
target_language_example: Ieri ha comprato una borsa nuova.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she bought a new bag.

additional_notes: Past tense with passato prossimo: ha (present of avere) + comprato (past participle). The subject (he/she) is often implied in Italian and understood from context. You can replace “una macchina” with details: una macchina nuova/usata/rossa, etc.
target_language_example: Ha comprato una macchina nuova ieri.
native_language_example: He/She bought a new car yesterday.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (past tense): "ha comprato" = "(he/she) bought/has bought". The subject is often omitted in Italian; it can mean "he" or "she" depending on context. "Una macchina fotografica" is the common way to say "a camera" (literally “a photographic machine”).
target_language_example: Ha comprato una macchina fotografica nuova per il viaggio.
native_language_example: He/She bought a new camera for the trip.

ha condiviso il suo pranzo con

target_language_multi_word_term: ha condiviso il suo pranzo con
meaning: 'shared his lunch with' / 'shared her lunch with'.
additional_notes: Used to say someone shared their lunch with another person. It’s in the passato prossimo (ha condiviso = 'he/she shared' or 'has shared'). "Il suo" can mean 'his' or 'her' depending on context. After "con" you can use a person/pronoun (lei, lui, me) or a noun (e.g., una senzatetto = 'a homeless woman').
target_language_example: Ha condiviso il suo pranzo con i colleghi.
native_language_example: He/She shared his/her lunch with his/her coworkers.

additional_notes: Present perfect of conoscere: used to say someone met a person (often for the first time) or came to know someone/something. It can be about a person (Ha conosciuto Maria?) or how you discovered something (Come ha conosciuto Tatoeba?). Formal/polite questions often use Lei + ha conosciuto.
target_language_example: Ha conosciuto il nuovo collega ieri?
native_language_example: Did you meet the new coworker yesterday?

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "consigliare". Common pattern: "[Someone] ha consigliato di + infinitive" to say someone advised doing something. Often used with professions giving advice (doctor, teacher, etc.). You can also specify who is being advised with "a + person": "Mi ha consigliato di..." = "He/She recommended that I..."
target_language_example: Il medico ha consigliato di bere più acqua.
native_language_example: The doctor recommended drinking more water.

additional_notes: Used to report advice in the past. It’s made of: "ha consigliato" (has advised/recommended) + "di non" (not to) + an infinitive verb (e.g., "uscire", "guidare", "mangiare"). The subject (he/she) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Il medico ha consigliato di non bere alcolici per una settimana.
native_language_example: The doctor advised not to drink alcohol for a week.

additional_notes: Used to report advice from a specific person ("ha consigliato" = "he/she advised"). It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb after the second "di": "ha consigliato di smettere di fumare" (advised to stop smoking). You can add who received the advice with an indirect object: "Mi ha consigliato di..." (He/She advised me to...).
target_language_example: Il medico mi ha consigliato di smettere di fumare.
native_language_example: The doctor advised me to stop smoking.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "continuare": "ha" (has) + "continuato" (continued) + "a" + infinitive (verb). It means someone kept doing the same action, often despite a reason to stop. Change "ha" to match the subject (e.g., "ho continuato a" = I continued to; "abbiamo continuato a" = we continued to).
target_language_example: Nonostante la pioggia, ha continuato a camminare.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, he/she kept on walking.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ha" + "continuato" (past participle of continuare) + "a" + infinitive. Used to say someone kept doing an activity, often despite a difficulty (e.g., being tired): "ha continuato a lavorare anche se...". You can change the subject by changing the auxiliary: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno continuato a lavorare".
target_language_example: Nonostante il mal di testa, ha continuato a lavorare fino a tardi.
native_language_example: Despite the headache, he/she kept working until late.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of “continuare a + infinitive” (to continue to do something). “Ha” is the auxiliary avere (3rd person singular), so the subject is usually “he” or “she” (or a named person). Often followed by an object: “ha continuato a leggere il libro/la lettera/dei libri,” but it can also stand alone (“Ha continuato a leggere.”).
target_language_example: Dopo la pausa, ha continuato a leggere in silenzio.
native_language_example: After the break, he/she kept reading quietly.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo: avere (ha) + past participle (corso). Used both for literal running (“He ran.”) and more general meanings like “to take/run a risk” (Ha corso un grande rischio) or “to do/complete laps” (Quanti giri ha corso?).
target_language_example: Oggi ha corso per prendere l’autobus.
native_language_example: Today he ran to catch the bus.

additional_notes: Past tense of "cucinare" (to cook), using "avere": "ha" + past participle "cucinato". The subject can be he/she/it (or a name) and is understood from context: "(Lorenzo) ha cucinato..." = "(Lorenzo) cooked...". With an indirect object pronoun, it often means cooking *for someone*: "Mi/ti/gli/le ha cucinato..." = "He/She cooked ... for me/you/him/her".
target_language_example: Ieri mi ha cucinato una pasta semplice.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she cooked me a simple pasta.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of dare for lui/lei/Lei (third-person singular). Literally it means "has given," but in many contexts English translates it simply as "gave." It is often followed by something given, and often also the person receiving it with a + noun or an indirect object pronoun like gli or le.
target_language_example: Marco ha dato il libro a sua sorella.
native_language_example: Marco gave the book to his sister.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of dare (“to give”) in the 3rd person singular: lui/lei (or a name) ha dato = “he/she gave/has given.” It’s followed by a + a person (the indirect object): ha dato a Maria… = “(he/she) gave to Maria…”. In speech, “a” often combines with names and articles (e.g., a Marco, al ragazzo).
target_language_example: Giulia ha dato a Paolo il suo numero di telefono.
native_language_example: Giulia gave Paolo her phone number.

additional_notes: From the expression “dare da mangiare (a qualcuno)”, meaning “to feed (someone/animals)”. It’s used with an indirect object for who is being fed: “alla gatta”, “ai cani”, “alle capre”. You can also add what food was given: “Ha dato da mangiare i suoi avanzi al cane.”
target_language_example: Ha dato da mangiare ai bambini prima di uscire.
native_language_example: She fed the children before going out.

meaning: “(he/she) fed the …” / “(he/she) has fed the …” (literally: “gave to eat to the …”).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the idiom “dare da mangiare a” = “to feed.” It takes an indirect object with “a”; with “il” it contracts to “al” (a + il). You can swap the subject or object: “Ho dato da mangiare al cane” = “I fed the dog”; “Ha dato da mangiare al cavallo” = “He/She fed the horse.”
target_language_example: Tom ha dato da mangiare al suo cane prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Tom fed his dog before going out.

meaning: “he/she gave food to the …” / “he/she fed the …”.
additional_notes: From the expression **dare da mangiare a [someone/animal]** = “to give [someone] something to eat / to feed.” **Ha dato** is the passato prossimo (past tense). **al** = **a + il** (“to the” masculine singular). You’ll also see **alla** (a+la), **ai** (a+i), **agli** (a+gli), **alle** (a+le).
target_language_example: Ha dato da mangiare al cane prima di uscire.
native_language_example: He fed the dog before going out.

additional_notes: Literally means “has given the,” from avere (ha) + past participle of dare (dato) + the masculine singular article (il). It’s usually incomplete by itself and needs a direct object after il (e.g., il libro, il permesso, il numero) and often an indirect object with a/alla (e.g., a me, alla ragazza). Note: in some common expressions you may see it followed by a fixed noun phrase, e.g. “ha dato il via (a ...)” = “(he/she) kicked off/started (something).”
target_language_example: Ha dato il libro a Marco.
native_language_example: He/She gave the book to Marco.

additional_notes: Used when someone authorizes another person to do something. Often follows the pattern: [Someone] ha dato il permesso a [person] di + infinitive (e.g., mi ha dato il permesso di entrare). In questions like “Chi ti ha dato il permesso di…?”, it can sound scolding: “Who gave you permission to…?”
target_language_example: Il capo mi ha dato il permesso di uscire prima.
native_language_example: My boss gave me permission to leave early.

meaning: “he/she did their part” (contributed what they could).
additional_notes: Commonly used as a shortened form of phrases like “ha dato il suo contributo” (“he/she made their contribution”). It suggests someone has done what was expected or all they could, and the task is essentially complete for them. You can also hear it about things (e.g., a machine) meaning it has “done its job” and may not work anymore.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: Marco ha dato il suo, ora tocca a noi finire il lavoro.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: Marco did his part; now it’s up to us to finish the work.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dare le dimissioni" = "to resign." Used for quitting a job or stepping down from an official position. You can change the auxiliary and ending for gender/number: "ho dato le dimissioni" (I resigned), "abbiamo dato le dimissioni" (we resigned), "ha dato le dimissioni" (he/she resigned).
target_language_example: Dopo lo scandalo, il ministro ha dato le dimissioni.
native_language_example: After the scandal, the minister resigned.

meaning: "has given everything that..." (introduces what someone gave or did).
additional_notes: Used when talking about a completed action in the past (passato prossimo): "ha dato" = "has given". It’s typically followed by a clause with "che" to specify what was given/done: "...tutto quello che poteva" (everything he/she could). "Ha" can refer to he/she/you (formal).
target_language_example: Ha dato tutto quello che poteva per aiutarmi.
native_language_example: He/She gave everything he/she could to help me.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "dare" (to give): "ha dato" = "has given / gave". It’s followed by a masculine singular noun with "un" (e.g., un premio, un dollaro, un osso, un pugno). Often used with an indirect object introduced by "a" (to someone): "ha dato un premio a John" = "gave John a prize".
target_language_example: Mi ha dato un consiglio molto utile.
native_language_example: He/She gave me a very useful piece of advice.

meaning: "(He/She) gave a present" / "has given a present".
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of **dare** (to give): **ha dato** = "gave/has given" (auxiliary **avere** + past participle **dato**). Italian often drops the subject, so it can mean **he** or **she** depending on context. To say **to whom** you gave it, use **a** + person: *Ha dato un regalo a Marco.*
target_language_example: Ha dato un regalo a sua madre per il compleanno.
native_language_example: He/She gave a present to his/her mother for her birthday.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has made a decision: "ha deciso di" + verb (infinitive). It’s the passato prossimo of "decidere" (3rd person singular), so it refers to a completed decision in the past or with present relevance.
target_language_example: Maria ha deciso di studiare medicina.
native_language_example: Maria has decided to study medicine.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has made the decision to travel/move to a place. "Ha deciso" is the present perfect (passato prossimo) of "decidere" and often translates as "has decided" or simply "decided." "Andare in" is used with many countries and larger places (e.g., "in Giappone", "in Australia"). With cities you usually use "andare a" (e.g., "andare a Roma").
target_language_example: Ha deciso di andare in Italia quest’estate.
native_language_example: He/She decided to go to Italy this summer.

additional_notes: Past tense with **ha deciso** (passato prossimo of *decidere*) + **di** + infinitive. **Non andare** means “not to go.” Change **ha** to match the subject (e.g., *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno deciso di non andare*). You can add a destination with **a/in** (e.g., *a casa*, *in Australia*) or specify company with **da solo/a**.
target_language_example: Tom ha deciso di non andare in Australia.
native_language_example: Tom decided not to go to Australia.

meaning: “(He/She) decided to study.” / “(He/She) has decided to study.”
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of decidere: “ha deciso” = “has decided/decided.” The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean “he” or “she” depending on context. You can swap the verb after “di” to say what someone decided to do (e.g., ha deciso di partire = decided to leave).
target_language_example: Ha deciso di studiare italiano ogni sera.
native_language_example: He/She decided to study Italian every evening.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has made the decision to sell something feminine singular introduced by **la** (e.g., *la casa*, *la macchina*). You normally add the noun after **la**. **Ha deciso** = “(he/she) has decided”; **di vendere** = “to sell”.
target_language_example: Ha deciso di vendere la casa.
native_language_example: He/She decided to sell the house.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone spent most of their life focused on a cause, profession, or goal. It’s in the passato prossimo (ha + dedicato). The object changes with gender/number: ha dedicato la sua vita (his/her life), ha dedicato le sue vite (rare), etc. It’s usually followed by "a" + infinitive (ha dedicato la sua vita a aiutare gli altri) or by "a" + a noun with the right article (ha dedicato la sua vita alla medicina / allo studio).
target_language_example: Ha dedicato la sua vita a proteggere l’ambiente.
native_language_example: He/She dedicated his/her life to protecting the environment.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of dire. The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean 'he said', 'she said', 'you said' (formal), or 'it said', depending on context. In English, it is often translated simply as 'said'.
target_language_example: Luca ha detto di no.
native_language_example: Luca said no.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of dire used with an indirect object introduced by a (to someone): ha detto a Tom = "he/she told Tom" / "said to Tom". Often followed by che + clause (ha detto a Tom che...) or di + infinitive (ha detto a Tom di...).
target_language_example: Mary ha detto a Tom che aveva sete.
native_language_example: Mary told Tom that she was thirsty.

meaning: "he/she told everyone that" / "he/she said to everyone that".
additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech: the person (often implied as “he” or “she”) told everybody some information. The verb is in the passato prossimo (ha detto), so it refers to something said in the past. After che, you usually get a full clause (e.g., che stava bene, che era a Boston).
target_language_example: Ha detto a tutti che non poteva venire alla festa.
native_language_example: He/She told everyone that he/she couldn’t come to the party.

ha detto a tutti che era

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto a tutti che era
additional_notes: Used to report what someone revealed or announced to everyone. It uses the past tense "ha detto" (passato prossimo of dire, “said/told”) followed by "che" (“that”) and "era" (imperfetto of essere, “was”). In context, Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so "ha detto" can mean “he said” or “she said.” You then add a description or situation after "era" (e.g., depresso, in pensione, adottata, al verde).
target_language_example: Ha detto a tutti che era stanco.
native_language_example: He/She told everyone that he/she was tired.

additional_notes: Used to introduce reported speech. In English, "that" is often optional: ha detto che... can often be translated as "said...". Ha can refer to he/she or to formal Lei ("you").
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che arriva domani.
native_language_example: Marco said that he's arriving tomorrow.

meaning: 'he/she said that to …' / in practice often part of the pattern 'he/she told … that …'.
additional_notes: This sequence is usually encountered within the structure **ha detto che … a + [person]** (“he/she said that … to [someone]”), or more commonly **ha detto a + [person] che …** (“he/she told [someone] that …”). The provided term **ha detto che a** is grammatical but less natural than **ha detto a … che …** in everyday Italian. **ha detto** is **passato prossimo** of *dire* (“said/told”); **che** introduces a clause; **a** introduces the indirect object (the person being told).
target_language_example: Ha detto che a Marco non avrebbe telefonato.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she wouldn’t call Marco.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment: **ha detto che...** = “he/she said that…”. **a lei** means “to her” (emphatic/clearer than just **le**). In natural Italian you’ll often see **Le ha detto che...** or **Ha detto a lei che...** depending on emphasis.
target_language_example: Le ha detto che a lei non interessa.
native_language_example: He/She told her that she isn’t interested.

ha detto che a lei piace

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che a lei piace
meaning: “she said that she likes …” / “she said she likes …”.
additional_notes: Used to report what a woman said (indirect speech). In Italian, piacere works like “to be pleasing to”: a lei piace = “she likes (it)” (literally “it is pleasing to her”). The verb usually agrees with the thing liked: Le piace ballare (“She likes dancing”), Le piacciono i libri (“She likes books”).
target_language_example: Ha detto che a lei piace questo ristorante.
native_language_example: She said that she likes this restaurant.

ha detto che a lei piaceva la

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che a lei piaceva la
meaning: “he/she said that she liked the …” (introducing reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "ha detto che" = "he/she said that". "a lei piaceva" uses the verb "piacere" (literally: "the … was pleasing to her"), so the thing liked comes after the verb (e.g., "la pizza"). You would normally complete the phrase with a noun: "… piaceva la pizza / la musica / la città".
target_language_example: Ha detto che a lei piaceva la pizza.
native_language_example: He/She said that she liked pizza.

meaning: “(he/she) said that to him” / “(he/she) told him that.”
additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll usually see in longer sentences. "ha detto" = "(he/she) said"; "che" introduces what was said ("that..."); "a lui" means "to him" and is often used for emphasis/contrast (e.g., "to him, not to someone else"). In everyday Italian you’ll often also hear "gli ha detto che..." ("he/she told him that...").
target_language_example: Ha detto che a lui non interessa.
native_language_example: He said that he’s not interested.

ha detto che a lui piace

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che a lui piace
meaning: 'he said that he likes' (reporting what someone said about what he likes).
additional_notes: Used to report someone’s words: **ha detto che** = “he said that…”. **a lui piace** uses the verb *piacere* (“to be pleasing to”), so the person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: **a lui** = “to him” (i.e., “he”). Often you can drop **a lui** if it’s clear: *Ha detto che gli piace la pizza.* The word order is flexible, but this structure commonly introduces a thing/verb he enjoys: *piace la pizza / piace studiare…*.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che a lui piace viaggiare in treno.
native_language_example: Marco said that he likes traveling by train.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. Italian often omits the subject pronoun, so “ha detto” can mean “he said” or “she said,” and “aveva” can mean “he had” or “she had.” Commonly followed by a past participle (e.g., “aveva finito / aveva trovato / aveva lavorato”) to describe something that was already completed at that time.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che aveva già pagato il conto.
native_language_example: Marco said that he had already paid the bill.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech to say what someone said. "Ha detto" is a completed past action (passato prossimo: “he/she said”), and "che" means “that.” "Aveva" (imperfetto of avere) is often used to show something was already true at the time of what was said (roughly: “had” / “was having”).
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che aveva dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: Marco said that he had forgotten his keys.

ha detto che aveva bisogno di

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che aveva bisogno di
additional_notes: Used in reported speech to say what someone said they needed. "Ha detto" = "(he/she) said" (passato prossimo), and "aveva bisogno di" = "needed" (imperfect), often used after a past reporting verb. Followed by a noun ("…di un favore", "…di una scatola") or by an infinitive ("…di parlare"). The subject can change: "ho detto che avevo bisogno di…", "hanno detto che avevano bisogno di…".
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che aveva bisogno di aiuto.
native_language_example: He told me that he needed help.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past (reported speech). Often follows the Italian “sequence of tenses”: **ha detto** (passato prossimo) + **aveva** (imperfetto) to show the fear was ongoing at that time. Subject can be “he” or “she” depending on context; you can also specify: *Lui ha detto...* / *Lei ha detto...*.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che aveva paura di guidare di notte.
native_language_example: Marco said that he was afraid of driving at night.

additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment used before a noun ("un" = "a" + masculine singular). It’s common in reported speech: after "ha detto che" (he/she said that), Italian often shifts the tense back, so "aveva" (imperfect) corresponds to English "had" (e.g., "He said he had a ticket"). To use it, add a masculine noun after "un" (e.g., un biglietto, un problema).
target_language_example: Ha detto che aveva un problema.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she had a problem.

meaning: “(he/she) said that (he/she) would …” (reported speech about a planned or promised action).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, followed by the conditional past (avrebbe + past participle or an infinitive in some contexts). It often corresponds to English “said (that) he/she would…” and is common when the main verb is in the past (ha detto). The subject is implied (he/she) unless you add a name (e.g., “Tom ha detto…”).
target_language_example: Luisa ha detto che avrebbe chiamato più tardi.
native_language_example: Luisa said she would call later.

meaning: “he/she said that … (to us / for us / about it / there)”.
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past: “ha detto che …” (“he/she said that …”). The little word “ci” is a pronoun that can mean “to us / for us” (e.g., “ci può aiutare” = “can help us”), “about it” (with verbs like “credere”: “ci credeva” = “he believed in it”), or “there” depending on the verb and context.
target_language_example: Ha detto che ci avrebbe chiamato più tardi.
native_language_example: He said that he would call us later.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech. "Ha detto" is passato prossimo (a completed statement in the past). After "che" (that), Italian often uses the imperfetto ("conosceva") to show the past relative to what was said (sequence of tenses). The subject is often omitted: it can mean "he said" or "she said" depending on context. "Conoscere" means “to know (a person/place/subject),” not “to know a fact” (for facts you often use "sapere").
target_language_example: Ha detto che conosceva Maria, ma non l’aveva vista da anni.
native_language_example: He said that he knew Maria, but he hadn’t seen her for years.

additional_notes: Past statement introducing reported speech: **ha detto che...** (“he/she said that...”), followed by **doveva** (imperfect of *dovere*, “had to/was supposed to”) and **andare** (“to go”). The subject (he/she) is often implied in Italian; use context to know who it refers to.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che doveva andare via subito.
native_language_example: Marco said he had to leave right away.

additional_notes: Used to report someone’s advice or opinion. “Ha detto” = “he/she said,” and “dovrei” is the conditional of “dovere” (to have to/should), meaning “I should / I ought to.” Often appears as “Mi ha detto che dovrei…” (“He/She told me that I should…”).
target_language_example: Ha detto che dovrei riposarmi un po'.
native_language_example: He/She said that I should rest a bit.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about a past state or situation. ha detto means "said" (literally "has said" in form), and era means "was." The person or thing after che is often understood from context, so in English you may need to supply "he," "she," or "it."
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che era pronto a partire.
native_language_example: Luca said that he was ready to leave.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech. "Ha detto" (she said) is the passato prossimo; "che" means "that". After "ha detto che...", Italian often uses the imperfect ("era") to describe what was true at that time. "Curiosa" agrees with a female subject; for a male subject you’d say "curioso".
target_language_example: Maria ha detto che era curiosa di sapere come finiva il film.
native_language_example: Maria said she was curious to know how the movie ended.

target_language_example: Mia sorella ha detto che ero stanco.
native_language_example: My sister said that I was tired.

meaning: “he/she said that (to him)…”, used to report what someone said, with **gli** = “to him” (often in phrases like “gli fa male…”, “gli piace…”).
additional_notes:
**Ha detto che…** introduces reported speech (“He/She said that…”). **Gli** is the indirect object pronoun meaning “to him.” In Italian it’s common with:
- **fare male**: *gli fa male lo stomaco / la schiena* = “his stomach/back hurts” (literally “the stomach/back hurts to him”).
- **piacere**: *gli sta piacendo la festa* = “he is liking/enjoying the party” (literally “the party is pleasing to him”).
You can swap **gli** for **le** (“to her”) or **mi/ti/ci/vi** depending on who is affected.

native_language_example: He said that he really liked this restaurant.

The thing he likes can be a noun (Gli piace il caffè) or an activity with the infinitive (Gli piace nuotare).
target_language_example: Ha detto che gli piace questa città.
native_language_example: He said that he likes this city.

meaning: “he/she said that he/she has …” / “he/she said that he/she did …” (reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said: **ha detto** (“he/she said”) + **che** (“that”) + **ha** (auxiliary for the next verb in the past tense, e.g. *ha visto, ha rotto, ha trovato*). The subject is often implied in Italian; **ha detto** can mean “he said” or “she said” depending on context (or you can add a name: *Tom ha detto che ha…*). English often uses “had” in this situation (“He said he had…”), but Italian commonly keeps **ha**.
target_language_example: Maria ha detto che ha perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: Maria said that she lost her keys.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said ("ha detto che" = "(he/she) said that") followed by an obligation in the past. "Ha dovuto" is the past of "dovere" (to have to / must) and is often followed by an infinitive: "ha dovuto aspettare" (had to wait), "ha dovuto chiamare" (had to call).

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said they heard. Often followed by what was heard (e.g., degli spari = some gunshots; tre spari = three gunshots; molti spari = many gunshots). native_language_example: The neighbor said that he heard a loud noise.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: **ha detto che** = “she said that…”. **le piace** comes from *piacere* (“to be pleasing”), so it literally means “it pleases her.” After **piace**, you can use a noun (*le piace la pizza*) or an infinitive verb (*le piace insegnare*).
target_language_example: Ha detto che le piace questo ristorante.
native_language_example: She said she likes this restaurant.

meaning: "he/she said that ... not" (introduces a negative reported statement).

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past (“ha detto che…” = “he/she said that…”). meaning: “(he/she) said that (someone) would …” (reported speech about a future event seen from the past).

meaning: “he said that he would come / would be coming.”

"Sembravo" is *sembrare* in the imperfect ("I seemed/ looked"), often used for ongoing impressions (e.g., hungry, sad). You can change the subject: *mi ha detto che sembravo…* (he/she told me I looked…), *ha detto che sembravi…* (you looked…), *ha detto che sembrava…* (he/she looked…).

meaning: “he/she said that he/she …” (introduces reported speech, often before a reflexive verb).

native_language_example: Marco said that he feels better today.

You can follow it with an adjective: “frustrata/o”, “nervosa/o”, “responsabile”, “intrappolata/o”.

- **si stava sentendo** = “(he/she) was feeling” (imperfect continuous); **si** is the reflexive pronoun used with **sentirsi** (“to feel”).
The adjective that follows agrees with the person’s gender/number: **stanco/stanca**, **nervoso/nervosa**, etc.
target_language_example: Ha detto che si stava sentendo male e voleva tornare a casa.
native_language_example: He said he was feeling sick and wanted to go home.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "Ha detto" is the past tense (passato prossimo) of dire (to say), and "voleva" is the imperfect of volere (to want), often used in reported speech. The "si" refers back to the subject (himself/herself), so in English you usually translate it as “he” or “she,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che si voleva trasferire a Milano.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wanted to move to Milan.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect/reported speech). After che, stava is the imperfect of stare and is commonly followed by: (1) a gerund to mean “was (doing)” (stava tornando = “was coming back”), or (2) per + infinitive to mean “was about to …” (stava per parlare = “was about to talk/speak”). The subject (he/she) is understood from context.
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che stava studiando quando l’hai chiamato.
native_language_example: Luca said that he was studying when you called him.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: **ha detto che...** (“(he/she) said that...”) introduces what someone reported. **stava andando** (imperfetto of *stare* + gerund) often corresponds to English “was going/was on the way/was leaving” in the past. The destination usually follows with **a/in/al** (e.g., *andare in Italia*, *andare al lavoro*). With **andare bene**, it means “to be going well,” so *ha detto che stava andando bene* = “(she) said it was going well.”
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che stava andando a casa.
native_language_example: He/She told me he/she was going home.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech: *ha detto che...* (“he/she said that...”) + *stava cercando* (imperfect progressive: “was looking for/was searching for”). The subject (who said it / who was looking) is understood from context and can be changed (e.g., *Tom ha detto...*, *Lei ha detto...*). Often followed by what someone was looking for: *aiuto*, *un lavoro*, *dei volontari*.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che stava cercando un appartamento in centro.
native_language_example: Marco said that he was looking for an apartment downtown.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "Ha detto" is past tense of *dire* (he/she said), "che" means "that", and "ti" refers to "you" in the following clause. Depending on the verb after it, "ti" can mean "you" as a direct object (e.g., *ti conosceva* = "knew you"), an indirect object (e.g., *ti ha telefonato* = "called you"), or a reflexive meaning (e.g., *ti devi riposare* = "you need to rest").
target_language_example: Ha detto che ti aspetta davanti al cinema.
native_language_example: He said that he’s waiting for you in front of the cinema.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech). The subject pronoun is often omitted in Italian, so "ha detto" can mean "he said" or "she said" depending on context. "che" = "that". "voleva" (imperfetto of "volere") often translates as "wanted" in the past and is commonly followed by an infinitive (e.g., voleva parlare = wanted to talk).
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva partire subito.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she wanted to leave right away.

meaning: “he/she said that he/she wanted to go.”
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "Ha detto" is passato prossimo (“said/has said”), and it’s commonly followed by "che" (“that”) plus an imperfect verb like "voleva" (“wanted”) for reported speech. The subject (he/she) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che voleva andare via presto.
native_language_example: Marco said that he wanted to leave early.

ha detto che voleva andare a

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che voleva andare a
meaning: “(He/She) said that (he/she) wanted to go to …”
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. **Ha detto** = “(he/she) said”; **che** = “that”; **voleva** (imperfetto of *volere*) = “wanted/was wanting”; **andare a** = “to go to” + a place (often followed by a city, a store, *casa*, etc.). You can change the subject: *ho detto* (I said), *hanno detto* (they said), and change the destination after **a**.
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva andare a Roma domani.
native_language_example: He said that he wanted to go to Rome tomorrow.

meaning: "he/she said that he/she wanted to do it."
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said in the past. "ha detto" is passato prossimo ("said"), and it’s followed by a clause introduced by "che" ("that"). "voleva" is imperfetto ("wanted"), common in reported speech. "farlo" = "fare" (to do) + "lo" (it). The subject of "ha detto" is often implied (he/she).
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che voleva farlo domani.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wanted to do it tomorrow.

ha detto che voleva parlare con

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che voleva parlare con
meaning: “he/she said that he/she wanted to talk to/with …” (used before the person’s name).
additional_notes: Used in reported speech (indirect speech) to say what someone said. It’s usually followed by the person someone wanted to speak to: “... parlare con Maria / con il dottore”. In context, “ha detto” can also mean “(he/she) told me/you/us…”.
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva parlare con il direttore.
native_language_example: He said he wanted to talk to the manager.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect/reported speech). It’s incomplete on its own: you must add a masculine singular noun after **un** (e.g., *un caffè, un taxi, un biglietto*). For a feminine noun, use **una** (e.g., *una pizza*), or **un’** before a vowel (e.g., *un’acqua*). The subject is often understood from context: **ha detto** can mean “he said” or “she said.”
target_language_example: Ha detto che voleva un caffè.
native_language_example: He/She said that he/she wanted a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech). Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so "ha detto" can mean "he said" or "she said" depending on context; and "vuole" means "he/she wants". What comes next is usually an infinitive (e.g., "vuole cambiare", "vuole mangiare") or a noun phrase ("vuole una pizza"). You can change the person/tense as needed: "ho detto che voglio" (I said I want), "hanno detto che vogliono" (they said they want).
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che vuole parlare con te domani.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wants to talk to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, introducing a subordinate clause with **che** (“that”). **Ha detto** is the *passato prossimo* of **dire** (“to say”), and **vuole** is the present tense of **volere** (“to want”). Italian often omits the subject pronoun, so it can mean “he said…” or “she said…”, depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che vuole cambiare lavoro.
native_language_example: He/She told me that he/she wants to change jobs.

meaning: 'he/she said that he/she wants to be…'
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (indirect speech). The subject is often implied: "ha detto" = "he/she said" (can also refer to a named person, e.g., "Mary ha detto"). After it, "vuole essere" means "wants to be". The next word often agrees with the person’s gender: "amico" (male friend), "amica" (female friend). Possessives like "sua/tua/vostro" show whose friend: "sua" can mean "his" or "her" depending on context.
target_language_example: Luca ha detto che vuole essere mio amico.
native_language_example: Luca said that he wants to be my friend.

meaning: "he/she said that (it) is" / "(someone) said that (someone/it) is".
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "Ha detto" = "(he/she) said" (the subject is often left out in Italian). "che" means "that" and introduces the next clause. "è" is the present of "essere" ("to be"), but it can change with tense and agreement: e.g. "ha detto che era" (was), "ha detto che è stata" (she has been / she was). Context tells you who "he/she" and "it" refer to.
target_language_example: Marco ha detto che è pronto, ma non lo vedo.
native_language_example: Marco said that he is ready, but I don’t see him.

ha detto che è andata a

target_language_multi_word_term: ha detto che è andata a
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (reported speech): **ha detto che** = “she said that…”. **è andata** is the past tense of **andare** with **essere** (passato prossimo) and agrees with a female subject (**andata**). Add a place after **a** (e.g., *a Roma*, *al supermercato*). For a male subject: **ha detto che è andato a**.
target_language_example: Maria ha detto che è andata a Roma ieri.
native_language_example: Maria said that she went to Rome yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said (“ha detto che…” = “he/she said that…”). “È stata” is passato prossimo of essere and agrees with a feminine subject (è stato = masculine; sono stati/state = plural). In English you often translate it as “was,” but in Italian it can also correspond to “has been,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha detto che è stata una giornata difficile.
native_language_example: He/She said it was a difficult day.

additional_notes: "Ha detto" is the "he/she said" form of dire. After di + infinitive, Italian often uses this structure where English may say "told someone to..." or "said that..." depending on context. It also appears in expressions like dire di sì / di no ("say yes / no") and with di + person/thing to mean "about."
target_language_example: Mi ha detto di aspettare qui.
native_language_example: He told me to wait here.

meaning: “he/she said to wait” / “he/she told (someone) to wait.”
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said. "Ha detto" is the passato prossimo of "dire" (he/she said), and "di aspettare" means "to wait". It often implies an understood object like "mi/ci" (me/us): "Ha detto di aspettare" = “He/She told us to wait.” You can change the subject: "hanno detto di aspettare" (they said to wait).
target_language_example: Il medico ha detto di aspettare in sala d’attesa.
native_language_example: The doctor said to wait in the waiting room.

meaning: "(he/she) said (that) he/she has/had" (followed by a past action).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about something they did. "Ha detto" = "(he/she) said" + "di aver" + past participle ("called / forgotten / won"). "Aver" is the infinitive "to have" used to form the past infinitive; it often corresponds to English "to have + past participle" ("to have called"), but in everyday translation you’ll often say "said he/she had..." (sequence of tenses).
target_language_example: Maria ha detto di aver perso il telefono.
native_language_example: Maria said she lost her phone.

additional_notes: Used to report what someone said when the subject stays the same: "Ha detto di..." + infinitive. With the past, Italian often uses the past infinitive: "di avere" + past participle (e.g., "di avere mangiato" = "that he/she had eaten"). You can also use "di aver" as a shorter form of "di avere" in many cases (same meaning).
target_language_example: Luca ha detto di avere dimenticato le chiavi.
native_language_example: Luca said he had forgotten his keys.

additional_notes: Used in reported speech. The past infinitive "avere visto" means "to have seen" and often corresponds to English "had seen" after a past reporting verb like "ha detto" (he/she said). You can change the subject: "ho detto di avere visto" (I said I had seen), "hanno detto di avere visto" (they said they had seen).
target_language_example: Ha detto di avere visto Luca ieri sera.
native_language_example: He said he had seen Luca last night.

meaning: “he/she said he/she was…” / “he/she said to be…” (reported speech).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said about themselves: **ha detto** (“he/she said”) + **di essere** (“to be”). In English you often translate it as “said (that) he/she was…,” especially when speaking in the past. What follows can be an adjective or noun (e.g., *stanco, canadese, un nuovo studente*) or an expression like *di fretta* (“in a hurry”).
target_language_example: Marco ha detto di essere pronto.
native_language_example: Marco said he was ready.

meaning: "he/she said not to…" / "he/she said that he/she didn’t…" (introduces a negative infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to report what someone said, followed by a negated infinitive: ha detto di non + infinitive (often in the past infinitive: aver/essere + past participle). It can mean either (1) the person reported they didn’t do something ("He said he didn’t…") or (2) they told someone not to do something ("He said not to…"), depending on context. Variants like “ha detto di non aver…” and “ha detto di non avere…” are both common.
target_language_example: Ha detto di non voler uscire stasera.
native_language_example: He said he doesn't want to go out tonight.

meaning: "he/she said (that) he/she was" (often: "he/she said he/she was feeling...").
additional_notes: Used in reported speech with the verb "stare" + an adjective/adverb (e.g., bene, male, meglio) to report someone’s condition or how they feel. The subject of "stare" is usually the same person as the subject of "ha detto" (so it often corresponds to English "he/she said he/she was..."). You’ll typically see it completed as: "Ha detto di stare bene/male".
target_language_example: Marco ha detto di stare meglio oggi.
native_language_example: Marco said he was feeling better today.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire" (to say/tell). "Ha" is the auxiliary "avere" (has), and "detto" is the past participle (said/told). The subject (lui/lei) is often omitted and understood from context, so it can mean “he told the truth” or “she told the truth.” Often used as an exclamation: "Ha detto la verità!" = “He/She told the truth!”
target_language_example: Non mi fido di lui, ma questa volta ha detto la verità.
native_language_example: I don’t trust him, but this time he told the truth.

additional_notes: Used with negative words like **non** or **nessuno**: **non ha detto niente** = “he/she didn’t say anything”; **nessuno ha detto niente** = “nobody said anything.” In Italian, **niente** often goes with another negative word (double negative) to express “anything/anybody” in negative sentences.
target_language_example: Non mi ha detto niente ieri.
native_language_example: He/She didn’t tell me anything yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of dire: ha detto = "has said/said". Qualcosa means "something". Used to report that someone said something, often without specifying what; in questions it can mean "Did he/she say anything?"
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ha detto qualcosa di utile.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she didn’t say anything useful.

additional_notes: Used to say that a third-person singular subject (he/she/it, or a named person) forgot something in the past. “Ha” is the present of avere used as an auxiliary; the subject (lui/lei/Name) is often understood from context. Plural: “hanno dimenticato” (they forgot).
target_language_example: Mary ha dimenticato il suo maglione.
native_language_example: Mary forgot her sweater.

additional_notes: Third-person singular passato prossimo of "dimenticare di" + infinitive. It means someone didn’t do something because they forgot. Related forms: ho dimenticato di (I forgot to), hai dimenticato di (you forgot to), abbiamo dimenticato di (we forgot to), avete dimenticato di (you all forgot to), hanno dimenticato di (they forgot to).
target_language_example: Tom ha dimenticato di spegnere il gas.
native_language_example: Tom forgot to turn off the gas.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone forgot something that belongs to them. Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so "ha" can mean "he has" or "she has" depending on context. "Il suo" is the possessive + article and must match the noun that follows in gender/number: il suo maglione (his/her sweater), la sua borsa (his/her bag), i suoi documenti (his/her documents), le sue chiavi (his/her keys).
target_language_example: Ha dimenticato il suo telefono a casa.
native_language_example: He/She forgot his/her phone at home.

additional_notes: "Ha dimenticato" is the passato prossimo of dimenticare (to forget) and can refer to either “he” or “she” depending on context. "Il suo ombrello" means “his/her umbrella” (suo can mean his or her). You can add a place with su/in + location: "su un autobus" (on a bus), "in auto" / "in automobile" (in the car).
target_language_example: Ha dimenticato il suo ombrello in ufficio.
native_language_example: He/She forgot his/her umbrella at the office.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "dormire" (to sleep), used to talk about a completed action in the past. It’s made with the auxiliary "avere" + past participle: (io) ho dormito, (lui/lei) ha dormito, (noi) abbiamo dormito, etc. Often translated as "slept" in English; can also be "has slept" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ieri notte Marco ha dormito molto bene.
native_language_example: Last night Marco slept very well.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb **dovere** (to have to / must). Used to say someone had an obligation or was compelled to do something. Very often followed by an infinitive: **ha dovuto + infinitive** (e.g., *ha dovuto partire* = he/she had to leave).
target_language_example: Ieri Marco ha dovuto lavorare fino a tardi.
native_language_example: Yesterday Marco had to work until late.

additional_notes: Used with a short time word (e.g., momento, secondo, attimo) to say someone paused briefly before acting or speaking. "Ha esitato" is past tense (passato prossimo) of "esitare" = to hesitate, and it agrees with the person implied by context.
target_language_example: Ha esitato per un attimo prima di rispondere.
native_language_example: He hesitated for a moment before answering.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of fare with a third-person singular subject: he/she/it did, or formal you did. Depending on context, it can mean "did" or "made" in English, and it also appears in common expressions like fare foto and fare domanda.
target_language_example: Giulia ha fatto tutto da sola.
native_language_example: Giulia did everything by herself.

additional_notes: Past tense of the expression “fare arrabbiare” (to make someone angry). It’s used with a person (direct object) who becomes angry: “X ha fatto arrabbiare Y” = “X made Y angry.” Often you’ll see it with object pronouns: “Mi ha fatto arrabbiare” (It made me angry), “Ci ha fatto arrabbiare” (It made us angry).
target_language_example: Quel commento mi ha fatto arrabbiare molto.
native_language_example: That comment made me really angry.

meaning: 'he/she did well' OR 'it did (someone) good' / 'it was good for (someone)'.
additional_notes:
From the verb phrase **fare bene**. It has two very common uses:
1) **Performing well / doing the right thing**: *Lui ha fatto bene* = “He did well / He did the right thing.” You can also add what was done well: *Ha fatto bene il suo lavoro*.
2) **Being good for someone (helping, benefiting)**: **fare bene a + person**. With pronouns: *Mi ha fatto bene* (“It did me good”), *Ti ha fatto bene la cura?* (“Did the treatment do you good?”). Often used for situations that help you feel better: *Stare con lui ti ha fatto bene*.
target_language_example: Hai riposato: ti ha fatto bene.
native_language_example: You rested: it did you good.

additional_notes: Used with the verb pattern "far(e) + infinitive" to mean "to make/lead someone to do something": "far cambiare idea a qualcuno" = to make someone change their mind. The person is usually shown with an indirect object pronoun: gli (to him), le (to her), vi (to you plural). "Ha fatto" is passato prossimo (3rd person singular): "(He/She/It) made".
target_language_example: Cosa ti ha fatto cambiare idea?
native_language_example: What made you change your mind?

additional_notes: Uses the causative pattern **fare + infinitive** to say that something caused someone to make a decision. Often appears in questions like **Che cosa/Cosa ti/vi/le ha fatto decidere di…?** (“What made you decide to…?”). The person affected can be shown with an indirect pronoun: **ti** (you singular informal), **vi** (you plural), **le** (you singular formal).
target_language_example: Che cosa ti ha fatto decidere di studiare italiano?
native_language_example: What made you decide to study Italian?

ha fatto del suo meglio per

target_language_multi_word_term: ha fatto del suo meglio per
additional_notes: Used to say someone tried as hard as they could to achieve something. It’s the passato prossimo of “fare del proprio meglio” + “per” + infinitive. Change the possessive to match the person: “ho fatto del mio meglio per…”, “hai fatto del tuo meglio per…”, “abbiamo fatto del nostro meglio per…”, etc.
target_language_example: Tom ha fatto del suo meglio per proteggere Mary.
native_language_example: Tom did his best to protect Mary.

meaning: 'he/she did his/her best' (tried as hard as possible).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "fare del proprio meglio" = "to do one’s best." "Suo" agrees with the subject: "ho fatto del mio meglio" (I did my best), "hai fatto del tuo meglio" (you did your best), "abbiamo fatto del nostro meglio" (we did our best), "hanno fatto del loro meglio" (they did their best). Often followed by a contrast with "ma/però" (but).
target_language_example: Ha fatto del suo meglio fino alla fine, ma non è bastato.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her best until the very end, but it wasn’t enough.

ha fatto del suo meglio per

target_language_multi_word_term: ha fatto del suo meglio per
additional_notes: Used to say someone tried as hard as they could to achieve a goal. The form "ha fatto" is passato prossimo (third-person singular) and works for both masculine and feminine subjects (lui/lei). "del suo" means “his/her” and changes with the person: del mio, del tuo, del nostro, etc. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (per + proteggere/salvare/sembrare...).
target_language_example: Ha fatto del suo meglio per proteggerla.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her best to protect her.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of fare i compiti (“to do homework”). Used to say someone completed their homework; “suoi” agrees with the person (i suoi compiti = his homework; i suoi compiti = her homework). You can add details like time (prima di cena) or doing it alone (da sola/da solo).
target_language_example: Ha fatto i suoi compiti ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She did his/her homework last night.

meaning: “he/she/it has done” / “did” (used with a noun: “did the …”, “had a …”, “took …”).
additional_notes: Past tense of **fare** (passato prossimo: *ha fatto*). It often appears as **ha fatto il + noun** to talk about an activity, experience, or procedure: *ha fatto il check-in* (“checked in”), *ha fatto il colloquio* (“had/did the interview”), *ha fatto il militare* (“did military service”), *ha fatto il dottorato* (“did a PhD”). In English you usually translate it with a more specific verb (“checked in”, “had”, “took”, “served”) rather than literally “did the”.
target_language_example: Ieri ha fatto il test di italiano.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she took the Italian test.

additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of fare (ha fatto = “has done/made”) plus molte (“many”, feminine plural). It must be followed by a feminine plural noun, e.g. molte foto (“many photos”). With foto, English usually says “take” (take photos), even though Italian uses fare (“make/do”).
target_language_example: Ha fatto molte domande durante la lezione.
native_language_example: He/She asked many questions during the lesson.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone made a lot of mistakes in something they did (writing, typing, homework, a report, etc.). It uses the passato prossimo with avere: “ha fatto” = “has done/made.” Often followed by more detail (e.g., “mentre…” / “nel…”).
target_language_example: Ha fatto molti errori mentre scriveva a computer il rapporto.
native_language_example: He/She made many mistakes while typing the report on the computer.

meaning: “(he/she) didn’t do anything” / “(he/she) has done nothing.”
additional_notes: Usually used with **non**: **non ha fatto niente** (“he/she didn’t do anything”). It’s in the **passato prossimo** (present perfect) and can be a statement (**Non ha fatto niente.**), a question (**Ha fatto niente? / Non ha fatto niente?**), or an exclamation (**Non ha fatto niente!**). You can also add details: **non ha fatto niente di sbagliato** (“did nothing wrong”).
target_language_example: Tranquillo: non ha fatto niente di male.
native_language_example: Relax: he/she didn’t do anything wrong.

additional_notes: Literally “(he/she) has done nothing illegal.” Used to say someone has not committed any crime or wrongdoing. **Ha fatto** is the passato prossimo of *fare* (did/has done). The subject is often implied: *Lui/Lei non ha fatto niente di illegale.* In standard Italian you usually include **non**: *non ha fatto niente di illegale* (without *non* can sound incorrect or dialectal). You can change the person: *non ho fatto niente di illegale* (I didn’t do anything illegal), *non hanno fatto niente di illegale* (they didn’t do anything illegal).
target_language_example: Tranquilli: non ha fatto niente di illegale.
native_language_example: Relax: he didn’t do anything illegal.

meaning: “(it) was nice / I was pleased (to hear/see…)” (past of fare piacere).
additional_notes: Used to say you appreciated something in the past. Most often you’ll hear it with an indirect object pronoun: **mi ha fatto piacere** = “I was pleased / I appreciated it”, **ci ha fatto piacere** = “we were pleased”, etc. Common after news, help, or meeting someone: **Mi ha fatto piacere conoscerti** (“It was nice to meet you”).
target_language_example: Mi ha fatto piacere sentirti ieri.
native_language_example: It was nice to hear from you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause explaining what someone did. "Ha fatto" is the past (passato prossimo) of *fare* and can translate as either simple past (“did”) or present perfect (“has done”) depending on context. Often followed by *doveva*, *poteva*, *voleva*, *ha promesso*, etc. (e.g., *Ha fatto quello che doveva fare* = “He did what he had to do”).
target_language_example: Marco ha fatto quello che poteva per aiutarti.
native_language_example: Marco did what he could to help you.

meaning: "(he/she) did this" or "(he/she) has done this."
additional_notes: Past tense of fare (to do/make) with the helper avere. "Ha" = he/she/it has, "fatto" = done/made, "questo" = this. Used to say someone did something, or to ask how/why they did it (e.g., "Come/Perché ha fatto questo?"). The subject (lui/lei/Tom/mamma) can be stated before it or understood from context.
target_language_example: Non so perché ha fatto questo.
native_language_example: I don't know why he/she did this.

additional_notes: Used to say someone did everything possible or everything required, followed by a clause that specifies what (e.g., what you told them to do, what they could do). It’s the passato prossimo of "fare" (ha fatto = has done/did) + "tutto ciò che" (= everything that/that which). Often paired with "poteva" (could) or "riusciva" (managed) to emphasize effort.
target_language_example: Lei ha fatto tutto ciò che poteva per finire il progetto in tempo.
native_language_example: She did everything she could to finish the project on time.

ha fatto tutto quello che poteva

target_language_multi_word_term: ha fatto tutto quello che poteva
