additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ha" (has) + "ricevuto" (received). It agrees with the subject (lui/lei) but "ricevuto" doesn’t change here because the auxiliary is "avere". Often followed by "da" to say who it was from: "ha ricevuto un regalo da lei/lui" = “received a gift from her/him.”
target_language_example: Ieri Marco ha ricevuto un regalo dai suoi amici.
native_language_example: Yesterday Marco received a gift from his friends.

meaning: 'he/she has received a' (followed by a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *ricevere* (“to receive”) with *avere*: *ha ricevuto* = “has received.” It’s used when the thing received is feminine singular (e.g., *una chiamata* “a call”, *una nota* “a note”, *una lettera* “a letter”). With *avere*, the past participle usually stays *ricevuto* (no agreement): *ha ricevuto una chiamata*.
target_language_example: Ha ricevuto una lettera ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She received a letter last night.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo (present perfect) of "ricevere". "Ha" is the auxiliary "avere" for 3rd person singular, so the subject is usually "lui" (he) or "lei" (she), often omitted in Italian. You can change the subject by changing the auxiliary: "ho/hai/abbiamo/avete/hanno ricevuto una lettera". Also common: "ha ricevuto una lettera da..." (from...).
target_language_example: Marco ha ricevuto una lettera da sua nonna.
native_language_example: Marco has received a letter from his grandmother.

additional_notes: Past tense with passato prossimo: ha ringraziato = “(he/she) thanked / has thanked.” The subject (lui/lei/a name) is often omitted in Italian. You can add the person being thanked with an indirect object pronoun: mi = “me,” ti = “you,” gli = “him,” le = “her,” ci = “us,” vi = “you (pl.),” li = “them (m.),” le = “them (f.).” The reason is introduced by per: per il regalo = “for the gift.”
target_language_example: Mi ha ringraziato per il regalo che le ho comprato.
native_language_example: She thanked me for the gift I bought her.

additional_notes: "Ha riparato" is the passato prossimo of *riparare* (to fix/repair), used for a completed action. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article (“the”) and changes with the noun: *ha riparato la stampante*, *ha riparato i telefoni*, *ha riparato le sedie*. You can add an object pronoun too: *L’ha riparato* (“He/She fixed it”).
target_language_example: Ha riparato il telefono ieri.
native_language_example: He/She fixed the phone yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ha" (has) + "risolto" (solved). It refers to a completed action. Use "Ha risolto il problema?" for a yes/no question. "Da solo/da sola" means "by himself/by herself."
target_language_example: Finalmente ha risolto il problema con il computer.
native_language_example: Finally, he/she solved the problem with the computer.

additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of rispondere (“to answer/reply”): ha + risposto. The subject is often understood from context (lui/lei). Common with al telefono (“on the phone”) and to answer someone: ha risposto a qualcuno.
target_language_example: Ho chiamato due volte, ma non ha risposto.
native_language_example: I called twice, but he/she didn’t answer.

additional_notes: Used to describe *how* someone replied, usually followed by an adjective: **in maniera errata/sbagliata** (wrongly), **in maniera scortese/sgarbata** (rudely). You can change the subject and tense: **ho risposto in maniera…** (I answered…), **hanno risposto in maniera…** (they answered…).
target_language_example: Mi ha risposto in maniera molto scortese.
native_language_example: He/She answered me in a very rude way.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of rivelare = “to reveal.” The subject is often omitted in Italian, so “Ha rivelato…” can mean “He revealed…” or “She revealed…”. You can add who received the secret with an indirect object: “Le ha rivelato il segreto” = “He/She revealed the secret to her,” “Gli ha rivelato il segreto” = “...to him,” or with “a + name” (e.g., “a Maria”).
target_language_example: Non dirlo a nessuno: ha rivelato il segreto!
native_language_example: Don’t tell anyone: he/she revealed the secret!

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "rompere" (to break). Used with a direct object: "ha rotto la bottiglia" = "(he/she) broke the bottle". With "con" it can mean ending a relationship: "ha rotto con Tom" = "(she) broke up with Tom".
target_language_example: Ha rotto il telefono ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She broke the phone last night.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun introduced by **il** (e.g., *il bicchiere*, *il vaso*). It’s the **passato prossimo** of **rompere** (to break): **ha** (present of *avere*) + **rotto** (past participle). In English you often translate it as simple past (“broke the”), even though Italian uses passato prossimo in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, Marco ha rotto il telefono.
native_language_example: Sorry, Marco broke the phone.

additional_notes: Past tense with passato prossimo: "ha rotto" (from "rompere", irregular past participle "rotto") + the object "la finestra". The subject can be a person or thing and is often understood from context (so it can mean “he/she/it broke the window”).
target_language_example: Chi ha rotto la finestra?
native_language_example: Who broke the window?

additional_notes: Used with liquids to say someone spilled something: *ha rovesciato il suo caffè/latte/drink*. The subject can be *ha* (he/she/it) + past participle *rovesciato* + possessive *il suo/la sua* (“his/her”). In questions, intonation or a question mark is enough: *Ha rovesciato il suo caffè?*
target_language_example: Ha rovesciato il suo bicchiere d’acqua sul tavolo.
native_language_example: He/She spilled his/her glass of water on the table.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "rubare" (to steal), used with the auxiliary "avere": "lui/lei ha rubato" = he/she has stolen (often translated as "he/she stole" in English depending on context). Often followed by a direct object ("ha rubato il portafoglio") or by "a" + person to mean stealing from someone ("ha rubato i soldi a Marco").
target_language_example: Qualcuno ha rubato la mia bici!
native_language_example: Someone stole my bike!

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun that takes "il" (e.g., il laptop, il diamante). "Ha rubato" is the passato prossimo of "rubare" (to steal): "ha" + past participle "rubato". For a feminine singular noun, you’d say "ha rubato la"; for plural: "ha rubato i/le".
target_language_example: Ha rubato il portafoglio.
native_language_example: He/She stole the wallet.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine noun (singular) that is understood or said right after, e.g. "ha rubato la mia borsa" = "he/she stole my bag". On its own, it feels incomplete in Italian unless the noun is implied from context (like "la mia macchina" = "my car"). "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" used to form the past (passato prossimo) with "rubare" (to steal).
target_language_example: Ha rubato la mia borsa!
native_language_example: He/She stole my bag!

additional_notes: Past tense of "salvare" with "avere" (passato prossimo). It agrees with the subject (ha = he/she/it). Used for rescuing someone/something, or more generally for saving (e.g., time/money/data) depending on context.
target_language_example: Mi ha salvato la vita.
native_language_example: He/She saved my life.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "scegliere" (to choose), used with the auxiliary "avere" + past participle "scelto". It can mean either "has chosen" (recent/present relevance) or "chose" (simple past idea), depending on context. The subject is not stated in Italian: it can be "he", "she", or "it" (and sometimes "you" formal). Often followed by "di" + infinitive: "ha scelto di + verb" = "he/she chose to + verb".
target_language_example: Ha scelto di restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: He/She chose to stay home tonight.

meaning: "he/she found out the truth" / "he/she discovered the truth."
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "scoprire" (to discover / to find out). "Ha" + past participle "scoperto" means a completed past action. The subject (he/she/you formal) is often understood from context. You can add the source with "da": "Ha scoperto la verità da lei" = "He found out the truth from her."
target_language_example: Ho mentito, ma poi ha scoperto la verità.
native_language_example: I lied, but then he/she found out the truth.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of scrivere. It is used with lui/lei/Lei or with a singular noun as the subject. In English, it can translate as either present perfect ('has written') or simple past ('wrote'), depending on context.
target_language_example: Maria ha scritto una lettera a sua nonna.
native_language_example: Maria wrote / has written a letter to her grandmother.

meaning: "(he/she) wrote a book" / "(he/she) has written a book."
additional_notes: "Ha scritto" is the passato prossimo of "scrivere" (to write) with the auxiliary "avere." It’s used for a completed action in the past, often connected to the present (similar to English "has written"), but it can also correspond to simple past "wrote" depending on context. The subject is not stated; it can mean "he" or "she" (or "you" formal) based on context.
target_language_example: Lei ha scritto un libro per bambini.
native_language_example: She wrote/has written a children’s book.

additional_notes: This is the passato prossimo of “scrivere” with “avere”: **ha scritto** = “he/she wrote” / “he/she has written.” It normally needs a noun after **una** (a feminine singular thing): *ha scritto una lettera* (“he wrote a letter”). In many contexts you’ll also see the pronoun subject: *Lui/Lei ha scritto una…*.
target_language_example: Ha scritto una lettera alla sua amica.
native_language_example: She wrote a letter to her friend.

meaning: “(He/She) wrote a letter” / “has written a letter.”
additional_notes: Past tense with avere: **ha scritto** (passato prossimo of *scrivere*). The subject is often understood from context (he/she/it), but you can add it: *Emily ha scritto una lettera.* You can also add details with **a** (to someone) or **dal** (from somewhere): *Ha scritto una lettera alla sua fidanzata; ha scritto una lettera dal carcere.* In questions, intonation or a question mark is enough: *Ha scritto una lettera?*
target_language_example: Mio padre ha scritto una lettera al sindaco.
native_language_example: My father wrote a letter to the mayor.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: **ha** (from *avere*) + past participle **scritto** (from *scrivere*). The subject is often implied in Italian, so it can mean **he** or **she** depending on context. Common in storytelling and everyday speech to talk about a completed action in the past.
target_language_example: Ieri ha scritto una lunga lettera ai suoi genitori.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she wrote a long letter to his/her parents.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *seguire* (to follow), used with *avere*: *ha seguito + (object)*. Meaning depends on context: following a person/animal (*Ha seguito il cane*), following tracks (*ha seguito le tracce*), or following advice/instincts/rules (*ha seguito i suoi istinti*). With pronouns: *Lo ha seguito a casa* = “He/She followed him home.”
target_language_example: Ha seguito le indicazioni fino alla stazione.
native_language_example: He/She followed the directions to the station.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of **sentire** (“to hear”, sometimes “to feel”). **Ha sentito…?** is also used as a polite/formal question with **Lei** (“Have you heard…?” / “Did you hear…?”). With another verb it often means “heard someone do something”: *ha sentito Mary gridare* = “heard Mary scream.”
target_language_example: Ha sentito quello che ho detto?
native_language_example: Did you hear what I said?

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone has stopped doing an action: "ha smesso di" + infinitive (e.g., "ha smesso di fumare" = "he/she stopped smoking"). It’s the 3rd-person singular present perfect of "smettere"; you can change it by person/tense (e.g., "ho smesso di" = "I stopped/I’ve stopped").
target_language_example: Lei ha smesso di lavorare alle sei.
native_language_example: She stopped working at six.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "smettere di" + infinitive. "Ha" is the auxiliary verb and "smesso" is the past participle; it agrees with the subject only in gender/number when using "essere" (not here). Use it for a completed action: "Ha smesso di fumare due anni fa." For "you stopped smoking", say "Hai smesso di fumare"; for "I stopped", "Ho smesso di fumare". Questions keep the same word order: "Quando ha smesso di fumare?"
target_language_example: Ha smesso di fumare perché si sentiva sempre stanco.
native_language_example: He stopped smoking because he always felt tired.

additional_notes: Used when a device, machine, or system no longer works (often suddenly). It’s the past tense (passato prossimo) of “smettere di funzionare” = “to stop working.” You can change it by person: “ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno smesso di funzionare.”
target_language_example: Il mio telefono ha smesso di funzionare ieri sera.
native_language_example: My phone stopped working last night.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ha" (from avere) + past participle "smesso" + "di" + infinitive. Used to say that someone no longer does an action. For other subjects: "ho smesso di piangere" (I stopped), "hai smesso..." (you stopped), "hanno smesso..." (they stopped).
target_language_example: Dopo qualche minuto, ha smesso di piangere.
native_language_example: After a few minutes, he/she stopped crying.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "sorridere" (to smile): "ha" (present of avere) + "sorriso" (past participle). Used for a completed action in the past (often translated with English simple past). The subject is understood from context (lui/lei/etc.).
target_language_example: Quando l'ho salutata, ha sorriso subito.
native_language_example: When I greeted her, she smiled right away.

additional_notes: Used with a drink right after it (e.g., "vino", "caffè"). "Il suo" means “his/her” and matches the noun (masc. singular here: il vino, il caffè). Often followed by an adverb like "lentamente" (“slowly”).
target_language_example: Ha sorseggiato il suo tè in silenzio.
native_language_example: He/She sipped his/her tea in silence.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "sparare" (to shoot/fire). Often followed by "a" + person/animal ("ha sparato a loro" = he/she shot at them) or "a" + article ("ha sparato al lupo" = he/she shot at the wolf). It can also mean "blurted out" or "told" (e.g., "ha sparato una bugia" = he/she told a lie), but in these examples it’s literal shooting.
target_language_example: Qualcuno ha sparato durante la notte.
native_language_example: Someone fired a gun during the night.

additional_notes: From the verb "sparare" (to shoot). "Ha sparato a + person" uses "a" before the person targeted. Depending on context, it can mean either “shot at” (maybe missed) or “shot” (hit).
target_language_example: Ha sparato a un uomo davanti alla banca.
native_language_example: He shot at a man in front of the bank.

additional_notes: “Ha” is the present tense of “avere” used to form the passato prossimo (past tense): ha spedito = “has sent/mailed.” “Spedire” is commonly used for sending mail or parcels (similar to “to ship”). The subject (lui/lei/Marco, etc.) is often omitted in Italian and understood from context.
target_language_example: Ha spedito una lettera ieri mattina.
native_language_example: He/She mailed a letter yesterday morning.

additional_notes: Used to say something caused deep emotional pain (often romantic, but also from bad news or disappointment). Usually you add an indirect object pronoun to say whose heart was broken: “mi ha spezzato il cuore” (broke my heart), “ti ha spezzato il cuore” (broke your heart), “gli/le ha spezzato il cuore” (broke his/her heart). Also common in other tenses: “mi hai spezzato il cuore” (you broke my heart), “mi sta spezzando il cuore” (it’s breaking my heart).
target_language_example: Mi ha spezzato il cuore quando se n’è andata.
native_language_example: It broke my heart when she left.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *spiegare* (to explain): *ha* (present of *avere*) + *spiegato* (past participle). Often used with an indirect object (to someone), frequently shown with pronouns: *mi* (to me), *ti* (to you), *gli* (to him), *le* (to her), *ci* (to us), *vi* (to you all), *gli* (to them). Can also introduce a reason with *perché*: *Ha spiegato perché...*
target_language_example: Mi ha spiegato come funziona questa app.
native_language_example: He/She explained to me how this app works.

additional_notes: Used with an expressed subject (lui/lei, a name) or implied from context. It’s the passato prossimo: "ha" + past participle "sposato". It can mean the event (“married” in the past) or, in some contexts, “has married” (recently). Often followed by the person married (direct object): "Ha sposato Maria" = "He/She married Maria."
target_language_example: Giulia ha sposato Luca l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: Giulia married Luca last year.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of sposare (“to marry”): ha sposato = “(he) married/has married.” The subject (usually “lui/he”) is often implied in Italian. Ragazza can mean “girl,” but in many contexts it also means “young woman.” You can add details after ragazza (e.g., canadese, ricca, di Boston).
target_language_example: Ha sposato una ragazza italiana l’anno scorso.
native_language_example: He married an Italian girl/young woman last year.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "studiare" with the auxiliary "avere" ("ha" + "studiato"). Used to talk about a completed action in the past; in English it can be "has studied" (present perfect) or often simply "studied" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha studiato italiano per due anni.
native_language_example: He/She studied Italian for two years.

additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of *studiare* (“to study”): **ha** (present of *avere*) + **studiato** (past participle). The subject is often understood from context: **lui/lei ha studiato francese** = “he/she studied French.” You can add details with **con** (with someone) or **per** (for a length of time).
target_language_example: Lei ha studiato francese all’università.
native_language_example: She studied French at university.

additional_notes: Past tense of studiare (“to study”) with the passato prossimo: ha (has) + studiato (studied). It agrees with the subject understood from context (lui/lei). Used to talk about completed study or life experience; add time expressions like ieri (yesterday), per tre anni (for three years), durante gli ultimi tre anni (during the last three years).
target_language_example: Lei ha studiato il francese all’università.
native_language_example: She studied French at university.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "tagliare i capelli". "Ha" can mean "he" or "she" (Italian doesn’t show gender here). Often implies a haircut (especially if it’s their own hair), even though the literal meaning is “has cut the hair.” To make it explicit that it’s their own hair, you’ll often hear the reflexive form: "si è tagliato/i capelli" (he) / "si è tagliata/i capelli" (she).
target_language_example: Ha tagliato i capelli ieri.
native_language_example: He/She got a haircut yesterday.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *tagliare* (to cut): **ha tagliato** = “(he/she) cut / has cut”. **La** is the feminine singular direct object (“the”), used before feminine nouns: *la mela* (the apple), *la torta* (the cake), *la corda* (the rope). Note: **tagliare la corda** can also be an idiom meaning “to take off / run away,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha tagliato la torta in due.
native_language_example: He/She cut the cake in two.

meaning: "(he/she) cut the rope"; also (idiomatically) "(he/she) ran away / took off."
additional_notes: Literally used when someone cuts a rope (e.g., with a knife or with their teeth). In everyday Italian, "tagliare la corda" is also a common idiom meaning to leave quickly or escape (like "to take off"), often without saying goodbye.
target_language_example: Quando ha visto la polizia, ha tagliato la corda.
native_language_example: When he saw the police, he took off.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: ha (present of avere) + tagliato (past participle). The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean “he cut” or “she cut” depending on context. Often followed by details like a metà / in due (“in half”).
target_language_example: Ha tagliato la mela a metà per condividerla.
native_language_example: He/She cut the apple in half to share it.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" used to form the passato prossimo. "Ha telefonato" means someone called (at an unspecified time in the recent past). Often followed by "a" + person (e.g., "Ha telefonato a loro?") or an indirect object pronoun like "mi/ti/ci/vi/gli/le" (e.g., "Mi ha telefonato").
target_language_example: Mi ha telefonato ieri sera, ma non ho risposto.
native_language_example: He/She called me last night, but I didn’t answer.

meaning: “has thrown,” “has pulled,” or “has taken out” (past tense of *tirare*).
additional_notes: *Ha tirato* is the **passato prossimo** (present perfect) of *tirare*, used for a completed action. Meaning depends on context: **tirare + object** = to throw (e.g., *tirare un sasso*), to pull (e.g., *tirare lo straccio*); **tirare fuori** = to pull/take out (e.g., from a pocket); **tirare su** = to lift up or (with a person) to raise/bring up (e.g., *mi ha tirato su da sola*). Often you’ll see **tirare + something + a + someone/animal** (“throw something at someone/animal”).
target_language_example: Ha tirato fuori il telefono dalla borsa.
native_language_example: She took the phone out of her bag.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "tirare fuori". Used when someone takes something out of a bag, pocket, etc. Often followed by the object + "da/dalla/dal" + the place it came from (e.g., "ha tirato fuori le chiavi dalla tasca").
target_language_example: Ha tirato fuori le chiavi dallo zaino.
native_language_example: He/She took the keys out of the backpack.

meaning: “he/she pulled out his/hers (feminine item),” with the noun implied by context.
additional_notes: From *tirare fuori* (“to pull out / take out”). *La sua* means “his/hers” referring to a feminine noun that’s understood (e.g., *la carta d’identità*, *la tessera*, *la pistola*, *la chiave*). You’ll usually hear it when everyone already knows what object is being talked about. It can also mean “he/she brought out / brought up his/hers” in some contexts, but without more words it’s most often literal (“pulled out”).
target_language_example: Al controllo ha tirato fuori la sua carta d’identità.
native_language_example: At the checkpoint he pulled out his ID card.

additional_notes: Commonly used to accuse someone of betraying their homeland (often “per denaro/per soldi” = “for money”). Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so “ha tradito…” can mean “he betrayed…” or “she betrayed…”. “Il suo paese” means “his/her country” (su = his/her, paese = country).
target_language_example: Ha tradito il suo paese per soldi.
native_language_example: He/She betrayed his/her country for money.

additional_notes: Past tense of *trascorrere* used with a time period (hours, days, weeks) or an occasion (e.g., Christmas) to say how someone spent that time. Often followed by a duration (*molto tempo*, *tre settimane*) or by *con* + person (*con la sua famiglia*), or by a place (*in prigione*, *a letto*).
target_language_example: Ha trascorso due giorni a Roma con degli amici.
native_language_example: He/She spent two days in Rome with some friends.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb "trascorrere" (to spend time). "Ha" is the auxiliary (avere) and "trascorso" is the past participle. Used for a completed period of time, often followed by what the time was spent doing or where: "ha trascorso molto tempo a studiare" (studying) / "ha trascorso molto tempo in Italia" (in Italy).
target_language_example: Ha trascorso molto tempo a studiare per l’esame.
native_language_example: He/She spent a lot of time studying for the exam.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "trattenere il fiato". Used literally (to stop breathing for a moment, e.g., while hiding or underwater) and also figuratively (to wait tensely/with suspense). The subject is implied by context: "ha" can mean "he" or "she".
target_language_example: Durante la scena finale, ha trattenuto il fiato fino ai titoli di coda.
native_language_example: During the final scene, he/she held their breath until the end credits.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of trovare. It is used with a third-person singular subject: he, she, it, or formal you (Lei). In English, it can translate as either present perfect ('has found') or simple past ('found'), depending on context.
target_language_example: Maria ha trovato le chiavi in cucina.
native_language_example: Maria found the keys in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *trovare* (to find): **ha** (present of *avere*) + **trovato** (past participle) + **il** ("the" for masculine singular nouns). Used when a single person (he/she) found something: *ha trovato il bottone* (he/she found the button). The thing found (direct object) comes after **il**. For feminine you’ll see **ha trovato la...**; for plural **ha trovato i/le...**. Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so **Ha trovato il...** can mean "He/She found the..." from context.
target_language_example: Ha trovato il telefono sotto il letto.
native_language_example: He/She found the phone under the bed.

meaning: he got what was coming to him; he got what he deserved.
additional_notes: Commonly said about someone who is finally punished or put in their place after behaving badly. Often used with an implied negative outcome (bad luck, consequences, a comeback). You can also change the pronoun: “ho trovato il mio”, “hai trovato il tuo”, “hanno trovato il loro”.
target_language_example: Dopo tutte le bugie, finalmente ha trovato il suo: nessuno si fida più di lui.
native_language_example: After all the lies, he finally got what was coming to him: nobody trusts him anymore.

meaning: "(he/she/you formal) found the" / "has found the" (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "trovare" (to find): "ha" (has) + "trovato" (found). It’s used with a direct object that is feminine singular, so it’s followed by "la" (e.g., "la chiave" = the key). In a question you’ll often see it like: "Ha trovato la ...?" = "Did you find the ...?"
target_language_example: Ha trovato la chiave sotto il divano.
native_language_example: He/She found the key under the couch.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun starting with a consonant (un): ha trovato un cadavere / un capello. It’s the passato prossimo of trovare (to find): ha (auxiliary avere) + trovato (past participle). In speech and in context it can translate as either “has found a” or simply “found a.”
target_language_example: Luca ha trovato un portafoglio per strada.
native_language_example: Luca found a wallet on the street.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): *ha trovato* = “has found/found,” with the subject implied from context (lui/lei). Used to say someone has found employment; in questions, intonation or a question mark signals “Did he/she find a job?”
target_language_example: Finalmente ha trovato un lavoro vicino a casa.
native_language_example: He/She finally found a job close to home.

meaning: '(he/she) found a' / '(he/she) has found a' (feminine noun).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "trovare" (to find). "Ha" is the auxiliary verb (has), and "trovato" is the past participle (found). The subject (lui/lei, or a name) is often implied. "Una" is used before a feminine singular noun (una bottiglia, una sorpresa, una fidanzata).
target_language_example: Ha trovato una soluzione al problema.
native_language_example: He/She found a solution to the problem.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of uccidere with a singular subject: he/she/it has killed. In English, it is often translated simply as "killed" depending on context.
target_language_example: Il lupo ha ucciso una pecora.
native_language_example: The wolf killed a sheep.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of uccidere: ha ucciso = "has/have killed" → usually "killed" in English. Used with a masculine singular direct object: il + noun (e.g., il ragno, il serpente). For feminine singular use "ha ucciso la"; for plural use "ha ucciso i/le".
target_language_example: Ha ucciso il cane per difendersi.
native_language_example: He killed the dog to defend himself.

additional_notes: Past tense of "usare" (to use) with the auxiliary "avere" in the passato prossimo. It agrees with the subject (lui/lei) and is followed by what was used: "ha usato la testa" (used his head = thought well), "ha usato un/uno...", "ha usato [nome]" (used a name). Often corresponds to English simple past.
target_language_example: Ha usato il mio telefono per chiamare un taxi.
native_language_example: He/She used my phone to call a taxi.

meaning: 'he/she used the' / 'has used the' (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Past tense of "usare" (to use): "ha usato" = he/she used or has used. "La" is the feminine singular "the" (la formula, la margarina, la via). Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so "ha usato la..." can mean "he used..." or "she used..." depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha usato la carta di credito per pagare.
native_language_example: He/She used the credit card to pay.

additional_notes: Used to say someone used a specific masculine singular thing in the past. "ha" (has) + past participle "utilizzato" (used) forms the passato prossimo; "il" is the masculine singular definite article. Change "il" depending on the noun: "ha utilizzato lo" (lo zaino), "ha utilizzato l'" (l'auto), "ha utilizzato la" (la macchina), "ha utilizzato i/le" (plural).
target_language_example: Ha utilizzato il telefono per chiamarti.
native_language_example: He/She used the phone to call you.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "vendere" (to sell): "ha" + past participle "venduto". It usually means a completed action in the past (“sold”), but can also translate as “has sold” depending on context. Often used with an indirect object pronoun: "Le ha venduto..." = “He/She sold (it) to her.” You can add "a + person" to say who it was sold to: "ha venduto ... a Tom".
target_language_example: Ha venduto la macchina a suo fratello.
native_language_example: He/She sold the car to his/her brother.

meaning: “he/she has sold his/hers” (with an implied noun).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of *vendere* (“to sell”): *ha venduto* = “has sold.” *La sua* means “his/hers” referring back to a feminine singular noun already known from context (e.g., *la macchina*, *la casa*). Often you’ll see it with the noun stated (*ha venduto la sua macchina*), but it can also stand alone when the noun is understood.
target_language_example: Io ho comprato una bici nuova; lui invece ha venduto la sua.
native_language_example: I bought a new bike; he, on the other hand, sold his.

additional_notes: Common Italian sentence without an explicit subject: “ha” already tells you it’s 3rd person singular (“he/she”). It uses the passato prossimo: avere (ha) + past participle (venduto) to talk about a completed past action. “La sua automobile” means “his/her car” (sua agrees with automobile, feminine singular). Often you’ll also hear “macchina” instead of “automobile.”
target_language_example: Ha venduto la sua automobile ieri mattina.
native_language_example: He/She sold his/her car yesterday morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ha venduto" = "has sold/sold". The subject is often omitted in Italian; it can mean “he” or “she” depending on context. "La sua" means “his/her/its” and agrees with the noun that follows (macchina is feminine). You can add time expressions (la settimana scorsa, tre settimane fa) or specify the buyer/price with "a" (a Mary) and "per" (per trecento dollari).
target_language_example: Ha venduto la sua macchina perché non la usava più.
native_language_example: He/She sold his/her car because he/she didn’t use it anymore.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "vincere" (to win), used with many subjects: a person/team (Ha vinto Tom.), a country (La Germania ha vinto la guerra.), or a prize/competition (ha vinto un premio). In English it can translate as either "has won" or "won" depending on context. Italian word order can put the subject after the verb (Ha vinto Tom. = Tom won.).
target_language_example: Alla fine ha vinto la squadra di Marco.
native_language_example: In the end, Marco's team won.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of **vincere** (“to win”) with **avere**: **ha vinto**. It’s followed by a noun with a definite article, often **il** for masculine singular (e.g., *il premio, il campionato*). The article changes with the noun: *ha vinto la gara*, *ha vinto lo scudetto*, *ha vinto i premi*. Can mean either “has won” (recent relevance) or simply “won” (past event), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ha vinto il torneo ieri sera.
native_language_example: He/She won the tournament last night.

meaning: "(he/she/you formal) won the" (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: From the verb "vincere" (to win). Used with a feminine singular noun after it: "ha vinto la gara/la corsa/la competizione". It can refer to winning a race, competition, bet, etc. The subject isn’t stated in Italian here and depends on context (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Maria ha vinto la partita.
native_language_example: Maria won the match/game.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): ha (has) + vinto (won). Used to say that someone has won the lottery; the subject is understood from context (lui/lei), or can be made explicit: "Lui/Lei ha vinto la lotteria."
target_language_example: Marco ha vinto la lotteria e non ci crede ancora.
native_language_example: Marco won the lottery and still can’t believe it.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): **ha vinto** = “has won / won” (from *vincere*, to win). **Le elezioni** can mean a single election event or elections in general; English often says “the election.” You can change the subject: *Ho vinto le elezioni* (I won), *Abbiamo vinto le elezioni* (we won), *Hanno vinto le elezioni* (they won).
target_language_example: Dopo una campagna lunga, ha vinto le elezioni.
native_language_example: After a long campaign, he/she won the election.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "visitare" (to visit). Used for a completed action in the past. It’s made with the auxiliary "avere" (ha) + past participle "visitato". The subject is often implied (e.g., "Ha visitato..." = "He/She/It visited/has visited...") and is understood from context.
target_language_example: Ha visitato il museo ieri pomeriggio.
native_language_example: He/She visited the museum yesterday afternoon.

additional_notes: Third-person singular of the passato prossimo of vivere (“to live”). Used to say where someone lived and for how long, often with time expressions like due anni, per sei settimane, tutta la sua vita, da quando…, sin da quando…. It can describe living in a place (ha vissuto a Boston) or a living situation (ha vissuto da solo = he lived alone).
target_language_example: Maria ha vissuto in Italia per tre mesi.
native_language_example: Maria lived in Italy for three months.

meaning: "he/she has lived a life" (often implying a full, intense, or difficult life).
additional_notes: Used with an implied subject (lui/lei) in the passato prossimo: "ha vissuto" = "has lived". In real speech it’s often followed by an adjective or phrase to add meaning: "ha vissuto una vita difficile" (a hard life), "una vita piena" (a full life), "una vita avventurosa" (an adventurous life). On its own, it can sound a bit incomplete unless the context already explains what kind of life is meant.
target_language_example: Mio nonno ha vissuto una vita difficile, ma è sempre rimasto positivo.
native_language_example: My grandfather lived a hard life, but he always stayed positive.

meaning: “(he/she) saw” / “has seen” (with a feminine direct object).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of **vedere** (“to see”): **ha** + past participle **visto/vista**. The participle becomes **vista** when the direct object is feminine and comes before the verb (common with pronouns like **ti**, **la**, **ne**): **Ti ha vista** = “He saw you” (to a woman/girl). With a masculine object you’ll see **ha visto**: **Ti ha visto** (to a man/boy).
target_language_example: Gianni ti ha vista ieri al supermercato.
native_language_example: Gianni saw you yesterday at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of vedere. It is used for he/she/it, and in everyday Italian it often corresponds to English simple past ('saw') as well as present perfect ('has seen'). With Lei, the formal 'you', the same form can also mean 'you have seen' or 'have you seen?'
target_language_example: Ha visto le mie chiavi?
native_language_example: Have you seen my keys?

additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of vedere (to see). It refers to a completed action in the past. "Ha" = has, "visto" = seen, "il" = the (masculine singular). With people, use "l'ha visto" (“has seen him/it”), not "ha visto il".
target_language_example: Ha visto il mio messaggio?
native_language_example: Did you see my message?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (with formal Lei) if they have seen something that belongs to you. Put the item after it: "Ha visto il mio cappotto?" (my coat), "Ha visto il mio cellulare?" (my phone). For feminine nouns use "la mia" (e.g., "Ha visto la mia borsa?").
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ha visto il mio passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my passport?

additional_notes: From vedere (to see), passato prossimo: ha visto = “has/have seen.” With a capital Lei (formal “you”), questions like “Ha visto la…?” mean “Have you seen the…?” (e.g., to ask a stranger). The la is the feminine singular definite article (“the”) and is used with feminine nouns (la gatta, la mamma, la serie, la versione).
target_language_example: Scusi, ha visto la mia borsa nera?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my black bag?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone (politely) if they have seen something that belongs to you. It uses the formal "Lei" form: "Ha visto…?" = "Have you seen…?" Add a noun after it: "Ha visto la mia borsa?" (my bag). For masculine nouns, use "il mio": "Ha visto il mio telefono?"
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ha visto la mia borsa?
native_language_example: Excuse me, have you seen my bag?

meaning: "(he/she) has seen a" / "(he/she) saw a" (masculine singular object).
additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of vedere (to see): ha (present of avere) + visto (past participle). Used with a masculine singular noun introduced by un (e.g., un edificio, un cammello). In context it can translate as either "has seen" or simple past "saw" in English.
target_language_example: Ha visto un cane vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: He/She saw a dog near the station.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say what something is connected to. Very common in questions with “Che cosa/Cosa … ha a che fare con …?” (“What does … have to do with …?”). You’ll also often hear it in the negative (variant): “Non ha nulla a che fare con …” (“It has nothing to do with …”).
target_language_example: Che cosa ha a che fare con questo?
native_language_example: What does this have to do with this?

meaning: "makes any sense" / "has any point" (usually in questions or negatives).
additional_notes: Used mostly with non-specific "alcun" (= any) in questions or negative sentences: "Non ha alcun senso" (It doesn’t make any sense). In a positive sentence, Italians more often say "ha senso" or "ha un senso" rather than "ha alcun senso".
target_language_example: Non ha alcun senso discutere di questo adesso.
native_language_example: It doesn’t make any sense to argue about this now.

additional_notes: Used with a third-person singular subject (he, she, it, or a name) to say that something continues to be true or remains in someone's possession. Here ancora means "still".
target_language_example: Giulia ha ancora il mio libro.
native_language_example: Giulia still has my book.

additional_notes: Form of the verb phrase "avere bisogno (di)" = "to need". "Ha bisogno" is used with a following "di" + noun/pronoun (Ha bisogno di te; ha bisogno della tua firma) or with "di cui" meaning "that (which) ... needs" (tutto quello di cui ha bisogno; ciò di cui ha bisogno).
target_language_example: Scusi, ha bisogno di aiuto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you need help?

additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive: "ha bisogno di denaro" (needs money), "ha bisogno di studiare" (needs to study). It’s the 3rd-person singular form of "avere bisogno di" (to need); you can change it depending on the subject (e.g., "ho bisogno di" = I need, "hai bisogno di" = you need).
target_language_example: Ha bisogno di aiuto per trovare la strada.
native_language_example: He/She needs help to find the way.

additional_notes: "Avere bisogno di" means "to need." "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular form, so it refers to he/she/it (or a singular formal "you" = "Lei"). Often used as a question: "Ha bisogno di aiuto?" = "Do you need help?"
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ha bisogno di aiuto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you need help?

meaning: "needs to be" (must be done to it).
additional_notes: Used to say something requires an action done to it. It’s often followed by a past participle (lavato, pitturata, sostituita) and agrees in gender/number with the thing: lavato (m. sg.), lavata (f. sg.), lavati (m. pl.), lavate (f. pl.). The subject is the thing that needs the action (e.g., the house), not the person doing it.
target_language_example: Questo documento ha bisogno di essere firmato oggi.
native_language_example: This document needs to be signed today.

additional_notes: Used to say something requires washing/cleaning. It literally combines: ha (has) + bisogno di (need of) + essere (to be) + lavata (washed, feminine singular). Use lavato for masculine singular (Il cane ha bisogno di essere lavato), lavate for feminine plural (Le camicie… lavate), lavati for masculine plural (I pantaloni… lavati).
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, la valigia ha bisogno di essere lavata.
native_language_example: After the trip, the suitcase needs to be washed.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" = "to need". "Ha" is present tense for lui/lei or Lei (polite "you"), so it can mean "he needs me", "she needs me", or "do you (formal) need me?" in a question. Often followed by a noun or infinitive: "ha bisogno di aiuto" (needs help), "ha bisogno di parlare" (needs to talk).
target_language_example: Se ha bisogno di me, sono qui.
native_language_example: If you need me, I'm here.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something needs a greater amount of something. It’s the present tense of "avere bisogno di" (to need) with "più" (more). The thing needed usually follows directly: "ha bisogno di più + noun" (e.g., più pratica, più sale).
target_language_example: Il tuo italiano ha bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: Your Italian needs more time.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "avere bisogno di" = "to need". "Ha" can mean "you have" (formal "Lei") or "he/she has" depending on context. Often used as a polite offer of help: "Ha bisogno di qualcosa?" = "Do you need anything?" With "Se ha bisogno di qualcosa..." it means "If you need anything..." (again usually formal "you").
target_language_example: Se ha bisogno di qualcosa, sono qui.
native_language_example: If you need anything, I'm here.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “avere bisogno di” = “to need.” Here, “ha” is 3rd person singular (he/she/it has), and “di te” means “of you” → “needs you.” Use it for a person (Lui/Lei) or a thing/organization (Il mondo, Tatoeba) that needs your help or presence.
target_language_example: Non andare via: ha bisogno di te adesso.
native_language_example: Don’t go away: he/she needs you now.

meaning: "he/she needs a" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a third-person singular subject (lui/lei/it; often implied). Followed by a masculine singular noun, so it takes the article "un" (e.g., un cappotto, un telefono). For feminine singular nouns, use "ha bisogno di una" (una chiave). For plural: "ha bisogno di" + "dei/delle" (or just the plural noun in some contexts).
target_language_example: Ha bisogno di un aiuto?
native_language_example: Does he/she need help?

additional_notes: Used with a noun after it: “ha bisogno di un altro + [noun]” = “needs another + [noun]” (e.g., un altro computer = another computer). The verb form “ha bisogno” is for he/she/it and for polite “you” (Lei).
target_language_example: Dice che ha bisogno di un altro computer.
native_language_example: He/She says that he/she needs another computer.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something needs a replacement. It’s the phrase "avere bisogno di" (to need) + "un nuovo" (a new [masculine singular] ...). It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., un nuovo capitano). For feminine nouns, use "ha bisogno di una nuova" (e.g., una nuova macchina).
target_language_example: La mia bici ha bisogno di un nuovo sellino.
native_language_example: My bike needs a new saddle.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: “ha bisogno di una + [noun]”. It literally means “has need of a”, but in natural English you translate it as “needs a”. For masculine nouns you say “ha bisogno di un …” (e.g., “ha bisogno di un medico”).
target_language_example: Ha bisogno di una pausa.
native_language_example: He/She needs a break.

additional_notes: “Avere bisogno di” means “to need” and is followed by a noun (as here) or an infinitive: “Ho bisogno di aiuto” (I need help), “Ho bisogno di parlare” (I need to talk). “Ha” is 3rd person singular (he/she/it has). In real life you’ll usually add context: “La città ha bisogno di una moschea” (The city needs a mosque).
target_language_example: Questa comunità ha bisogno di una moschea.
native_language_example: This community needs a mosque.

additional_notes: Formed by **ha** (he/she has) + **dei** (partitive article meaning “some” with masculine plural nouns). Used before plural countable nouns: *ha dei gusti / ha dei parenti / ha dei rimpianti*. In questions, word order stays the same: *Ha dei…?* (Does he/she have any…?). For feminine plural nouns you typically use **delle** (*ha delle idee*).
target_language_example: Marco ha dei dubbi su questo progetto.
native_language_example: Marco has some doubts about this project.

additional_notes: Used to say or ask what someone intends to do for a time/event (oggi, stasera, Halloween, Natale) or to do something (e.g., "ha dei piani per farlo" = "he/she has plans to do it"). In questions, "Ha..." is formal/polite (Lei). You can change the subject: ho/hai/abbiamo/hanno dei piani per...
target_language_example: Ha dei piani per stasera?
native_language_example: Do you have plans for tonight?

additional_notes:
Used with different prepositions depending on what the problem is:
- **ha dei problemi a + infinitive** = has trouble doing something: *Ha dei problemi a dormire.*
- **ha dei problemi con + noun/pronoun** = has problems with something/someone: *Ha dei problemi con quello.*
- **ha dei problemi alla/con la schiena** = has back problems (pain/issues).
- **ha dei problemi di + noun** = has problems of (e.g., credibility): *problemi di credibilità.*
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi ha dei problemi a concentrarsi.
native_language_example: Sorry, today he/she is having trouble concentrating.

additional_notes: Used to say someone finds it hard to do something. It’s followed by the preposition "a" + an infinitive verb (e.g., "a dormire") or "a" + infinitive with a reflexive pronoun (e.g., "a farsi delle amicizie"). You can change the subject and tense: "ho dei problemi a...", "aveva dei problemi a...", "avrà dei problemi a...". Similar: "fa fatica a".
target_language_example: Tom ha dei problemi a gestire lo stress.
native_language_example: Tom has trouble managing stress.

additional_notes: Composed of ha ('has') + delle ('some'). It is used with feminine plural nouns to say that someone or something has some amount of something: ha delle idee = 'has some ideas', ha delle prove = 'has some evidence/proofs'.
target_language_example: Maria ha delle domande importanti.
native_language_example: Maria has some important questions.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”) + the number due (“two”) to say that someone has two of something (objects, family members, homes, jobs, etc.). In Italian the subject pronoun is often omitted: “Ha due figli” = “(He/She) has two children.” The verb form ha is for lui/lei/Lei (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Marta ha due fratelli e una sorella.
native_language_example: Marta has two brothers and a sister.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere fame" = to be hungry. "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular present (lui/lei/Lei): "Lui ha fame" (He’s hungry), "Lei ha fame" (She’s hungry), also polite "Lei ha fame?" (Are you hungry?). To say "I’m hungry": "Ho fame".
target_language_example: Scusa, ma lei ha fame?
native_language_example: Excuse me, but are you hungry?

meaning: “(he/she) has eyes” / “has (the) eyes …” (to describe eye color or look).
additional_notes: Used with a following description: eye color (marroni, verdi, azzurri), size/shape (molto piccoli), or a comparison/metaphor (di un leopardo). You can also add an adjective like rossi. Literally “has the eyes,” but in English you typically drop “the” when talking about someone’s eye color (e.g., “She has green eyes”).
target_language_example: Lei ha gli occhi neri.
native_language_example: She has black eyes.

meaning: "has (the) hair"; used to describe someone’s hair (color, type, length, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with a hair description: *Ha i capelli + adjective* (Ha i capelli rossi/biondi/lunghi/corti/ricci/lisci). For a single feature you can also say *Ha i capelli* + *castani* (brown), etc. You can add comparisons: *Ha i capelli simili ai suoi* = “He/She has hair similar to his/hers.” In Italian you normally include the article *i* with body parts.
target_language_example: Lei ha i capelli lunghi e ricci.
native_language_example: She has long, curly hair.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s appearance. The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean “he has…” or “she has…”, depending on context. You can use it in statements or as a yes/no question (with rising intonation or a question mark in writing).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha i capelli lunghi e ricci.
native_language_example: My sister has long, curly hair.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the present tense of avere for he/she/it, and "il" means "the" before many masculine singular nouns. Italian often leaves out the subject pronoun, so "ha il" can mean "he has the," "she has the," or "it has the" depending on context.
target_language_example: Anna ha il telefono in borsa.
native_language_example: Anna has the phone in her bag.

meaning: "has the desire to be" / "wants to be".
additional_notes: Formal-sounding phrase, often used in writing or polite speech. "Ha" is 3rd person singular (he/she/it has). It’s followed by an infinitive with "di" ("di essere" = "to be"). In everyday conversation you often just say "vuole essere" ("wants to be").
target_language_example: Ha il desiderio di essere indipendente.
native_language_example: He/She has the desire to be independent.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is entitled/allowed (legally or morally) to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., sapere, votare, arrabbiarsi). You can change the subject/verb for other people: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno il diritto di.
target_language_example: Ognuno ha il diritto di avere una propria opinione.
native_language_example: Everyone has the right to have their own opinion.

meaning: "(he/she) has a …ache" (literally: has the pain of …).
additional_notes: This is part of the expression **avere il mal di + body part** to say someone has pain in a specific place. You must add what hurts: **ha il mal di testa** (has a headache), **ha il mal di denti** (has a toothache), **ha il mal di pancia** (has a stomachache). For “my/your…” change the verb: **ho il mal di…**, **hai il mal di…**.
target_language_example: Oggi ha il mal di testa, quindi resta a casa.
native_language_example: Today he has a headache, so he’s staying home.

additional_notes: Used with masculine singular nouns (il suo = his/its; can also mean “its own”). It emphasizes possession or that something is specific to that person/thing: “his own website/apartment,” “its own destiny/path/deepest point.” For feminine singular you use “ha la sua,” and for plural “ha i suoi / ha le sue.” Often you’ll see it with body/essential items too: “ha il suo bastone” = “has his cane.”
target_language_example: Ogni famiglia ha il suo modo di fare le cose.
native_language_example: Every family has its own way of doing things.

additional_notes: Used with a subject (often implied): "(Questo) ha importanza" = "This matters." Most commonly heard in the negative: "Non ha importanza" = "It doesn't matter" / "No big deal." You can also use it in questions: "Ha importanza?" = "Does it matter?"
target_language_example: Se arrivo cinque minuti tardi, ha importanza?
native_language_example: If I arrive five minutes late, does it matter?

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s intention or plan. It’s the present tense (lui/lei) of "avere intenzione di" + infinitive: "Ho intenzione di..." (I intend to), "Hai intenzione di...?" (Do you intend to?), "Abbiamo intenzione di..." (We intend to). Often implies a deliberate plan rather than just a wish.
target_language_example: Ha intenzione di partire domani mattina.
native_language_example: He/She intends to leave tomorrow morning.

meaning: "he/she intends to go" / "he/she plans to go".
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s intention or plan to go somewhere or to leave. It’s formal/neutral and common in speaking and writing. Structure: (avere) intenzione di + infinitive. Here: ha = "he/she has" (3rd person singular), so it can mean either "he" or "she"; you can make it explicit with lui/lei.
target_language_example: Ha intenzione di andare via presto.
native_language_example: He/She intends to leave early.

meaning: "he/she intends to do it" / "he/she plans to do it".
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has the intention/plan to do something. You can change the subject: "ho intenzione di farlo" (I intend to do it), "hai intenzione di farlo?" (do you intend to do it?), "non ha intenzione di farlo" (he/she doesn’t intend to do it). Often paired with a time word like "oggi" (today) or "domani" (tomorrow).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che ha intenzione di farlo.
native_language_example: He told me that he intends to do it.

meaning: 'has the' (referring to a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Made of the verb "ha" (he/she/it has) + the definite article "la" (the, feminine singular). Used before feminine singular nouns: "ha la macchina" = "has the car". For masculine singular you’ll usually see "ha il" (or "ha l’" before vowels).
target_language_example: Lei ha la chiave.
native_language_example: She has the key.

additional_notes: From the verb *avere* (“to have”): *ho la febbre* (I have a fever), *hai la febbre* (you have a fever), *ha la febbre* (he/she has a fever). Often used with adjectives like *alta* (“high”) or with a cause/type: *febbre da fieno* (“hay fever”).
target_language_example: Non può venire a scuola oggi: ha la febbre.
native_language_example: He/She can’t come to school today: he/she has a fever.

additional_notes: Used to say someone (or something) has the same age as someone/something else. It’s the 3rd-person singular form of the expression "avere la stessa età di" (to be the same age as). You can change the verb to match the subject: "Ho/Hai/Ha/Abbiamo/Avete/Hanno la stessa età di...".
target_language_example: Mary ha la stessa età di Tom.
native_language_example: Mary is the same age as Tom.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone/something possesses something that belongs only to them (not shared). The possessive changes with the owner: ho la mia propria…, hai la tua propria…, ha la sua propria…, abbiamo la nostra propria…, avete la vostra propria…, hanno la loro propria…. Often you can also say simply “ha la sua…”; “propria” adds emphasis (“own”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ha la sua propria macchina.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he has his own car.

meaning: "tends to" / "has a tendency to" (usually does something).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a typical habit or pattern. It’s most common with "a" + infinitive: "ha la tendenza a + verb" (Ha la tendenza a parlare...). You may also see "di" in some contexts, but "a" is generally preferred.
target_language_example: Mio fratello ha la tendenza a rimandare tutto all’ultimo minuto.
native_language_example: My brother tends to put everything off until the last minute.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) in the 3rd person singular: "lui/lei/Lei/esso(a) ha". "Le" is the definite article for feminine plural nouns (e.g., "le idee", "le ruote", "le pulci"). In speech and writing, Italian often uses the article where English might drop it (e.g., "ha le guance rosse" = "has red cheeks").
target_language_example: Giulia ha le chiavi in borsa.
native_language_example: Giulia has the keys in her bag.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or phrase to describe someone’s hands or their condition. Common patterns: "ha le mani + aggettivo" (ha le mani piccole = he has small hands; ha le mani fredde = she has cold hands) and "ha le mani piene" = he/she has their hands full (busy). Italian typically uses the definite article "le" where English often uses a possessive (his/her).
target_language_example: Lei ha le mani fredde.
native_language_example: She has cold hands.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t specify the noun because it’s understood from context: ha le sue ragioni (has his/her reasons), ha le sue colpe (has his faults), ogni rosa ha le sue spine (every rose has its thorns). The possessive agrees with what’s owned (le sue = feminine plural), not with the person who owns it.
target_language_example: Non giudicarlo: ha le sue ragioni.
native_language_example: Don’t judge him: he has his reasons.

additional_notes: Used with the verb avere ("to have"): ha = "he/she has" (also "you have" in formal address: Lei ha). Molte agrees with feminine plural nouns (e.g., molte foto, molte riviste). For masculine plural nouns, use molti (e.g., ha molti amici). In questions, intonation often changes: Ha molte foto?
target_language_example: Lei ha molte valigie.
native_language_example: She has many suitcases.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has lots of female friends. The subject is often understood from context (e.g., “lui/lei” isn’t stated). “Amiche” is feminine plural (female friends); for male friends you’d say “ha molti amici.”
target_language_example: Giulia ha molte amiche all’università.
native_language_example: Giulia has many (female) friends at university.

meaning: “he/she has a lot of things to do.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone is busy and has several tasks to do. The subject can change: "ho molte cose da fare" (I have...), "hai..." (you have...), "abbiamo..." (we have...). Often followed by a time phrase (e.g., "questa mattina/stamattina") or something that must happen first ("prima di..." + infinitive / "prima che..." + subjunctive).
target_language_example: Oggi non può venire: ha molte cose da fare.
native_language_example: He/She can’t come today: he/she has a lot of things to do.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the 3rd person singular of avere ("to have"). "Molti" means "many" and is used with masculine plural nouns. For feminine plural nouns, Italian uses "ha molte" instead. This phrase can describe possession or more abstract things, like homework, problems, or grammatical cases.
target_language_example: Lui ha molti amici in città.
native_language_example: He has many friends in the city.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has a lot of friends. "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular of "avere" (to have), so it goes with "lui/lei" or a singular noun (e.g., Tom, il musicista). In questions, intonation often rises: "Tom ha molti amici?"
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha molti amici in città.
native_language_example: My sister has many friends in the city.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" (to have) for he/she/it (also used with "Lei" formal “you”). "Molti" agrees with the masculine plural noun "libri". Often followed by where the books are ("in camera sua / nella sua camera" = in his/her room) or what kind ("libri religiosi" = religious books, "per giovani" = for young people).
target_language_example: Lei ha molti libri in casa.
native_language_example: She has many books at home.

ha niente a che vedere con

target_language_multi_word_term: ha niente a che vedere con
meaning: "has nothing to do with" / "is unrelated to".
additional_notes: From the verb phrase "avere (qualcosa/niente) a che vedere con" = "to have (something/nothing) to do with". It’s used to say there is no connection between two things. You can change it for other subjects/tenses: "non ho niente a che vedere con..." (I have nothing to do with...), "non c'entra niente con..." is a common alternative.
target_language_example: Questo non ha niente a che vedere con il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: This has nothing to do with my job.

additional_notes:
Third-person singular of “avere paura” (“to be afraid”). It refers to he/she/it (or a singular noun/name): “Tom ha paura.” Often followed by:
- di + person/thing: “ha paura di lui” (afraid of him)
- di + infinitive: “ha paura di parlare” (afraid to speak)
- che + clause: “ha paura che…” (afraid that…).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha paura del buio.
native_language_example: My sister is afraid of the dark.

meaning: “is afraid of” (he/she is scared of + plural noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb avere (“to have”): avere paura di = “to be afraid of.” Here ha = “he/she has.” With plural masculine nouns you often get di + i → dei (e.g., dei cani, dei ragni). For plural feminine nouns it becomes delle (e.g., delle api). You can negate it with non: non ha paura dei cani = “he/she isn’t afraid of dogs.”
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha paura dei temporali.
native_language_example: My sister is afraid of thunderstorms.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **avere paura di** (“to be afraid of”). **ha** = “(he/she) has” and **paura** = “fear,” but in English you usually translate it as “is afraid.” **del** is **di + il** (“of the”), used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *del cane*). With other nouns you’ll see: **della** (fem. sing.), **dei/degli** (masc. plural), **delle** (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Luca ha paura del buio.
native_language_example: Luca is afraid of the dark.

additional_notes: Used with a third-person singular subject (lui/lei) to say someone is afraid. It can be followed by a noun ("ha paura di quel cane" = afraid of that dog) or by an infinitive verb to say someone is afraid to do something ("ha paura di dirlo" = afraid to say it). For other subjects: "ho paura di" (I’m afraid), "hai paura di" (you’re afraid), "hanno paura di" (they’re afraid).
target_language_example: Luca ha paura di parlare davanti a tutti.
native_language_example: Luca is afraid to speak in front of everyone.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) + "qualche" to ask or say that someone has an unspecified small number/amount of something. "Qualche" is typically followed by a singular noun even though it often translates as "some" or "a few" (e.g., "qualche domanda" = "some/a few questions"). In questions it often matches English "any" ("Ha qualche notizia?" = "Do you have any news?").
target_language_example: Ha qualche minuto libero?
native_language_example: Do you have a few free minutes?

meaning: "(he/she/it) has something to …" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say someone has something to say/ask/do/hide, etc. It can introduce a direct or indirect object after the infinitive (e.g., "Ha qualcosa da dirle" = "He has something to tell her"). Change "ha" to match the subject: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno qualcosa da".
target_language_example: Scusi, ha qualcosa da aggiungere?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have something to add?

additional_notes: Used to agree with someone’s opinion or to say they’re correct. It’s the 3rd-person singular of "avere ragione" (to be right): lui/lei ha ragione = he/she is right; Lei ha ragione = you (formal) are right. Often appears with contrast words like "ma/però" (but): "Ha ragione, però..."
target_language_example: Odio dirlo, ma Tom ha ragione.
native_language_example: I hate to say it, but Tom is right.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is logical or reasonable: “Non ha senso” = “It doesn’t make sense.” Often used as a short reply (“Ha senso.” / “Ha senso?”). You can also ask if something is appropriate or worth doing in a situation: “Ha senso qui…?” = “Does it make sense here…?”
target_language_example: Non ha senso discutere adesso: ne parliamo domani.
native_language_example: It doesn’t make sense to argue now: we’ll talk about it tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something possesses or contains three of something. "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular present of "avere" (to have): lui/lei/Lei ha tre… (he/she/you formal has three…). The noun is usually plural after the number: "ha tre fratelli".
target_language_example: La mia famiglia ha tre gatti.
native_language_example: My family has three cats.

additional_notes: Used with a third-person singular subject (lui/lei, a name, etc.). In Italian, "avere" (to have) is used for family relationships: "ha tre figli" = has three children (sons and/or daughters). You’ll often see time words added like "adesso/ora" (now) or extra details like "da mantenere" (to support).
target_language_example: Marco ha tre figli e lavora molto.
native_language_example: Marco has three children and works a lot.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the 3rd person singular of avere, so it means "he/she/it has" (and also formal "you have"). "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article, used before a masculine noun.
target_language_example: Maria ha un cane molto affettuoso.
native_language_example: Maria has a very affectionate dog.

additional_notes: Used mainly in crime/legal contexts to say someone has evidence or an explanation showing they couldn’t have committed a crime (e.g., they were somewhere else). The verb changes with the subject: ho un alibi (I have), hai un alibi (you have), ha un alibi (he/she has), abbiamo un alibi (we have), avete un alibi (you all have), hanno un alibi (they have).
target_language_example: Non può essere stato lui: ha un alibi.
native_language_example: It couldn't have been him: he has an alibi.

additional_notes: Used with an adjective or descriptive phrase to say how someone or something looks. Literally it’s avere (“to have”) + un aspetto (“an appearance”), and it typically refers to a third-person singular subject (lui/lei/esso/essa) or a named person/thing: “(he/she/it) has an appearance…”. In English it’s often translated more naturally as “looks.” You can change person/tense as needed: ho un aspetto, hai un aspetto, aveva un aspetto, ecc.
target_language_example: Oggi ha un aspetto stanco.
native_language_example: Today he/she looks tired.

meaning: "looks much better" / "has a much better appearance."
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something appears improved compared to before, often with time words like adesso/oggi/ora (now/today). It can also be used with a comparison: "molto migliore di..." (much better than...). In everyday Italian you also commonly hear "ha un aspetto molto migliore" or "sembra molto meglio" for "looks much better."
target_language_example: Dopo una buona notte di sonno, ha un aspetto molto migliore.
native_language_example: After a good night’s sleep, he/she looks much better.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (ha = he/she/it has) to compliment something someone possesses. "Bel" is a shortened form of "bello" used before most masculine singular nouns (e.g., bel cane, bel nome). For feminine nouns use "una bella" (Ha una bella casa). For masculine plural: "dei bei" (Ha dei bei libri).
target_language_example: Lei ha un bel sorriso.
native_language_example: She has a nice smile.

meaning: “(he/she/it) has a good …” (before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to say someone/something “has a good” quality, object, or reason (e.g., buon cervello, buon profumo, buon alibi, buon motivo). **Buon** is the shortened form of **buono** and is used before most masculine singular nouns (especially those starting with a consonant). With feminine nouns you’ll use **una buona** (e.g., *ha una buona idea*).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante ha un buon servizio.
native_language_example: This restaurant has good service.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has a pleasant smell. Literally “has a good smell.” The subject can be food, a place, or a thing. You’ll often hear it without naming the subject if it’s obvious: "Qua dentro ha un buon odore" (“It smells good in here”).
target_language_example: Il caffè appena fatto ha un buon odore.
native_language_example: The freshly made coffee smells good.

meaning: “it tastes good” / “it has a good flavor.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about the taste of food or drinks. Often paired with a subject (e.g., Il vino/Questa minestra/Questo latte ha un buon sapore). It’s a neutral, everyday phrase; in conversation you can also say “È buono/a” (“It’s good”).
target_language_example: Questo formaggio ha un buon sapore, ma è un po' salato.
native_language_example: This cheese tastes good, but it’s a bit salty.

additional_notes: From the verb **avere** (“to have”), 3rd person singular: **lui/lei ha** = “he/she has.” Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so **ha un cane** can mean “he has a dog” or “she has a dog,” depending on context. In questions, you can raise intonation or use a question mark in writing: **Ha un cane?** = “Does he/she have a dog?” Note: **cane** means “dog” (it can look like English **cane**, but that’s a different word).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha un cane molto piccolo.
native_language_example: My sister has a very small dog.

meaning: “it smells bad” / “it has a bad smell.”
additional_notes: Used to say that something (food, a room, a person/animal, etc.) has an unpleasant smell. The verb is avere (“to have”): ha un cattivo odore = “it has a bad smell.” You can change the subject (e.g., Il cane ha..., Questa carne ha...) and the tense (e.g., aveva un cattivo odore = “it smelled bad”).
target_language_example: Non mangiarlo: ha un cattivo odore.
native_language_example: Don’t eat it: it smells bad.

additional_notes: "Ha" is the 3rd-person singular of avere (“to have”), so it can refer to lui (he) or lei (she) depending on context. "Un figlio" literally means “a son,” but it’s also sometimes used more generally to mean “a child” (especially when the gender isn’t important or in a general statement). For a daughter, you say "ha una figlia".
target_language_example: Maria ha un figlio che studia all’università.
native_language_example: Maria has a son who studies at university.

additional_notes: Used with "avere" (to have) in the 3rd person singular present: "lui ha" = he has, "lei ha" = she has (and "Lei ha...?" with capital L is also the formal "Do you have...?"). To ask a yes/no question, you often just raise your intonation: "Lei ha un fratello?"
target_language_example: Maria ha un fratello più grande.
native_language_example: Maria has an older brother.

meaning: "has a big/great ..." (used before a masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has a lot of a quality or has a large object/amount. It’s normally followed by a noun: "ha un grande entusiasmo" (a great enthusiasm) or "ha un grande secchio" (a big bucket). With a feminine noun, use "ha una grande ..." (e.g., "ha una grande idea").
target_language_example: Ha un grande talento per le lingue.
native_language_example: He/She has great talent for languages.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is called something, or to ask whether something has a name. The verb is "avere" (to have): "ha" = he/she/it has (used with "cosa", "hotel", etc.). For "you have" (tu), it’s "hai un nome".
target_language_example: Questo piatto ha un nome difficile da pronunciare.
native_language_example: This dish has a name that’s hard to pronounce.

additional_notes: Used to describe the smell of something. Often followed by an adjective (ha un odore buono/strano/forte) or by “di + noun” to say what it smells of (ha un odore di fumo = it smells of smoke).
target_language_example: Questa stanza ha un odore di fumo.
native_language_example: This room smells of smoke.

additional_notes: From avere (“to have”) + un piano (“a plan”). In Italian, the subject pronoun is often omitted, so it can mean “he has a plan,” “she has a plan,” etc., depending on context. Note: piano can also mean “piano” (the musical instrument), but in this phrase it means “plan.” You can add details with per (“for”) or di (“to”): “ha un piano per te” = “has a plan for you.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ha un piano per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he/she has a plan to solve the problem.

meaning: "has a problem with" (has an issue with someone/something).
additional_notes: Used to say someone has a difficulty, complaint, or disagreement related to a person, thing, plan, or idea. It can be a practical problem (e.g., a device) or a personal/attitude issue (e.g., with someone or with a suggestion). You can change the subject and tense: "ho un problema con" (I have a problem with), "abbiamo un problema con" (we have a problem with), "aveva un problema con" (he/she had a problem with).
target_language_example: Ha un problema con questo piano?
native_language_example: Does he have a problem with this plan?

meaning: “has a lot of / has loads of”.
additional_notes: Used with a noun to say someone/something has a large quantity of something. Common in everyday speech and slightly informal. You can swap the verb for other people/tenses (e.g., “ho/hai/abbiamo un sacco di...”). Sometimes you’ll also hear “ha un sacco” without “di” to mean “has a lot” in general.
target_language_example: Bob ha un sacco di libri nella sua camera.
native_language_example: Bob has a lot of books in his room.

additional_notes: Used to describe how food or drink tastes. It’s followed by an adjective (dolce, amaro, buono, eccellente) or other description. You can also specify the taste more precisely with di: Ha un sapore di limone = “It has a lemon flavor.”
target_language_example: Questo tè ha un sapore forte.
native_language_example: This tea has a strong flavor.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: ha ("he/she/it has") + una ("a/an" for feminine nouns). The subject can be a person or a thing: "Tom ha una…" = "Tom has a…"; "ha una natura generosa" = "he/she has a generous nature".
target_language_example: Lei ha una macchina nuova.
native_language_example: She has a new car.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun: ha (he/she/it has) + una (a) + bella (nice/beautiful). You normally complete it with what is nice: "Ha una bella calligrafia" = "She has nice handwriting." For a masculine noun you’d say "ha un bel ..." (e.g., "Ha un bel sorriso").
target_language_example: Marta ha una bella voce.
native_language_example: Marta has a beautiful voice.

additional_notes: Used to compliment someone’s speaking or singing voice. 'Ha' = 'has' and can refer to 'he', 'she', or a named person (e.g., Maria). Often extended with context like 'al telefono' (on the phone) or 'quando canta' (when he/she sings).
target_language_example: Marco ha una bella voce quando canta.
native_language_example: Marco has a beautiful voice when he sings.

additional_notes: Used to say someone “has a good …” followed by a feminine singular noun. "Buona" agrees with the feminine noun (e.g., una buona idea, una buona ragione, una buona opinione). With masculine nouns you use "ha un buon…" (e.g., ha un buon lavoro).
target_language_example: Giulia ha una buona idea per risolvere il problema.
native_language_example: Giulia has a good idea to solve the problem.

additional_notes: Form of the verb "avere" (to have): "ha" = "he/she has" (also "you have" formal: Lei ha). Used both for owning a house and for having a place to live (a home). In negatives: "non ha una casa" = "he/she doesn’t have a home/house."
target_language_example: Lei ha una casa in città, ma lavora in campagna.
native_language_example: She has a house in the city, but she works in the countryside.

additional_notes: Used to describe that someone has a scar somewhere on their body. Often followed by the location: "ha una cicatrice sul braccio" (on the arm), "sulla fronte" (on the forehead). "su" + "il/la" becomes "sul/sulla".
target_language_example: Ha una cicatrice sulla mano destra.
native_language_example: He/She has a scar on his/her right hand.

additional_notes: Used to say someone feels romantic interest (often not serious or not officially a relationship) toward a person. It changes with the subject: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno una cotta per…; you can ask: Hai una cotta per lui/lei?
target_language_example: Marco ha una cotta per la nuova collega.
native_language_example: Marco has a crush on the new coworker.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has a family (e.g., a spouse/partner and/or children). It’s the verb "avere" (to have) in the 3rd person singular present: "ha" = "he/she has"; the subject (lui/lei or a name) is often omitted because it’s understood from context.
target_language_example: Non posso restare tardi: ha una famiglia che lo aspetta a casa.
native_language_example: I can’t stay late: he has a family waiting for him at home.

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s family has many members (often many children/siblings). You can change the subject (e.g., "ho" = I have, "hanno" = they have) or make it a question with rising intonation or a question mark in writing.
