target_language_example: Ho conosciuto Maria durante un viaggio in Italia.
native_language_example: I met Maria during a trip to Italy.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "continuare": "ho continuato" = "I continued/I kept". It’s followed by "a" + an infinitive to say you kept doing something: "ho continuato a + fare/dirridere...". You can replace the subject/auxiliary for other people (e.g., "hai continuato a" = you kept on; "abbiamo continuato a" = we kept on).
target_language_example: Nonostante la pioggia, ho continuato a camminare.
native_language_example: Despite the rain, I kept walking.

meaning: 'I gave' / 'I have given' (past tense of dare, 'to give').
additional_notes: Used with many common patterns: **dare [something] a [someone]** (Ho dato tre matite a ognuna di loro.); **dare da mangiare** = “to feed” (Ho dato da mangiare al gatto.); **dare per scontato (che...)** = “to take for granted (that...)”; **dare una + noun** can mean “to give a quick/one-time action” (Ho dato una spazzolata... = “I gave it a brush / I brushed it”). With pronouns: **vi ho dato** = “I gave you (plural) / I have given you”.
target_language_example: Ti ho dato il mio numero ieri.
native_language_example: I gave you my number yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dare" (to give): "ho dato" = "I gave / I have given". Use "a" before an indirect object that is a person (or an animal), like "a Tom" = "to Tom". Word order is often "Ho dato a Marco il libro" (I gave Marco the book). With pronouns, "a" disappears: "Gli ho dato il libro" = "I gave him the book".
target_language_example: Ho dato a Maria il mio numero di telefono.
native_language_example: I gave Maria my phone number.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you made a serious promise or commitment. Often said as "Ti ho dato la mia parola" (I gave you my word) or "Ho dato la mia parola che..." (I promised that...). In the past tense because the promise has already been made, but it refers to keeping it now.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ho dato la mia parola che ti aiuterò.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I gave you my word that I’ll help you.

meaning: "I gave a" / "I have given a" (first-person past of *dare* + "a").
additional_notes: Used to say you gave something (or delivered an action) in the past: *ho dato un [oggetto]* (I gave a [thing]) or *ho dato un [colpo]* (I gave a [hit/kick]). Often followed by **a + person/thing** for who receives it: *ho dato un sedativo a Tom* (I gave Tom a sedative). Italian commonly uses the **passato prossimo** (*ho dato*) where English often uses the simple past (“I gave”).
target_language_example: Ho dato un regalo a mia sorella.
native_language_example: I gave my sister a gift.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "decidere" ("io ho deciso"). Used to say you have made a decision. Often followed by "di" + infinitive ("ho deciso di uscire" = "I've decided to go out"), or by a direct object ("ho deciso la stessa cosa" = "I decided the same thing"). It can also be used alone to announce a firm decision, sometimes followed by what will happen next.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di restare a casa stasera.
native_language_example: I've decided to stay home tonight.

additional_notes: Past tense of decidere (passato prossimo) used to say you made a decision. It is followed by an infinitive verb: ho deciso di + (verb in infinitive), e.g., ho deciso di andare, ho deciso di restare. Often corresponds to either simple past (“I decided to”) or present perfect (“I’ve decided to”) in English, depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di andare al cinema stasera.
native_language_example: I've decided to go to the movies tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you made a decision to *not* do an action. Pattern: **Ho deciso di non + infinitive** (e.g., andare, bere, dire, fare). With object pronouns you can attach them to the infinitive: **farla** = “do it (feminine/it)”.
target_language_example: Ho deciso di non uscire stasera.
native_language_example: I decided not to go out tonight.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the passato prossimo of "dire" (to say/tell). Used to talk about something you said in the past, often with a link to the present ("I've said..."). In dialogue it can be used emphatically like “I said!” to insist or repeat an order.
target_language_example: Ho detto che non posso venire oggi.
native_language_example: I said (that) I can’t come today.

additional_notes:
Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire": "ho detto" = "I said / I told". It’s used with an indirect object introduced by "a" (a Maria, a Tom, a lui/lei). Often followed by:
- "che" + a full sentence: "Ho detto a Tom che ero impegnata." (I told Tom that I was busy.)
- "di" + infinitive: "Ho detto a Tom di venire presto." (I told Tom to come early.)
target_language_example: Ho detto a mia sorella che torno tardi.
native_language_example: I told my sister that I'm coming back late.

additional_notes: Used to report what you said, often introducing a statement with che (= “that”). The verb is past tense (passato prossimo) of dire: ho detto = “I said / I have said”. It can be followed by different tenses depending on what you reported (e.g., avevo, avrei).
target_language_example: Ho detto che non potevo venire.
native_language_example: I said that I couldn’t come.

meaning: “I said that I don’t / I didn’t …” (introducing a negative statement).
additional_notes: Used to report something you already said, followed by a verb in the negative (non + verb). It often adds emphasis, like “I told you that I don’t…” / “I said I wasn’t…”. You can change the person: hai detto che non… (you said you don’t/didn’t), ha detto che non… (he/she said … not).
target_language_example: Ho detto che non posso venire oggi.
native_language_example: I said that I can’t come today.

meaning: “I said what …” / “I said that …” (introducing what you said).
additional_notes: Used to report your own words and introduce a clause. It’s often followed by something like: “ho detto ciò che pensavo” (“I said what I thought”) or “ho detto ciò che dovevo dire” (“I said what I had to say”). You can change the tense/person: “hai detto ciò che…”, “ha detto ciò che…”, “avevo detto ciò che…”.
target_language_example: Ho detto ciò che pensavo, ma non mi hanno ascoltato.
native_language_example: I said what I thought, but they didn’t listen to me.

meaning: “I said to …” / “I told (someone) to …” (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to report an instruction or request you gave. The person you told can be explicit (e.g., “Ti ho detto di…” = “I told you to…”) or implied by context. Pronouns can attach to the infinitive: lasciarla (to let her go), lasciarle (to let them [feminine] go), lasciarli (to let them [masculine] go), lasciarlo (to let him/it go), prenderti/prendervi (to take your time).
target_language_example: Ti ho detto di aspettarmi qui.
native_language_example: I told you to wait for me here.

meaning: "I told (you) to do" / "I said to do" (giving an instruction).
additional_notes: Past tense of "dire" + "di" + infinitive. It’s used to report an order or instruction you gave. Very often you’ll add what should be done (or a pronoun): "Ho detto di farlo" = "I told you to do it"; "Ho detto di non farlo" = "I told you not to do it". If you want to specify who you told, add it: "Ho detto a Marco di farlo" = "I told Marco to do it".
target_language_example: Ho detto di fare i compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I said to do the homework before going out.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire di no" = to say no, to refuse. Often used to clearly state you didn’t accept something or you turned down a request. You can add who you refused with "a": "Ho detto di no a Jamal" (I said no to Jamal). For emphasis you can say it alone: "Ho detto di no!"
target_language_example: Mi ha chiesto di aiutarlo, ma ho detto di no.
native_language_example: He asked me to help him, but I said no.

ho detto di non dirlo a

target_language_multi_word_term: ho detto di non dirlo a
meaning: “I told (you/someone) not to tell it to …”
additional_notes: Used before naming the person you shouldn’t tell: *Ho detto di non dirlo a Marco.* **dirlo** = “to say/tell it” (lo refers to something already known in context, like a secret or news). The person you told is understood from context, or you can add it: *Ti ho detto di non dirlo a…*
target_language_example: Ti ho detto di non dirlo a nessuno!
native_language_example: I told you not to tell anyone!

additional_notes: "Ho detto" is the passato prossimo of dire (to say/tell). "Loro" means “to them” (indirect object) and is often used before a clause with che (“that…”) or before di + infinitive to report instructions (e.g., "ho detto loro di andare" = “I told them to go”).
target_language_example: Ho detto loro di aspettarmi fuori.
native_language_example: I told them to wait for me outside.

additional_notes: Used to report what you said to other people. "Ho detto" is the passato prossimo of "dire" (to say/tell). "loro" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to them"; "che" introduces the clause with the information you told them. You can change the verb and pronoun: e.g., "ha detto loro che" (he/she told them that), "ho detto loro di…" is used before an infinitive (I told them to…).
target_language_example: Ho detto loro che arrivo tra dieci minuti.
native_language_example: I told them that I’ll arrive in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to report what you said about your past state/condition. Structure: **ho detto** (passato prossimo of *dire*, “I said/told”) + **loro** (“to them”) + **che** (“that”) + **ero** (imperfect of *essere*, “I was”), followed by an adjective or noun. The ending of what follows often changes for gender/number (e.g., *affamat**o** / affamat**a***, *sposat**o** / sposat**a***).
target_language_example: Ho detto loro che ero stanco e che volevo tornare a casa.
native_language_example: I told them that I was tired and that I wanted to go home.

meaning: "I told them to" (I said to them to do something).
additional_notes: Used to report an instruction you gave to a group of people ("loro" = "them"). It’s the passato prossimo of "dire" (ho detto = I said/I told). After "di" you normally use an infinitive verb: "ho detto loro di + infinitive" (e.g., di andare, di partire).
target_language_example: Ho detto loro di non fare rumore.
native_language_example: I told them not to make noise.

additional_notes: Used to report a negative instruction/advice you gave to a group of people. Structure: **ho detto loro di non + infinitive** (e.g., *venire, guidare, usare*). **loro** = “to them” (indirect object). In speech you may also hear **gli ho detto di non...** meaning “I told them not to...”
target_language_example: Ho detto loro di non parlare durante il film.
native_language_example: I told them not to talk during the movie.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the content of what you said, usually followed by a clause (often with a verb like pensavo, volevo, sapevo): "Ho detto quello che pensavo." Literally "I have said what", but in English it’s often just "I said what" depending on context. Commonly used to insist or clarify that you already expressed something.
target_language_example: Ho detto quello che pensavo, non quello che volevi sentire.
native_language_example: I said what I thought, not what you wanted to hear.

additional_notes: Past tense of "dimenticare" used with "io" (passato prossimo). Use "ho dimenticato + [noun]" to say you forgot an object/person/thing ("Ho dimenticato il libro"). Use "ho dimenticato di + infinitive" to say you forgot to do something ("Ho dimenticato di chiamarti"). With "tutto di/su di + [person/thing]" it means "everything about" someone/something.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato di risponderti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to reply to you.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb after "di" to say you forgot to do an action: "Ho dimenticato di + infinitive" (e.g., "ho dimenticato di chiamare"). It’s the passato prossimo of "dimenticare" for "io" (I). You can swap the subject: "Hai dimenticato di...?" (Did you forget to...?).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato di mandarti il messaggio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to send you the message.

additional_notes: Used to say you didn’t remember to purchase something. Structure: (io) ho dimenticato di + infinitive (comprare) + the item. You can add "Oh" at the start to show you just realized it.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato di comprare il caffè.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to buy the coffee.

additional_notes: Used when you forgot a specific masculine singular thing. It’s incomplete by itself: you normally add a noun after it (e.g., il passaporto, il telefono). In Italian the past tense here is commonly formed with avere + past participle: ho dimenticato = “I forgot / I have forgotten.” For a feminine singular object, use “ho dimenticato la …”.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato il passaporto a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot my passport at home.

meaning: “I forgot my …” (speaking as a man; with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say you forgot something that belongs to you. It’s made of: ho (I have) + dimenticato (forgot) + la mia (my, feminine singular). Use it before a feminine noun: “Ho dimenticato la mia giacca / la mia password / la mia carta…”. If the item is masculine, you say “Ho dimenticato il mio …” (e.g., “Ho dimenticato il mio passaporto”).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho dimenticato la mia tessera a casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot my card at home.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “dormire”: ho (I have) + dormito (slept). Used to say you slept for a duration (Ho dormito due ore), how well/deeply (Ho dormito bene / profondamente), or when (Ho dormito ieri / la scorsa notte). In phrases like “Ho dormito con …”, it can mean either “I slept (in the same place) with …” or “I slept with …” (had sex), depending on context—be careful.
target_language_example: Stanotte ho dormito poco.
native_language_example: Tonight I slept little / I didn’t sleep much.

additional_notes: First-person singular of dovere in the passato prossimo. It is usually followed by an infinitive and expresses something that was necessary or obligatory in the past.
target_language_example: Ho dovuto chiamare un taxi.
native_language_example: I had to call a taxi.

additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of fare. It often translates as English simple past too: 'I did' or 'I made'. fare is very flexible, so with some nouns English may use a different verb, for example ho fatto un giro = 'I went/took a drive' and ho fatto un esame = 'I took an exam'.
target_language_example: Ho fatto i compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I did my homework before going out.

additional_notes: Used to say you tried as hard as you could, often as an explanation or apology when the result wasn’t good. Literally "I have done of my best" (passato prossimo of fare). You can swap the subject: "hai fatto del tuo meglio" (you), "ha fatto del suo meglio" (he/she/you formal).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace se non è bastato: ho fatto del mio meglio.
native_language_example: I’m sorry if it wasn’t enough: I did my best.

ho fatto del mio meglio per

target_language_multi_word_term: ho fatto del mio meglio per
meaning: "I did my best to" / "I tried my best to".
additional_notes: Used to say you made your strongest effort to do something (often as an explanation or defense). Follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., aiutare, proteggere) after "per". The pronouns attached to the infinitive show who is being helped/protected: aiutarla (her), aiutarlo (him), aiutarle (them/feminine or formal "you").
target_language_example: Ho fatto del mio meglio per arrivare in orario.
native_language_example: I did my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: "Ho fatto" is the past tense (passato prossimo) of *fare* (to do/make). In the pattern "ho fatto il + noun", it often means you *did/performed* an action or activity: *ho fatto il check-in* (I checked in), *ho fatto il giro* (I went for a drive/round), *ho fatto il vaccino* (I got the vaccine), *ho fatto il buffone* (I acted like a clown / I played the fool), *ho fatto il percorso* (I did/took the route). English usually doesn’t translate it word-for-word as “I have done the…”, but as a natural verb for the activity.
target_language_example: Oggi ho fatto il bagno e poi sono uscito.
native_language_example: Today I took a bath and then I went out.

additional_notes: Almost always used with **non**: **(Io) non ho fatto niente**. It often sounds defensive, like protesting innocence (“But I didn’t do anything!”). With an object, it can mean “I didn’t do anything to you,” e.g. **Non ti ho fatto niente**. A more formal/standard alternative is **non ho fatto nulla**.
target_language_example: Ma non ho fatto niente!
native_language_example: But I didn't do anything!

meaning: "I did everything that…" / "I’ve done everything that…"
additional_notes: Used to say you completed all the actions required or possible, followed by a clause (often with a past tense or conditional) explaining what was asked/needed: "…avete chiesto" (you asked), "…avrei dovuto fare" (I should have done), "…potevo" (I could). In Italian the tense is "ho fatto" (passato prossimo), which can translate as either "I did" or "I have done" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho fatto tutto quello che potevo per aiutarti.
native_language_example: I did everything I could to help you.

meaning: "I did/made a" (used with a noun to say you did something).
additional_notes: Past tense of "fare" ("to do/make"): "io ho fatto" + "un/uno/una" + noun. Very common with actions/events: "ho fatto un errore" (I made a mistake), "ho fatto un pisolino" (I took a nap), "ho fatto un viaggio" (I took a trip), "ho fatto un test" (I did/took a test), "ho fatto un selfie" (I took a selfie). Choose the article based on the noun’s gender/starting sound (un/uno/una).
target_language_example: Ho fatto un errore, scusa.
native_language_example: I made a mistake, sorry.

additional_notes: Used to admit or acknowledge that you did something wrong. It often comes with an apology (e.g., “Spiacente,” / “Mi dispiace,”). Grammar note: it’s the passato prossimo of *fare* (ho fatto) + *un errore*; you can change the subject (e.g., *hai fatto un errore* = “you made a mistake”, *abbiamo fatto un errore* = “we made a mistake”).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho fatto un errore nel modulo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mistake on the form.

additional_notes: Literally “I made a dream,” but in Italian you say fare un sogno (“to have a dream”). Used to talk about what you dreamed while sleeping, often followed by an adjective (divertente, strano, triste) or by su (“about”): Ho fatto un sogno su…
target_language_example: Ho fatto un sogno su di te stanotte.
native_language_example: I had a dream about you last night.

meaning: "I made a" / "I did a" (past: I have done/made).
additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of fare (ho fatto) + una + noun, used for things you do or create: ho fatto una promessa (I made a promise), ho fatto una dichiarazione (I made a statement), ho fatto una bambola (I made a doll). With many actions, Italian uses fare where English might use different verbs (make/do).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho fatto una promessa e devo mantenerla.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a promise and I have to keep it.

meaning: 'I made a promise' / 'I've made a promise.'
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of fare (ho fatto) to talk about a completed action in the past with a present relevance. Often followed by the person you promised (a mia madre) or what you promised: "Ho fatto una promessa: non fumerò più" / "Ho fatto una promessa che sarei tornato".
target_language_example: Ho fatto una promessa a mia sorella: l'aiuterò domani.
native_language_example: I made a promise to my sister: I’ll help her tomorrow.

additional_notes: Literally means "I have finished." Used to say you completed something or that you are finished for now. With con, as in "non ho finito con te," it means "I'm not finished with you."
target_language_example: Ho finito i compiti, adesso possiamo uscire.
native_language_example: I've finished my homework, now we can go out.

additional_notes: "Ho" + past participle "giocato" is the passato prossimo (past tense) of "giocare" for "io" (I). It’s typically followed by "a" + the game/sport: "ho giocato a calcio" (I played soccer). You can add who you played with using "con" (with): "ho giocato a scacchi con Tom".
target_language_example: Ho giocato a calcio con mia sorella sabato.
native_language_example: I played soccer with my sister on Saturday.

meaning: "I have already" / "I already" (used with the past tense).
additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo: "ho" (I have) + "già" (already) + past participle (e.g., "ho già letto" = "I’ve already read"). With object pronouns, "già" often comes after the pronoun: "l’ho già visto" (I’ve already seen it). You can also say "già ho...", but "ho già..." is more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Ho già finito i compiti.
native_language_example: I’ve already finished my homework.

additional_notes: Used to say you have already talked to someone about something. It’s the passato prossimo of parlare: ho (I have) + già (already) + parlato (spoken) + con (with). It must be followed by a person or group: con Maria, con il dottore, con loro.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ho già parlato con il responsabile.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve already spoken with the manager.

meaning: 'I looked', 'I watched', or 'I checked' (past: I did look/watch/check).
additional_notes: "Ho guardato" is the passato prossimo (past tense) of *guardare* for "I". Use it for watching something (TV, a game), looking somewhere (*ho guardato nella stanza*, *sotto al letto*), or witnessing something happen (*ho guardato morire Tom* = "I watched Tom die"). On its own, it can mean "I looked!/I checked!" (for example, answering someone who asked you to look). Note: *guardare* is a false friend with English *to guard*; it usually means "to look/watch," not "to protect."
target_language_example: Hai cercato le chiavi? Sì, ho guardato sotto il divano.
native_language_example: Did you look for the keys? Yes, I checked under the couch.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "imparare" (to learn). Used for something learned in the past; in English it can often be translated as either "I learned" (simple past) or "I've learned" (present perfect), depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho imparato molto durante quel corso.
native_language_example: I learned a lot during that course.

meaning: “I learned to …” / “I have learned to …” (I acquired the ability or habit of doing something).
additional_notes: Used to say you learned how to do something, often through experience or practice. It’s the passato prossimo of “imparare” (to learn): "ho imparato" + "a" + infinitive (e.g., ho imparato a guidare = I learned to drive). With time expressions it can emphasize a result up to now (“I’ve learned to…”).
target_language_example: Ho imparato a cucinare piatti semplici.
native_language_example: I learned to cook simple dishes.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): ho (I have) + imparato (learned) + molto (a lot). Used to say you gained a lot of knowledge/experience, often followed by da (“from”): Ho imparato molto da questa esperienza.
target_language_example: Ho imparato molto dal corso di italiano.
native_language_example: I learned a lot from the Italian course.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "incontrare" (1st person singular): literally "I have met" but often translated as "I met" in English. Used for meeting someone either by chance (running into them) or by arrangement; context makes it clear. Can also be used for “first met” (e.g., "il giorno in cui ti ho incontrato" = "the day I met you").
target_language_example: Ti ho incontrato per caso in centro.
native_language_example: I ran into you by chance downtown.

meaning: “I met a …” / “I ran into a …” (masculine singular).
additional_notes: This is a common past-tense pattern: **ho incontrato** = “I met / I have met” (passato prossimo of *incontrare*). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: **un ragazzo, un amico, un turista**. For feminine, use **ho incontrato una …**.
target_language_example: Ieri ho incontrato un amico al supermercato.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ran into a friend at the supermarket.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "iniziare" with "a" + infinitive to say you began doing something. Used to describe the start of an action in the past; you can change the subject (e.g., "hai iniziato a", "ha iniziato a", "abbiamo iniziato a").
target_language_example: Ho iniziato a studiare italiano la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I started studying Italian last week.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of *lasciare* for "I" (auxiliary *avere* + past participle *lasciato*). Used for leaving a place/person/thing behind (e.g., *Ho lasciato Boston* = I left Boston; *Ho lasciato tutto alle spalle* = I left everything behind). With **che** + subjunctive it means "I let / I allowed" (*Ho lasciato che lo facessero* = I let them do it).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi a casa.
native_language_example: I left the keys at home.

meaning: "I left my..." / "I’ve left my..." (used before naming the thing).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase: you normally add a masculine singular noun after it (e.g., *ho lasciato il mio telefono* = “I left my phone”). On its own it sounds unfinished unless the object is understood from context. For feminine nouns use *ho lasciato la mia...*; for plural *i miei / le mie*. In Italian, *ho lasciato* (passato prossimo) can mean either “I left” or “I have left” depending on context.
target_language_example: Scusi, ho lasciato il mio passaporto in camera.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I left my passport in the room.

meaning: “I left a message” / “I left a voicemail.”
additional_notes: Past tense with *ho lasciato* (passato prossimo of *lasciare*, “to leave”). Used when you contacted someone (often by phone) but they didn’t answer, so you left a message. Use **a + person** to say who you left it to (*Ho lasciato un messaggio a Tom*), and **per + pronoun/person** to say it’s intended for them (*per lui/lei*).
target_language_example: Ti ho chiamato ieri, ma non hai risposto: ho lasciato un messaggio.
native_language_example: I called you yesterday, but you didn’t answer: I left a message.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): "ho lavato" = "I have washed / I washed" (lavare + avere). "I piatti" literally means "the plates," but in everyday Italian it often refers to the dishes in general. Used to say you did the dishwashing, often after a meal: "Dopo cena, ho lavato i piatti."
target_language_example: Stasera ho lavato i piatti io.
native_language_example: Tonight I washed the dishes.

meaning: “I worked” / “I have worked” (past: I did work).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of the verb “lavorare” (to work): ho (I have) + lavorato (worked). Used for actions completed in the past and often connected to the present (English can be either “I worked” or “I have worked,” depending on context). You can add details with: a/in + place (Ho lavorato a Boston / in questa fabbrica), insieme a + person (Ho lavorato insieme a Tom), come + job (Ho lavorato come cameriere), and time expressions (la scorsa notte, per tre anni). “Io ho lavorato …” adds emphasis to “I.”
target_language_example: Ho lavorato tutto il giorno e adesso sono stanco.
native_language_example: I worked all day and now I’m tired.

meaning: "I read" / "I have read" (past: "I read" in English).
additional_notes: First-person singular passato prossimo of "leggere" (to read): "ho" (I have) + "letto" (read). Used to say you completed reading something in the past, often with time words like "ieri" (yesterday) or "questa notte" (last night). In relative clauses it can mean "that I read" (e.g., "il libro che ho letto").
target_language_example: Ho letto le email stamattina.
native_language_example: I read the emails this morning.

meaning: "I read many" / "I have read many" (said by a male speaker).
additional_notes: Past tense with passato prossimo: "ho letto" = "I have read" / often simply "I read" in English. "Molti" agrees with a masculine plural noun (molti romanzi, molti autori). For feminine plural use "molte" (molte storie). You can add "io" for emphasis: "Io ho letto...".
target_language_example: Ho letto molti libri in italiano quest'anno.
native_language_example: I read / I have read many books in Italian this year.

meaning: "I read a book" / "I've read a book."
additional_notes: Passato prossimo (completed action in the past). Literally "I have read a book," but in English it’s often translated as simple past: "I read a book" (especially with a finished time like "yesterday"). Structure: ho (present of avere) + letto (past participle of leggere) + un libro. You can add time phrases like "ieri sera" or "la scorsa notte" before or after the verb.
target_language_example: Oggi ho letto un libro sul treno.
native_language_example: Today I read a book on the train.

additional_notes:
*Ho* is the present tense of **avere** (“to have”) for **io** (“I”). With **mai** (“ever/never”), it’s very common in:
- **Questions** (often rhetorical): *Ho mai... ?* = “Have I ever...?”
- **Negative sentences**: **Non** + *ho mai* + past participle = “I have never ...” (e.g., *Non ci ho mai pensato* = “I’ve never thought about it”).
You’ll also see it inside relative clauses: *le uniche cose che ho mai fatto* = “the only things I’ve ever done.”
target_language_example: Ho mai detto una cosa del genere?
native_language_example: Have I ever said something like that?

meaning: "I ever said/told (you/him/her/them) to…" (almost always used with "non" = "I never told … to …").
additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary "ho" (present perfect of "dire" = to say/tell) plus "mai" (ever/never) and then "di" + infinitive (what someone was told to do). In real sentences it’s typically negative: "Non ho mai detto di…" = "I never said/told (anyone) to…". Change "ho" to match the subject (e.g., "hai mai detto di…?" = "have you ever told… to…?").
target_language_example: Non ho mai detto di farlo.
native_language_example: I never told you to do it.

meaning: “(I) have ever done”; with non: “(I) have never done.”
additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of fare: ho fatto = “I did / I have done.” Adding mai means “ever.” Very often you’ll see it with negation: non ho mai fatto = “I have never done.” With object pronouns it becomes, for example, Non le ho mai fatto del male = “I never hurt her/them.” Without non, it’s common in questions: Hai mai fatto…? = “Have you ever done…?”
target_language_example: Non ho mai fatto questo prima.
native_language_example: I’ve never done this before.

meaning: “(I) have ever learned to…?” / usually (with non): “(I) have never learned to…”
additional_notes: This chunk is most commonly used with **non**: **non ho mai imparato a + infinitive** = “I never learned to + verb” (e.g., nuotare, guidare, cucinare). Without **non**, **mai** is typically used in questions or with special emphasis, but beginners will most often meet it in the negative form.
target_language_example: Non ho mai imparato a nuotare.
native_language_example: I never learned to swim.

meaning: '(I) have ever heard'—usually used in the negative: 'I have never heard'.
additional_notes: Often appears as "non ho mai sentito..." = "I’ve never heard...". You can also use it with "di" or "parlare": "non ho mai sentito di..." / "non ne ho mai sentito parlare" = "I’ve never heard of..." / "I’ve never heard about it." ("ne" = "about it/of it").
target_language_example: Non ho mai sentito parlare di questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I've never heard of this restaurant.

additional_notes: In Italian, *mai* (“ever/never”) normally needs *non* to mean “never”: **non ho mai visto** = “I have never seen.” It’s the *passato prossimo*: **ho visto** (I have seen) + **mai** (ever) → with **non** becomes “never.” With **ti** it means “I’ve never seen you” / “I’ve never seen you there”: **Non ti ho mai visto (lì)**. Often used with **ne** (“of it/them”): **Non ne ho mai visto uno** = “I’ve never seen one (of them).”
target_language_example: Non ho mai visto una pizza così grande!
native_language_example: I’ve never seen such a big pizza!

meaning: "I have ever wanted" (usually used with *non* as *non ho mai voluto* = "I never wanted / I never meant to").
additional_notes: Most commonly you’ll hear it in the negative: **non ho mai voluto + infinitive** (“I never wanted to…”) or **non ho mai voluto + noun/pronoun** (“I never wanted that”). It can also express intention in apologies: **non ho mai voluto ferirti** = “I never meant to hurt you.”
target_language_example: Non ho mai voluto offenderti.
native_language_example: I never meant to offend you.

additional_notes: First-person singular of the past tense (passato prossimo) of "mangiare". Use it to say you ate something in the past; it’s often translated as either simple past ("I ate") or present perfect ("I have eaten") depending on context. Negation: "non ho mangiato" = "I didn’t eat / I haven’t eaten."
target_language_example: Oggi ho mangiato solo un panino.
native_language_example: Today I only ate a sandwich.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of “mangiare”: ho (I have) + mangiato (eaten). “della pizza” means “some pizza” (an unspecified amount). You can add time expressions like “ieri” (yesterday), “la settimana scorsa” (last week), or “per pranzo” (for lunch).
target_language_example: Ieri ho mangiato della pizza con i miei amici.
native_language_example: Yesterday I ate some pizza with my friends.

meaning: 'I put' / 'I placed' / 'I put on' (clothes); sometimes 'it took me' (time).
additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "mettere" with "avere": "io ho messo". Common uses: (1) put/place something somewhere: "Ho messo le chiavi sul tavolo"; in questions about location: "Dove ho messo...?". (2) put on/wear clothing: "Ho messo i pantaloni". (3) with time + "per": means "it took me": "Ci ho messo un anno per..." (= I took a year). (4) figurative with "ci": "Ci ho messo il cuore" = I put my heart into it. Also appears in phrasal verbs like "mettere giù" (to put down).
target_language_example: Scusa, dove ho messo il telefono?
native_language_example: Sorry, where did I put my phone?

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "pagare" (to pay): "ho" + past participle "pagato". In everyday Italian it often translates to simple past English (“I paid”), especially for completed actions. You can use it with a direct object (Ho pagato il conto.) or with "per" to say who/what you paid for (Ho pagato per Tom.).
target_language_example: Ho pagato il conto con la carta.
native_language_example: I paid the bill with a card.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "parlare" with "avere": ho parlato = I spoke / I have spoken. Often followed by "con" (with someone) or "di" (about something). In "Ti ho parlato", "ti" means "to you" (I spoke to you / I told you).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con il dottore stamattina.
native_language_example: I spoke with the doctor this morning.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "parlare con" = "to talk/speak with (someone)". Use it with a person or group: "Ho parlato con Tom", "Ho parlato con tutti". If you add a topic, you often use "di": "Ho parlato con Tom di quello che è successo" (I spoke with Tom about what happened).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con la mia insegnante dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: I spoke with my teacher after the lesson.

meaning: “I spoke to him” / “I have spoken to him.”
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (ho parlato) to talk about a completed conversation in the recent past; in English it can be either simple past (“I spoke…”) or present perfect (“I’ve spoken…”), depending on context. “Con lui” means “with him/to him” (parlare con = to talk with/to). You can swap the person: ho parlato con lei (her), ho parlato con loro (them).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con lui ieri sera, ma non ho capito tutto.
native_language_example: I spoke to him last night, but I didn’t understand everything.

additional_notes: Used to say you communicated in French with someone. Structure: ho parlato (passato prossimo of “parlare” = I spoke/I have spoken) + in francese (in French) + con (with) + person/pronoun. Change the ending depending on who you spoke with (con lui/lei/loro, con Tom).
target_language_example: Ho parlato in francese con il professore dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: I spoke in French with the teacher after the lesson.

additional_notes: This is the passato prossimo of *passare* for “io” (I): *ho passato* = “I have passed/spent.” Very often it means “I spent (a period of time)” with expressions like *ore, giorni, anni* + *a* (doing something) or *in* (a place): *Ho passato due ore a studiare*; *Ho passato la giornata in biblioteca*. It can also mean “I passed/got through” (e.g., an exam, a test), so the meaning depends on context.
target_language_example: Ho passato una settimana a Roma.
native_language_example: I spent a week in Rome.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "pensare" (used for a completed thought in the past). Common patterns: "ho pensato a + noun/pronoun" = "I thought about ..." (Ci ho pensato a lungo = "I thought about it for a long time"); "ho pensato che + sentence" = "I thought that ..." (often meaning "I assumed/figured that ..."); "ho pensato + noun" can mean "I thought (the same thing)" in the sense of forming an idea/opinion.
target_language_example: Ho pensato che fosse una buona idea.
native_language_example: I thought it was a good idea.

meaning: “I thought of / about …” (I had the idea of …).
additional_notes: Past tense of *pensare a* (“to think of/about”). Use **a** + a noun/pronoun/person: *ho pensato a Tom / a te*. It can mean something came to mind, or that you came up with an idea/plan: *ho pensato a un finale*.
target_language_example: Ieri ho pensato a te mentre ascoltavo quella canzone.
native_language_example: Yesterday I thought of you while I was listening to that song.

additional_notes: Used to introduce what you believed or assumed in the past. It’s the passato prossimo of pensare (“to think”) + che (“that”). After che, Italian often uses the subjunctive (congiuntivo), especially when the thought is uncertain: Ho pensato che fosse...; but you may also see the indicative in everyday speech: Ho pensato che era....
target_language_example: Ho pensato che fosse già partita.
native_language_example: I thought that she had already left.

meaning: “I thought that it was / he was / she was …”
additional_notes: Used to report what you believed in the past. After "ho pensato che" Italian typically uses the imperfect subjunctive (congiuntivo imperfetto): fosse (from essere). You usually add more information after it: un aggettivo (serio), un nome (una buona idea), or an expression (il momento, fuori di testa).
target_language_example: Ho pensato che fosse la scelta giusta.
native_language_example: I thought it was the right choice.

meaning: “I thought of / I thought I’d (do something).”
additional_notes: Used to say you got the idea or made the decision to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., chiedere, passare, cambiare). Literally “I have thought of,” but often translates naturally as “I thought I’d …” or “so I decided to …” in English.
target_language_example: Pioveva, così ho pensato di prendere un taxi.
native_language_example: It was raining, so I thought I’d take a taxi.

additional_notes: Past tense of perdere for “I” (passato prossimo): ho + perso. Used for losing objects (keys, money, a phone number), losing track (“ho perso il conto” = I lost count), and figuratively (“ho perso la speranza” = I lost hope). It can also mean “I missed” with transport/appointments (e.g., ho perso il treno = I missed the train).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho perso le chiavi di casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I lost my house keys.

additional_notes: Literally 'I have lost the', but in natural English it is often just 'I lost the'. It uses the passato prossimo of perdere. It can be used for physical things, but also for more abstract things like a game, context, or a place/seat. Because it ends with il, it is followed by a masculine singular noun; with other nouns, the article changes. In some contexts, perdere can also mean 'miss' (for example, ho perso il treno = 'I missed the train').
target_language_example: Ho perso il biglietto del treno.
native_language_example: I lost the train ticket.

additional_notes: Past tense of perdere (“to lose/miss”). Use it for missing scheduled transport (ho perso il treno/il volo/l’autobus) and for losing belongings (ho perso il mio telefono/portafoglio). The “mio” (“my”) changes with the noun: il mio (masc. sing.), la mia (fem. sing.), i miei (masc. pl.), le mie (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Scusi, ho perso il mio volo e ho perso anche il mio telefono.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I missed my flight and I also lost my phone.

meaning: “I lost the / I’ve lost the …” (feminine singular object).
additional_notes: Used with the passato prossimo of perdere (“to lose”): ho perso + a noun. It can be literal (losing an object) or figurative (losing a bet, losing your mind/reason, losing your sight). Because la is feminine singular (“the”), it must match the noun: ho perso il… (masc.), ho perso i/gli… (masc. plural), ho perso le… (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Ho perso la chiave di casa.
native_language_example: I lost the house key.

meaning: “I lost my …” (referring to a feminine singular thing you own).
additional_notes: Used when the noun is feminine singular (la mia + feminine noun), e.g., “la mia fede (nuziale)” = “my (wedding) ring.” In normal speech you usually include the noun: “Ho perso la mia borsa.” It’s in the passato prossimo: ho perso = “I lost / I’ve lost.”
target_language_example: Ho perso la mia borsa sul treno.
native_language_example: I lost my bag on the train.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "portare" with "avere": "ho portato" + object. Often used with a destination: "ho portato [qualcosa] a casa / al lavoro" = "I brought [something] home / to work". Depending on context it can mean bring, take, or carry.
target_language_example: Ho portato i documenti in ufficio stamattina.
native_language_example: I brought the documents to the office this morning.

additional_notes: Used to say you brought something (or someone) with you. It's the passato prossimo of *portare* (to bring/carry): *ho portato* = “I have brought / I brought”. It must be followed by a noun with the masculine singular article *il* (e.g., *il pane, il succo*). If the noun is feminine or plural, you change the article: *ho portato la…*, *ho portato i…*, *ho portato le…*.
target_language_example: Scusa il ritardo: ho portato il pane e il vino.
native_language_example: Sorry I’m late: I brought the bread and the wine.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of *potere* used to say you managed to do something or had the possibility/ability to do it. Often with an infinitive: *non ho potuto venire* = “I couldn’t come.” It can also be used alone when the verb is understood: *Appena ho potuto* = “As soon as I could.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho potuto chiamarti ieri.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn’t call you yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say you got something ready in the past, often with a present result. Common with an indirect object to show who it’s for: *ti ho preparato…* (I prepared … for you), *gli ho preparato…* (for him). Word order with pronouns: *Ti ho preparato un elenco* / *Gli ho preparato una tazza di tè*.
target_language_example: Ti ho preparato un panino per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I prepared (I’ve prepared) you a sandwich for the trip.

meaning: “I made/prepared some …” (talking about an unspecified amount).
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of preparare: ho preparato = “I have prepared / I prepared” (often “I made” with food). Dei is the partitive plural meaning “some” before a masculine plural noun (e.g., dei biscotti). It’s usually followed by a plural noun: ho preparato dei cookie = “I made some cookies.”
target_language_example: Ho preparato dei panini per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I made some sandwiches for the trip.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of prendere: ho preso = 'I have taken' literally, but in English it’s usually 'I took' or 'I got'. Very common when talking about buying or picking up items (e.g., at a bar/shop): Ho preso una birra = 'I got/bought a beer.' Also used for physically taking something: Ho preso la coppa = 'I took the cup/trophy.'
target_language_example: Scusa, ho preso l'ultimo pezzo di pizza.
native_language_example: Sorry, I took the last piece of pizza.

meaning: "I borrowed" (I took something on loan, usually to give it back).
additional_notes: Past tense of "prendere in prestito" (= to borrow). Often followed by what you borrowed, and then who you borrowed it from: "Ho preso in prestito un libro da lui" / "dalla mia amica". You can also say "in prestito" by itself: "Posso prenderlo in prestito?"
target_language_example: Ho preso in prestito la tua penna e te la restituisco domani.
native_language_example: I borrowed your pen and I’ll give it back to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun that starts with a consonant: ho preso in prestito il libro (I borrowed the book). For masculine singular nouns that start with a vowel or z/s+consonant, Italian uses l’ / lo instead of il (e.g., ho preso in prestito l’ombrello, ho preso in prestito lo zaino). The base expression is prendere in prestito = “to borrow” (often from a person: da Marco, dalla biblioteca).
target_language_example: Ho preso in prestito il libro da Luca.
native_language_example: I borrowed the book from Luca.

meaning: "I took the" / "I caught the" (with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Past tense of prendere (passato prossimo): ho preso + feminine singular noun (la medicina, la metro/metropolitana). Used for taking medicine ("I took the medicine") and for using/catching transport ("I took/caught the subway/metro"). Often translates as simple past in English ("I took"), not "I have taken" in everyday context.
target_language_example: Oggi ho preso la medicina dopo pranzo.
native_language_example: Today I took the medicine after lunch.

meaning: "I got/bought/had a" (often: "I had" something to eat/drink).
additional_notes: Literally "I have taken a" (passato prossimo of prendere). Very common when talking about what you ordered or consumed: Ho preso un caffè = I had/got a coffee. The noun after "un" is masculine singular; for feminine use "ho preso una" (e.g., Ho preso una pizza).
target_language_example: Al bar ho preso un panino e un'acqua.
native_language_example: At the bar I got/had a sandwich and a water.

additional_notes: Past tense of provare (passato prossimo): ho (I have) + provato (tried). Often followed by a + infinitive to say you tried to do something: Ho provato a chiamarti. It can also mean you tried something/experienced something: Ho provato tutto (I tried everything). With davvero it emphasizes sincerity (I really tried); with invano it means without success (I tried in vain).
target_language_example: Ho provato a chiamarti, ma non ho ricevuto risposta.
native_language_example: I tried to call you, but I didn’t get an answer.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamare, parlare, convincere) to say you made an effort to do something, often implying it didn’t work or wasn’t successful. It’s the passato prossimo of provare (io ho provato). You can change the subject: hai provato a… (you tried), ha provato a… (he/she tried), abbiamo provato a… (we tried).
target_language_example: Ho provato a prenotare un tavolo, ma non c'era posto.
native_language_example: I tried to book a table, but there were no seats.

meaning: 'I tried not to…' (I attempted to avoid doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a verb in the infinitive to say you made an effort not to do something: "Ho provato a non + [infinitive]". Literally it’s "I tried to not…" but in natural English it’s usually "I tried not to…". Common in everyday speech to describe self-control or restraint (not laughing, not worrying, etc.).
target_language_example: Ho provato a non rispondere subito, ma non ci sono riuscito.
native_language_example: I tried not to reply right away, but I couldn’t do it.

meaning: "I tried to talk to / speak with".
additional_notes: Used when you want to say you attempted to have a conversation with someone. It’s in the past tense (passato prossimo): "ho provato" = "I tried". It’s normally followed by a person: "ho provato a parlare con Marco". You can also add "ma..." to explain it didn’t work out (e.g., they weren’t available).
target_language_example: Ho provato a parlare con il direttore, ma non era in ufficio.
native_language_example: I tried to talk to the manager, but he wasn't in the office.

additional_notes: Used to say you made an effort to do an action. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive (e.g., ho provato ad chiamare / a chiamare). In speech you may also hear it with an extra pronoun like ci (“I really did try / I tried (at it)”), adding emphasis: ci ho provato ad….
target_language_example: Ho provato ad chiamarti, ma non rispondevi.
native_language_example: I tried to call you, but you weren’t answering.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "ricevere" = "to receive". Used for things you receive physically (a letter, gifts, mail) and also for information/news ("una notizia"). Often followed by a direct object: "Ho ricevuto un invito".
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto la tua email ieri sera.
native_language_example: I received your email last night.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (past tense): **ho** (I have) + **ricevuto** (received). **Un** is the masculine singular indefinite article; change it as needed: **ho ricevuto una** (a feminine noun), **ho ricevuto dei/delle** (some). Often used for messages, invitations, gifts, etc.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto un'email dal mio insegnante.
native_language_example: I received an email from my teacher.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of ricevere una chiamata (“to receive a call”). It’s often followed by da (“from”) + a person (da lui/lei) or from a place/organization (dalla scuola = da + la). You can add context with quando… (“when…”) or just say it on its own.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una chiamata da mia madre mentre ero al lavoro.
native_language_example: I received a call from my mother while I was at work.

additional_notes: Used to say you got a written letter and to introduce the sender with da (“from”). This is in the passato prossimo: ho ricevuto (I have received / I received). You can change the person: hai ricevuto (you), ha ricevuto (he/she), abbiamo ricevuto (we), hanno ricevuto (they).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una lettera da mia madre ieri.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my mother yesterday.

additional_notes: Past tense of *sbagliare* (“to make a mistake”). Used to admit you were wrong or that you did something incorrectly. Often followed by what you got wrong (e.g., *ho sbagliato strada* = “I took the wrong road”). In conversation, *Ho sbagliato, va bene?* can sound frustrated: “I was wrong, OK?”
target_language_example: Scusa, ho sbagliato: l’appuntamento è domani, non oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I was wrong: the appointment is tomorrow, not today.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of scegliere (“to choose”), made with ho + scelto (past participle). In English it can often be translated as either simple past (“I chose”) or present perfect (“I’ve chosen”), depending on context. It can be followed by di + infinitive (ho scelto di partire = “I chose to leave”) or by a noun (ho scelto questa strada = “I chose this path”).
target_language_example: Alla fine ho scelto di restare a casa.
native_language_example: In the end I chose to stay home.

additional_notes: It’s the passato prossimo of scoprire (“to discover/find out”): ho (I have) + scoperto (discovered). Used for discovering information (a truth, how to do something) or meeting/finding something/someone (“Finché non ho scoperto te” = “Until I discovered/found you”). Often followed by a noun (la verità) or by a clause with come/cosa/che (how/what/that).
target_language_example: Ho scoperto che il negozio è chiuso oggi.
native_language_example: I found out that the shop is closed today.

additional_notes: Past tense of scordare (to forget), used with the auxiliary avere. It’s interchangeable in many situations with "ho dimenticato" (more common/neutral). Use it to say you forgot an object, information, or rules: "Ho scordato + noun".
target_language_example: Scusa, ho scordato il tuo nome.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot your name.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (e.g., chiamare, dire, scrivere) to say you forgot to do something. It’s the passato prossimo of "scordarsi" (to forget), and is interchangeable with "ho dimenticato di". With indirect object pronouns you may see forms like "chiamarle" (to call her/them politely) and "dirglielo" (to tell it to him/her).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho scordato di mandarti un messaggio.
native_language_example: Sorry, I forgot to send you a message.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "scrivere" for "I": "ho" (present of "avere") + "scritto" (past participle). Use it to say you wrote something, or you’ve written something (often with a result that matters now). It’s commonly followed by what you wrote ("ho scritto una canzone") or used with pronouns ("Le ho scritto" = "I wrote to her" / "I wrote her"; "ci ho scritto" = "I wrote on it/in it").
target_language_example: Ho scritto un messaggio, ma non l'ho ancora inviato.
native_language_example: I wrote a message, but I haven’t sent it yet.

meaning: “I wrote three letters” / “I have written three letters.”
additional_notes: A complete sentence in the passato prossimo (present perfect). "ho" = “I have” (auxiliary verb), "scritto" = “written” (past participle of *scrivere*), "tre lettere" = “three letters.” In Italian the subject pronoun *io* (“I”) is usually omitted: *(io) ho scritto...*. Depending on context it can mean either “I wrote” (simple past meaning) or “I have written.”
target_language_example: Oggi ho scritto tre lettere per lavoro.
native_language_example: Today I wrote three letters for work.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo: ho (present of avere) + scritto (past participle of scrivere). It means you completed the action of writing a letter. You can add who it’s to with a + person (a mia madre) or to/for someone with a + article + person (al mio professore). Time expressions often go at the beginning or end: ieri sera, la scorsa notte.
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera al comune per chiedere informazioni.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to the town hall to ask for information.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of *scrivere* (to write): *ho scritto* = “I wrote / I have written.” *una lettera* = “a letter.” *a* introduces the recipient (a person or organization): *Ho scritto una lettera a Maria / al direttore*.
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera a mia nonna ieri.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my grandma yesterday.

additional_notes: Literally “I have always”: present tense of avere (ho) + sempre (“always”). It’s most commonly followed by a past participle to make the passato prossimo: “ho sempre amato” = “I’ve always loved,” “ti ho sempre protetto” = “I’ve always protected you.” Word order is usually “ho sempre + past participle.”
target_language_example: Ho sempre pensato che avevi ragione.
native_language_example: I’ve always thought you were right.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo): present of **avere** (ho) + past participle **avuto**. Used to say something has been true/possessed/experienced for a long time up to now (e.g., **ho sempre avuto paura**, **ho sempre avuto fede**, **ho sempre avuto la sensazione che...**). Often followed by a noun or by expressions like **paura di + infinitive** (“fear of doing”).
target_language_example: Ho sempre avuto difficoltà a parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: I’ve always had trouble speaking in public.

meaning: "I have always wanted" / "I’ve always wished for."
additional_notes: Used to say you’ve wanted something for a long time, up to now. It’s the passato prossimo of desiderare (to desire/want), used with ho because the subject is io. Often followed by: an infinitive (e.g., comprare, saperla suonare) or a noun phrase (e.g., una borsa, due figli).
target_language_example: Ho sempre desiderato visitare il Giappone.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to visit Japan.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a belief/opinion you’ve had for a long time. It’s the past tense of “penso che” (I think that). It’s usually followed by a full clause (subject + verb). In Italian, after “pensare che” you often use the subjunctive (e.g., “sia”, “fosse”), though in everyday speech you may also hear the indicative (e.g., “era”).
target_language_example: Ho sempre pensato che fosse una buona idea.
native_language_example: I’ve always thought it was a good idea.

additional_notes: Used to say you have been sure about something for a long time (often from the beginning), and it introduces a clause with che + verb. You can also say Io ho sempre saputo che... for emphasis. Tense: ho saputo is passato prossimo of sapere, but with sempre it often means an ongoing certainty up to now.
target_language_example: Ho sempre saputo che saresti tornato.
native_language_example: I always knew that you would come back.

additional_notes: Used to say you have wanted something for a long time, from the past up to now. It’s the passato prossimo of volere (to want): ho (I have) + sempre (always) + voluto (wanted). Often followed by an infinitive (ho sempre voluto studiare...) or a noun (ho sempre voluto un cane). You can add emphasis with io: Io ho sempre voluto...
target_language_example: Ho sempre voluto visitare Napoli.
native_language_example: I've always wanted to visit Naples.

meaning: "I have always wanted to be" / "I always wanted to be."
additional_notes:
Used to talk about a long-time ambition or dream. It’s usually followed by a noun (a job/role) or an adjective: 
- Ho sempre voluto essere medico. (a doctor)
- Ho sempre voluto essere indipendente. (independent)
In conversation, English often uses "I’ve always wanted to be..." even though Italian uses the passato prossimo (ho voluto).
target_language_example: Ho sempre voluto essere un insegnante, ma ho cambiato idea.
native_language_example: I’ve always wanted to be a teacher, but I changed my mind.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of sentire. It is used to say that you heard something, and in some contexts it can also mean "I felt" depending on what follows. In English, it is often translated with the simple past: "I heard."
target_language_example: Ho sentito un rumore strano fuori.
native_language_example: I heard a strange noise outside.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information you learned from someone else or from somewhere (news, rumors, word of mouth). It’s followed by a clause introduced with "che" (that). Often implies you’re not stating it as a certain fact, just what you heard.
target_language_example: Ho sentito che domani il museo è chiuso.
native_language_example: I heard that the museum is closed tomorrow.

meaning: "I heard that..." (a rumor / something you were told).
additional_notes: Used to report second-hand information (gossip, rumors, or something you heard from someone else). It introduces a clause with che. You can change the subject/tense: "Hai sentito dire che...?" (Have you heard that...?), "Abbiamo sentito dire che..." (We heard that...).
target_language_example: Ho sentito dire che il nuovo ristorante è molto buono.
native_language_example: I heard that the new restaurant is really good.

meaning: "I heard (that) he/she has…" (reporting something you’ve heard).
additional_notes: Used to introduce information you heard from other people (a rumor, news, or hearsay). Literally it’s “I have heard say that…”, but in natural English it’s usually “I heard that…”. The final “ha” is the start of what the other person has done (e.g., ha detto, ha cambiato, ha comprato). You can also say: “Ho sentito dire che…” without adding “ha” right away.
target_language_example: Ho sentito dire che ha cambiato lavoro.
native_language_example: I heard that he/she changed jobs.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive verb (e.g., parlare, fumare, ascoltare) to say you stopped doing an activity. It’s the passato prossimo of "smettere" (to stop/quit): "ho smesso" = I stopped. For other people: "hai smesso di" (you stopped), "ha smesso di" (he/she stopped).
target_language_example: Ho smesso di fumare l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I quit smoking last year.

additional_notes: Past tense phrase: "ho smesso" (I have stopped) + "di" + infinitive. Used to say you quit an activity; the time is often added with "due anni fa" (two years ago), "sei mesi fa" (six months ago). You can swap the verb to talk about other habits: "Ho smesso di bere" (I quit drinking), "Ho smesso di mangiare carne" (I stopped eating meat).
target_language_example: Ho smesso di fumare perché non mi faceva bene.
native_language_example: I quit smoking because it wasn’t good for me.

additional_notes: Past tense of "studiare" (to study) with "avere": ho studiato = I studied / I have studied. Used for a completed action in the past or past experience; often followed by what you studied ("ho studiato il berbero") or when you studied ("ho studiato prima di cena"). Negative: "non ho studiato".
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per due ore ieri sera.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for two hours last night.

meaning: “I spent the whole …” (talking about a period of time).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular time period (e.g., la giornata = the day, la notte = the night, la settimana = the week). It’s in the passato prossimo: ho trascorso = I spent / I have spent. You typically finish the phrase with the time period and often add where/with whom (e.g., al mare, con gli amici).
target_language_example: Ho trascorso tutta la giornata al mare.
native_language_example: I spent the whole day at the beach.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "trovare" used with "io" (I). Commonly means you found something/someone (often physically), but it can also mean you found something to be a certain way (an opinion), e.g. "Ho trovato l’esame difficile" = "I found the exam difficult."
target_language_example: Ho trovato le chiavi sotto il divano.
native_language_example: I found the keys under the sofa.

additional_notes: "Ho trovato" is the passato prossimo of "trovare" (to find) and can mean either "I found" or "I have found" in English, depending on context. "Il" is the masculine singular definite article ("the") and changes with the noun (e.g., "ho trovato la...", "ho trovato lo...", "ho trovato l'...", "ho trovato i/gli...", "ho trovato le..."). It’s used both for literally finding something (an object/place) and for discovering/realizing something (e.g., finding something comfortable, finding north).
target_language_example: Ho trovato il mio telefono sotto il divano.
native_language_example: I found my phone under the couch.

meaning: "I found the" / "I have found the" (past tense, feminine singular object).
additional_notes: "Ho trovato" is the passato prossimo of "trovare" (to find). It’s followed by a direct object; "la" is the feminine singular definite article (“the”), so it must match a feminine noun (e.g., la bicicletta, la scatola, la maniera). In English you may translate it as either “I found the …” or “I have found the …” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho trovato la chiave sul tavolo.
native_language_example: I found the key on the table.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of *trovare* (“to find”): *io ho trovato* + object. Use **un** before a masculine singular noun (e.g., *un albergo, un fungo*). With a feminine noun, use **ho trovato una…** (e.g., *una chiave*). In speech, Italians often add where/which one: *Ho trovato un albergo in centro.*
target_language_example: Ho trovato un ristorante vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I found a restaurant near the station.

additional_notes: Past tense of "trovare" (to find) using "avere": "ho trovato" = "I found / I have found". Use "una" before feminine singular nouns (una pianta, una scatola, una foto, una tartaruga). It can refer to finding something physical (an object/animal) or something more abstract (e.g., "una splendida solitudine").
target_language_example: Ho trovato una farmacia vicino a casa.
native_language_example: I found a pharmacy near my house.

additional_notes: Past tense with avere: ho + ucciso (past participle of uccidere). Used to say you killed someone/something; the direct object can follow (e.g., ho ucciso i topi = I killed the rats). In Italian, the passato prossimo often translates to simple past in English (“I killed”) depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho ucciso una zanzara in cucina.
native_language_example: I killed a mosquito in the kitchen.

additional_notes: "Ho venduto" is the passato prossimo of "vendere" (to sell). "la mia" means “my” for a feminine singular noun (e.g., auto, macchina, bici, casa, chitarra). You normally add the noun after it ("Ho venduto la mia auto"). It can also stand alone if the noun is understood from context (like “I sold mine”).
target_language_example: Ho venduto la mia chitarra ieri.
native_language_example: I sold my guitar yesterday.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of **vincere** (“to win”): **ho** (I have) + **vinto** (won). Used for winning a prize, a game, money, etc. You can add what you won: **Ho vinto il primo premio.** Sometimes you may also see an indirect pronoun to mean “for someone”: **Le ho vinto…** = “I won her …” (i.e., for her), though more common wording is **Ho vinto … per lei**.
target_language_example: Ho vinto due biglietti per il concerto.
native_language_example: I won two tickets to the concert.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of "visitare" (to visit): "ho" (I have) + "visitato" (visited). Used to talk about a completed visit in the past, often translated as simple past in English ("I visited"). With places it means you went there (Ho visitato Boston). With people it usually implies you went to see them (Ho visitato i miei genitori = I visited my parents / went to see my parents).
target_language_example: Ho visitato Roma due anni fa.
native_language_example: I visited Rome two years ago.

additional_notes: Past tense of vedere (to see) with avere: ho visto/ho vista. The past participle agrees in gender/number (vista/viste) when the direct object is a pronoun that comes before the verb (e.g., l’ho vista = I saw her/it; le ho viste = I saw them [fem.]). With ne you often add a quantity/one: ne ho vista una = I saw one (of them).
target_language_example: L’ho vista ieri al bar.
native_language_example: I saw her yesterday at the café.

additional_notes: Used with the verb vedere in the passato prossimo. You’ll often see it with the pronoun “ne” (“some/of them”): “Ne ho viste tante” = “I’ve seen lots (of them).” When a direct object pronoun comes before the verb (like “le” or “ne” referring to feminine plural things), the past participle can agree: visto → viste. Common in expressions like “Ne ho viste di peggiori” = “I’ve seen worse.”
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: ne ho viste di peggiori.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve seen worse.

additional_notes: Past tense of vedere (to see) with the auxiliary avere: ho visto/ho vista/ho visti/ho viste. The past participle can agree in gender/number with a direct object pronoun placed before the verb (e.g., li ho visti = I saw them (m. pl.); le ho viste = I saw them (f. pl.)). In your examples, it often appears with ne (“some/of them”), where agreement is common in informal speech: ne ho visti alcuni = I saw some (of them).
target_language_example: Li ho visti ieri al cinema.
native_language_example: I saw them yesterday at the movie theater.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of vedere ('to see'): ho + visto. It can describe a completed past action. In English, it may be translated as either 'I've seen' or 'I saw' depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho visto Marco al supermercato.
native_language_example: I saw Marco at the supermarket.

meaning: "I saw the" / "I have seen the" (masculine singular).
additional_notes: Passato prossimo of vedere (to see): ho visto = "I saw" or "I have seen" depending on context. Il is the definite article "the" used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., il film, il semaforo). Use it when the thing you saw is masculine singular; for feminine use la (ho visto la...), and for plural use i/gli/le (ho visto i/gli/le...).
target_language_example: Ho visto il film ieri sera.
native_language_example: I saw the movie last night.

meaning: “I saw that movie/film” or “I’ve seen that movie/film.”
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo (ho visto) to talk about a completed past event. With a specific time expression (e.g., lunedì scorso, sabato, tre anni fa), it usually translates as simple past (“I saw…”). Without a specific time, it can be “I’ve seen…”. "Quel" means “that” (over there/previously mentioned) and agrees with masculine singular "film".
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: ho visto quel film, quindi non mi spoilerare il finale.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I’ve seen that movie, so don’t spoil the ending for me.

additional_notes: Common way to say you saw something: "ho visto" is the passato prossimo of vedere (literally "I have seen"), often used like English simple past "I saw" in conversation. "un" is the masculine form of "a/an" and is used before a masculine singular noun (e.g., un aereo, un alieno). If the noun is feminine, use "una" instead (e.g., ho visto una casa). You can also use it before an infinitive phrase: "Ho visto un fulmine cadere..." = "I saw lightning strike/fall...".
target_language_example: Ho visto un gatto nel giardino.
native_language_example: I saw a cat in the garden.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of vedere (“to see”): ho visto = “I saw / I have seen”. Add a feminine singular noun after una (e.g., una zebra, una capanna). For a masculine noun, use ho visto un / uno; for plural, ho visto dei / delle.
target_language_example: Ho visto una macchina rossa davanti a casa.
native_language_example: I saw a red car in front of the house.

meaning: (not used on its own; usually in “non ho alcun/alcuna …”)
additional_notes: “Alcun” (like “any”) normally needs a noun after it and is most common in negative sentences: “non ho alcun + noun” (masc.) / “non ho alcuna + noun” (fem.) = “I don’t have any …”. On its own, “ho alcun” sounds incomplete/incorrect in standard Italian. Example patterns: “Non ho alcun problema.” / “Non ho alcuna idea.”
target_language_example: Non ho alcuna domanda.
native_language_example: I don’t have any questions.

additional_notes: Used with "ancora" to say something continues to be true. Often followed by a noun ("Ho ancora degli amici" = "I still have friends") or by an expression like "intenzione di..." ("Ho ancora intenzione di..." = "I still intend to..."). Note: "ancora" can also mean "again" in other contexts.
target_language_example: Ho ancora tempo per un caffè.
native_language_example: I still have time for a coffee.

meaning: “I still have doubts / I’m still not sure.”
additional_notes: Used to express that you’re still uncertain or not fully convinced. Literally: “I have still some doubts.” You can change the subject: *hai ancora dei dubbi?* (“do you still have doubts?”), *abbiamo ancora dei dubbi* (“we still have doubts”). Often followed by *su* + topic: *Ho ancora dei dubbi su questa scelta.*
target_language_example: Ho ancora dei dubbi su quale treno prendere.
native_language_example: I’m still not sure which train to take.

additional_notes: Literally means "I have need." This is the 1st person singular form of avere bisogno, and it is usually followed by di + noun or infinitive: ho bisogno di aiuto = "I need help," ho bisogno di dormire = "I need to sleep."
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un po' d'acqua.
native_language_example: I need some water.

additional_notes: Used to express a need/requirement followed by a verb clause introduced by che. The verb after che is typically in the present subjunctive (congiuntivo): Ho bisogno che tu vada / che mi aiuti / che capiscano. It often implies you need another person (or people) to do something.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno che tu venga subito.
native_language_example: I need you to come right away.

meaning: "I need you to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to say you need someone to do something. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive (e.g., capisca, prenda, sappia, traduca, collabori). Often used for requests, instructions, or expressing an important need.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno che tu mi aiuti con questo esercizio.
native_language_example: I need you to help me with this exercise.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something: “ho bisogno di …” = “I need …”. “del” is the contraction of “di + il”, so it’s used before a masculine singular noun with “il” (e.g., il cacciavite → del cacciavite). With other articles you get: “dello” (lo), “della” (la), “dei” (i), “degli” (gli), “delle” (le).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho bisogno del tuo aiuto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need your help.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone directly for help. You can change the person: “Ho bisogno del suo aiuto” (formal: I need your help), “Ho bisogno del vostro aiuto” (to more than one person). Often followed by a name or a time word like “ora” (now).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho bisogno del tuo aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Sorry, I need your help with this form.

additional_notes: Literally “I have need of.” Used to say you need something: ho bisogno di + noun (Ho bisogno di soldi.). With an action, use ho bisogno di + infinitive (Ho bisogno di parlare.). You can change the person/tense as needed (hai bisogno di…, aveva bisogno di…).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di dormire un po’.
native_language_example: I need to sleep a bit.

additional_notes: Literally “I have need of help.” Use it to ask for assistance in general or in a specific situation. You can add details with: "da" (from someone), "per" (for/with a problem), "qui" (here), or address someone: "Ho bisogno di aiuto, dottore."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ho bisogno di aiuto con questo modulo.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need help with this form.

additional_notes: Used to say you need to go somewhere. It’s made of: ho bisogno di = “I need” + andare = “to go” + in = “to/into” (often used with countries, regions, and some places like in Italia, in Toscana, in banca). After this phrase you normally add a place: Ho bisogno di andare in Italia / in ufficio. You can change the subject: ho/hai/ha bisogno di andare in… (I/you/he/she need(s) to go to…).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di andare in ufficio oggi.
native_language_example: I need to go to the office today.

additional_notes: Used to say you need to speak with someone. It’s followed by a person (a name, role, or pronoun): “Ho bisogno di parlare con Maria / con il dottore / con te.” Structure: “ho bisogno di” + infinitive (“parlare”) + “con” + person. Often used for requests or urgent matters.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di parlare con il responsabile, per favore.
native_language_example: I need to talk to the manager, please.

additional_notes: Used to say you need a greater quantity or amount of something. It’s often followed by a noun (e.g., più acqua, più tempo). You can also use it without naming the thing if it’s understood: “Ne ho bisogno di più” (“I need more of it”).
target_language_example: Mi piace questa ricetta, ma ho bisogno di più tempo per prepararla.
native_language_example: I like this recipe, but I need more time to make it.

additional_notes: Used to say you need someone's help, presence, or support. It can be emotional (“I need you”) or practical (“I need you to help me”). Often said with emphasis in urgent or serious situations.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di te adesso: puoi venire qui?
native_language_example: I need you now: can you come here?

additional_notes: First-person singular of avere bisogno di, a common way to say “to need” (literally “to have need of”). This pattern is used before many masculine singular nouns or quantity expressions: ho bisogno di un medico, ho bisogno di un litro d'acqua. With feminine nouns, use una instead; with some masculine nouns, use uno.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un caffè.
native_language_example: I need a coffee.

additional_notes: Used to say you need something. It’s made of: ho (I have) + bisogno (need) + di (of) + una (a/an, feminine). Use it before a feminine singular noun: “Ho bisogno di una busta/scrivania.” For masculine: “Ho bisogno di un…”. For plural: “Ho bisogno di…” + article (e.g., “dei/delle”).
target_language_example: Scusi, ho bisogno di una penna.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I need a pen.

additional_notes: Used to say you need to see someone/something. It’s built from: "ho" (I have) + "bisogno" (need) + "di" + infinitive ("vedere" = to see). You can add a person/thing after it (e.g., "ho bisogno di vedere Tom") and often add time words like "adesso/ora" (now). "Io" is optional and usually omitted unless you want emphasis.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di vedere il medico oggi.
native_language_example: I need to see the doctor today.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re occupied or can’t do something right now. Often said on its own (“Ho da fare.”) or to end a conversation (“Vai, ho da fare.”). Similar in meaning to “Ho qualcosa da fare.” and “Sono impegnato/a.”
target_language_example: Non posso venire adesso: ho da fare.
native_language_example: I can’t come right now: I’m busy.

additional_notes: Used to strongly express necessity or desire. It’s followed by: (1) an infinitive verb (e.g., "parlare") meaning "I really need to...", or (2) a noun/pronoun (e.g., "te", "un amico", "una tazza di caffè") meaning "I really need ...". Note the verb agreement: "ho" is 1st person singular (I have).
target_language_example: Ho davvero bisogno di dormire un po'.
