native_language_example: Let’s wait until we have all the documents in hand before signing.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like essere/andare (e.g., essere bravo/a, andare bene/male) to say how someone performs in the subject of math. You can also hear "a matematica" in some contexts, but "in matematica" is common for talking about skill/performance.
target_language_example: Non sono molto bravo in matematica, ma ci provo.
native_language_example: I'm not very good at math, but I try.

meaning: in the matter of; in the field/subject of.
additional_notes: Used to mean “regarding” a specific topic or area of expertise, often with “di” + topic: “in materia di diritto” (in matters of law / in the legal field). It frequently appears with words like “esperto” (expert) or verbs like “sapere” (to know).
target_language_example: Non sono molto preparato in materia di tasse.
native_language_example: I’m not very knowledgeable when it comes to taxes.

meaning: on average; on an average basis.
additional_notes: Used with numbers, amounts, or frequencies to express a typical average. It can come before or after the quantity (e.g., “guadagna in media…” / “…al giorno in media”).
target_language_example: In media arrivo al lavoro in trenta minuti.
native_language_example: On average, I get to work in thirty minutes.

meaning: less than; fewer than; ... younger than (by).
additional_notes: Used with numbers to compare amounts or time. With time expressions it means “in under …” (in less than ten minutes). With age it can mean “... years younger than” (quattro anni in meno di lui = four years younger than him). Often follows the number: “dieci minuti” + “in meno di” + reference, or “in meno di” + number + unit.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in meno di mezz’ora.
native_language_example: We arrived in under half an hour.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere (“to have”) and venire (“to come”) to talk about what someone is thinking, planning, or remembering: “avere in mente” = “to have in mind”; “venire in mente” = “to come to mind” (an idea/reminder pops into your head). In commands, “mett(it)elo bene in mente” means “keep it firmly in mind / remember this well,” and “non ti/vi venga più in mente!” means “don’t you ever think of (doing that) again!”
target_language_example: Avevo in mente di chiamarti ieri, ma mi sono dimenticato.
native_language_example: I had in mind to call you yesterday, but I forgot.

meaning: in the middle; in between; (also figuratively) involved/dragged in; in the way.
additional_notes: Most commonly means a physical position: "in mezzo alla strada" (in the middle of the road), "in mezzo alla stanza" (in the middle of the room). With verbs like "tirare/mettere qualcuno in mezzo" it means to involve someone (often unwillingly) or to bring someone into an argument/problem. In "in mezzo ai piedi" it means "underfoot / in the way".
target_language_example: Non mettermi in mezzo, per favore: non c’entro niente.
native_language_example: Don’t drag me into it, please: I have nothing to do with it.

meaning: in the middle of; among (in the middle of a group).
additional_notes: Used for physical position inside a group or crowd ("in mezzo a dei bambini", "in mezzo a tutta la gente"). It can also be used figuratively to mean being among certain people/things, sometimes with a negative tone depending on the context ("in mezzo a questa feccia" = "among this scum"). Often followed by an article: in mezzo a + i/gli/le/una/un/degli/dei.
target_language_example: Mi sono ritrovato in mezzo a una folla enorme.
native_language_example: I found myself in the middle of a huge crowd.

meaning: "in the middle of" / "among" (with masculine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used to say something is located or moving among a group of things/people: *in mezzo ai fiori* = “among the flowers.” It can also be used in set expressions like *in mezzo ai piedi* (“in the way/underfoot”). Grammar: *in mezzo a* + article; *ai* = *a + i* and is used before masculine plural nouns (e.g., *i fiori, i pini, i denti*).
target_language_example: Mi sono seduto in mezzo ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I sat in the middle of my friends.

meaning: in the middle of the street/road.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is literally out in the street (often in a place where you’re not supposed to be) or to emphasize that something is happening publicly, out in the open. Can also be used more loosely for “out on the street,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non lasciare la bici in mezzo alla strada!
native_language_example: Don’t leave the bike in the middle of the street!

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone does something, usually followed by an adjective: in modo incredibile (in an incredible way), in modo strano (in a strange way). Often comes right after the verb it describes.
target_language_example: Parla in modo chiaro.
native_language_example: He/She speaks in a clear way.

additional_notes: Introduces a purpose or intended result. Usually followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo): "in modo che non si noti", "in modo che nessuno lo veda". In the fixed expression "fare/fate in modo che..." it means "make sure that...".
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta in modo che il gatto non esca.
native_language_example: Close the door so that the cat doesn’t go out.

meaning: "so that" / "in such a way as to" (in order to achieve a result).
additional_notes: Introduces the goal or intended result of an action, similar to “so that” or “in order to.” It’s often followed by an infinitive (e.g., in modo da + stare/risolvere/nascondere). When the subject changes, Italian commonly uses “in modo che” + subjunctive instead.
target_language_example: Parla lentamente in modo da farsi capire.
native_language_example: Speak slowly so that people can understand you.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone does something or thinks/sees something differently from before or from other people. Often follows the verb: vedere/guardare le cose in modo diverso (“to see/look at things differently”), fare qualcosa in modo diverso (“to do something differently”).
target_language_example: Proviamo a risolvere il problema in modo diverso.
native_language_example: Let’s try to solve the problem differently.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "comportarsi" (to behave) or "agire" (to act): "comportarsi/agire in modo strano" = to behave/act strangely. It describes the manner of an action and can imply something unusual or suspicious.
target_language_example: Perché ti comporti in modo strano oggi?
native_language_example: Why are you acting weird today?

in molti negozi a cercare il libro

target_language_multi_word_term: in molti negozi a cercare il libro
meaning: to (go) to many shops to look for the book.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like andare/andare in or essere andato/a (past tense) to say you went to several stores with the purpose of searching for a specific book. Often appears as: (sono) andato/a in molti negozi a cercare il libro.
target_language_example: Sono andata in molti negozi a cercare il libro, ma non l’ho trovato.
native_language_example: I went to many shops to look for the book, but I didn’t find it.

meaning: start the car (get the engine running).
additional_notes: Most often used with the verb "mettere": "mettere in moto la macchina" = to start the car. It literally means "put the car in motion," and you’ll also hear it with other vehicles or engines: "mettere in moto lo scooter / il motore".
target_language_example: Non riesco a mettere in moto la macchina: la batteria è scarica.
native_language_example: I can’t start the car: the battery is dead.

additional_notes: Used to say you are acting with someone’s authority (on behalf of a person/organization) or invoking a value/reason (e.g., “in the name of justice/peace”). Often followed by a noun or name: in nome di Maria, in nome della legge.
target_language_example: Parlo in nome di tutta la squadra.
native_language_example: I’m speaking on behalf of the whole team.

meaning: “for God’s sake!” / “in God’s name!” (an exclamation showing shock, anger, or urgency).
additional_notes: Used as a strong interjection, often at the beginning of a sentence, to express frustration, disbelief, or to demand an explanation. Depending on tone it can sound rude or blasphemous to some people; a milder alternative is “Per favore!” or “Dai!” In formal/religious contexts it can also mean “in the name of God,” but in these examples it’s an emotional exclamation.
target_language_example: In nome di Dio, smettila e ascoltami!
native_language_example: For God’s sake, stop and listen to me!

additional_notes: Used to say something is true or should be done no matter what (often to conclude a point, change topic, or insist on an action). Common with negatives like “In ogni caso non…” (= “Anyway, it doesn’t…”).
target_language_example: Non so se arriverò in orario; in ogni caso, ti chiamo appena arrivo.
native_language_example: I don’t know if I’ll arrive on time; in any case, I’ll call you as soon as I get there.

meaning: in every way; by all means possible.
additional_notes: Used to say someone does something using all possible ways/efforts. Often follows verbs like aiutare (to help), sostenere (to support), fare (to do), and can be strengthened with words like possibile (“in every way possible”).
target_language_example: Ti sosterrò in ogni modo.
native_language_example: I’ll support you in every way.

additional_notes: Used for radio/TV/live streams when a program is currently broadcasting (“Siamo in onda” = “We’re on air”). Also appears in the noun phrase “messa in onda” meaning “broadcasting/airing” (e.g., the airing of a show).
target_language_example: Tra due minuti siamo in onda, pronti?
native_language_example: In two minutes we’re on air—ready?

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something arrives/starts at the expected time (often with verbs like essere, arrivare). You can also negate it: non essere in orario = to be late.
target_language_example: Cerco sempre di essere in orario per le riunioni.
native_language_example: I always try to be on time for meetings.

additional_notes: Used to say things are arranged neatly or as they should be. Very common with the verb phrase "mettere in ordine" (to put in order / to tidy up). It can also be used as a question: "È/Siete in ordine?" = "Is everything/Are you (all) ready/in order?"
target_language_example: Prima che arrivino gli ospiti, voglio che la cucina sia in ordine.
native_language_example: Before the guests arrive, I want the kitchen to be tidy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about how something/someone was at the beginning or in the past (its original state, name, owner, purpose, etc.). With people, it can also mean “originally from” a place (your origins). Often placed near the verb: “In origine si chiamava…”, “apparteneva… in origine”.
target_language_example: In origine questo edificio era una scuola.
native_language_example: Originally this building was a school.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of being/staying (essere/stare) to mean "in the hospital" (location): "Sono in ospedale." With verbs of motion (andare/portare) it often means "to the hospital": "Andiamo in ospedale." Also used in phrases like "visitare qualcuno in ospedale" = "to visit someone in the hospital."
target_language_example: Devo andare in ospedale per una visita.
native_language_example: I have to go to the hospital for an appointment.

meaning: in the hospital for a week.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was staying in the hospital for one week. Often follows verbs like stare/restare/rimanere/essere (“to be/stay/remain”).
target_language_example: Mia madre è stata in ospedale per una settimana dopo l’operazione.
native_language_example: My mother was in the hospital for a week after the operation.

additional_notes: Common with "lasciare" to mean "to leave (someone) alone": "Lasciami in pace!" = "Leave me alone!". With "essere in pace con" it means "to be at peace with" (a person/country). In contexts about death, it can mean "peacefully" or "rest in peace" ("riposare in pace").
target_language_example: Dopo una giornata lunga, voglio stare in pace.
native_language_example: After a long day, I want to be left in peace.

meaning: at the gym; to the gym.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/being to talk about going to or being at the gym. Often with andare (vado in palestra = I go to the gym) and essere (sono in palestra = I’m at the gym).
target_language_example: Oggi non posso: sono già in palestra.
native_language_example: I can’t today: I’m already at the gym.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true/possible only to some extent, not completely. Often goes with expressions like "solo in parte" (only partly) or with responsibility/blame: "in parte responsabile" = partly responsible.
target_language_example: Capisco in parte quello che dici, ma non del tutto.
native_language_example: I partly understand what you’re saying, but not completely.

additional_notes: Used to highlight a specific item within a general statement. Common in both spoken and written Italian, often placed at the start of a sentence or right before the detail you want to emphasize.
target_language_example: Mi piace la cucina italiana, in particolare la pizza.
native_language_example: I like Italian food, especially pizza.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an earlier time (either long ago or simply before now). It often appears at the start of a sentence as a time marker: “In passato, …”. You can also use it after a verb to mean “before/previously”.
target_language_example: In passato ho vissuto a Milano, ma ora vivo a Roma.
native_language_example: In the past I lived in Milan, but now I live in Rome.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is retired (no longer working) or has entered retirement. Often with essere (to be): “Sono in pensione” = “I’m retired.” With andare in pensione it means “to retire” (to stop working and start receiving a pension).
target_language_example: Mio padre è in pensione da due anni.
native_language_example: My father has been retired for two years.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to say someone/something is in danger: "Sono in pericolo" (I’m in danger). It can also be used with mettere (“to put”) or mettere in pericolo (“to endanger”): "Lo metti in pericolo" (You put him in danger). You may also hear "in pericolo immediato" for “in immediate danger.”
target_language_example: Sei in pericolo? Chiamo la polizia.
native_language_example: Are you in danger? I’ll call the police.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that someone is physically present, not represented by someone else or via phone/email. Often placed after the person it refers to (e.g., "il presidente in persona" = "the president himself in person"). It can also be used alone as a short reply meaning “in person.”
target_language_example: Preferirei parlarne con te in persona.
native_language_example: I’d rather talk about it with you in person.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like tagliare (to cut), rompere (to break), ridurre (to reduce) to mean “into pieces.” It can also describe the result/state: essere/andare in pezzi = “to be/fall apart (be broken).”
target_language_example: Ho rotto il bicchiere: adesso è in pezzi.
native_language_example: I broke the glass: now it’s in pieces.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is standing rather than sitting or lying down: “essere/stare in piedi” = “to be/stand up.” It can also be used as an order: “In piedi!” = “Stand up!” You can add a place: “in piedi in giardino” (standing in the garden), or “in piedi su uno sgabello” (standing on a stool).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti in piedi per tutta la lezione.
native_language_example: We stayed standing for the whole lesson.

meaning: in the middle of; in full (at the height of).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is happening right at that moment/point (e.g., in pieno inverno = in the middle of winter; in pieno centro = right in the city center; in pieno giorno = in broad daylight). Often followed by a noun.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in pieno centro in dieci minuti.
native_language_example: We arrived right in the city center in ten minutes.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is at the pool or going there, often with verbs like essere (to be), andare (to go), and portare (to take/bring). You can also use it for pool-related events: una festa in piscina = a pool party.
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio andiamo in piscina con gli amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon we’re going to the pool with friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an added amount or an additional thing/action beyond what’s already there. Common patterns: (1) "qualcosa in più" = "something extra / more"; (2) "X anni in più" = "X years older" (literally "X years more"); (3) "un passo in più" = "one more step" (also figuratively: making extra effort or going further); (4) sentence-initial "In più, ..." = "Besides/On top of that, ...".
target_language_example: Mi puoi dare un minuto in più?
native_language_example: Can you give me one more minute?

meaning: In short; in a few words.
additional_notes: Used to summarize what was just said or to get to the main point. Often placed at the start of a sentence (followed by a comma), but it can also stand alone as a quick “So, basically…” / “In short.”
target_language_example: In poche parole, non posso venire domani.
native_language_example: In short, I can’t come tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the real situation (how things work in reality), often contrasting with "in teoria" (in theory). In conversation it can also mean "so, basically..." or "the bottom line is..." to summarize or push for a practical answer.
target_language_example: In teoria è semplice, ma in pratica ci vuole molto tempo.
native_language_example: In theory it’s simple, but in practice it takes a lot of time.

additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "prendere" (prendere in prestito) to mean "to borrow" (books, pens, money, etc.). The opposite is "dare in prestito" = "to lend". Often followed by "da" + person/place you borrow from: "prendere in prestito qualcosa da qualcuno/dalla biblioteca".
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito questa penna per un minuto?
native_language_example: Can I borrow this pen for a minute?

meaning: (some) money as a loan; borrowed money.
additional_notes: Used mainly with the verb "prendere" ("prendere in prestito dei soldi" = to borrow money) and the opposite is "dare dei soldi in prestito" (= to lend money). You can add who you borrow from with "da": "prendere in prestito dei soldi da un amico".
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito dei soldi da te?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money from you?

additional_notes: Used when talking about borrowing something. "In prestito" means "on loan / borrowed"; "dei" is a partitive article meaning "some" with plural nouns (e.g., "dei libri" = "some books"). Often appears as "prendere in prestito dei ..." (to borrow some ...) or "avere in prestito dei ..." (to have some ... on loan).
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito dei libri?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some books?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "prendere" ("prendere in prestito") to mean "to borrow" something and then return it. You can add who you borrow from with "da/dal/dai/dalle": "Prendo in prestito dei gioielli da un’amica" (I borrow some jewelry from a friend). "Dei gioielli" means "some jewelry" (unspecified quantity).
target_language_example: Ho preso in prestito dei gioielli da mia sorella per la festa.
native_language_example: I borrowed some jewelry from my sister for the party.

additional_notes: Usually used with the verb "prendere": "prendere in prestito (dei) libri" = to borrow (some) books. The lender can be introduced with "da" ("da lui" = from him), and places with "da" or "dalla/dal" ("dalla biblioteca" = from the library).
target_language_example: Prendo in prestito dei libri dalla biblioteca ogni settimana.
native_language_example: I borrow some books from the library every week.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "prendere" ("prendere in prestito") to mean "to borrow" (not "to lend"). Often followed by "da" + person: "prendere in prestito dei soldi da lui" = "to borrow money from him". You can also say "chiedere dei soldi in prestito" = "to ask to borrow money".
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito dei soldi da te fino a domani?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money from you until tomorrow?

additional_notes: Most commonly used with the verb phrase "prendere in prestito" (to borrow). You’ll usually say: "prendere in prestito del denaro" = to borrow some money. The lender would say "prestare del denaro" = to lend money.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito del denaro fino a domani?
native_language_example: Can I borrow some money until tomorrow?

additional_notes: You’ll almost always see this as **in prestito** followed by a noun, often with an article: **in prestito il libro** (“the book on loan / the borrowed book”). Very common verbs are **prendere in prestito** (“to borrow”) and **dare in prestito** (“to lend”).
target_language_example: Ho in prestito il libro della biblioteca.
native_language_example: I have the library book on loan.

meaning: “his (one) on loan” / “borrow his (one)” (i.e., borrow something that belongs to him, with the noun understood from context).
additional_notes: This phrase is used when the thing being borrowed belongs to a man (or to ‘he’ in context) and the noun is implied (e.g., *il suo libro*, *il suo telefono*). In practice, Italian more commonly uses *prendere in prestito il suo [nome]* or *prendere in prestito il suo* when the object is clear from context. Note: agreement depends on the implied noun; if the implied noun is feminine, you’d say *in prestito la sua*.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio caricatore: posso prendere in prestito il suo?
native_language_example: I forgot my charger: can I borrow yours (his)?

additional_notes: Used when you want to borrow something that belongs to the person you’re speaking to. It usually appears in a longer sentence with a noun that may be said or implied: “Posso prendere in prestito il tuo (libro)?” = “Can I borrow your (book)?” You can also say “il tuo” by itself if the object is clear from context.
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito il tuo telefono per un minuto?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Usually used as part of the verb phrase **prendere in prestito** = “to borrow” (literally “to take on loan”). **Il vostro** means “yours/your” (formal or plural “you”), and it agrees with the noun it refers to (e.g., **il vostro libro** = “your book”, **la vostra penna** = “your pen”). Often you’ll see it in a question like **Posso prendere in prestito il vostro (…)?**
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il vostro libro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow your book?

meaning: 'to borrow your car' / 'on loan, your car'.
additional_notes: Used with a verb like prendere/avere/chiedere: "Posso prendere in prestito la vostra macchina?". "In prestito" means "as a loan" (temporarily, with the idea you’ll give it back). "Macchina" commonly means "car" in Italian (not just "machine"). "Vostra" is the formal/plural "your".
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito la vostra macchina per un’ora?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your car for an hour?

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "prendere" or "avere" to talk about borrowing something for a short time: "Posso prendere [X] in prestito per un minuto?" It’s a polite, neutral phrase; in everyday speech you can also say "un attimo" instead of "un minuto".
target_language_example: Posso prendere il tuo telefono in prestito per un minuto?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your phone for a minute?

meaning: to borrow a book from (someone/a place).
additional_notes: Usually used with the verb **prendere**: **prendere in prestito un libro da + person/place** = “to borrow a book from…”. The opposite is **dare in prestito** = “to lend”. You can also say **prendere in prestito un libro dalla biblioteca** (“from the library”).
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito un libro da te?
native_language_example: Can I borrow a book from you?

additional_notes: Means someone is imprisoned/being held. Common with verbs like essere (to be), finire (to end up), andare (to go), mettere/mandare (to put/send), and passare (to spend time): “È in prigione” = “He/She is in prison.” In Italian you often use “in” (not “a”) with places seen as institutions/conditions like prigione.
target_language_example: Se continui così, finirai in prigione.
native_language_example: If you keep going like this, you'll end up in prison.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was in prison because of a specific crime or reason ("per" = "for"). Often followed by a noun (omicidio, rapina) or by a time expression in related phrases like "in prigione per dieci anni" (= in prison for ten years).
target_language_example: È finito in prigione per frode.
native_language_example: He ended up in prison for fraud.

additional_notes: Used to say someone spent a total duration of three years in prison. With essere, the past participle agrees with the subject: sono stato (male) / sono stata (female). You can swap the time: in prigione per due mesi, per cinque anni, etc.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è stato in prigione per tre anni, ma ora lavora e sta bene.
native_language_example: My brother was in prison for three years, but now he works and is doing well.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is sitting or standing in the first row (e.g., at school, a theater, a meeting, a ceremony). Often answers “Where?” (Dove?) or is used as a short instruction (e.g., “In prima fila!” = “Front row!”).
target_language_example: Siediti in prima fila, così vedi meglio.
native_language_example: Sit in the front row so you can see better.

meaning: first of all; first and foremost.
additional_notes: A formal, somewhat bureaucratic/academic expression (a Latinism). Used to introduce the most important point or the first item in a list. In everyday speech, Italians more often say "prima di tutto" or "innanzitutto".
target_language_example: In primis, dobbiamo capire quanto costa il progetto.
native_language_example: First of all, we have to understand how much the project costs.

meaning: first (of all); in the first place.
additional_notes: Used to introduce the first point in a list or argument ("First of all..."). It can also mean "in the first place" = "to begin with" (often in questions/negatives: "Why ... in the first place?", "He never called in the first place"). Word order is flexible, but it often appears at the start of the sentence followed by a comma.
target_language_example: In primo luogo, dobbiamo capire che cosa è successo.
native_language_example: First of all, we need to understand what happened.

meaning: in private; privately (not in front of others).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like parlare/discutere/dire to ask for a one-on-one conversation or to keep something confidential. Often implies stepping aside so others can’t hear.
target_language_example: Possiamo parlarne in privato un momento?
native_language_example: Can we talk about it in private for a moment?

additional_notes: Used with avere/essere (e.g., "ho/abbiamo in programma...") to say you have something planned. Common patterns: "avere in programma + noun" (a visit, a meeting) and "avere in programma di + infinitive" (to travel, to do something). Often used for plans that are somewhat organized or intended, not just a vague idea.
target_language_example: Domani ho una riunione in programma.
native_language_example: I have a meeting scheduled for tomorrow.

meaning: in public; in front of other people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about actions done where others can see/hear you (e.g., in the street, at a party, on stage). Often contrasts with "in privato" (in private).
target_language_example: Preferisco non discutere in pubblico.
native_language_example: I prefer not to argue in public.

additional_notes: Idiom: literally “in (the) fist,” meaning you have someone/something firmly under control or at your mercy. Often used with verbs like avere/tenere (“to have/keep”) and with pronouns: mi/ti/lo/la/li/le (e.g., “Mi tieni in pugno” = “You’ve got me in your grip”).
target_language_example: La polizia ha il sospetto in pugno.
native_language_example: The police have the suspect under control.

meaning: on tiptoe; quietly/softly (as if on tiptoe).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like camminare/andare/uscire/entrare to say someone moves on their toes, often to avoid making noise or to be discreet. Literally means “on the tips of the feet.”
target_language_example: Sono entrato in punta di piedi per non svegliare il bambino.
native_language_example: I came in on tiptoe so I wouldn’t wake the baby.

meaning: exactly (at a specific time); also: on the point of (e.g., death).
additional_notes:
Used mainly in two patterns:
1) With a time to mean “exactly / on the dot”: "alle sei in punto" = “at six o’clock sharp.”
2) In the fixed phrase "in punto di morte" to mean “at the point of death / on one’s deathbed.”
Often placed right after the time expression (alle cinque in punto).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle otto in punto davanti alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at eight o’clock sharp in front of the station.

additional_notes: Used when the exact method or reason is unknown, unspecified, or not important. It can mean “somehow (I’ll manage)” in problem-solving contexts, or “in some way” to say something is partly/indirectly true (e.g., “limited in some way”). Common in offers of help: “Posso aiutarti in qualche modo?”
target_language_example: Non so come, ma in qualche modo ce la faremo.
native_language_example: I don’t know how, but somehow we’ll make it.

meaning: “in which?” / “in what?” (asking which one, within a category).
additional_notes: Used in questions to ask which specific place, folder, direction, neighborhood, school, way/manner, etc. something is in. It’s often followed by a noun (in quale cartella/direzione/quartiere) or by words like “modo” (“in what way”). Similar meaning to “in che…”, but “in quale” is a bit more specific/formal.
target_language_example: In quale ristorante vuoi andare stasera?
native_language_example: Which restaurant do you want to go to tonight?

meaning: in the capacity of; as (someone’s role).
additional_notes: Used before a job title or role to specify what function someone has (officially or temporarily). Common in formal or written Italian: "in qualità di direttore", "in qualità di testimone". In more casual speech you can often just say "come" (as).
target_language_example: Parlo in qualità di responsabile del progetto.
native_language_example: I’m speaking in my capacity as the project manager.

additional_notes: Used to say something can happen or be done at an unspecified time, without restrictions. Often with the future tense to mean “any moment now” (e.g., something is expected to happen soon).
target_language_example: Puoi chiamarmi in qualsiasi momento.
native_language_example: You can call me anytime.

meaning: at any time; whenever you like.
additional_notes: Used to say there is no restriction on timing (you can do it now, later, day or night). Common with invitations or permission, often with the verb in the present or future: “puoi chiamarmi in qualunque momento,” “sarai/ sarà il benvenuto/a in qualunque momento.” Similar to “in qualsiasi momento.”
target_language_example: Puoi scrivermi in qualunque momento se hai domande.
native_language_example: You can write to me at any time if you have questions.

additional_notes: Used in more formal Italian to introduce a role/identity (“as a…”) or a reason/justification (“since/because…”). Often followed by a noun (“in quanto studente”) or by a clause (“in quanto non ho tempo…”). In everyday speech, Italians may prefer alternatives like “come” (as) or “perché” (because).
target_language_example: In quanto cittadino, ho il diritto di fare domanda.
native_language_example: As a citizen, I have the right to apply.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun to point to a specific place/time/thing already known or indicated: in quel periodo (in that period), in quel caso (in that case), in quel villaggio (in that village). It’s the contraction of "in" + "quel" (from "quello"). Feminine: "in quella"; plural: "in quei" / "in quegli" / "in quelle".
target_language_example: Non voglio entrare in quel negozio.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go into that shop.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to a situation just mentioned and to introduce what to do or what follows as a consequence. It often comes at the start of a sentence followed by a comma: “In quel caso, …”.
target_language_example: In quel caso, possiamo partire domani.
native_language_example: In that case, we can leave tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific way of speaking, behaving, doing something, or even looking at someone—often with a negative or disapproving tone depending on context (e.g., "Don’t talk to me like that"). Can also refer to leaving a situation "that way" (unresolved, messy, etc.).
target_language_example: Non guardarmi in quel modo, mi metti a disagio.
native_language_example: Don’t look at me like that, you’re making me uncomfortable.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific point in time being talked about (in the past, present, or in a story). Often appears with past tenses (e.g., imperfetto) to describe what was happening then. Similar to "in quel momento" = "at that moment" and "in quel periodo" = "during that period" (longer time span).
target_language_example: In quel momento non potevo rispondere al telefono.
native_language_example: At that moment I couldn't answer the phone.

additional_notes: Used to point to a specific shop (usually one you’ve mentioned already or can indicate in context). Often answers “Where?” (Dove?): *Hai comprato la penna dove?* → *In quel negozio.* You can swap in other determiners: *in questo negozio* (in this shop), *in quel supermercato* (in that supermarket).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in quel negozio alle cinque.
native_language_example: See you in that shop at five.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific restaurant that’s already known from context (you can point to it, have mentioned it before, etc.). "in" + "quel" (that, masculine singular) + "ristorante" (restaurant). Often used with verbs like mangiare (to eat) and andare (to go).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in quel ristorante vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you at that restaurant near the station.

additional_notes: Means “in that” when referring to a specific place/setting/thing already known from context, and it’s used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., in quella città = in that city; in quella stanza = in that room). For masculine singular, you’ll see in quel / in quello.
target_language_example: Non posso parlare in quella sala: è troppo rumorosa.
native_language_example: I can't talk in that room: it's too noisy.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being inside a specific house already identified in context. "Quella" is the feminine singular demonstrative (“that”) and matches "casa" (feminine). Often implies the house is not the one near the speaker (contrast with "in questa casa" = “in this house”).
target_language_example: Non voglio entrare in quella casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go into that house.

additional_notes: Used to indicate being inside/attending a specific school already known from context. "Quella" = "that" (not "this"), pointing to a particular school (often not the one you’re in right now). Common with verbs like andare (to go), studiare (to study), trasferirsi (to transfer).
target_language_example: Mio fratello studia in quella scuola da due anni.
native_language_example: My brother has been studying at that school for two years.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun to mean “in this” place/thing/time period: in questa classe (in this class), in questa biblioteca (in this library), in questa stagione (in this season). “Questa” agrees with feminine nouns; with masculine singular it’s “in questo.”
target_language_example: Non posso parlare adesso: sono in questa riunione fino alle tre.
native_language_example: I can’t talk now: I’m in this meeting until three.

meaning: in this house; in this home.
additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is (or happens) inside this specific house. Often used when talking about where you lived or grew up ("Sono cresciuto in questa casa"), or when setting a rule about what/who is allowed inside ("Non la voglio in questa casa!" = “I don’t want her/it in this house!”).
target_language_example: In questa casa non si fuma.
native_language_example: In this house, no one smokes / Smoking is not allowed.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is (or stays/lives) within the current city being talked about. Common with verbs like abitare (to live), restare (to stay), vivere (to live), and rimanere (to remain). You can swap questa with other demonstratives: in quella città = in that city.
target_language_example: Non lavoro più in questa città.
native_language_example: I don’t work in this city anymore.

additional_notes: Used to say someone or something is inside/part of the particular class you’re talking about. Often follows phrases like “Ci sono…” (There are…), “Quanti sono…” (How many are…), or “essere in…” (to be in…). “Classe” can mean a school class, a course group, or sometimes a category/grade level—context makes it clear.
target_language_example: Oggi in questa classe siamo in venti.
native_language_example: Today in this class there are twenty of us.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something is located inside the room you are currently in (or the room being referred to). Common with "essere/ci sono" (to be/there are) and with action verbs like "succedere" (to happen) or "rimanere" (to stay). "Questa" agrees with the feminine noun "stanza".
target_language_example: Non fumare in questa stanza, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t smoke in this room, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something happening or existing nearby (in the local area). Common in questions about whether something has been seen/found locally, or statements about what people are like in the area.
target_language_example: C'è un buon ristorante in questa zona?
native_language_example: Is there a good restaurant in this area?

meaning: these days; lately; in the last few days.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a recent period around now (often the last few days or the current period). It can mean “these days” in general or “lately/recently,” depending on context. Often placed at the beginning or end of the sentence.
target_language_example: In questi giorni sono molto impegnato con il lavoro.
native_language_example: These days I’m very busy with work.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun. It can refer to place, time, or an abstract situation: in questo lago, in questo istante, in questo caso. Compare with in questa (feminine singular), in questi (masculine plural), and in queste (feminine plural).
target_language_example: In questo momento sono molto occupato.
native_language_example: At this moment I'm very busy.

meaning: in this case; in this situation.
additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific situation or set of circumstances being discussed. Often introduces what is true or what should happen given those circumstances. With legal meanings, "caso" can also mean a court case (e.g., "il procuratore in questo caso" = the prosecutor on this case).
target_language_example: In questo caso, è meglio chiamare la polizia.
native_language_example: In this case, it's better to call the police.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone/something is located or happens inside this specific building (often one you’re in or have just mentioned). Common with verbs like vivere (to live), lavorare (to work), trovarsi (to be located), and fare (to do).
target_language_example: C'è un ascensore in questo edificio?
native_language_example: Is there an elevator in this building?

additional_notes: Used to describe the way something happens or is done, often referring to a specific situation (sometimes with a negative tone: “treated me like this”). It can also mean “end up like this” (finire in questo modo) or mean “it doesn’t have to be like this” (non deve essere in questo modo).
target_language_example: Per favore, non parlare con me in questo modo.
native_language_example: Please, don’t talk to me like this.

additional_notes: Used to talk about what is happening now, at the present time. Often refers to a temporary situation (it may change later).
target_language_example: Non posso parlare in questo momento, ti richiamo dopo.
native_language_example: I can’t talk right now, I’ll call you back later.

meaning: in this world; in this life/reality.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the world as we know it (life on Earth, reality, society). Often appears in general statements or contrasts (e.g., “In questo mondo, …”) and can also be used in fictional contexts to mean “in this world/universe” (as opposed to another world).
target_language_example: In questo mondo, niente è perfetto.
native_language_example: In this world, nothing is perfect.

meaning: in this country (or: in this town/village).
additional_notes: Means “in this place” with paese most often understood as “country,” but in some contexts it can also mean “town/village” (especially when talking about a small local place). Used for location or being present/absent in that place.
target_language_example: Non ho mai vissuto in questo paese prima d’ora.
native_language_example: I’ve never lived in this country before.

additional_notes: Used to say someone lives or is located in the same neighborhood you’re currently talking about or pointing to. Often with verbs like abitare (to live) and vivere (to live). You can swap the demonstrative: in quel quartiere = “in that neighborhood.”
target_language_example: C'è una buona pizzeria in questo quartiere.
native_language_example: There’s a good pizzeria in this neighborhood.

additional_notes: Used to say where an action happens (a place). With restaurants you typically use "in" (in/at) to mean you eat there. You can change the noun: "in questo bar" (in this bar), "in questo hotel" (in this hotel).
target_language_example: Non ho mai mangiato in questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I’ve never eaten in this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to correct or уточнить what was just said, often contrasting appearances/assumptions with the true situation. It can go at the beginning, in the middle, or at the end of the sentence: “In realtà, … / …, in realtà.”
target_language_example: Pensavo fosse chiuso, ma in realtà è aperto.
native_language_example: I thought it was closed, but actually it’s open.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a correction, the real situation, or a contrast with what someone thinks/said. Often follows a name/topic: "Tom in realtà è…" = "Tom is actually…". In speech it can sound like "Well, actually…".
target_language_example: Scusa, in realtà è domani l’appuntamento.
native_language_example: Sorry, the appointment is actually tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say something is correct and meets requirements (often legal/official): paperwork, documents, permits, inspections, equipment, a situation (“è tutto in regola”). Common with avere/essere: “avere i documenti in regola” (to have valid papers), “essere in regola” (to be compliant/up to date).
target_language_example: Non posso partire se non ho il passaporto in regola.
native_language_example: I can’t leave if my passport isn’t in order.

additional_notes: Used to tell people to form a line (often for organization/discipline: at school, in the military, before entering somewhere). Common with verbs like mettersi in riga (to line up), mettere qualcuno in riga (to line someone up / get them in order), restare/stare in riga (to stay in line).
target_language_example: Ragazzi, mettetevi in riga davanti alla porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Kids, line up in front of the door, please.

additional_notes: Used to say that a person, event, train, payment, etc. is not on time. Often follows essere: essere in ritardo = to be late.
target_language_example: Siamo in ritardo per la lezione.
native_language_example: We're late for class.

additional_notes: Used with essere (e.g., sono/sei/è/eravamo) to say you are late for an event, appointment, meeting, school, work, etc. It’s often followed by an article + noun (per il lavoro, per una riunione, per gli appuntamenti).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo per la lezione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late for class.

additional_notes: Used with essere (to be) or arrivare (to arrive) to say someone won’t make it to dinner on time. You can replace la cena with another event: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work), in ritardo per l'appuntamento (late for the appointment).
target_language_example: Scusa, sono in ritardo per la cena.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m late for dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (to be): essere in ritardo per la scuola = to be late for school. Common in talking about schedules and obligations. You can swap the destination: in ritardo per il lavoro (late for work), in ritardo per l’appuntamento (late for the appointment).
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo per la scuola, devo andare subito!
native_language_example: I’m late for school, I have to go right away!

meaning: late for class / late for lessons.
additional_notes: Used to say someone arrives after the scheduled start time of their classes. Common pattern: "essere in ritardo per ..." (to be late for ...) + what you’re late for (e.g., le lezioni, la scuola, una riunione).
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo per le lezioni perché l'autobus non è arrivato.
native_language_example: I'm late for class because the bus didn't come.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "essere" (or similar) to say someone is doing well health-wise: "Sono in salute" = "I’m in good health." It often implies “healthy/doing well” rather than just “not sick,” and can be strengthened with words like "molto" or contrasted with age/conditions ("per la sua età").
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, è finalmente in salute.
native_language_example: After the operation, he’s finally in good health.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "mettere" (to put) or "mettersi" (to get) to mean getting someone/yourself to safety: "mettere qualcuno in salvo" = to get someone to safety; "mettersi in salvo" = to get to safety. Common in emergencies, warnings, or dangerous situations.
target_language_example: Dopo l'incendio, tutti sono riusciti a mettersi in salvo.
native_language_example: After the fire, everyone managed to get to safety.

additional_notes: Used after a noun to say it’s preserved and sold in a can: frutta in scatola (canned fruit), manzo in scatola (canned beef), salmone in scatola (canned salmon). Often contrasts with fresco (fresh).
target_language_example: Preferisco il tonno in scatola perché dura a lungo.
native_language_example: I prefer canned tuna because it lasts a long time.

additional_notes: Used to say something is done privately so others don’t know about it. Often goes with verbs like continuare (continue), incontrarsi (meet), leggere (read), fare (do). You can also ask “Perché in segreto?” = “Why in secret?”
target_language_example: L'hanno organizzato in segreto per non rovinare la sorpresa.
native_language_example: They organized it in secret so they wouldn’t ruin the surprise.

additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens after another event or at a later time. Common both at the end of a sentence (Avverrà in seguito = It will happen later) and at the beginning with commas (In seguito, ... = Afterwards, ...). Often interchangeable with "poi" or "dopo" depending on context; "in seguito" can sound a bit more formal/neutral, like "subsequently."
target_language_example: Ne parleremo in seguito, adesso non ho tempo.
native_language_example: We’ll talk about it later; right now I don’t have time.

meaning: in store (kept in reserve for later).
additional_notes: Used especially with "avere qualcosa in serbo (per qualcuno/per un’occasione)" to mean you have something planned, saved, or prepared for later—often a surprise. It can also be used more generally about what the future will bring: "non sapevo cosa avesse in serbo per me..." = "I didn’t know what ... had in store for me."
target_language_example: Non sai cosa ho in serbo per il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: You don’t know what I have in store for your birthday.

meaning: on duty; at work (in an official role).
additional_notes: Used for jobs with shifts or official responsibilities (police, security, military, medical staff, public services). It means you are currently working/active and responsible, often contrasted with "fuori servizio" (off duty). Common with verbs like "essere" (sono/ero in servizio) and "andare" (andare in servizio = start your shift/go on duty).
target_language_example: Il medico è in servizio fino alle otto.
native_language_example: The doctor is on duty until eight.

meaning: safe; secured; in a safe state.
additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "mettere" or "portare": "mettere in sicurezza" = to make safe / to secure (an area, a building, a situation). Common in instructions and emergency contexts (e.g., securing a perimeter). It can refer both to people (getting them to safety) and to places/things (making them secure).
target_language_example: Prima dell’arrivo della tempesta, abbiamo messo in sicurezza le finestre.
native_language_example: Before the storm arrived, we secured the windows.

additional_notes: Used to say someone stays or does something quietly, without talking or making noise. Often with verbs like essere/stare (to be/stay), rimanere (to remain), andare/uscire/entrare (to go out/in).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti in silenzio durante il film.
native_language_example: We stayed silent during the movie.

meaning: “in silence for the whole …” / “quietly for the entire …”
additional_notes: Used to say someone stays quiet for an entire period of time. It’s usually followed by a noun: per tutto il tempo (the whole time), per tutto il viaggio (the whole trip), per tutto il giorno (the whole day). You can also use it with feminine nouns by changing it to: in silenzio per tutta la … (e.g., per tutta la notte).
target_language_example: È rimasto in silenzio per tutto il viaggio.
native_language_example: He stayed quiet for the whole trip.

meaning: in sync; on the same wavelength; in harmony.
additional_notes: Used to say people understand each other well, work well together, or share the same feelings/ideas. Common with verbs like "essere" (essere in sintonia con...), "entrare" (entrare in sintonia con...) and "mettersi" (mettersi in sintonia con...). It can also be used more generally for being aligned with values or desires (e.g., "in sintonia con i desideri").
target_language_example: Dopo qualche incontro, siamo finalmente in sintonia.
native_language_example: After a few meetings, we're finally on the same wavelength.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that happens during sleep, often with verbs like "parlare in sonno" (to talk in your sleep), "russare in sonno" (to snore while asleep), or in more formal/medical contexts (e.g., "apnea in sonno"). It can also describe something happening without waking up (e.g., "è morto in sonno" = he died in his sleep).
target_language_example: A volte parlo in sonno.
native_language_example: Sometimes I talk in my sleep.

meaning: pending; unfinished (still to be dealt with).
additional_notes: Used for tasks, issues, questions, payments, or business that haven’t been resolved yet and are still “hanging.” Common collocations: "questioni in sospeso" (pending issues), "pagamento in sospeso" (payment pending), "lasciare qualcosa in sospeso" (to leave something unfinished).
target_language_example: Preferisco risolvere tutto oggi, senza lasciare nulla in sospeso.
native_language_example: I prefer to sort everything out today, without leaving anything unfinished.

additional_notes: Means being located at the beach ("at the beach") or going there (often after verbs of movement like "andare": "andare in spiaggia" = "to go to the beach").
target_language_example: Domani andiamo in spiaggia con gli amici.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to the beach with friends.

meaning: at the train station; to the train station.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement to mean “to the station” (andare/arrivare/portare qualcuno in stazione). With verbs describing being somewhere, it means “at the station” (essere/vedere qualcuno in stazione). In Italian, "stazione" usually refers to the train station unless specified (e.g., stazione degli autobus).
target_language_example: Puoi accompagnarmi in stazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take me to the train station, please?

meaning: 'in itself' / 'within oneself'; also 'not oneself' in set phrases.
additional_notes: Often means “in itself” (a quality contained within something): *aveva un certo fascino in sé* (“it had a certain charm in itself”). With people, it commonly appears in fixed expressions like **non essere in sé** (“to not be oneself; to be out of it”) and **tornare in sé** (“to come to; to regain consciousness / composure”). **sé** is the stressed form of “oneself” used after prepositions (like *in*).
target_language_example: Dopo lo shock, finalmente è tornato in sé.
native_language_example: After the shock, he finally came to.

meaning: in your pocket; in a pocket.
additional_notes: Used to say something is inside a pocket (your own or someone else’s), often with verbs like avere (to have), mettere/mettersi (to put), and tenere (to keep/carry). Common in everyday situations for carrying small objects. Also in the phrase "mettere le mani in tasca" (to put your hands in your pockets).
target_language_example: Ho il telefono in tasca, non in borsa.
native_language_example: I have my phone in my pocket, not in my bag.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dire/parlare/scrivere to say something is spoken or written in German. Often answers the question “In che lingua?” (“In what language?”).
target_language_example: Puoi scriverlo in tedesco, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write it in German, please?

meaning: on time; in time (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used for meeting a deadline or arriving by the required time: "arrivare in tempo" = to arrive on time / in time. Very common also with "fare in tempo" (often in the negative: "non ho fatto in tempo") meaning "to manage to (do something) in time / before it was too late".
target_language_example: Sbrigati, così arriviamo in tempo.
native_language_example: Hurry up, so we arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to specify the aspect or point of view you’re talking about (money, time, quality, business, etc.). Often followed by a noun: "in termini di prezzo/tempo/qualità". Common in neutral to formal speech and writing.
target_language_example: In termini di tempo, oggi non posso aiutarti.
native_language_example: In terms of time, I can't help you today.

meaning: in/on (your) head; (figuratively) on your mind / in your head.
additional_notes: Literal meaning: in or on someone’s head (body part), often after verbs like colpire in testa (hit on the head). Figurative meaning: what someone is thinking about or obsessed with (avere una cosa in testa = have one thing on your mind). With mettersi in testa (che...) it means “to get it into your head (that...) / to convince yourself.” In aggressive expressions like farti un buco in testa or una pallottola in testa, it refers to shooting someone in the head.
target_language_example: Mettiti in testa che non cambierò idea.
native_language_example: Get it into your head that I won’t change my mind.

meaning: in a circle; around and around.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement like correre/girare/volare to describe circular motion (e.g., “girare in tondo” = to go round in circles). Figuratively, it means making no progress in a discussion or situation (“stiamo girando in tondo”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo discusso per ore, ma alla fine stavamo ancora girando in tondo.
native_language_example: We talked for hours, but in the end we were still going around in circles.

meaning: in three days; within three days (time needed to finish).
additional_notes: Used with completed actions to say how long it took to finish something (duration needed), often with verbs like fare, completare, leggere. It answers “How long did it take?” or “Can you do it in X days?” For time spent doing something without focusing on completion, Italian often uses "per" (e.g., "per tre giorni" = for three days).
target_language_example: Abbiamo preparato tutto in tre giorni.
native_language_example: We prepared everything in three days.

meaning: by train; on the train (as a means of travel).
additional_notes: Used to say you travel using the train as your transportation method, especially with verbs like andare/venire/partire/arrivare (e.g., andare in treno = to go by train).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a Milano in treno.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to Milan by train.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens everywhere or in every case within a group of feminine plural nouns: in tutte le situazioni (in all situations), in tutte le parti (in all parts). With masculine plural nouns, use “in tutti i” (e.g., in tutti i casi).
target_language_example: Cerco di essere puntuale in tutte le riunioni.
native_language_example: I try to be punctual in all meetings.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens or is true everywhere in the world. Often follows verbs like vivere/viaggiare (to live/travel) or expressions like essere famoso (to be famous). Similar options: "nel mondo" = in the world (more general), "in giro per il mondo" = around the world.
target_language_example: Questo film è conosciuto in tutto il mondo.
native_language_example: This movie is known all over the world.

additional_notes: Used in two common ways: (1) with verbs/adjectives to mean “in everything / at everything” (Faccia del suo meglio in tutto. = “Do your best in everything.”); (2) with numbers/amounts to mean “in total / altogether” (Dieci libri in tutto. = “Ten books in total.”). Position is often at the end of the clause, especially for the “in total” meaning.
target_language_example: Abbiamo speso 50 euro in tutto.
native_language_example: We spent 50 euros in total.

meaning: in the office; at the office (at work).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically at their workplace/office or that something happens there. Very common with verbs like essere/stare (to be), andare/venire (to go/come), arrivare (to arrive), aspettare (to wait). Contrast: "a casa" (at home).
target_language_example: Oggi lavoro in ufficio fino alle sei.
native_language_example: Today I’m working in the office until six.

additional_notes: Used mostly in formal speech or writing to introduce a final argument, consideration, or item in a list (similar to “infine” or “da ultimo”). You may also see the longer form “in ultimo luogo”.
target_language_example: In ultimo, vorrei ringraziare tutti per la partecipazione.
native_language_example: Lastly, I’d like to thank everyone for taking part.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun. It usually means "in a/an," but with verbs of movement it can also be "into a/an" (for example, cadere in un pozzo = "fall into a well"). It is also common in time expressions like in un istante ("in an instant").
target_language_example: Viviamo in un piccolo appartamento.
native_language_example: We live in a small apartment.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or works/stays inside a hotel. "In" + "un" (a) + "albergo" (hotel). Often interchangeable with "in hotel" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Soggiorniamo in un albergo vicino al centro.
native_language_example: We’re staying in a hotel near the city center.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun after it: **in un altro** + *mondo / universo / posto / momento* (“in another world/universe/place/time”). It often implies something different from the current or usual one. Common set phrase: **in un modo o in un altro** = “one way or another.”
target_language_example: Scusami, ne parliamo in un altro momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, we'll talk about it another time.

additional_notes: Used to suggest changing the method or approach, or to ask someone to rephrase what they said (often with verbs like provare “to try” and dire “to say/tell”).
target_language_example: Puoi spiegarmelo in un altro modo, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me in another way, please?

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is in a different location than here/now, or to imagine a different situation (“somewhere else you’d be right, but not here”). Often answers “Dove?” (Where?) or contrasts with “qui” (here).
target_language_example: Non posso parlare qui: andiamo in un altro posto.
native_language_example: I can’t talk here: let’s go somewhere else.

meaning: in an apartment / in a flat.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like "abitare" or "vivere" to say where someone lives. "In" + a place (here, an apartment) expresses location. You can add details after it, e.g. "in un appartamento sopra un negozio" (in an apartment above a shop).
target_language_example: Vivo in un appartamento in centro.
native_language_example: I live in an apartment in the city center.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside a bar, or to describe meeting/going/working there. In Italian, "bar" often means a café where you get coffee and snacks, not only a place for alcohol. With motion verbs like "andare/entrare", "in un bar" can mean going/entering into a bar.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in un bar vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: Let’s meet in a bar near the station.

meaning: "in a way" / "in a certain sense" (partly; from one point of view).
additional_notes: Used to soften or qualify a statement: you agree only to some extent, or only from a particular perspective. Often followed by a contrast like "però/ma" (but).
target_language_example: In un certo senso ti capisco, ma non posso essere d'accordo su tutto.
native_language_example: In a way I understand you, but I can’t agree with everything.

meaning: in one day; within a day.
additional_notes: Used to say something happens or can be done in the time span of a single day (a 24-hour period). Often answers “How long does it take?” (Quanto ci vuole?). Can also be used in fixed expressions like “Roma non è stata costruita in un giorno” (“Rome wasn’t built in a day”).
target_language_example: Non posso finire questo lavoro in un giorno.
native_language_example: I can’t finish this work in one day.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is/was staying, working, or located at a hotel. Often appears with verbs like essere (to be), stare (to stay), soggiornare (to stay), and lavorare (to work). Note: in Italian, hotel is masculine, so you say un hotel (not *una*).
target_language_example: Abbiamo dormito in un hotel vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: We slept in a hotel near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (often injury or death) happened as the result of an accident. Very common with verbs like "morire/perdere la vita" (to die), "rimanere ucciso" (to be killed), and "ferirsi" (to get injured). You can specify the type: "in un incidente stradale" (in a road accident), "in un incidente di caccia" (in a hunting accident).
target_language_example: È rimasto ferito in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: He was injured in a road accident.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened as a result of a traffic accident (often serious, e.g., injuries or death). You’ll also see related phrases like "essere coinvolto in un incidente stradale" (to be involved in a traffic accident) and "morire/perdere la vita in un incidente stradale" (to die in a traffic accident).
target_language_example: Due persone sono rimaste ferite in un incidente stradale.
native_language_example: Two people were injured in a traffic accident.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the present situation, often to show surprise, disbelief, or criticism (especially in rhetorical questions or exclamations): “...now, of all times?” You can also say "in un momento come questo, ..." at the start of a sentence to emphasize the context.
target_language_example: In un momento come questo, dovremmo restare uniti.
native_language_example: At a time like this, we should stick together.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the world in general (Viviamo in un mondo complicato) or to create a more figurative/poetic idea. Very common in expressions like "in un mondo tutto suo" (= "in a world of his/her own"), meaning someone is mentally absorbed or not paying attention to what’s around them.
target_language_example: A volte mi sembra di vivere in un mondo completamente diverso.
native_language_example: Sometimes it feels like I’m living in a completely different world.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "stare", "restare", "rimanere" to say you are staying/living temporarily at a motel. "Un" is the masculine indefinite article (“a”).
target_language_example: Stiamo in un motel vicino all’aeroporto per una notte.
native_language_example: We’re staying in a motel near the airport for one night.

meaning: “in a (type of) shop/store for …” (e.g., donuts, groceries, hardware).
additional_notes: Use it to say you work/are inside a shop that specializes in something: “in un negozio di + noun”. Common examples: negozio di alimentari (grocery store), negozio di ferramenta (hardware store), negozio di musica (music store), negozio di dolciumi (candy shop). In the expression “come un bambino in un negozio di dolciumi”, it means “like a kid in a candy store” (very excited).
target_language_example: Lavora in un negozio di abbigliamento in centro.
native_language_example: She works in a clothing store downtown.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like essere portato/a (to be taken) or essere mandato/a (to be sent) to say someone is taken/sent to a psychiatric hospital for mental health care. The preposition “in” is used for being taken/sent into institutions/places. “Ospedale psichiatrico” is a formal term; in everyday language you may also hear “ospedale/clinica psichiatrica” or “reparto di psichiatria” (psychiatry ward).
target_language_example: Dopo la crisi, l'hanno portato in un ospedale psichiatrico.
native_language_example: After the crisis, they took him to a psychiatric hospital.

additional_notes: Used to talk about being/going/staying abroad. It’s often used with travel/life-experience questions like “Sei mai stato/a…?” (“Have you ever been…?”). Note agreement in questions: stato (male), stata (female), stati (mixed/plural male), state (plural female).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto in un paese straniero per un anno.
native_language_example: I lived in a foreign country for a year.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives. Often goes with verbs like abitare/vivere (“to live”) and can be expanded with extra details, e.g. con lui/lei (“with him/her”), da solo/a (“alone”).
target_language_example: Viviamo in un piccolo appartamento vicino al centro.
native_language_example: We live in a small apartment near downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives or grew up. Often followed by extra detail with "di..." (e.g., "un villaggio di pescatori" = a fishing village) or by a place name.
target_language_example: Sono nato in un piccolo villaggio vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I was born in a small village near the sea.

meaning: in a place; to a place.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of being/staying (è/sta/tenere) to mean “in a place,” and with movement verbs (andare/portare) to mean “to a place.” Often followed by an adjective: in un posto tranquillo/carino/fresco. In phrases like “in un posto migliore,” it can mean “in a better place” (sometimes said about someone who has died).
target_language_example: Mettilo in un posto sicuro.
native_language_example: Put it in a safe place.

meaning: in a place like this / in such a place.
additional_notes: Used to describe the kind of place you’re in, often followed by an adjective (e.g., così buio = so dark, così freddo = so cold, così bello = so beautiful, così rumoroso = so noisy). It can also be used on its own (“in un posto così”) when the context makes the description clear, often expressing surprise or emphasis.
target_language_example: Non pensavo di finire in un posto così lontano.
native_language_example: I didn’t think I’d end up in a place this far away.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located somewhere safe, or will be taken somewhere safe. Common with verbs like essere (to be) and portare (to take/bring).
target_language_example: Metti i documenti in un posto sicuro.
native_language_example: Put the documents in a safe place.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happens inside/at a restaurant. Very common with verbs like mangiare (to eat), lavorare (to work), andare (to go). You can change the article depending on the restaurant: in un ristorante (a restaurant), nel ristorante (in the/the specific restaurant), in un ristorante asiatico/costoso (in an Asian/expensive restaurant).
target_language_example: Ci vediamo in un ristorante vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: See you in a restaurant near the station.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una = “a/an”). With verbs of movement it often means “into a” (Ci ha portato in una palude! = “He took us into a swamp!”); with states/locations it means “in a” (Ero in una band. = “I was in a band.”).
target_language_example: Siamo entrati in una stanza molto piccola.
native_language_example: We went into a very small room.

meaning: in a bank (inside a bank / at a bank).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is physically inside a bank or works at a bank. Often follows verbs like lavorare (to work), entrare (to enter), andare (to go), aprire un conto (to open an account).
target_language_example: Vado in una banca per prelevare contanti.
native_language_example: I’m going to a bank to withdraw cash.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "in" + an indefinite article ("una") to say someone/something is inside a library or works there. If you mean a specific library, you’d usually say "in biblioteca" (without "una") or "nella biblioteca" (= in the/the one library).
target_language_example: Sto studiando in una biblioteca vicino a casa.
native_language_example: I’m studying in a library near my house.

meaning: in a house; into a house.
additional_notes: Uses "in" + indefinite article "una" (a/an) + "casa" (house/home). With verbs like "abitare" it means being/living in a house (location). With verbs of movement/change like "trasferirsi" it can mean moving into a (different) house. "Casa" can mean either "house" or "home" depending on context.
target_language_example: Vivono in una casa vicino al mare.
native_language_example: They live in a house near the sea.

meaning: in a city; living/being in an (unspecified) city.
additional_notes: Uses "in" + a place to say where someone lives, is, or grew up. "Una" is the indefinite article, so it often means an unspecified city (not naming which one). You can add adjectives or details: "in una città grande" (in a big city), "in una città vicino a Boston" (in a city near Boston).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto per anni in una città molto rumorosa.
native_language_example: I lived for years in a very noisy city.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives or where something happens. "In" is used with most cities in Italian (e.g., "abito in una grande città").
target_language_example: Lavoro in una grande città, ma vivo in periferia.
native_language_example: I work in a big city, but I live in the suburbs.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is inside a mosque (often for praying) or going there; with verbs of movement like "andare" it implies destination (going to a mosque).
target_language_example: Domani andiamo in una moschea per visitarla.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to a mosque to visit it.

meaning: in a small town (in a small city).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives/lived or grew up. Italian often uses "città" even when English would say "town." You can change the adjective or size: "in una grande città" (in a big city), "in una città tranquilla" (in a quiet town/city).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto per anni in una piccola città vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I lived for years in a small town near the sea.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of going/being to say you went/are inside a place. "In" + "una" = "in a"; "pizzeria" is a pizza place, and "italiana" (feminine singular) agrees with "pizzeria". Often used with "andare" (to go) and "essere" (to be).
target_language_example: Stasera andiamo in una pizzeria italiana vicino a casa.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re going to an Italian pizzeria near home.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (to be) to say someone is/was in a relationship where the partners live far apart (often in different cities or countries). You’ll often hear it in questions like “Sei mai stata…?” (“Have you ever been…?”).
target_language_example: Siamo stati in una relazione a distanza per due anni.
native_language_example: We were in a long-distance relationship for two years.

additional_notes: Used to say something is placed inside a box. Often follows verbs like mettere (to put), mettere via (to put away), or tenere (to keep).
target_language_example: Metti questi libri in una scatola, per favore.
native_language_example: Put these books in a box, please.

meaning: in a situation; in a (particular) set of circumstances.
additional_notes: Used with an adjective or description to explain the circumstances someone is in: "in una situazione difficile/delicata/impossibile". With verbs like "trovarsi" (to find oneself), "mettere" (to put), "finire" (to end up), it describes being placed in or ending up in certain circumstances.
target_language_example: Non voglio metterti in una situazione imbarazzante.
native_language_example: I don't want to put you in an embarrassing situation.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is located or happens inside a zoo. Italian uses "uno" (not "un") before words that start with z (zoo), s+consonant, ps, gn, x, etc.: "in uno zoo".
target_language_example: I bambini si divertono in uno zoo.
native_language_example: The kids have fun at a zoo.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "andare" (to go) to talk about going on vacation: "andare in vacanza". It can also describe your current status: "Sono in vacanza" = "I’m on vacation." You can add the destination with "a" (city) or "in" (country/region): "in vacanza a Roma", "in vacanza in Italia".
target_language_example: Siamo in vacanza in Italia per due settimane.
native_language_example: We’re on vacation in Italy for two weeks.

additional_notes: Used to ask or say that something is being sold (available to buy). Common in shops and on signs/ads. Often with essere: "È in vendita?" / "Non è in vendita."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, questo modello non è in vendita oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, this model isn’t for sale today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or emphasize what you really think or what is truly the case, often like English “actually” or “to be honest.” It can go at the beginning of a sentence (“In verità, …”) or as an aside at the end (“, in verità.”). In everyday speech, Italians often use alternatives like “in realtà” or “a dire il vero.”
target_language_example: In verità, non mi va di uscire stasera.
native_language_example: Actually, I don’t feel like going out tonight.

meaning: in the process of; on the way to (doing something).
additional_notes: Used with a noun or an infinitive to say something is underway or being completed soon. Common with states/changes (e.g., repairs, approval, completion): “in via di approvazione” (being approved), “in via di riparazione” (being repaired), “in via di definizione” (being finalized). Often translated as “under way” / “in the process of” rather than word-for-word.
target_language_example: Il progetto è in via di approvazione.
native_language_example: The project is in the process of being approved.

additional_notes: Used after a noun (often with "essere") to describe a species, language, or other thing that is disappearing and may die out soon. Common pattern: "una specie in via di estinzione" / "X è in via di estinzione".
target_language_example: Questo animale è in via di estinzione e va protetto.
native_language_example: This animal is endangered and must be protected.

meaning: traveling; on a trip; on the way (while traveling).
additional_notes: Used mainly with essere to say someone is currently traveling or en route: "Sono/è/siamo in viaggio." You can also combine it with verbs like "andare in viaggio" (to go on a trip) or "mettersi in viaggio" (to set off/start a journey).
target_language_example: Scusa se rispondo tardi: sono in viaggio.
native_language_example: Sorry for the late reply: I’m traveling.

meaning: in sight; in view; (figuratively) coming soon / likely to happen.
additional_notes: Used for something you can see (“Bersaglio in vista.” = “Target in sight.”) and also figuratively for something approaching or expected (“Guai in vista.” = “Trouble ahead.” / “La fine è in vista.” = “The end is in sight.”). With verbs like “tenere/mettere”, it means “to keep/put something in view/visible” (“Non tenerlo in vista.” = “Don’t keep it in sight.”).
target_language_example: Con le nuvole nere, un temporale è in vista.
native_language_example: With the dark clouds, a storm is on the way.

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like "tenere" (to keep) or "rimanere" (to remain) to mean "alive" (e.g., "tenere in vita" = keep alive, "rimasto in vita" = still alive). It can also appear in the fixed expression "in vita sua" meaning "in his/her life" = "ever" (e.g., "non ha mai... in vita sua" = has never... in his/her life).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo tenerlo in vita finché arriva l’ambulanza.
native_language_example: We have to keep him alive until the ambulance arrives.
