additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "miei" (plural of "mio"). It often appears with an article when it’s part of a noun phrase ("i miei amici" = "my friends"), but the article is commonly omitted after forms of "essere" ("Sono miei amici" = "They are my friends").
target_language_example: Questi sono miei amici.
native_language_example: These are my friends.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about your friends. "I miei amici" = "my (male or mixed-group) friends"; "sono" is the 3rd person plural of "essere" (to be). For a group of only female friends, say "le mie amiche sono..." (e.g., "Le mie amiche sono simpatiche").
target_language_example: I miei amici sono di Milano.
native_language_example: My friends are from Milan.

additional_notes: In Italian, "capelli" is usually plural even when English uses the uncountable "hair" ("i miei capelli" = "my hair"). You’ll often see it with the article: "i miei capelli". In some contexts it can also be used figuratively to complain someone is too close/annoying (e.g., "Stai sui miei capelli!" ≈ "You’re in my hair!").
target_language_example: Non toccare i miei capelli!
native_language_example: Don’t touch my hair!

additional_notes: Usually you’ll see it with the article: **i miei compiti** (“my homework/my tasks”). **Compiti** is plural; it commonly means **homework** (school assignments), but can also mean **tasks/duties** depending on context.
target_language_example: Devo finire i miei compiti prima di uscire.
native_language_example: I have to finish my homework before going out.

additional_notes: "Miei" is the masculine plural form of the possessive "my". Use "i miei figli" for "my children/sons" (or "my kids" in a neutral sense). If you mean "my daughters," say "le mie figlie".
target_language_example: Oggi porto i miei figli al parco.
native_language_example: Today I'm taking my children to the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your own mother and father. It’s plural masculine because it refers to a mixed group (mother + father). Common with prepositions: "con/coi miei genitori" = "with my parents", "dai miei genitori" = "from my parents", "dei miei genitori" = "of my parents".
target_language_example: Nel weekend vado a trovare i miei genitori.
native_language_example: On the weekend I go visit my parents.

additional_notes: Used at the start of a sentence to say something your parents have done. It’s typically followed by a past participle in the passato prossimo (e.g., mi hanno chiamato = they called me). "Mi" means "to me" and can often be translated as "me" in English.
target_language_example: I miei genitori mi hanno chiamato ieri sera.
native_language_example: My parents called me last night.

additional_notes: Used to introduce information about your parents (an adjective, a job, where they are from, etc.). In a full sentence you usually say **I miei genitori sono...** (with the article **i**). The verb **sono** is 3rd-person plural of *essere* (“to be”), so what follows is typically plural (e.g., **simpatici**, **insegnanti**, **americani**).
target_language_example: I miei genitori sono insegnanti.
native_language_example: My parents are teachers.

additional_notes: "Miei" is the plural form of "mio" (my) and agrees with the plural noun "libri" (books). It’s usually used with a possessive + noun, often with an article in Italian: "i miei libri" = "my books" (literally "the my books").
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato i miei libri a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my books at home.

meaning: “my (own) eyes” (used to stress you personally saw something).
additional_notes: Most often used in the phrase **con i miei occhi** (“with my own eyes”) to emphasize direct, first-hand experience. Italian often adds **proprio** for extra emphasis: **con i miei propri occhi**. In everyday speech you may hear **coi miei occhi** (short for **con i miei occhi**).
target_language_example: Non ci credo finché non lo vedo con i miei occhi.
native_language_example: I won’t believe it until I see it with my own eyes.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the glasses you wear. "Occhiali" is plural in Italian, so you say "i miei occhiali" (literally "the my glasses"). You can also use it for sunglasses: "i miei occhiali da sole".
target_language_example: Non trovo i miei occhiali.
native_language_example: I can't find my glasses.

additional_notes: Means the speaker’s thoughts/ideas. It’s made of the possessive adjective **miei** (“my”, masculine plural) + **pensieri** (“thoughts”, masculine plural). Common in phrases like **nei miei pensieri** (“in my thoughts”) or to express sympathy/support: **Sei nei miei pensieri** (“You’re in my thoughts”).
target_language_example: Sei sempre nei miei pensieri.
native_language_example: You’re always in my thoughts.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your own emotions, often in personal, intimate, or relationship contexts. Very common with verbs like parlare di (to talk about) and in the expression giocare con i miei sentimenti (“to play with my feelings,” i.e., to toy with my emotions or lead me on). Note that it usually appears as dei miei sentimenti after prepositions like di (e.g., parlare dei miei sentimenti).
target_language_example: Preferirei non parlare dei miei sentimenti.
native_language_example: I’d rather not talk about my feelings.

meaning: "my money" (the money that belongs to me).
additional_notes: "Miei" is the plural form of "mio" (my) and agrees with the plural noun "soldi". Often used to stress ownership or responsibility: "con i miei soldi" = "with my own money" (not someone else’s). "Soldi" is commonly used for money in general (cash/finances).
target_language_example: Non voglio spendere i miei soldi per questo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to spend my money on this.

additional_notes: Plural masculine: miei (my) agrees with vestiti (clothes/outfits). Often you’ll hear it with the article: i miei vestiti (“my clothes”). Used when talking about what you’re wearing, packing, washing, or looking for.
target_language_example: Non trovo i miei vestiti.
native_language_example: I can’t find my clothes.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to indicate a very large number (plural). Often followed by a plural noun: “migliaia di dollari/uomini/avventure”. You can also intensify it as “migliaia e migliaia di” (“thousands and thousands of”).
target_language_example: Ci sono migliaia di persone in piazza.
native_language_example: There are thousands of people in the square.

additional_notes: Used before a noun to say you want to get better at something you possess/your own ability, very often a language: "migliorare il mio italiano/francese/inglese". The possessive changes with the person (il mio, il tuo, il suo, il nostro, il vostro, il loro) and must agree with the noun’s gender/number (e.g., "la mia pronuncia", "i miei voti").
target_language_example: Sto cercando di migliorare il mio italiano prima dell’esame.
native_language_example: I’m trying to improve my Italian before the exam.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a girl/woman who is your closest friend. It agrees with the gender of the friend: migliore amico (male), migliore amica (female). Common with possessives: la mia/tuа/sua migliore amica; la vostra migliore amica (your, plural/formal).
target_language_example: Laura è la mia migliore amica da anni.
native_language_example: Laura has been my best friend for years.

additional_notes: Used for a person’s closest friend. With articles/possessives you’ll often see it as il mio/tuo/suo migliore amico. For a female best friend, say migliore amica.
target_language_example: Marco è il mio migliore amico da quando eravamo bambini.
native_language_example: Marco has been my best friend since we were kids.

meaning: “better than mine” (referring to something feminine singular, e.g., vista, macchina, idea).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons where the omitted noun is feminine singular: migliore = “better,” della = “than the/of the” (di + la), mia = “mine” (fem. sing.). Often the noun is stated once and then implied: “una vista migliore della mia” = “a view better than mine.” If what’s “mine” is masculine or plural, it changes: migliore del mio (masc. sing.), migliore dei miei (masc. pl.), migliore delle mie (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Hai una vista migliore della mia.
native_language_example: You have a view better than mine.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone (or something) to yourself. Common patterns: "essere migliore di me" (to be better than me), "qualcuno migliore di me" (someone better than me), and you can add an area with "in + noun" (e.g., "in matematica", "in questo"). In more formal Italian you may hear "migliore di quanto lo sia io" (better than I am), but "migliore di me" is very common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sei migliore di me a cucinare.
native_language_example: You're better than me at cooking.

additional_notes: Used to state an amount of money in dollars. You’ll often see it after prepositions like per (“for”) when giving a price, or da/di (“of/from”) when describing a compensation or amount received. The structure is number + milione + di + currency (e.g., un milione di euro / un milione di dollari).
target_language_example: Quel contratto vale un milione di dollari.
native_language_example: That contract is worth a million dollars.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate a very large quantity (e.g., "milioni di persone"). You can also use it with money amounts: "milioni di euro" = "millions of euros". With specific numbers, Italian often says the number + "milioni" + the currency: "dieci milioni di yen" = "ten million yen".
target_language_example: Ci sono milioni di turisti in città d’estate.
native_language_example: There are millions of tourists in the city in summer.

additional_notes: Used to talk about very large amounts of money measured in dollars. It’s a noun phrase: "milioni" (millions) + "di" (of) + "dollari" (dollars). Often used after a number (e.g., "cinque milioni di dollari") or in expressions like "milioni di dollari in gioco" (millions of dollars at stake).
target_language_example: Non spenderò milioni di dollari per una macchina.
native_language_example: I won’t spend millions of dollars on a car.

additional_notes: Used to express a very large number of people. Often followed by a relative clause ("milioni di persone che...") or a verb ("milioni di persone muoiono..."). You can specify an exact figure too ("quattro/nove milioni di persone"), and it’s also common to say "milioni di" + noun in general.
target_language_example: Milioni di persone usano i mezzi pubblici ogni giorno.
native_language_example: Millions of people use public transportation every day.

additional_notes: Used to talk about threats to kill someone. It often appears in the plural ("delle minacce di morte") and commonly goes with verbs like "ricevere" (to receive) or "avere" (to have): "Ho ricevuto delle minacce di morte" = "I received death threats."
target_language_example: Ha denunciato tutto perché ha ricevuto minacce di morte.
native_language_example: He reported everything because he received death threats.

additional_notes: Used to say how long ago something happened. Put the number (or an approximate amount like circa) before it: "tre minuti fa" = "three minutes ago". Very common with "circa" (about) and informal "tipo" (like/around).
target_language_example: Ti ho scritto cinque minuti fa.
native_language_example: I texted you five minutes ago.

meaning: “a minute, please” (asking someone to wait briefly).
additional_notes: Used as a polite request to ask for a short pause or a moment of someone’s time. Very common with “solo/un attimo”: “Solo un minuto, per favore.” You can add “mi scusi” for extra politeness, especially with strangers or in formal situations.
target_language_example: Aspetti un minuto, per favore: arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait a minute, please: I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used to talk about help that you provide. Often appears in the set phrase “venire in mio aiuto” = “to come to my aid” (literally “to come in my help”).
target_language_example: Grazie per essere venuto in mio aiuto.
native_language_example: Thanks for coming to my aid.

additional_notes: Means a male friend who belongs to the speaker's circle. mio is the masculine singular possessive and agrees with amico. In many sentences Italian often uses an article with possessives (for example il mio amico), while un mio amico means 'a friend of mine'. As a predicate, the article is often omitted: Marco è mio amico.
target_language_example: Marco è mio amico da molti anni.
native_language_example: Marco has been my friend for many years.

additional_notes: Means “my dog.” Often appears with an article: “il mio cane” (my dog) as the subject/object, and with prepositions: “del mio cane” (of my dog), “col mio cane” (with my dog). In everyday Italian you’ll usually hear/see “il mio cane” more than just “mio cane.”
target_language_example: Non posso uscire: devo portare fuori il mio cane.
native_language_example: I can't go out: I have to take my dog out.

additional_notes: Used as a form of address (often with a comma: “..., mio caro.”). It can sound affectionate, polite, or sometimes slightly ironic/condescending depending on tone and context. Common variants: “mia cara” (to a woman), “miei cari” (plural), “cara/caro” on its own.
target_language_example: Non è così semplice, mio caro.
native_language_example: It’s not that simple, my dear.

additional_notes: Usually you’ll hear it as **il mio cavallo** (“my horse”), with the definite article **il**. **Mio** agrees with the noun: **il mio cavallo** (masc. sing.), **i miei cavalli** (plural).
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio cavallo?
native_language_example: Where is my horse?

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (è/era/sarà) to say when your birthday is (e.g., "È il mio compleanno" = "It’s my birthday"). Often used with time expressions like "tra..."/"fra..." (in...) and "quanti giorni mancano..." (how many days are left...).
target_language_example: Oggi è il mio compleanno: vieni a cena con me?
native_language_example: Today is my birthday: are you coming to dinner with me?

additional_notes: "Mio" is the possessive adjective "my" and agrees with the noun: "il mio computer" (my computer). Often used with prepositions: "sul mio computer" (onto/on my computer), "nel mio computer" (in my computer), "di fronte al mio computer" (in front of my computer).
target_language_example: Non toccare il mio computer, per favore.
native_language_example: Don't touch my computer, please.

additional_notes: "Mio" means "my" (used with masculine singular nouns). "Computer portatile" is the common way to say "laptop" in Italian; literally it’s "portable computer." Often you’ll also hear just "il portatile" (the laptop) when the context is clear.
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio computer portatile a casa.
native_language_example: I forgot my laptop at home.

meaning: "my computer is ..." (start of a sentence describing your computer).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment made of: **mio** (“my”) + **computer** + **è** (“is”). You typically use it to introduce an adjective or description: *Mio computer è lento* (“My computer is slow”). Note: in standard Italian you often include the article with family/possession nouns, so you may also hear **Il mio computer è ...**.
target_language_example: Il mio computer è molto lento oggi.
native_language_example: My computer is very slow today.

additional_notes: Used when you’re giving your personal suggestion or opinion. Often appears in phrases like “Il mio consiglio è…” (My advice is…) or “Ti do un consiglio” (I’ll give you some advice). Note: “consiglio” can also mean “council/board” in other contexts (e.g., consiglio comunale), but “mio consiglio” is normally about advice.
target_language_example: Il mio consiglio è di prenotare in anticipo.
native_language_example: My advice is to book in advance.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your male cousin. In Italian, with singular family members you usually don’t use the article: "mio cugino" (not *"il mio cugino"*). For a female cousin: "mia cugina". For plural you typically use the article: "i miei cugini / le mie cugine".
target_language_example: Mio cugino vive a Milano.
native_language_example: My cousin lives in Milan.

additional_notes: Literal meaning is the physical heart, but very often it’s used in emotional/poetic expressions. Common patterns: “dal profondo del mio cuore” = “from the bottom of my heart” (strong, sincere feeling), and “nel mio cuore” / “è nel mio cuore” = “in my heart” (you hold someone/something dear). “La chiave del mio cuore” (“the key to my heart”) is a romantic, poetic metaphor.
target_language_example: Grazie di tutto, dal profondo del mio cuore.
native_language_example: Thank you for everything, from the bottom of my heart.

additional_notes: Means “my son.” It’s the singular masculine form: mio (my) + figlio (son). In Italian, possessives usually agree with the noun (mio/mia/miei/mie). Often used without an article with close family members in the singular (e.g., “mio figlio,” not usually “il mio figlio”).
target_language_example: Mio figlio ha cinque anni.
native_language_example: My son is five years old.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your son with the verb essere (“to be”). Italian often omits the subject pronoun (io/tu/lui…), so starting with “Mio figlio è…” is very common. It can be followed by an adjective (stanco, alto), a noun phrase, or a place/status expression (e.g., “alle superiori”).
target_language_example: Mio figlio è a casa oggi.
native_language_example: My son is at home today.

additional_notes: A basic possessive phrase: mio + fratello. In Italian, singular close family nouns usually take no article with possessives, so you say mio fratello, not il mio fratello.
target_language_example: Mio fratello studia a Roma.
native_language_example: My brother studies in Rome.

additional_notes: Used to identify your brother who is younger than you. In Italian, possessives (mio, tuo, suo, etc.) usually take the definite article (il mio fratello), but with singular family members the article is often omitted: "mio fratello" / "mio fratello minore" (without "il"). "Fratello minore" can also be used without a possessive to mean "younger brother" in general.
target_language_example: Mio fratello minore ha dodici anni.
native_language_example: My younger brother is twelve.

additional_notes:
Used to describe your brother or give information about him. After è (“is”), you can use:
- an adjective: Mio fratello è basso. (“My brother is short.”)
- a job/noun; often with an article (un/uno/una): Mio fratello è un dottore. (“My brother is a doctor.”) Some professions are commonly used without an article: Mio fratello è insegnante. (“My brother is a teacher.”)
- a phrase like appena + past participle to mean “has just …”: Mio fratello è appena tornato. (“My brother has just come back.”)
target_language_example: Mio fratello è molto gentile.
native_language_example: My brother is very kind.

additional_notes: Means “my cat.” With a masculine singular noun like gatto, mio becomes il mio (e.g., il mio gatto). You’ll often see it after prepositions too: al mio gatto (“to my cat”), con il mio gatto (“with my cat”), per il mio gatto (“for my cat”).
target_language_example: Il mio gatto dorme sempre sul divano.
native_language_example: My cat always sleeps on the sofa.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective mio (“my”) before the noun insegnante (“teacher”). Insegnante can refer to a male or female teacher (the article may change: il mio insegnante / la mia insegnante). Often used when talking about a specific teacher you have (at school, a course, etc.).
target_language_example: Domani parlerò con il mio insegnante di italiano.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll talk with my Italian teacher.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a male teacher (or a teacher referred to with masculine grammar). If the teacher is female, you often say "la mia insegnante di francese". "di francese" means "of French" (i.e., who teaches French). You can also say "il mio professore di francese" (more common for middle/high school, university).
target_language_example: Domani ho un colloquio con il mio insegnante di francese.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a meeting with my French teacher.

additional_notes: "Mio" is the possessive adjective "my" and "lavoro" means "job/work." Used to talk about your employment, tasks, or school/work assignments depending on context. Often appears with the article: "il mio lavoro" (my job/my work).
target_language_example: Domani devo finire il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have to finish my work.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: the adjective mio (“my”) agrees with the noun. With masculine singular nouns like libro, use mio. Often used with the definite article: il mio libro (“my book”).
target_language_example: Dov'è il mio libro?
native_language_example: Where is my book?

additional_notes: Means “my husband.” In Italian, close family members (like marito, moglie, madre, padre) are often used without an article in the singular when a possessive is used: “mio marito” (not usually *il mio marito* in neutral contexts).
target_language_example: Mio marito lavora in banca.
native_language_example: My husband works at a bank.

meaning: "my husband is" (used to describe or identify your husband).
additional_notes: "Mio" agrees with "marito" (masculine singular). Use "è" (from *essere*, "to be") to give information like nationality, job, health condition, location, etc. Often followed by an adjective (canadese, disoccupato), a noun with an article (un dottore), or a place with a preposition (a Singapore, in prigione).
target_language_example: Scusi, mio marito è allergico alle arachidi.
native_language_example: Excuse me, my husband is allergic to peanuts.

meaning: 'my best to' (usually in the phrase 'fare del mio meglio per' = 'to do my best to').
additional_notes: On its own, 'mio meglio per' sounds incomplete in Italian. You’ll most often hear it as part of: 'fare del mio meglio per + infinitive' (e.g., 'fare del mio meglio per aiutarti' = 'to do my best to help you'). You can also say 'dare il mio meglio' = 'to give my best'.
target_language_example: Farò del mio meglio per arrivare in orario.
native_language_example: I’ll do my best to arrive on time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to your closest friend (a man/boy). In a full sentence you’ll often add the article: "il mio migliore amico". For a female best friend, say "la mia migliore amica".
target_language_example: Luca è il mio migliore amico.
native_language_example: Luca is my best friend.

additional_notes: Use this to introduce or describe your best (male) friend. “mio” and “migliore amico” agree with a masculine singular noun. For a female friend: “la mia migliore amica è …”. You can follow it with a name, a noun, or an adjective.
target_language_example: Il mio migliore amico è Marco.
native_language_example: My best friend is Marco.

meaning: “my nephew” or “my grandson” (Italian *nipote* can mean either).
additional_notes: Italian uses *nipote* for both a nephew/niece and a grandchild (grandson/granddaughter). Context usually makes it clear; if needed, you can specify *mio nipote (figlio di mio fratello/sorella)* = my nephew, or *mio nipote (figlio di mio figlio/figlia)* = my grandson.
target_language_example: Mio nipote ha dieci anni.
native_language_example: My nephew/grandson is ten years old.

additional_notes: Means “my name.” In Italian, the possessive adjective agrees with the noun, so with masculine singular nome you say mio (not *mia*). Often used when talking about signing or registering something “under my name” (sotto il mio nome), or when asking someone not to mention you (non fare il mio nome = “don’t say/mention my name”).
target_language_example: Puoi scrivere il mio nome qui, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you write my name here, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce yourself and say your name. In Italian you’ll often hear and say the full phrase “Il mio nome è…”, but in casual speech “mio nome è…” can be used too. More common alternatives are “Mi chiamo …” and “Sono …”.
target_language_example: Ciao, il mio nome è Luca.
native_language_example: Hi, my name is Luca.

additional_notes: Used to talk about your grandfather. In Italian, family members are often used without an article after a possessive (mio nonno, mia nonna, mio padre). The adjective agrees with the noun: mio nonno (masc.), mia nonna (fem.).
target_language_example: Mio nonno vive in campagna e cucina benissimo.
native_language_example: My grandfather lives in the countryside and cooks really well.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a personal goal or purpose, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., "il mio obiettivo è imparare...") or by a noun phrase (e.g., "il mio obiettivo è la qualità"). In natural Italian, you’ll very often include the article: "il mio obiettivo è...". You can change the possessive: "il tuo obiettivo è..." (your goal is), "il nostro obiettivo è..." (our goal is).
target_language_example: Il mio obiettivo è migliorare il mio italiano.
native_language_example: My goal is to improve my Italian.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: mio = “my” (masculine singular), ombrello = “umbrella.” Used when asking where it is, whether someone took it, or inviting someone to stand under it ("sotto il mio ombrello").
target_language_example: Scusa, dov'è finito il mio ombrello?
native_language_example: Sorry, where did my umbrella go?

additional_notes: Most often means “my watch” (a wristwatch). Italian "orologio" can also mean a clock depending on context (e.g., "orologio da parete" = wall clock). "mio" agrees with the masculine singular noun "orologio". In questions like "È il mio orologio?" it means “Is it my watch?”
target_language_example: Non trovo il mio orologio: l’hai visto?
native_language_example: I can’t find my watch—have you seen it?

additional_notes: Used to refer to your father. In Italian, singular close family members usually take a possessive without the article: mio padre, mia madre, mio fratello.
target_language_example: Mio padre lavora in ospedale.
native_language_example: My father works in a hospital.

additional_notes: Used to refer to both of your parents together. In Italian you normally repeat the possessive and article with each family member: "mio padre" and "mia madre" (not *mio padre e madre*). Often interchangeable with "i miei genitori" (my parents), which is shorter and more common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Vado a trovare mio padre e mia madre questo fine settimana.
native_language_example: I’m going to visit my father and mother this weekend.

additional_notes: "Era" is the imperfect past tense of *essere* (to be). Use it to describe who/what someone was, their nationality/job, where they were, or ongoing states/habits in the past (e.g., *era occupato*, *era sempre arrabbiato*). Often followed by an adjective (*era algerino*), a noun with an article (*era un insegnante*), or a place with *a/in* (*era a caccia*, *era in Svezia*).
target_language_example: Quando ero piccolo, mio padre era molto paziente.
native_language_example: When I was little, my father was very patient.

mio padre era ancora a casa quando

target_language_multi_word_term: mio padre era ancora a casa quando
meaning: “my father was still at home when …”
additional_notes: Used to set up a time relationship: the situation “era ancora a casa” (imperfect = ongoing state in the past) was happening when another past event occurred. Often followed by a completed action in the past (e.g., passato prossimo: “quando sono uscito/a”, “quando me ne sono andato/a”). “Ancora” = “still”; “a casa” = “at home.” The verb after “quando” changes depending on the speaker’s gender in some forms: “andato/andata”, “partito/partita.”
target_language_example: Mio padre era ancora a casa quando ho chiamato.
native_language_example: My father was still at home when I called.

meaning: "my father has" (used to talk about something your father did, has done, or has been doing).
additional_notes: "Mio padre" means "my father." "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" (to have) and is very often used as the auxiliary verb to form the passato prossimo (a common past tense) with a past participle: "mio padre ha + [past participle]" (e.g., ha abitato, ha giocato, ha insistito). With some verbs (often movement/change of state), Italian uses "essere" instead of "avere" ("mio padre è andato").
target_language_example: Mio padre ha lavorato tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: My father worked all day.

additional_notes: Used when the subject is "mio padre" (my father) and "mi" is an unstressed object pronoun placed before the verb. With many verbs it means "to me/for me" (indirect object), e.g., "Mio padre mi comprò..." = "My father bought me...". With some verbs it can be the direct object, e.g., "Mio padre mi odiava" = "My father hated me".
target_language_example: Mio padre mi ha chiamato ieri sera.
native_language_example: My father called me last night.

meaning: "My father has" / "my father (did)" + "to me" (introduces an action done by my father to me).
additional_notes: This is the start of a sentence in the passato prossimo (present perfect / simple past in English): "mio padre" = "my father", "mi" = "me" (object pronoun), "ha" = "has" (auxiliary for the past tense). It must be followed by a past participle (e.g., avvertito/a = warned, portato/a = took/brought, proibito = forbade). With "mi" meaning "me" as a direct object, the past participle can agree with the speaker: "mi ha avvertito" (male speaker) / "mi ha avvertita" (female speaker); similarly "mi ha portato" / "mi ha portata".
target_language_example: Mio padre mi ha chiamata ieri.
native_language_example: My father called me yesterday.

meaning: “my father bought me … / has bought me …” (i.e., bought something for me).
additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo of comprare (“to buy”): ha comprato = “bought/has bought.” The pronoun mi means “to me/for me” (an indirect object): he bought something for me, not “he bought me.” You normally add the thing that was bought right after this phrase (e.g., un computer, dei libri).
target_language_example: Mio padre mi ha comprato un regalo per il compleanno.
native_language_example: My father bought me a birthday present.

meaning: “my father doesn’t / isn’t / will not …” (introduces a negative statement about your father).
additional_notes: “Mio padre” means “my father.” In Italian negation, “non” goes directly before the verb: "Mio padre non mangia" (doesn’t eat), "Mio padre non è" (isn’t), "Mio padre non sarà" (won’t be). Often followed by extra negatives like “mai” (never): “non … mai”.
target_language_example: Mio padre non vuole uscire stasera.
native_language_example: My father doesn’t want to go out tonight.

additional_notes: Used to describe your dad (his personality, feelings, job, etc.). Often followed by an adjective or a noun phrase (e.g., "mio padre è gentile", "mio padre è medico").
target_language_example: Mio padre è molto paziente.
native_language_example: My father is very patient.

additional_notes: Uses the passato prossimo with essere (è morto). In Italian, this form can mean either "died" (at a specific time in the past, often with a time expression like due anni fa/quando...) or simply "is dead" (stating the fact).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, mio padre è morto l'anno scorso.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, my father died last year.

meaning: “my country” or “my hometown/home region” (depending on context).
additional_notes: Paese can mean “country” (a nation) or “town/village” (your place of origin). Context usually makes it clear: “La Francia è il mio paese” = “France is my country,” while “una specialità del mio paese” can mean a specialty from your hometown/region. In patriotic or political statements like “quello che è meglio per il mio paese,” it typically means “my country.”
target_language_example: Mi manca il mio paese quando sono all’estero.
native_language_example: I miss my country when I’m abroad.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a plan that belongs to you or that you came up with. Often appears with an article ("il mio piano" = "my plan"), and you can add an adjective for more detail ("il mio piano segreto" = "my secret plan").
target_language_example: Non cambierò il mio piano, anche se è difficile.
native_language_example: I won’t change my plan, even if it’s difficult.

additional_notes: Used for the specific place where you sit/stand (e.g., a seat) or more generally your position/role (even in a job). Very common with the verb "prendere" ("prendere il mio posto" = "take my place").
target_language_example: Scusi, credo che lei sia nel mio posto.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I think you're in my seat.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun: *il mio primo giorno* (“my first day”), *il mio primo film* (“my first movie/film”). It changes with gender/number: *mia prima* (feminine singular), *miei primi* (masculine plural), *mie prime* (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Questo è il mio primo viaggio in Italia.
native_language_example: This is my first trip to Italy.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the first person you loved romantically. It can also be used more loosely or figuratively for a first big passion (e.g., a hobby), but most often it refers to a person. You can change the possessive: "il tuo primo amore" (your first love), "il suo primo amore" (his/her first love).
target_language_example: Lei è stata il mio primo amore.
native_language_example: She was my first love.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase: mio = “my”, primo = “first”, bacio = “kiss”. Italian often puts a possessive (mio) before the noun, while the adjective (primo) can appear before the noun for emphasis or in common phrases like this. You can change the possessive: il tuo primo bacio (“your first kiss”), il suo primo bacio (“his/her first kiss”).
target_language_example: Ricordo ancora il mio primo bacio.
native_language_example: I still remember my first kiss.

additional_notes: Uses the possessive adjective "mio" before "telefono" to show ownership. Context tells you which phone: often a mobile phone, but you can specify (e.g., "telefono di casa" = home phone).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il mio telefono in macchina.
native_language_example: I forgot my phone in the car.

additional_notes: Possessive phrase: "mio" (my) + "ufficio" (office). Often used to say where your office is or to talk about your workspace/room at work. You can change the owner: "il tuo ufficio" (your office), "il suo ufficio" (his/her office). Usually with the article: "il mio ufficio".
target_language_example: Puoi venire nel mio ufficio alle tre?
native_language_example: Can you come to my office at three?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a friend you’ve known for a long time (not necessarily an elderly friend). When addressing someone directly, Italian often drops the article: “Mio vecchio amico, come stai?” In narration you’ll often see it with an article: “il mio vecchio amico.”
target_language_example: Sono contento di rivederti, mio vecchio amico.
native_language_example: I’m happy to see you again, my old friend.

additional_notes: Means your uncle (your parent’s brother, or an uncle by marriage). In Italian, the possessive agrees with the noun: "mio" (masculine singular) + "zio". With family members in the singular, Italian often drops the definite article: "mio zio" (not *"il mio zio"*).
target_language_example: Domani vado a trovare mio zio.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to visit my uncle.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase + time expression. "mio zio" = "my uncle"; "la scorsa settimana" = "last week". In a full sentence, you often place the time expression at the end: "Ho visto mio zio la scorsa settimana" (I saw my uncle last week). You can also move it to the beginning for emphasis: "La scorsa settimana ho visto mio zio."
target_language_example: Ho parlato con mio zio la scorsa settimana.
native_language_example: I spoke with my uncle last week.

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase + time expression. "mio zio" means "my uncle" (male). "la settimana scorsa" means "last week" and is commonly used to say when something happened; it can also appear at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Ho visto mio zio la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I saw my uncle last week.

meaning: “my uncle has … (to me)” — a sentence starter before a past action or something given/told.
additional_notes: Used to begin a sentence about something your uncle did in the past. "mi" usually means “to me” (indirect object), and "ha" is “has” used to form the passato prossimo (e.g., ha detto = “has said/told”, ha dato = “has given”). You normally need a past participle after "ha" (detto, dato, fatto, ecc.).
target_language_example: Mio zio mi ha detto che domani piove.
native_language_example: My uncle told me that it’s going to rain tomorrow.

meaning: “my uncle lives” (either lives somewhere / is alive).
additional_notes: A simple subject + verb sentence: **mio zio** = “my uncle”, **vive** = “lives.” Often followed by a place: *Mio zio vive a Roma* (“My uncle lives in Rome”). Depending on context, **vive** can also mean “is alive” (e.g., *Mio zio vive ancora* = “My uncle is still alive”).
target_language_example: Mio zio vive a Milano.
native_language_example: My uncle lives in Milan.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase "mettere giù" (to put down). "Mise" is the remote past (passato remoto), often used in written stories or in some regions for past events. It’s typically followed by an object: "mise giù la sua penna" = he/she put down his/her pen.
target_language_example: Dopo aver scritto, mise giù la sua matita.
native_language_example: After writing, he/she put down his/her pencil.

additional_notes: Set phrase used to announce that an assignment has been successfully completed, often in a military, police, or action-movie context. It can also be used jokingly or proudly after finishing something in everyday life. Often said on its own as a complete statement.
target_language_example: Ho finito il progetto: missione compiuta!
native_language_example: I finished the project: mission accomplished!

meaning: "way of" (a way to do something / a way of living, etc.).
additional_notes: Used before an infinitive or a noun to talk about the manner, method, or style of doing something: "un modo di vivere" (a way of living), "un modo di risparmiare" (a way to save). Very common with "un modo di + infinitive" (one way to...).
target_language_example: C’è un modo di arrivare lì senza prendere l’autostrada?
native_language_example: Is there a way to get there without taking the highway?

meaning: an idiom; a common set expression (not meant literally).
additional_notes: Literally “a way of saying (something).” Used to talk about idioms/proverbs or fixed expressions. Very common in the phrase “È solo un modo di dire,” meaning “It’s just an expression,” i.e., don’t take it literally.
target_language_example: Non prenderla alla lettera: è solo un modo di dire.
native_language_example: Don’t take it literally: it’s just an expression.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s typical way of reasoning or their general attitude/opinion style. Often followed by a possessive (il mio/il tuo/il suo modo di pensare) or a demonstrative (questo modo di pensare).
target_language_example: Il mio modo di pensare è cambiato dopo quel viaggio.
native_language_example: My way of thinking changed after that trip.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is done/said/understood in another way. Often appears with prepositions like "in modo diverso" (in a different way) or "in un modo diverso" (in a different way). Note: Italian "diverso" usually means "different," not "diverse" (in the sense of a varied group).
target_language_example: Possiamo risolvere il problema in modo diverso.
native_language_example: We can solve the problem in a different way.

meaning: "the way (that)" / "how" (the manner in which something happens).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause that explains the manner or style of something: "the way in which...". Often follows a verb like amare/cambiare/capire/ricordare, etc. You can also use it after prepositions like "dal modo in cui..." (= "from the way...") or "per il modo in cui..." (= "because of the way...").
target_language_example: Non mi piace il modo in cui mi parli.
native_language_example: I don’t like the way you talk to me.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause describing how you do/feel something. It’s often followed by a verb: "il modo in cui mi parli" = “the way you talk to me”, "il modo in cui mi sento" = “the way I feel”. You may also hear the shorter version "modo in cui" or "modo che" depending on the sentence.
target_language_example: Non mi piace il modo in cui mi parli.
native_language_example: I don’t like the way you talk to me.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a woman (often someone’s wife) together with her children. In a full sentence you’ll often see an article: "la moglie e i suoi figli". Here "i suoi" means "her" (their gender depends on who owns them, not on the noun: "suo/sua/suoi/sue").
target_language_example: Lui vive con la moglie e i suoi figli.
native_language_example: He lives with his wife and her children.

meaning: 'wife is' (used to say what someone's wife is/does).
additional_notes: "Moglie" means "wife" (often with a possessive: "mia moglie" = my wife, "sua moglie" = his/her wife). "È" is the 3rd-person singular of "essere" (to be): "is". You’ll usually see this in a full sentence like "Mia moglie è…" followed by an adjective, job, or description.
target_language_example: Mia moglie è insegnante.
native_language_example: My wife is a teacher.

additional_notes: Uses the verb “mollare” (informal: to quit/ditch/let go of something). This phrase is typically used with an auxiliary verb, e.g. “Ha mollato il suo impiego” = “He quit his job.” “Suo” changes with the person (mio/tuo/suo/nostro/vostro/loro), and “impiego” is a somewhat formal word for “job” (often interchangeable with “lavoro”).
target_language_example: Ha mollato il suo impiego perché non era più felice.
native_language_example: He quit his job because he wasn’t happy anymore.

meaning: a lot of water; plenty of water.
additional_notes: Used with uncountable nouns like acqua to mean “a lot of” in everyday situations (health advice, needs, consumption). Molta agrees with the feminine singular noun acqua (molta + acqua). Common with verbs like bere (to drink), avere bisogno di (to need), servire (to need/to be necessary), usare/utilizzare (to use).
target_language_example: Dopo lo sport, bevi molta acqua.
native_language_example: After sports, drink a lot of water.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large quantity of beer. Agreement: since birra is feminine singular, you say molta (not molto). Can also be plural: molte birre (“many beers”). Often used with verbs like bere (“to drink”).
target_language_example: Stasera non voglio bere molta birra.
native_language_example: Tonight I don’t want to drink a lot of beer.

meaning: very hungry; a lot of hunger.
additional_notes: Used to say someone is very hungry. It’s common with avere (“to have”): avere molta fame = “to be very hungry.” You can also ask it as a question: Hai molta fame?
target_language_example: Dopo la camminata avevamo molta fame.
native_language_example: After the walk we were very hungry.

meaning: many people; a lot of people.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general. It’s often followed by a verb in the singular (because "gente" is singular): "Molta gente pensa..." You can also use it after prepositions: "per molta gente" = "for many people."
target_language_example: In estate molta gente va al mare.
native_language_example: In summer, a lot of people go to the beach.

additional_notes: Feminine plural: *molte* agrees with *amiche* (female friends). Use it when the group of friends is all women/girls, or when you’re talking about friends who are women. For a mixed group or when gender isn’t specified, you’ll often hear *molti amici* or just *molti amici* (male/mixed). Note: in the example sentences, the verb *scopare* is vulgar slang; the phrase *molte amiche* itself is neutral.
target_language_example: Ho molte amiche a Roma.
native_language_example: I have many (female) friends in Rome.

additional_notes: Means “many things” (plural). Used to talk about a large number of tasks, facts, questions, etc. It can be followed by “da + infinitive” to mean “many things to (do)”: “molte cose da fare”.
target_language_example: Ho ancora molte cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I still have many things to do today.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with che (“that/which”) describing the things being talked about: molte cose che devo fare (“many things that I have to do”). Often follows ci sono (“there are”) or avere (“to have”). Che stays the same regardless of singular/plural.
target_language_example: Ho molte cose che devo finire oggi.
native_language_example: I have many things that I have to finish today.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive after **da** to say there are many tasks/actions to be done: **molte cose da fare/spiegare/vedere**. Often appears with **ci sono** (“there are”) or **ho** (“I have”). You may also see **molte cose da dover + infinitive** to stress obligation.
target_language_example: Oggi ho molte cose da fare, quindi torno tardi.
native_language_example: Today I have many things to do, so I’ll be back late.

additional_notes: Used to say you (or someone) are busy because there are several tasks to complete. Common with avere (“to have”) or esserci (“there are”): “Abbiamo molte cose da fare” = “We have many things to do”; “Ci sono molte cose da fare” = “There are many things to do.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso uscire stasera: ho molte cose da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have many things to do.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot of questions (to ask or to answer). Often followed by "su" (about) or by an infinitive like "da fare" (to ask) / "a cui rispondere" (to answer). "Molte" agrees with the feminine plural noun "domande."
target_language_example: Se hai molte domande, possiamo parlarne dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: If you have many questions, we can talk about them after the lesson.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a large number of people in general. It’s the feminine plural of "molto" (many/a lot of) + "persone" (people). Often used as a subject: "Molte persone fanno..." You can negate it with "non": "Non molte persone..." (= not many people).
target_language_example: Molte persone preferiscono pagare con la carta.
native_language_example: Many people prefer to pay by card.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened repeatedly in the past or happens frequently. It often goes near the verb: "L'ho visto molte volte" / "Molte volte mi chiama". For "very often," you can also hear "molto spesso."
target_language_example: Sono stato in Italia molte volte.
native_language_example: I've been to Italy many times.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase: plural adjective "molti" (many) + plural noun "amici" (friends). It’s often used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere molti amici" = "to have many friends." The masculine plural "amici" can refer to a mixed group; for only female friends, you can say "molte amiche."
target_language_example: In questa città ho molti amici.
native_language_example: In this city I have many friends.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a long period of time, often with "per" (for): "per molti anni" = "for many years." You can also use it with "da" to mean "for many years (up to now)": "da molti anni". Often refers to duration in the past or continuing to the present, depending on the verb tense.
target_language_example: Vivo in questa città da molti anni.
native_language_example: I’ve lived in this city for many years.

additional_notes: Used to say that something happened a long time in the past. It often appears at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed at the beginning for emphasis. It can refer to events, relationships, deaths, disappearances, visits, etc.
target_language_example: Molti anni fa vivevo a Roma.
native_language_example: Many years ago I lived in Rome.

meaning: many mistakes / a lot of errors.
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something has a large number of mistakes. "Molti" agrees with masculine plural "errori". Common with verbs like "fare" (to make) and with "contenere" (to contain): "fare molti errori", "contenere molti errori".
target_language_example: Ho fatto molti errori, ma sto imparando.
native_language_example: I made many mistakes, but I'm learning.

additional_notes: "Molti" agrees with masculine plural nouns like "libri" (singular: "molto libro" is rare; usually you’d say "molti libri"). It’s often used to talk generally about a large number of books, as the subject ("Molti libri sono...") or object ("Ho/leggo molti libri").
target_language_example: In biblioteca ci sono molti libri interessanti.
native_language_example: In the library there are many interesting books.

additional_notes: Used to say that there are (or someone reads/has) a large number of books written in English. Note the structure: molti (plural of 'much/many') + libri (books) + in inglese (in English).
target_language_example: A casa mia ci sono molti libri in inglese.
native_language_example: At my house there are many books in English.

molti negozi a cercare il libro

target_language_multi_word_term: molti negozi a cercare il libro
meaning: (I went to) many shops to look for the book.
additional_notes: As written, this phrase sounds incomplete/unnatural in Italian on its own. You’ll usually see it inside a full sentence, often with a verb like "ho girato" (I went around/visited) or "sono andato in" (I went to): e.g. "Ho girato molti negozi cercando il libro" or "Sono andato in molti negozi a cercare il libro". "a cercare" expresses purpose (“to look for”).
target_language_example: Sono andato in molti negozi a cercare il libro, ma non l'ho trovato.
native_language_example: I went to many shops to look for the book, but I didn’t find it.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a lot of difficulties or issues. Common with verbs like avere (to have) and causare (to cause): “avere molti problemi” = “to have many problems,” “causare molti problemi” = “to cause a lot of trouble.” Can also be followed by “da + infinitive” to mean “many problems to + verb” (e.g., “molti problemi da affrontare” = “many problems to face”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo molti problemi da risolvere prima di partire.
native_language_example: We have many problems to solve before leaving.

additional_notes: Common way to say someone has/saved/spent a large amount of money. 'Molti' agrees with the plural noun 'soldi' (not *molto soldi*). Often used with verbs like dare (to give), risparmiare (to save), spendere (to spend), guadagnare (to earn).
target_language_example: Ho speso molti soldi per il biglietto.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of money on the ticket.

meaning: many types of / many kinds of.
additional_notes: Used to say there are several different categories or varieties of something. It’s followed by a plural noun (often without an article): molti tipi di musica, molti tipi di fiori. You can also use it with an article in some contexts (e.g., molti tipi di cibo / molti tipi di cibi).
target_language_example: In questo negozio trovi molti tipi di pane.
native_language_example: In this shop you can find many types of bread.

additional_notes: You repeat molto to intensify an adjective or adverb. In speech it’s a strong, often emotional emphasis; in writing it can sound a bit informal or dramatic. Similar in meaning to "molto" alone, but stronger.
target_language_example: Sono molto, molto stanco oggi.
native_language_example: I’m very, very tired today.

meaning: "very beautiful" (said about a female person or a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to compliment someone or describe something feminine. "Molto" = "very" and "bella" = feminine form of "beautiful" (singular). For a masculine noun/person use "molto bello"; for plural use "molto belle" (feminine) / "molto belli" (masculine or mixed).
target_language_example: Questo vestito è molto bello, ma quella gonna è molto bella.
native_language_example: This dress is very beautiful, but that skirt is very beautiful.

additional_notes: Means “very beautiful/very nice.” It agrees with the noun/person it describes: molto bello (masc. singular), molto bella (fem. singular), molto belli (masc. plural), molto belle (fem. plural). Often used to compliment places, things, or people.
target_language_example: Che panorama molto bello!
native_language_example: What a very beautiful view!

additional_notes: Used to strengthen bene. It can describe doing something well, knowing something/someone well, or feeling well, depending on the verb.
target_language_example: Parli italiano molto bene.
native_language_example: You speak Italian very well.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is very good at an activity or skill. Often followed by “a + noun” (molto bravo a nuotare = very good at swimming) or “con + noun” (molto bravo con la chitarra = very good with the guitar). It changes for gender/number: molto brava (f.), molto bravi (m. pl./mixed), molto brave (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Sei molto bravo a cucinare!
native_language_example: You’re very good at cooking!

additional_notes: Used to say someone is skilled at an activity. It’s usually followed by an infinitive (a cucinare, a parlare italiano) or sometimes a noun (a calcio). Note: Italian *bravo* means “good / skilled / well-behaved,” not “brave.”
target_language_example: Sei molto bravo a cucinare.
native_language_example: You’re very good at cooking.

additional_notes: Used to strongly praise the quality of something (a speech, concert, service, weather, etc.) or to say someone is a very good person. It agrees in gender/number with the noun: molto buono (m. sg.), molto buona (f. sg.), molto buoni (m. pl.), molto buone (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Il suo concerto fu molto buono.
native_language_example: His concert was very good.

additional_notes: Used to compliment a woman/girl or to describe something grammatically feminine (e.g., città, casa, bandiera). Match gender/number: molto carino (masc. sing.), molto carina (fem. sing.), molto carini (masc. pl./mixed), molto carine (fem. pl.). Depending on context, it can mean “lovely/nice” as much as “cute.”
target_language_example: La mia città natale è molto carina.
native_language_example: My hometown is very nice/lovely.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is hard, challenging, or complicated. It can describe tasks, situations, exams, or relationships. Word order is typically: molto + adjective (molto difficile).
target_language_example: Per me, imparare i verbi irregolari è molto difficile.
native_language_example: For me, learning irregular verbs is very difficult.

additional_notes: Used to say something (a person, joke, story, situation, job, etc.) is highly amusing or enjoyable. It agrees in gender/number with what it describes: molto divertente (sing.), molto divertenti (pl.). Often said on its own as a comment: “Molto divertente.” = “Very funny.” (can be sincere or sarcastic depending on tone/context).
target_language_example: Il film era molto divertente.
native_language_example: The movie was very entertaining.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the effort someone puts into an activity, especially with verbs like "lavorare" (to work) and "studiare" (to study). It describes how something is done (an adverb phrase).
target_language_example: Sto preparando l'esame e sto studiando molto duramente.
native_language_example: I'm preparing for the exam and I'm studying very hard.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective felice (“happy”) with molto (“very/a lot”). It can describe a person’s state (Sono molto felice) or how someone seems (Sembra molto felice). With sentirsi (“to feel”), it commonly appears as mi sento molto felice (“I feel very happy”).
target_language_example: Sono molto felice di vederti.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pleasure about an action or event. It’s commonly followed by an infinitive: molto felice di + verb (e.g., vedere, conoscerla). In greetings you can also drop the subject: “Molto felice di vederti/vedervi” = “Very happy to see you.”
target_language_example: Sono molto felice di aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: I’m very happy to help you today.

additional_notes: Used to intensify the adjective "felici" (happy). "Felici" is plural: use it with plural subjects (e.g., noi, loro, Tom e Mary). For a single person, use "molto felice".
target_language_example: Siamo molto felici di vederti.
native_language_example: We’re very happy to see you.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *essere* (“to be”) or *sentirsi* (“to feel”) to express pride: *essere/sentirsi molto fiera di…*. The adjective agrees with the person who feels proud: *molto fiero di* (male), *molto fiera di* (female); plural *molto fieri/fiere di*. Followed by *di* + a noun or pronoun: *di sua figlia*, *di te*, *di lei/lui*.
target_language_example: Sono molto fiera di te per questo esame.
native_language_example: I’m very proud of you for this exam.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pride in someone or something. Typically used with *essere* (e.g., "Sono molto fiero di...") or *sentirsi* ("Mi sento molto fiero di..."). Agreement note: *fiero* changes with the subject (masc. sing. **fiero**, fem. sing. **fiera**, masc./mixed pl. **fieri**, fem. pl. **fiere**). In this fixed term, **di** introduces the person/thing you’re proud of (e.g., *di te, di voi, di lui/lei, di loro, di mio figlio*).
target_language_example: Mi sento molto fiero di voi.
native_language_example: I feel very proud of you (plural).

additional_notes: Used both literally (strong taste, alcohol, smell, noise, etc.) and figuratively for someone with a strong character or strong opinions ("una personalità molto forte"). Word order is fixed: molto + adjective.
target_language_example: Questo caffè è molto forte, ne vuoi uno più leggero?
native_language_example: This coffee is very strong—do you want a lighter one?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s kind, courteous behavior (a person can be gentile, or an action can be gentile). You can also say it as a polite reply to thank someone, like “That’s very kind (of you).” Often used with essere: “è/era/stato molto gentile”. With a + infinitive, it means “kind of (someone) to do something”: “È stato molto gentile a prestarmi dei soldi.”
target_language_example: Sei stato molto gentile ad aiutarmi oggi.
native_language_example: It was very kind of you to help me today.

additional_notes: Used to describe how someone treats you: *essere gentile con qualcuno* = “to be kind to someone.” In Italian you say **con** (“with”) + a person: *con me, con te, con lui/lei*. **Gentile** can mean “kind” or “polite.”
target_language_example: Sei stato molto gentile con me, grazie.
native_language_example: You’ve been very kind to me, thank you.

additional_notes: Used to thank someone politely for something they did or offered. Usually followed by a possessive: **molto gentile da parte tua** (of you), **da parte sua** (formal: of you / of him/her), **da parte vostra** (of you all). Often used with **È**: **È molto gentile da parte tua.**
target_language_example: È molto gentile da parte sua aiutarmi con i bagagli.
native_language_example: It’s very kind of you to help me with the luggage.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a lot to do or not much free time. Often followed by a time expression (e.g., oggi, questa settimana) or a context like work: “molto impegnato al lavoro / col suo lavoro.” Note: “impegnato” alone can also mean “committed” or “engaged” (e.g., in a relationship), but with “molto” in these contexts it usually means “busy.”
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi sono molto impegnato e non posso venire.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I’m very busy and I can’t come.

additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize importance. "Molto" works like "very" and can intensify many adjectives (e.g., molto bello = very beautiful). It can appear after the noun with the adjective (un elemento molto importante), after verbs like "sembrare" (mi sembra molto importante), or in the common structure "è molto importante che + (subjunctive)" to say it’s very important that something happens.
target_language_example: È molto importante che tu arrivi in orario.
native_language_example: It’s very important that you arrive on time.

additional_notes: Usually used as **molto imprudente da parte di + person/pronoun** to judge someone’s action as careless or risky: *È stato molto imprudente da parte tua...* (“It was very imprudent of you...”); you’ll often see it with **è stato / sarebbe / è**.
target_language_example: È stato molto imprudente da parte tua uscire senza guardare il traffico.
native_language_example: It was very imprudent of you to go out without watching the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to strongly compliment someone’s intelligence. It agrees in gender and number with the person described: molto intelligente (m./f. singular), molto intelligenti (plural).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è molto intelligente e impara in fretta.
native_language_example: My sister is very smart and learns quickly.

additional_notes: Used to react to information, an idea, or a story. Often said on its own as a comment, or followed by a detail/question: "Molto interessante, ma…" (Very interesting, but…).
target_language_example: Molto interessante! Puoi spiegarmelo meglio?
native_language_example: Very interesting! Can you explain it to me better?

additional_notes: Used to compare improvement (health, mood, situation): sentirsi molto meglio = “to feel much better.” It can also mean “much more clearly/better” about how something is said or explained: Puoi dirmelo molto meglio! = “You can tell/explain it to me much better!”
target_language_example: Dopo una notte di riposo, mi sento molto meglio.
native_language_example: After a night of rest, I feel much better.

additional_notes: Used to compare someone’s ability/performance to yours. It often follows a verb (e.g., nuotare, parlare) or “essere” and can be completed with a context phrase like “negli sport” (at sports). In more formal Italian, you may also hear “molto meglio di me” replaced with “molto meglio di quanto faccia io” depending on the structure, but “molto meglio di me” is common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Lei cucina molto meglio di me.
native_language_example: She cooks much better than me.

additional_notes: Used to say you have little or no free time. It agrees with the person described: molto occupato (male), molto occupata (female), molto occupati/occupate (plural). Often used with time words like oggi (today) or this week.
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso uscire stasera: sono molto occupato.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can't go out tonight: I'm very busy.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pride in someone/something. "Orgogliosa" is feminine singular; masculine is "orgoglioso" (e.g., "molto orgoglioso di mio figlio"). It’s followed by "di" + a noun ("di mio figlio") or a stressed pronoun: "di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro". Often used with "essere" ("sono") or "sentirsi" ("mi sento").
target_language_example: Mi sento molto orgogliosa di te per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I feel very proud of you for what you did.

additional_notes: Used to express pride about someone or something. The adjective agrees with the subject: orgoglioso (m. sing.), orgogliosa (f. sing.), orgogliosi (m./mixed plural), orgogliose (f. plural). It’s followed by di + person/thing: di te (of you, informal singular), di voi (of you, plural/formal), di lei (of her/you formal).
target_language_example: Siamo molto orgogliosi di questo progetto.
native_language_example: We’re very proud of this project.

additional_notes: Used to express strong pride in someone or something. It’s followed by a person/thing (often a pronoun) and can change for gender/number: molto orgoglioso (m. sing.), molto orgogliosa (f. sing.), molto orgogliosi (m. pl.), molto orgogliose (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Sono molto orgoglioso di te.
native_language_example: I'm very proud of you.

additional_notes: Used to intensify a comparison, meaning ‘by a large amount’. Often followed by "di" + noun/pronoun ("molto più di Mary" = much more than Mary). It can also be used without an explicit comparison when the context makes it clear ("Ora so molto più" = now I know much more).
target_language_example: Questo esercizio è molto più difficile del primo.
native_language_example: This exercise is much more difficult than the first.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages. Put the person/thing you’re comparing to after di: “X è molto più giovane di Y” = “X is much younger than Y.” (più giovane = younger; molto = much).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è molto più giovane di me.
native_language_example: My sister is much younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to say something is liked by a particular group of people. It’s typically followed by a plural noun or group: **tra i giovani** (among young people), **tra gli studenti** (among students), **tra i turisti** (among tourists). You can also say **molto popolare fra** (same meaning).
target_language_example: Questo ristorante è molto popolare tra i turisti.
native_language_example: This restaurant is very popular with tourists.

additional_notes: Used to express strong concern about a person or situation. It’s often followed by a person (per lei/te/voi) or by a noun phrase (per la sua salute). The adjective changes for gender/number: molto preoccupata (f. sg.), molto preoccupati (m. pl. or mixed), molto preoccupate (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Sono molto preoccupato per il tuo esame domani.
native_language_example: I'm very worried about your exam tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize the speed of an action or change. It can modify many verbs (crescere, imparare, mangiare, guarire, ecc.). Word-by-word it’s “very” (molto) + “quickly” (rapidamente).
target_language_example: Abbiamo finito il lavoro molto rapidamente.
native_language_example: We finished the work very quickly.

additional_notes: Used most naturally with the verb "giocare" (to play): "giocare a tennis" = "to play tennis". "Molto spesso" means "very often / quite often" and can be moved around in the sentence (e.g., "Gioco molto spesso a tennis" or "Molto spesso gioco a tennis").
target_language_example: Io gioco molto spesso a tennis il sabato.
native_language_example: I play tennis very often on Saturdays.

additional_notes: "Molto" = "very" and "stanca" is the feminine form of "tired" (male: "molto stanco"). Often used with "essere" (Sono molto stanca) or "sentirsi" (Mi sento molto stanca) to describe how you feel.
target_language_example: Oggi sono molto stanca, vado a letto presto.
native_language_example: Today I'm very tired, I'm going to bed early.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize how tired someone feels or looks. It agrees with the person: molto stanco (male), molto stanca (female), molto stanchi (plural male/mixed), molto stanche (plural female). Often used with essere (sono/era) or sembrare (sembra).
target_language_example: Sono davvero molto stanco.
native_language_example: I’m really very tired.

additional_notes: Used with essere/sembrare or to describe how someone feels (often after rendere + person + adjective: “to make someone very sad”). Agreement: triste stays the same for masculine/feminine singular; plural is tristi (molto tristi).
target_language_example: Sono molto triste perché ho perso le chiavi.
native_language_example: I’m very sad because I lost my keys.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has, wants, earns, needs, gives, or asks for a large amount of money. Very common with verbs like avere (to have), volere (to want), fare (to make/earn), chiedere (to ask for), dare (to give), and avere ... a disposizione (to have available).
target_language_example: Per aprire un ristorante serve molto denaro.
native_language_example: To open a restaurant, you need a lot of money.

meaning: a lot of work to do.
additional_notes: Used to say you still have many tasks left. Often follows a form of avere (ho/hai/abbiamo…) and can be intensified with ancora (“still”): Ho ancora molto lavoro da fare. You can also say tanto lavoro da fare with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso uscire stasera: ho molto lavoro da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t go out tonight: I have a lot of work to do.

additional_notes: Used to say you need/have a large amount of time. With "passare" it often appears as "non passerà molto tempo prima che..." = "it won’t be long before...".
target_language_example: Ci vuole molto tempo per arrivare lì in autobus.
native_language_example: It takes a long time to get there by bus.

meaning: “a long time to” (with a verb) or “a lot of time in/at” (with a place).
additional_notes: Used after verbs like metterci/volerci, passare, trascorrere, perdere to say that something takes a long time or that someone spends a lot of time doing something or being somewhere. Structure: (1) molto tempo a + infinitive: "Ci vorrà molto tempo a costruire..." / "Passo molto tempo a guardare..."; (2) molto tempo a + place: "Ho passato molto tempo a Boston." With actions, Italian often uses "a" before the infinitive (passare/trascorrere/perdere tempo a fare qualcosa).
target_language_example: Ci ho messo molto tempo a trovare questa strada.
native_language_example: It took me a long time to find this street.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like passare/trascorrere (“to spend”) to say you spent a long time with someone. Word order stays the same: (ho) passato/trascorso + molto tempo con + person.
target_language_example: Ho passato molto tempo con i miei amici quest’estate.
native_language_example: I spent a lot of time with my friends this summer.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened far in the past. Often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also be placed earlier for emphasis. Commonly used with past tenses (e.g., passato prossimo, imperfetto).
target_language_example: Ho imparato a nuotare molto tempo fa.
native_language_example: I learned to swim a long time ago.

additional_notes: Used with a verb after it (often in the subjunctive, e.g. “prima che si faccia vivo”) to say something will happen only after quite a while. Very common in the pattern “Non passerà / Non ci vorrà molto tempo prima che …” meaning “It won’t be long before …” (so despite “molto tempo”, the whole sentence often expresses that something will happen soon).
target_language_example: Non passerà molto tempo prima che arrivi il treno.
native_language_example: It won’t be long before the train arrives.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say there is a lot that needs to be done, explained, eaten, celebrated, etc. Common patterns: "avere molto da + infinitive" (to have a lot to...), "c'è molto da + infinitive" (there’s a lot to...). Example: "Ho molto da fare" = "I have a lot to do."
target_language_example: Oggi ho molto da fare, quindi non posso uscire.
native_language_example: Today I have a lot to do, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like avere (“to have”): avere molto da fare = “to have a lot to do.” It often implies being busy and not having much free time. You can add time phrases: oggi/questa settimana ho molto da fare (“today/this week I have a lot to do”).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso venire: oggi ho molto da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t come: I have a lot to do today.

additional_notes: Used to say someone still has many things to learn (skills, knowledge, experience). Structure: molto (“a lot”) + da + infinitive (“to” do something). Often said as advice or a mild criticism: Hai molto da imparare (“You have a lot to learn”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo ancora molto da imparare.
native_language_example: We still have a lot to learn.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere molto in comune con qualcuno" = to have many shared interests, traits, or experiences with someone. You can also say "avere qualcosa in comune" (something in common) or "avere poco/niente in comune" (little/nothing in common).
target_language_example: Abbiamo molto in comune, per esempio ci piace la stessa musica.
native_language_example: We have a lot in common, for example we like the same music.

additional_notes: Used to say two people or things share many similarities (interests, habits, characteristics). It’s often used with the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho molto in comune con...". You can also say "abbiamo molto in comune" (we have a lot in common).
target_language_example: Ho molto in comune con mia sorella: ci piace la stessa musica.
native_language_example: I have a lot in common with my sister: we like the same music.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a specific point in time when something happens. Often follows phrases like "è il momento in cui..." (it’s the moment when...) or appears inside "dal momento in cui..." meaning "from the moment when" / "since".
target_language_example: È il momento in cui dobbiamo prendere una decisione.
native_language_example: It’s the moment when we have to make a decision.

additional_notes: Usually used as **Il mondo è pieno di + noun** to say there are many of something (often in a general, sometimes negative or ironic way). You can use it literally (people/objects) or figuratively (problems, opportunities).
target_language_example: Il mondo è pieno di persone gentili.
native_language_example: The world is full of kind people.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb *stare* to describe a current state: *sto/stavo/stanno morendo di fame* (“I’m/was/they’re starving”). It can be literal (not having food) or exaggerated in everyday speech to mean “very hungry.”
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro sto morendo di fame, mangiamo qualcosa?
native_language_example: After work I’m starving—shall we eat something?

additional_notes: “Morì” is the passato remoto (simple past), common in written narratives and in some regions when speaking about completed past events. “Morire di + illness” means “to die of/from + illness” (e.g., “morì di cancro”). You can add details with “a/al/alla + body part,” e.g., “morì di cancro allo stomaco” = “died of stomach cancer.”
target_language_example: Il nonno morì di cancro quando ero piccolo.
native_language_example: Grandpa died of cancer when I was little.

additional_notes: "Mostrò" is the passato remoto (simple past) of mostrare (“to show”), used often in stories or formal writing (especially in central/southern Italy). It typically takes an indirect object (e.g., ci = “to us”, mi = “to me”) plus a direct object: la sua nuova + a feminine singular noun (e.g., macchina, automobile, casa). "Sua" can mean “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Ci mostrò la sua nuova casa.
native_language_example: He/She showed us his/her new house.

meaning: a motel in the area / nearby.
additional_notes: Used when asking or talking about accommodation close to your current location or a specific place. "Nella zona" literally means "in the zone/area" and is often translated as "around here" or "nearby" depending on context.
target_language_example: C'è un motel nella zona?
native_language_example: Is there a motel in the area?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an explanation or justification. Often followed by a clause with a verb: "Questo è il motivo per cui..." (= "This is why..."). You may also see "il motivo per cui" or "un motivo per cui" depending on whether it’s a specific reason or just one possible reason.
target_language_example: Questo è il motivo per cui non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: This is the reason why I can’t come tonight.

additional_notes: Used for an internet tool/site that lets you search the web (e.g., Google). Often appears with articles: "un/il motore di ricerca". You can also say "cercare su un motore di ricerca" (to search on a search engine).
target_language_example: Ho trovato la risposta con un motore di ricerca.
native_language_example: I found the answer using a search engine.

meaning: a heap/pile of; (informally) a bunch of / lots of.
additional_notes: Literally means “heap/pile of” for things you can pile up (giornali, lettere). Very often used informally as a quantity expression meaning “a lot of” with almost any noun (un mucchio di cose/idee). With insults or negative nouns (mucchio di idioti, mucchio di merda) it’s strongly offensive and means “a bunch/heap of …”. Often used with the article: “un/quel mucchio di …”.
target_language_example: Ho un mucchio di cose da fare oggi.
native_language_example: I have a lot of things to do today.

additional_notes: Literal farm/ranch expression. "Mungere" means "to milk" (an animal), and it’s used with a direct object: "mungere le mucche" / "mungere una mucca". You may also hear it in commands: "Vai a mungere le mucche" (informal) or "Vada a mungere le mucche" (formal).
target_language_example: Ogni mattina devo mungere le mucche prima di colazione.
native_language_example: Every morning I have to milk the cows before breakfast.

additional_notes: Used for the action of extracting milk from a cow, typically on a farm. Often appears with "sapere" (to know how): "Sai/Sapete mungere una mucca?" = "Do you know how to milk a cow?"
target_language_example: Non ho mai provato a mungere una mucca.
native_language_example: I’ve never tried to milk a cow.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from the verb "mungere" (to milk). It’s used with "avere" to form the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha munto la mucca" = "I/you/he/she milked the cow" (or "has milked the cow"). Often you’ll hear the infinitive form in general statements or instructions: "mungere la mucca" = "to milk the cow".
target_language_example: Stamattina ho munto la mucca prima di colazione.
native_language_example: This morning I milked the cow before breakfast.

additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar. Used as a strong command to tell someone to hurry, stop wasting time, or start moving/doing something. Can also be used jokingly (e.g., to tell someone to dance), but it’s still rude in many situations. Similar in tone to “Get your ass moving!”
target_language_example: Muovi il culo, siamo in ritardo!
native_language_example: Move your ass, we’re late!

additional_notes: Common genre label used after verbs like ascoltare (to listen to), suonare (to play), or when introducing the topic: Parlando di musica classica... (= Speaking of classical music...).
