target_language_example: Non ho mai detto che non voglio aiutarti.
native_language_example: I never said that I don’t want to help you.

non ho mai detto che era

target_language_multi_word_term: non ho mai detto che era
additional_notes: Used to deny having made a specific claim about something. It’s typically followed by an adjective or noun phrase: “Non ho mai detto che era facile” (easy), “Non ho mai detto che era colpa tua” (your fault). In conversation you might also hear it with “fosse” instead of “era” depending on the sentence, but “non ho mai detto che era …” is common and understandable.
target_language_example: Non ho mai detto che era una buona idea.
native_language_example: I never said it was a good idea.

meaning: "I never said I would / I never said to..." (denying you said something).
additional_notes: Used to correct a misunderstanding or defend yourself when someone claims you said something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive (often in the past): "Non ho mai detto di voler partire" = "I never said I wanted to leave." If you want to deny saying a full clause with “that…”, you often use "non ho mai detto che..." instead.
target_language_example: Non ho mai detto di voler cambiare lavoro.
native_language_example: I never said I wanted to change jobs.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done an action at any time up to now. Common in denials or assurances: non ho mai fatto del male a… = “I’ve never hurt…”. You can add an object (non ho mai fatto del male) or use it with niente/nulla (“anything”): non ho mai fatto niente/nulla a loro = “I never did anything to them / I never hurt them.”
target_language_example: Non ho mai fatto una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: I’ve never done anything like that.

meaning: "I never learned to" / "I've never learned to".
additional_notes: Used to say you never acquired a skill or never learned how to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (e.g., usare, fare, guidare). Grammatically it uses the passato prossimo: non + ho + mai + imparato + a + [verb].
target_language_example: Non ho mai imparato a guidare.
native_language_example: I never learned to drive.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never met/come across a person before. It’s the negative past of "incontrare" (to meet) with "mai" = "ever/never". Often followed by "nessuno" (no one) or "qualcuno" (someone): "Non ho mai incontrato nessuno..." = "I’ve never met anyone...".
target_language_example: Non ho mai incontrato una persona così gentile.
native_language_example: I’ve never met a person so kind.

additional_notes: Uses the present perfect (ho sentito) with mai (“ever/never”) to talk about something you have never heard up to now. Often followed by a direct object (Non ho mai sentito questo nome) or by di + person/thing meaning “heard of” (Non ho mai sentito di lei).
target_language_example: Non ho mai sentito parlare di questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I’ve never heard of this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never seen someone or something at any time up to now. Literally: "I do not have ever seen" (Italian uses "avere" + past participle for the present perfect: ho visto = I have seen). Often followed by a person/thing (Non ho mai visto Tom) or by something like niente / nulla (Non ho mai visto niente di simile = I've never seen anything like that).
target_language_example: Non ho mai visto un posto così bello.
native_language_example: I've never seen a place this beautiful.

additional_notes: Used when the noun is understood from context and it’s feminine singular (una). For a masculine noun you’d say: non ho mai visto uno / non ne ho mai visto uno (or simply non ne ho mai visto uno). Often used as a reply to a question like “Hai mai visto una…?”
target_language_example: Hai mai visto una balena? No, non ho mai visto una.
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a whale? No, I’ve never seen one.

additional_notes: Used to say you never had the desire or intention to do something. It’s the negative of "ho voluto" (past tense of "volere" = to want), and it’s commonly followed by an infinitive: "non ho mai voluto + andare/fare/cantare..." It can also imply “I never meant to” in contexts like "Non ho mai voluto farvi del male" (no intention to hurt you).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho mai voluto offenderti.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I never meant to offend you.

additional_notes: Passato prossimo of *potere* (to be able to): *non ho potuto + infinitive* to say you were unable to do something in the past (often because of circumstances). Can also be used alone as an explanation: *Non ho potuto!* = “I couldn’t (do it)!”
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho potuto venire ieri.
native_language_example: Sorry, I couldn't come yesterday.

additional_notes: Common negative form of the verb "avere" (to have) in the present tense, 1st person singular: "(io) non ho". Use it before a noun: "Non ho la macchina" (I don't have a car). You can also emphasize with words like "neanche"/"nemmeno" = "not even": "Non ho neanche un diploma".
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho contanti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have cash.

meaning: "I have no / I don’t have any" (with a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express having zero of something (stronger than "non ho" alone). It’s followed by a masculine singular noun (e.g., "alcun piano", "alcun amico"). With feminine nouns, use "non ho alcuna..." (e.g., "non ho alcuna idea"). In plural, use "non ho alcuni/alcune..." though often Italians prefer "non ho" + plural ("non ho amici").
target_language_example: Non ho alcun problema a venire domani.
native_language_example: I have no problem coming tomorrow.

meaning: "I have no" / "I don’t have any" (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to express a total absence of something: non ho alcuna + noun (e.g., alcuna idea, alcuna intenzione, alcuna prova). It’s the feminine singular form; with masculine singular you use "non ho alcun" (non ho alcun dubbio), and with plurals you use "non ho alcuna" is not used (instead: non ho nessuna + feminine singular, or non ho alcun/alcuna + singular; for plural: non ho (nessun) + plural). Common in more formal or emphatic statements, similar to "no ... whatsoever."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non ho alcuna informazione su quel volo.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t have any information about that flight.

meaning: “I have absolutely no …” / “I don’t have any … at all.”
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize having zero of something. It’s a negative structure: non ho (“I don’t have”) + assolutamente (“absolutely”) + alcun + masculine singular noun (alcuna for feminine nouns). Common with abstract nouns like talento, rimpianto, dubbio.
target_language_example: Non ho assolutamente alcun dubbio.
native_language_example: I have absolutely no doubt.

meaning: "I don’t need" / "I have no need for".
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t need something. It’s the negative of "ho bisogno di" (I need). Often followed by a noun ("non ho bisogno di aiuto" = I don’t need help) or by an infinitive ("non ho bisogno di parlare" = I don’t need to talk). You can replace "ho" with other forms: "non hai bisogno di" (you don’t need), "non ha bisogno di" (he/she doesn’t need), "non abbiamo bisogno di" (we don’t need).
target_language_example: Grazie, ma non ho bisogno di aiuto.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I don’t need help.

meaning: “I have no idea (about) …” / “I don’t know … at all.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something. It’s commonly followed by an indirect question word: di che (what it’s about), di chi (who), di dove (where), di quanto (how much), etc. Often interchangeable with “non ne ho idea” or “non ne ho la minima idea” (stronger).
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho idea di a che ora arrivi il treno.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no idea what time the train arrives.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the identity of a person (or which people) being referred to. It’s typically followed by the subjunctive with indirect questions: di chi sia / di chi siano. You can also see it before other verbs to mean “I have no idea who is supposed to…”.
target_language_example: Non ho idea di chi sia quella persona.
native_language_example: I have no idea who that person is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about “what” something is/means/does/wants. It’s typically followed by a verb (often in the subjunctive in more careful Italian): “Non ho idea di cosa significhi.” You can also say “Non ho idea di cosa fare” (= “I have no idea what to do”).
target_language_example: Non ho idea di cosa stia succedendo.
native_language_example: I have no idea what’s happening.

non ho idea di dove sia

target_language_multi_word_term: non ho idea di dove sia
meaning: "I have no idea where it is."
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the location of something/someone. After "non ho idea" (I have no idea), Italian often uses "di" + an indirect question like "dove" (where) + the subjunctive "sia" (from "essere", to be). You can change "sia" based on the subject (e.g., "dove siano" = where they are).
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho idea di dove sia il mio telefono.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have no idea where my phone is.

meaning: "I have no intention of" / "I don’t intend to" (followed by a verb).
additional_notes: Used to clearly say you do not plan or want to do something. It’s often firm and can sound defensive or reassuring depending on tone. Structure: non ho intenzione di + infinitive (e.g., dire, fare, andare). You can change the subject: non hai intenzione di… (you don’t intend to), non abbiamo intenzione di… (we don’t intend to).
target_language_example: Non ho intenzione di cambiare idea.
native_language_example: I don’t intend to change my mind.

additional_notes: Common way to say you don’t have something (objects, money, time, etc.). Italian typically uses double negation: "non" + "niente" (even though in English you usually avoid double negatives). Often followed by structures like "non ho niente da + infinitive" (nothing to do) or "non ho niente di cui + infinitive" (nothing to worry about / be afraid of).
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho niente da darti in questo momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have anything to give you right now.

meaning: "I have nothing to" (followed by an infinitive).
additional_notes: Used to say you have nothing to do/say/give/offer, etc. It’s followed by a verb in the infinitive: Non ho niente da + dire/fare/darti/offrirti. You can also hear the equivalent with "nulla": Non ho nulla da....
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho niente da aggiungere.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to add.

meaning: “I have nothing to say.” / “I have nothing to add.”
additional_notes: Used to say you have no comment or no explanation to give. It can be neutral (“I don’t have anything else to add”) or sound defensive/annoyed, especially with exclamations like “!” or words like “basta!” (“enough!”). In Italian, double negatives are normal: “non” + “niente”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho niente da dire su questa storia.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I have nothing to say about this situation.

meaning: “I have nothing … / I don’t have anything …” (used before an adjective or a “di + noun” phrase).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have something, especially when describing a quality: **Non ho niente di speciale** (“I’m nothing special / I don’t have anything special”). Very often it’s followed by an adjective (di speciale, di nuovo, di interessante) or by **di + noun** (e.g., di soldi = “any money”). In everyday Italian you may also hear **non ho niente** on its own.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho niente di contante.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any cash.

meaning: “I have nothing / I don’t have anything.”
additional_notes: Used to say you have nothing (to do, to say, to eat, etc.). Very common in set patterns like: “Non ho nulla da fare” (I have nothing to do), “Non ho nulla da dire” (I have nothing to say), “Non ho nulla contro di lui/lei” (I have nothing against him/her), and “Non ho nulla in comune con…” (I have nothing in common with…). In English you often translate it as “I don’t have anything…”.
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi non ho nulla da fare.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have anything to do today.

meaning: “I have nothing to …” (followed by an infinitive verb).
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have anything to do/say/write/share, etc. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: non ho nulla da + fare/dire/scrivere/condividere. Italian uses a double negative (non + nulla), but in English you normally translate it as “I have nothing to …” (not “I don’t have nothing to …”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho nulla da aggiungere.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have nothing to add.

meaning: "I have nothing to ... about" (e.g., worry about / be ashamed of / apologize for).
additional_notes:
This phrase is usually followed by an infinitive (often with a reflexive verb), because it needs a verb to complete the meaning: 
- non ho nulla di cui preoccuparmi = I have nothing to worry about
- non ho nulla di cui vergognarmi = I have nothing to be ashamed of
- non ho nulla di cui scusarmi = I have nothing to apologize for
Literally it’s “I don’t have anything of which…”, but in natural English you translate it as “nothing to … about.”
target_language_example: Non ho nulla di cui preoccuparmi: andrà tutto bene.
native_language_example: I have nothing to worry about: everything will be fine.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t fear someone or something. It’s followed by a person/thing (often with a pronoun like te, loro, questo) or by an infinitive verb (e.g., non ho paura di parlare = I’m not afraid to speak). You can also use it with niente: Non ho paura di niente! = I’m not afraid of anything!
target_language_example: Non ho paura di parlare in pubblico.
native_language_example: I’m not afraid to speak in public.

meaning: "I no longer have" / "I don't have anymore".
additional_notes: Used with the present tense of avere (ho) + più (“anymore/no longer”) to say you’ve stopped having something (fear, need, time, objections, etc.). Often followed by a noun (Non ho più tempo), or by expressions like bisogno di (Non ho più bisogno di…).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho più tempo per parlarne.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't have time anymore to talk about it.

meaning: “I don’t have any money on me.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have cash with you right now (e.g., you forgot your wallet or don’t have coins/bills). You can add a time word like “ora/adesso” (now). Often followed by an alternative: paying later, paying by card, or giving something in exchange (“in cambio”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non ho soldi con me: posso pagare con la carta?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have any money on me—can I pay by card?

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy or unavailable to do something. Often followed by “di” + infinitive to say what you don’t have time to do: “Non ho tempo di aiutarti.” You can add “ora/adesso” to mean “right now”: “Non ho tempo ora.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho tempo di parlare adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time to talk right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy to do an activity, followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., fare, andare, parlare). You can change the subject: non hai tempo di (you don’t have time to), non abbiamo tempo di (we don’t have time to).
target_language_example: Scusa, non ho tempo di parlare adesso.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have time to talk right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re too busy to do something, often followed by a noun (i miei hobby, queste cose) or an infinitive verb (scrivere, chiacchierare). With people it can sound dismissive ("Non ho tempo per te" = "I don’t have time for you"). You can also change the subject: non hai tempo per… (you don’t have time for…), non abbiamo tempo per… (we don’t have time for…).
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi non ho tempo per parlare: devo lavorare.
native_language_example: Sorry, today I don’t have time to talk: I have to work.

meaning: “I don’t feel like …” / “I don’t want to … (right now).”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have the desire/energy/mood to do something. It’s followed by an infinitive (non ho voglia di uscire = I don’t feel like going out) or by a noun (non ho voglia di feste = I’m not in the mood for parties). Often implies a temporary feeling rather than a strong refusal.
target_language_example: Oggi non ho voglia di cucinare.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel like cooking.

additional_notes: Used to say that something doesn’t change even if the amount or degree changes. It’s often followed by a verb (e.g., "non importa quanto io ci pensi") or an adjective/adverb idea (e.g., "non importa quanto (sia) difficile/veloce").
target_language_example: Non importa quanto sia tardi, voglio finire questo lavoro.
native_language_example: No matter how late it is, I want to finish this work.

additional_notes: "Non" is the negation (not), and "la" is a direct object pronoun meaning "her" or "it" (feminine singular, referring to a feminine noun like "la cosa", "la verità", "la macchina"). It usually comes right before the verb: "non la vedo" = "I don’t see her/it". The exact meaning depends on context (who/what "la" refers to).
target_language_example: Non la capisco, questa regola.
native_language_example: I don’t understand it, this rule.

additional_notes: "Non" makes the verb negative, and "le" is an indirect object pronoun meaning "to her" or "to you" (formal, singular). It commonly appears before a verb: "Non le dico" = "I don’t tell her/you." With a past tense, you’ll often see it as "non le ha..." or "non le sono...".
target_language_example: Non le dico niente adesso.
native_language_example: I’m not telling her/you anything right now.

additional_notes: "Non" makes the verb negative, and "li" is a direct-object pronoun meaning "them" (usually masculine plural or a mixed group). In Italian, object pronouns like "li" usually come before the conjugated verb: "Non li vedo" = "I don’t see them." With an infinitive, the pronoun can attach to the end: "Non vederli" = "Not to see them / Don’t see them." The exact English verb depends on context (see, understand, take, etc.).
target_language_example: Non li conosco, sono nuovi qui.
native_language_example: I don’t know them; they’re new here.

additional_notes: Used with the direct object pronoun lo before the verb. Usually it means 'not it' or 'not him' depending on context. With essere, lo can stand for a quality, role, or identity already mentioned: non lo sono = 'I'm not' / 'they aren't'. English often translates the whole sentence less literally.
target_language_example: Dicono che sia facile, ma non lo è.
native_language_example: They say it's easy, but it isn't.

meaning: “I don’t do it / I won’t do it.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t do something (as a habit or in general) or you refuse to do it in a specific situation. Literally: “I don’t do it,” with **lo** = “it/that.” Often appears with extras like **mai** (never), **da sola** (alone), **a nessuno** (to anyone), or **di mestiere** (for a living).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non lo faccio.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I won’t do it.

additional_notes: From sapere (“to know”): non (not) + lo (“it”) + sa (“knows”). The subject is often omitted in Italian, so it can mean “he/she doesn’t know it” or “you (formal: Lei) don’t know it,” depending on context. With a question mark it can be a surprised or rhetorical “Don’t you know?” / “You don’t know?”
target_language_example: Vuole entrare senza biglietto? Non lo sa che è vietato?
native_language_example: He wants to come in without a ticket? Doesn’t he know it’s forbidden?

meaning: “you don’t know (it)” / “you have no idea (about it).”
additional_notes: Used when talking to one person ("sai" = "you know" singular). "Lo" refers to “it/that” (something already mentioned or understood). Often said with surprise or disbelief: "Ah, non lo sai?" / "Come non lo sai?" = “You don’t know?” / “How do you not know?”
target_language_example: Non lo sai? Domani c’è lo sciopero.
native_language_example: You don’t know? There’s a strike tomorrow.

additional_notes: Very common way to say you don’t know. Literally it’s “I don’t know it/that” (lo refers to the thing you’re talking about), but in English you usually just say “I don’t know.” Often used by itself as an answer, or followed by extra info: “Non lo so di preciso” = “I don’t know exactly.”
target_language_example: Scusa, non lo so: non ho visto niente.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know: I didn’t see anything.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a guess, opinion, or warning while admitting you’re not sure. Very common in conversation. You can also hear: "Non so, ma..." (shorter) or "Non lo so, però..." (same meaning).
target_language_example: Non lo so, ma mi sembra una cattiva idea.
native_language_example: I don’t know, but it seems like a bad idea to me.

meaning: "I don’t know, (not...)" (often followed by what you don’t know / don’t think / don’t want).
additional_notes: Used to start a reply by saying you don’t know, and then adding more information that begins with another negation (non): e.g. non ho idea (I have no idea), non molto (not much), non penso (I don’t think so), non voglio (I don’t want…). In speech it can be repeated for emphasis: Non lo so, non lo so!
target_language_example: Non lo so, non credo che sia aperto oggi.
native_language_example: I don’t know, I don’t think it’s open today.

non me ne frega un cazzo

target_language_multi_word_term: non me ne frega un cazzo
meaning: “I don’t give a damn / I don’t give a f***.”
additional_notes: Very vulgar and aggressive way to say you don’t care at all. Often followed by “di + [thing]” (“Non me ne frega un cazzo di X” = “I don’t give a damn about X”). “Me ne” refers to “about it/that.” Avoid in polite conversation; use milder options like “Non mi importa (di...)” or “Non me ne frega niente.”
target_language_example: Non me ne frega un cazzo di quello che pensano gli altri.
native_language_example: I don’t give a f*** what other people think.

meaning: "I don’t care" / "it doesn’t matter to me."
additional_notes: Used to say you are not interested or it doesn’t concern you. The "ne" refers back to what you’re talking about (e.g., "of it/them"): "Non me ne importa delle vostre scarpe" = "I don’t care about your shoes." Very common with "niente" for emphasis: "Non me ne importa niente!" ("I don’t care at all!").
target_language_example: Non me ne importa di quello che dicono gli altri.
native_language_example: I don’t care about what other people say.

additional_notes: Common spoken way to say you can’t recall something. "lo" = “it” (the thing you’re trying to remember), and "me" adds emphasis (“I don’t remember it”). You’ll often hear variants like: "non me lo ricordo bene" (I don’t remember it well), "non me lo ricordo nemmeno" (I don’t remember it either / at all), "non me lo ricordo più" (I don’t remember it anymore).
target_language_example: Scusa, non me lo ricordo: quando è il tuo compleanno?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember: when is your birthday?

meaning: "I won't ..." with Italian pronouns (often: 'I won’t leave/go away' or 'I won’t forget it').
additional_notes: This is the negative form of the clitic pronoun cluster **me ne**. **me** = “to/for me”, and **ne** often means “of it / about it” or “from here/from there,” depending on the verb. It commonly appears with verbs like **andarsene** (to leave/go away), **dimenticarsene** (to forget about it), and **starsene** (to stay/keep oneself). The exact English translation depends on the verb that follows: e.g. **Non me ne vado** = “I’m not leaving,” **Non me ne dimenticherò** = “I won’t forget it.”
target_language_example: Non me ne vado finché non finiamo.
native_language_example: I’m not leaving until we finish.

meaning: "I didn't" (used with verbs like *accorgersi*: "I didn’t notice/realize").
additional_notes: This is a common pronoun + auxiliary chunk that normally needs a past participle after it, e.g. *non me ne sono accorto/a* = “I didn’t notice/realize (it)”. *me* = “to me”, *ne* often means “about it/of it”, *sono* is the auxiliary used with *accorgersi* (which takes *essere*). The ending changes for gender/number: *accorto* (male), *accorta* (female), *accorti/accorte* (plural).
target_language_example: Scusa, non me ne sono accorto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t notice.

additional_notes: non negates the verb, and mi means 'me' or sometimes 'to/for me'. In Italian, mi usually comes before the verb, so non mi + verb often corresponds to English phrases like 'don't ... me', 'doesn't ... me', or 'won't ... forgive me'. In structures like finché ... non ('until'), non can appear without adding a real negative meaning.
target_language_example: Non mi ascolti mai.
native_language_example: You never listen to me.

additional_notes: Literally the negative imperative of "dire" (to tell/say): "don’t tell me." It can be used (1) as a real request not to say something, often followed by "che..." or "così" (e.g., "Non mi dire così" = “Don’t say that to me / Don’t talk to me like that”), and (2) as a stand-alone exclamation of surprise or disbelief, similar to “You don’t say!” or “No way!” Tone is conversational and common in speech.
target_language_example: —Ho trovato due biglietti gratis per il concerto. —Non mi dire!
native_language_example: —I found two free tickets for the concert. —No way!

additional_notes: Used to say that someone never informed you about a fact. Built from: non (not) + mi (to me) + disse (said/told, past historic of dire; in everyday speech you’ll often hear “non mi ha mai detto che …”) + mai (ever/never) + che (that). The verb and pronouns can change: “non ci disse mai che …” (never told us), “non gli dissi mai che …” (I never told him).
target_language_example: Non mi disse mai che avrebbe cambiato lavoro.
native_language_example: He/She never told me that he/she was going to change jobs.

meaning: “(he/she/it) didn’t … to me” / “hasn’t … (me)” (negative with indirect object “me”).
additional_notes: Used with many past tenses that take the auxiliary avere (passato prossimo, trapassato, etc.). It means “(he/she/it) did not” or “has not” with “mi” = “to me” or “me,” depending on the verb. Word order: Non + mi + ha + past participle (e.g., non mi ha detto = “he/she didn’t tell me”). With “più” it often means “no longer” (non mi ha più parlato = “he/she didn’t speak to me anymore”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non mi ha risposto ieri.
native_language_example: Sorry, but he/she didn’t reply to me yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has never happened to you, up to now. It’s typically followed by a past participle (e.g., chiamato/a, pagato/a, amato/a). The past participle may agree with you: -o (male) / -a (female), especially with verbs that take "avere" and a direct object pronoun like "mi".
target_language_example: Non mi ha mai ascoltato.
native_language_example: He has never listened to me.

meaning: '(he/she) never told me' / '(he/she) has never told me'.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone has never told you something. It’s in the past tense (passato prossimo): non + mi (to me) + ha detto (has said/told) + mai (ever/never). The subject (lui/lei, or a name like Mary/Tom) is often stated before it or understood from context. Commonly followed by a clause with che (“that”) or by question words like perché (why), cosa (what), dove (where).
target_language_example: Non mi ha mai detto come si chiama.
native_language_example: He/She never told me what his/her name is.

additional_notes: Used to say that someone has not done something for you or to you. Literally: “not + to me + you have.” It’s followed by a past participle: Non mi hai detto (you didn’t tell me / you haven’t told me), Non mi hai aiutato/a (you didn’t help me), Non mi hai risposto (you didn’t answer me). Often used when complaining or asking why something wasn’t done.
target_language_example: Perché non mi hai detto la verità?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you tell me the truth?

meaning: “you’ve never … (to/for me)” / “you never …” (with a past action).
additional_notes: Used with **passato prossimo** to say someone has *never* done something to/for you up to now. Structure: **non + mi + hai + mai + past participle** (e.g., *non mi hai mai detto / aiutato*). **mi** = “to me/me” (object pronoun). **mai** = “ever,” but with **non** it means “never.” With some verbs, the past participle can agree with the direct object pronoun implied (*Non mi hai mai ascoltata* = said by a woman).
target_language_example: Non mi hai mai spiegato come funziona.
native_language_example: You’ve never explained to me how it works.

non mi hanno mai detto che

target_language_multi_word_term: non mi hanno mai detto che
additional_notes: Used to say you were never informed about a fact. Common pattern: non + indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi) + hanno mai detto + che + clause. Often implies surprise or complaint.
target_language_example: Non mi hanno mai detto che la riunione era stata annullata.
native_language_example: They never told me that the meeting had been canceled.

meaning: I don’t care / it doesn’t matter to me.
additional_notes:
Used to say something is not important to you. Often followed by:
- “se …” + clause: “Non mi importa se piove.” (I don’t care if it rains.)
- “di …” + noun/infinitive: “Non mi importa di essere espulsa.” (I don’t care about being expelled.)
You can intensify it with “più”: “Non mi importa più.” (I don’t care anymore.) and “Non mi importa più niente.” (I don’t care about anything anymore.)
target_language_example: Non mi importa se arriviamo tardi: l’importante è stare insieme.
native_language_example: I don’t care if we arrive late; what matters is being together.

additional_notes: Used to say something doesn’t matter to you or doesn’t interest you. It can refer to a person, a thing, or a detail (often followed by a clause like “non mi interessa come…” = “I don’t care how/what…”). Tone depends on context: it can sound blunt or dismissive, so in polite situations you can soften it (e.g., “non mi interessa molto” = “I’m not very interested”).
target_language_example: Non mi interessa dove vuoi andare, scegli tu.
native_language_example: I don’t care where you want to go— you choose.

meaning: "I don't like the ..." (for masculine plural nouns).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine plural noun starting with i (e.g., i dottori, i ricchi). Italian uses piacere with an inverted structure: literally "the ... are not pleasing to me". For feminine plural you’d say: Non mi piacciono le .... For singular: Non mi piace il/la ....
target_language_example: Non mi piacciono i film horror.
native_language_example: I don't like horror movies.

additional_notes: Used to express dislike. You can follow it with a noun (Non mi piace la mia posizione.) or with a clause introduced by "che/come" (Non mi piace come tratti Raleigh.). You can strengthen it with words like "mica" (not at all / not really) or "per niente" (not at all): "Non mi piace mica" / "Non mi piace per niente."
target_language_example: Non mi piace questo ristorante: è troppo rumoroso.
native_language_example: I don't like this restaurant: it's too noisy.

meaning: “I don’t like the …” (about a masculine singular thing).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”): the thing you don’t like is the grammatical subject (e.g., Il tè verde non mi piace = “Green tea isn’t pleasing to me”). You can swap il for other articles depending on the noun: non mi piace lo / la; non mi piacciono i / gli / le (plural). Word order is flexible, but non mi piace + noun is very common.
target_language_example: Non mi piace il rumore qui dentro.
native_language_example: I don’t like the noise in here.

additional_notes: Common way to say you can’t recall something. Often followed by **se** (“whether/if”): *Non mi ricordo se…* (“I don’t remember if…”). You can add **niente** for emphasis: *Non mi ricordo niente* (“I don’t remember anything”). With a person/thing you can use **di**: *Non mi ricordo di lui/lei* (“I don’t remember him/her”).
target_language_example: Scusa, non mi ricordo il tuo nome.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t remember your name.

meaning: "I don’t feel" (well / guilty / alone / at peace, etc.).
additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb *sentirsi* to describe how you feel physically or emotionally: *non mi sento bene* (I don’t feel well), *non mi sento sola* (I don’t feel alone), *non mi sento in pace* (I don’t feel at peace). Often followed by an adjective or phrase; *io* is usually omitted.
target_language_example: Oggi non mi sento molto bene, resto a casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel very well, I’m staying home.

meaning: "I don’t need it" / "it’s no use to me."
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t needed or useful to you. It comes from "servire" = "to be useful / to be needed" (literally: “it doesn’t serve me”). Often used with a noun: "Non mi serve un avvocato" (I don’t need a lawyer), or by itself when “it” is understood from context.
target_language_example: Grazie, ma non mi serve: ne ho già uno.
native_language_example: Thanks, but I don’t need it: I already have one.

additional_notes: Used to say you have never done/experienced something up to now. It’s made of: non (not) + mi (myself) + sono (I am / I have, auxiliary) + mai (ever/never). It’s typically followed by a past participle: non mi sono mai accorto/a (I never noticed), non mi sono mai fidato/a (I never trusted), non mi sono mai sentito/a (I never felt). The past participle often changes for gender/number: accorto (male), accorta (female).
target_language_example: Non mi sono mai svegliato così presto.
native_language_example: I’ve never woken up this early.

non mi sono mai preoccupato per

target_language_multi_word_term: non mi sono mai preoccupato per
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb preoccupare (preoccuparsi) in the passato prossimo: mi sono preoccupato/a = “I got worried / I worried.” Add mai to mean “never,” and per + person/thing you’re worried about. Change preoccupato to preoccupata if the speaker is female. Often used to emphasize you didn’t feel concern about someone/something.
target_language_example: Non mi sono mai preoccupato per l'esame.
native_language_example: I have never worried about the exam.

meaning: “I don’t feel like (doing something)”; “I’m not in the mood to.”
additional_notes: Used to say you don’t want to do something (because you don’t feel up to it), often in everyday conversation. It’s followed by an infinitive: non mi va di + verbo (e.g., non mi va di uscire). You can change the pronoun: non ti va di… (you don’t feel like), non gli/le va di… (he/she doesn’t feel like), non ci va di… (we don’t feel like).
target_language_example: Oggi non mi va di uscire, resto a casa.
native_language_example: Today I don’t feel like going out; I’m staying home.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened to you or you have never felt/thought something. Literally: "not to me is ever". It often comes before a past participle (e.g., piaciuto/piaciuta, capitato, successo, passato) and agrees in gender/number where needed (piaciuto vs. piaciuta). Common with expressions like "non mi è mai capitato/successo" (it’s never happened to me) and "non mi è mai passato per la testa" (it never crossed my mind).
target_language_example: Non mi è mai successo di perdere il treno.
native_language_example: It’s never happened to me to miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to say you’ve never liked someone or something, from the past up to now. It literally means “it has never pleased me,” so the thing/person you didn’t like is the grammatical subject (e.g., Non mi è mai piaciuto Tom/il Natale). With plural subjects, use piaciuti/piaciute (e.g., Non mi sono mai piaciute le feste). You can also follow it with an infinitive to talk about an activity: Non mi è mai piaciuto andare a scuola (“I never liked going to school”).
target_language_example: Non mi è mai piaciuto questo ristorante, anche se tutti lo adorano.
native_language_example: I’ve never liked this restaurant, even though everyone loves it.

additional_notes: "Non" is the negation (not/don’t) and "ne" is a pronoun meaning "of it / of them" or "about it" (referring back to something already mentioned). It’s very common with verbs like "sapere" and expressions like "avere idea": "non ne so nulla" = "I don’t know anything about it"; "non ne ha idea" = "he/she has no idea". It can also appear with other verbs where English would use "it/them" or "about it": "non ne sarà felice" = "he/she won’t be happy about it".
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non ne so niente.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t know anything about it.

meaning: "you don’t have any" / "you don’t have (any) of it/them."
additional_notes: Uses the pronoun **ne** to mean “(any) of it/them” or “any,” often referring back to something already mentioned (a quantity, a type, etc.). Common with partitive ideas: *Non ne hai?* = “Don’t you have any?” It can also be followed by a noun phrase to mean “you don’t have the right/permission/ability (to do that)”: *Non ne hai il diritto* = “You don’t have the right (to).”
target_language_example: Hai del pane? No, non ne hai più.
native_language_example: Do you have any bread? No, you don’t have any left.

meaning: “I don’t have any (of it/them).” (often: “I have no…”)
additional_notes: Used with **avere** + **ne** to mean you don’t have any of something already mentioned or understood. Very common in fixed expressions like **Non ne ho idea** (“I have no idea”) and with nouns like **voglia**: **Non ne ho voglia** (“I don’t feel like it / I’m not in the mood”). **Ne** roughly means “of it/of them/any.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non ne ho tempo oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I don’t have time for it today.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know something. The little word “ne” means “about it/of it” and refers back to the topic (often it’s already understood from context). You can also hear “non ho idea” (less precise) or “non ne ho la minima idea” (“I have absolutely no idea”).
target_language_example: —Sai dov’è Marco? —Non ne ho idea.
native_language_example: —Do you know where Marco is? —I have no idea.

meaning: "I can’t take it anymore" / "I’m fed up."
additional_notes: Used to express that you’ve reached your limit (with a situation, a place, a person, or something you’re doing). Often followed by **di + noun/infinitive** (e.g., *non ne posso più di aspettare*) or **di/del/della/dei/degli/delle + noun** (e.g., *non ne posso più di questa città*, *non ne posso più delle tisane*). It can also be said alone: *Non ne posso più!* Common in everyday speech and can sound quite strong depending on tone.
target_language_example: Non ne posso più di aspettare in fila.
native_language_example: I can’t take waiting in line anymore.

meaning: “it’s not worth it / it’s not worth the trouble.”
additional_notes: Used to discourage doing something because the effort, risk, or cost isn’t justified. Often said on its own as advice or a warning. "Ne" refers to "about it/for it" (the thing you’re talking about), so the whole phrase is literally like “it’s not worth the effort (of it).”
target_language_example: Lascia perdere: non ne vale la pena.
native_language_example: Forget it: it’s not worth it.

additional_notes: "Non possiamo" is the negative form of "possiamo" (from "potere" = can/to be able to) in the "we" form. It’s usually followed by an infinitive: "non possiamo farlo" = "we can’t do it". You can also use it alone when the action is understood: "Non possiamo." = "We can’t."
target_language_example: Scusa, oggi non possiamo venire.
native_language_example: Sorry, today we can’t come.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is not possible or not allowed. It’s usually followed by a noun (the thing you can’t do) or more information: "Non possiamo fare la foto" (We can’t take the photo), "Non possiamo fare questa cosa da soli" (We can’t do this alone). Common pattern: "non possiamo fare più niente" = "there’s nothing more we can do."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non possiamo fare niente oggi: è troppo tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can't do anything today: it's too late.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to help or take action in a situation. Often followed by “per + someone” (e.g., “Non possiamo fare niente per lei/lui” = “We can’t do anything for her/him”), and it’s commonly softened with “Mi dispiace, ma…” (“I’m sorry, but…”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non possiamo fare niente per lei oggi.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but we can't do anything for you today.

additional_notes: Present-tense form of potere with non. Used to say you are unable to do something, cannot do something, or sometimes that something feels impossible. It is often followed by an infinitive verb, as in non posso restare ('I can't stay').
target_language_example: Non posso venire stasera.
native_language_example: I can't come tonight.

additional_notes: Used to refuse something (a gift, an apology, an offer) or to say you can’t come to terms with a situation/fact (“I can’t accept the fact that…”). Often followed by a noun (non posso accettare il regalo / una scusa) or by “che …” / “il fatto che …”. Can also stand alone: “Non posso accettare.” = “I can’t accept it.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non posso accettare questa offerta.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but I can’t accept this offer.

meaning: “I can’t agree/consent to (the fact) that…” / “I can’t allow that…”
additional_notes: Used to express strong refusal or non-approval. It is typically followed by the subjunctive (congiuntivo), as in: che andiate / che vada. Common in formal or serious contexts (rules, authority, moral objection).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso acconsentire che tu esca così tardi.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, I can’t allow you to go out that late.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise, shock, or disbelief, often before a clause introduced by che (“that”). In careful Italian you’ll often see the subjunctive after che (e.g., Non posso credere che abbia mentito), though in informal speech many people use the indicative (e.g., Non posso credere che sei scappato).
target_language_example: Non posso credere che tu sia già qui!
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’re already here!

meaning: I can’t do anything about it.
additional_notes: Used to express that you’re unable to change a situation, often with a tone of apology or resignation. "Farci" = "do about it" (fare + ci), referring to the situation just mentioned: "Non posso farci niente" = there’s nothing I can do (about that).
target_language_example: Vorrei aiutarti, ma non posso farci niente.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but I can’t do anything about it.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re not able to do something or it’s not possible for you. What comes next can be an action (Non posso fare di più = I can’t do more), something you make/do as a task (Non posso fare la marmellata = I can’t make jam), or an expression like fare tardi (“be late”). Often followed by an object or phrase that completes the meaning.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso fare tutto oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do everything today.

additional_notes: Often followed by **di + infinitive** to mean “I can’t help doing something”: *Non posso fare a meno di ridere* (I can’t help laughing). It can also mean “I can’t do without (something)”: *Non posso fare a meno del caffè* (I can’t do without coffee).
target_language_example: Non posso fare a meno di pensare a te.
native_language_example: I can't help thinking about you.

additional_notes: Used to say you are unable to do something. Often followed by more information, e.g. "senza..." (without...) or "perché..." (because...). You can also say "Non posso farlo" on its own as a complete sentence.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso farlo oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t do it today.

additional_notes: Used to refuse or say something is impossible for you to do, often as a firm boundary. It can be followed by an infinitive (e.g., "Non posso venire" = "I can’t come") or used alone as a short reply ("Non posso." = "I can’t.").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non posso aiutarti oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t help you today.

additional_notes: Used to say that a group of people or things are not able/allowed to do something. It’s made of non (“not”) + possono (they can, from potere). Often followed by an infinitive: non possono venire (they can’t come), non possono uscire (they can’t go out).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non possono entrare.
native_language_example: Sorry, today they can’t come in.

additional_notes: Used with "voi" (you all) or as the polite/formal "you" in some regions. It’s the negative of "potete" (you can/are able to). With an infinitive it means “you can’t do (something)”: "non potete farlo" = you can’t do it. In commands/signs it often means “you must not”: "Non potete entrare!" = You can’t/mustn’t enter.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non potete parcheggiare qui.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t park here.

additional_notes: Uses the imperfect tense of potere (poteva) with non to describe an ongoing/repeated inability in the past, or something that was not possible due to circumstances. It can also appear in a rhetorical question to complain or suggest an alternative: “Non poteva…?” = “Couldn’t you…?”
target_language_example: Ieri non poteva venire perché lavorava.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she couldn’t come because he/she was working.

meaning: “I couldn’t” / “I wasn’t able to” (in the past).
additional_notes: Past tense of potere (“can/to be able to”) in the imperfect: (io) potevo = “I could/was able to”. Used for ongoing situations in the past or to describe inability/it wasn’t possible at that time. Often followed by an infinitive: non potevo farlo (I couldn’t do it), non potevo saperlo (I couldn’t have known), non potevo permettermelo (I couldn’t afford it).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma ieri non potevo venire.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but yesterday I couldn’t come.

meaning: I could never / I would never (do something).
additional_notes: Used to express that you would be unable to do something or would never do it (often for moral/emotional reasons). It’s built from: non (not) + potrei (I could, conditional of potere) + mai (ever/never). Usually followed by an infinitive: non potrei mai farlo (I could never do it).
target_language_example: Non potrei mai mentire ai miei amici.
native_language_example: I could never lie to my friends.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to be anxious about a situation. Often said on its own, or followed by “per …” (e.g., “non preoccuparti per noi” = don’t worry about us). Grammatically it’s the negative informal (tu) imperative of “preoccuparsi” (to worry). For a formal version with Lei, use “non si preoccupi.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, ci penso io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Used to tell someone that something is impossible, not allowed, or not a good idea. It’s the negative of "puoi" (you can), from "potere". Often followed by an infinitive: "non puoi + verb" (e.g., "non puoi entrare" = you can’t enter). Can also be used more emphatically as "non puoi mica..." (informal: you really can’t / you can’t just...).
target_language_example: Non puoi entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: You can’t go in without a ticket.

additional_notes: Means that someone is not able to do something or is not allowed to do it, depending on context. It uses the 3rd person singular of "potere" (può): "lui/lei non può" = "he/she can't". With formal "Lei", it can mean "you can't" (e.g., "Non può fumare" addressed politely/formally). Often followed by an infinitive: "non può + verb" (non può andare, non può fermare).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non può entrare qui.
native_language_example: Sorry, you can’t come in here today.

additional_notes: Used with a past participle in the passive voice to say something is impossible: non può essere + past participle (e.g., fermato, rimossa). It agrees with the thing affected (fermato = masculine singular; rimossa = feminine singular). You can also use it more generally to mean “it can’t be” (impossible/untrue), depending on context.
target_language_example: Questo problema non può essere risolto oggi.
native_language_example: This problem can’t be solved today.

meaning: "It can’t be" / "That can’t be true" ("No way!").
additional_notes: Used either literally to say something is impossible or someone can’t be somewhere (often followed by a place or person: “non può essere con lui”), or as a standalone exclamation to show surprise/disbelief (“Non può essere!”).
target_language_example: Hai già finito? Non può essere!
native_language_example: You’ve already finished? No way!

additional_notes: From "riuscire a" = "to manage to". "Non riesce a" is the 3rd person singular present (he/she/it doesn't manage to). It’s followed by an infinitive: "non riesce a + verb". You can change the subject: "non riesco a" (I can’t), "non riesci a" (you can’t), "non riusciamo a" (we can’t).
target_language_example: Scusa, non riesce a venire oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she can’t make it today.

meaning: "you can't" / "you're not able to" (to manage to do something).
additional_notes: Second-person singular (tu) of "non riuscire a" + infinitive: "non riesci a dormire" = "you can’t sleep". Often suggests difficulty or failure to manage to do something (not just lack of permission). Other common forms: "non riesco a" (I can’t), "non riesce a" (he/she can’t), "non riusciamo a" (we can’t), "non riuscite a" (you all can’t), "non riescono a" (they can’t).
target_language_example: Non riesci a trovare le chiavi?
native_language_example: Can’t you find the keys?

additional_notes: Used to say that you are unable to do something or can't manage it. It is often followed by a + infinitive: non riesco a capire = I can't understand.
target_language_example: Non riesco a dormire stanotte.
native_language_example: I can't sleep tonight.

additional_notes: Used before an infinitive to say you can’t manage to do something (because it’s difficult, not working, or you don’t have the ability in that moment). Structure: "non riesco a" + infinitive (e.g., non riesco a capire, non riesco a dormire).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non riesco a venire oggi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t make it today.

meaning: “I can’t understand / I can’t figure it out.”
additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to understand something or make sense of a situation. Often followed by a question word (perché = why, cosa = what, che/cosa le/gli passa per la testa = what someone is thinking) or by an object (non riesco a capire il perché = I can’t understand why). You can change the subject: non riesci a capire (you can’t), non riesce a capire (he/she can’t), non riusciamo a capire (we can’t).
target_language_example: Scusa, non riesco a capire questa parola.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t understand this word.

additional_notes: Used to express surprise or disbelief. The verb after che often follows Italian sequence-of-tenses: commonly the subjunctive (e.g., "che sia successo"), though in casual speech many people also use the indicative (e.g., "che hai ricordato"). You can also hear "Non riesco a credere a questo!" = "I can’t believe this!"
target_language_example: Non riesco a credere che tu sia già qui.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’re already here.

additional_notes: Literally “I don’t manage to sleep.” Used when you’re unable to fall asleep or stay asleep. You can swap in other verbs after non riesco a… (e.g., non riesco a capire = I can’t understand).
target_language_example: Sono stanco, ma non riesco a dormire.
native_language_example: I’m tired, but I can’t sleep.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to stop an action/habit/thought (often emotional or repetitive). Structure: non riesco a smettere di + infinitive (piangere, ascoltare, pensarci). You can add what you can’t stop thinking about with a + noun/pronoun: non riesco a smettere di pensare a/alla…
target_language_example: Non riesco a smettere di ridere quando lo vedo.
native_language_example: I can’t stop laughing when I see him.

meaning: "I can't manage to / I can't (do it)".
additional_notes: Used to say you’re unable to do something (physically, mentally, or practically), often implying difficulty or repeated failed attempts. It’s followed by an infinitive. The "ad" is the preposition "a" + "d" used before a verb starting with a vowel (e.g., "ad aprire", "ad arrivare"); before consonants you usually see "a" (e.g., "non riesco a dormire").
target_language_example: Scusa, non riesco ad aprire questa bottiglia.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t manage to open this bottle.

meaning: "we can't / we aren't able to" (to do something).
additional_notes: From the verb "riuscire a" = "to manage to / to be able to" + an infinitive. "Non riusciamo a" is the negative, used when something is impossible or difficult (because of circumstances, ability, time, etc.). Often followed by an infinitive: "non riusciamo a dormire". It can imply struggling rather than a simple lack of permission.
target_language_example: Scusa, non riusciamo a venire stasera.
native_language_example: Sorry, we can’t make it tonight.

meaning: “couldn’t / wasn’t able to” (he/she wasn’t managing to).
additional_notes: Imperfect tense of "non riuscire a" + infinitive, used for an ongoing difficulty or repeated inability in the past. It can mean physical inability (non riusciva a camminare) or not being able to bring yourself to do something (non riusciva a dire di no / non riusciva a credere...). Often translated as “couldn’t manage to.”
target_language_example: Era troppo stanco e non riusciva a concentrarsi.
native_language_example: He was too tired and couldn’t concentrate.

additional_notes: From riuscire a (“to manage to / be able to”) + non (not) + più (anymore). Used to say someone has reached a limit and can’t keep doing something. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., reggere, sopportare, contenere, nascondere). Tense can change: non riesco più a… (I can’t anymore), non riuscivo più a… (I couldn’t anymore), non riuscirà più a… (he/she won’t be able to anymore).
target_language_example: Dopo ore di lavoro, non riusciva più a tenere gli occhi aperti.
native_language_example: After hours of work, he couldn’t keep his eyes open anymore.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive (non riuscivo a + verb) to say you were unable to do something in the past, often because it was difficult emotionally or mentally (e.g., believe, understand, stop thinking). It’s the imperfect tense of riuscire (to manage to / succeed in), describing an ongoing situation or repeated difficulty in the past. Present: non riesco a (I can’t).
target_language_example: Non riuscivo a dormire per l’ansia.
native_language_example: I couldn’t sleep because of anxiety.

meaning: "(he/she/it) doesn’t know" or "(he/she/it) can’t / doesn’t know how to."
additional_notes: Used with a 3rd-person singular subject (lui/lei/Lei/it, or a named person/thing). With an infinitive, it often means “doesn’t know how to” (e.g., non sa nuotare = he can’t swim / doesn’t know how to swim). In questions, it can mean “doesn’t he/she know…?” (e.g., Non sa quando ritorna? = Doesn’t he/she know when he/she is coming back?).
target_language_example: Mia sorella non sa guidare.
native_language_example: My sister can’t drive / doesn’t know how to drive.

additional_notes: Uses the present tense of sapere (“to know”) with non ... niente (“not ... anything”). Often followed by di/su (“about”): non sa niente di/su di lui = “he/she doesn’t know anything about him.” You can change the subject: io non so niente, tu non sai niente, loro non sanno niente.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non sa niente di questa storia.
native_language_example: Sorry, he/she doesn’t know anything about this story.

meaning: "you don’t know" / "you can’t" / "you don’t know how to" (said to one person).
additional_notes:
Used with:
- a verb (often infinitive): "non sai + [verb]" = you can’t / you don’t know how to do something (e.g., "Non sai leggere" = You can’t read).
- a clause: "non sai che..." / "non sai cosa..." = you don’t know that... / you don’t know what...
Often sounds critical or accusatory in context (like "You have no idea" / "You don’t know what you’re saying").
target_language_example: Non sai cosa stai dicendo.
native_language_example: You don’t know what you’re saying.

additional_notes: A common way to start a sentence with a reason or situation. It uses the gerund (sapendo) and often means “since/because I/they didn’t know what to do.” Usually the subject is the same as in the main clause (e.g., “Non sapendo cosa fare, ho chiesto aiuto.”).
target_language_example: Non sapendo cosa fare, ho chiamato un amico.
native_language_example: Not knowing what to do, I called a friend.

additional_notes: Past tense (imperfetto) of *sapere* used to describe a previous state of not knowing, often giving background or setting the scene. Common patterns: **non sapevo che + clause** (“I didn’t know that…”), **non sapevo cosa/come/dove + infinitive** (“I didn’t know what/how/where to…”), **non sapevo niente** (“I didn’t know anything”).
target_language_example: Scusa, non sapevo che oggi era il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: Sorry, I didn’t know that today was your birthday.

additional_notes: Used to introduce new or surprising information you just learned. It’s the imperfect of "sapere" (sapevo = I knew), so it often implies you didn’t know at the time (and maybe still didn’t until now). After "che", Italian typically uses the subjunctive in this structure (e.g., che fossi, che avessi, che esistessero, che facessi).
target_language_example: Non sapevo che oggi fosse festa.
native_language_example: I didn’t know that today was a holiday.

additional_notes: It’s the negative conditional of "essere" (sarebbe = would be). Common in hypothetical sentences, especially with "se" (if): "Se..., non sarebbe..." = "If..., it wouldn’t be...". It’s also used in reported speech or expectations: "Credevo che non sarebbe..." = "I thought it wouldn’t...".
target_language_example: Se fosse più tardi, non sarebbe un problema.
native_language_example: If it were later, it wouldn’t be a problem.

additional_notes: Used to make a negative prediction/statement about the future. The subject is often implied from context (it/he/she/that). Common patterns: **non sarà + adjective/noun** (non sarà facile = it won’t be easy; non sarà sufficiente = it won’t be enough), **non sarà così** (it won’t be like that), **non sarà finita** (it won’t be over/finished), **non sarà in grado di + infinitive** (he/she won’t be able to…).
target_language_example: Domani non sarà possibile entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow it won’t be possible to enter without a ticket.

meaning: “(someone) doesn’t … it / doesn’t … about it” (used with verbs that take the pronouns *se* + *ne*, e.g. *accorgersene* = “to notice it”).
additional_notes:
*Non se ne* is not usually a standalone phrase; it’s a chunk you’ll see inside **pronominal verbs** like **accorgersene** (“to notice it”) or expressions like **darsene pensiero** (“to worry about it”).
- **se** = “(to) oneself” (part of the verb: *accorgersi* = to realize/notice)
- **ne** = “of it / about it” (refers back to something previously mentioned)
Common patterns:
- **Non se ne accorge.** = “He/She doesn’t notice (it).”
- **Non se ne dia pensiero.** (formal) = “Don’t worry about it.”
target_language_example: Non se ne sono accorti in tempo.
native_language_example: They didn’t notice it in time.

meaning: "No way / out of the question." (Also: "it won’t be talked about.")
additional_notes: Often used as a firm refusal: "Non se ne parla!" = "No way!" It can also mean "it’s not happening/it won’t be discussed (until...)" as in "fino a lunedì non se ne parla" = "not until Monday." In phrases like "Non se ne parla mai abbastanza", it keeps its literal sense: "it’s never talked about enough." Here, "ne" = "about it" and "se" is an impersonal "one/people" (si).
target_language_example: Uscire stasera? Non se ne parla proprio!
native_language_example: Go out tonight? Absolutely not!

additional_notes: Negative command using the formal Lei form. It comes from the verb “andarsene” (to go away/leave). “se ne” adds the idea of leaving from here/going away. Often used with polite phrases like “La prego” (please) or “Si accomodi” (please, have a seat).
target_language_example: Non se ne vada ancora, la prego.
native_language_example: Please don’t leave yet.

additional_notes: Negative form of "sei" ("you are", for "tu") from the verb "essere" (to be). It’s used before an adjective or noun: "non sei stanco" (you’re not tired), "non sei mio fratello" (you’re not my brother). Often appears with "più" to mean "no longer": "non sei più lo stesso" (you’re not the same anymore).
target_language_example: Non sei pronto per uscire.
native_language_example: You're not ready to go out.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has changed compared to before. It’s the pattern **non + essere + più** followed by an adjective or noun: **Non sei più te stesso** (You’re not yourself anymore), **Non sei più il benvenuto/la benvenuta** (You’re no longer welcome). You can also use it for other persons: **non sono più**, **non è più**, **non siete più**, etc.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non sei più il benvenuto in questa casa.
native_language_example: I'm sorry, but you're no longer welcome in this house.

meaning: “you’re not a …” (talking to one person, masculine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is not a certain type of person/thing: Non sei un + noun/adjective used as a noun (e.g., codardo = coward). It’s 2nd-person singular (tu) of essere: sei. For a feminine noun, use “non sei una …” (e.g., non sei una bugiarda). For formal “you” (Lei), use “non è un/una …”.
target_language_example: Non sei un bugiardo.
native_language_example: You’re not a liar.

meaning: "it’s no use / it’s pointless"; "it doesn’t help."
additional_notes: Used to say something is useless or won’t change the situation. Very common with an infinitive: “Non serve a niente + verb” (e.g., Non serve a niente discutere). It can also be said about a thing/person to mean “(it’s) good for nothing,” which can sound harsh or insulting depending on context.
target_language_example: Non serve a niente preoccuparsi adesso.
native_language_example: There’s no point in worrying now.

additional_notes: Used to negate verbs with si. The si can be reflexive (non si comporta = doesn't behave), reciprocal (non si incontreranno = they won't meet each other), or impersonal/passive (non si compra = you can't buy it / it isn't bought). The exact English translation depends on the verb and context.
target_language_example: In Italia non si mangia la pizza con il cappuccino.
native_language_example: In Italy, people don't eat pizza with cappuccino.

additional_notes: Used with the reflexive verb "lamentarsi" (= to complain). "Non" + "mai" together mean "never." You can add "di ..." to say what someone complains about: "non si lamenta mai di niente" = "never complains about anything."
target_language_example: Mio fratello non si lamenta mai, anche quando è stanco.
native_language_example: My brother never complains, even when he’s tired.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone or tell them not to worry in a polite/formal way. It uses the Lei form (3rd person singular): si + verb, as in “Non si preoccupi, andrà tutto bene.” With friends you often hear the informal version: “Non ti preoccupare.”
target_language_example: Non si preoccupi, posso occuparmene io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can take care of it.

additional_notes: Polite/formal way to reassure someone, used with Lei (e.g., to a stranger, older person, customer). It can stand alone or be followed by “di …” to specify what not to worry about (e.g., “Non si preoccupi di me”). More informal: “Non ti preoccupare.”
target_language_example: Non si preoccupi, ci penso io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’ll take care of it.

additional_notes: Impersonal form with **si** (like “one can’t / people can’t”), used to express impossibility, rules, or what is not allowed/acceptable. It can sound like a general statement (“you just can’t do that”) rather than aimed at one specific person. Often followed by an infinitive: **non si può + verb** (e.g., *non si può discutere così* = “you can’t discuss like this”).
target_language_example: Non si può entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: You can’t enter without a ticket.

meaning: "There's nothing you can do" / "Nothing can be done."
additional_notes: An impersonal expression using "si" + "potere" ("si può" = "one/you can"). It’s used to say a situation can’t be changed or that no solution is possible. Often said as a frustrated statement or as a rhetorical question: "Ma non si può fare niente?" = "So there’s really nothing we can do?"
target_language_example: Ho provato a chiamare, ma non si può fare niente.
native_language_example: I tried calling, but there’s nothing you can do.

additional_notes: Impersonal form with "si" meaning "one/people" + "può" (can). Used to say something is impossible, not allowed, or can’t be done (because of a rule, situation, or practical problem). Often works as a stand-alone reply: "Non si può."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, oggi non si può entrare senza biglietto.
native_language_example: Sorry, today you can’t go in without a ticket.

meaning: you never know; you never can tell.
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty and to justify being cautious or prepared (often like “just in case”). Literally “it’s never known,” with an impersonal "si".
target_language_example: Porta un ombrello: non si sa mai.
native_language_example: Bring an umbrella—you never know (just in case).

meaning: “You can’t hear (it)” / “it can’t be heard”; sometimes “you don’t feel (it)”.
additional_notes: Uses the impersonal/passive “si” with sentire (“to hear/feel”). Often followed by an object: non si sente niente/nulla (“you can’t hear anything”). It can also refer to feelings/engagement: non si sente coinvolto (“doesn’t feel involved”).
target_language_example: Scusi, non si sente bene: può ripetere?
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t hear well—can you repeat?

additional_notes: Used to say someone is unwell (physically or sometimes emotionally). It’s the negative form of “si sente bene” (“feels well”). “Si” is the reflexive pronoun used with “sentirsi” (to feel). Most commonly used about a third person (he/she/they, or a polite form), e.g., “Lei non si sente bene.” For “I don’t feel well,” use “non mi sento bene.”
target_language_example: Mia moglie non si sente bene, quindi resto con lei.
native_language_example: My wife doesn’t feel well, so I’m staying with her.

meaning: “it’s not about …” / “it’s not a matter of …”
additional_notes: Impersonal expression from **(non) si tratta di + noun/pronoun/infinitive**. It’s used to correct someone or clarify the real issue: *Non si tratta di me* = “This isn’t about me.” Often said firmly in arguments or explanations. (Positive form: **Si tratta di…** = “It’s about… / It’s a matter of…”.)
target_language_example: Non si tratta di soldi: si tratta di rispetto.
native_language_example: It’s not about money; it’s about respect.

meaning: “you can’t see” / “it can’t be seen” (there is no visibility).
additional_notes: Impersonal form with **si**: it means something isn’t visible (because it’s dark, hidden, missing, etc.). Often used with **niente/nessuno/da nessuna parte** (“you can’t see anything/anyone/anywhere”). With time expressions like **da un migliaio di anni**, it can also mean “it hasn’t been seen (for…)”.
target_language_example: È troppo buio: non si vede niente.
native_language_example: It’s too dark: you can’t see anything.

meaning: "didn’t / hasn’t" (used with si + è in the past tense).
additional_notes:
Used in the passato prossimo (past) with verbs that take essere. 
- With a reflexive verb (si = himself/herself/yourself): "Non si è presentato" = "He didn’t show up." 
- With impersonal si (meaning “people/one” in general): "Non si è fatto niente" = "Nothing was done." 
Word order is fixed: non + si + è + past participle (e.g., non si è lamentato, non si è guardato).
target_language_example: Ieri non si è visto nessuno in ufficio.
native_language_example: Yesterday nobody was seen at the office / Nobody showed up at the office.

additional_notes: Used to say something has never happened up to now. It’s common with the passato prossimo: "non" + "si è" (or "si sono") + "mai" + past participle. With reflexive verbs you’ll often see it with a pronoun too: "Non si è mai perdonato" = “He never forgave himself.” For plural: "Non si sono mai sposati" = “They never got married.”
target_language_example: Non si è mai lamentato del lavoro.
native_language_example: He has never complained about work.

additional_notes: 1st person plural negative of essere (“to be”). Used before a noun/adjective or a place phrase: Non siamo una squadra. / Non siamo pronti. / Non siamo a casa. Often followed by articles or prepositions (al, alla, una, dei/degli/delle, etc.).
target_language_example: Scusa, non siamo pronti.
native_language_example: Sorry, we’re not ready.

additional_notes: Used to correct an assumption or clarify that one fact does not imply another. Often follows a statement (or "solo perché" = "just because") and is followed by the subjunctive: "non significa che sia...", "non significa che dobbiamo...".
target_language_example: Ha detto di essere stanco, ma non significa che non venga alla festa.
native_language_example: He said he’s tired, but that doesn’t mean he won’t come to the party.

additional_notes: Used to say you don't know or aren't sure. It's the 1st-person singular form of sapere ('to know'), so it specifically means 'I don't know'. Often followed by a question word or an infinitive clause, as in non so cosa fare ('I don't know what to do').
target_language_example: Scusa, non so dove sia la stazione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know where the station is.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question or uncertainty about a specific thing to do/say/think, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., non so che fare/dire) or by a full clause (non so che succedeva / non so che pensi). In everyday speech you’ll also hear the shorter form "non so cosa" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Sono stanco e non so che dire.
native_language_example: I’m tired and I don’t know what to say.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t know the way/method to do something, or you can’t understand how something is possible. It can be followed by a clause ("Non so come farà...") or used alone at the end of a sentence meaning "I don’t know how (to help/do it)." Often expresses confusion, disbelief, or uncertainty.
target_language_example: Vorrei aiutarti, ma non so come.
native_language_example: I’d like to help you, but I don’t know how.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re unsure of the way/method to do something, often followed by an infinitive (e.g., dirlo, esprimerlo, prenderlo, ringraziare). It can also introduce an indirect question: "Non so come dirtelo" = "I don’t know how to tell you." With object pronouns it’s very common (dirtelo = dirlo + te lo; ringraziarti = ringraziare + ti).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non so come aiutarti in questo momento.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know how to help you right now.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know what something is, what you’re doing, or what’s happening. It’s typically followed by a clause (often with a verb in the present continuous: “sto …”): “Non so cosa sto facendo” = “I don’t know what I’m doing.” You can also hear “Non so cosa dire” (“I don’t know what to say”).
target_language_example: Non so cosa dire adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t know what to say now.

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question about a place/location. It’s often followed by an infinitive (non so dove andare = “I don’t know where to go”) or by a full clause (non so dove siamo = “I don’t know where we are”). You can also add it before other verbs like trovare (“to find”), mettere (“to put”), ecc.
target_language_example: Scusa, non so dove sia la fermata dell’autobus.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know where the bus stop is.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you don’t know something at all (often with surprise, frustration, or annoyance). It’s commonly followed by a question word (chi, cosa, dove, perché, come) or by più (“anymore”): “Non so neanche più…”
target_language_example: Scusa, non so neanche dove ho messo le chiavi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t even know where I put the keys.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that you really don’t know something (often with surprise, frustration, or feeling lost). It’s commonly followed by a question word or phrase: chi (who), cosa (what), dove (where), da dove (from where), come (how), da dove cominciare (where to start).
target_language_example: Non so nemmeno come si chiama.
native_language_example: I don't even know what his/her name is.

additional_notes: Common way to say you have no information or knowledge. Italian normally uses double negatives (non + niente) where English uses a single negative. Often followed by “di” + topic/person: “non so niente di...” = “I don’t know anything about...”.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non so niente di questa storia.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don't know anything about this story.

meaning: "I don’t know anything about …" / "I know nothing about …"
additional_notes: Used to say you have no knowledge or experience of a person, thing, or topic. It’s followed by "di" + noun/pronoun (e.g., "Non so niente di Tom"), or "di" + a clause introduced by "ciò che" (e.g., "Non so niente di ciò che fa...").
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, non so niente di questa città.
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t know anything about this city.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t know the reason for something. Often followed by a full clause (non so perché + verb: "non so perché è...", "non so perché sto..."). In speech you may also hear it shortened to "non so perché, ma..." = "I don’t know why, but...".
target_language_example: Non so perché, ma oggi mi sento nervoso.
native_language_example: I don’t know why, but today I feel nervous.

additional_notes: Used to introduce uncertainty about something that may be true or may happen. It’s often followed by the present tense ("non so se riesco" = I don’t know if I can) or by another clause with "se" for alternatives ("non so se… o se…" = I don’t know whether… or whether…).
target_language_example: Non so se domani piove, quindi porto l’ombrello.
native_language_example: I don’t know if it will rain tomorrow, so I’ll bring an umbrella.

additional_notes: Negative form of sono (from essere, “to be”). Italian often drops the subject pronoun, so non sono can mean “I am not” or “they are not,” depending on context.
target_language_example: Non sono pronto.
native_language_example: I'm not ready.

additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) to say something hasn’t happened/arrived/been done up to now. It’s often followed by a past participle in the passive: “non sono ancora state trovate/scritte” (“they still haven’t been found/written”). Person/number can change (non sei ancora, non siamo ancora, non sono ancora).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma non sono ancora pronto.
native_language_example: Sorry, but I’m not ready yet.

meaning: 'I am/they are never' or 'I/they have never' (with essere).
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (present: sono; past: sono stato/a/i/e) to express 'never'. The exact English meaning depends on tense and context: present + a place/habit = 'I’m never…' (Non sono mai a casa la domenica.); past participle = 'I’ve never…' / 'I never…' (Non sono mai uscito/a…). Note agreement in the past participle with essere: sono mai tornata, sono mai cambiato.
target_language_example: Non sono mai stato a Roma.
native_language_example: I've never been to Rome.

meaning: "I have never been" / "I was never" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used by a female speaker: "sono stata" is the past of "essere" (to be), and "mai" means "ever/never". It’s a common way to say you have never been in a certain state or situation up to now (e.g., good at something, in love, so happy). For a male speaker: "non sono mai stato". You can also add emphasis with "così": "Non sono mai stata così felice" = "I’ve never been so happy."
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata a Roma, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome, but I’d like to go.

meaning: "I have never been" / "I’ve never been" (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to say you have never been in a place or situation before. It’s the negative of the present perfect with "essere": "sono stata" = "I have been" (female speaker), "non" = not, "mai" = ever/never. Common with places: "Non sono mai stata in Canada". For a man: "non sono mai stato". You can also add "neanche" to mean "not even".
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata a Roma, ma vorrei andarci.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome, but I’d like to go.

meaning: “I have never been to …” (said by a woman).
additional_notes: Used to say you have never visited a place. The verb is in the passato prossimo (sono stata). Change it depending on the speaker: non sono mai stato a… (man); non siamo mai stati/e a… (we); non è mai stato/a a… (he/she). Common with cities/countries/islands; use a + place name.
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata a Roma, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I’ve never been to Rome, but I’d like to go there.

meaning: "I've never been to/in" (said by a woman).
additional_notes:
Used to say you have never visited a place. 
- donna: non sono mai stata in… 
- uomo: non sono mai stato in… 
With countries, regions, and cities you usually use “in” (in America, in Cina, in Florida).
target_language_example: Non sono mai stata in Italia, ma mi piacerebbe andarci.
native_language_example: I've never been to Italy, but I'd like to go there.
