additional_notes: Used to indicate the person responsible for an action, especially in formal or dramatic contexts (e.g., something happens, is destroyed, or someone is killed “at the hands of” someone). It often appears with passive forms like "fu/è stato" (was/has been).
target_language_example: Il castello fu distrutto per mano di un esercito invasore.
native_language_example: The castle was destroyed at the hands of an invading army.

additional_notes: Usually means something is done for your benefit or on your behalf. In some expressions, English may translate it differently: era preoccupata per me = she was worried about me; tenere qualcosa per me = keep something to myself.
target_language_example: Puoi aprire la porta per me?
native_language_example: Can you open the door for me?

meaning: “for me, it is…” / “to me, it is…”.
additional_notes: Used to give your personal opinion, judgment, or perspective about something (“in my view”). It’s often followed by an adjective or description: Per me è diverso/innocente/importante. It can also appear inside a longer sentence (e.g., “che per me è…” = “which, for me, is…”). Not the same as “il tuo amore per me è…” (“your love for me is…”), where “per me” means “for me” (the recipient).
target_language_example: Per me è un buon ristorante, ma è un po' caro.
native_language_example: For me, it’s a good restaurant, but it’s a bit expensive.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens using a tool, method, or intermediary. Common in formal/written Italian; in everyday speech you often hear alternatives like "con" (with) or "tramite" (via/through).
target_language_example: Ti contatteremo per mezzo di e-mail.
native_language_example: We’ll contact you by email.

additional_notes: Uses the preposition "per" to show who something is intended for (a gift, medicine, a cake) or a dedication/toast. With singular family members in Italian, you often use the possessive without an article: "mio padre" (not *"il mio padre"* in most everyday contexts). You may also see it in formal identifications: "Per mio padre, [Name]" = "For my father, [Name]" (e.g., on a dedication or document).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un regalo per mio padre.
native_language_example: I bought a gift for my father.

meaning: for many years; for a long time.
additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted in the past or up to the present. It often follows the verb or comes at the end of the sentence. Similar idea to "per molto tempo" (for a long time).
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per molti anni.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for many years.

additional_notes: Used to say that something lasts/d lasted a long period. Often placed after the verb or at the end of the sentence. As a question ("Per molto tempo?") it means "For a long time?" to confirm or show surprise.
target_language_example: Ho aspettato per molto tempo, ma non è arrivato nessuno.
native_language_example: I waited for a long time, but nobody arrived.

meaning: not at all; for nothing / in vain.
additional_notes: Often used with a negative to mean “not at all” (Non mi piace per niente. = I don’t like it at all.). It can also mean “for nothing / in vain,” especially about doing something with no result or purpose (Siamo venuti per niente. = We came for nothing.). As a standalone answer, “Per niente.” means “Not at all.” / “You’re welcome.” Depending on context, “Non per niente...” can mean “It’s no coincidence that...” / “No wonder...”
target_language_example: Ho aspettato un’ora, ma lui non è arrivato: ho perso tempo per niente.
native_language_example: I waited an hour, but he didn’t show up: I wasted my time for nothing.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition "per" + the pronoun "noi" to say that something is intended for you/your group, done to help you/your group, or meant to benefit you/your group. In slogans like "Vota/Voti per noi!", it means "vote for us".
target_language_example: Puoi prenotare un tavolo per noi?
native_language_example: Can you book a table for us?

meaning: just in case; for any eventuality.
additional_notes: Used to say you want to be prepared if something unexpected happens. Common with doing something “extra” (bringing, writing down, preparing) as a precaution. You’ll also hear the shorter variant “per ogni evenienza” without changing the meaning.
target_language_example: Porto una batteria esterna per ogni evenienza.
native_language_example: I bring a power bank just in case.

additional_notes: Used to say something is true only at the present moment, with the idea that it may change later. It can appear at the beginning of the sentence ("Per ora, ...") or at the end ("... per ora").
target_language_example: Per ora va tutto bene, poi vediamo.
native_language_example: For now everything is fine, then we’ll see.

meaning: for hours and hours; for a very long time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something lasted a long time (often longer than expected). Common with verbs like aspettare (to wait), piovere (to rain), parlare (to talk), camminare (to walk). The repetition "ore e ore" adds emphasis.
target_language_example: Abbiamo parlato per ore e ore al telefono.
native_language_example: We talked on the phone for hours and hours.

meaning: "to talk/speak with" (in order to talk with).
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose: *per parlare* = “to/in order to talk.” Add **con + person** for “with [someone].” Often used after verbs of coming/being somewhere (*venire*, *essere qui*) or to explain why you did something.
target_language_example: Sono qui per parlare con il dottore.
native_language_example: I'm here to talk with the doctor.

additional_notes: A polite expression used to make a request or appeal, similar to "please" in English. It often comes at the end of a sentence. In everyday Italian, "per favore" is more common.
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per piacere.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to hand you something or give you something. **Dammi** is the imperative of **dare** (“to give”) + **mi** (“to me”) attached: **da’ + mi = dammi**. Often followed by a noun (e.g., *dammi una penna*) or something abstract (e.g., *dammi la tua attenzione* = “give me your attention”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, dammi il menu.
native_language_example: Please, give me the menu.

meaning: "Please, give me …" (addressing "you" plural or a polite/formal "you").
additional_notes: "Datemi" is the command form of "dare" (to give) for "voi" (you all). It’s used when speaking to more than one person, or as a polite/formal way to address a single person in some contexts (e.g., in customer service). Often followed by what you want: "Per piacere, datemi il menù" / "...due hot dog".
target_language_example: Per piacere, datemi un caffè e un bicchiere d’acqua.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee and a glass of water.

meaning: 'Please, (to me)…' used to make a polite request (often with 'mi' + a verb).
additional_notes: Common pattern for polite requests: “Per piacere, mi + verb (Lei form)” = “Please + verb (for me).” Here “mi” is an object pronoun meaning “to me/me,” used with verbs like ascoltare (listen), passare (pass), prestare (lend), perdonare (forgive), richiamare (call back). Often paired with formal “Lei” verb forms (e.g., mi ascolti, mi passi) to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi può dire dov’è la stazione?
native_language_example: Please, can you tell me where the station is?

meaning: "Please call me" (on the phone / contact me).
additional_notes: Used as a polite request. "Mi chiami" is the polite (Lei) form, like saying “please call me.” For an informal request to a friend (tu), you’d usually say "Per favore, chiamami". It can also be followed by a name (“Call me Joe”) or a time (“this evening/tonight”).
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi chiami domani mattina.
native_language_example: Please call me tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request, especially with strangers, in shops, restaurants, or formal situations. “Mi dia” is the formal (Lei) command form of dare (“to give”). For friends/family you’d usually say “Per favore, dammi …” or “Mi dai …?”. You can add what you want after it: “mi dia un caffè”, “mi dia la borsa”, etc.
target_language_example: Per piacere, mi dia un caffè.
native_language_example: Please, give me a coffee.

meaning: 'please, speak' (polite request to more than one person or to someone you address with 'voi').
additional_notes: "Per piacere" means "please." "Parlate" is the present-tense imperative for "you (plural) speak"; it’s used when talking to a group, or as a polite/formal address to one person in some contexts/regions. It’s often followed by "con ..." (with/to someone) or "in ..." (in a language), and can be modified with adverbs like "più forte" (louder) or "più lentamente" (more slowly).
target_language_example: Per piacere, parlate più lentamente: non capisco bene.
native_language_example: Please, speak more slowly: I don’t understand well.

additional_notes: Used to politely ask someone to come somewhere, addressing them with Lei (formal “you”). Venga is the formal command form of venire (“to come”). For an informal request to a friend, you’d say: Per favore/piacere, vieni. It can also introduce polite instructions like “come tomorrow” or “come well-dressed” (venga vestito/a bene).
target_language_example: Per piacere, venga qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please, come here for a moment.

additional_notes: Commonly used to say something almost happened, often in the pattern: “Per poco non + verb” (e.g., “Per poco non cadevo” = “I almost fell”). Literally it’s “for little,” but in this usage it means “almost.”
target_language_example: Per poco non perdevo il treno.
native_language_example: I almost missed the train.

meaning: "in order to be able to" (so that someone can).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: *per* + infinitive *potere* + another infinitive. Often followed by a verb like *fare, andare, studiare*, etc. You can use it with different subjects: *Sono venuto per poter parlare con te* (“I came so I can talk with you”). In everyday speech, *per* + infinitive is also common without *poter* when ability isn’t the focus.
target_language_example: Ho messo la sveglia per poter alzarmi presto.
native_language_example: I set an alarm so I can get up early.

meaning: so that I can rest; in order to be able to rest.
additional_notes: Used to express purpose with **per + infinitive**. **potermi** = **potere** (to be able to) + **mi** (myself/me), so it literally means “to be able (for me)”. Commonly follows a main clause like *Mi fermo…* (I’m stopping…) or *Ho bisogno di una pausa…* (I need a break…).
target_language_example: Mi fermo un attimo per potermi riposare.
native_language_example: I’m stopping for a moment so I can rest.

additional_notes: Used to say what you eat/have at lunchtime, or to invite someone to stay for lunch ("Resta per pranzo" = "Stay for lunch"). Often answers questions like "Cosa mangi per pranzo?" (What do you eat for lunch?).
target_language_example: Oggi mangiamo pasta per pranzo.
native_language_example: Today we’re having pasta for lunch.

additional_notes: Used to say what happens first in time or what you should do first in a sequence of actions. Often placed at the beginning of a sentence as an introductory phrase: “Per prima cosa, …” It can also appear later: “Cosa faresti per prima cosa?” = “What would you do first?”
target_language_example: Per prima cosa, devo chiamare il dottore.
native_language_example: First of all, I have to call the doctor.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something before everyone else, often about taking turns (speaking, going, choosing, being served). It can refer to a person ("io/tu/lui per primo") or to order in a sequence ("porterò lui per primo" = "I’ll take him first").
target_language_example: Chi vuole parlare per primo?
native_language_example: Who wants to speak first?

meaning: for a few days; for a couple of days.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts for a short period of several days (not exact). Common with verbs like restare/rimanere (to stay), stare (to be/stay), fermarsi (to stop/stay), or with actions done over a short span of days.
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per qualche giorno, poi torno a casa.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a few days, then I’m going home.

meaning: for a few minutes; for a little while (minutes).
additional_notes: Used to say an action or situation lasts a short, not exact amount of time (usually just several minutes). Common in requests ("Puoi aspettare/lasciarci...") and announcements ("sospese per qualche minuto").
target_language_example: Aspetta qui per qualche minuto, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait here for a few minutes, please.

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something, similar to “perché?” but a bit more formal/explicit. It can be a direct question (Per quale motivo mi hai chiamato?) or part of a longer sentence (Non so per quale motivo...).
target_language_example: Per quale motivo non vuoi venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why don’t you want to come with us?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason something is happening. It’s a more formal/explicit version of "perché?" and is common in careful speech or writing. Often followed by a full sentence (e.g., "Per quale ragione sei qui...?"), and you can swap "qui" and "qua" with no real change in meaning.
target_language_example: Per quale ragione non vuoi venire con noi?
native_language_example: Why don’t you want to come with us?

meaning: as much as; as far as (to the extent that).
additional_notes: Used to express extent/degree, often followed by an adjective or adverb like possibile (as much as possible), riguarda (as far as … is concerned), or ne so (as far as I know). In many cases it introduces a limit or scope: “to the extent possible.”
target_language_example: Cerco di aiutarti per quanto posso.
native_language_example: I try to help you as much as I can.

additional_notes: Used to ask about duration (the length of time something lasts), often with verbs like aspettare (wait), rimanere (stay), essere (be), prendere in prestito (borrow). In questions it’s very common at the start: Per quanto tempo...?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Italy?

meaning: "how long has ...?" / "for how long have you (formal) ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration. It’s often followed by a past participle (passato prossimo) to mean “How long have you/he/she...?”: "Per quanto tempo ha lavorato qui?". "Ha" can mean “has” (he/she/it has) or “have” with formal "Lei" (you).
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo ha vissuto a Roma?
native_language_example: How long have you lived in Rome?

meaning: "How long were you...?/How long have you been...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about the duration of a state or stay, followed by a past participle (e.g., sei stato/a, sei rimasto/a, sei restato/a, sei stata innamorata). Choose the ending to match the person’s gender/number: sei stato (male), sei stata (female). Often followed by a place or situation: a Roma, in Giappone, allo zoo, innamorato/a di qualcuno.
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo sei stato in Italia?
native_language_example: How long were you in Italy?

meaning: "How long were you (all)?" / "For how long did you (all) stay...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration with "voi" (you plural) or the polite "Lei" in formal speech (same verb form: siete). It’s usually followed by a past participle (e.g., "siete rimasti/e", "siete stati/e") and/or a place: "Per quanto tempo siete rimasti a Caracas?" The past participle can agree in gender/number: "stati" (mixed/masculine plural) and "state" (feminine plural).
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo siete rimasti in Italia?
native_language_example: How long did you stay in Italy?

meaning: 'how long has/was' (asking the duration of something).
additional_notes: Used to ask about duration. It’s typically followed by a past participle with the auxiliary verb essere (è + stato/a, è rimasto/a, è restato/a, etc.). The past participle often agrees with the subject: è rimasto (he stayed) / è rimasta (she stayed). Often completed with a place or situation: Per quanto tempo è stata via? = How long was she away?
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo è stata in Italia?
native_language_example: How long was she in Italy?

meaning: for how long; for as much/as many as.
additional_notes: Used in questions about duration: "Per quanto (tempo)...?" = "For how long...?" It can also refer to an amount (less common in beginner use): "per quanto" + number/quantity = "for as much/as many as" (e.g., for six or seven months). Often paired with "tempo" (time) or a stated period.
target_language_example: Per quanto tempo resti a Roma?
native_language_example: How long are you staying in Rome?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the topic you’re talking about (often followed by a noun or pronoun): per quanto riguarda il lavoro, tua sorella, me, ecc. It’s a fairly formal/neutral connector, common in speech and writing. Often interchangeable with "riguardo a" or "per quanto concerne" (more formal).
target_language_example: Per quanto riguarda la cena, possiamo mangiare alle otto.
native_language_example: As for dinner, we can eat at eight.

meaning: "as far as" (someone knows) / "for what" (e.g., "for what it's worth").
additional_notes: Commonly used with verbs like "sapere" to limit a statement to the information available: "Per quel che ne so" = "As far as I know." Often appears as "Per quel che ne sappiamo" (as far as we know) or in the fixed expression "Per quel che vale" = "For what it's worth."
target_language_example: Per quel che ne so, oggi il museo è chiuso.
native_language_example: As far as I know, the museum is closed today.

meaning: "for what" / "because of what" (for something that happened or was done).
additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or cause, usually followed by a clause with **che** (e.g., *per quello che hai detto/fatto*). Common after verbs and expressions about feelings or reactions: *arrabbiarsi per...*, *essere triste/furioso per...*, *incolpare qualcuno per...*, *perdonare qualcuno per...*.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che ho detto ieri.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for what I said yesterday.

meaning: for what he/she has done; for what he/she did
additional_notes:
Used to refer to a specific action someone did/has done, often with the idea of consequences (punishment, blame, payment). The auxiliary and ending agree with the subject:
- per quello che ho fatto = for what I did/have done
- per quello che hai fatto = for what you did/have done
- per quello che hanno fatto = for what they did/have done
Note: with feminine subject it becomes *per quello che ha fatta* only in some contexts with object pronouns/older usage; in standard modern Italian you usually keep *fatto* regardless.
target_language_example: Tom verrà punito per quello che ha fatto.
native_language_example: Tom will be punished for what he did.

meaning: 'for what you did' / 'for what you have done'.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific action someone did (often something already known in the conversation). Common after verbs expressing feelings or judgments like rispettare (respect), perdonare (forgive), odiare (hate), ringraziare (thank), biasimare (blame). The tense hai fatto is passato prossimo, implying a completed action with relevance now.
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che hai fatto.
native_language_example: I'm sorry for what you did.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to your previous words, often in apologies or when asking if someone is upset. Common with "Mi dispiace" / "Mi scusi" and adjectives like "(essere) arrabbiato". You can change the subject: "per quello che hai detto" (you said), "per quello che abbiamo detto" (we said), "per quello che ha detto" (he/she said).
target_language_example: Non volevo offenderti per quello che ho detto.
native_language_example: I didn’t mean to offend you with what I said.

meaning: for what happened; because of what happened.
additional_notes: Used to refer back to a specific event that has occurred. Often follows expressions of blame, apology, explanations, or consequences (e.g., "I blame myself...", "the lines are busy..."). In speech it can also be shortened to "per quello che è successo" as a standalone answer ("Yes, about what happened"). Note: "successo" here means "happened/occurred," not "success."
target_language_example: Mi dispiace per quello che è successo.
native_language_example: I’m sorry for what happened.

additional_notes: Literally means "for this." It can refer back to something already mentioned (for example, a task, object, or situation), and at the start of a sentence it often means "for this reason" or "that's why."
target_language_example: Per questo non voglio aspettare.
native_language_example: That's why I don't want to wait.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the reason or explanation for what was just said. Very common with "è": "(Ed) è per questo che…" = "And that's why…". It can also appear in negative questions: "Non è per questo che…?" = "Isn't that why…?".
target_language_example: È per questo che dobbiamo partire adesso.
native_language_example: That's why we have to leave now.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened unintentionally or due to an error. It commonly goes with verbs like prendere (to take), fare (to do), dire (to say), and can be placed after the verb or near the action it describes (e.g., "Ho preso per sbaglio...", "Per sbaglio ho...", "L'ho fatto per sbaglio").
target_language_example: Scusa, ho chiamato per sbaglio il numero sbagliato.
native_language_example: Sorry, I accidentally called the wrong number.

additional_notes: Means “forever / always,” often with the idea of something lasting indefinitely. It can also mean “for good” when talking about leaving or something ending permanently (e.g., “se n’è andato, forse per sempre” = “he left, maybe for good”). Common in emotional phrases like “addio per sempre” (“goodbye forever”).
target_language_example: Non voglio perderti per sempre.
native_language_example: I don’t want to lose you forever.

meaning: on the street; out in the street (sometimes: homeless).
additional_notes: Often means being/meeting someone outside while walking or passing by (“in the street”). In contexts like vivere/dormire per strada, it means living/sleeping on the street (without a home).
target_language_example: L'ho visto per strada mentre andavo al lavoro.
native_language_example: I saw him on the street while I was going to work.

meaning: 'to study French' / 'in order to study French'.
additional_notes: Uses **per + infinitive** to express purpose (“in order to…”). The verb stays in the infinitive (**studiare**). You can replace **il francese** with another subject: *per studiare l’italiano / per studiare la matematica*.
target_language_example: Ho scaricato un’app per studiare il francese.
native_language_example: I downloaded an app to study French.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is intended for, given to, suggested for, or done for someone's benefit. After the preposition per, Italian uses te, not tu.
target_language_example: Questo regalo è per te.
native_language_example: This gift is for you.

meaning: in time; early enough (before it’s too late).
additional_notes: Used to say that something happens with enough time to spare, often to avoid missing a deadline, train, appointment, etc. Common with verbs like arrivare (to arrive), essere (to be), finire (to finish), and in phrases like: “Siamo arrivati per tempo” (We arrived in time/early enough).
target_language_example: Siamo partiti per tempo per non perdere il treno.
native_language_example: We left early enough so we wouldn’t miss the train.

meaning: on the ground; onto the ground.
additional_notes: Used with verbs of putting/throwing to mean “onto the ground” (e.g., gettare/posare per terra). With verbs describing position it means “on the ground” (e.g., stare/steso per terra). In some contexts it implies “on the floor” indoors. Common in set phrases like "dormire per terra" (sleep on the floor/ground) and actions done downward like "sputare per terra" (spit on the ground).
target_language_example: Ho lasciato le chiavi per terra vicino alla porta.
native_language_example: I left the keys on the floor near the door.

meaning: 'to go back home' / 'in order to return home.'
additional_notes: Used after a verb to express purpose ("per" + infinitive = "to/in order to"). "Tornare" means "to return/come back"; "a casa" means "home" (literally "to house"). You’ll often hear it with travel/transport words like "volo" (flight), "passaggio" (ride), "soldi" (money).
target_language_example: Mi serve un taxi per tornare a casa.
native_language_example: I need a taxi to get back home.

additional_notes: Used in two very common ways: (1) in math to mean multiplication ("X per tre" = "X times three"); (2) to express duration/quantity with a time or unit word ("per tre minuti/notti" = "for three minutes/nights"). You’ll often see it as part of a longer phrase like "in fila per tre" (= in rows of three / three abreast).
target_language_example: Rimaniamo qui per tre giorni.
native_language_example: Let’s stay here for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted. It often goes with the passato prossimo (e.g., ho abitato/ho vissuto/ho lavorato/sono stato) to describe a completed period of time in the past. You can swap the number: per due anni, per cinque anni, etc.
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per tre anni.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for three years.

additional_notes: Used with time expressions to say how long something lasts (duration). Often follows verbs like stare (to stay), rimanere (to remain), essere (to be) or describes weather/events. Not the same as "in tre giorni" (= in three days, within three days).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a Roma per tre giorni.
native_language_example: We stayed in Rome for three days.

additional_notes: Used to say how long something lasted (duration). It can refer to time in the past, present, or future. Often used with verbs like studiare (to study), vivere (to live), uscire con (to date/go out with), non vedere (not see), etc.
target_language_example: Lavorerò a Milano per tre mesi.
native_language_example: I will work in Milan for three months.

additional_notes: Used with an action or state to say its duration. Often follows the verb: “aspettare per tre ore” (to wait for three hours), “studiare per tre ore” (to study for three hours). You can change the number: “per due ore”, “per mezz’ora”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo camminato per tre ore senza fermarci.
native_language_example: We walked for three hours without stopping.

meaning: for the whole (time period); for the entire.
additional_notes: Used to say something continues during an entire period of time. It’s usually followed by a feminine singular noun (la mattina, la settimana, la sera, la vita). With masculine nouns you use “per tutto il” (per tutto il giorno). With plural nouns: “per tutta/e i/le” (e.g., per tutti i giorni, per tutte le settimane). In “per tutta la famiglia”, it means “for the whole family” (for everyone in the family), not time.
target_language_example: Resterò qui per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: I’ll stay here all night.

additional_notes: Used with a following noun phrase introduced by "di/del/della/dei..." (e.g., "per tutta la durata del film") to mean that something happens continuously from beginning to end. Often placed at the start of the sentence for emphasis ("Per tutta la durata della visita...").
target_language_example: Per tutta la durata del viaggio, abbiamo parlato e riso.
native_language_example: For the whole duration of the trip, we talked and laughed.

meaning: for the whole morning / all morning.
additional_notes: Used with a duration (how long something lasts). It often implies continuously or throughout the morning. You can swap in other time periods: per tutto il giorno (all day), per tutta la settimana (all week).
target_language_example: Abbiamo camminato per tutta la mattina.
native_language_example: We walked all morning.

meaning: all night (long); for the whole night.
additional_notes: Used with an action that lasts continuously throughout the night. Often follows a verb (e.g., dormire/studiare/ballare/aspettare per tutta la notte).
target_language_example: Abbiamo studiato per tutta la notte.
native_language_example: We studied all night.

meaning: for his/her whole life; all his/her life.
additional_notes: Used to say something was true throughout someone’s entire lifetime. It refers to a third person (sua = his/her); you can change the possessive as needed: per tutta la mia vita (my), per tutta la tua vita (your), per tutta la nostra vita (our), per tutta la loro vita (their), etc. Often follows a verb (Ha lavorato... / È stato...).
target_language_example: Ha lavorato per tutta la sua vita.
native_language_example: He/She worked his/her whole life.

additional_notes: Used to say something lasts your entire life (a memory, consequence, promise, etc.). Often follows the thing that lasts: “... per tutta la vita.” Can also be used with possessives for clarity: “per tutta la mia/sua vita.”
target_language_example: Questa esperienza me la ricorderò per tutta la vita.
native_language_example: I’ll remember this experience for the rest of my life.

additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun (il) to mean duration or extent: time periods (per tutto il weekend = for the whole weekend) or places/routes (per tutto il paese/tragitto = throughout the country/the whole route). With things like help/support, it often means “for all (the) …”: per tutto il tuo aiuto = for all your help. It changes with the article: per tutta la, per tutto lo, per tutti i, per tutti gli, per tutte le.
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a casa per tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: We stayed at home for the whole afternoon.

meaning: all day (long); for the whole day.
additional_notes: Used to express duration: something happens continuously or for most of the day. Often with the passato prossimo/imperfetto (e.g., “ha piovuto…”, “camminava…”). Similar idea: “tutto il giorno” = “all day”; adding “per” emphasizes “for the whole day/for the entire day.”
target_language_example: Ho lavorato per tutto il giorno e ora sono stanco.
native_language_example: I worked all day long and now I'm tired.

additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time period to say something lasts the entire afternoon (duration). Often goes with verbs like essere (to be), restare (to stay), lavorare/cucinare (to work/cook), etc. You can swap in other time words: "per tutta la mattina" (all morning), "per tutta la sera" (all evening).
target_language_example: Resterò a casa per tutto il pomeriggio.
native_language_example: I'll stay at home all afternoon.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened continuously for the entire period being talked about. Very common in questions and accusations (e.g., “Were you with him the whole time?” / “You knew all along”).
target_language_example: Sono rimasto in casa per tutto il tempo.
native_language_example: I stayed at home the whole time.

additional_notes: Used to refer back to all actions/words/events in a broad way, often when apologizing, thanking, or blaming. It’s usually followed by a verb clause: per tutto quello che ho detto/fatto, per tutto quello che è successo. You can also hear it with an implied verb in context: Per tutto quello che hai fatto per me. (= For everything you’ve done for me.)
target_language_example: Grazie per tutto quello che hai fatto oggi.
native_language_example: Thanks for everything you did today.

meaning: for all this time; for this whole time.
additional_notes: Used to talk about the entire period up to now or up to a point being discussed, often with surprise or emphasis (especially as a standalone question: “Per tutto questo tempo?” = “All this time?”). It can refer to how long someone did something, stayed somewhere, or felt something.
target_language_example: Hai lavorato qui per tutto questo tempo?
native_language_example: Have you worked here all this time?

meaning: last; as the last one (in order).
additional_notes: Used to say someone/something was the last in a sequence (e.g., the last to leave, arrive, speak, or do something). Often placed after the verb: “sono partito per ultimo”, “me ne andai per ultimo”. Note agreement: with a female subject it becomes “per ultima”, and plural is “per ultimi/ultime”.
target_language_example: Sono arrivato per ultimo e ho trovato tutti già seduti.
native_language_example: I arrived last and found everyone already seated.

additional_notes: A very common combination of the preposition per and the masculine singular indefinite article un. It is used before a masculine singular noun. Depending on the verb and context, it can also mean 'because of a' or 'over a'.
target_language_example: Cerco un regalo per un amico.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a gift for a friend.

meaning: for a moment; for a second.
additional_notes: Used to say something lasts a very short time, or to ask someone to do/stop something briefly. Common with requests (e.g., watch something, wait, be quiet) and with thoughts/feelings that happened briefly (e.g., 'I thought for a moment that...').
target_language_example: Aspettami per un attimo, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me a moment, I'll be right back.

meaning: for a minute; for a moment (briefly).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time expression to say how long something lasts or to ask for a short amount of time (e.g., to talk, to borrow something, to wait/relax). Often means “just a moment” rather than exactly 60 seconds.
target_language_example: Aspettami per un minuto, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait for me a minute, I’ll be right back.

meaning: for a moment; for a second (briefly).
additional_notes: Used to say something happens only for a very short time. Often follows the verb (es. “esitò per un momento”) or is used to politely ask to borrow or do something briefly (“Posso… per un momento?”). It can also introduce a temporary thought/feeling (“Per un momento mi sentii…”).
target_language_example: Aspetta qui per un momento, per favore.
native_language_example: Wait here for a moment, please.

meaning: for a couple of days (about two days).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a short period of time, usually around two days (sometimes loosely meaning “a few days”). Common with the present/past tense to say how long something lasts or lasted: “restare/essere/stare … per un paio di giorni.”
target_language_example: Rimango a Roma per un paio di giorni.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a couple of days.

meaning: by a hair; just barely (almost not).
additional_notes: Used to say something happened (or didn’t happen) with a very small margin—an escape, a near miss, or a narrow win. Often said alone as an exclamation: “Per un pelo!” It can also follow a verb: “Sono arrivato per un pelo” (I arrived just in time).
target_language_example: Siamo riusciti a prendere il treno per un pelo.
native_language_example: We managed to catch the train by a hair (just barely).

additional_notes: Used to indicate a very short time. Common in polite requests to pause or to speak briefly: "Scusi per un secondo" (Excuse me for a second), "Posso parlarle per un secondo?" (Can I talk to you for a second?). You can also extend it as "per un secondo o due" (for a second or two).
target_language_example: Aspetta per un secondo, torno subito.
native_language_example: Wait a second, I’ll be right back.

additional_notes: Used when the speaker doesn’t know (or doesn’t want to say) the exact reason. Often implies the reason is unclear or unexplained. Common in everyday speech; you can also hear "per qualche ragione" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Per una qualche ragione, oggi il computer non si accende.
native_language_example: For some reason, the computer won’t turn on today.

meaning: for a week (for the duration of one week).
additional_notes: Used with "per" + a time period to say how long something lasts (stay, rent, be sick, etc.). Very common with verbs like restare/rimanere (to stay), noleggiare (to rent), andare (to go), and essere (to be). You can change the time period: per due settimane (for two weeks), per una settimana o due (for a week or two).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a Firenze per una settimana.
native_language_example: We stayed in Florence for a week.

meaning: for once; just this one time.
additional_notes: Used to ask for or highlight an exception to the usual situation (often implying it doesn’t normally happen). It can sound like a mild complaint or encouragement: “for once, do X.”
target_language_example: Per una volta, ascoltami fino alla fine.
native_language_example: For once, listen to me until the end.

meaning: in order to see; to see.
additional_notes: Uses "per" + infinitive to express purpose (why someone does something): "Vado al museo per vedere i quadri". It can be followed by a noun/pronoun/name ("per vedere Mary") or a clause ("per vedere che era possibile" = to see/check that it was possible).
target_language_example: Siamo usciti presto per vedere l’alba.
native_language_example: We went out early to see the sunrise.

meaning: 'to see if' / 'to check whether' (in order to find out).
additional_notes: Used to express purpose: you do an action *in order to find out* if something is true. Very common before a clause with the verb (often with indicative; with uncertainty or reported/indirect context you may see the subjunctive, e.g. "per vedere se fossi...").
target_language_example: Ho chiamato l’hotel per vedere se hanno camere libere.
native_language_example: I called the hotel to see if they have any rooms available.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason or cause, often with a negative or explanatory tone. It’s normally followed by **di** + a noun: **per via di** + noun, which becomes **per via del/della/dei/degli/delle** (e.g., *per via del caldo*, *per via dello sciopero*). Similar to *a causa di*.
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati tardi per via del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason, followed by a noun or noun phrase. It’s common in speech and writing. The article changes with the noun: per via del (masc. sing.), della (fem. sing.), dei/degli (masc. plural), delle (fem. plural). Similar to "a causa di"; if you want to emphasize blame, you can use "per colpa di".
target_language_example: Siamo arrivati in ritardo per via del traffico.
native_language_example: We arrived late because of the traffic.

additional_notes: Used to give the cause/reason for something, usually followed by a feminine singular noun: per via della malattia = “because of the illness.” With masculine singular nouns use “per via del” (e.g., per via del traffico). It’s common in speech and writing; “a causa di” is a close synonym.
target_language_example: Ero assente da scuola per via della malattia.
native_language_example: I was absent from school because of the illness.

additional_notes: Used to express the cause/reason for something, typically followed by a noun, pronoun, or situation: per via di Jason / per via di una lunga passeggiata / per via di quello. Similar in meaning to "a causa di" and common in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Non sono venuto per via di un imprevisto.
native_language_example: I didn’t come because of something unexpected.

additional_notes: Used to indicate something is intended for, addressed to, or meant from the point of view of "voi". "Voi" is the plural "you" (to a group). In some contexts (older, regional, or very formal), "voi" can also be used as a polite singular "you".
target_language_example: Ho preparato un tavolo per voi vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: I reserved a table for you near the window.

additional_notes: Used with quantities or frequency to mean “on each occasion” or “at one time.” Common with numbers: "due (tre) per volta" = “two (three) at a time,” and with expressions like "una volta per volta" = “one at a time.”
target_language_example: Puoi entrare solo in due per volta.
native_language_example: Only two people can go in at a time.

additional_notes: Used to propose an idea, invite someone, or challenge a reason for not doing something. It’s followed by a verb (often in the present tense) and can sound friendly (“Why don’t you come with me?”) or slightly critical depending on tone (“Why didn’t you come pick me up?”). Often corresponds to English “Why don’t you…?” or simply “Why not…?”.
target_language_example: Perchè non andiamo a prendere un caffè?
native_language_example: Why don’t we go get a coffee?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. "Perché" means "why" here, and "avete" is "you (plural) have" (present tense of avere). It’s followed by a past participle to make the passato prossimo (e.g., "Perché avete venduto...?" = "Why did you sell...?"), or it can introduce a clause in the present (less common in these examples).
target_language_example: Perché avete chiamato la polizia?
native_language_example: Why did you call the police?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a purchase. "Perché" = why; "avete comprato" is passato prossimo of "comprare" with "voi" (you all) or formal "you" when addressing more than one person. Often followed by an object ("questo…") or by "così tanto" (so much).
target_language_example: Perché avete comprato due biglietti invece di uno?
native_language_example: Why did you buy two tickets instead of one?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s decision. "Avete" is 2nd person plural (you all) or the polite form used with "voi" in some contexts; it’s followed by "deciso di" + infinitive (e.g., comprare, divorziare, restare).
target_language_example: Perché avete deciso di cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why did you decide to change jobs?

meaning: "why do you need (to)…?" (you = plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a need/requirement. Structure: perché + avete bisogno di + noun ("...of two bikes") or + infinitive ("...to do this"). "Avete" is 2nd person plural (voi) and can also be used as a polite/formal "you" in some contexts.
target_language_example: Perché avete bisogno di parlare con il direttore?
native_language_example: Why do you need to speak with the manager?

additional_notes: "Perché" means “why” (or “because,” depending on context). Here it’s used in questions: “Why…?” "Ci" is a very common pronoun meaning “us / to us” (e.g., "Perché ci dici questo?" = “Why are you telling us this?”). With some verbs it can also be part of a fixed expression, like "metterci" (“to take [time]”): "Perché ci mette così tanto?" = “Why is it taking so long?”
target_language_example: Perché ci chiami così tardi?
native_language_example: Why are you calling us so late?

meaning: 'why did you … to us?' / 'why have you … to us?'.
additional_notes: Used to start a question asking the reason for something someone did to 'us' (ci = to us). It’s followed by a past participle to form the passato prossimo with "avere": e.g., "Perché ci hai invitati?" (Why did you invite us?). The ending of the past participle can agree with the direct object pronoun "ci" when it refers to people: "invitati" (us, masculine/mixed group) vs "invitate" (us, all female).
target_language_example: Perché ci hai chiamati così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call us so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason or to challenge an idea/suggestion: “Why should I do that?”. Literally “why” + “I should/would have to” (from dovere). Often sounds skeptical or rhetorical, depending on tone and context.
target_language_example: Perché dovrei accettare questa offerta?
native_language_example: Why should I accept this offer?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s past state or behavior. "Era" is the imperfect tense of "essere" (was), and "così" means "so" and is usually followed by an adjective: "Perché era così stanco?" (Why was he so tired?). The subject (he/she/it) is often understood from context.
target_language_example: Perché era così arrabbiata ieri?
native_language_example: Why was she so angry yesterday?

meaning: why (he/she) was late; the reason (he/she) was late.
additional_notes: Used after verbs like *spiegare* (to explain), *dire* (to tell/say), *sapere* (to know) to introduce the reason for someone’s lateness: *spiegare/dire/sapere perché...*. Note that *perché* can mean both “why” and “because”; in these examples it means “why” (= “the reason”). *Era* is the imperfect of *essere* (“was”), commonly used for background situations like being late.
target_language_example: Non so perché era in ritardo stamattina.
native_language_example: I don’t know why he/she was late this morning.

meaning: "why they were late" (or "because they were late," depending on context).
additional_notes: In sentences like "spiegare/dire perché..." it usually means "explain/tell (someone) why...". "Perché" can mean both "why" (question/indirect question) and "because" (reason). "Erano" is the imperfect of "essere" (they were). "In ritardo" means "late" (literally "in delay").
target_language_example: Non capisco perché erano in ritardo.
native_language_example: I don’t understand why they were late.

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a state/attitude in the past. "Eravate" is the imperfect of "essere" for "voi" (you plural / formal you). "Così" means "so" and is usually followed by an adjective that agrees in gender/number: curiose/preoccupate (female plural), preoccupati/sorpresi (male or mixed plural).
target_language_example: Perché eravate così stanchi ieri?
native_language_example: Why were you all so tired yesterday?

additional_notes:
Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior or state in the past. 
- perché = “why”
- eri = “you were” (past, informal singular “tu”)
- così = “so” (intensifier before an adjective)
It’s typically followed by an adjective that agrees with the person (e.g., scortese works for all genders; sgarbato/sgarbata, sorpreso/sorpresa change).
target_language_example: Perché eri così nervoso ieri?
native_language_example: Why were you so nervous yesterday?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone bought something. "Ha comprato" is the passato prossimo of "comprare" with "avere" and can refer to he/she/you (formal) depending on context; the subject is often implied.
target_language_example: Perché ha comprato quel telefono invece di questo?
native_language_example: Why did he/she/you (formal) buy that phone instead of this one?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason behind a decision. "Ha deciso di" is the passato prossimo of "decidere" and can refer to **he** (lui), **she** (lei), or the polite **you** (Lei), depending on context. It is followed by an infinitive verb: "ha deciso di + [infinitive]" (e.g., "ha deciso di partire").
target_language_example: Perché ha deciso di cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why did he/she decide to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone stopped an activity. "ha smesso di" is the passato prossimo of "smettere di" + an infinitive (e.g., smesso di fumare = stopped smoking). "ha" can refer to "he" or "she"; you can also change it: "Perché hai smesso di..." (you), "Perché hanno smesso di..." (they).
target_language_example: Perché ha smesso di venire qui?
native_language_example: Why did he/she stop coming here?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s need. "Ha" is the present tense of "avere" (he/she/you-formal has). "Bisogno di" means "need (of)" and is followed by a noun ("di due biciclette") or by an infinitive ("di farlo"). You can change the subject: "perché ho bisogno di…" (why do I need…), "perché hai bisogno di…" (why do you need…), "perché abbiamo bisogno di…" (why do we need…).
target_language_example: Perché ha bisogno di chiamare un taxi?
native_language_example: Why does he/she/you (formal) need to call a taxi?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone did something. Hai is the 2nd person singular of avere and often works as an auxiliary with a past participle in the passato prossimo, so in English this is often translated as "why did you ...?".
target_language_example: Perché hai cambiato idea?
native_language_example: Why did you change your mind?

meaning: "why did you buy" / "why have you bought".
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for a purchase. It’s a question in the passato prossimo: "hai comprato" = "you bought / you have bought" (literally "you have bought"). Usually followed by the thing bought (e.g., "Perché hai comprato questo...?"), and it can imply surprise or criticism depending on tone.
target_language_example: Perché hai comprato due biglietti se non possiamo andare?
native_language_example: Why did you buy two tickets if we can’t go?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for the reason behind a past decision. Follow it with an infinitive verb (e.g., andare, diventare, restare). You can also use it more generally as a polite question about motivation: Perché hai deciso di + [infinitive] ?
target_language_example: Perché hai deciso di cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why did you decide to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone needs to do something or needs something. Follow it with an infinitive (perché hai bisogno di andare/fare/leggere…) or a noun (perché hai bisogno di una motosega?). Often implies surprise or curiosity about the necessity.
target_language_example: Perché hai bisogno di parlare con il manager?
native_language_example: Why do you need to talk to the manager?

additional_notes: Used inside a question after verbs like sapere (“to know”) to ask if someone knows the reason for something. Note the difference between perché (why/because) and che (“that”): Tu sai perché il cielo è blu? = “Do you know why the sky is blue?”
target_language_example: Non so perché il cielo è blu, ma posso cercarlo su internet.
native_language_example: I don’t know why the sky is blue, but I can look it up online.

additional_notes: Used to ask a general question about people in general (not specific individuals). Often followed by a verb phrase: "Perché la gente + verbo...?" (e.g., fa, ha, pensa, spreca). In Italian, "perché" can mean both "why" (question) and "because" (answer), but here it’s the question form.
target_language_example: Perché la gente parla così in metro?
native_language_example: Why do people talk like that on the subway?

additional_notes: Used at the beginning of a question to ask for the reason behind what people do or what happens. In Italian, perché can mean both “why” (in questions) and “because” (in answers), so punctuation and context matter.
target_language_example: Perché le persone sono sempre di fretta?
native_language_example: Why are people always in a hurry?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. "Perché" means "why" in questions. "Le" is a clitic pronoun placed before the verb: most often an indirect object meaning "to her" (e.g., Perché le ha detto…? = Why did you tell her…?). In some sentences it can be a direct object meaning "them" (feminine plural), and then the past participle often agrees in the feminine plural (e.g., Perché le ha portate qua? = Why did you bring them here?).
target_language_example: Perché le hai parlato così?
native_language_example: Why did you talk to her like that?

additional_notes: Used when asking “why” with the direct object pronoun **lo** (“him/it”) placed before the verb: **Perché lo stiamo ascoltando?** = “Why are we listening to him/it?” **Lo** usually refers to a masculine singular person (“him”) or thing (“it”). In answers, **perché** can also mean “because,” but you typically wouldn’t keep **lo** right after it unless the sentence continues (e.g., *Perché lo voglio.* = “Because I want it.”).
target_language_example: Perché lo stai facendo?
native_language_example: Why are you doing it?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for an action done by “you” plural (voi). "Perché" means “why/because.” "Lo" is a direct object pronoun meaning “it” or “him” (depending on context). "Avete" is the "you (plural)" form of *avere* and is often used with a past participle (e.g., *detto, colpito, gettato via, licenziato, ucciso*) to form the past tense (passato prossimo).
target_language_example: Perché lo avete comprato se non vi serve?
native_language_example: Why did you buy it if you don’t need it?

additional_notes: Used in questions to add emphasis, surprise, disbelief, or irritation. Often introduces rhetorical questions like "Perché mai dovrei..." (= "Why would I ever...?"). You can also use it alone: "Perché mai?"
target_language_example: Perché mai dovrei accettare una cosa del genere?
native_language_example: Why on earth would I accept something like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something that someone is doing to/for you. It’s made of perché (“why/because”) + mi (“me”), and it’s normally followed by a verb: Perché mi odi? (“Why do you hate me?”). mi can mean “me” as a direct object (“hate me”, “imitate me”) or indirect object (“ask me”, “give me”).
target_language_example: Perché mi guardi così?
native_language_example: Why are you looking at me like that?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason about something a group of people (“voi”) did that affects the speaker (“mi” = to me). It’s followed by a past participle to form the passato prossimo: perché mi avete + lasciato/scelto/abbandonata, etc. The past participle may agree with the speaker when a direct-object pronoun is used (e.g., abbandonata if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Perché mi avete chiamato così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

meaning: “why did you … to me?” / “why have you … to me?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason when someone did something that affects you. It’s typically followed by a past participle (passato prossimo): “Perché mi hai invitato?” (Why did you invite me?). “mi” means “to me” (object pronoun), and “hai” is “you have” (tu) used to form the past tense.
target_language_example: Perché mi hai chiamato così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you call me so late?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an indirect question explaining the reason someone isn’t trusted. The verb is "fidarsi di" (reflexive) = "to trust" and it takes "di" before a person/thing: "si fida di Tom" (he/she trusts Tom). You can change "nessuno" (nobody) to "tutti" (everyone) or swap in a pronoun: "di lui/lei" (him/her), "di me" (me).
target_language_example: Mi spieghi perché nessuno si fida di lui?
native_language_example: Can you explain to me why nobody trusts him?

additional_notes: Used to accept or agree to a suggestion, often with a casual, open-minded tone (similar to “sure” or “might as well”). It can also be a real question asking for a reason not to do something, depending on context and intonation. Often appears alone as a short reply: “Sì, perché no?” / “Perché no?”.
target_language_example: Andiamo a prendere un gelato? Sì, perché no?
native_language_example: Shall we go get an ice cream? Yes, why not?

additional_notes: perché can mean both 'why' and 'because'. In questions, perché non + verb asks why someone doesn't or didn't do something; by itself, Perché no? means 'Why not?'. In statements, it introduces a reason: 'because ... not'.
target_language_example: Perché non vieni con noi?
native_language_example: Why don't you come with us?

meaning: "why don't ..." with "ci" (= there / to it / about it / us), depending on the verb.
additional_notes: Used to ask why someone doesn’t do something, or to make a suggestion. "Ci" is a pronoun that changes meaning with the verb: e.g. "andarci" = to go there, "crederci" = to believe it, "entrarci"/"farci entrare" = to let us in, "metterci" = to put (something) in it/there. In speech, "ci" often attaches to an infinitive: "perché non ci andare?" (less common) / "perché non andarci?" (more natural).
target_language_example: Perché non ci vai domani?
native_language_example: Why don't you go there tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used at the start of a question/complaint: perché = “why”, non = “not”, mi = “me/to me”. It’s followed by a verb (often with a subject like tu/lei/voi implied): “Perché non mi aiuti?” = “Why don’t you help me?” The verb form changes depending on who you’re speaking to (e.g., vieni = you come, fate = you all do, ha = he/she has).
target_language_example: Perché non mi ascolti?
native_language_example: Why don’t you listen to me?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone did not do something. It’s typically followed by a past participle (passato prossimo): “Perché non mi hai chiamata/chiamato?” Note: with some verbs, the past participle can agree with the person being referred to by “mi” when “mi” is the direct object and comes before the verb (e.g., a female speaker may say “mi hai chiamata / mi hai svegliata”). With other verbs, there’s no agreement (e.g., “mi hai detto…” when the direct object is the clause that follows; “mi hai telefonato” because “telefonare” takes an indirect object).
target_language_example: Perché non mi hai scritto ieri?
native_language_example: Why didn’t you write to me yesterday?

meaning: "Why aren’t you…?" (asking why someone is not in a certain situation/state).
additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s followed by an adjective or noun phrase (perché non sei malato? = why aren’t you sick?), or by a place with “a/in” (perché non sei a scuola? = why aren’t you at school?). “Sei” is the “you are” form (tu) of essere.
target_language_example: Perché non sei pronto?
native_language_example: Why aren’t you ready?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone the reason/evidence for their opinion or belief. "Pensa" is formal "you think" (Lei). After "che," Italian often uses the subjunctive in indirect statements (e.g., "sia", "sia capitato", "stesse piangendo"), though you may also hear the indicative in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Perché pensa che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Why do you think it’s a good idea?

meaning: “Why do you think that…?” (asking a group).
additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason/opinion. "Pensate" is 2nd-person plural (you all/you plural), and it’s often followed by "che" + a verb in the subjunctive (e.g., "sia", "abbia", "fosse"). For one person, you’d usually say "Perché pensi che…?".
target_language_example: Perché pensate che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: Why do you think it’s a good idea?

additional_notes: Used to ask for someone’s reason or explanation for an opinion/belief. It’s followed by a clause introduced by che, typically with the subjunctive (e.g., sia, stia, abbia, stesse). Often used when asking about someone’s assumptions: Perché pensi che…?
target_language_example: Perché pensi che sia successo questo?
native_language_example: Why do you think this happened?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone's state, identity, or action. Sei is the present tense of essere and means "you are" for one person in the informal singular (tu).
target_language_example: Perché sei in ritardo?
native_language_example: Why are you late?

meaning: “why are you still…?” (asking why someone hasn’t changed/stopped yet).
additional_notes: Used to question why a situation continues. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., *sveglio/sveglia*, *celibe/scapolo*) or by a phrase like *con lui* (“with him”) or *lì* (“there”). *Sei* is 2nd person singular (“you are”), so it’s used when speaking to one person.
target_language_example: Perché sei ancora qui?
native_language_example: Why are you still here?

additional_notes: Used to ask why someone has a particular quality, mood, or behavior. It is usually followed by an adjective or similar description. Depending on the adjective and tone, it can sound neutral, concerned, or critical.
target_language_example: Perché sei così nervoso oggi?
native_language_example: Why are you so nervous today?

additional_notes: Used to ask (often with frustration or surprise) why someone consistently behaves in a certain way. It’s typically followed by an adjective or description (e.g., geloso = jealous, lenta = slow, stanco = tired). You can change the subject: perché siete sempre così… (you plural/formal), perché è sempre così… (he/she/it).
target_language_example: Perché sei sempre così pessimista?
native_language_example: Why are you always so pessimistic?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s coming/arriving. Literally “why are you come,” but in Italian this present tense form (“sei venuta”) is the normal way to express the past (“you came/you have come”). Venuta is feminine, so you say it to a woman; to a man: “perché sei venuto?”. You can add a place/time: “Perché sei venuta qui/qua stamattina?” In a blaming tone it can mean “why did you even come?”
target_language_example: Perché sei venuta qui oggi?
native_language_example: Why did you come here today?

meaning: “why did you come?” / “why have you come?” (to a male).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone came/arrived. It’s addressed to a man (venuto). For a woman: “perché sei venuta?”. You can add place/time details: “Perché sei venuto qui/qua?” (here), “a casa” (home), “così tardi/presto” (so late/early).
target_language_example: Perché sei venuto qui oggi?
native_language_example: Why did you come here today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for something about a group of people, using the present tense of essere (siete = you all are). It’s followed by an adjective (Perché siete felici?), a preposition phrase (Perché siete in ritardo?), or a past participle as an adjective (Perché siete arrabbiati?). For mixed or all-male groups use siete venuti/tornati/arrabbiati; for all-female groups use siete venute/tornate/arrabbiate.
target_language_example: Perché siete qui così presto?
native_language_example: Why are you here so early?

meaning: "why are you so …?" (asking the reason for a quality or reaction).
additional_notes: Used to ask why a group of people ("voi") has a certain characteristic or feels/reacts a certain way. "Siete" is the "you" plural/formal form of "essere" (to be). "Così" means "so" and is usually followed by an adjective: "così generose/popolari/sorpresi".
target_language_example: Perché siete così stanchi oggi?
native_language_example: Why are you so tired today?

meaning: "why are you (plural, feminine) so good at …?"
additional_notes:
Used to ask why a group of women/girls are very skilled at something. 
- perché = why
- siete = you are (plural)
- così = so
- brave = good/capable (feminine plural; masculine would be bravi)
- a = at (used before many activities; also before nouns like baseball/scacchi)
Often followed by a noun (a scacchi, a baseball) or an infinitive verb (a nuotare, a cucinare, a farlo).
target_language_example: Perché siete così brave a parlare italiano?
native_language_example: Why are you (all, women/girls) so good at speaking Italian?

meaning: "Why are you always like this?" / "Why are you always so…?" (to a group).
additional_notes: Used to ask a group of people ("voi") why they repeatedly behave in a certain way. Often followed by an adjective: "Perché siete sempre così felici/gelosi/irritabili/tranquilli?". Can sound accusing or teasing depending on tone; for one person you’d say "Perché sei sempre così…?".
target_language_example: Perché siete sempre così in ritardo?
native_language_example: Why are you always so late?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what someone is doing right now. It’s typically followed by a gerund (sta + -ando/-endo): e.g., “Perché sta piangendo?” = “Why is he/she crying?” The subject (lui/lei/Lei/it) is often implied from context.
target_language_example: Perché sta parlando così piano?
native_language_example: Why is he/she speaking so quietly?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what someone is doing or how they are behaving. Very often followed by a gerund (stai + verb-ando/-endo) or an adjective: “Perché stai ridendo?” (Why are you laughing?), “Perché stai zitto?” (Why are you quiet?). On its own it usually sounds unfinished—you normally add what the person is doing/like.
target_language_example: Perché stai piangendo?
native_language_example: Why are you crying?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason behind someone’s action. You can add details after this, like a person (Perché stai facendo questo a Fadil? = Why are you doing this to Fadil?), a time (…adesso? = …now?), or a beneficiary (…per me? = …for me?). Often said with a name or attention-getter: "Senti, ..." (Listen, ...).
target_language_example: Perché stai facendo questo? Non capisco.
native_language_example: Why are you doing this? I don’t understand.

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for what a group of people (or “you” plural) are doing. Often followed by the present continuous with a gerund: “Perché state + verb-ando/-endo …?” (e.g., “Perché state aspettando?” = “Why are you waiting?”).
target_language_example: Perché state parlando così forte?
native_language_example: Why are you speaking so loudly?

additional_notes: Used mostly to start a question with perché (“why”) followed by ti, which is an unstressed pronoun placed before the verb. ti can mean “you” as an indirect object (“to you”) or be reflexive (“yourself”), depending on the verb: Perché ti serve…? = “Why do you need…?”; Perché ti lamenti? = “Why are you complaining?” (lit. “complaining to yourself”). Note: perché can also mean “because,” but in that case it’s usually not followed immediately by ti (e.g., Perché ti ho chiamato = “Because I called you”).
target_language_example: Perché ti arrabbi così facilmente?
native_language_example: Why do you get angry so easily?

meaning: "Why did you..." (talking to one person, using the past tense with a reflexive verb).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s past action/state when the verb is reflexive (verb with “si”), in the passato prossimo: perché + ti sei + past participle (e.g., ti sei svegliato/a, ti sei fermato/a, ti sei arrabbiato/a). The past participle often agrees with the person’s gender/number (svegliaTa for a woman, svegliaTo for a man).
target_language_example: Perché ti sei preoccupato così tanto?
native_language_example: Why did you worry so much?

meaning: “why are you behaving in…?” (introduces the way/manner someone is behaving).
additional_notes: This is an incomplete lead-in that normally needs something after it, such as *questo modo* (“this way”) or a noun phrase: *Perché ti stai comportando in questo modo?* More common alternatives are *Perché ti stai comportando così?* (“Why are you behaving like that?”) or *Perché ti comporti così?* (less emphatic, same meaning). Uses *stare + gerundio* (*ti stai comportando*) to emphasize “right now / these days.”
target_language_example: Perché ti stai comportando in questo modo?
native_language_example: Why are you behaving this way?

meaning: 'why you…' (addressing more than one person, or formal 'you').
additional_notes: Used at the start of a question. "Perché" means "why" and "vi" is the object/reflexive pronoun for "you" plural (or formal "you"), placed before the verb (e.g., "Perché vi importa…?" = "Why do you care…?"; "Perché vi state comportando…?" = "Why are you behaving…?").
target_language_example: Perché vi siete arrabbiati con me?
native_language_example: Why did you get angry with me?

meaning: “Why did you (all) …?” (introduces a question in the past).
additional_notes: Used with Passato Prossimo, especially with reflexive verbs: **vi** = “you (plural)”, **siete** is the auxiliary for **voi**. It’s followed by a past participle: *Perché vi siete fermati?* = “Why did you stop?” If the group is all female, the past participle is usually feminine plural (*fermate, separate*).
target_language_example: Perché vi siete svegliati così tardi?
native_language_example: Why did you wake up so late?

meaning: “Why are you hiding?” (talking to more than one person).
additional_notes: Used to ask the reason for someone’s behavior. "Vi" = to/you (plural). "Stare" + gerund ("state nascondendo") expresses an action happening right now: "you are hiding". Often followed by "da" + person ("da lui/da me/da Tom") meaning "from" someone.
target_language_example: Perché vi state nascondendo qui?
native_language_example: Why are you hiding here?

additional_notes: Used to ask someone for the reason they want something or want to do something. In Italian you don’t need to invert the subject and verb like in English: literally it’s “why you want…?”. Often followed by an infinitive: “perché vuoi + verb” (e.g., perché vuoi andare…?).
target_language_example: Perché vuoi cambiare lavoro?
native_language_example: Why do you want to change jobs?

additional_notes: Used to ask for a reason. It’s the question word perché (“why”) + è (“is,” from essere). In writing it’s usually followed by a question mark: “Perché è …?”. Don’t confuse with perché meaning “because” in statements (no question mark).
target_language_example: Perché è così difficile?
native_language_example: Why is it so difficult?

additional_notes: Used to ask for the reason someone or something has a certain quality/state. You typically add an adjective after it (e.g., assonnato/a, divertito/a, egoista). The verb agrees with the subject (è = 'is'), and the adjective often changes for gender/number (assonnato/assonnata; divertito/divertita).
target_language_example: Perché è così arrabbiata oggi?
native_language_example: Why is she so angry today?

additional_notes: Used to ask the reason someone is consistently a certain way. Often followed by an adjective (e.g., burbero, felice, geloso/a). You can change the subject pronoun: Perché sono sempre così...? (Why am I always like this?), Perché sei sempre così...? (Why are you always like that?).
target_language_example: Perché è sempre così nervoso?
native_language_example: Why is he always so nervous?

additional_notes: Used to introduce a reason that is negative: perché + non + verb. Often followed by a verb in the present/past: "perché non ho potuto" (because I couldn’t), "perché non hai dormito" (because you didn’t sleep). Note: with a question mark, "Perché non...?" can also mean "Why don’t you...? / Why not...?".
target_language_example: Sono in ritardo perché non ho trovato parcheggio.
native_language_example: I’m late because I couldn’t find parking.

additional_notes: Used to give a reason for something in the past. "Perché" means "because/why"; here it means "because." "Stava piovendo" is the imperfect progressive (stare + gerund), meaning "it was raining" (ongoing at that time).
target_language_example: Siamo rimasti a casa perché stava piovendo.
native_language_example: We stayed at home because it was raining.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "stare" to describe something happening right now: "sto/stai/sta/stiamo/state/stanno perdendo sangue" = "I’m/you’re/he’s… bleeding." Common in emergencies; you can also say "Sta sanguinando" (He/She is bleeding).
target_language_example: Chiama un’ambulanza: sta perdendo sangue!
native_language_example: Call an ambulance: he’s bleeding!

meaning: to lose sight of; to lose track of (someone/something).
additional_notes: Used both literally (you can’t see someone/something anymore) and figuratively (you stop keeping in touch, or you stop following a situation). Often followed by a person or thing: “Ho perso di vista Marco” / “Abbiamo perso di vista l’obiettivo.” In the literal sense, you may also see “perdere qualcuno di vista” (lose someone from view).
target_language_example: Nel caos della stazione ho finito per perdere di vista mia sorella.
native_language_example: In the chaos of the station I ended up losing sight of my sister.

additional_notes: Used when you don’t arrive in time for a departure. Often said with urgency, especially with phrases like “per non perdere il treno” (so as not to miss the train) or “non posso perdere il treno” (I can’t miss the train).
target_language_example: Se non ci sbrighiamo, rischiamo di perdere il treno.
native_language_example: If we don’t hurry up, we might miss the train.

meaning: to lose patience; to get impatient.
additional_notes: Used when someone can’t stay calm anymore (often after waiting or dealing with something annoying). Very common in everyday speech. Often with "con" + person/thing: "Ho perso la pazienza con lui" (I lost patience with him).
target_language_example: Dopo mezz’ora in fila, ho iniziato a perdere la pazienza.
native_language_example: After half an hour in line, I started to lose patience.

meaning: to lose your head; to go crazy; to lose control (sometimes: to fall madly in love).
additional_notes: Used when someone stops thinking clearly or acting rationally because of panic, anger, excitement, or love. Common with “per” + person: “Ha perso la testa per lei/lui” = “He/She fell head over heels for her/him.”
target_language_example: Ho paura di perdere la testa quando sento quella notizia.
native_language_example: I’m afraid I’ll lose my head when I hear that news.

meaning: to lose one’s life; to die (often in an accident or tragedy).
additional_notes: A fairly formal, indirect way to say someone died, common in news reports and serious contexts (accidents, wars, disasters). Frequently appears conjugated (e.g., "ha perso la vita"), but the base term is "perdere la vita".
target_language_example: Due persone rischiavano di perdere la vita nell’incidente.
native_language_example: Two people were at risk of losing their lives in the accident.

meaning: to lose your temper; to fly off the handle.
additional_notes: Used when someone suddenly gets very angry and can’t control themselves. Common in everyday speech; you can use it with different subjects and tenses (e.g., "ha perso le staffe", "stavo per perdere le staffe").
target_language_example: Cerco di restare calmo, ma a volte rischio di perdere le staffe.
native_language_example: I try to stay calm, but sometimes I risk losing my temper.

additional_notes: Commonly used when giving advice about health or dieting. It’s built from perdere (“to lose”) + peso (“weight”). You can also say: Devo perdere peso. / Vorrei perdere peso.
target_language_example: Sto cercando di perdere peso prima dell’estate.
native_language_example: I’m trying to lose weight before summer.

additional_notes: Used when time is being spent in an unproductive or unnecessary way. Often appears in the causative form "far perdere tempo (a qualcuno)" = "to make someone waste time" (e.g., "Ci stai facendo perdere tempo!"), and with "non" to reassure someone you won’t waste their time ("per non farvi perdere tempo").
target_language_example: Non voglio perdere tempo: andiamo subito.
native_language_example: I don’t want to waste time: let’s go right away.

additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t worth doing because it doesn’t bring results or value. Often appears with intensifiers like una pura/una totale/una tale perdita di tempo (“a pure/total/such a waste of time”). Can be exclaimed: Che perdita di tempo! (“What a waste of time!”).
target_language_example: Fare la fila per due ore è stata una perdita di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting in line for two hours was a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to say someone is allowed to do something: "avere/ottenere/chiedere il permesso di + infinitive". It can also be used as a polite request on its own, especially in formal contexts: "Permesso di + infinitive" (e.g., asking to speak or to come aboard). In some situations it can refer to an official permit (e.g., "permesso di viaggio" = travel permit).
target_language_example: Devo chiedere il permesso di uscire prima.
native_language_example: I have to ask permission to leave early.

additional_notes: “Perse” is the passato remoto (simple past) of *perdere* (“to lose”). In everyday spoken Italian you’ll more often hear *ha perso i suoi occhiali* (passato prossimo). *I suoi occhiali* means “his/her glasses” (owned by the subject).
target_language_example: Ieri perse i suoi occhiali e non riuscì più a leggere.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she lost his/her glasses and couldn’t read anymore.

additional_notes: "Perse" is the simple past (passato remoto) of "perdere" (to lose), common in writing and storytelling; in everyday conversation many people use "ha perso" instead. "Il suo" means "his/her/its" and agrees with a masculine singular noun (e.g., "il telefono" → "perse il suo telefono").
target_language_example: Durante il viaggio perse il suo passaporto.
native_language_example: During the trip, he/she lost his/her passport.

additional_notes: “Perse” is the passato remoto (remote past) of perdere (“to lose”). It’s common in writing and storytelling; in everyday conversation you’ll often hear “ha perso il suo lavoro.” The possessive and article can change: “persi il mio lavoro” (I lost my job), “perse il suo lavoro” (he/she lost his/her job), “persero il loro lavoro” (they lost their job). Often used without naming the person when the subject is clear from context.
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente, perse il suo lavoro.
native_language_example: After the accident, he lost his job.

meaning: “(he/she) lost his/her …” (past simple of perdere, used with a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to say someone lost something they possessed or something abstract (like credibility). The verb is in the passato remoto (common in storytelling, history, and in some regions; in everyday speech many people use passato prossimo: “ha perso”). “La sua” agrees with the thing owned (feminine singular): la sua borsetta, la sua fede, la sua terra, la sua credibilità. With a masculine singular noun you would use “perse il suo …”.
target_language_example: Durante il viaggio, perse la sua valigia.
native_language_example: During the trip, he/she lost his/her suitcase.

meaning: "he/she/it lost all of his/her/its" (followed by a noun).
additional_notes: "Perse" is the passato remoto (past historic) of "perdere" (to lose), used mainly in narratives, books, news reports, and in some regions in everyday speech instead of "ha perso". "tutti" agrees with the noun that follows: "tutti i suoi" + masculine plural noun (soldi, risparmi, libri), but "tutte le sue" + feminine plural noun (chiavi, cose). You’ll usually add the thing lost right after: "perse tutti i suoi soldi".
target_language_example: Durante la crisi, perse tutti i suoi risparmi.
native_language_example: During the crisis, he lost all his savings.

meaning: “(have) lost sight of” / “(have) lost track of.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb phrase **perdere di vista**. In the past tense you’ll often see **ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno perso di vista + [person/thing]** (“I/you/he… lost sight of”).
