It can be literal (can’t see someone anymore, e.g., in a crowd) or figurative (you’re no longer in contact / you don’t know where or how someone is doing).
target_language_example: Ti ho perso di vista per un attimo, poi ti ho ritrovato.
native_language_example: I lost sight of you for a moment, then I found you again.

additional_notes: Past participle of perdere followed by il. It is used with a masculine singular noun: perdere can mean either to lose something (perso il lavoro = lost the job) or to miss something like a bus, train, or event (perso il compleanno = missed the birthday).
target_language_example: Abbiamo perso il treno di mattina.
native_language_example: We missed the morning train.

additional_notes: Past tense (passato prossimo) of "perdere il controllo". Used both literally (losing physical control) and figuratively (losing self-control or temper). You can add "di" to specify what you lost control of: "ho perso il controllo di/delle..."
target_language_example: Ho perso il controllo e ho detto cose che non pensavo.
native_language_example: I lost control and said things I didn’t mean.

meaning: “lost mine / I lost mine” (usually as in: Ho perso il mio).
additional_notes: This is typically an incomplete fragment on its own. In full, you usually say **Ho perso il mio** (“I lost mine”) where **perso** is the past participle of *perdere* (“to lose”) and **il mio** means “mine” (masculine singular). It refers to something already understood from context (e.g., *il mio telefono / il mio biglietto*). For a feminine item you’d say **Ho perso la mia**.
target_language_example: Non posso usare il tuo: ho perso il mio.
native_language_example: I can’t use yours: I lost mine.

additional_notes: From the verb **perdere** (“to lose”). With transport, **perdere l’autobus / il treno / il volo** usually means **to miss** it (arrive too late), not literally “lose” it. **Suo** can mean **his** or **her** depending on context; you can swap the possessive: **perso il mio autobus** (my bus), **perso il nostro autobus** (our bus), **perso il loro autobus** (their bus).
target_language_example: Ha appena perso il suo autobus e ora deve aspettare il prossimo.
native_language_example: He/She just missed his/her bus and now has to wait for the next one.

additional_notes: Often seen as a shortened phrase (e.g., in headlines or summaries) where the auxiliary verb is omitted. In full, you’ll commonly say: “Ha perso il suo impiego” (He/She lost his/her job). “Impiego” is a fairly formal word for “job/employment”; in everyday speech, “lavoro” is more common.
target_language_example: Ha perso il suo impiego il mese scorso.
native_language_example: He/She lost his/her job last month.

additional_notes: From the verb "perdere" (to miss/lose) in the past participle "perso" + "il suo treno" (his/her train). In Italian you commonly use "perdere" to mean "to miss" a train, bus, flight, appointment, etc. The literal translation is "lost his/her train," but the natural meaning is "missed his/her train."
target_language_example: Mary ha perso il suo treno e ora deve aspettare il prossimo.
native_language_example: Mary missed her train and now she has to wait for the next one.

meaning: "missed the train" (arrived too late to catch it).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "perdere" (to miss/lose). In the past it’s usually in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha perso il treno" = "I/you/he/she missed the train." It can also be used more generally to mean “missed the chance/opportunity” ("Hai perso il treno" = “You missed your chance”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ho perso il treno e arrivo più tardi.
native_language_example: Sorry, I missed the train and I’ll arrive later.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary essere/avere depending on the verb form: most commonly "ho perso la..." = "I lost/missed the...". With events/calls/parts of something, it often means "to miss" (e.g., "ho perso la chiamata" = "I missed the call"). Some common expressions: "perdere la memoria" (to lose one’s memory), "perdere la fiducia" (to lose trust), "perdere la vita" (to lose one’s life). The article "la" agrees with a feminine singular noun (la ricevuta, la chiamata, la parte, la vita).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho perso la chiave di casa.
native_language_example: Sorry, I lost the house key.

additional_notes: Used with the verb *perdere* (to lose): *Hai/Abbiamo/Avete perso la partita* = “You/We/You all lost the match.” In the reflexive form (*perdersi*), it often means “to miss” an event: *Ti sei perso la partita?* = “Did you miss the match?” (auxiliary *essere*: *mi/ti/si/ci/vi sono perso/a*).
target_language_example: Ho perso la partita, ma mi sono divertito lo stesso.
native_language_example: I lost the match, but I still had fun.

additional_notes: "Perso" is the past participle of "perdere" (to lose). With "avere" (e.g., "ha perso", "di aver perso", "sembra aver perso"), it expresses a completed action: "(someone) has lost...". "La sua" means "his/her" and usually refers back to the subject (e.g., Mary → her key).
target_language_example: Credo che abbia perso la sua chiave.
native_language_example: I think he/she has lost his/her key.

meaning: to lose your head; to lose control or go crazy (figuratively).
additional_notes: Common idiom used when someone panics, acts irrationally, or stops thinking clearly. In romance contexts it can also mean “to fall head over heels.” Conjugates normally: ho perso la testa, hai perso la testa, ha perso la testa, etc.
target_language_example: Quando ho visto il conto, ho perso la testa e ho iniziato a urlare.
native_language_example: When I saw the bill, I lost my head and started shouting.

meaning: to lose your temper; to snap.
additional_notes: Idiomatic expression used when someone suddenly gets very angry and loses self-control. Often appears in the past tense: (ho/ha) perso le staffe. It’s common in everyday speech and not vulgar, but it can sound strong depending on the situation.
target_language_example: Scusa, ieri ho perso le staffe.
native_language_example: Sorry, yesterday I lost my temper.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing which person you mean. Often preceded by an article or demonstrative (la/una/questa/quella persona che...). With 'persona' (feminine), the relative pronoun is still 'che' for both genders: "la persona che...", "la sola persona che...".
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli inglese.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a person who speaks English.

meaning: “the person (that/who) …” (used to introduce a clause with di cui = “about whom/that”).
additional_notes: Used when you refer to a specific person and then add information in a relative clause introduced by **di cui**. Most often it means **“the person (that) you’re talking about”** or **“a person you can trust.”** The verb after **di cui** often takes **parlare (di)** (“talk about”) or **fidarsi (di)** (“trust”). With **fidarsi**, you’ll see forms like **di cui mi posso fidare / di cui posso fidarmi** (same meaning).
target_language_example: Non è una persona di cui mi posso fidare.
native_language_example: He/She isn’t a person I can trust.

additional_notes: In Italian, *molto* (“very”) normally modifies an adjective, so this expression is typically incomplete by itself and is used like: *una persona molto gentile / molto simpatica / molto paziente* (“a very kind / very nice / very patient person”). On its own, *persona molto* sounds unfinished; you usually need the adjective after *molto*.
target_language_example: È una persona molto gentile.
native_language_example: She is a very kind person.

meaning: "people who" (introduces a relative clause about people).
additional_notes: Used when you’re describing a group of people and then adding information about them with a clause starting with che (= who/that). Often appears after "(ci) sono" or "delle/le" (e.g., "Ci sono persone che...", "le persone che...").
target_language_example: Conosco persone che parlano tre lingue.
native_language_example: I know people who speak three languages.

meaning: "but ... not" / "however, ... not" (introduces a contrast with a negative).
additional_notes: Used to contrast what you expect with what actually happens, followed by a verb in the negative. Often comes after a comma: "..., però non ...". Similar to "ma non", but "però" can sound a bit more like "however".
target_language_example: Volevo uscire, però non ho tempo.
native_language_example: I wanted to go out, but I don't have time.

meaning: Literally: “to draw/fish out the previous/last one.” (Not a standard set phrase; sounds incomplete without a noun after *scorso*.)
additional_notes: *Pescare* is commonly used for “drawing” something (a card, a name, a number): *pescare una carta / pescare un nome*. *Lo scorso* (“last/previous”) normally modifies a time word (*lo scorso anno, la scorsa settimana*) or is used with an implied noun only in very specific contexts. As a standalone phrase, *pescare lo scorso* is unusual; a more natural version would specify what is “previous” (e.g., *pescare la carta precedente / pescare il biglietto precedente*).
target_language_example: Nel gioco, non dovresti pescare lo scorso: pesca una nuova carta.
native_language_example: In the game, you shouldn’t draw the previous one: draw a new card.

meaning: goldfish; (figurative) someone with a very short memory.
additional_notes: Literally “red fish.” Most often it means the pet fish (“a goldfish”). In the expression “avere la memoria di un pesce rosso,” it’s a humorous way to say someone forgets things quickly.
target_language_example: Scusa, ho la memoria di un pesce rosso: come ti chiami?
native_language_example: Sorry, I have a goldfish memory—what’s your name?

additional_notes: Used to indicate a portion or chunk of something, often food: "un pezzo di pizza/pane". It’s usually preceded by an article ("un/uno/una", "questo") and followed by a noun. With amounts you’ll often hear "un altro pezzo di..." = "another piece of...".
target_language_example: Mi dai un pezzo di torta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of cake, please?

additional_notes: Used for any sheet/bit of paper (a note, message, scrap). It’s a normal, literal expression: pezzo = piece, carta = paper.
target_language_example: Puoi darmi un pezzo di carta per scrivere il numero?
native_language_example: Can you give me a piece of paper to write the number?

additional_notes: Extremely vulgar and aggressive. Used to insult someone directly (often like “You piece of shit!”) or to call someone a terrible person (“Sei un pezzo di merda”). Avoid in polite conversation; it can easily start a fight. In speech it may be used alone as an exclamation (“Pezzo di merda!”).
target_language_example: Non parlarmi così, pezzo di merda!
native_language_example: Don’t talk to me like that, you piece of shit!

additional_notes: Used when offering, requesting, or talking about a serving of cake. With one portion, Italian often says "un pezzo di torta" (literally “a piece of cake”).
target_language_example: Posso avere un pezzo di torta, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a piece of cake, please?

meaning: a big shot; an important/influential person.
additional_notes: Informal. Used for someone with power, status, or authority (in a company, the government, the police, even criminal groups). Often said with irony or annoyance (like “Listen here, big shot”). You’ll also hear it with articles: "un pezzo grosso" (a big shot), "il pezzo grosso" (the top person/the main boss).
target_language_example: Se vuoi una decisione veloce, devi parlare con il pezzo grosso.
native_language_example: If you want a quick decision, you have to talk to the big shot.

meaning: “(I/you/etc.) really like the …” (with a plural feminine noun).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”), so the person who likes something is an indirect object: mi piace/piacciono = “I like”, ti piace/piacciono = “you like”, gli/le piace/piacciono = “he/she likes”, ci/vi piace/piacciono = “we/you(pl) like”. Use piacciono (plural) because the thing liked is plural; le is the feminine plural article (le canzoni, le torte). Word order is often: [to me] + piacciono + davvero + le + [things].
target_language_example: Mi piacciono davvero le tue idee.
native_language_example: I really like your ideas.

meaning: "(Do/does) … like the …?" / "… like(s) the …" (with plural masculine nouns starting with a vowel, s+consonant, z, gn, ps, pn, x, y).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say that someone likes something; the thing liked is the grammatical subject (piacciono = plural). The person who likes it is introduced with an indirect pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with a + name (A Tom…). “Gli” is the plural masculine article used before certain sounds (e.g., gli sport, gli orologi, gli asiatici, gli ananas, gli involtini). Word order often starts with the person: “Mi piacciono gli …” = “I like the …”.
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono gli involtini primavera.
native_language_example: Marco likes spring rolls.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to express likes. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Tom..."); the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you often use a pronoun like "gli/le" (to him/to her). Because "gli animali" is plural, you use the plural verb form "piacciono" (vs. singular "piace").
target_language_example: A me piacciono gli animali, soprattutto i cani.
native_language_example: I like animals, especially dogs.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”): the thing you like is the grammatical subject. So you say: Mi piacciono gli uomini = “I like men” (literally, “Men please me”). Verb is plural (piacciono) because uomini is plural. Often used with an indirect object pronoun: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli.
target_language_example: Ti piacciono gli uomini o le donne?
native_language_example: Do you like men or women?

meaning: "(They) like the ..." (plural masculine) / "the ... are pleasing to (someone)".
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to talk about liking things. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you often add an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: mi piacciono i... (I like...), ti piacciono i... (you like...), gli/le piacciono i... (he/she likes...), ci piacciono i... (we like...), vi piacciono i... (you all like...), gli piacciono i... (they like...). Use piacciono (plural) because i + noun is plural; for singular use piace: mi piace il.... With feminine plural use piacciono le....
target_language_example: Mi piacciono i film italiani.
native_language_example: I like Italian movies.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (indirect object): "A Tom piacciono i cani" = "Tom likes dogs." The thing that is liked ("i cani") is grammatically the subject, so the verb is plural: "piacciono" (because dogs = plural). With a singular thing you use "piace" (e.g., "A Tom piace il cane").
target_language_example: A mia sorella piacciono i cani, ma non le piacciono i gatti.
native_language_example: My sister likes dogs, but she doesn't like cats.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”). The thing you like is the grammatical subject, so it often appears after the verb: piacciono (plural) i cani piccoli. The person who likes them is shown with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) or with “a + person”: Mi piacciono… / A te piacciono… / Le piacciono…
target_language_example: A me piacciono i cani piccoli, ma a mio fratello piacciono i cani grandi.
native_language_example: I like small dogs, but my brother likes big dogs.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works differently from English: the thing liked (i cavalli) is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it (piacciono = plural). The person who likes it is introduced with a + stressed pronoun/name (a me, a Mary) or an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli). Example patterns: A me piacciono i cavalli. / Ti piacciono i cavalli? / Perché vi piacciono i cavalli?
target_language_example: A loro piacciono i cavalli, ma a me piacciono i cani.
native_language_example: They like horses, but I like dogs.

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the thing liked (i film) is the grammatical subject, so you use the 3rd-person plural verb form piacciono. The person who likes is introduced with a + indirect object pronoun/name: A me/te/lui/lei/Lei/noi/voi/loro piacciono i film. If the thing liked is singular, use piace (e.g., Mi piace questo film).
target_language_example: A me piacciono i film d’azione.
native_language_example: I like action movies.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). Grammatically, "i fiori" is the subject, and the person who likes them is introduced with "a" (e.g., "a lui", "a Layla") or an indirect object pronoun ("mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi"). Because "i fiori" is plural, it takes the plural verb form "piacciono" (singular would be "piace").
target_language_example: A mia madre piacciono i fiori, soprattutto le rose.
native_language_example: My mother likes flowers, especially roses.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing liked (i frutti di mare) is the grammatical subject, so you use piacciono (plural). The person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (a lui/a noi/a loro) or with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): e.g., Ci piacciono i frutti di mare = We like seafood.
target_language_example: Ti piacciono i frutti di mare?
native_language_example: Do you like seafood?

meaning: (they) like cats / cats are pleasing (to someone).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The thing liked (“i gatti”) is the grammatical subject, so you often add the person with a + pronoun/name: “A me/A Susan…”. With plural things (like i gatti), use piacciono; with a singular thing, use piace.
target_language_example: A Marco piacciono i gatti, ma a sua sorella piacciono i cani.
native_language_example: Marco likes cats, but his sister likes dogs.

additional_notes: Uses piacere (to be pleasing) with an indirect object: Mi/Ci/Gli/Le piacciono i giochi = “I/We/He/She like games.” The person who likes something is introduced with a (A Tom piacciono i giochi). With plural things (i giochi), use piacciono; with a singular thing (il gioco), use piace.
target_language_example: A mia sorella piacciono i giochi da tavolo.
native_language_example: My sister likes board games.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The thing liked is the grammatical subject: "i libri piacciono" = "books are pleasing". Add the person with "a + pronoun/name": "A me/te/lui/lei piace/piacciono..." Use "piacciono" with plural nouns like "i libri" (use "piace" with singular: "Mi piace il libro").
target_language_example: A te piacciono i libri di avventura?
native_language_example: Do you like adventure books?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere (to be pleasing). The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: a me, a lui, a voi, etc. Because "i pomodori" is plural, you use the plural verb form "piacciono" (singular would be "piace"). Common patterns: "A me piacciono i pomodori" = I like tomatoes; "Gli piacciono i pomodori?" = Does he like tomatoes? (gli = to him).
target_language_example: A Maria piacciono i pomodori, ma non le piacciono le cipolle.
native_language_example: Maria likes tomatoes, but she doesn’t like onions.

meaning: 'they are liked' / 'they please' (used to say someone likes things—plural feminine).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing to”: the person who likes is an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli) and the thing liked is the subject. "Piacciono" is 3rd-person plural to match a plural thing, and "le" is the feminine plural article (le auto, le acciughe). Structure: A + person + piacciono le + plural noun. Example: "A me piacciono le..." = "I like...".
target_language_example: A me piacciono le fragole.
native_language_example: I like strawberries.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing). The thing liked (le arance) is the grammatical subject, so it takes piacciono (plural). The person who likes them is introduced with a + name/pronoun: A Tom piacciono le arance. With pronouns you often use indirect object pronouns: Gli piacciono le arance? (= Does he like oranges?). For one item you use piace: Mi piace l’arancia / Mi piace questa arancia.
target_language_example: A me piacciono le arance, ma a mia sorella no.
native_language_example: I like oranges, but my sister doesn’t.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say someone likes something. The thing liked ("le mele") is the grammatical subject, so the verb agrees with it: "piacciono" for plural, "piace" for singular. The person who likes it is introduced with "a" (e.g., "a me", "a te", "a lei", "a noi"). In questions, intonation often changes or you can add a question mark in writing: "A te piacciono le mele?" For negation: "non piacciono".
target_language_example: A Marco non piacciono le mele, ma gli piacciono le pere.
native_language_example: Marco doesn’t like apples, but he likes pears.

additional_notes: This is used with the verb piacere, which works differently from English “to like.” The thing you like is the grammatical subject: Le persone piacciono… To say who likes them, you add an indirect object pronoun: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli/le (to him/her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). So in a full sentence you’ll usually say: Mi piacciono le persone. (Without mi/ti/etc., it can sound incomplete.)
target_language_example: Mi piacciono le persone gentili.
native_language_example: I like kind people.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”). The person who likes is usually introduced with an indirect object: a me/a te/a lui/a lei/a noi/a loro, or pronouns like gli/le/mi/ti/ci/gli. Because ragazze is plural, you use piacciono (plural) rather than piace (singular). Word order can vary: Le ragazze gli piacciono = “He likes girls.”
target_language_example: A te piacciono le ragazze?
native_language_example: Do you like girls?

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: **mi piace andare in…** (I like going to…), **ti piace andare in…** (you like…), **gli/le piace…** (he/she likes…), **ci piace…** (we like…). With plural things/activities, use **piacciono** instead of **piace**. The place often follows with **in** for countries/regions and many place types (e.g., **in Italia, in montagna, in palestra**), while **a** is common for cities (**a Roma**).
target_language_example: Mi piace andare in montagna nel weekend.
native_language_example: I like going to the mountains on the weekend.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing to”), so the person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: mi piace… (I like…), ti piace… (you like…), gli/le piace… (he/she likes…), ci piace… (we like…), vi piace… (you all like…). You can also use a + name/pronoun: A Tom piace… (“Tom likes…”). With an infinitive, use piace (singular): Mi piace ascoltare…
target_language_example: A Lucia piace ascoltare il jazz la sera.
native_language_example: Lucia likes listening to jazz in the evening.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally: “to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: "A me piace…" or "Mi piace…" (I like…), "A Tom piace…" (Tom likes…). You can add a genre or details after "la musica": "la musica pop", "la musica jazz", "la musica degli anni ottanta".
target_language_example: Mi piace ascoltare la musica mentre studio.
native_language_example: I like listening to music while I study.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with “a + name/pronoun.” The thing liked (here: “cantare”) is the subject, so you say “Mi piace cantare” = “Singing is pleasing to me” → “I like to sing.” You can add what you like to sing: “Mi piace cantare canzoni italiane.”
target_language_example: Mi piace cantare quando sono da solo in macchina.
native_language_example: I like to sing when I’m alone in the car.

additional_notes: Used with piacere, where the thing liked is the grammatical subject and the person who likes it is introduced by an indirect object (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): e.g., «Perché ti piace così tanto Boston?» = “Why do you like Boston so much?” Often appears in questions with «Perché…?» and can refer to a specific thing («ti piace così tanto il basket») or just “it” («ti piace così tanto?»).
target_language_example: Mi piace così tanto questa città che vorrei viverci.
native_language_example: I like this city so much that I’d like to live here.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to express that someone likes doing something. The person who likes it is an indirect object: mi piace cucinare (I like to cook), ti piace cucinare? (Do you like to cook?), le/vi piace cucinare? (Do you/you all like to cook? formal/plural). The activity (cucinare) is treated as the thing that is pleasing, so you use piace (singular).
target_language_example: Mi piace cucinare la pasta la domenica.
native_language_example: I like cooking pasta on Sundays.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to emphasize that someone genuinely likes something/someone. Remember the "piacere" structure is reversed compared to English: "A Tom piace davvero Mary" literally means "Mary is really pleasing to Tom" = "Tom really likes Mary." The person who likes is introduced by "a" (a me/ti/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro), and the thing liked is the subject. With verbs, you often use the infinitive: "Mi piace davvero farlo" = "I really like doing it."
target_language_example: Mi piace davvero questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I really like this restaurant.

additional_notes: This is a fragment you’ll usually see with an indirect object pronoun: "Mi/ti/gli/le piace davvero il ..." (= "I/you/he/she really likes the ..."). With "piacere", the thing liked is the grammatical subject, so use "piace" for singular nouns (il/la) and "piacciono" for plural (i/le): "Mi piacciono davvero i ...".
target_language_example: Mi piace davvero il tuo cappotto.
native_language_example: I really like your coat.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing), so the person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Mary...") or with an indirect object pronoun ("gli" = to him, "le" = to her). "Il suo impiego" means “his/her job/employment,” and "davvero" adds emphasis (“really”).
target_language_example: A Marco piace davvero il suo impiego, anche se è stancante.
native_language_example: Marco really likes his job, even if it's tiring.

additional_notes: Used with piacere to compare preferences (more than something else) or to say what you like the most. Often appears in questions with a choice (Cosa ti piace di più, X o Y?) and in relative clauses: Il/La ... che mi piace di più = “my favorite ...”. Remember the grammar: the thing you like is the subject (Mi piace...), and the person is an indirect object (mi/ti/le/gli/ci/vi/gli).
target_language_example: Tra questi due ristoranti, quale ti piace di più?
native_language_example: Between these two restaurants, which one do you like more?

meaning: “to like doing / to like to do”.
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive to say someone likes an activity. The person who likes it is marked with an indirect object pronoun (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with “a + name”: “Mi piace fare…”, “A Maria piace fare…”. Often used in questions about hobbies: “Cosa ti piace fare…?”
target_language_example: Mi piace fare una passeggiata dopo cena.
native_language_example: I like to go for a walk after dinner.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive. The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (a me, a te, a Mary, a loro). With an infinitive like giocare, you normally use piace (singular). Note: piace looks like English “please,” but here it means “(to) like,” so it can be confusing.
target_language_example: A mio fratello piace giocare a calcio dopo scuola.
native_language_example: My brother likes to play soccer after school.

meaning: “(someone) likes to play (a game/sport)” (literally: “it pleases (someone) to play”).
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive. The person who likes something is an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): “Mi piace giocare a …” = “I like to play …”. Use “giocare a” before many games and sports: a calcio (soccer), a tennis, a carte (cards). For plural activities, you may hear “Mi piace giocare a…” anyway, but the strict agreement is “Mi piacciono …” when the thing liked is plural (e.g., “Mi piacciono i videogiochi”).
target_language_example: Mi piace giocare a calcio nel weekend.
native_language_example: I like playing soccer on the weekend.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere. The person who likes it is introduced with "a" (A me/te/lei/lui/noi/voi/loro) and the thing liked is the activity: "piace" + infinitive (giocare...). For questions, raise intonation or use a question mark: "A te piace giocare a badminton?".
target_language_example: A Marco piace giocare a badminton il sabato.
native_language_example: Marco likes to play badminton on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with "a" (a me, a te, a lui/lei, a noi, a voi, a loro). The thing liked is the subject: "giocare a calcio" (to play soccer) + "piace" (singular, because an activity counts as one thing). You can turn it into a question by raising your intonation: "A te piace...?"
target_language_example: A loro piace giocare a calcio dopo scuola.
native_language_example: They like to play soccer after school.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally “to be pleasing”), so you normally add an indirect object pronoun: "Mi piace giocare a carte" = “I like playing cards,” "Ti piace..." = “You like...,” "Gli/Le piace..." = “He/She likes...”. "Giocare a carte" means “to play cards” (card games in general).
target_language_example: Mi piace giocare a carte con gli amici.
native_language_example: I like playing cards with friends.

additional_notes: This uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). In real sentences you normally add the indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: mi piace… (I like…), ti piace… (you like…), gli/le piace… (he/she likes…), ci piace… (we like…), vi piace… (you all like…), gli piace… (they like…). With an infinitive like giocare (“to play”), you typically use the singular: Mi piace giocare a mahjong. To ask: Ti piace giocare a mahjong?
target_language_example: Mi piace giocare a mahjong la sera.
native_language_example: I like playing mahjong in the evening.

additional_notes: In Italian, piacere works like “to be pleasing” to someone. You almost always add an indirect object pronoun: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli. So you normally say: “Mi piace giocare a tennis” = “I like playing tennis” (literally: “Playing tennis is pleasing to me”). You can also use it with a name: “A Marco piace giocare a tennis.”
target_language_example: Mi piace giocare a tennis il sabato.
native_language_example: I like playing tennis on Saturdays.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the thing being watched is the grammatical subject. Common patterns: “Mi piace guardare…” = “I like to watch…”, “Ti piace guardare…?” = “Do you like to watch…?”, “A Tom piace guardare…” = “Tom likes to watch…”. You can also use “piace guardare + noun” (e.g., “piace guardare le serie TV”).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare film in italiano con i sottotitoli.
native_language_example: I like watching movies in Italian with subtitles.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked is the subject (guardare la TV), and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (a me, a lui, a Felicja). Example patterns: A me piace guardare la TV. / A loro piace guardare la TV mentre mangiano. With a plural thing liked, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i film).
target_language_example: A me piace guardare la TV la sera.
native_language_example: I like to watch TV in the evening.

additional_notes: Used with piacere when the thing liked is singular and masculine: e.g. A Tom piace il tennis. Literally, Italian structures this as 'the tennis is pleasing to Tom,' so the person is marked with a, mi, ti, gli, le, ci, or vi. With plural things, Italian uses piacciono instead.
target_language_example: Mi piace il caffè italiano.
native_language_example: I like Italian coffee.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked (il basket) is the subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli + a Tom). So it’s literally “basketball is pleasing to (someone),” even though in English we say “(someone) likes basketball.” Questions are often formed just with intonation: A Tom piace il basket?
target_language_example: Ti piace il basket o preferisci il calcio?
native_language_example: Do you like basketball, or do you prefer soccer?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom…, A loro…). With singular thing: piace; with plural things: piacciono. Common forms: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace il caffè.
target_language_example: Mi piace il caffè, ma non mi piace il tè.
native_language_example: I like coffee, but I don't like tea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object (a me, a te, a Tom, a tutte le mie amiche). Because calcio is singular, you use piace (not piacciono). Word order is flexible: A Tom piace il calcio / Il calcio piace a Tom.
target_language_example: A me piace il calcio, ma a mio fratello piace il basket.
native_language_example: I like soccer, but my brother likes basketball.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (A Tom, A me, A tutti), and the thing liked is the grammatical subject: A Tom piace il cibo = “Tom likes food” (literally: “Food is pleasing to Tom”). With plural things, use piacciono: A Tom piacciono i dolci (“Tom likes sweets”).
target_language_example: A me piace il cibo italiano.
native_language_example: I like Italian food.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with an indirect object (often with a + pronoun/noun): a me/mi (I), a te/ti (you), a lui/gli (he), a lei/le (she), a noi/ci (we), a voi/vi (you all), a loro/gli. The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so with a singular noun you use piace; with plural nouns you use piacciono.
target_language_example: Mi piace il cibo cinese, ma oggi preferisco la pizza.
native_language_example: I like Chinese food, but today I prefer pizza.

meaning: “(someone) likes the color” / “the color is nice (to someone).”
additional_notes: With piacere, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: **il colore piace** = “the color is pleasing.” In real sentences you almost always add an indirect object pronoun to say *who* likes it: **Mi piace il colore** (I like the color), **Ti piace il colore?** (Do you like the color?), **Le piace il colore** (She likes the color / You [formal] like the color).
target_language_example: Mi piace il colore di questa maglietta.
native_language_example: I like the color of this T-shirt.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes something. The thing liked (il gelato) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi piace il gelato (I like ice cream), ti piace...? (do you like...?), le piace...? (formal you), a chi piace...? (who likes...?). With plural things, use piacciono (e.g., Mi piacciono i gelati).
target_language_example: Mi piace il gelato al cioccolato, ma non mi piace quello alla vaniglia.
native_language_example: I like chocolate ice cream, but I don’t like vanilla one.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (A me/ a te/ a lui/ a lei/ a Tom...), and the verb agrees with what is liked: "piace" + singular thing (il jazz), "piacciono" + plural things (i film).
target_language_example: A me piace il jazz, ma a mio fratello no.
native_language_example: I like jazz, but my brother doesn't.

additional_notes: Used to say you like (or don’t like) someone’s behavior/style of doing something. Italian often uses the structure "A + person + piace" (e.g., "A Maria piace...") or "Mi piace / Non mi piace...". "il modo" = “the way/manner,” and "in cui" = “in which/that.” You can also use the plural: "Mi piacciono i modi in cui..." (“I like the ways (that) ...”).
target_language_example: Mi piace il modo in cui parli italiano.
native_language_example: I like the way you speak Italian.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”), so the person who likes something is marked with an indirect object (a me/mi, a te/ti, a lei/le, etc.). The thing liked (il purè) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is usually singular here: mi piace il purè (“I like mashed potatoes”). You can form a question with intonation or a question mark: Ti piace il purè?
target_language_example: A noi piace il purè, ma a loro no.
native_language_example: We like mashed potatoes, but they don’t.

additional_notes: Used with piacere: the thing liked (il riso) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace...). Common pattern: (A me/Marco) piace il riso; (A noi) piace il riso.
target_language_example: A me piace il riso, ma non mi piace la pasta.
native_language_example: I like rice, but I don’t like pasta.

meaning: (lit.) “likes his/her own”; used like “to each their own / everyone has their own taste.”
additional_notes: Usually appears in a fuller phrase like “A ciascuno piace il suo” or “A ognuno piace il suo,” meaning different people like different things. “Suo” can also change to match the person: “il mio” (mine), “il tuo” (yours), “il nostro” (ours), etc.
target_language_example: Non a tutti piace lo stesso film: a ciascuno piace il suo.
native_language_example: Not everyone likes the same movie: to each their own.

meaning: “you like your coffee” (literally: “your coffee is pleasing to you”).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing to.” The person who likes something is usually expressed with an indirect object pronoun (Le/ti/mi/ci/vi), and the thing liked is the subject: “(Le) piace il suo caffè?” = “Do you like your coffee?” In polite/formal speech you’ll often see it with “Le” and “suo/sua/suoi/sue.” On its own, “piace il suo caffè” sounds incomplete—you normally include the pronoun: “Le piace il suo caffè.”
target_language_example: Le piace il suo caffè?
native_language_example: Do you like your coffee?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere: the person who likes something is introduced with a + pronoun/name (A me piace il tennis = I like tennis; A Tom piace il tennis? = Does Tom like tennis?). Negative: non piace. You can swap order: Il tennis mi piace.
target_language_example: A te piace il tennis?
native_language_example: Do you like tennis?

meaning: “(I) like yours” / “your one pleases (me)” (used with an indirect object like mi/ti).
additional_notes: In Italian, piacere works differently from English “to like”: the thing you like is the grammatical subject. So you normally say **Mi piace il tuo** = “I like yours” (literally: “Yours pleases me”). **Il tuo** means “yours” (masculine singular), usually referring to a masculine noun understood from context (e.g., *il telefono*, *il cappotto*). You can also use **Ti piace il tuo?** = “Do you like yours?”
target_language_example: Mi piace il tuo, ma preferisco il mio.
native_language_example: I like yours, but I prefer mine.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing): the thing liked (il tè) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object (a/ad + pronoun/name), e.g., Mi piace il tè = I like tea; A lui piace il tè = He likes tea; Ti piace il tè? = Do you like tea?
target_language_example: Mi piace il tè, ma preferisco il caffè.
native_language_example: I like tea, but I prefer coffee.

additional_notes: With the verb **piacere** (“to be pleasing”), the thing you like is the grammatical subject. You usually add an indirect object pronoun to show **who** likes it: **Mi piace il vino** = “I like wine”; **Ti piace il vino?** = “Do you like wine?” For plural things: **Mi piacciono** + plural noun (e.g., *Mi piacciono i formaggi*).
target_language_example: Mi piace il vino, ma preferisco la birra.
native_language_example: I like wine, but I prefer beer.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: **Mi piace il vostro** = “I like yours.” It refers to something already understood (e.g., your car/idea). **Il vostro** is masculine singular (“your [one]” to multiple people or in formal address). Variations: **la vostra** (fem. sing.), **i vostri / le vostre** (plural). Italian often prefers **Mi piace il vostro** rather than **Io piaccio il vostro** (because the thing liked is the grammatical subject).
target_language_example: Mi piace il vostro, ma preferisco il nostro.
native_language_example: I like yours, but I prefer ours.

additional_notes: This uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). In real sentences you normally add an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: "Mi piace insegnare il francese" = "I like teaching French" (literally: "Teaching French pleases me"). You can change the pronoun: "Ti piace..." (you like), "Gli/Le piace..." (he/she likes), "Ci piace..." (we like), "Vi piace..." (you all like), "Gli piace..." (they like).
target_language_example: Mi piace insegnare il francese, ma oggi sono stanco.
native_language_example: I like teaching French, but today I’m tired.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to express liking. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (or a pronoun like "mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli"). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, so you use "piace" for singular ("la ...") and "piacciono" for plural. Example: "A Maria piace la macchina" = "Maria likes the car" (literally: "To Maria, the car is pleasing").
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza.
native_language_example: I like pizza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, where the thing liked (la birra) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect pronoun: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli/le (to him/her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). Often: A me piace la birra / Mi piace la birra. With plural things: Mi piacciono le birre artigianali.
target_language_example: A noi piace la birra, ma non ci piace il vino.
native_language_example: We like beer, but we don’t like wine.

additional_notes: With piacere, the thing liked (here, la cioccolata) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is expressed with an indirect object pronoun or with a + name/pronoun: mi piace... (I like...), ti piace...? (Do you like...?), a Paul piace... (Paul likes...). Use piace (singular) with one thing; use piacciono with plural things (e.g., Mi piacciono i biscotti).
target_language_example: Ti piace la cioccolata fondente?
native_language_example: Do you like dark chocolate?

meaning: “(Do you) like mine?” (usually: “Ti piace la mia?”).
additional_notes: As written, it’s incomplete in standard Italian: you normally need an indirect object pronoun with piacere (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli), e.g. “Ti piace la mia?” = “Do you like mine?”. “La mia” means “mine” (feminine), and it refers to a feminine noun understood from context (e.g. la macchina, la borsa, la pizza, la foto). For a masculine noun you’d use “il mio”.
target_language_example: Ti piace la mia macchina?
native_language_example: Do you like my car?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally “to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (indirect object): "A Nancy piace la musica" = “Nancy likes music.” The thing liked (“la musica”) is the grammatical subject, so the verb is singular (piace). With pronouns you’ll often hear: "Mi piace la musica" (I like music), "Ti piace la musica" (Do you like music?).
target_language_example: A Marco piace la musica classica.
native_language_example: Marco likes classical music.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes it is introduced with a + indirect object: A Tom piace la musica classica = “Tom likes classical music” (literally, “Classical music is pleasing to Tom”). Question form: A te piace la musica classica? (“Do you like classical music?”).
target_language_example: A mia sorella piace la musica classica, ma a me piace il rock.
native_language_example: My sister likes classical music, but I like rock.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere": the thing liked ("la pasta") is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with "a" (often combined with an article: "a + il = al"). So "A Tom piace la pasta" is literally “To Tom, pasta is pleasing.” For more than one person, use "piacciono" (e.g., "A Tom e Maria piacciono i film").
target_language_example: A me piace la pasta, ma a mia sorella piace il riso.
native_language_example: I like pasta, but my sister likes rice.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works differently from English “to like.” The person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun (or an indirect object pronoun: mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli). The thing that is liked is the grammatical subject: piace with singular nouns (la pizza), and piacciono with plural nouns (Le pizze mi piacciono). Common pattern: A Marco piace la pizza / A loro piace la pizza.
target_language_example: A me piace la pizza, ma a mia sorella piacciono gli hamburger.
native_language_example: I like pizza, but my sister likes hamburgers.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing liked (la root beer) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli; e.g., A me piace..., A te piace...?). Often used as a question: Ti piace la root beer? = “Do you like root beer?”
target_language_example: A me piace la root beer, ma a lui non piace.
native_language_example: I like root beer, but he doesn’t like it.

meaning: “(Someone) likes his/her new …” (feminine noun implied or follows).
additional_notes: This is likely part of a longer sentence such as “Mi piace la sua nuova macchina.” In Italian, *piacere* works like “to please”: the thing liked is the grammatical subject (*la sua nuova … piace*), and the person who likes it is an indirect object (often *mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli*). *La sua nuova* means “his/her new” and agrees with a feminine singular noun (e.g., *auto*, *borsa*, *casa*) that may follow or be understood from context.
target_language_example: Mi piace la sua nuova auto.
native_language_example: I like his/her new car.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (literally "to be pleasing"), so the person who likes something is marked with "a" (A me/A te/A Tom) or with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/le/gli). The thing liked is the subject: "leggere" (to read) or what you read ("Mi piace leggere romanzi"). Common forms: "Mi piace leggere" = I like reading; "Ti piace leggere...?" = Do you like reading...?; "Le piace leggere" (polite) = You like reading.
target_language_example: Ti piace leggere prima di dormire?
native_language_example: Do you like reading before going to sleep?

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”), so the person who likes something is introduced with a + name/pronoun: A Maria piace… (“Maria likes…”). With pronouns you often use indirect object forms: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli piace… (“I/you/he/she/we/you(pl)/they like…”). Example: Gli piace leggere… = “He likes reading…”. You can add an adjective for the type of literature: la letteratura inglese/francese.
target_language_example: A me piace leggere la letteratura italiana.
native_language_example: I like reading Italian literature.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A Tom piace leggere libri = “Tom likes reading books” (literally: “Reading books is pleasing to Tom”). The thing liked is the subject (here: leggere libri). Question form is the same word order, with rising intonation or a question mark in writing.
target_language_example: Ti piace leggere libri in italiano?
native_language_example: Do you like reading books in Italian?

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to say someone likes doing an activity. The person who likes it is an indirect object: mi piace mangiare (I like to eat), ti piace mangiare? (Do you like to eat?), a Marco piace mangiare… (Marco likes to eat…), ai conigli piace mangiare… (Rabbits like to eat…). Use piace (singular) because the thing liked is the action “mangiare.”
target_language_example: Ti piace mangiare la pizza?
native_language_example: Do you like eating pizza?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say someone likes something a lot. Italian structure is different from English: the thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with "a" or an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli). Example: "Mi piace molto questo posto" = "I really like this place" (literally: "This place pleases me a lot").
target_language_example: Mi piace molto questa canzone.
native_language_example: I really like this song.

additional_notes: This is a common fragment you’ll see inside a full sentence like “Mi piace molto il …” = “I really like the …”. Italian uses the verb piacere (to be pleasing), so the thing you like is the grammatical subject: “Mi piace il caffè” (Coffee is pleasing to me). Use “il” before a masculine singular noun (il caffè, il film). Often you’ll need a pronoun before it: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli. For plural nouns you’d use “piacciono molto i/gli/le …”.
target_language_example: Mi piace molto il caffè.
native_language_example: I really like coffee.

meaning: “(Someone) really likes his/her new …” (literally: “his/her new … is very pleasing”).
additional_notes:
This chunk is incomplete on its own: it normally needs (1) who likes it (often with an indirect object pronoun) and (2) what the “new” thing is.

With **piacere**, the thing liked is the grammatical subject: **A Marco piace molto il suo nuovo telefono** = “Marco really likes his new phone” (literally: “Marco is very pleased by his new phone”). Common pattern: **(a + person) + piace molto + (the thing)**.

**il suo / la sua / i suoi / le sue** = “his/her/your (formal) …”; **nuovo/nuova/nuovi/nuove** must agree with the noun that follows.
target_language_example: A Giulia piace molto il suo nuovo lavoro.
native_language_example: Giulia really likes her new job.

additional_notes: Used with indirect object pronouns to say what someone enjoys discussing: "Mi piace parlare di..." (I like to talk about...), "Ti piace parlare di...?" (Do you like to talk about...?). After "di" you can use a noun ("di musica"), or "di" + infinitive to talk about an activity/topic ("di viaggiare").
target_language_example: Mi piace parlare di musica con i miei amici.
native_language_example: I like to talk about music with my friends.

meaning: “to like to go for a walk / to like strolling.”
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere + infinitive: literally “(it) is pleasing to (someone) to stroll.” The person who likes it is shown with an indirect object pronoun: mi piace… (I like…), ti piace… (you like…), le piace… (you like…, formal or “she likes…”), gli piace… (he likes…). You can also specify with A me / A lei / A Marco, etc.: A lei piace passeggiare? = Do you (formal) like to go for a walk? Note: piace looks like English “please” but it doesn’t mean “please!” here.
target_language_example: Ti piace passeggiare in centro la sera?
native_language_example: Do you like strolling downtown in the evening?

additional_notes: Uses the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). The thing liked is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with "a + person" (A te piace... = You like...) or an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli). Negative: "Non mi piace questo..." = "I don’t like this...". Often followed by a noun: "piace questo colore/cibo".
target_language_example: Ti piace questo ristorante?
native_language_example: Do you like this restaurant?

additional_notes: This is a common structure with the verb "piacere" (to be pleasing). In Italian, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: "questo tipo di musica". The person who likes it is expressed with an indirect object pronoun: "Mi piace questo tipo di musica" (I like this kind of music), "Ti piace...?" (Do you like...?), "Le piace...?" (Do you like...? formal).
target_language_example: Mi piace questo tipo di musica, ma non mi piace il jazz.
native_language_example: I like this kind of music, but I don’t like jazz.

additional_notes: In Italian, *piacere* works like “to be pleasing to.” You normally need an indirect object pronoun to say who likes it: **Mi piace studiare il francese** (I like studying French), **Ti piace...** (you like...), **Gli/Le piace...** (he/she likes...). Without the pronoun, the phrase sounds incomplete in most situations.
target_language_example: Mi piace studiare il francese, ma è un po' difficile.
native_language_example: I like studying French, but it's a bit difficult.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere to emphasize a strong liking. Remember the structure: A + person + piace + thing/activity (literally “To [someone], [thing] is pleasing”). With pronouns: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi piace veramente… (e.g., Gli piace veramente = He really likes it).
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente questa pizza.
native_language_example: I really like this pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "piacere" to say that something is really pleasing to someone. It normally appears with an indirect object pronoun (mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli): e.g., "Mi piace veramente il caffè" = "I really like coffee." Word order can vary, but "mi piace veramente il..." is very common. Agreement note: use "piace" with a singular thing ("il libro"), and "piacciono" with plural things ("i libri").
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente il tuo libro.
native_language_example: I really like your book.

additional_notes: Usually used with an indirect object pronoun: **Mi piace veramente il suo** = “I really like his/hers/yours (formal).” **Il suo** is a possessive pronoun meaning “his/hers/its/your (formal)” and it refers back to something already understood (e.g., his car, her jacket, your idea). Often you’ll hear **Mi piace molto il suo** (“I like his/hers a lot”) as a more common alternative.
target_language_example: Mi piace veramente il suo, ma preferisco il mio.
native_language_example: I really like his/hers, but I prefer mine.

additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere: the thing you like (here, viaggiare = “to travel”) is the grammatical subject, and the person who likes it is introduced with a + pronoun/name: A me piace viaggiare (I like traveling), A Tom piace viaggiare (Tom likes traveling). With an infinitive like viaggiare, you typically use piace (singular).
target_language_example: Ti piace viaggiare in treno?
native_language_example: Do you like traveling by train?

additional_notes: Uses the verb *piacere* (to be pleasing). You normally say **Mi piace viaggiare da solo** = “I like traveling alone” (literally: “Traveling alone is pleasing to me”). You can change the person: **Ti/Gli/Le/Ci/Vi piace…**
target_language_example: Mi piace viaggiare da solo, perché posso decidere tutto io.
native_language_example: I like traveling alone because I can decide everything myself.

additional_notes: Used when you meet someone for the first time in a formal/polite context. It uses the formal object pronoun “La” (= you), so you say it to someone you would address with “Lei” (e.g., a stranger, a boss, an older person). Less formal: “piacere di conoscerti”. Often said on its own as “Piacere.”
target_language_example: Buongiorno, piacere di conoscerla, dottore.
native_language_example: Good morning, nice to meet you, doctor.

additional_notes: A common greeting when you meet someone for the first time. Often said after exchanging names. You’ll also hear variations: “piacere di conoscerla” (formal, to someone you address as Lei), “piacere di conoscerti” (informal, to someone you address as tu), or simply “Piacere!” (“Nice to meet you!”).
target_language_example: Ciao, sono Emma. Piacere di conoscerti!
native_language_example: Hi, I'm Emma. Nice to meet you!

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense. The person who likes something is introduced with "a" (e.g., "A Fadil..."), and the thing liked is grammatically the subject. "Piaceva" is for singular things; for plural things use "piacevano". It agrees with the noun after it (here "la" + a feminine singular noun). Often translates to English as "liked" in the past.
target_language_example: Da bambino, a me piaceva la pizza.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the imperfect tense (piaceva) to talk about liking in the past, often in reported speech after che (e.g., Ha detto che...). Remember the structure: the thing liked is the subject (la mia idea), and the person who likes it is an indirect object pronoun (gli/le/mi) or a + pronoun (a lui/a loro).
target_language_example: Mi ha detto che le piaceva la mia idea.
native_language_example: He/She told me that she liked my idea.

meaning: "(Someone) liked the snow" (in the past / used to like the snow).
additional_notes: Uses the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing”: a lei piaceva la neve = “she liked the snow” (literally, “the snow was pleasing to her”). Piaceva is the imperfect tense, common in reported speech after ha detto che… and for describing past preferences/habits. The person who likes something is shown with an indirect object (mi, ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli) or with a + pronoun (a me, a lei, a loro).
target_language_example: Da bambino, mi piaceva la neve, ma ora preferisco il sole.
native_language_example: As a child, I liked the snow, but now I prefer the sun.

meaning: “(he/she) liked the rain” / “(he/she) used to like the rain.”
additional_notes: Imperfect of piacere (“to be pleasing”). The person who likes something is expressed with an indirect object: mi (to me), ti (to you), gli (to him), le (to her), ci (to us), vi (to you all), gli (to them). So “A lui piaceva la pioggia” literally means “To him, the rain was pleasing,” i.e., “He liked the rain,” often describing a past habit or ongoing feeling.
target_language_example: Da bambino, gli piaceva la pioggia perché poteva saltare nelle pozzanghere.
native_language_example: As a child, he liked the rain because he could jump in puddles.

meaning: “(someone) liked pizza” / “pizza was pleasing to (someone)” (past, imperfect).
additional_notes: With piacere, the thing liked is the grammatical subject (la pizza), and the person who likes it is introduced with an indirect object: a Ziri, a lei, mi, gli, le, etc. Piaceva is the imperfect tense, used for a past state or habitual liking (“used to like,” “liked (back then)”). Word order can vary: A lei piaceva la pizza / La pizza le piaceva.
target_language_example: Quando era bambina, a Marta piaceva la pizza margherita.
native_language_example: When she was a child, Marta liked margherita pizza.

additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere in the past: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject, so you say Mi è piaciuta la cena (“The dinner pleased me” = “I liked the dinner”). Piaciuta agrees with a feminine singular noun (la cena, la scuola, la minestra). Often appears with an indirect object pronoun or phrase: mi/ti/gli/le/ci/vi/gli, or a + person (A me, a te).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la mostra?
native_language_example: Did you like the exhibition?

meaning: “(you) liked the party” / “did you like the party?”
additional_notes: This is a common fragment from the verb *piacere* in the past: **Ti è piaciuta la festa?** = “Did you like the party?” Literally, the party is the subject (“the party pleased you”), so it uses **essere** as the auxiliary and agrees with **la festa** (feminine singular): *piaciuta*. With a masculine noun you’d say *piaciuto* (e.g., *Ti è piaciuto il film?*).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuta la festa ieri sera?
native_language_example: Did you like the party last night?

additional_notes: Used with the verb **piacere** (“to be pleasing/liked”), which works differently from English: the thing that is liked is the grammatical subject (**il mio libro**), and the person who likes it is introduced with **a + person** (e.g., **a lei**, **a loro**). In the past tense (**è piaciuto**), the verb agrees with what is liked: **è piaciuto** (masc. singular, for **il libro**), **è piaciuta** (fem. singular), **sono piaciuti/piaciute** (plural).
target_language_example: Ti è piaciuto il mio libro?
native_language_example: Did you like my book?

additional_notes: Used to indicate the position of a planet when you count outward starting from a reference point (usually the Sun): “il quarto pianeta a partire dal Sole” = “the fourth planet from the Sun.” The pattern is: [number + pianeta] a partire da/dal + [starting point]. Use “dal” before masculine singular nouns like “il Sole” (a partire dal Sole) and “dalla” before feminine singular nouns (a partire dalla Terra).
target_language_example: Giove è il quinto pianeta a partire dal Sole.
native_language_example: Jupiter is the fifth planet from the Sun.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens repeatedly whenever a certain situation occurs. “Ogni volta che” (“every time that/whenever”) is followed by a verb (often in the present tense for a general habit): e.g., “piango ogni volta che lo vedo” = “I cry every time I see it/him.”
target_language_example: Piango ogni volta che penso a quei giorni.
native_language_example: I cry every time I think about those days.

additional_notes: Used with a noun (piani per un picnic = plans for a picnic) or with an infinitive (piani per andare = plans to go). Common with "avere": "Ho dei piani per..." = "I have plans to/for...".
target_language_example: Hai già dei piani per il weekend?
native_language_example: Do you already have plans for the weekend?

additional_notes: Common in spoken Italian. It can mean doing something carefully/softly (often with verbs like sedersi, parlare, andare) or that something happens gradually over time (“little by little”).
target_language_example: Cammina piano piano: la strada è scivolosa.
native_language_example: Walk slowly/carefully: the road is slippery.

meaning: the upstairs floor; the floor above.
additional_notes: Used to refer to an upper level in a building (often in a house). Common with verbs of movement like andare/salire (to go up) or with sounds coming from above (sentire qualcuno al piano di sopra).
target_language_example: Il bagno è al piano di sopra, a destra.
native_language_example: The bathroom is upstairs, on the right.

meaning: the floor downstairs; the lower floor.
additional_notes: Used to refer to the level below where you are (often the ground floor from an upstairs room). It can be used with verbs of movement (andare/tornare/scendere al piano di sotto) or location (essere/aspettare al piano di sotto).
target_language_example: Vado al piano di sotto a prendere un bicchiere d'acqua.
native_language_example: I'm going downstairs to get a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used with the subjunctive verb form "sia" (from "essere" = to be), typically after expressions like "penso che..." (I think that...) to give an opinion. "Piuttosto" often means "rather/pretty" (a bit, fairly). Note: "piano" here means "plan" (not the musical instrument).
target_language_example: Penso che questo piano sia piuttosto stupido, ma possiamo discuterne.
native_language_example: I think this plan is rather stupid, but we can discuss it.

additional_notes: A simple, literal phrase: **pianta** (verb, from *piantare*) means “(he/she) plants,” and **una pianta** means “a plant” (e.g., a tree, flower, rose bush). Used for actions like planting something in a garden, or ceremonially planting in someone’s memory (often with *in memoria di...*).
target_language_example: Ogni primavera, mio nonno pianta una pianta nuova sul balcone.
native_language_example: Every spring, my grandfather plants a new plant on the balcony.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used with the auxiliary avere to form the passato prossimo: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno piantato un albero. In Italian, piantare means “to plant” (a tree, flowers, seeds) and also “to stick/drive in” something (like a pole), so context helps. The phrase can be used literally or in a humorous/angry way (“Who the hell planted a tree on my ship?”).
target_language_example: L'anno scorso abbiamo piantato un albero in giardino.
native_language_example: Last year we planted a tree in the garden.

additional_notes: Used for a meal eaten outside (often in a park or countryside). In Italian it’s commonly written as one word ("picnic") or two ("pic nic"). Plural: "i picnic" / "i pic nic".
target_language_example: Domani facciamo un pic nic al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having a picnic in the park.

additional_notes: Used to describe a village that is small in size/population. Often follows a preposition like "in" ("in the small village"). "Piccolo" agrees with the noun: "piccolo villaggio" (masc. sing.), "piccoli villaggi" (masc. plural).
target_language_example: In quel piccolo villaggio tutti si conoscono.
native_language_example: In that small village everyone knows each other.

meaning: pickup truck (a small truck with an open cargo bed).
additional_notes: In Italian, "pick-up" is a loanword used for the vehicle type (often masculine: *il pick-up*; plural usually *i pick-up*). It’s common when talking about cars/vehicles (e.g., *pick-up o SUV*).
target_language_example: Abbiamo noleggiato un pick-up per trasportare i mobili.
native_language_example: We rented a pickup truck to transport the furniture.

additional_notes: A tool used to pry things open or pull out nails. Literally “pig’s foot,” but in Italian it means the tool, not an animal body part. It’s masculine: un/il piede di porco.
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi il piede di porco?
native_language_example: Can you pass me the crowbar?

additional_notes: Used with feminine nouns/adjectives (e.g., una scatola/stanza/persona è piena di...). With masculine nouns use "pieno di"; plural: "pieni di" (masc.) / "piene di" (fem.). Can describe something literally filled ("una scatola piena di mele") or figuratively ("piena di energia/curiosità").
target_language_example: Sono piena di impegni questa settimana.
native_language_example: I'm full of commitments this week.

additional_notes: Used mostly about women/girls (piena is feminine). For a man/boy, say pieno di energia. Common with verbs like essere (“to be”) and sembrare (“to seem”): Sono/Lei sembra piena di energia.
target_language_example: Dopo il caffè, sono piena di energia.
native_language_example: After coffee, I’m full of energy.

additional_notes: Used to say that people/things are filled with something. It agrees with what’s “full”: pieno di (masc. singular), piena di (fem. singular), pieni di (masc. plural), piene di (fem. plural). Common with emotions/substances: occhi pieni di lacrime/speranza (“eyes full of tears/hope”). In informal contexts with certain nouns it can also imply “loaded with”: pieni di grana (“loaded with money”).
target_language_example: Hanno gli occhi pieni di speranza.
native_language_example: They have eyes full of hope.

additional_notes: Used to say something contains a lot of something (literal: "full of salt") or to describe someone’s state/feelings ("full of anger"). Common fixed expression: "pieno di sé" = "full of himself" (self-important, conceited). It agrees with what it describes: pieno/piena/pieni/piene di + noun.
target_language_example: Perché dovrei essere pieno di rabbia?
native_language_example: Why should I be full of anger?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who has an inflated opinion of themselves and acts smug or conceited. Note: in standard Italian it’s written with the accent: “pieno di sé” (“of himself/herself/themself”). It agrees with the person described: pieno (m.), piena (f.), pieni (m. pl.), piene (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Da quando ha avuto quella promozione, è sempre più pieno di sè.
native_language_example: Since he got that promotion, he’s more and more full of himself.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like riuscire a (manage to), sapere (know how to), and potere (can) to talk about having the ability to operate and fly a helicopter. In everyday English you’d usually say “fly a helicopter,” while Italian commonly uses pilotare (“to pilot/operate”) for aircraft and other vehicles.
target_language_example: Non so pilotare un elicottero, ma so pilotare un aereo.
native_language_example: I can’t fly a helicopter, but I can fly a plane.

additional_notes: A loanword used for the sport played on a table with small paddles and a light ball. Very common in everyday Italian; often used interchangeably with "tennis da tavolo" (more formal/official). With "giocare": "giocare a ping-pong" = to play ping-pong.
target_language_example: Giochiamo a ping-pong dopo cena?
native_language_example: Shall we play ping-pong after dinner?

additional_notes: Common noun for the sport (same as "tennis da tavolo"). Often used with verbs like "giocare a ping pong" (to play ping-pong) and "fare ping pong" (to play ping-pong). In casual speech it can also be used as a quick question or suggestion: "Ping pong?" = "Ping-pong?" / "Want to play?".
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio giochiamo a ping pong al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon we’ll play ping-pong at the park.

meaning: To rain very heavily; to pour down ("to rain cats and dogs").
additional_notes: Common idiom used to emphasize intense rain. You can conjugate the verb in any tense (e.g., "ha piovuto a catinelle", "pioverà a catinelle"). Often used in weather contexts.
target_language_example: Oggi sembra proprio piovere a catinelle, quindi meglio prendere l’ombrello.
native_language_example: It really looks like it’s going to pour down today, so it’s better to take an umbrella.

additional_notes: Commonly used with the auxiliary verb "avere" in the passato prossimo: "ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno pitturato" + "le pareti" (the walls). You can add a color with "di" + color: "pitturare le pareti di bianco" = "to paint the walls white".
target_language_example: Abbiamo pitturato le pareti di grigio chiaro.
native_language_example: We painted the walls light gray.

additional_notes: Used to say someone does something fairly well (often better than expected, but not necessarily perfectly). It can sound a bit modest/understated. Position: usually after the verb (e.g., parlare piuttosto bene).
target_language_example: Me la cavo piuttosto bene in italiano.
native_language_example: I get by pretty well in Italian.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or talking about a specific pizza topping. "Salame piccante" is spicy salami (often like pepperoni), and "con" means "with." In questions like "Le piace...?" and "Vi piace...?" it means "Do you like...?" (formal singular / plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una pizza con il salame piccante, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a spicy salami pizza, please.

meaning: Sal’s pizzeria (a pizzeria owned by/associated with Sal).
additional_notes: In Italian, **di + name** is a common way to show possession or association, like **“Sal’s …”** in English. You’ll also see it with businesses and shops: *il bar di Marco* (Marco’s bar), *la farmacia di Anna* (Anna’s pharmacy). In the examples, *la famosa pizzeria di Sal (e figli)* means “the famous pizzeria of Sal (and sons).”
target_language_example: Prendiamo una pizza alla pizzeria di Sal stasera?
native_language_example: Shall we get a pizza at Sal’s pizzeria tonight?

additional_notes: Used to compare duration ("more long"), often with verbs like vivere, restare/rimanere, parlare, aspettare. It can be followed by "di/che" to compare two durations: "più a lungo di/che...".
target_language_example: Possiamo restare qui più a lungo?
native_language_example: Can we stay here longer?

additional_notes: Comparative form of "alta" (feminine singular), used when comparing two things or people: "più alta di..." = "higher/taller than...". Use it with feminine nouns (e.g., "una montagna più alta") or a woman/girl ("Lei è più alta"). For masculine, use "più alto"; for plural, "più alti/alte". Related superlative: "la più alta" = "the tallest/highest" (feminine).
target_language_example: Questa torre è più alta di quella.
native_language_example: This tower is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: This is part of a comparison pattern: **più + adjective + di + [noun phrase]** (“more + adjective + than …”). Here **più alta** = “taller” (feminine singular), and **sua** is a possessive (“his/her”) that normally must be followed by a noun (e.g., **sua sorella**, **sua madre**). On its own, **di sua** sounds unfinished; you’d typically say **più alta di sua sorella** (“taller than his/her sister”) or, with a pronoun, **più alta di lei** (“taller than her”).
target_language_example: Giulia è più alta di sua sorella.
native_language_example: Giulia is taller than her sister.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons with di: più alto di me = taller than me. With il/la/i/le + più alto it forms the superlative: il ragazzo più alto = the tallest boy. You can strengthen it with molto (much) or ancora (even): molto più alto, ancora più alto. "Alto" can describe people (tall) and things/positions (high).
target_language_example: Mio figlio è più alto di me.
native_language_example: My son is taller than me.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective + di. Use it to compare height (people) or level/height (objects). Often intensified with molto (much) or only slightly with soltanto leggermente. After di you can use a noun or pronoun (e.g., di Mary, di lui). Superlative pattern: il più alto di tutti = “the tallest of all”.
target_language_example: Questo edificio è più alto di quello.
native_language_example: This building is taller/higher than that one.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages or how old someone looks. It agrees in gender/number with the person described: più anziano di (male singular), più anziana di (female singular), più anziani di / più anziane di (plural). You can also use it with expressions like “quel che” to mean “than (what)”: più anziano di quel che sembra = older than he seems.
target_language_example: Lui è più anziano di quel che sembra.
native_language_example: He is older than he seems.

additional_notes: Used to compare: **più bella di + noun/pronoun** = “prettier than…”. With **la/le + più bella** it becomes a superlative: **la più bella** = “the most beautiful (one)”. Feminine singular form, so it describes a feminine noun/person (e.g., *ragazza, spiaggia*).
target_language_example: Secondo me, questa foto è più bella dell’altra.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this photo is prettier than the other one.

meaning: more beautiful / nicer; (with articles) the most beautiful.
additional_notes: Used to compare: "più bello di ..." = "more beautiful/nicer than ...". With a superlative: "il/la/i/le posto più bello" = "the most beautiful place". It can also be used emphatically to mean "even nicer/better" (e.g., "ancora più bello" = "even more beautiful").
target_language_example: Questo parco è più bello di quello vicino a casa mia.
native_language_example: This park is more beautiful than the one near my house.

meaning: mostly; more than anything else; rather.
additional_notes: Used to highlight the main thing among several possibilities, often to correct/nuance what you just said (“not so much X, but mainly Y”). Common with verbs like ricordare, cercare, volere, essere/sembrare.
target_language_example: Non è che mi dispiace: più che altro sono stanco.
native_language_example: It’s not that I mind; I’m mostly just tired.

meaning: more than ever (now more than at any other time).
additional_notes: Used to strongly emphasize that something is true/important especially now, compared to any time in the past. Often follows the idea it intensifies ("ne ho bisogno più che mai") or can stand alone as a short emphatic reply ("Più che mai!").
target_language_example: In questo periodo, abbiamo bisogno di restare uniti più che mai.
native_language_example: In this period, we need to stick together more than ever.

additional_notes: Used to compare quantities or to say something exceeds a number or amount: più di 30 miglia (more than 30 miles), più di ottanta pagine (over 80 pages). It can also compare people/things: Lei mangia più di suo padre (She eats more than her father). Often followed by a number, a noun, or a person/thing being compared.
target_language_example: Abbiamo aspettato più di due ore.
native_language_example: We waited more than two hours.

più di cinque fette di pizza al mese

target_language_multi_word_term: più di cinque fette di pizza al mese
meaning: more than five slices of pizza per month.
additional_notes: A quantity phrase used to talk about frequency/amount over a month. Structure: "più di" (more than) + number + noun ("fette di pizza") + time period ("al mese" = per month). Often used in questions with "Di solito" or "Solitamente" (usually).
target_language_example: Non mangio più di cinque fette di pizza al mese.
native_language_example: I don't eat more than five slices of pizza per month.

meaning: more than me (i.e., more than I do / more than I am).
additional_notes: Used in comparisons: "più" (more) + "di" (than) + stressed pronoun "me" (me). After "di" you use the stressed pronoun ("me"), not "io". Common with verbs to compare degree/amount: "lavora più di me" (works more than me / than I do), "ti ama più di me" (loves you more than me / than I do).
target_language_example: Lei ha lavorato più di me.
native_language_example: She worked more than me (than I did).

meaning: more than anything else; above all (else).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the top priority or the strongest preference (or dislike) compared to everything else. It can be placed after the verb/object, or set off by commas in the middle of the sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Desidero, più di ogni altra cosa, passare del tempo con la mia famiglia.
native_language_example: More than anything else, I want to spend time with my family.
