additional_notes: Used to compare quantities/degree: “more than” + a clause (often with the subjunctive in formal Italian), meaning “more than I thought/expected/wanted/should.” You may also see “più di quanto non …” where “non” doesn’t negate; it’s just an idiomatic/formal extra often used with comparisons.
target_language_example: Ho speso più di quanto pensassi.
native_language_example: I spent more than I thought.

additional_notes: Used to compare degrees/amounts with a clause: più di quanto + verb (often in the subjunctive), meaning “more than I/you/he thought/expected/believed.” You may also see the optional "non" in the following clause (più di quanto non...), which doesn’t make it negative; it’s a common expletive "non" in comparisons.
target_language_example: Mi piace questo posto più di quanto pensassi.
native_language_example: I like this place more than I thought.

meaning: more than a year; over a year.
additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration of time that exceeds one year. Often follows expressions like "da" (for/since) to say how long something has been happening: "da più di un anno" = "for more than a year."
target_language_example: Studio italiano da più di un anno.
native_language_example: I've been studying Italian for more than a year.

additional_notes: Used with verbs to say someone should increase their effort or intensity (e.g., cercare/guardare più duramente = look/search more thoroughly; lavorare/provare più duramente = work/try harder). Common in advice or commands. In everyday Italian you may also hear "più forte" (especially for physical effort) or "di più" (more in general).
target_language_example: Se vuoi passare l’esame, devi studiare più duramente.
native_language_example: If you want to pass the exam, you have to study harder.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective (facile) = “more …”. Used to compare things (più facile di … = “easier than …”) or to say something becomes easier (diventare più facile). With object pronouns: lo/la rende più facile = “it makes it easier.”
target_language_example: Con questo metodo, è più facile imparare l'italiano.
native_language_example: With this method, it’s easier to learn Italian.

additional_notes: Comparative form: più + adjective/adverb. With forte it usually means “stronger” (physically/mentally, or a stronger drink/medicine), but in volume contexts it means “louder” (e.g., Parla più forte! = Speak louder!).
target_language_example: Dopo l’allenamento mi sento più forte.
native_language_example: After training I feel stronger.

additional_notes: Used to compare strength or power: "più" (more) + "forte" (strong/strongly) + "di" (than). Often appears with intensifiers like "molto" (much): "molto più forte di...". You can use it literally for physical strength or more generally for power, influence, or effect.
target_language_example: Questa squadra è molto più forte di quella dell’anno scorso.
native_language_example: This team is much stronger than last year’s one.

additional_notes: Used to compare intensity. Very common with speaking/volume: "Parla più forte" = "Speak louder." With actions or forces it means "more strongly/harder" (wind, blow, hit, push). You can intensify it with words like "ancora" (even) or "possibile" (as possible): "il più forte possibile" = "as loud/strong as possible."
target_language_example: Puoi mettere la musica più forte, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you turn the music up louder, please?

additional_notes: Used to compare ages, often with "di" (più giovane di lui = younger than him) and can add the difference: "di due anni". With "il/la ... più giovane" it means "the youngest" (e.g., il figlio più giovane). "Non è più giovane" usually means "He/She isn’t young anymore" (no longer young).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è più giovane di me di cinque anni.
native_language_example: My sister is five years younger than me.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages (or how old someone looks). It follows the common comparative pattern "più + adjective + di" (= "more + adjective + than"). It can also be followed by a clause: "più giovane di quel che pensi" = "younger than you think."
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più giovane di me, ma sembra più grande.
native_language_example: My brother is younger than me, but he looks older.

additional_notes: Used as the comparative of grande. It can refer to physical size/importance ("bigger") or to age ("older"). For comparisons, it’s often followed by di + person/thing: "più grande di te" = "bigger/older than you". With a noun, it can form a superlative idea: "la moschea più grande" = "the biggest mosque" (literally "the most big").
target_language_example: Mio fratello è più grande di me.
native_language_example: My brother is older than me.

additional_notes: Used to make comparisons: più + adjective + di/che. With grande you usually use di, which combines with the definite article: di + la = della, di + il = del, di + lo = dello, di + i = dei, di + gli = degli, di + le = delle. You can also use di + pronoun: più grande di te/lui/lei. Often the noun is omitted when it’s clear: La mia (casa) è più grande della tua.
target_language_example: La mia casa è più grande della tua.
native_language_example: My house is bigger than yours.

additional_notes: Used for comparisons: X è più grande di Y. With people, it often refers to age (older). You can intensify with numbers/expressions (e.g., tre volte più grande di = three times bigger than) or make it negative: non più grande di = no bigger than.
target_language_example: Questo appartamento è più grande di quello, ma è più caro.
native_language_example: This apartment is bigger than that one, but it's more expensive.

additional_notes: Plural comparative form of "grande" (big/great). Use it to compare size/quantity: "più grandi di ..." = "bigger than ...". With family members, it commonly means older: "sorelle più grandi" = "older sisters". It can also appear in superlative structures: "una delle (cose/città) più grandi" = "one of the biggest". Agreement: use "più grande" (singular) vs. "più grandi" (plural).
target_language_example: I cani sono più grandi dei gatti.
native_language_example: Dogs are bigger than cats.

additional_notes: Used with comparisons and superlatives. With "più" + adjective you get a comparison: "A è più importante di B" (A is more important than B). With an article + "più" you often get a superlative: "la cosa più importante" (the most important thing). In phrases like "cosa ancora più importante" it means "something even more important".
target_language_example: Per me, la cosa più importante è stare bene.
native_language_example: For me, the most important thing is to be well.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a higher position or level (physically or sometimes figuratively). Often used with nouns like "la mensola più in alto" (“the highest shelf / the shelf up higher”) or with comparisons like "due piani più in alto" (“two floors higher”). You can also say it alone as a direction: "Più in alto!" (“Higher up!”).
target_language_example: Puoi mettere la scatola più in alto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you put the box higher up, please?

additional_notes: Used to say you want to reach the maximum height you can. Often appears with verbs like volare (to fly) and saltare (to jump). You’ll also commonly see it with the article: il più in alto possibile (“as high as possible”).
target_language_example: Metti la valigia più in alto possibile.
native_language_example: Put the suitcase as high up as possible.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed or to urge doing something with more speed. Often follows a verb (e.g., "andare più in fretta" = "to go faster"), and it can be reinforced with "possibile" ("più in fretta possibile" = "as fast as possible").
target_language_example: Dobbiamo finire più in fretta, altrimenti perdiamo il treno.
native_language_example: We have to finish faster, otherwise we’ll miss the train.

additional_notes: Used to make a comparison. It’s built with the comparative pattern “più + adjective + di” (more + adjective + than). With a clause, you often see “di quanto …” or “di quel che …” (e.g., “più intelligente di quanto sembri” = “more intelligent than you seem”).
target_language_example: Secondo me, questo esercizio è più intelligente di quello di ieri.
native_language_example: In my opinion, this exercise is more intelligent than yesterday’s one.

additional_notes: Used to ask someone to slow down (walking, talking, driving, etc.). Often appears in polite requests with "Per favore/Per piacere". With commands you may see either informal "Parla/Cammina" (to a friend) or formal "Parli/Camini" (to a stranger). You can also compare speeds with "più lentamente di ..." (more slowly than ...).
target_language_example: Mi puoi spiegare più lentamente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you explain it to me more slowly, please?

additional_notes: Used to say something is not exact or only partially true/known. Common after numbers and times ("le quattro, più o meno" = "around four"), and also to mean "kind of / sort of" with verbs like sapere/capire ("lo capisco più o meno" = "I kind of understand"). It can sound vague; in some contexts it may be criticized ("Più o meno non è abbastanza!").
target_language_example: Arrivo tra dieci minuti, più o meno.
native_language_example: I’ll arrive in about ten minutes, more or less.

additional_notes: Used when comparing vertical position, usually followed by a noun or pronoun: "più su di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro" (= higher up than me/you/him…). Similar meaning: "più in alto di" or "più sopra di". On its own, Italians more often just say "più su" (= further up / higher up).
target_language_example: La mensola è più su di quella che abbiamo in cucina.
native_language_example: The shelf is higher up than the one we have in the kitchen.

meaning: 'more about her' or 'higher up on her' (depending on context).
additional_notes: "più" = more, "su" = on/about, "di lei" = of her (or "you" in the formal sense). Most often you’ll see it when asking for more information about a woman: "qualcosa di più su di lei" = "something more about her." In physical/location contexts, "più su" means "higher up" (e.g., moving something further up on someone’s body or clothing).
target_language_example: Vorrei sapere qualcosa di più su di lei.
native_language_example: I’d like to know something more about her.

meaning: more about him; more on him.
additional_notes: Literally “more on him.” Use it when you want additional information about a man already mentioned (similar to “more about him / more on him” in English). In some contexts, “su di lui” can also be physical (“on him” / “on top of him”), but with information it commonly means “about him.”
target_language_example: Voglio sapere più su di lui prima di decidere.
native_language_example: I want to know more about him before deciding.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens at a later time. Very common with time expressions: “qualche minuto/giorno più tardi” = “a few minutes/days later.” In “Lo posso fare più tardi”, it means “I can do it later (on).” Literally it’s “more late,” but English normally just says “later.”
target_language_example: Ci sentiamo più tardi.
native_language_example: We’ll talk later.

additional_notes: Used to compare ages: "più + adjective + di" = "more + adjective + than". With age, Italians often also say "più grande di". It agrees with the person described: "più vecchio" (masc.), "più vecchia" (fem.). "Di" is used before a noun or pronoun (di Maria, di noi, di me).
target_language_example: Tom è molto più vecchio di Mary.
native_language_example: Tom is much older than Mary.

additional_notes: Comparative: più veloce = faster (often followed by “di …” for “than …”). Superlative: il/la più veloce = the fastest (e.g., Tu sei la più veloce). Common in commands and encouragement: “Più veloce!” = “Faster!” With “possibile/che puoi” it means “as fast as possible / as fast as you can.”
target_language_example: Possiamo andare più veloce, ma non troppo.
native_language_example: We can go faster, but not too fast.

additional_notes: Used to compare speed: più + adjective/adverb (veloce) + di + person/thing. With verbs, it often appears as "correre più veloce di..." (to run faster than...). You can also use it with nouns: "un corridore più veloce di..." (a faster runner than...).
target_language_example: Questo treno è più veloce di quello.
native_language_example: This train is faster than that one.

additional_notes: Comparative adverb used to say someone does something at a higher speed than before or than someone else. Often followed by a comparison: "più velocemente di..." (faster than...).
target_language_example: Puoi parlare più velocemente, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you speak faster, please?

additional_notes: Used to compare amounts of money or to say someone wants/has/earns a larger amount. Often followed by a comparison: “più soldi di me/dei suoi genitori” (more money than me/his parents). With verbs like “fare” it commonly means “to earn”: “fare più soldi” = “to make/earn more money.”
target_language_example: Vorrei più soldi per comprare un computer nuovo.
native_language_example: I’d like more money to buy a new computer.

additional_notes: Used to say you need additional time to finish something or to ask someone to wait longer. Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "dare" (to give), "servire" (to need), and "bisognare" (to be needed): "Mi serve più tempo" = "I need more time."
target_language_example: Possiamo parlarne domani? Ho bisogno di più tempo.
native_language_example: Can we talk about it tomorrow? I need more time.

più tempo a casa o al lavoro

target_language_multi_word_term: più tempo a casa o al lavoro
meaning: more time at home or at work
additional_notes: Used to ask/compare where someone spends most of their time, typically with verbs like *passare* or *trascorrere* (“to spend (time)”). Often framed as a question; you can swap in other places (e.g., *più tempo in ufficio o in viaggio?*).
target_language_example: In questo periodo passi più tempo a casa o al lavoro?
native_language_example: These days, do you spend more time at home or at work?

additional_notes: Used to talk about spending additional time in someone’s company. It normally appears with a verb like "passare" (to spend) or "avere" (to have): "Vorrei passare più tempo con..." / "Ho bisogno di più tempo con...". The "con" introduces the person/people you want to be with.
target_language_example: Vorrei passare più tempo con te.
native_language_example: I’d like to spend more time with you.

più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro

target_language_multi_word_term: più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro
meaning: “more time outside and less time inside.”
additional_notes: A straightforward comparative phrase (più = more, meno = less). Often used as advice or a slogan about spending more time outdoors and less time indoors. You can adjust it (e.g., più tempo al parco e meno tempo a casa).
target_language_example: Quest’estate voglio più tempo fuori e meno tempo dentro.
native_language_example: This summer I want more time outside and less time inside.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened repeatedly or on multiple occasions. Often placed after the verb (è successo più volte) or before an infinitive (ho pensato più volte di...).
target_language_example: Te l’ho detto più volte: non lasciare la porta aperta.
native_language_example: I’ve told you several times: don’t leave the door open.

additional_notes: Used to say a small number of people (not many). It can be the subject or object of the sentence: “Poche persone…” = “Few people…”, “ci sono poche persone” = “there are few people.” Often contrasts with “molte persone” (many people).
target_language_example: Oggi al museo ci sono poche persone.
native_language_example: Today there are few people at the museum.

additional_notes: Means a small number of days. Often used with time expressions like "entro pochi giorni" (within a few days) or "pochi giorni più tardi" (a few days later).
target_language_example: Ritorno tra pochi giorni.
native_language_example: I'll be back in a few days.

additional_notes: Used to say you have only a short amount of time, or that something will happen soon (e.g., “in a few minutes,” “a few minutes later”). With distances/travel time, it can mean “a few minutes away” (Siamo a pochi minuti = We’re a few minutes away).
target_language_example: Aspettami: arrivo tra pochi minuti.
native_language_example: Wait for me: I’ll be there in a few minutes.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that improves, grows, or changes slowly over time, often step by step. Common with verbs like migliorare (to improve), crescere (to grow), riprendersi (to recover), and can go at the end of the sentence.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: andrà meglio poco a poco.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: it will get better little by little.

meaning: a short while ago; just now.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happened recently (a few minutes or a little time ago). It can go at the end of the sentence (common) or near the verb: “Mi ha chiamato poco fa” / “Poco fa mi ha chiamato”.
target_language_example: Sono arrivato poco fa, scusa il ritardo.
native_language_example: I arrived a short while ago, sorry I’m late.

additional_notes: Used to say you don’t have much time available, or that something lasts only a short time. Common patterns: "in poco tempo" = "in a short time"; "per poco tempo" = "for a short time"; "(mi) resta/rimane poco tempo" = "I have little time left"; "poco tempo fa" = "a short time ago".
target_language_example: Scusa, ho poco tempo: possiamo parlare domani?
native_language_example: Sorry, I don’t have much time: can we talk tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used especially at school or performances to mean a poem learned and recited without reading (similar to English “by heart” / “from memory”). Often said with verbs like imparare/studiare (to learn) or recitare/dire (to recite/say): “imparare una poesia a memoria”, “recitare una poesia a memoria”.
target_language_example: Devo imparare una poesia a memoria per domani.
native_language_example: I have to memorize a poem for tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about reading or performing poetry for an audience (or simply not silently). You may also hear it as a category of events: “serata di poesia ad alta voce” (an evening of poetry readings). Related phrase: “leggere ad alta voce” = “to read out loud.”
target_language_example: Stasera c’è un evento di poesia ad alta voce in biblioteca.
native_language_example: Tonight there’s a poetry reading event at the library.

additional_notes: Less common as two words; usually written as one word: **poiché** (more standard, somewhat formal). Used similarly to *perché* when giving a reason. Typically followed by the indicative.
target_language_example: Poi che non ho tempo, lo farò domani.
native_language_example: Since I don't have time, I'll do it tomorrow.

additional_notes: News/reporting-style phrase using the passato prossimo: ha arrestato (has arrested/arrested). In everyday speech you’ll often see an article: la polizia ha arrestato… (“the police arrested…”). Add the person/object after it: la polizia ha arrestato un uomo / il sospetto (“the police arrested a man / the suspect”).
target_language_example: La polizia ha arrestato il sospetto ieri sera.
native_language_example: The police arrested the suspect last night.

meaning: “the police are looking for / searching for”.
additional_notes: Uses the present continuous: “sta” (is) + “cercando” (looking/searching). It’s usually followed by what/whom they are looking for, often with “di” (e.g., “La polizia sta cercando di capire…” = “The police are trying to figure out…”), or by a direct object (“La polizia sta cercando un uomo…”).
target_language_example: La polizia sta cercando un uomo con una giacca nera.
native_language_example: The police are looking for a man wearing a black jacket.

additional_notes: A food item. Often used with an article: "il pollo fritto" (the fried chicken). You can also use it on its own as an answer/order: "Pollo fritto!"
target_language_example: Per cena prendo il pollo fritto.
native_language_example: For dinner I’ll have fried chicken.

additional_notes: Used to refer to the business that handles funerals (the company/office that organizes the funeral and related services). Often used with a place word like “casa di pompe funebri” (funeral home).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo chiamare le pompe funebri per organizzare il funerale.
native_language_example: We have to call the funeral home to arrange the funeral.

meaning: “Fuck!” / “For fuck’s sake!” (a very strong swear word).
additional_notes: Very vulgar Italian exclamation used to show sudden anger, frustration, shock, or emphasis—similar to English “fuck!” or “for fuck’s sake!”. It can be shouted on its own ("Porca puttana!") or added at the end of a sentence for emphasis. Avoid in polite situations, with strangers, at work, or around children.
target_language_example: Porca puttana, ho perso le chiavi!
native_language_example: Fuck, I lost my keys!

meaning: a very strong, vulgar swear word (like “for fuck’s sake!” / “goddamn it!”).
additional_notes: Used to express strong anger, frustration, or emphasis, either on its own ("Porca troia!") or added to a sentence. It’s offensive/vulgar and should be avoided in polite situations; it can sound aggressive if directed at someone.
target_language_example: Porca troia, ho perso le chiavi!
native_language_example: For fuck’s sake, I lost my keys!

meaning: to put an end to; to end (something).
additional_notes: Used in formal or serious contexts to mean ending a situation, activity, conflict, or relationship. It’s often followed by "a" + noun/infinitive: "porre fine a una guerra" (end a war), "porre fine agli insulti" (put an end to the insults). Less common in casual speech than "finire" or "mettere fine a".
target_language_example: È ora di porre fine a questa discussione.
native_language_example: It’s time to put an end to this discussion.

additional_notes: Used to politely refer to the door when making a request, most commonly in phrases like “Apri la porta, per favore.” The comma shows a pause: you’re adding “please” to soften the request. “Porta” here is the noun “door” (not the verb “he/she brings”).
target_language_example: Chiudi la porta, per favore.
native_language_example: Close the door, please.

additional_notes: Used to locate something: *accanto a* means “next to.” *Alla nostra* = “next to ours” (feminine singular), because *porta* is feminine. You can swap in other possessives: *alla mia* (next to mine), *alla tua* (next to yours).
target_language_example: L’appartamento è quello con la porta accando alla nostra.
native_language_example: The apartment is the one with the door next to ours.

meaning: an open door; (left) the door open.
additional_notes: Used literally to describe a door that is open or has been left open. Often appears with verbs like lasciare (to leave): "Hai lasciato la porta aperta?" = "Did you leave the door open?".
target_language_example: Per favore, non lasciare la porta aperta.
native_language_example: Please, don’t leave the door open.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "portare" to talk about wearing items like glasses, contact lenses, clothes, etc. It describes a usual or current characteristic (often with "solitamente" = usually). In questions, subject pronouns are often omitted: "Porta gli occhiali?" = "Do you wear glasses?"
target_language_example: Mio padre porta gli occhiali da lettura.
native_language_example: My father wears reading glasses.

meaning: "always carries (it) with him/her" / "always keeps (it) on them".
additional_notes: Used to say someone habitually has an object with them. The item usually follows the phrase: "Porta sempre con sé + [object]". "Con sé" literally means "with oneself" and refers back to the subject (so you can change it: "porto sempre con me" = I always carry with me; "porta sempre con te" = you always carry with you).
target_language_example: Lei porta sempre con sé un ombrello, anche quando c'è il sole.
native_language_example: She always carries an umbrella with her, even when it’s sunny.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **portare via**. It’s used when something is removed from a place or when something (like wind) carries something off. In the imperative (**Porta via…**), it’s a direct command meaning “Take … away.”
target_language_example: Per favore, porta via questi piatti dal tavolo.
native_language_example: Please take these plates away from the table.

additional_notes: Common with direct object pronouns (ti, lo, la, li, le): "Ti porto a casa" = "I’ll take you home." It can mean either taking someone home (e.g., giving them a ride) or bringing something back home; context tells you which. In the passato prossimo it uses "avere": "Ti ho portato/a a casa".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, ti porto a casa dopo la festa: devo proprio portare a casa anche queste borse.
native_language_example: If you want, I’ll take you home after the party: I really need to bring these bags home too.

meaning: to finish; to carry through to completion.
additional_notes: Used for completing a task, project, plan, or goal. It often implies seeing something through until the end (sometimes despite difficulty). In contexts like pregnancy ("portare a termine la gravidanza"), it means carrying it to full term.
target_language_example: Sono stanco, ma voglio portare a termine questo lavoro entro stasera.
native_language_example: I'm tired, but I want to finish this work by tonight.

meaning: to carry on; to continue; to pursue (a project/plan).
additional_notes: Used with activities, work, plans, or projects: “portare avanti un progetto/il lavoro/le trattative” = keep it going and make progress. It can also mean “to carry forward” in a more literal sense, and in some contexts “portare avanti una gravidanza” = to carry a pregnancy to term.
target_language_example: Non è facile, ma dobbiamo portare avanti il progetto.
native_language_example: It’s not easy, but we have to carry on with the project.

additional_notes: Common household chore meaning to bring the garbage outside (often to the bins/curb). You may also hear: "buttare la spazzatura" (throw away the trash) or "portare giù la spazzatura" (take the trash down, e.g., to the building’s dumpster).
target_language_example: Puoi portare fuori la spazzatura prima di uscire?
native_language_example: Can you take out the trash before you go out?

meaning: to take away; to carry off; to take (someone) away.
additional_notes: Used for removing or taking something from a place (often ‘away from here’), or taking a person away from someone/somewhere. With direct objects: portare via il pacco = take the package away. With a person: portare via qualcuno = take someone away (sometimes in the sense of being taken from someone’s care). In polite requests you may see it with ‘mi’: Mi può portare via…? = Can you take me away/with you?
target_language_example: Può portare via questi piatti, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take these dishes away, please?

additional_notes: Most often used in the fixed expression **a portata di mano** (“within reach”). It can be literal (something you can physically reach) or figurative (something easily available, e.g., information or help).
target_language_example: Tieni il telefono a portata di mano, per favore.
native_language_example: Keep your phone within reach, please.

additional_notes: You’ll most often see this as **portare a spasso** + an object, especially **portare a spasso il cane** (“to take the dog for a walk”). **Portato** is the past participle of *portare* and is used with *avere* in the passato prossimo: *Ho portato a spasso il cane.* The word order in your term is incomplete by itself; it normally needs the thing/person being walked (e.g., *il cane*, *i bambini*).
target_language_example: Ho portato a spasso il cane dopo cena.
native_language_example: I took the dog for a walk after dinner.

meaning: taken away; carried off (sometimes: swept away, figuratively).
additional_notes: Past participle of **portare via** (“to take/carry away”). Often used for someone being removed or taken somewhere (e.g., by force), for stealing (“He took it away”), and in the passive: **è stato portato via** (“he was taken away”). It can also be figurative: **portato via dalla passione** = “carried/swept away by passion.” You may see it with pronouns: **se lo sono portato via** = “they took him/it away (with them).”
target_language_example: La polizia lo ha portato via in ambulanza.
native_language_example: The police took him away in an ambulance.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase **portare a casa** (“to take/bring home”). **Porti** is the present tense used with **Lei** (polite “you”) and is also used as a formal imperative: **La prego, mi porti a casa** = “Please take me home.” With **tu**, you’ll often hear **mi porti a casa** (informal present) or **portami a casa** (informal command). It can also mean “bring someone home” in a dating/romantic sense: **Scegli meglio chi ti porti a casa** = “Be more careful about who you bring home (with you).”
target_language_example: La prego, mi porti a casa.
native_language_example: Please take me home.

additional_notes: "Possiamo" is the 1st-person plural of "potere" (can/to be able to). Used to offer help (often as a question: "Come possiamo aiutare?"), or to say you’re able/willing to help ("Possiamo aiutare."). With pronouns, it becomes more specific/polite: "La/Le possiamo aiutare?" = “Can we help you?” (formal; La = you singular, Le = you plural or polite singular in some contexts).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, possiamo aiutare con i bagagli.
native_language_example: If you want, we can help with the luggage.

meaning: "we can go" / "can we go?" (permission or possibility).
additional_notes: Used to talk about being able to go somewhere, or asking for permission to leave/go. Often followed by a destination with "a" (possiamo andare a casa/a scuola) or "in/nel" (possiamo andare nel cortile). In questions, intonation (or a question mark in writing) makes it mean “Can we go?”; as a statement it means “We can go.” Related: "ce ne possiamo andare" = “we can leave / we can go away.”
target_language_example: Se hai finito, possiamo andare.
native_language_example: If you’re done, we can go.

additional_notes: Formed by possiamo (we can) + fare (to do/make). Used to say what is possible/feasible (“we can do this”) or to ask about options (“Possiamo fare qualcosa?”). Often followed by an object (qualcosa, questo) or an activity (un passo, una pausa). In contexts like “non possiamo fare più niente”, it means “there’s nothing more we can do.”
target_language_example: Possiamo fare una pausa adesso?
native_language_example: Can we take a break now?

meaning: "can we do to ...?" / "what can we do to ...?"
additional_notes: Used to ask what actions are possible in order to achieve a goal. It’s often followed by an infinitive (per aiutare, per fermare, per risolvere) or a noun (per te, per il problema). In questions, it commonly appears as: Che cosa possiamo fare per...? / Come possiamo fare per...?
target_language_example: Che cosa possiamo fare per risolvere questo problema?
native_language_example: What can we do to solve this problem?

additional_notes: From the verb "fidarsi" = "to trust." It’s used with "di" before a person/pronoun/thing you trust: "fidarsi di qualcuno/qualcosa". "Possiamo" means "we can" (also "can we" in questions). With a pronoun, use: "possiamo fidarci di lui/lei/loro"; often "di" + name: "possiamo fidarci di Maria".
target_language_example: Possiamo fidarci di questo sito?
native_language_example: Can we trust this website?

additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or possibility to talk, often meaning “Can we talk (for a moment/in private)?” If you add an object, you specify who you want to talk to: "Possiamo parlare con lui/lei/loro?" (= Can we talk to him/her/them?). With "di" you specify the topic: "Possiamo parlare di..." (= Can we talk about...?).
target_language_example: Scusa, possiamo parlare un attimo?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can we talk for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to talk about how likely something is to happen. Often followed by a noun (possibilità di successo = chance of success) or by an infinitive verb (possibilità di vincere/essere eletto/salvarsi = chance of winning/being elected/saving oneself). Common with negatives and quantifiers: nessuna/alcuna possibilità di (no chance of), qualche possibilità di (some chance of), una possibilità di (a chance of).
target_language_example: Abbiamo ancora una possibilità di finire in tempo.
native_language_example: We still have a chance of finishing on time.

additional_notes: Used to offer help or say you’re able to help. In questions, you’ll often hear it as **Posso aiutare?** (“Can I help?”). With the formal polite object pronoun, **La posso aiutare?** means “Can I help you?” (to a stranger/customer). With an informal person you can say **Ti posso aiutare?**.
target_language_example: Posso aiutare con le valigie?
native_language_example: Can I help with the suitcases?

meaning: “Can I help you?” (formal, to a woman / using polite ‘Lei’).
additional_notes: Used in customer service, phone calls, or when speaking politely to someone you don’t know well. It literally means “I can help you,” but in questions like “Come posso aiutarla?” it’s the standard formal way to offer help. The pronoun “-la” refers to “her/you (formal).” For a man you can also hear “posso aiutarla?” (still Lei), and informally with friends you’d usually say “posso aiutarti?”
target_language_example: Buongiorno, posso aiutarla?
native_language_example: Good morning, can I help you?

additional_notes: Literally 'I can go'. It is the 1st person singular form, so it refers to 'I'. Used to say you are able or allowed to go somewhere; as a question, it often asks permission ('can/may I go?'). A destination or expression of transport can follow, like a casa or in treno.
target_language_example: Se finisco presto, posso andare a casa.
native_language_example: If I finish early, I can go home.

meaning: 'can I go to…?' / 'I can go to…'.
additional_notes: Used with a place or activity after "a" (e.g., a casa, a scuola, al ristorante). With a question intonation it often asks permission ("Can/May I go to…?"); as a statement it expresses possibility/ability ("I can go to…"). You can also use "Posso andare a + infinitive" to mean "Can I go and (do)…?" (e.g., "Posso andare a comprare il pane?").
target_language_example: Posso andare al bagno?
native_language_example: Can I go to the bathroom?

additional_notes: A common polite way to ask for something, such as an object, food, or information. It is often followed by a noun phrase: posso avere un caffè? / posso avere il tuo numero?
target_language_example: Posso avere un bicchiere d'acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a glass of water, please?

meaning: “Can I have a …?” (polite way to ask for something).
additional_notes: Used to request an item or a serving (often in cafés, restaurants, shops, or at an event). It’s a polite, common formula; you can also use it with feminine nouns: “Posso avere una…?” (e.g., una bottiglia). Often preceded by “Scusi/Scusami/Scusatemi” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a glass of water, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely order a drink (especially in a bar/restaurant). Put the drink after di: "posso avere un bicchiere di vino?" (a glass of wine). You can also use it when asking for water: "posso avere un bicchiere d’acqua?" (d’ before a vowel).
target_language_example: Posso avere un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have a glass of red wine, please?

meaning: “Can I have a…?” / “May I have a…?” (polite request).
additional_notes: Used to ask for something you want to receive (a drink, an item, a document, an opinion). It’s often followed by a noun: “Posso avere una birra…?”, “Posso avere una lista…?”, “Posso avere una seconda opinione?”. Add “per favore” or “per piacere” to be extra polite. The “una” changes with gender/number: “un” (masc. singular), “una” (fem. singular), “due” + plural (e.g., “Posso avere due biglietti?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una bottiglia d’acqua?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a bottle of water?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone is reliable or willing to help. It’s the verb phrase “contare su” (to count on / rely on) with “posso” (can I). Often followed by a person (su Tom, su di lei) or by an action: “Posso contare su di te per…” (Can I count on you to…). “su di lei” is formal (“you” = Lei).
target_language_example: Posso contare su di te domani mattina?
native_language_example: Can I count on you tomorrow morning?

meaning: "can I believe that…?" / "I can believe that…"
additional_notes: Used before a clause introduced by "che" to say you find something believable (or, often as a question, to express disbelief: "Posso credere che…?"). In the clause after "che", Italian commonly uses the subjunctive, especially in questions or when there’s uncertainty (e.g., "posso credere che sia vero?").
target_language_example: Posso credere che tu abbia fatto tutto da solo?
native_language_example: Can I believe that you did everything by yourself?

additional_notes: Used when you expect to see someone and want to relay a message to them for another person. Often combined with an indirect object pronoun: Gli posso dare un messaggio? (to him), Le posso dare un messaggio? (to her). You can also specify the person: Posso dare un messaggio a Tom?
target_language_example: Visto che lo vedrò domani, gli posso dare un messaggio se vuoi.
native_language_example: Since I’ll see him tomorrow, I can pass him a message if you want.

meaning: "can I give you" / "I can give you" (offering to give someone something).
additional_notes: Used to offer something to someone (an object, information, help, or even a ride: "posso darti un passaggio"). It can be a question ("Posso darti...?" = "Can I give you...?") or a statement ("Posso darti..." = "I can give you..."). The pronoun "-ti" means "to you" (informal singular).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso darti una mano con i compiti.
native_language_example: If you want, I can give you a hand with your homework.

additional_notes: From potere (posso = “I can”) + dire (“to say”). Used in questions to look for words or soften what you’re about to say: “Come posso dire?” often means “How can I put it?”. In negative form (non posso dire) it can mean “I can’t say / I can’t tell (you)” or “I can’t say that…”.
target_language_example: Non posso dire che sia facile, ma ci provo.
native_language_example: I can’t say it’s easy, but I’m trying.

additional_notes: First-person singular of potere + fare. It is used to talk about ability or possibility ('I can do') and, in questions, permission or offers ('can I do...?'). Depending on context, fare can also mean 'make'. In expressions like ce la posso fare, it is part of the idiom ce la fare, meaning 'to manage' or 'to make it'.
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso fare la spesa io.
native_language_example: If you want, I can do the shopping.

meaning: "I can do without" / "I can go without" (I don’t need to).
additional_notes: Used to say something isn’t necessary, or that you can refrain from doing something. Often followed by a noun or an infinitive verb: "posso fare a meno del caffè" (I can do without coffee), "posso fare a meno di uscire" (I can go without going out). In questions or negatives it can sound like "I can’t do without" / "I can’t go without": "Non posso fare a meno di...".
target_language_example: Oggi posso fare a meno di prendere la macchina.
native_language_example: Today I can go without taking the car.

meaning: 'what can I do to/for …?' (asking how to help or achieve something).
additional_notes: Used when asking what action you can take to help someone or to reach a goal, usually followed by an infinitive (e.g., "aiutare", "migliorare") or by a person/pronoun ("te", "Lei"). Very common in polite help-offers: "Che cosa posso fare per aiutarla?" (formal).
target_language_example: Che cosa posso fare per aiutarti?
native_language_example: What can I do to help you?

meaning: "can I do for you?" / "what can I do for you?" (offering help).
additional_notes: Used to offer help or ask what someone needs. With "per te" it’s the informal "you" (tu). In polite/formal situations, you’ll often hear "Cosa posso fare per Lei?". The phrase can sound neutral and helpful in customer service, but tone and extra words (e.g., swearing) can make it aggressive.
target_language_example: Buongiorno, cosa posso fare per te?
native_language_example: Good morning, what can I do for you?

meaning: May I ask you a question? (formal)
additional_notes: Used to politely ask permission to ask a question in formal situations. "farle" = "fare" (to ask/make) + "Le" (to you, formal). You can add an adjective to specify the type: "una domanda personale" (a personal question), "indiscreta" (nosy), etc. Informal version: "Posso farti una domanda?"
target_language_example: Mi scusi, posso farle una domanda?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I ask you a question?

meaning: “Can I do it?” / “I can do it.”
additional_notes: From the verb phrase “potere + fare” (“to be able to do”). It can be a question asking for permission or possibility (“Posso farlo?” = “Can I do it?/May I do it?”) or a statement of ability (“Posso farlo oggi.” = “I can do it today.”). The pronoun “lo” means “it” (a previously mentioned thing). You can add a time or method: “oggi”, “adesso”, “in modo diverso”.
target_language_example: Non posso farlo adesso, ma posso farlo più tardi.
native_language_example: I can’t do it now, but I can do it later.

additional_notes: Used to offer instruction: posso = “I can”, insegnare = “to teach”, come = “how”. It’s normally followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., come guidare = “how to drive”). Often includes an object pronoun before posso (e.g., Le posso… = “I can teach you…” formal; vi posso… = “I can teach you all…”).
target_language_example: Ti posso insegnare come cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to cook pasta.

meaning: “I can teach you (formal) to …” / “I can teach her to …”.
additional_notes: Used to offer or say you are able to teach someone how to do something. The pronoun **-le** means “to her” or “to you” when speaking formally with **Lei** (it can also be used formally for “to him”). It’s followed by **a + infinitive** (e.g., *a cantare* = “to sing”).
target_language_example: Posso insegnarle a cucinare un piatto semplice.
native_language_example: I can teach you (formal) to cook a simple dish.

additional_notes: Used to offer to teach a skill. "posso" = I can; "insegnarvi" = teach you (to you all / to you in formal "voi"); followed by "a" + an infinitive verb (e.g., scrivere, tradurre, cantare). In everyday modern Italian, for one person you’ll more often hear "posso insegnarti a…" (informal "tu") or "posso insegnarle a…" (formal "Lei").
target_language_example: Se vuoi, posso insegnarvi a cucinare piatti semplici.
native_language_example: If you want, I can teach you to cook simple dishes.

additional_notes: Used to ask permission or make a polite request to speak. Often followed by a person: "posso parlare con + [person]?" (Can I speak with ...?). With pronouns: con lei (formal you), con te (informal you), con loro (them/you plural formal). In statements it can mean "I can speak"/"I’m able to speak" (e.g., "Non posso parlare ora" = "I can’t talk now").
target_language_example: Scusi, posso parlare con il responsabile, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I speak with the person in charge, please?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to speak with someone, especially on the phone or in a polite request. Follow with a name or a person: "Posso parlare con Mike?" / "Posso parlare con il direttore?". With pronouns it changes: "con lei" (formal you/her), "con te" (informal you), "con voi" (you all or formal you in some regions). Often paired with "per favore".
target_language_example: Buongiorno, posso parlare con la responsabile, per favore?
native_language_example: Good morning, can I speak to the manager, please?

additional_notes: Uses the verb potere (posso = “I can / may I”) + infinitive portare (“to bring/carry/take”). It can refer to bringing an object (Posso portare questo a lui.) or taking someone somewhere (Posso portare Tom a casa? / Ti posso portare da lei.). With object pronouns, Italian often places them before posso: Lo posso portare… (= “I can bring it…”).
target_language_example: Posso portare una bottiglia di vino?
native_language_example: Can I bring a bottle of wine?

additional_notes: Literally “I can take.” Used to ask permission or to request something politely, especially in shops, bars, or restaurants (similar to “Can I get...?”). With an object: “Posso prendere un caffè?” = “Can I have a coffee?” It can also be used more generally to mean you’re able/allowed to take something: “Posso prendere qualunque cosa.”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere un biglietto per Roma?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I get a ticket to Rome?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission to borrow something temporarily. Very common in polite requests; you can make it more formal by using Lei forms (e.g., i suoi / il suo). Often followed by an object and a time expression (per un minuto, per un momento, per oggi).
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito la tua penna per un attimo?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your pen for a moment?

meaning: 'Can I borrow the…?' (asking to borrow a masculine singular item).
additional_notes: Use this to politely ask to borrow something. It’s followed by a masculine singular noun: "Posso prendere in prestito il libro?" If the item is feminine, use "la" ("posso prendere in prestito la…"); plural: "i/le". You can also say "Posso prenderlo in prestito?" = "Can I borrow it?"
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito il tuo caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your charger?

posso prendere in prestito il suo

target_language_multi_word_term: posso prendere in prestito il suo
additional_notes: Uses the verb phrase "prendere in prestito" = "to borrow" (literally "to take on loan"). "il suo" means "yours" in a formal/polite way (addressing someone as "Lei"). It often refers to something understood from context (e.g., your pen/phone), and you may add the noun for clarity: "Posso prendere in prestito la sua penna?"
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il suo caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I borrow your charger?

posso prendere in prestito il tuo

target_language_multi_word_term: posso prendere in prestito il tuo
meaning: “Can I borrow your …?” (asking to borrow something of yours).
additional_notes: Common polite request. Use it with a masculine singular noun (il tuo coltello / il tuo laptop). For feminine singular, say: “Posso prendere in prestito la tua …?” (la tua penna). You can also add “per un attimo/un momento” (for a moment) or “per un giorno” (for a day).
target_language_example: Scusa, posso prendere in prestito il tuo caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I borrow your charger?

posso prendere in prestito il vostro

target_language_multi_word_term: posso prendere in prestito il vostro
additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow something from the person you’re addressing. “Prendere in prestito” = “to borrow.” “Il vostro” agrees with a masculine singular noun (il coltello, il computer, il laptop); for feminine singular use “la vostra” (la penna), masculine plural “i vostri,” feminine plural “le vostre.” You can add the item after it: “Posso prendere in prestito il vostro coltello?”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il vostro caricabatterie?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow your charger?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask to borrow an object. Literally “can I take it on loan.” Often followed by a time limit: “per un secondo/un minuto/per quanto tempo…”. Use “Scusa” (informal) or “Scusi” (formal) to sound more polite.
target_language_example: Posso prenderlo in prestito per un attimo?
native_language_example: Can I borrow it for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to ask for something that belongs to you to be returned. You normally add the noun after it (e.g., “Posso riavere il mio telefono?”). If the item is feminine, change it to “la mia” (e.g., “Posso riavere la mia borsa?”).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso riavere il mio passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have my passport back?

meaning: "Can I sit down?" / "May I sit (here/with you)?"
additional_notes: Common polite way to ask permission to sit. Often followed by a place or person: "Posso sedermi qui?" (here), "Posso sedermi con te/voi/loro?" (with you/you all/them). You can add "un attimo" to mean “for a moment.” It can also be used more generally as “I can’t just sit here…” in expressions like "Non posso sedermi qui e...".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso sedermi qui vicino alla finestra?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I sit here near the window?

meaning: “can I find” / “I can find” (also: “can I get/locate?”).
additional_notes: From "potere" (to be able to/can) + "trovare" (to find). Used to ask where something/someone is or how to reach/locate them: "Dove lo/la/le posso trovare?" = "Where can I find it/her/them?" In other contexts it can mean “I can manage to find” something (time, a job, a person): "Posso trovare del tempo" = "I can find/make some time." Pronouns often appear in the middle: "la/le/lo".
target_language_example: Scusi, dove lo posso trovare?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I find it?

additional_notes: "Posso" is the 1st-person singular of "potere" (to be able to / can). It’s followed by an infinitive like "usare" (to use). Use it to ask permission (especially with a question mark and rising intonation): "Posso usare…?" or to say you’re allowed/able to use something: "Posso usare…".
target_language_example: Scusa, posso usare il tuo telefono per un minuto?
native_language_example: Sorry, can I use your phone for a minute?

meaning: "Can I use the…?" (asking permission to use something; masculine singular).
additional_notes: Used to ask if you’re allowed to use an item or service. It must be followed by a masculine singular noun (il bagno, il telefono, il Wi‑Fi). If the noun is feminine, use "posso usare la…"; if it starts with s+consonant or z, you often need "posso usare lo…" (e.g., lo scanner).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso usare il bagno?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I use the bathroom?

additional_notes: Used to ask permission or to request to look at something (often politely). It can be followed by a noun ("Posso vedere la tua licenza?") or by a place/direction ("Posso vedere dietro?"). Adding "per favore" makes it more polite.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso vedere il menu, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, may I see the menu, please?

meaning: "Can I see the…?" / "May I see the…?" (for a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to politely ask to see something (a menu, a person, a document, a video, etc.). It’s made of: posso (I can/may) + vedere (to see) + il (the). Change "il" depending on the noun: "posso vedere lo…", "posso vedere l’…", "posso vedere la…", "posso vedere i/le…".
target_language_example: Scusi, posso vedere il passaporto?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I see the passport?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask to see something. It’s followed by a feminine singular noun (la lista, la documentazione, la torre). For a masculine noun, use “posso vedere il/lo …?”; for plural, “posso vedere i/le …?”. You can add “per favore” to be extra polite.
target_language_example: Posso vedere la carta dei dolci, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I see the dessert menu, please?

additional_notes: 3rd-person plural of "potere" + infinitive "essere". Used to say something is possible, allowed, or generally true about multiple things/people (loro). Often followed by an adjective or noun ("possono essere diversi", "possono essere un dolore") or a past participle in the passive ("possono essere visti" = "can be seen").
target_language_example: Questi problemi possono essere risolti facilmente.
native_language_example: These problems can be solved easily.

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s employment/job (often the specific position), or sometimes the workplace in a general sense. Common in questions like "Qual è il tuo posto di lavoro?" (= What’s your job/position?) and in phrases like "cercare un posto di lavoro" (= to look for a job) or "domande di posto di lavoro" (= job applications).
target_language_example: Sto cercando un nuovo posto di lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a new job.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a specific place and introduce a clause with information about what happens there (who lives/works there, where something happened, etc.). It’s often followed by a verb: "il posto dove vivere" (the place to live), "il posto dove ci siamo conosciuti" (the place where we met). In everyday Italian you may also hear "il posto in cui" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cerco un posto dove studiare in pace.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place where I can study in peace.

meaning: a place to stay (somewhere you can live/sleep temporarily).
additional_notes: Used when you need accommodation or a temporary place to sleep/live, often when traveling or in an emergency. You’ll often hear it with a time phrase (e.g., “per stanotte”, “per qualche giorno”): “Cerco un posto dove stare per stanotte.”
target_language_example: Cerco un posto dove stare per due notti.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a place to stay for two nights.

meaning: a place where (…); a place in which (…).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that describes what happens/exists in that place: “un posto in cui + verb” (e.g., abitare, dormire, lavorare, nascondersi). It’s similar to “dove” (“where”), but a bit more explicit because it names the place (posto). You can also see it after a comma as an apposition: “Laramie, posto in cui…”.
target_language_example: Cerco un posto in cui studiare in pace.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place where I can study in peace.

meaning: a place to go (often: ‘nowhere to go’).
additional_notes: Literally “a place where to go.” Very common after negatives like non… nessun/alcun (“no/any”), especially to express having no options or no home/safe place: Non ho nessun posto in cui andare = “I have nowhere to go.” You can also add altro (“other”) to mean “no other place to go.”
target_language_example: Dopo la lite, non avevo nessun posto in cui andare.
native_language_example: After the argument, I had nowhere to go.

meaning: a place to stay (somewhere you can live/sleep, often temporarily).
additional_notes: Used when talking about having accommodation or somewhere to sleep/live, often in a practical or urgent context (e.g., after moving, traveling, or if someone might be homeless). You’ll often hear it in questions like “Hai un posto in cui stare?” = “Do you have a place to stay?” Literally “place in which to stay.”
target_language_example: Se vieni a Roma, posso aiutarti a trovare un posto in cui stare.
native_language_example: If you come to Rome, I can help you find a place to stay.

additional_notes: Used to describe a location as suitable for living there, or to say you have accommodation. Often follows adjectives like bello/buon (nice/good): “un bel/buon posto in cui vivere.” In everyday speech you may also hear “un posto dove vivere” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Cerco un posto in cui vivere vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a place to live near work.

meaning: “you can count on …” / “you can rely on …”.
additional_notes: Uses the polite/plural form potete (“you [all] can” or formal “you can”). It’s followed by su di + a stressed pronoun: su di me (on me), su di te, su di lui/lei, su di noi, su di voi, su di loro. In everyday speech you’ll also often hear just contare su di me or contare su di lui/lei.
target_language_example: Non preoccupatevi: potete contare su di noi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: you can count on us.

additional_notes: Imperfetto of "potere" + infinitive "aiutare". Often used in reported speech (after verbs like "disse", "chiese", "pensava") to talk about ability or possibility to help in the past. Depending on context it can mean a general past ability (“could”) or a specific possibility (“might be able to”).
target_language_example: Non sapevo se poteva aiutare, ma ho chiesto lo stesso.
native_language_example: I didn't know if he/she could help, but I asked anyway.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty. It is the conditional form of potere + essere. Before a noun or adjective, it usually means "could/might be"; before a past participle, it often means "could/might have," as in Potrebbe essere arrivata = "She might have arrived."
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere una buona idea.
native_language_example: It could be a good idea.

meaning: “it could be in …” / “it might be in …” (expressing uncertainty about a location or situation).
additional_notes: Used to guess or suggest a possibility. "Potrebbe" is the conditional of "potere" (can/may), often translated as “might/could.” It’s typically followed by a place ("in cucina", "in ufficio") or by a condition/state ("in ritardo" = late, "in pericolo" = in danger).
target_language_example: Il tuo telefono potrebbe essere in macchina.
native_language_example: Your phone might be in the car.

meaning: might be able to / could be able to.
additional_notes: Used to express possibility or uncertainty about someone’s ability to do something. It combines the conditional of "potere" (potrebbe = could/might) with "essere in grado di" (= to be able/capable of) + an infinitive (e.g., aiutare, venire). Often sounds a bit formal compared with "potrebbe + infinitive" (e.g., "potrebbe aiutarti").
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere in grado di finire il lavoro oggi.
native_language_example: He/She might be able to finish the work today.

additional_notes: Used to express possibility/uncertainty that someone is innocent. It’s built from the conditional of potere (“potrebbe” = “could/might”) + essere (“to be”) + innocente (“innocent”). Very common in questions like “Pensi/Pensate davvero che…?” (“Do you really think that…?”).
target_language_example: Non lo so: potrebbe essere innocente.
native_language_example: I don’t know: he might be innocent.

meaning: "it could be a / he could be a" (a possibility).
additional_notes: Used to express uncertainty or a guess about what something/someone is. It’s the conditional of essere (to be): potrebbe = “could/might”. Often followed by a noun: potrebbe essere un cancro (“it could be cancer”), potrebbe essere un guaio (“it could be trouble”). For feminine nouns use una: potrebbe essere una buona idea. For plural use dei/degli/delle: potrebbero essere dei turisti (“they could be tourists”).
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere un errore, ricontrolliamo.
native_language_example: It could be a mistake; let’s double-check.

additional_notes: Used to express a possibility or speculation. Potrebbe is the conditional of potere (“can/to be able to”) and is often used for “might/could.” In questions like “Pensi/Pensate che…?” it stays “potrebbe” because it refers to what someone might be, not what they can do.
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere un alieno, ma non ne siamo sicuri.
native_language_example: He could be an alien, but we’re not sure.

additional_notes: Uses the conditional of potere ("could/might") + essere ("to be") to express possibility or speculation. Common in questions ("Che altro potrebbe essere?" = "What else could it be?") and when thinking out loud ("Mi chiedo cosa potrebbe essere" = "I wonder what it might be"). It can also be used alone to mean "Could be."
target_language_example: Potrebbe essere una buona idea, ma non ne sono sicuro.
native_language_example: It could be a good idea, but I'm not sure.

meaning: “they could be / they might be” (conditional of “essere,” used for possibility).
additional_notes: Used to talk about a possibility (not certain). It’s the conditional tense of “essere” with the subject “they” (loro / a plural noun). With adjectives or nouns: “potrebbero essere vere” = “might be true.” With a place/state: “potrebbero essere in ritardo” = “might be late.” It can also be followed by another verb: “potrebbero essere in grado di…” = “they might be able to…”. With past participle it forms the conditional perfect passive, matching gender/number: “potrebbero essere stati” (masc. plural) / “potrebbero essere state” (fem. plural).
target_language_example: Domani potrebbero essere chiuse molte strade.
native_language_example: Tomorrow many roads might be closed.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request in shops, cafés, restaurants, or when asking for someone’s time/attention. Literally “I could have,” from potere (can/could) + avere (to have), but it functions like “Could I have…?” Common with items (una tazza di caffè), time (un minuto, un momento), or to speak with someone (con lei = with you/formal).
target_language_example: Potrei avere il conto, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have the bill, please?

additional_notes: Used to politely ask for something (a drink, an item, a moment of someone’s time). It’s the conditional of "potere" (I could) + "avere" (to have), making the request softer than "posso avere…?". Usually followed by a noun; change the article as needed: "potrei avere una…?", "potrei avere dell’…?".
target_language_example: Potrei avere un caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used to suggest (politely and a bit indirectly) that you may be able to connect someone with a person who can help. Often followed by an infinitive like "aiutare" (to help): "Potrei conoscere qualcuno che può aiutarti." You can add the person being helped with a pronoun: "aiutarla" (help her/you polite), "aiutarti" (help you informal), "aiutarvi" (help you plural).
target_language_example: Potrei conoscere qualcuno che può risolvere questo problema.
native_language_example: I might know someone who can solve this problem.

meaning: “I could never …” (it would be impossible/unthinkable for me).
additional_notes: Used to express strong impossibility or refusal, often with "non": "non potrei mai" = “I could never.” It’s the conditional of "potere" ("potrei" = “I could”) plus "mai" (“ever/never”), so it often corresponds to English “never” even though "mai" literally means “ever” unless it’s with negation.
target_language_example: Non potrei mai dirti una cosa del genere.
native_language_example: I could never tell you something like that.

additional_notes: Very common polite way to ask to borrow something. Literally “I could take on loan,” but it’s used like “Could I borrow…?” It’s conditional (potrei), so it sounds softer/more courteous than “posso…”. Often followed by a noun: “Potrei prendere in prestito il tuo/il suo…?” (your/formal your). You can also add “per un attimo/un momento” (for a moment) or “per un giorno” (for a day).
target_language_example: Potrei prendere in prestito la tua penna per un attimo?
native_language_example: Could I borrow your pen for a moment?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a possibility (“you might be…”) or to make a polite/soft suggestion. It’s made of potresti (“you could,” conditional of potere) + essere (“to be”). In questions it can ask if someone could be something (“Could you be my teacher?”), though in many contexts Italian would more naturally use "Potresti fare da insegnante?" or "Potresti insegnarmi?".
target_language_example: Potresti essere stanco: hai lavorato tutto il giorno.
native_language_example: You might be tired: you worked all day.

additional_notes: Imperative form (tu) of "premere" (to press), used to give a direct instruction: "Press the button." Often followed by a color or purpose (e.g., "premi il pulsante rosso" / "per aprire..."). For a more polite request, you can say "Premi il pulsante, per favore" or use the formal form "Prema il pulsante".
target_language_example: Premi il pulsante e aspetta cinque secondi.
native_language_example: Press the button and wait five seconds.

additional_notes: 3rd-person singular present of the verb phrase **prendere in prestito** = “to borrow.” It takes a direct object (the thing borrowed) and often **da/dal/dalla/dai/dalle** + person/source you borrow from: *Prende in prestito la macchina dal suo vicino.* Can also be used figuratively (e.g., “borrowing” ideas or even lives in a story).
target_language_example: Prende in prestito la macchina dal suo vicino.
native_language_example: He/She borrows the car from his/her neighbor.

additional_notes: From the verb phrase “prendere in prestito” = “to borrow” (literally “to take on loan”). “Prende” is 3rd person singular present tense (“he/she borrows”). “dei” means “some” (masculine plural) and is used before a plural noun: “dei libri” = “some books”. You can change “dei” depending on the noun: “delle” (feminine plural), “dell’” (singular before a vowel), “del/dello/della” (singular).
target_language_example: Prende in prestito dei libri dalla biblioteca.
native_language_example: He borrows some books from the library.

meaning: “often borrows the” (talking about a feminine noun).
additional_notes: “Prendere in prestito” means “to borrow” (to take something temporarily and give it back). “Prende” is the present tense for “he/she takes/borrows,” “spesso” = “often,” and “la” is “the” for feminine singular nouns (e.g., la macchina, la sua auto). For masculine nouns you’d use “il/lo” (e.g., prende in prestito il libro).
target_language_example: Luca prende spesso in prestito la mia macchina.
native_language_example: Luca often borrows my car.

meaning: making fun of me; teasing me; messing with me.
additional_notes: From the expression "prendere in giro" = "to make fun of / tease". It’s often used when you feel someone is joking at your expense or not being serious. "Prendendo" is the gerund (“-ing”), used with "stare" to mean “is/are making fun of…”; you can change the pronoun: "di te" (of you), "di lui/lei" (of him/her), "di noi" (of us), etc.
target_language_example: Non stai prendendo gioco di me, vero?
native_language_example: You’re not making fun of me, are you?

additional_notes: Gerund of "prendere in giro" (to tease/make fun of / mess with someone). Often used in questions like "Mi stai prendendo in giro?" meaning "Are you kidding me?" or "Are you making fun of me?" Depending on tone, it can range from playful teasing to accusing someone of not being serious.
target_language_example: Dai, mi stai prendendo in giro?
native_language_example: Come on, are you kidding me?

additional_notes: Very common but vulgar/impolite expression. Used especially in questions like “Mi stai prendendo per il culo?” to show disbelief or annoyance (“Are you serious?” / “Are you messing with me?”). Can mean either joking with someone or mocking them. Literally it would be “taking (someone) by the ass,” but that’s not how you translate it in English.
target_language_example: Dai, mi stai prendendo per il culo? Non può essere vero.
native_language_example: Come on, are you kidding me? That can’t be true.

meaning: to take care of; to look after.
additional_notes: Used to talk about caring for a person, animal, or thing (looking after them, helping them, making sure they’re okay). In everyday Italian it’s most commonly used in the reflexive form: prendersi cura di (mi prendo cura di…, ti prendi cura di…, si prende cura di…, ci prendiamo cura di…, vi prendete cura di…, si prendono cura di…). Often followed by a pronoun (di lui/lei/loro/me/te) or a noun (di un bambino, di un cane).
target_language_example: Ti devi prendere cura di lui.
native_language_example: You have to take care of him.

meaning: to panic; to be overcome by panic.
additional_notes: Almost always used with a reflexive/causative form: "farsi prendere dal panico" (to let yourself panic) and "lasciarsi prendere dal panico" (to let yourself be overcome by panic). Common in negatives as advice: "Non farti prendere dal panico" = “Don’t panic.”
target_language_example: Durante l’esame mi sono fatto prendere dal panico e ho dimenticato tutto.
native_language_example: During the exam I panicked and forgot everything.

meaning: to target; to single out (often for criticism or teasing).
additional_notes: Used both literally (to aim at something) and, very commonly, figuratively (to pick someone as a target for jokes, bullying, or repeated criticism). Often used with a direct object: "prendere qualcuno di mira".
target_language_example: A scuola prendevano sempre di mira lui per il suo accento.
native_language_example: At school they always picked on him for his accent.

meaning: to catch fire; to start burning.
additional_notes: Used when something (a building, car, pan, clothes, etc.) starts burning, often suddenly or accidentally. Common in news and safety contexts. Past: “ha preso fuoco” (it caught fire).
target_language_example: Attenzione: la padella può prendere fuoco sul fornello.
native_language_example: Careful: the pan can catch fire on the stove.

additional_notes: A very common combination meaning "to take" or "to get" followed by a masculine singular noun with il. The exact English translation depends on the noun: prendere il treno = "take the train," prendere il farmaco = "take the medicine," prendere il covid = "catch covid." In reflexive expressions like prendersi il suo tempo, it can mean "take one’s time."
target_language_example: Devo prendere il treno delle otto.
native_language_example: I have to take the eight o'clock train.

additional_notes: Used to talk about traveling by train or catching a specific train. With an object pronoun it becomes: prendere il treno → prenderlo (to take it). In negatives, "non" goes before the verb: Non prendere il treno. Common future/ability forms: sarò/sarai in grado di prendere il treno (I/you will be able to take the train).
target_language_example: Devo prendere il treno delle otto.
native_language_example: I have to take the 8 o’clock train.

meaning: to rent (to lease, as the tenant).
additional_notes: Used when YOU are the one renting something from someone else (an apartment, a car, a room). It contrasts with "dare in affitto" = to rent out (as the owner/landlord). Common pattern: "prendere in affitto + [thing]" or "prendere in affitto + [thing] + per + [time period]".
target_language_example: Vorrei prendere in affitto un appartamento per tre mesi.
native_language_example: I’d like to rent an apartment for three months.

meaning: to consider; to take into account.
additional_notes: Used when you want someone to think carefully about an idea, fact, or option before deciding. Very common with nouns like "il fatto" (the fact), "il consiglio" (advice), "il tempo" (time), and can also mean "to consider (doing something)" in serious contexts.
target_language_example: Prima di decidere, devi prendere in considerazione tutte le opzioni.
native_language_example: Before deciding, you have to consider all the options.

meaning: to make fun of; to tease; to kid/joke with (someone); sometimes: to fool/deceive (someone).
additional_notes: Very common idiom. Usually takes a direct object (a person) and often appears with pronouns: "prendere in giro qualcuno" (to tease/make fun of someone). Depending on tone and context it can range from light teasing to mocking, and in some contexts it can imply tricking or not being serious. Related form: "Non mi faccio prendere in giro" = "I won’t let myself be fooled/made fun of."
target_language_example: Perché mi devi prendere in giro?
native_language_example: Why do you have to make fun of me? / Why are you teasing me?

additional_notes: Used when you borrow something (an object) or money from someone, with the idea that you will give it back later. You can add who you borrow from with "da": "Posso prendere in prestito dei soldi da te?" The opposite is "prestare" / "dare in prestito" (to lend).
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito la tua penna per un minuto?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your pen for a minute?

additional_notes: Used when you borrow something temporarily and plan to return it. The article changes with the noun: prendere in prestito il libro (the book), lo zaino (the backpack), la penna (the pen), i soldi (the money). Often followed by “da” to say who you borrow from: prendere in prestito il libro da Marco.
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito il tuo libro?
native_language_example: Can I borrow your book?

additional_notes: Used when you borrow something that belongs to a male person ("il suo" = "his"). It normally refers to a specific noun that’s understood from context or said earlier (e.g., "il suo libro" = "his book"). Italian possessives agree with the noun being borrowed: il suo (masc. singular), la sua (fem. singular), i suoi (masc. plural), le sue (fem. plural). Often you’ll also hear "prendere in prestito" without the possessive if the owner is stated differently (e.g., "prendere in prestito il libro di Marco").
target_language_example: Posso prendere in prestito il suo libro per un giorno?
native_language_example: Can I borrow his book for one day?

additional_notes: Used when the thing you’re borrowing is understood from context and you refer to it with a possessive pronoun. "Il tuo" agrees with a masculine singular item (e.g., "il libro" → "il tuo"). You’ll often hear it as a question: "Posso prendere in prestito il tuo?" Note: "prendere in prestito" means "to borrow" (not *to lend*).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato il caricatore: posso prendere in prestito il tuo?
native_language_example: I forgot my charger: can I borrow yours?

additional_notes: Based on the verb phrase prendere in prestito (“to borrow”). Il vostro means “yours” (masculine singular) and is used with the article il; it can refer to an item understood from context (e.g., a pen, phone, charger). Vostro is also used for formal “your” (to one person) or plural “your” (to multiple people).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso prendere in prestito il vostro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I borrow yours?

meaning: to borrow mine (referring to a feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used when you’re saying someone can borrow something that belongs to you, where the thing is feminine in Italian (e.g., *la macchina* = the car, *la penna* = the pen). It usually needs context or the noun to be clear: *Puoi prendere in prestito la mia macchina?* / *Puoi prendere in prestito la mia?* = “Can you borrow mine?” Literally it’s “to take on loan,” so it doesn’t translate word-for-word as “borrow.”
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi prendere in prestito la mia macchina.
native_language_example: If you want, you can borrow my car.

meaning: "to take/get/pick up the …" (followed by a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun after it: prendere la barca (take/get the boat), prendere la pillola (take the pill), prendere la roba (pick up/get your stuff). Often appears with "andare a" to mean "go and get/pick up": vado a prendere la….
target_language_example: Aspettami: vado a prendere la valigia.
native_language_example: Wait for me: I’m going to get the suitcase.

additional_notes: Used when someone needs to take medication. You can change the possessive to match the person: prendere la mia medicina (my), la tua (your), la sua (his/her), la nostra (our), la vostra (your plural), la loro (their). In Italian the possessive agrees with the noun (medicina is feminine singular → la mia/sua, not *il mio/suo*). Often used with reminders: “Devi prendere la tua medicina.”
target_language_example: Tom si è dimenticato di prendere la sua medicina stamattina.
native_language_example: Tom forgot to take his medicine this morning.

additional_notes: This is the verb pattern "prendere" + possessive pronoun + noun. "Le sue" means "her" or "his/its" when the noun is feminine plural (e.g., *le pillole, le medicine, le decisioni, le difese, le impronte digitali*). Often used for routine actions like taking medicine (*prendere le sue pillole*) or more generally “take his/her own …”. The exact English verb may change by context (e.g., *prendere le sue decisioni* = “make her own decisions”).
target_language_example: Ricordati di prendere le sue medicine prima di uscire.
native_language_example: Remember to take her medicine before going out.

additional_notes: Used with "a" + an activity/event: "prendere parte a una riunione / a un corso / a una gara". It’s slightly more formal than "partecipare" in everyday speech but very common in announcements and invitations.
target_language_example: Vuoi prendere parte alla riunione di domani?
native_language_example: Do you want to take part in tomorrow’s meeting?

meaning: to make fun of someone; to mess with someone (vulgar).
additional_notes: Very informal and vulgar expression. Often used to accuse someone of mocking you or not being serious. Structure: prendere per il culo + [person] (e.g., "Mi stai prendendo per il culo?" = "Are you messing with me?"). A more polite/common alternative is "prendere in giro" (to tease/make fun of).
target_language_example: Mi stai prendendo per il culo o dici sul serio?
native_language_example: Are you messing with me, or are you serious?

meaning: to take a seat; to sit down.
additional_notes: Used when inviting someone to sit (often polite/formal): "Prego, prenda/prendete posto." It can also mean "to take one’s place" (e.g., in a line or in a group). Don’t confuse it with English "take place" (= "happen").
target_language_example: Prego, potete prendere posto: lo spettacolo sta per cominciare.
native_language_example: Please take your seats: the show is about to start.

additional_notes: Common, everyday way to talk about getting food (often casually or quickly), e.g., at a bar, café, or on the go. Uses "prendere" in the sense of "to get" rather than literally "to take".
target_language_example: Prima del treno, possiamo prendere qualcosa da mangiare.
native_language_example: Before the train, we can grab something to eat.

meaning: to take/get this medicine without a prescription.
additional_notes: Used to say a medicine can be taken or obtained without a doctor’s prescription. In Italian, with medicines you’ll often hear prendere (take) or comprare (buy). Senza ricetta means “without a prescription” (over-the-counter). Si può… is an impersonal way to say “you can/it’s possible to…”.
target_language_example: Scusi, si può prendere questa medicina senza ricetta?
