additional_notes: Used before a verb like dice/dico/ho detto (“say/tell”) to mean “everything that (someone) says/tells to her.” **le** is an indirect object pronoun meaning “to her” (or “to you” in the polite/formal form). It must match who receives the information (e.g., le dice = “says to her/you”).
target_language_example: Non credere a tutto quello che le dicono.
native_language_example: Don’t believe everything they tell you/her.

meaning: "everything that (someone) … to me" / "all that … to me".
additional_notes: Used to introduce a clause meaning “everything that …,” followed by the indirect object pronoun mi (“to me”). It’s typically followed by a verb: tutto quello che mi dice (“everything he says to me”), tutto quello che mi rimane (“everything that remains to me”), tutto quello che mi serviva (“everything I needed”). You can change mi to other pronouns (ti, gli/le, ci, vi, gli).
target_language_example: Ho capito tutto quello che mi hai spiegato.
native_language_example: I understood everything you explained to me.

meaning: everything (that) he/she owned; all (that) he/she possessed.
additional_notes: A relative clause meaning “all that … owned.” It’s often used with verbs like dare (to give), perdere (to lose), vendere (to sell). The verb possedeva is the imperfect (“owned/used to own”), describing what someone had up to that point; in the present you’d say tutto quello che possiede (“everything he/she owns”).
target_language_example: Dopo l’incendio, ha perso tutto quello che possedeva.
native_language_example: After the fire, he lost everything he owned.

additional_notes: Used to say someone is doing as much as possible, often implying they’re trying their best. The subject can change: tutto quello che posso (I can), può (he/she can), possiamo (we can), potete (you all can), possono (they can). It’s often followed by a purpose phrase with “per” + infinitive: “tutto quello che può per + verb” (everything (they) can to do something).
target_language_example: Tom sta facendo tutto quello che può per risparmiare soldi.
native_language_example: Tom is doing everything he can to save money.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause meaning “everything that someone does/says to you” or “everything that I can do/tell you.” It’s often followed by a verb like dice (says/tells you), fa (does), posso dire (I can tell you). The pronoun ti means “to you” (informal singular).
target_language_example: Ho fatto tutto quello che ti ho promesso.
native_language_example: I did everything I promised you.

additional_notes: Used to talk about the one thing (or everything) you desire. It’s built from: tutto (“everything/all”) + quello che (“what/that which”) + voglio (“I want”). It can be the subject or object of the sentence: Tutto quello che voglio è... (“All I want is...”). With “to be,” Italian agrees with what comes after: Tutto quello che voglio sei tu (“All I want is you”)—using sei because tu is “you (singular).”
target_language_example: In vacanza, tutto quello che voglio è rilassarmi.
native_language_example: On vacation, all I want is to relax.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the one thing (or main things) someone desires or asks for. It’s often followed by a noun (il tuo amore), a phrase (pace e tranquillità), or an infinitive action (sedermi qui e bere...). In speech you’ll also hear: "Tutto quello che voglio è che..." (All I want is that...).
target_language_example: Tutto quello che voglio è un po' di tempo per riposarmi.
native_language_example: All I want is a bit of time to rest.

additional_notes: Literally “all that (he/she) wanted.” Uses the imperfect tense of volere (voleva = “wanted/was wanting”), often to talk about what someone wanted at that time in the past. It can refer to things someone received, bought, had, or was given. You can change the verb to match the person: volevo (I), volevi (you), voleva (he/she), volevamo (we), volevate (you plural), volevano (they).
target_language_example: Alla fine, ha ottenuto tutto quello che voleva.
native_language_example: In the end, he got everything he wanted.

meaning: whatever you want; anything you want.
additional_notes: Used to give someone freedom of choice: after a verb it often means “as much/as many as you want” (e.g., eat/watch as much as you want). Said on its own, it can mean “anything you like/whatever you want,” sometimes with a tone of indifference (“fine, whatever you want”).
target_language_example: Scegli tutto quello che vuoi dal menu.
native_language_example: Choose whatever you want from the menu.

meaning: “everything (that) he/she wants” or “all that he/she wants.”
additional_notes: Used to talk about having/being able to get whatever someone wants. It’s a relative clause: tutto (“everything”) + quello che (“that which”) + vuole (“he/she wants”). The verb changes with the person: tutto quello che vuoi (you want), tutto quello che vogliono (they want). In a question it can also mean “Is that all you want (to know)?”
target_language_example: Se ha soldi, può comprare tutto quello che vuole.
native_language_example: If he has money, he can buy everything he wants.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with di cui (“of which/that”), very common with avere bisogno di (“to need”). Pattern: tutto quello di cui + subject + verb (often: ho bisogno) = “everything that … needs”. You can also replace tutto with only what fits: quello di cui (“what/that which … needs”), or add a noun: tutte le cose di cui… (“all the things that…”).
target_language_example: Ho comprato tutto quello di cui avevo bisogno per il viaggio.
native_language_example: I bought everything I needed for the trip.

meaning: all this time; this whole time.
additional_notes: Used to emphasize how long something has been happening or how much time has passed. Often appears with prepositions: "per tutto questo tempo" = "for all this time" (duration up to now or up to a point), "dopo tutto questo tempo" = "after all this time" (after a long period).
target_language_example: Non posso credere che tu lo sapessi da tutto questo tempo.
native_language_example: I can’t believe you’ve known all this time.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a whole situation, event, or set of things that is present, obvious, or already mentioned. It can stand alone or refer broadly to everything involved.
target_language_example: Non posso credere a tutto questo.
native_language_example: I can't believe all this.

additional_notes: Common, everyday phrase used to ask if someone is okay or if everything is fine, and to answer that things are fine. Often said as a quick check-in (like “You good?”) or to confirm there’s no problem. Can also appear as “È tutto a posto.”
target_language_example: Hai trovato le chiavi? Tutto a posto?
native_language_example: Did you find the keys? Everything okay?

additional_notes: Common, friendly way to ask if someone is okay or if things are going well. Often used as a quick check-in (like “How are you?”). You can answer with “Tutto bene.” (Everything’s fine.) or “Sì, tutto bene.” / “Non tanto.” (Not so much.)
target_language_example: Ehi, tutto bene?
native_language_example: Hey, everything ok?

meaning: “all by myself” (said by a female speaker).
additional_notes: Used to say you did everything on your own, without help. The form changes with gender/number: tutto da solo (male), tutto da soli (group of males/mixed), tutto da sole (group of females). Often used with verbs like fare (“to do”).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: posso farlo tutto da sola.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: I can do it all by myself.

meaning: all by yourself; on your own (without help).
additional_notes: Used to say someone did something without anyone’s help or company. With people, it agrees in gender/number: tutto da solo (male singular), tutta da sola (female singular), tutti da soli (male/mixed plural), tutte da sole (female plural). Often used with verbs like fare (to do) or andare (to go).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, posso farlo tutto da solo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can do it all by myself.

additional_notes: Used to say that something has completely ended (a situation, a relationship, a problem, an event). Very common with the verb essere: “È tutto finito” = “It’s all over.” It can sound final or dramatic depending on context.
target_language_example: Tranquillo, è tutto finito: possiamo andare a casa.
native_language_example: Relax, it’s all over: we can go home.

meaning: “everything in terms of (…); with (something) as the main way of thinking/measuring.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone interprets or evaluates everything using one main criterion (often money, profit, etc.). Common with verbs like pensare a / vedere: “pensa a tutto in termini di denaro” = “she thinks about everything in terms of money.” Also works with other nouns (tempo, costi, vantaggi).
target_language_example: Non pensare a tutto in termini di soldi: conta anche il tempo.
native_language_example: Don’t think about everything in terms of money: time matters too.

additional_notes: Very common informal way to ask if things are fine or to reassure someone that there’s no problem. Often used as a short reply on its own (no verb needed): "Tutto ok." It can also be a question: "Tutto ok?" Tone depends on context and can be sarcastic or aggressive if paired with an insult (e.g., "stronzetto").
target_language_example: Ehi, tutto ok? Ti vedo un po' stanco.
native_language_example: Hey, everything OK? You look a bit tired.

meaning: "that's all / that's it"; sometimes literally "everything here".
additional_notes: Common in conversation to downplay or conclude: it means “nothing more than that” or “that’s it” (often after an explanation). It can also be used literally to mean “everything here/right here,” especially with gestures or when telling someone where to put things (e.g., "Metti tutto qua" = "Put everything here"). Often said as a short standalone comment: "Tutto qua." / "Tutto qua?" ("Is that it?").
target_language_example: Volevo solo farti una domanda, tutto qua.
native_language_example: I just wanted to ask you a question, that's all.

additional_notes: Used to say that a situation is managed and going as planned, or to ask for reassurance (often as a short question: “Tutto sotto controllo?”). Common with avere/essere: “Ho tutto sotto controllo” / “È tutto sotto controllo.”
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è tutto sotto controllo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is under control.

additional_notes: Used to reassure someone that there are no problems (“Everything’s fine”). With *se* (“if”), it means “if all goes well” and introduces a condition about the future. *Tutto* = “everything”, *va* (andare) = “goes”, *bene* = “well”.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: tutto va bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything is fine.

additional_notes: Used to offer or ask someone to choose between tea and coffee (informal "vuoi" or formal "vuole"). You’ll often hear it as a quick choice question: "Tè o caffè?"
target_language_example: Per colazione preferisci tè o caffè?
native_language_example: For breakfast, do you prefer tea or coffee?

additional_notes: A type of tea. Often used with an article (il tè verde = the green tea) or without one when speaking generally (Bevo tè verde = I drink green tea). You can contrast it with “tè nero” (black tea).
target_language_example: Preferisco il tè verde al tè nero.
native_language_example: I prefer green tea to black tea.

meaning: the last word; the final say (final decision).
additional_notes: Literally “last word.” Often used in the expression “avere l’ultima parola” = “to have the final say” (the person who makes the final decision). Can also mean the last thing someone says in a conversation or argument.
target_language_example: In questa scelta, i miei genitori hanno l’ultima parola.
native_language_example: In this decision, my parents have the final say.

additional_notes: Used with the verb dare (“to give”): dare un abbraccio a qualcuno = “to give someone a hug.” You’ll also hear it as a greeting/closing in messages: Un abbraccio! (“Hugs!” / “A hug!”).
target_language_example: Quando l'ho vista, le ho dato un abbraccio.
native_language_example: When I saw her, I gave her a hug.

additional_notes: Used for an arrangement or deal between people, companies, or countries. Common with verbs like fare/raggiungere (make/reach), avere (have), and firmare (sign). It can be formal (a contract or treaty) or informal (a personal deal).
target_language_example: Possiamo raggiungere un accordo entro domani?
native_language_example: Can we reach an agreement by tomorrow?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to talk about any one airplane (not a specific one). In questions it often means “a/any plane?” (e.g., “a private plane?”). The plural is “degli aerei” = “some airplanes/planes.”
target_language_example: Devo prendere un aereo domani mattina.
native_language_example: I have to catch a plane tomorrow morning.

additional_notes: Used when talking about finding/booking a place to stay. After the verb "essere" it means "a hotel" (e.g., "Questa casa è un albergo?"). "Albergo" is masculine, so it takes "un" in the singular; plural: "degli alberghi".
target_language_example: Cerco un albergo vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a hotel near the station.

additional_notes: Means “a tree” in general (not a specific one). Use “un” because “albero” is a masculine singular noun. Common with verbs like “piantare” (to plant) and with places like “sotto un albero” (under a tree) or “da un albero” (from/out of a tree).
target_language_example: C'è un albero davanti a casa mia.
native_language_example: There’s a tree in front of my house.

meaning: an alibi (proof/excuse that you were somewhere else).
additional_notes: Used especially in crime/police contexts to mean evidence or a story that shows you couldn’t have done something because you were elsewhere. It can also be used more generally as a “pretext/excuse” (often with a negative tone).
target_language_example: Se hai un alibi, dillo subito alla polizia.
native_language_example: If you have an alibi, tell the police right away.

meaning: an alien (a non-human being from another planet).
additional_notes: Used both literally (in sci‑fi: “I saw an alien”) and figuratively to mean “I’m not a weirdo/stranger; I’m normal like you.” Singular masculine; feminine: "un'aliena". Plural: "gli alieni".
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non sono un alieno: lavoro qui da anni.
native_language_example: Relax, I’m not an alien: I’ve worked here for years.

additional_notes: Used to say someone coaches a particular sport. Put the sport after di: un allenatore di basket/tennis/nuoto. Feminine: un’allenatrice di.
target_language_example: Tom è un allenatore di basket molto bravo.
native_language_example: Tom is a very good basketball coach.

additional_notes: Used before a singular noun. Depending on context, it can mean either an additional one ('another, one more') or a different one. Before a feminine singular noun, it becomes "un'altra".
target_language_example: Vorrei un altro caffè, per favore.
native_language_example: I'd like another coffee, please.

additional_notes: Used when you want to change how you do something or how you say something (e.g., try a different method, rephrase). Often appears with verbs like provare (to try) and dire (to say): "in un altro modo" = "in another way".
target_language_example: Possiamo farlo in un altro modo?
native_language_example: Can we do it another way?

meaning: “another planet” (often: completely different; out of touch/doesn’t fit in).
additional_notes: Used literally (science/space) or figuratively to say someone is so different that it’s like they’re “from another planet.” Common with verbs like "venire da" (to come from) or "appartenere a" (to belong to): "Vengo da un altro pianeta" / "Appartieni a un altro pianeta."
target_language_example: Quando parla di tecnologia, sembra venire da un altro pianeta.
native_language_example: When he talks about technology, he seems like he’s from another planet.

meaning: another place; another spot (e.g., a seat/location).
additional_notes: Used when you want a different location than the one you have now or than the one being discussed. Common in everyday situations like looking for a different seat, a new place to stay, or another location to meet. You can also say "un posto diverso" (a different place).
target_language_example: Scusi, possiamo trovare un altro posto per sederci?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can we find another place to sit?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a different man than the one already mentioned or expected. In relationship contexts it can imply “someone else/a lover” (e.g., “She has another man in her life”), but it can also be neutral (“Another man is coming”). Often contrasts with a specific man: “non… che un altro uomo…” = “not… that another man…”.
target_language_example: Non voglio vedere un altro uomo con lei.
native_language_example: I don’t want to see another man with her.

additional_notes: Used before a masculine singular noun (or on its own) to mean “another/one more.” It agrees in gender and number: un altro (m. sg.), un'altra (f. sg.), altri (m. pl.), altre (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere un altro caffè?
native_language_example: Can we have another coffee?

additional_notes: Used when you want one more serving of wine (after already having one). In a polite offer or request you’ll often hear: “Vorrebbe un altro bicchiere di vino?” (formal singular) or “Vorrebbe...” / “Vorresti...” depending on how formal you want to be. "Bicchiere" = glass (the container/serving), "un altro" = another/one more.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un altro bicchiere di vino, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have another glass of wine, please?

additional_notes: Used when referring to an additional or different item/person, often replacing a noun already understood: "Ne voglio un altro" = "I want another one." It agrees in gender/number: "un altro" (masc. sing.), "un'altra" (fem. sing.), "altri/altre" (plural). Common fixed expression: "in un modo o in un altro" = "one way or another."
target_language_example: Non mi piace questo caffè: ne prendo un altro.
native_language_example: I don’t like this coffee: I’ll have another one.

additional_notes: "Un amante" can mean (1) a romantic/sexual partner, often implying a secret affair (like “a lover” in English), or (2) someone who really loves something (“an enthusiast/fan”), often used with "di": "un amante del vino rosso" = “a red-wine lover.” Feminine: "un'amante" (a lover / a female lover).
target_language_example: Marco è un amante della musica jazz.
native_language_example: Marco is a jazz music lover.

additional_notes: Means “a friend,” referring to a male friend (or to “a friend” when gender isn’t important). The feminine form is “un’amica.” Used with common patterns like “un amico di + name” (a friend of ...) and “chiedere a un amico di + infinitive” (to ask a friend to ...).
target_language_example: Ho parlato con un amico ieri sera.
native_language_example: I talked with a friend last night.

meaning: “a friend who …” (introduces a description of a friend).
additional_notes: Used to add more information about a friend using a relative clause with che (“who/that”). With a specific friend, you’ll often use the indicative: Avevo un amico che si chiamava Tom. With an unknown or hypothetical friend (often in questions), Italian commonly uses the subjunctive: Hai un amico che possa aiutarti?
target_language_example: Cerco un amico che parli inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a friend who speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to mention or introduce someone by where they live. Add a city (or other place) after a (e.g., “a Roma”, “a Milano”). You can also change it for gender/number: “un’amica che vive a …” (female), “degli amici che vivono a …” (plural).
target_language_example: Ho un amico che vive a Firenze.
native_language_example: I have a friend who lives in Florence.

meaning: a CEO / managing director (the top executive of a company).
additional_notes: Used mainly in business contexts for the person who runs a company’s day-to-day operations and has executive authority. Often abbreviated as “AD” in Italian (Amministratore Delegato).
target_language_example: Abbiamo incontrato un amministratore delegato per discutere del futuro dell’azienda.
native_language_example: We met a CEO to discuss the company’s future.

additional_notes: Literally means an angel (the spiritual/religious being). Very often used figuratively as a compliment: "È un angelo" = he/she is so kind, patient, helpful. Common comparisons: "come un angelo" (like an angel), especially about singing/voice, and "sembra un angelo" (he/she looks like an angel), sometimes referring to wearing white.
target_language_example: Sei un angelo, grazie per l'aiuto!
native_language_example: You’re an angel—thanks for the help!

additional_notes: Basic noun phrase using the indefinite article (un). Used literally for an animal, and sometimes figuratively about a person behaving in a rough/violent or out-of-control way ("He’s not an animal!"). The plural is "animali".
target_language_example: In fattoria c’è un animale che fa molto rumore di notte.
native_language_example: On the farm there’s an animal that makes a lot of noise at night.

additional_notes: Used for animals kept at home for companionship (e.g., a dog or cat). Often in the plural: “animali domestici.” Related: “cane/gatto domestico” = domestic dog/cat.
target_language_example: Nel mio appartamento non posso avere un animale domestico.
native_language_example: In my apartment I can’t have a pet.

additional_notes: Means “one year” (a period of 12 months). Used for durations (per un anno = for a year; da un anno = for a year / since a year ago, depending on context) and in fixed expressions like un anno di prigione (“one year in prison”).
target_language_example: Ho studiato italiano per un anno.
native_language_example: I studied Italian for a year.

un anno da quando mi sono

target_language_multi_word_term: un anno da quando mi sono
meaning: “a year since I …” (it’s been a year since I …).
additional_notes: Used with time expressions like "È passato un anno" (“A year has passed”) to say how much time has passed since a past event involving yourself. "da quando" = “since/ever since (the time when)”, and "mi sono" starts a past tense with "essere" (passato prossimo) for reflexive verbs (e.g., mi sono sposato/a = “I got married”). You normally continue the sentence with a past participle (e.g., "mi sono trasferito/a", "mi sono laureato/a").
target_language_example: È passato un anno da quando mi sono trasferito a Milano.
native_language_example: It’s been a year since I moved to Milan.

meaning: a year and a half (18 months).
additional_notes: Used to express a duration or amount of time. You can use it after a verb to say how long something lasted (e.g., ha lavorato un anno e mezzo), or with "è passato" to say that much time has gone by. Similar pattern: "un mese e mezzo" (a month and a half), "due anni e mezzo" (two and a half years).
target_language_example: Ho vissuto a Roma un anno e mezzo.
native_language_example: I lived in Rome for a year and a half.

additional_notes: Used to say something happened one year before now (or before another reference time in a story). Common with the past tense: "È successo un anno fa". With amounts other than one year, Italian often uses "X anni fa" (e.g., "due anni fa") or "più di un anno fa" (more than a year ago).
target_language_example: Ho iniziato questo lavoro un anno fa.
native_language_example: I started this job a year ago.

additional_notes: Used for a self-contained home unit in a building. The indefinite article changes depending on gender/number: un appartamento (masc. sing.), un appartamento di tre camere = a three-bedroom apartment; vivo in un appartamento sopra un negozio = I live in an apartment above a shop.
target_language_example: Stiamo affittando un appartamento vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: We are renting an apartment near the station.

additional_notes: Used for scheduled meetings (e.g., with a doctor, at an office) and also for a romantic date. Common patterns: "Ho un appuntamento dal dentista" (appointment with the dentist), "prenotare/fissare un appuntamento" (to book/set an appointment), "chiedere un appuntamento" (to ask someone out / request a meeting), "andare a un appuntamento" (to go to an appointment/date).
target_language_example: Domani ho un appuntamento con il medico alle 10.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an appointment with the doctor at 10.

additional_notes: Used to say you are meeting someone at a planned time. "Appuntamento" can mean a formal appointment (doctor, meeting) or a romantic date; the context makes it clear. Often followed by a time expression (oggi, domani, questo pomeriggio).
target_language_example: Stasera ho un appuntamento con il medico.
native_language_example: Tonight I have an appointment with the doctor.

meaning: an artist (male; or “a person who is very skilled” in a joking/admiring way).
additional_notes: Usually means an artist in the arts (painter, sculptor, etc.). It’s masculine singular: un artista. The feminine is also artista: un’artista (a female artist). In informal speech, “È un artista!” can mean “He’s really good at it” (sometimes ironic).
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un artista: dipinge quadri bellissimi.
native_language_example: My brother is an artist: he paints beautiful paintings.

additional_notes: A very common noun in travel/hotel situations (bathroom, beach, gym). Plural: asciugamani. In Italian the indefinite article changes with gender/starting sound; here it’s masculine so you say un asciugamano.
target_language_example: Mi può portare un asciugamano, per favore?
native_language_example: Could you bring me a towel, please?

additional_notes: Used mainly to describe someone’s physical appearance or the impression they give: “avere un aspetto + adjective” (to look + adjective), e.g. un aspetto splendido/terribile. It can also mean “an aspect” (a part of something), but in these examples it’s about how someone looks.
target_language_example: Oggi hai un aspetto stanco: hai dormito poco?
native_language_example: Today you look tired: did you sleep little?

additional_notes: Used to compare how someone looks (often health/tiredness/condition). It follows the pattern: avere + un aspetto + adjective + di + person/thing. The adjective changes for gender/number: peggiore stays the same for masculine/feminine and singular/plural.
target_language_example: Dopo il viaggio, ho un aspetto peggiore di ieri.
native_language_example: After the trip, I look worse than yesterday.

additional_notes: Means a person who kills someone (often intentionally). Used with the indefinite article: un assassino (male), una assassina (female). Plural: assassini / assassine. In everyday Italian, you may also hear "un killer" (loanword), but "assassino" is common and not slang.
target_language_example: La polizia pensa che l'uomo sia un assassino.
native_language_example: The police think the man is a murderer.

additional_notes: Used to mean “a very short time.” Common in requests: "Aspetta un attimo" = “Wait a moment.” With time expressions: "un attimo fa" = “a moment ago / just a second ago.” Also used with verbs like "parlare" or "restare" to mean “for a moment”: "Devo parlare un attimo" = “I need to talk for a moment.”
target_language_example: Aspetta un attimo, arrivo subito.
native_language_example: Wait a moment, I’ll be right there.

additional_notes: Used for a male actor; the feminine form is "un’attrice". Plural: "attori" (male or mixed group), "attrici" (all female). Often used with adjectives like "famoso" (famous) or to describe someone’s job: "Lui è un attore".
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un attore e lavora a teatro.
native_language_example: My brother is an actor and works in the theater.

additional_notes: Most commonly means a pay raise: "chiedere un aumento" (to ask for a raise), often "un aumento di stipendio". More generally it means an increase in something measurable: "un aumento del rumore/temperatura/prezzi" (an increase in noise/temperature/prices).
target_language_example: Ho chiesto un aumento perché il costo della vita è aumentato.
native_language_example: I asked for a raise because the cost of living has gone up.

additional_notes: Indefinite form: use when talking about one bus (not a specific one). Plural: "degli autobus" or "alcuni autobus". Often used with "prendere" (to take/catch): "prendere un autobus".
target_language_example: Scusi, dove posso prendere un autobus per il centro?
native_language_example: Excuse me, where can I catch a bus to the city center?

additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s profession or to say you need legal help. The article changes with gender/number: un avvocato (male), un’avvocata / un avvocato (female, depending on preference), un avvocato e una avvocata; plural: degli avvocati (mixed or all male), delle avvocate (all female). Common phrases: parlare con un avvocato (to talk to a lawyer), mi serve un avvocato (I need a lawyer).
target_language_example: Mi serve un avvocato per questo contratto.
native_language_example: I need a lawyer for this contract.

additional_notes: Used for a single kiss. Common in romantic contexts, but also for a quick affectionate kiss with family (often on the cheek). With verbs like dare (to give) and volere (to want): “Dategli un bacio” = “Give him a kiss.”
target_language_example: Mi dai un bacio prima di andare via?
native_language_example: Will you give me a kiss before you leave?

additional_notes: Often used with verbs like fare (to take/give): fare un bagno = to take a bath; fare un bagno a qualcuno/qualcosa = to give someone/something a bath (e.g., a dog). Note: bagno can also mean “bathroom” (more often il bagno), but in these examples it means “bath.”
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra, faccio un bagno caldo.
native_language_example: After the gym, I take a hot bath.

additional_notes: Means “a (male) child/boy.” Often used about someone’s age or to emphasize innocence/youngness: “Lui è solo un bambino” (“He’s just a child”). The feminine is “una bambina” (“a little girl”).
target_language_example: Quando ero un bambino, giocavo sempre in strada.
native_language_example: When I was a child, I always played in the street.

additional_notes: In Italy, a "bar" is usually a casual café where people go for espresso/cappuccino, pastries, sandwiches, and sometimes alcohol (especially aperitivo). It can feel more like a coffee bar than an English-style pub. Common collocations: "andare in un bar" (go to a bar/café), "prendere un caffè in un bar" (have a coffee at a bar/café).
target_language_example: Siete mai andati in un bar spagnolo?
native_language_example: Have you ever been to a Spanish bar?

additional_notes: 'bel' is the shortened masculine singular form of bello after un, used before many masculine nouns: un bel viaggio, un bel cane. It can also mean nice, lovely, or good depending on context; before some sounds, Italian uses un bello or un bell' instead.
target_language_example: Abbiamo passato un bel pomeriggio insieme.
native_language_example: We spent a nice afternoon together.

additional_notes: Used with negation (non/nessuno) for emphasis: it means “not a thing.” Often sounds a bit blunt or dismissive. Common with verbs like valere (to be worth), fare (to do), capire (to understand), dire (to tell), riuscire a (to manage to).
target_language_example: Oggi non ho fatto un bel niente.
native_language_example: Today I didn’t do a thing.

meaning: a nice place; a beautiful place.
additional_notes: Used to say a place is pleasant/attractive. "Bel" is a shortened form of "bello" used before a noun (especially before a consonant): "un bel posto", "un bel giorno". With questions like "Non è un bel posto?" it often means "Isn’t it a nice place?"
target_language_example: Questo è proprio un bel posto per rilassarsi.
native_language_example: This is really a nice place to relax.

meaning: a nice gift; a lovely present.
additional_notes: Means “a nice/lovely gift,” with bel as the shortened form of bello used before a masculine singular noun starting with most consonants (bel regalo). Often used when giving something to someone: fare/dare un bel regalo (to give someone a nice gift) or comprare un bel regalo per qualcuno (to buy a nice gift for someone).
target_language_example: Ti ho comprato un bel regalo per il tuo compleanno.
native_language_example: I bought you a nice gift for your birthday.

additional_notes: A common compliment about someone’s smile. "Bel" is the shortened form of "bello" used before a masculine singular noun ("un bel sorriso"). Often used with "avere" ("ha un bel sorriso" = "he/she has a nice smile").
target_language_example: Hai proprio un bel sorriso!
native_language_example: You have a really nice smile!

meaning: a glass (drinking glass); also “a drink” (one glassful).
additional_notes: Literally “a glass.” In everyday Italian it can mean the physical glass (e.g., break a glass, take a bigger glass) or a serving of an alcoholic drink (“bere/offrire un bicchiere” = to have/offer a drink). Often used in invitations and toasts: “Ti offro un bicchiere” (I’ll buy you a drink).
target_language_example: Vuoi un bicchiere d'acqua?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of water?

meaning: 'a glass of' (used to order drinks or specify a quantity served in a glass).
additional_notes: Common in bars/restaurants to ask for a drink served in a glass: "Un bicchiere di vino/birra/acqua, per favore." It can also be used generally to indicate a quantity of liquid in a glass. Plural: "due bicchieri di...".
target_language_example: Un bicchiere di vino, per favore.
native_language_example: A glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Common when ordering a drink or asking someone to pour you beer. In Italy you might also hear/see specific sizes or containers (es. una birra piccola/media/grande, una birra alla spina, una bottiglia di birra), but this phrase is always understood as “a glass of beer.”
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un bicchiere di birra, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a glass of beer, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single serving of milk. Often appears with verbs like bere (to drink) and versare (to pour). “Che ne dice/dite di…?” means “How about…?” when making a suggestion.
target_language_example: Vuoi un bicchiere di latte prima di andare a letto?
native_language_example: Do you want a glass of milk before going to bed?

additional_notes: Common when ordering in a bar/restaurant or describing what someone drank. Use it with polite requests like "Posso avere..." or "Vorrei...". "Un bicchiere" = "a glass" (quantity/container), "di vino" = "of wine".
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Common in cafés/restaurants when ordering a drink. “Un bicchiere di…” = “a glass of…”. You may also hear “Vorrebbe…?” as a polite way to ask what someone would like.
target_language_example: Dopo cena prendo un bicchiere di vino rosso.
native_language_example: After dinner I have a glass of red wine.

meaning: a ticket (e.g., for a train, bus, concert).
additional_notes: Used for a pass you buy to travel or enter an event/place. Often followed by “del/della + [thing]”: “un biglietto del treno” (a train ticket), “un biglietto dell’autobus” (a bus ticket). You can also specify one-way/round-trip: “un biglietto di sola andata” / “un biglietto di andata e ritorno”.
target_language_example: Vorrei un biglietto del treno per Firenze, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a train ticket to Florence, please.

un biglietto andata e ritorno per

target_language_multi_word_term: un biglietto andata e ritorno per
additional_notes: Used when buying travel tickets (train, bus, plane). Follow it with the destination: “...per Roma / per Chicago”. “Andata e ritorno” literally means “outbound and return.” You can also hear “biglietto di andata e ritorno” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Vorrei un biglietto andata e ritorno per Roma, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a round-trip ticket to Rome, please.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying, getting, reserving, or asking for a concert ticket. "Un biglietto" = "a ticket"; "per" indicates what the ticket is for (the concert). Often used with verbs like prendere (to get/buy), comprare (to buy), ottenere (to obtain), and with questions like "Mi prendi...?" (Can you get me...?).
target_language_example: Devo comprare un biglietto per il concerto di stasera.
native_language_example: I have to buy a ticket for tonight’s concert.

meaning: a pack of / a bunch of (a group of).
additional_notes: Used mainly for animals (dogs, wolves) meaning “a pack.” With people, it’s usually insulting or angry (“a bunch of idiots / murderers”), suggesting they act like a pack. The verb that follows is typically singular (e.g., “Un branco di lupi ha…”).
target_language_example: C'era un branco di ragazzi davanti alla scuola.
native_language_example: There was a bunch of kids in front of the school.

additional_notes: "Bravo" means "good" or "skilled" about a person (often their ability or role): un bravo avvocato = a good lawyer. It’s commonly placed before the noun (un bravo insegnante), especially in everyday speech, to mean “a good/nice” person in that role. Don’t confuse it with the English/Italian exclamation "Bravo!" (= “well done!”).
target_language_example: Vorrei parlare con un bravo medico.
native_language_example: I’d like to speak with a good doctor.

additional_notes: "Bravo" means "good" in the sense of capable or skilled (often about a person doing their job well). "Avvocato" is a lawyer/attorney. Often used when someone is in legal trouble or needs legal help: "avere bisogno di un bravo avvocato" = "to need a good lawyer."
target_language_example: Se vai in tribunale, ti serve un bravo avvocato.
native_language_example: If you go to court, you need a good lawyer.

meaning: a good boy / a good guy.
additional_notes: Used to describe a male (often a young man) as kind, well-behaved, and generally trustworthy. With "essere" or "sembrare": "È un bravo ragazzo" (He’s a good guy), "Sembra un bravo ragazzo" (He seems like a good guy). "Bravo" can also mean “skilled,” but in this phrase it usually means “good/nice” as a person.
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare: è un bravo ragazzo.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s a good guy.

meaning: "a bad" / "an unpleasant" (masculine singular, before a noun).
additional_notes: Used with a masculine singular noun to describe something negative (an error, feeling, pain, moment, temperament, etc.). It’s the form of the adjective "brutto" that comes before the noun: "un brutto errore", "un brutto momento", "un brutto carattere", "un brutto mal di...". With feminine nouns you’d say "una brutta..." (e.g., "una brutta giornata").
target_language_example: Oggi è stato un brutto giorno per me.
native_language_example: Today was a bad day for me.

meaning: a bad (ache/pain) in… (used before the body part).
additional_notes: This phrase is usually completed by adding the body part after it: e.g. "un brutto mal di testa" (a bad headache), "un brutto mal di stomaco" (a bad stomachache). "Mal di" literally means something like "pain of", but in English you typically translate it as "ache" or "pain" depending on context.
target_language_example: Ho un brutto mal di testa.
native_language_example: I have a bad headache.

additional_notes: Used to say you have a strong cold. Very common with: "avere" (to have) → "Ho un brutto raffreddore"; "prendere" (to catch) → "Ho preso un brutto raffreddore"; and "soffrire di" (to suffer from) → "Ha sofferto di un brutto raffreddore". "Brutto" here means "bad" in the sense of "severe," not "ugly."
target_language_example: Non vengo a lavoro oggi: ho un brutto raffreddore.
native_language_example: I’m not coming to work today: I have a bad cold.

meaning: a hole; (figurative) a gap/void; (informal) a mess/trouble; (threat) a gunshot hole.
additional_notes: Literal: a physical hole you dig or fall into ("scavare un buco", "cadere in un buco"). Figurative: a painful emptiness or absence ("un buco nel cuore"). It can also mean being in a bad situation ("trovarsi in un buco"). In threats, "ti faccio un buco in..." means “I’ll shoot you / put a bullet hole in...”, and is aggressive slang.
target_language_example: Dopo la sua partenza, ho sentito un buco dentro.
native_language_example: After he left, I felt an emptiness inside.

additional_notes: Noun used to accuse or describe someone who lies. It’s masculine; for a woman you say "una bugiarda". Often used with "sei" (you are): "Sei un bugiardo".
target_language_example: Non fidarti di lui: è un bugiardo.
native_language_example: Don’t trust him: he’s a liar.

additional_notes: Used before a singular masculine noun: un buon libro, un buon ristorante. Here buon is the shortened form of buono commonly used in this position.
target_language_example: Cerco un buon hotel in centro.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a good hotel in the city center.

additional_notes: Used in holiday wishes. Often with verbs like augurare (“to wish”) or passare (“to spend”): "Vi auguriamo un buon Natale" = “We wish you a Merry Christmas”; "Passate/Passi un buon Natale" = “Have a Merry Christmas” (plural/formal). You can also ask "Ha passato un buon Natale?" = “Did you have a good Christmas?” (formal).
target_language_example: Ti auguro un buon Natale e un felice anno nuovo.
native_language_example: I wish you a Merry Christmas and a happy new year.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "avere" (to have) to describe how someone looks (health, style, general appearance): "avere un buon aspetto" = "to look good" / "to look well." In the plural it becomes "un buon aspetto" → "un buon aspetto" stays the same if referring to one person; for multiple people you typically still say "hanno un buon aspetto" (the thing they “have” is the singular "aspetto").
target_language_example: Dopo le vacanze hai un buon aspetto!
native_language_example: You look good after the vacation!

additional_notes: Used to talk about having or needing a competent lawyer, often in legal trouble or court contexts. It’s masculine singular: un avvocato; with the adjective buon before a noun starting with a vowel: buon avvocato (instead of buono avvocato). Feminine: una buona avvocata / una buona avvocatessa (less common).
target_language_example: Se vai in tribunale, ti serve un buon avvocato.
native_language_example: If you go to court, you need a good lawyer.

additional_notes: Used when recommending or asking for a reliable dictionary. Often followed by a language with "di" (un buon dizionario di esperanto = a good Esperanto dictionary). "A portata di mano" means "within reach/handy" (keep a good dictionary handy).
target_language_example: Per iniziare a studiare italiano, ti consiglio un buon dizionario.
native_language_example: To start studying Italian, I recommend a good dictionary.

additional_notes: Uses the noun "impiego" (employment/job) with the adjective "buon" (= "buono" before a noun). Common in statements about having/looking for stable or desirable work (often implying good conditions, pay, or security). Typically used with "avere": "Ho un buon impiego" = "I have a good job."
target_language_example: Dopo la laurea, ha trovato un buon impiego in banca.
native_language_example: After graduating, he found a good job at a bank.

meaning: a good job (good work; or a good job/employment).
additional_notes: Most often means “good work” in phrases like “fare un buon lavoro” (to do a good job). With verbs like “trovare/avere/cercare un buon lavoro,” it usually means “a good job” as in good employment/position. Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Hai fatto un buon lavoro con questa presentazione.
native_language_example: You did a good job with this presentation.

additional_notes: Used when asking for a recommendation nearby. Often appears in questions with conoscere (“to know”) or consigliare (“to recommend”), especially when speaking to staff or locals. You can swap in other places: un buon hotel/un buon ristorante/un buon bar nella zona.
target_language_example: Scusi, conosce un buon motel nella zona?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you know a good motel in the area?

un buon nome per un cane

target_language_multi_word_term: un buon nome per un cane
meaning: a good name for a dog.
additional_notes: Used when suggesting or asking for a suitable dog name. Literally: “a good name for a dog.” You can change the animal or the article: “un buon nome per un gatto” (a good name for a cat). “Buon” is the shortened form of “buono” before a noun (buon nome).
target_language_example: Secondo te, "Luna" è un buon nome per un cane?
native_language_example: Do you think “Luna” is a good name for a dog?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have) or "fare" (to give off) to say something or someone smells nice: "avere un buon odore" = to smell nice; "fare un buon odore" = to have/give off a nice smell (e.g., books, food, flowers).
target_language_example: Questa crema per le mani fa un buon odore.
native_language_example: This hand cream smells nice.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone as being a good dad/father (good at being a parent). You can change the article to fit the context: “è un buon padre” (he is a good father), “sei un buon padre” (you are a good father).
target_language_example: Penso che sia un buon padre.
native_language_example: I think he is a good father.

meaning: a good seat/spot; a good place.
additional_notes: Used for a seat (e.g., at a concert, on a train) or a physical spot/location. Often with verbs like avere/trovare (“to have/find”) and with a clause like “un buon posto dove…” (“a good place to…”).
target_language_example: Abbiamo trovato un buon posto vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: We found a good spot near the window.

meaning: a good taste / a good flavor.
additional_notes: Used to say that food or drink tastes good. In everyday speech you might also hear similar phrases like "ha un buon sapore" (it has a good flavor) or "ha un buon sapore di..." (it has a nice ... flavor).
target_language_example: Questa zuppa ha un buon sapore.
native_language_example: This soup has a good taste.

additional_notes: Used for a person who tracks down and captures fugitives in exchange for a reward (a “taglia” is a bounty/reward offered for someone’s capture). Singular: “un cacciatore di taglie”; plural: “i cacciatori di taglie”.
target_language_example: Nel film, un cacciatore di taglie dà la caccia a un fuggitivo.
native_language_example: In the movie, a bounty hunter hunts down a fugitive.

additional_notes: In Italy, asking for “un caffè” in a bar usually means a single espresso. It’s also commonly used as an invitation to take a short coffee break: “Prendiamo un caffè?” = “Shall we grab a coffee?”
target_language_example: Prendiamo un caffè prima di tornare al lavoro?
native_language_example: Shall we grab a coffee before going back to work?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" = "a" (masculine singular). "Camion" is a masculine noun (il camion / i camion) and commonly refers to a (usually large) truck used for transporting goods; in accidents you’ll often see "travolto da un camion" = "run over/struck by a truck".
target_language_example: In città è difficile parcheggiare un camion.
native_language_example: In the city it’s hard to park a truck.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" is the masculine singular form of "a/an". For some masculine nouns you use "uno" instead (e.g., "uno zaino"), but with "cane" you use "un": "un cane". Plural: "dei cani" (some dogs) or "i cani" (the dogs).
target_language_example: C'è un cane davanti alla porta.
native_language_example: There’s a dog in front of the door.

additional_notes: Used to describe a man whose job or role is singing. Feminine form: una cantante (same word, with feminine article). Plural: cantanti. Often used with essere (to be): “Lui è un cantante.”
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un cantante, ma canta solo nei weekend.
native_language_example: My brother is a singer, but he only sings on weekends.

additional_notes: "Cappello" is a masculine singular noun; "un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). Plural: "dei cappelli" (some hats) or simply "cappelli" (hats). Used when shopping or describing clothing.
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare un cappello nero.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a black hat.

additional_notes: Uses the pattern "un/una + noun + da + role/use" to describe what something is for or associated with. Here, "cappello" = hat and "da cowboy" = cowboy-style/for a cowboy. Common verbs with it: "comprare" (to buy) and "indossare" (to wear).
target_language_example: Ho visto un uomo con un cappello da cowboy.
native_language_example: I saw a man with a cowboy hat.

additional_notes: Used for a military tank in war/action contexts. Plural: "carri armati". In everyday speech it can also be used figuratively for someone/something extremely strong or unstoppable (like “a tank”).
target_language_example: Non puoi fermare un carro armato con le mani.
native_language_example: You can’t stop a tank with your hands.

additional_notes: Used when a vehicle has broken down or needs to be towed away. Often with the verb chiamare (“to call”): chiamare un carro attrezzi = to call a tow truck.
target_language_example: La macchina non parte: chiamo un carro attrezzi.
native_language_example: The car won’t start: I’m calling a tow truck.

meaning: a mess; a big mess; a screw-up (trouble).
additional_notes: Very common informal expression meaning you’ve caused confusion, disorder, or trouble (often by mistake). It does NOT mean a gambling casino in these contexts. Often used with verbs like "fare" (fare un casino = make a mess), "combinare" (combinare un casino = screw things up), or "succedere" (è successo un casino = a big mess happened).
target_language_example: Scusa, ho fatto un casino con i documenti.
native_language_example: Sorry, I made a mess with the documents.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an unpleasant smell in a place or coming from something. Often with expressions like “C’è un cattivo odore” (There’s a bad smell) or “Sento un cattivo odore” (I smell something bad). Also common: “Che cattivo odore!” = “What a bad smell!”
target_language_example: C'è un cattivo odore in cucina.
native_language_example: There’s a bad smell in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine indefinite article "un" to mean "a/one" with the singular noun "cavallo" (horse). In questions it often means "Do you have a horse?"; with numbers it can be the subject (e.g., "How many teeth does a horse have?").
target_language_example: Vorrei un cavallo, ma non ho spazio.
native_language_example: I'd like a horse, but I don't have space.

meaning: a very vulgar intensifier: “fucking / damn / shitty” (before a noun).
additional_notes: Strong profanity (literally “a dick of…”), used to show anger, frustration, or emphasis: *un cazzo di X* = “a fucking/damn X.” Common in insults like *Non sai un cazzo di niente* (“You don’t know shit about anything”). Not appropriate in polite situations; avoid using it with or about people (it can be highly offensive).
target_language_example: Ho perso un cazzo di treno e ora arrivo tardi.
native_language_example: I missed a fucking train and now I’m late.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person, thing, time, or quantity that isn’t named or isn’t important to specify. Common patterns: "un certo periodo (di tempo)" = "a certain period (of time)"; "un certo numero di..." = "a certain number of... / some ...".
target_language_example: Ci vuole un certo tempo per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: It takes a certain amount of time to learn Italian.

meaning: a certain point; (often) at some point.
additional_notes: Literally “a certain point.” Very commonly used with a preposition: **a un certo punto** = “at a certain point / at some point (in a story, process, conversation, or time).” You can also see **fino a un certo punto** (“up to a point”) or **da un certo punto di vista** (“from a certain point of view”).
target_language_example: A un certo punto ho capito che dovevo andare via.
native_language_example: At some point I realized I had to leave.

meaning: a certain sense; (often in un certo senso) “in a way / to some extent”.
additional_notes: Most commonly used with the preposition **in**: **in un certo senso**. It softens what you say, meaning your statement is true only partly or from a particular point of view (similar to “in a way” or “to some extent”).
target_language_example: In un certo senso, hai ragione.
native_language_example: In a way, you’re right.

meaning: “a certain Mr. …” (a man named …, usually not well-known to the speaker).
additional_notes: Used when introducing someone by name but implying the person is unknown, only vaguely known, or being referred to with some distance (e.g., in phone messages: “There’s a Mr. Brown on the line”). It can sound neutral or slightly dismissive depending on tone/context. Often followed by a surname: “un certo signor Rossi”.
target_language_example: C'è un certo signor Rossi che chiede di parlarle.
native_language_example: There’s a certain Mr. Rossi asking to speak to you.

additional_notes: Used for a meeting where you talk with an employer about a job. Common verbs: avere un colloquio di lavoro (to have a job interview), andare a un colloquio di lavoro (to go to a job interview). Often followed by a time expression: domani, stamattina, domani pomeriggio, etc.
target_language_example: Oggi ho un colloquio di lavoro alle tre, quindi devo vestirmi bene.
native_language_example: Today I have a job interview at three, so I need to dress well.

meaning: a blow/strike; a sudden shock (also used in idioms like “to have a stroke/heart attack”).
additional_notes: Basic meaning: a hit or blow (physical impact), often with adjectives like “un colpo secco” = “a sharp/dry knock.” By extension it can mean a sudden shock or hard emotional impact: “La notizia è stata un colpo per lui” (“The news was a shock/a blow to him”). In idioms with “venire”: “Mi/ti/gli viene un colpo” = “I/you/he gets a stroke/heart attack” (often exaggerated: “Ti verrà un colpo!” = “You’ll have a heart attack!”). “Gli venga un colpo!” is a curse like “Hope he drops dead / has a stroke!” “Battere un colpo” means “to give a sign / make yourself heard” (“Anyone alive, give a sign!”).
target_language_example: Quando ho visto il conto, mi è venuto un colpo.
native_language_example: When I saw the bill, I nearly had a heart attack.

meaning: “a (sudden) bout/fit of …”, “a hit/blow of …”, or “a stroke of …” (depending on the noun).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a single sudden event or action. Very common with things like un colpo di tosse (a cough), un colpo di fortuna (a stroke of luck), un colpo di sole (sunstroke), un colpo di scena (a plot twist). The best English translation changes with the expression, and it’s not usually translated word-for-word as “a blow of”.
target_language_example: Abbiamo avuto un colpo di fortuna e abbiamo trovato un taxi subito.
native_language_example: We had a stroke of luck and found a taxi right away.

meaning: a gunshot (a shot fired from a pistol).
additional_notes: Used with verbs like sentire (to hear) or sembrare (to seem/sound like): “Ho sentito un colpo di pistola” = “I heard a gunshot.” Can also refer to the injury caused by being shot: “vittima di un colpo di pistola” = “the victim of a gunshot.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo sentito un colpo di pistola vicino al parco.
native_language_example: We heard a gunshot near the park.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like dare/fare: "dare un colpo di telefono (a qualcuno)" = to give someone a quick call. Very common in requests and suggestions (imperative or conditional), often with an indirect object pronoun: "dagli" (to him), "dalle" (to her), "dateci" (to us), etc. Similar to "fare una telefonata" but more like “just give a call.”
target_language_example: Quando arrivi, fammi un colpo di telefono.
native_language_example: When you arrive, give me a quick call.

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "un" is used for a masculine singular countable noun, meaning "a/an". Used when you mean any knife (not a specific one). For a specific knife, use "il coltello" ("the knife").
target_language_example: C'è un coltello sul tavolo.
native_language_example: There is a knife on the table.

additional_notes: Uses the masculine indefinite article "un" before the noun "computer" (a loanword). The plural is usually "i computer". Common with verbs like "usare" (to use), "comprare" (to buy), and "cercare" (to look for).
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un computer per studiare.
native_language_example: I need a computer to study.

additional_notes: Common noun phrase with the indefinite article (un) + noun (computer, masculine) + adjective (nuovo). The adjective usually comes after the noun: un computer nuovo. With plural: dei computer nuovi (some new computers).
target_language_example: Mi serve un computer nuovo per lavorare da casa.
native_language_example: I need a new computer to work from home.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a laptop. Gender: masculine (un/il). Plural: (dei/i) computer portatili. You can also just say "un portatile" in context. "Computer" is invariable in Italian (same in singular/plural), while "portatile" changes to "portatili" in the plural.
target_language_example: Ho bisogno di un computer portatile per studiare.
native_language_example: I need a laptop to study.

additional_notes: Used to name the animal (common as a pet) or to describe something that looks like a rabbit (e.g., a cloud). Masculine noun: il coniglio; plural: i conigli.
target_language_example: Abbiamo visto un coniglio nel parco.
native_language_example: We saw a rabbit in the park.

meaning: a farmer; a peasant (rural farm worker).
additional_notes: Refers to a male farmer or country person who works the land. Feminine: "una contadina". Plural: "contadini/contadine". It can be neutral (job) but in some contexts can sound old-fashioned or slightly insulting if used to mean "peasant" (e.g., "Sembri un contadino").
target_language_example: Mio nonno era un contadino e lavorava nei campi.
native_language_example: My grandfather was a farmer and worked in the fields.

additional_notes: Used to say what event/occasion the pirate costume is intended for. Structure: "un costume" (a costume) + "da pirata" (pirate-style / pirate) + "per" (for) + occasion (e.g., Halloween, una festa, carnevale).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un costume da pirata per la festa di domani.
native_language_example: I bought a pirate costume for tomorrow’s party.

additional_notes: Used to say something is (or isn’t) illegal or seriously wrong: “Non è un crimine” = “It’s not a crime.” Often followed by an adjective (e.g., “un crimine violento” = “a violent crime”) or a relative clause (“un crimine che ho commesso” = “a crime I committed”). More formal/stronger than “un reato” in everyday speech, and stronger than “una trasgressione/infrazione” (a violation).
target_language_example: Non è un crimine chiedere aiuto.
native_language_example: It’s not a crime to ask for help.

meaning: a nervous breakdown (a sudden mental/emotional collapse).
additional_notes: Used to describe someone becoming overwhelmed by stress or emotional strain to the point they can’t cope or function normally. Often appears with the verb "avere" (to have): "ha avuto un crollo nervoso". In everyday speech it can be used loosely for a strong emotional breakdown, but it can also refer to a serious mental health crisis depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo settimane di stress, ha avuto un crollo nervoso.
native_language_example: After weeks of stress, he had a nervous breakdown.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a spoon (a utensil for eating or stirring). In requests, you’ll often hear polite forms like “Mi dia un cucchiaio” (formal) or “Posso avere un cucchiaio?” (more neutral/polite). Plural: “dei cucchiai” / “due cucchiai”.
target_language_example: Per favore, mi porta un cucchiaio?
native_language_example: Could you bring me a spoon, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe a supernatural/evil creature, common in fantasy and religious contexts. It’s masculine; plural: "demoni". The feminine form is "una demone" (also sometimes "una demonessa"). Often used with "diventare" (to become): "diventare un demone".
target_language_example: Non voglio diventare un demone.
native_language_example: I don’t want to become a demon.

additional_notes: Often used with the verb "esprimere" ("to express"), especially about making a wish (e.g., when you see a shooting star). You can also use "un desiderio di + infinitive" to say you have a desire to do something: "un desiderio di cambiare lavoro" = "a desire to change jobs".
target_language_example: Ho un desiderio di viaggiare di più quest’anno.
native_language_example: I have a desire to travel more this year.

additional_notes: Used to describe something that went very badly or is in a chaotic/bad state (an event, situation, plan, relationship, your life, etc.). It can refer to real catastrophes (like an earthquake) or be an exaggeration for everyday problems. Often used with "è" / "era": "È un disastro" = "It’s a disaster."
target_language_example: Senza internet, lavorare da casa è un disastro.
native_language_example: Without internet, working from home is a disaster.

additional_notes: Used for a book (or app) that lists words and their meanings/translations. With "avere" (to have), "comprare" (to buy), or "prendere in prestito" (to borrow). In the phrase "un dizionario ambulante," it means "a walking dictionary"—a person who knows a lot of words/facts.
target_language_example: Hai un dizionario italiano-inglese?
native_language_example: Do you have an Italian-English dictionary?

additional_notes: Used to ask for or talk about a dictionary in French. Often extended as “un dizionario francese-inglese” (a French–English dictionary). In questions, it’s common with “avere” (to have) or “servire” (to need): “Avete…?” / “Lei ha…?” / “Mi serve…”.
target_language_example: Mi serve un dizionario francese-inglese, per favore.
native_language_example: I need a French–English dictionary, please.

additional_notes: Used to describe physical pain in your side/upper hip area (the “flank”), often with body verbs like avere (“to have”), sentire (“to feel”), or svegliarsi con (“to wake up with”). The usual pattern is: avere un dolore + in/nel + body part (e.g., un dolore nel fianco).
target_language_example: Da ieri ho un dolore nel fianco destro.
native_language_example: Since yesterday I’ve had a pain in my right side.

meaning: a gift; a talent (a special ability).
additional_notes: Means either a physical present (“a gift”) or an inborn/special ability (“a talent,” “a gift”). Commonly used with verbs like fare/ricevere un dono (to give/receive a gift) and avere un dono (to have a talent).
target_language_example: Lei ha un dono per le lingue.
native_language_example: She has a gift for languages.

additional_notes: Means “a doctor” in the general sense (a medical doctor). In Italian, dottore can also be used as a title for someone with a university degree, but in everyday contexts like calling for help (Chiama un dottore!) it typically means a physician. The feminine is una dottoressa.
target_language_example: Se non ti senti bene, chiama un dottore.
native_language_example: If you don’t feel well, call a doctor.

additional_notes: Common in bars and casual speech, borrowed from English. Often implies an alcoholic drink (like a cocktail), though context can vary. You may hear it with verbs like prendere/ordinare: “Prendiamo/Ordiniamo un drink?”.
target_language_example: Dopo cena andiamo a prendere un drink?
native_language_example: After dinner, shall we go have a drink?

meaning: “an elephant” (a male elephant; often used for the species in general).
additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: un (a/an) + elefante (elephant). Used when mentioning one elephant in general or introducing one for the first time. For a female elephant you can also say “un’elefante” (less common) or more clearly “un’elefantessa”.
target_language_example: Nel parco ho visto un elefante enorme.
native_language_example: In the park I saw a huge elephant.

meaning: "an ermine and a weasel" (two small mammals).
additional_notes: A literal noun phrase: un = “a” (masculine), una = “a” (feminine), e = “and”. Use it when listing or contrasting the two animals. Not a fixed idiom in standard Italian.
target_language_example: Nel bosco ho visto un ermellino e una donnola.
native_language_example: In the woods I saw an ermine and a weasel.

additional_notes: Used with the indefinite article "un" ("a") before the noun "eroe" ("hero"). Often appears with "diventare" (to become) or "rendere" (to make someone) to say someone became/was made a hero: "è diventato un eroe", "lo rese un eroe". For a female hero, say "un'eroina".
target_language_example: Dopo il salvataggio, è diventato un eroe per tutti.
native_language_example: After the rescue, he became a hero to everyone.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone seen as a hero by an entire country (often for bravery, important achievements, or historical actions). Common with verbs like "diventare" (to become) and "considerare" (to consider).
target_language_example: Dopo il suo gesto, è stato celebrato come un eroe nazionale.
native_language_example: After his action, he was celebrated as a national hero.

additional_notes: Used to refer to something wrong you did or found (a mistake/error). Often appears with verbs like fare/commettere un errore (to make an error), correggere un errore (to correct an error), and trovare/imbattersi in un errore (to come across an error). "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”).
target_language_example: Ho fatto un errore nel modulo.
native_language_example: I made a mistake on the form.

meaning: an exam; a test; (medical) an examination.
additional_notes: Usually means a school/college exam (you can pass it: *superare un esame*; or fail it: *fallire un esame*). With *del/di* + noun it often means a specific test or check, including medical/lab tests: *un esame del sangue / del DNA*.
target_language_example: Domani ho un esame di matematica.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have a math exam.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person with a lot of knowledge or skill in a field. Often followed by "di" + topic: "un esperto di arti marziali" (an expert in martial arts). In more formal contexts (e.g., court), it can mean an appointed expert/consultant: "il giudice ha chiesto a un esperto". The feminine form is "un’esperta".
target_language_example: Per questo problema informatico, serve un esperto.
native_language_example: For this computer problem, we need an expert.

additional_notes: Common, neutral way to refer to a person as a member of the human species (often used in comparisons with animals, aliens/robots, or in general statements). Plural: "esseri umani". You can also say "un umano", but "un essere umano" is more common/formal-sounding.
target_language_example: Non sono un robot: sono un essere umano.
native_language_example: I'm not a robot: I'm a human being.

meaning: a ghost; (figuratively) someone who looks very pale/ghost-like.
additional_notes: Means a ghost in the literal sense (a spirit). It can also be used jokingly/figuratively when someone looks very pale or blurry in a photo: "Sembri un fantasma" / "Pare un fantasma".
target_language_example: In quella foto sembro un fantasma!
native_language_example: In that photo I look like a ghost!

additional_notes: Used when asking someone to do something for you (often with verbs like fare: "fammi/facci un favore" = "do me a favor") or when talking about helping someone ("farti un favore" = "do you a favor"). You can also say "chiedere un favore" = "to ask for a favor".
target_language_example: Mi fai un favore e mi mandi questo file?
native_language_example: Can you do me a favor and send me this file?

additional_notes: "Figlio" usually means "son". It can also mean "child" in the sense of someone’s offspring, especially when the gender is known or when contrasting with "figlia" (daughter). Plural: "figli" = children/sons (mixed group can be "figli").
target_language_example: Mio padre ha un figlio e una figlia.
native_language_example: My father has a son and a daughter.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Film" is commonly used in Italian (often invariable: un film, due film). You’ll hear it with verbs like "fare" (to make) and "girare" (to shoot/film) when talking about making or shooting a movie.
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo un film a casa?
native_language_example: Shall we watch a movie at home tonight?

additional_notes: Refers to one single flower. Often used with verbs like dare (to give) or mettere (to put/wear), e.g., giving someone a flower or wearing one in your hair. Plural: i fiori (the flowers), dei fiori (some flowers).
target_language_example: Ho comprato un fiore per la mia amica.
native_language_example: I bought a flower for my friend.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a single piece/sheet of paper (e.g., to write something down). In requests you’ll often see it with polite forms like per favore/per piacere, or formal commands like Prenda… / Portatemi….
target_language_example: Mi serve un foglio di carta per prendere appunti.
native_language_example: I need a sheet of paper to take notes.

additional_notes: Refers to the kitchen appliance used to heat food quickly. Often used with the verb "usare" (to use) or "utilizzare" (more formal: to use). You may also hear the shorter form "un microonde" in everyday speech.
target_language_example: Sai usare un forno a microonde?
native_language_example: Do you know how to use a microwave?

additional_notes: Masculine noun: (il) fucile. With the indefinite article it’s “un fucile” = “a rifle.” Often used in contexts like hunting or being in the woods (e.g., “nel bosco”). Common related phrase: “fucile da caccia” = “hunting rifle.”
target_language_example: Non ho un fucile, quindi non posso andare a caccia.
native_language_example: I don’t have a rifle, so I can’t go hunting.

additional_notes: Means “a (male) cat.” With “un” it’s an indefinite noun phrase (“a cat”). For a female cat you can say “una gatta.”
target_language_example: Vorrei un gatto, ma il mio coinquilino preferisce un cane.
native_language_example: I’d like a cat, but my roommate prefers a dog.

un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato

target_language_multi_word_term: un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato
meaning: a lost cat that was being searched for.
additional_notes: "Gatto smarrito" means “lost cat.” "Che stava venendo cercato" is a passive form meaning “that was being looked for / searched for,” often followed by "da" + the person searching (e.g., "dalla sua padrona" = “by its owner,” female). You may also hear the simpler active form: "un gatto smarrito che cercavano" (“a lost cat they were looking for”).
target_language_example: Ho visto un gatto smarrito che stava venendo cercato dai vicini.
native_language_example: I saw a lost cat that the neighbors were searching for.

meaning: a genius (a very intelligent or exceptionally talented person).
additional_notes: Used with the verb essere (“to be”) or with verbs like considerare (“to consider”) to describe someone as extremely smart or brilliant. It can be sincere praise, and in some contexts it can also be said sarcastically (tone-dependent). Plural: un genio → dei geni.
target_language_example: Sei un genio: hai risolto tutto in cinque minuti!
native_language_example: You're a genius: you solved everything in five minutes!

meaning: “a (male) player of …” / “a … player” (a person who plays a sport).
additional_notes: Use before a sport to say someone plays it: un giocatore di rugby/tennis/football. It agrees with gender and number: una giocatrice di (female), un giocatore (male), dei giocatori (plural). You’ll also hear “gioco a …” (“I play …”) as a verb alternative.
target_language_example: Mio fratello è un giocatore di basket.
native_language_example: My brother is a basketball player.

meaning: a game; (figuratively) something not serious / a risky “game”.
additional_notes: Used literally for games (board games, sports, etc.): "Facciamo un gioco" = “Let’s play a game.” It can also be figurative: "È solamente un gioco" can mean “It’s just a game” (don’t take it too seriously). With an adjective it can describe the nature of what someone is doing, e.g. "un gioco pericoloso" = “a dangerous game.”
target_language_example: Dai, è solo un gioco: non te la prendere.
native_language_example: Come on, it’s just a game—don’t take it personally.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a day” as a unit of time (often with durations like “per un giorno” = “for a day” or “fra un giorno o due” = “in a day or two”). It can also mean “one day / someday” when talking about an unspecified time in the future (e.g., “un giorno lo farò” = “I’ll do it someday”).
target_language_example: Un giorno andremo a Roma insieme.
native_language_example: One day we'll go to Rome together.

meaning: a walk/quick trip around; a round.
additional_notes: Common with fare: fare un giro = to go for a walk, to go for a spin/quick tour, or to go out and come back later. In an imperative, “Fai un giro!” often means “Go away for a bit / Take a walk,” sometimes in an annoyed tone. Can also mean a ‘round’ (e.g., a round of drinks) depending on context.
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo un giro in centro.
native_language_example: After dinner, let's take a walk around downtown.

meaning: "a great / big" (used before a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Gran” is a shortened form of “grande” used before a noun (typically masculine singular): un gran lavoro, un gran caos, un gran numero. It often expresses emphasis (“really great / really big”), and you’ll also see it in phrases like “un gran bel …” (e.g., un gran bel giorno).
target_language_example: È stato un gran successo.
native_language_example: It was a great success.

additional_notes: Before a noun, grande can mean 'great' or 'big' depending on context: un grande uomo = 'a great man', un grande errore = 'a big/serious mistake'. Used by itself about a person, especially after essere (Sei un grande!), it is a colloquial compliment meaning 'you're great' or 'you're awesome'.
target_language_example: Per avermi aiutato così, sei un grande.
native_language_example: For helping me like that, you're awesome.

additional_notes: Used to say that something is important or difficult to deal with. Often appears with verbs like essere (Questo è un grande problema) and causare (ha causato un grande problema). You can change the adjective for emphasis: un enorme problema (a huge problem), un grosso problema (a big problem).
target_language_example: Se perdi il passaporto, è un grande problema.
native_language_example: If you lose your passport, it’s a big problem.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that a mistake has important consequences. Common with verbs like "fare" (to make) and "commettere" (to commit): "fare/commettere un grave errore".
target_language_example: Se firmi senza leggere, è un grave errore.
native_language_example: If you sign without reading, it’s a serious mistake.

additional_notes: "Grosso" is an adjective meaning "big/large". With "un" it often works like "a big one" or "a big [noun]" (e.g., un grosso pesce = a big fish). It can also mean "major/serious" with abstract nouns like "errore" (mistake) or "favore" (favor). Agreement: un grosso (masc. sing.); una grossa (fem. sing.); dei grossi / delle grosse (plural).
target_language_example: Mi serve un grosso aiuto per traslocare domani.
native_language_example: I need a big help to move tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to talk about several people or things seen as a unit (friends, coworkers, a theater/music group, etc.). Often followed by “di” to specify what it’s a group of: “un gruppo di studenti”. Plural: “gruppi”. Contrast with “una folla” = a crowd.
target_language_example: Siamo un gruppo di amici e andiamo al cinema insieme.
native_language_example: We’re a group of friends and we go to the cinema together.

meaning: "a group of" (a number of people or things together).
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to indicate multiple people/things seen or considered as one set: un gruppo di studenti/bambini/soldati. Very common in everyday descriptions. It agrees in number/gender with the verb as a singular unit (e.g., Un gruppo di bambini stava giocando).
target_language_example: C'era un gruppo di turisti davanti al museo.
native_language_example: There was a group of tourists in front of the museum.

additional_notes: "Un" is the masculine singular indefinite article (“a/an”). "Hamburger" is a common loanword in Italian; the plural is usually "hamburger" (invariable): "due hamburger".
target_language_example: Vorrei un hamburger, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a hamburger, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or ask for a hot dog (the food). In Italian it’s a masculine noun, so you’ll often see it with articles like un (a) or il (the): un hot dog, il hot dog. Plural is usually hot dog (unchanged) or sometimes hot dogs.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere un hot dog, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a hot dog, please?

additional_notes: Masculine noun. Use the indefinite article “un” (because it starts with a vowel sound): “un hotel”. Often interchangeable with “un albergo” (more traditionally Italian). Plural is usually invariable in writing: “due hotel”.
target_language_example: Cerco un hotel economico vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a cheap hotel near the station.

additional_notes: An insult meaning a very stupid or annoying person, or a self-criticism meaning “I feel like such a fool.” Uses the masculine article un; for a woman you often hear una idiota (many speakers keep idiota the same form).
target_language_example: Ho dimenticato le chiavi: sono proprio un idiota.
native_language_example: I forgot my keys: I’m such an idiot.

additional_notes: Used for a job or work position, often in a fairly general or formal way. You’ll also hear it in phrases like “trovare un impiego” (to find a job) and “un impiego migliore” (a better job). Similar in meaning to “un lavoro,” but “impiego” can sound a bit more like “employment/position.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando un impiego a tempo pieno.
