additional_notes: Used to refer to one full bottle of champagne. Common after verbs like portare (to bring), comprare (to buy), bere (to drink), or aprire (to open). Note the structure: una bottiglia di + drink (e.g., una bottiglia di vino, una bottiglia d’acqua).
target_language_example: Per festeggiare, abbiamo aperto una bottiglia di champagne.
native_language_example: To celebrate, we opened a bottle of champagne.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying, bringing, giving, or drinking a single bottle of wine. "Una" = "a/one" (feminine), "bottiglia" = "bottle" (feminine), "di" = "of", "vino" = "wine".
target_language_example: Per cena porto una bottiglia di vino.
native_language_example: For dinner I’m bringing a bottle of wine.

additional_notes: Used with a feminine singular noun (e.g., una brava madre, una brava insegnante, una brava chitarrista) to say someone is good at something or a good person in that role. It agrees in gender/number: un bravo (male), una brava (female), dei bravi / delle brave (plural). Note: it can look like English “brave,” but it usually means “good/capable,” not “brave” (coraggiosa).
target_language_example: Giulia è una brava cuoca.
native_language_example: Giulia is a good cook.

additional_notes: Used to compliment a woman’s cooking skills. Both words agree with a feminine noun: una (fem. singular) + brava (fem. singular of bravo/a) + cuoca (female cook). Note: brava usually means “good/skilled” here (not “brave”). For a man: un bravo cuoco.
target_language_example: Mia nonna è una brava cuoca.
native_language_example: My grandma is a good cook.

additional_notes: Used to describe a woman as a good/caring mother. Often used as praise ("Sei una brava madre") or in self-judgment ("Non sarò mai una brava madre"). Grammar: feminine singular—brava agrees with madre. For a man you’d say "un bravo padre" (a good father). Note: "brava" can look like English "brave," but here it usually means "good" (kind, capable, doing the right thing) rather than "courageous."
target_language_example: Secondo me, sei una brava madre e stai facendo del tuo meglio.
native_language_example: In my opinion, you’re a good mother and you’re doing your best.

meaning: a good person; a decent/nice person.
additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character or morals in a general way. "Bravo/brava" agrees with the person (una brava persona, un bravo ragazzo). You can negate it (Non è una brava persona) or use it with verbs like essere (to be) and fingere (to pretend).
target_language_example: Secondo me, è una brava persona e ti vuole aiutare.
native_language_example: In my opinion, he’s a good person and he wants to help you.

meaning: a good girl (well-behaved / nice young woman).
additional_notes: "Brava" agrees with the feminine noun "ragazza". It’s a common, everyday compliment meaning someone is kind, decent, or well-behaved; depending on context it can also sound a bit moralizing/patronizing (especially said to an adult). For a male: "un bravo ragazzo".
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è una brava ragazza, puoi fidarti di lei.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: she’s a good girl, you can trust her.

additional_notes: Literally “a bad (female) one.” Often used before a feminine noun (una brutta notizia = “bad news”, una brutta giornata = “a bad day”, una brutta sensazione = “a bad feeling”). In speech it can also stand on its own with the noun understood from context: Che brutta! / È una brutta. = “How awful!” / “It’s a bad thing/situation.”
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma è una brutta: il treno è stato cancellato.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but it’s bad news: the train has been canceled.

meaning: a banana peel; (figuratively) a trap or something that can make you slip up.
additional_notes: Literally means “a peel of banana.” In everyday speech it most often refers to the actual banana peel on the ground. Figuratively, it can mean an easy mistake, a hidden obstacle, or a situation designed to trip someone up (similar to “a banana skin”/“a trap”).
target_language_example: Attento: c’è una buccia di banana per terra!
native_language_example: Careful: there’s a banana peel on the ground!

additional_notes: Feminine noun: una bugia (sing.), le bugie (pl.). Common with verbs like dire una bugia (to tell a lie) and raccontare una bugia (to tell/make up a lie). You can also use it after "è" to say something is a lie: È una bugia.
target_language_example: Non dire una bugia: dimmi la verità.
native_language_example: Don’t tell a lie: tell me the truth.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form of “a good”. It agrees with a feminine noun (expressed or understood). Often used with a noun (e.g., “una buona domanda” = “a good question”), but it can also stand alone to mean “a good one” when the feminine noun is implied (e.g., ordering/choosing something feminine). Common collocation: “dare una buona occhiata” = “to take a good look.”
target_language_example: Ne vuoi una buona o una economica?
native_language_example: Do you want a good one or a cheap one?

meaning: "have a good summer" / "a good summer" (a summer greeting/wish).
additional_notes: Used as a seasonal wish, especially when people won’t see each other for a while (e.g., before the summer holidays). Often said as: "Ti auguro una buona estate" (I wish you a good summer) or "Buona estate!" (Have a good summer!). Note: Italian "estate" means "summer" and is a false friend with English "estate".
target_language_example: Ci vediamo a settembre—ti auguro una buona estate!
native_language_example: See you in September—have a good summer!

additional_notes: Used to describe that the day went well, or as a wish/goodbye meaning “Have a good day.” Often with verbs like "passare" (to spend) or "avere" (to have): "passare/avere una buona giornata". It can be made plural: "Passate una buona giornata" (to more than one person), or adjusted for different levels of formality with "Lei": "Passi una buona giornata".
target_language_example: Spero che tu abbia una buona giornata!
native_language_example: I hope you have a good day!

additional_notes: Used to say that something is a sensible or smart plan/suggestion. Often appears with verbs like "essere" (È/è stata una buona idea), "sembrare" (sembra una buona idea), and in opinions like "Non credo che sia una buona idea". It can also describe a general choice: "I fiori sono sempre una buona idea" (Flowers are always a good idea).
target_language_example: Portare un ombrello oggi è una buona idea.
native_language_example: Bringing an umbrella today is a good idea.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere una buona memoria" = to be good at remembering things (names, facts, dates, etc.). It can also be used more figuratively, e.g., "è la sua arma" (“it’s his/her weapon/strength”).
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha una buona memoria per i nomi.
native_language_example: My sister has a good memory for names.

meaning: a good opinion of; to think well of.
additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" (to have): "avere una buona opinione di qualcuno" = to have a positive view of someone / to respect them. The "di" is followed by a person or thing (di lui/lei/me/te, di Marco, di questo ristorante).
target_language_example: Ho una buona opinione di questo ristorante.
native_language_example: I have a good opinion of this restaurant.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one (unspecified) song. You’ll often see it after verbs like scrivere (to write), cantare (to sing), and suonare (to play an instrument): scrivere/cantare/suonare una canzone. For a specific song, use la canzone (“the song”).
target_language_example: Puoi cantarmi una canzone?
native_language_example: Can you sing me a song?

additional_notes: Used when talking about paying in shops, restaurants, hotels, or online. Often used with verbs like usare (to use), avere (to have), and pagare (to pay). In questions, you’ll often hear: “Posso usare una carta di credito?” (Can I use a credit card?).
target_language_example: Accettate una carta di credito?
native_language_example: Do you accept a credit card?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: una is used with feminine singular nouns like casa. It can mean either the physical building (“a house”) or the idea of having somewhere to live (“a home”), depending on context.
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una casa vicino al centro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a house near downtown.

meaning: "a big house and two …" (often: “a big house and two cars”).
additional_notes: This is the start of a quantity/list pattern: “una/uno + noun + adjective + e + number + (plural noun)”. In normal Italian you usually include what “due” refers to (e.g., “due auto / due macchine”). The examples show it as “una casa grande e due auto/macchine” = “a big house and two cars.”
target_language_example: Ha una casa grande e due auto.
native_language_example: He has a big house and two cars.

additional_notes: Used when buying or carrying beer in a packaged quantity (a box/crate containing multiple bottles or cans). In shops you might also hear "una cassa di bottiglie" (a crate of bottles).
target_language_example: Per la festa prendiamo una cassa di birra e del ghiaccio.
native_language_example: For the party, let's get a case of beer and some ice.

additional_notes: Used to say that a plan, choice, or action is not wise or will likely have negative consequences. Very common with "è/era/fu" (it is/was) and "stata" (has been/was, feminine to match "idea"): "È stata una cattiva idea" = “It was a bad idea.”
target_language_example: Andare senza prenotazione è una cattiva idea.
native_language_example: Going without a reservation is a bad idea.

additional_notes: Used for a telephone call in general. Common with verbs like fare (to make) and ricevere (to receive): fare una chiamata, ricevere una chiamata. You’ll also hear it in set phrases like chiamata persa (“missed call”) and una chiamata urgente (“an urgent call”).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo rispondere: ho una chiamata importante.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to answer: I have an important call.

additional_notes: Used to say who is calling (often in phone notifications or when reporting you received a call): “Ho ricevuto una chiamata da …”. You can also hear “una telefonata da …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una chiamata da Laura ieri sera.
native_language_example: I got a call from Laura last night.

additional_notes: Used for a physical key (house, room, car). Common with verbs like: avere/bisognare di (to have/need), prendere (to take), dare (to give), servire (to be needed). Example: "Le servirà una chiave" = "You will need a key" (formal "you").
target_language_example: Mi serve una chiave per questa porta.
native_language_example: I need a key for this door.

additional_notes: Used when talking about an extra key kept for emergencies (at home, for a car, etc.). Often asked as a yes/no question: "Hai/Avete una chiave di riserva?" You can add where it is: "Ho una chiave di riserva sotto lo zerbino" (under the doormat).
target_language_example: Scusa, hai una chiave di riserva per l'appartamento?
native_language_example: Sorry, do you have a spare key for the apartment?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: "una" = "a/an" for feminine singular nouns, and "città" (city) is feminine. Used when talking about any (not specific) city: "vivere in una città" = "to live in a city." For a specific city, you’ll often use "la città" (the city) or the city name (e.g., "Roma").
target_language_example: Mi piacerebbe vivere in una città vicino al mare.
native_language_example: I’d like to live in a city near the sea.

meaning: a coincidence; something that happens by chance.
additional_notes: Used to say that two events (or meeting someone) is accidental and not planned. Very common with phrases like “È solo una coincidenza” (It’s just a coincidence) and in the negative “Non è una coincidenza” / “Non è una coincidenza che…” to suggest it’s NOT by chance (there’s a reason behind it).
target_language_example: Incontrarti qui non è una coincidenza.
native_language_example: Meeting you here is not a coincidence.

additional_notes: Used for a duplicate of a document, photo, file, etc. Common with verbs like fare (to make) or avere (to have): fare una copia = to make a copy.
target_language_example: Puoi fare una copia di questo documento, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you make a copy of this document, please?

una copia dei miei piani appena

target_language_multi_word_term: una copia dei miei piani appena
meaning: a copy of my plans; “appena” = “just/only” or “as soon as”.
additional_notes: “Una copia” = “a copy”. “Dei miei piani” means “of my plans” (dei = di + i). “Piani” usually means “plans” (it can also mean “floors/levels” in other contexts). “Appena” is incomplete on its own here: it can mean “just” (time: “just now”), “barely/hardly”, or it’s commonly used in phrases like “appena possibile” = “as soon as possible”.
target_language_example: Vorrei una copia dei miei piani appena possibile.
native_language_example: I’d like a copy of my plans as soon as possible.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a single copy of something masculine singular: una copia del documento (= a copy of the document). It’s the contraction of “di + il” → “del.” For feminine singular, use “una copia della …”; for plural, “una copia dei/delle …”.
target_language_example: Potrei avere una copia del biglietto, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a copy of the ticket, please?

meaning: a couple (two people together, often romantically).
additional_notes: Used for two people seen as a pair, especially partners in a relationship (dating, engaged, married). It can also mean “a pair/two of something” in other contexts (e.g., una coppia di scarpe = a pair of shoes), and you often see it with “di” + noun (una coppia di fidanzati = a couple of fiancés).
target_language_example: Siamo una coppia da cinque anni.
native_language_example: We’ve been a couple for five years.

additional_notes: Literally 'a thing'. Used for an unspecified object, fact, idea, or matter. In everyday Italian it often translates naturally as 'something', especially in phrases like dire una cosa ('say something') or sapere una cosa ('know one thing / know something').
target_language_example: Devo dirti una cosa importante.
native_language_example: I have to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause describing a thing or idea (like English “something/a thing that …”). Often appears in negative statements (“Non è una cosa che…”) to mean “That’s not something we do/that people like.” It can also be used to highlight one specific aspect: “Una cosa che odio…” = “One thing I hate…”.
target_language_example: C’è una cosa che devo dirti prima di partire.
native_language_example: There’s something I have to tell you before I leave.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an action or event described (or obvious) in context, often with an adjective: "una cosa così crudele" = "such a cruel thing". It commonly appears with negatives or doubts ("non farei una cosa così...") to express that something is hard to imagine or unacceptable.
target_language_example: Non direi mai una cosa così cattiva.
native_language_example: I would never say such a mean thing.

additional_notes: Used to refer to an unspecified thing or event of that kind, often with surprise, disbelief, or disapproval. Common in questions and negative statements: Hai mai visto una cosa del genere? (Have you ever seen something like that?), Non ho una cosa del genere (I don’t have anything like that).
target_language_example: Non dire una cosa del genere!
native_language_example: Don’t say something like that!

additional_notes: Used to introduce or refer to a significant fact, event, or point. Common in phrases like “Ho una cosa importante da…” (I have something important to…) and “È successa una cosa importante” (Something important happened).
target_language_example: Prima di andare via, devo dirti una cosa importante.
native_language_example: Before leaving, I have to tell you something important.

additional_notes: Used to stress that something is important, real, or should be taken seriously (not a joke or not casual). Common with verbs like essere/ diventare (“to be/become”) and sembrare (“to seem”): È una cosa seria. / Non sembra una cosa seria. Often refers to situations like a problem, an illness, a commitment, or a relationship becoming “serious.”
target_language_example: Dobbiamo parlarne: è una cosa seria.
native_language_example: We need to talk about it: it’s serious.

meaning: “such a thing” / “something like that” (often: something shocking or unacceptable).
additional_notes: Literally “a similar thing.” Very common after verbs like dire (to say), pensare (to think), fare (to do), succedere (to happen). Often used in questions or exclamations to show disbelief or disapproval: “How can you say/think/do such a thing?”
target_language_example: Non riesco a credere che abbia fatto una cosa simile.
native_language_example: I can’t believe he/she did such a thing.

additional_notes: Used to say that something very bad has happened or will happen. Common with verbs like succedere (“to happen”) or accadere (“to happen”): È successa una cosa terribile! You can also use it as a general judgment: È una cosa terribile (“It’s a terrible thing”).
target_language_example: Ieri è successa una cosa terribile al lavoro.
native_language_example: Yesterday something terrible happened at work.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere": "avere una cotta per qualcuno" = to have a crush on someone (often a light, sometimes short-term romantic interest). You can also say "Mi sono preso/a una cotta per..." (I got a crush on...).
target_language_example: Ho una cotta per una ragazza della mia classe.
native_language_example: I have a crush on a girl in my class.

additional_notes: In Italian, **avere una cotta per** means “to have a crush on / to be infatuated with.” Here **la sua** (“his/her”) is a possessive that normally needs a noun after it (e.g., *la sua collega*, *la sua amica*, *la sua sorella*). Without the noun, the phrase sounds incomplete unless it’s clearly understood from context.
target_language_example: Ho una cotta per la sua collega.
native_language_example: I have a crush on his/her colleague.

additional_notes: “Avere una cotta per (qualcuno)” means to have a romantic crush (often secret or not serious yet). “Lei” can mean “her” or the formal “you” (to a woman), depending on context. You can swap the person: “una cotta per lui / per te / per Maria”.
target_language_example: Credo che Marco abbia una cotta per lei.
native_language_example: I think Marco has a crush on her.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re romantically interested in a boy/man, often in a light or not-too-serious way. You can change the pronoun: una cotta per lei (on her), una cotta per te (on you). Common with the verbs avere (to have) and essere (to be): Hai una cotta per lui? / Ho una cotta per lui. / È una cotta per lui (less common than avere).
target_language_example: Credo che Giulia abbia una cotta per lui.
native_language_example: I think Giulia has a crush on him.

additional_notes: A feminine noun: (una) cravatta. Used with clothing verbs like indossare (“to wear”) and with colors/adjectives: una cravatta gialla, una cravatta nuova. Often refers to a necktie worn with a shirt, especially for work or formal situations.
target_language_example: Devo mettere una cravatta per la riunione.
native_language_example: I have to wear a tie for the meeting.

additional_notes: Means a choice you make after thinking about options. Often used with the verb "prendere" (to make/take): "prendere una decisione" = "to make a decision". You may also see it in passive form: "Deve essere presa una decisione" = "A decision must be made."
target_language_example: È una decisione difficile, ma dobbiamo prenderla oggi.
native_language_example: It’s a difficult decision, but we have to make it today.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to do/take”): fare una doccia = “to take a shower.” With reflexive forms (farsi una doccia), it means the same and emphasizes that the subject takes the shower themself: Mi faccio una doccia / Si è fatto una doccia. Often used with time expressions like ogni giorno (“every day”).
target_language_example: Dopo la palestra, faccio una doccia veloce.
native_language_example: After the gym, I take a quick shower.

additional_notes: Means “a question.” Very common with verbs like: **fare una domanda** / **porre una domanda** = “to ask a question.” You can also say **avere una domanda** = “to have a question” (e.g., *Ho una domanda*). In sentence 3 (*Mi chiese una domanda*), beginners more often say **Mi fece una domanda** or **Mi chiese** + the question.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso fare una domanda?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I ask a question?

additional_notes: Means “a woman” (indefinite: one/any woman). Often used to introduce someone new or describe an unknown/unspecified woman. Compare: “la donna” = “the woman”. “Donna” can also mean “lady” depending on context.
target_language_example: In treno ho parlato con una donna molto simpatica.
native_language_example: On the train I talked to a very nice woman.

meaning: an elderly woman; an old woman.
additional_notes: “Donna” means “woman” and “anziana” means “elderly/old.” It’s a neutral, common description; “anziana” is often more polite than “vecchia” (“old,” which can sound rude when talking about people). Agreement: una donna anziana (feminine singular); un uomo anziano (masculine singular); donne anziane (feminine plural); uomini anziani (masculine plural).
target_language_example: Ho aiutato una donna anziana a salire sull’autobus.
native_language_example: I helped an elderly woman get on the bus.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a quantity of 12 items. It’s followed by a plural noun: “una dozzina di uova/matite/banane”. In everyday speech it can also mean “about twelve” (roughly a dozen).
target_language_example: Prendiamo una dozzina di uova, per favore.
native_language_example: We’ll take a dozen eggs, please.

additional_notes: Used when shopping or talking about quantities. "Una dozzina" means "a dozen" (12) and is followed by "di" + the item (often plural): "una dozzina di uova", "una dozzina di biscotti". You can also say "una dozzina d’uova" (di + uova).
target_language_example: Scusi, mi dà una dozzina di uova, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a dozen eggs, please?

additional_notes: Indefinite article + noun: used to talk about “a/one family” in general or an unspecified family. For a specific one, you’d typically use “la famiglia” (“the family”).
target_language_example: Ha una famiglia numerosa.
native_language_example: He/She has a big family.

meaning: a family to take care of; family responsibilities.
additional_notes: Used to say someone has responsibilities toward their family (supporting them, providing for them, looking after them). The structure “a cui + verb” means “to whom/which + verb,” so literally it’s “a family to think about,” but the natural sense is “a family to look after.” Often used to remind someone to be careful or responsible.
target_language_example: Non posso trasferirmi all'estero: ho una famiglia a cui pensare.
native_language_example: I can’t move abroad: I have a family to take care of.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has many people in their family, often implying many children or siblings. You can change the article depending on context (e.g., "ho una famiglia numerosa" = I have a big family; "vengo da una famiglia numerosa" = I come from a big family).
target_language_example: Vengo da una famiglia numerosa: siamo in sette.
native_language_example: I come from a big family: there are seven of us.

additional_notes: Means “a party” (a social event). Often followed by “di + event/holiday” (una festa di Halloween = a Halloween party) or “a casa di…” / “a casa sua” (una festa a casa sua = a party at his/her place).
target_language_example: Stasera c'è una festa a casa mia.
native_language_example: Tonight there's a party at my place.

additional_notes: Used to say what kind of party it is or what it’s for: una festa di Halloween (a Halloween party), una festa di addio (a farewell/goodbye party), una festa di strada (a street party). The “di” links the party to its theme/purpose.
target_language_example: Domani facciamo una festa di compleanno per mia sorella.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re having a birthday party for my sister.

additional_notes: Used to talk about an event that happened in the previous week. "La settimana scorsa" means "last week" and usually goes at the end of the sentence, but it can also go near the beginning for emphasis. Note: "festa" often means "party/celebration" (not necessarily a big "festival").
target_language_example: Ho fatto una festa la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: I had a party last week.

meaning: “a slice of” (a thin, flat piece of food).
additional_notes: Used with foods you can cut into slices (cake, pie, cheese, ham, bread, etc.). It’s feminine: una fetta. In a café/restaurant you can order with “Vorrei/mi porti una fetta di …”
target_language_example: Mi dà una fetta di torta al cioccolato, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me a slice of chocolate cake, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one single slice of bread (often from a loaf). With amounts, you may also see: "due fette di pane" (two slices). Often appears with food verbs like mangiare (to eat), tagliare (to cut), and spalmare ... su (to spread ... on).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo una fetta di pane con marmellata.
native_language_example: For breakfast I have a slice of bread with jam.

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering pizza by the slice. "Una fetta" means "a slice" (a portion cut from a larger pizza). Common with verbs like "mangiare" (to eat), "passare" (to pass/hand), and "servirsi" (to serve oneself/take).
target_language_example: Possiamo prendere una fetta di pizza ciascuno?
native_language_example: Can we each get a slice of pizza?

additional_notes: Used when offering, ordering, or talking about eating cake. The key structure is “una fetta di + [food]” = “a slice of + [food]” (e.g., una fetta di pizza, una fetta di pane). “Torta” is a general word for cake (often a whole cake, but here it’s the cake you’re slicing).
target_language_example: Per dessert, prendo una fetta di torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For dessert, I’ll have a slice of chocolate cake.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a (female) child. You’ll often see it after the verb avere (to have): Ho una figlia. It can be followed by details with che (who/that) or called/named: una figlia che si chiama…, una figlia chiamata…. Article changes with context (e.g., mia figlia = my daughter; due figlie = two daughters).
target_language_example: Ho una figlia di otto anni.
native_language_example: I have an eight-year-old daughter.

meaning: (1) good luck; a lucky thing. (2) a fortune (a very large amount of money).
additional_notes: Common with essere: "È una fortuna" = "It’s lucky / it’s a good thing." Also used with costare: "costa una fortuna" = "it costs a fortune" (very expensive). Context makes the meaning clear: luck/fortunate situation vs. lots of money.
target_language_example: È una fortuna che tu sia arrivato in tempo.
native_language_example: It’s lucky that you arrived on time.

additional_notes: Common in everyday speech. Often used with verbs like fare una foto (take a photo), scattare una foto (snap/take a photo), and farsi fare una foto (have someone take a photo of you). You can specify the subject with di (una foto di Roma = a photo of Rome) or the person/thing being photographed with a (ha scattato una foto alla mia casa = he took a photo of my house).
target_language_example: Mi fai una foto, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you take a photo of me, please?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the subject of a photo (the person/thing shown). Often followed by a noun or a possessive phrase: “una foto di mia nonna”, “una foto di sua madre”.
target_language_example: Hai una foto di tuo fratello sul telefono?
native_language_example: Do you have a photo of your brother on your phone?

additional_notes: Use "una" because "fotografia" is feminine. "di" means "of" here, showing who is in the photo. "mia nonna" means "my grandmother/grandma" ("mia" agrees with the feminine noun "nonna"). Often used with "solo/solamente/soltanto" to mean you have only one photo.
target_language_example: Vorrei incorniciare una fotografia di mia nonna.
native_language_example: I'd like to frame a photo of my grandma.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a sentence” in everyday Italian (a complete unit with a subject/verb), especially in learning contexts: *capire una frase*, *leggere una frase*. It can also mean “a phrase/wording” (how something is expressed), often with qualifiers like *una frase del genere* (“a phrase/sentence like that”).
target_language_example: Puoi ripetere una frase, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you repeat a sentence, please?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one (unspecified) leg, often in accidents/injuries: "rompersi una gamba" = "to break a leg". With "a" after a verb (e.g., "sparare a una gamba"), it means "shoot (someone) in the leg". If you mean a specific leg, use the article: "la gamba" (the leg).
target_language_example: Mi sono fatto male a una gamba giocando a calcio.
native_language_example: I hurt one of my legs playing soccer.

meaning: a day (often emphasizing what the day was like or how it was spent).
additional_notes: Common with adjectives to describe the day (una giornata bella/calda/fredda/orribile/speciale). Also used in phrases like “prendere una giornata libera” = to take a day off. Can refer to a specific day (e.g., Monday) or a day in general.
target_language_example: Domani sarà una giornata lunga, quindi vado a dormire presto.
native_language_example: Tomorrow will be a long day, so I’m going to bed early.

meaning: "a great / big" (emphatic form of *una grande* before a noun/adjective).
additional_notes: *Gran* is a shortened form of *grande* used before another word to add emphasis (similar to “a really great/big…”). It’s common in fixed patterns like **una gran bella casa** (“a really beautiful house”) or **una gran cosa** (“a great thing”). For masculine you’ll see **un gran** (e.g., *un gran problema*).
target_language_example: È stata una gran sorpresa!
native_language_example: It was a big (great) surprise!

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (e.g., una grande famiglia = “a big family”). "grande" can describe physical size (big/large) or importance/quality (great). It agrees with the noun: un grande (masc. sing.), una grande (fem. sing.), grandi (plural).
target_language_example: Ho avuto una grande idea per il progetto.
native_language_example: I had a great idea for the project.

additional_notes: Literally “a great city,” but in everyday Italian it usually means “a big/large city” (size). Use with the indefinite article una (“a”). For “a great city” in the sense of “wonderful,” you might also hear una città bellissima / una città fantastica.
target_language_example: Mi piace vivere in una grande città, ma è molto rumorosa.
native_language_example: I like living in a big city, but it's very noisy.

meaning: a big/large family; (figuratively) one big family.
additional_notes: Literally refers to a family with many members. It can also be used figuratively for a close-knit group (e.g., a school, workplace, or community) that treats each other like family: "come una grande famiglia" = "like one big family." The adjective agrees with the noun: una grande famiglia (feminine singular), una grande famigliare? (not here), una famiglia grande is also possible but slightly different emphasis.
target_language_example: Nel nostro ufficio siamo come una grande famiglia.
native_language_example: In our office we’re like one big family.

meaning: a great fortune; a big piece of luck.
additional_notes: Often means a large amount of money (especially with verbs like ereditare “to inherit” or accumulare “to build up”). In expressions like “È una grande fortuna…”, it means “it’s very fortunate / it’s a great stroke of luck,” not necessarily money.
target_language_example: È una grande fortuna avere amici così.
native_language_example: It’s a great stroke of luck to have friends like that.

additional_notes: Refers to a (written) letter/message on paper. Common with verbs like scrivere (to write), spedire/inviare (to send), ricevere (to receive), and leggere (to read). With an indirect object you’ll often see: "scriverti una lettera" = "to write you a letter". "Lettera" is feminine; plural: "lettere".
target_language_example: Domani ti mando una lettera.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’ll send you a letter.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition “a” + a person’s name to indicate the recipient of the letter: “una lettera a Judy” = “a letter to Judy.” Often appears with verbs like scrivere (to write), consegnare (to deliver), and spedire (to send).
target_language_example: Ho scritto una lettera a mia nonna ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote a letter to my grandma last night.

additional_notes: Used when saying who a letter is from. With places, it can mean a letter sent from that place (e.g., “una lettera da Boston”). Often follows verbs like ricevere (to receive), leggere (to read), arrivare con (to arrive with).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una lettera da mia nonna ieri.
native_language_example: I received a letter from my grandmother yesterday.

additional_notes: Used to specify that the letter (a written message or document) is written in the English language. You can swap the language: “una lettera in italiano / in francese”. In Italian, “in inglese” means “in English” (language), not “to England”.
target_language_example: Devo scrivere una lettera in inglese per il mio lavoro.
native_language_example: I have to write a letter in English for my job.

additional_notes: Use it for (1) a teaching session (a lesson/class/lecture): “una lezione di storia”, “tenere una lezione su…”; and (2) a life lesson or a harsh experience that teaches you something: “La vita mi ha dato una lezione.” Also in the expression “insegnare una lezione (a qualcuno)”, meaning “to teach someone a lesson” (often in a negative/punishing sense).
target_language_example: Domani ho una lezione di italiano alle nove.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I have an Italian class at nine.

additional_notes: Used for a line that doesn’t curve, especially in math, geometry, maps, or drawing instructions. Often follows verbs like "disegnare" (to draw) or "tracciare" (to trace). In questions like "La chiami una linea retta?" it can be sarcastic: “You call that a straight line?”
target_language_example: Per arrivare più velocemente, vai in una linea retta verso la piazza.
native_language_example: To get there faster, go in a straight line toward the square.

additional_notes: Used for a spoken language in general. After "una lingua" you can add an adjective: "una lingua difficile" (a difficult language), "una lingua nuova" (a new language). Also common in menus or settings: "Scelga una lingua" = "Choose a language."
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera.
native_language_example: I'm learning a foreign language.

additional_notes: Used for any language that is not your native language. Often appears with verbs like imparare (to learn), studiare (to study), parlare (to speak). With a specific language you’d usually say: una lingua + adjective (e.g., una lingua italiana/inglese) or simply the language name (l’italiano, l’inglese).
target_language_example: Sto imparando una lingua straniera per lavoro.
native_language_example: I’m learning a foreign language for work.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to say something lasted a long time or covered a lot (e.g., una lunga discussione, una lunga passeggiata, una lunga assenza, una lunga storia). It agrees with the noun: masculine is “un lungo …” (un lungo viaggio), feminine plural “delle lunghe …” (delle lunghe giornate). In “È una lunga storia,” it can imply “it’s a long story” (often meaning the explanation is complicated).
target_language_example: Scusa se sono in ritardo: ho avuto una lunga riunione.
native_language_example: Sorry I’m late: I had a long meeting.

additional_notes: Used to say someone wrote/sent a letter that is long (often implying detailed or lengthy). The adjective *lunga* agrees with *lettera* (feminine singular), so it’s *una lunga lettera*.
target_language_example: Ti ho scritto una lunga lettera ieri sera.
native_language_example: I wrote you a long letter last night.

meaning: a car; (also) a machine (depending on context)
additional_notes: In everyday Italian, "una macchina" most often refers to "a car" (especially with verbs like guidare "to drive", noleggiare "to rent", parcheggiare "to park"). Depending on context, it can also mean "a machine" (e.g., industrial equipment). "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article ("a/an").
target_language_example: Vorrei noleggiare una macchina.
native_language_example: I’d like to rent a car.

additional_notes: Used for a device that takes photographs. Often just "macchina fotografica" without the article. In everyday speech you may also hear "fotocamera". Plural: "macchine fotografiche".
target_language_example: Hai una macchina fotografica? Vorrei fare qualche foto.
native_language_example: Do you have a camera? I’d like to take a few photos.

additional_notes: Literally means “a hand” (the body part), as in "con una mano" = “with one hand.” Very commonly used in the expression "dare una mano (a qualcuno)" = “to give someone a hand / to help someone.” With pronouns: "dammi una mano" (help me), "dagli una mano" (help him).
target_language_example: Mi dai una mano a portare queste valigie?
native_language_example: Can you give me a hand carrying these suitcases?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a physical or digital map. Often followed by "di/del/della" to specify what kind of map it is (e.g., "una mappa della città" = a city map; "una mappa del tesoro" = a treasure map).
target_language_example: Hai una mappa della città?
native_language_example: Do you have a map of the city?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single pencil. "Una" is the feminine form of "a/an"; plural: "delle matite" (some pencils) or "matite" (pencils). Often paired with "una penna" (a pen).
target_language_example: Mi serve una matita per scrivere.
native_language_example: I need a pencil to write.

additional_notes: Refers to the piece of sports equipment used to hit the ball in baseball. With an indefinite article (una) it means “a baseball bat”; without the article (mazza da baseball) it can mean “baseball bat” in general.
target_language_example: Ho lasciato una mazza da baseball in macchina.
native_language_example: I left a baseball bat in the car.

additional_notes: Used for awards in sports/competitions. In Italian you can also say simply “il bronzo” to mean “the bronze (medal)” in contexts like the Olympics.
target_language_example: Alle Olimpiadi ha conquistato una medaglia di bronzo.
native_language_example: At the Olympics he/she won a bronze medal.

additional_notes: "Una" is the feminine singular form of the indefinite article "a/an" and can also mean "one" in some contexts. Used when asking for, offering, or referring to a single apple.
target_language_example: Posso avere una mela, per favore?
native_language_example: Can I have an apple, please?

additional_notes: Used to describe someone who remembers things well (names, facts, dates, details). It often follows the verb "avere" (to have): "Ho una memoria molto buona". You can change the intensity: "una memoria buona" (a good memory), "una memoria eccellente" (an excellent memory), "una memoria pessima" (a terrible memory).
target_language_example: Ho una memoria molto buona per i nomi.
native_language_example: I have a very good memory for names.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or mention one of your female friends. It’s a very common way to say “a friend of mine” (not necessarily your best friend). For a male friend: “un mio amico”. You can also use it with names: “Rita, una mia amica” = “Rita, a friend of mine.”
target_language_example: Stasera esco con una mia amica.
native_language_example: Tonight I’m going out with a friend of mine.

meaning: a mission; an important task/assignment (often with a specific goal).
additional_notes: Used for an official or organized assignment (military, diplomatic, rescue, space, etc.) or, more generally, a personal goal you feel you must accomplish. Often followed by "per" + infinitive to say the purpose (e.g., "una missione per trovare...").
target_language_example: Siamo partiti per una missione di soccorso.
native_language_example: We left on a rescue mission.

additional_notes: Used to say someone has a wife or to describe a woman as a wife. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), and the plural is "due/tre mogli" (“two/three wives”). With negation: "non ho una moglie" = “I don’t have a wife / I’m not married.”
target_language_example: Marco ha una moglie e due bambini.
native_language_example: Marco has a wife and two kids.

additional_notes: Used for a single coin (loose change). It can also mean “a currency” in general when talking about money systems, but with “una” it usually means one physical coin.
target_language_example: Hai una moneta da un euro?
native_language_example: Do you have a one-euro coin?

meaning: a mosque (a Muslim place of worship).
additional_notes: Feminine noun: la moschea / una moschea. Plural: le moschee. Used with common verbs like andare in (to go to), pregare in (to pray in), visitare (to visit), vivere accanto a (to live next to).
target_language_example: C'è una moschea vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There is a mosque near the station.

meaning: a move; a step/action (also used to mean “a quick move” in expressions like darsi una mossa = to hurry up).
additional_notes: Literally “a move.” Common in games (chess, cards, etc.) meaning “one move/turn”: Non ripetere mai una mossa… (“Never repeat a move…”). In everyday speech it’s often part of the phrase darsi una mossa / darsi una mossa! (or plural: datevi una mossa!) meaning “to hurry up!” / “Get a move on!” (informal/colloquial).
target_language_example: Se vogliamo arrivare in orario, dobbiamo darci una mossa.
native_language_example: If we want to arrive on time, we have to hurry up.

additional_notes: Indefinite phrase: "una" = "a/one" (feminine singular) + "mucca" = "cow". Used to talk about an unspecified cow. For a male, use "un toro" (a bull).
target_language_example: C'è una mucca nel campo.
native_language_example: There’s a cow in the field.

additional_notes: "Nave" is a feminine noun (la nave / una nave). It usually means a large ship (bigger than a "barca"), and it can also mean a spacecraft in phrases like "nave spaziale".
target_language_example: Dal porto si vede una nave enorme.
native_language_example: From the port you can see a huge ship.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (or a feminine adjective used as a noun). It agrees in gender/number with what follows: una nuova scuola = “a new school”, una nuova fase = “a new phase”. For masculine you use un nuovo (e.g., un nuovo problema).
target_language_example: Abbiamo bisogno di una nuova idea.
native_language_example: We need a new idea.

additional_notes: Used to talk about buying, needing, or choosing a new car. "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), "nuova" means “new,” and "auto" means “car” (feminine in Italian).
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova auto per la famiglia.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new car for the family.

additional_notes: Literally “a new automobile.” Use it when talking about buying, needing, or choosing a new car. Note the feminine agreement: una (feminine singular) + nuova (feminine singular) + automobile (feminine). In everyday Italian, people very often say “una nuova macchina” instead of “una nuova automobile.”
target_language_example: Sto cercando una nuova automobile, ma costa troppo.
native_language_example: I'm looking for a new car, but it costs too much.

meaning: a new house; a new home.
additional_notes: Used when talking about building, buying, or moving into a different house/home. "Casa" can mean both the physical house and the idea of a home; "una" is feminine singular (“a”), and "nuova" agrees with "casa".
target_language_example: Stiamo cercando una nuova casa vicino al lavoro.
native_language_example: We’re looking for a new home near work.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase. "Macchina" often means "car" in Italian (short for "macchina (automobile)"). "Una" is the feminine singular indefinite article (“a”), and "nuova" agrees with the feminine noun "macchina". You can swap the adjective: "una macchina nuova" also means “a new car.”
target_language_example: Vorrei comprare una nuova macchina quest'anno.
native_language_example: I’d like to buy a new car this year.

meaning: a new life; a fresh start.
additional_notes: Used when someone starts over or begins a different chapter in life (after moving, changing jobs, recovering from a difficult period, etc.). Often with verbs like cominciare/iniziare (to begin) or avere (to have).
target_language_example: Dopo il divorzio, ha deciso di cominciare una nuova vita in un'altra città.
native_language_example: After the divorce, he decided to start a new life in another city.

meaning: a ball (a round object used for playing; also used for spherical shapes).
additional_notes: Literally “a ball.” Used for a physical ball you throw/kick (e.g., in sports). It can also describe something that is round/spherical: “La Terra è una palla blu” = “The Earth is a blue ball.”
target_language_example: Mi presti una palla per giocare in spiaggia?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a ball to play with at the beach?

additional_notes: Used to name a type of ball by adding the sport after da: una palla da basket (a basketball), una palla da golf (a golf ball). In Italian you can also say palla da + sport, or use a more specific sport name (e.g., palla da pallacanestro).
target_language_example: Hai una palla da tennis?
native_language_example: Do you have a tennis ball?

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single word in general or in a text. In negative expressions it often means “a word” = “anything”: "non dire una parola" / "non mi ha detto una parola" = “don’t say a word / he didn’t say a word.”
target_language_example: Non dire una parola, per favore.
native_language_example: Don’t say a word, please.

additional_notes: Used to talk about one chess match. Common with invitations or suggestions (e.g., “Che ne dici di…?” = “How about…?”) and with “sfidare qualcuno in…” (“to challenge someone to…”).
target_language_example: Dopo cena, facciamo una partita a scacchi?
native_language_example: After dinner, shall we play a game of chess?

additional_notes: Used to talk about one game of a sport, either playing it ("giochiamo una partita di...") or going to watch it ("andiamo a una partita di..."). It’s usually followed by the sport: "una partita di tennis", "una partita di hockey", "una partita di calcio". "Partita" is feminine, so: una/la partita; due/le partite.
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo una partita di calcio in TV.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re watching a soccer match on TV.

additional_notes: Used with sports to mean a single game/match. With "fare" or "giocare" it means to play a game; with "guardare" it means to watch a game. In plural: "due/tre partite di baseball".
target_language_example: Domani giochiamo una partita di baseball al parco.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re playing a baseball game at the park.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a single game of soccer. "Partita" = match/game; "calcio" = soccer (called "football" in the UK). You can change the article depending on context: "la partita di calcio" (the match), "una partita di calcio" (a match).
target_language_example: Stasera guardiamo una partita di calcio in TV.
native_language_example: Tonight we’re watching a soccer match on TV.

additional_notes: Used with the verb fare (“to take/go for”): fare una passeggiata = to go for a walk. It can be a short, relaxed walk (often in a park or around town). In the idiom La vita non è una passeggiata, it means “Life isn’t easy” (literally, “Life isn’t a walk in the park”).
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo una passeggiata in centro.
native_language_example: After dinner we go for a walk downtown.

additional_notes: Most commonly used literally to mean going for a walk in a park. In English, “a walk in the park” is also an idiom meaning “something very easy”; in Italian that exact full phrase is less fixed as an idiom—more common are “È una passeggiata” (It’s easy) or “È una passeggiata di salute.”
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo una passeggiata al parco.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s take a walk in the park.

additional_notes: Used to invite or suggest going for a walk together. Often appears in questions or invitations like “Vuoi fare una passeggiata con me?” (Do you want to go for a walk with me?). You can swap “me” for another person: “con te” (with you), “con noi” (with us).
target_language_example: Vuoi fare una passeggiata con me dopo cena?
native_language_example: Do you want to go for a walk with me after dinner?

additional_notes: A simple noun phrase you can use when talking about plans or routines. Often used with verbs like *fare* (to do/take) or *andare a* (to go): *Faccio una passeggiata dopo la colazione.* Note: *colazione* means “breakfast” in Italian (it can look like English “collation,” but that’s not the meaning).
target_language_example: Di solito faccio una passeggiata dopo la colazione.
native_language_example: I usually take a walk after breakfast.

additional_notes: A common everyday phrase for going for a stroll in a park. Used with verbs like fare (“to take/do”): fare una passeggiata nel parco = “to go for a walk in the park.” In Italian it can also be used figuratively to mean something is very easy (like in English), but in your examples it’s literal.
target_language_example: Dopo cena facciamo una passeggiata nel parco.
native_language_example: After dinner, let’s go for a walk in the park.

meaning: a break; a pause (a short rest).
additional_notes: Used for a short rest from an activity (work, walking, cooking, etc.). Common with verbs like fare una pausa (to take a break), prendersi una pausa (to take a break for yourself), and dare una pausa (to give someone a break / let them rest). It can also mean a pause in speaking or action.
target_language_example: Facciamo una pausa di dieci minuti.
native_language_example: Let’s take a ten-minute break.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: the animal. "Pecora" is a feminine noun, so it uses "una" in the singular (una pecora) and "pecore" in the plural (due pecore). It can also be used figuratively to mean someone who is very naive or who follows others blindly (like "a sheep").
target_language_example: Al mercato ho comprato una pecora.
native_language_example: At the market I bought a sheep.

additional_notes: Used when asking for or referring to a pen. With the indefinite article "una" (feminine singular), it means “a pen”; the plural is "delle penne". Often appears with verbs like "avere" (to have), "prendere" (to take), and "prendere in prestito" (to borrow).
target_language_example: Mi presti una penna, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you lend me a pen, please?

additional_notes: Used to say an activity, meeting, lesson, etc. wasn’t useful or worth doing. Often follows “è stata” (it was) or “è” (it is): “È/È stata una perdita di tempo.”
target_language_example: Aspettare qui senza informazioni è una perdita di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting here with no information is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Indefinite phrase meaning one unspecified person. Often used when you don’t want or don’t know the name (similar to “someone”): "una persona mi ha chiamato" = “someone called me.” With "frequentare una persona" it can mean “to see/date someone.”
target_language_example: C'è una persona che ti aspetta fuori.
native_language_example: There’s someone waiting for you outside.

meaning: “a person who …” (used to describe someone by what they do/are).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause that defines or describes someone: una persona che + verb (e.g., fuma, disegna, è…). It’s singular; plural is “delle persone che” / “persone che.” Often used for general statements and definitions.
target_language_example: Cerco una persona che parli bene inglese.
native_language_example: I’m looking for a person who speaks English well.

meaning: “a very … person” (used to describe yourself or someone else).
additional_notes: Used before an adjective to say someone is very [adjective]. Common in self-descriptions: “Sono una persona molto …” (“I’m a very … person”). The adjective changes with gender/number (e.g., una persona molto impegnata/occupata/umile).
target_language_example: Mia sorella è una persona molto paziente.
native_language_example: My sister is a very patient person.

additional_notes: Used to describe someone’s character (honest, trustworthy). Often with verbs like essere (to be), considerarsi (to consider oneself), or conoscere qualcuno come… (to know someone as…).
target_language_example: Mi fido di lei: è una persona onesta.
native_language_example: I trust her: she’s an honest person.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun (una + feminine adjective piccola) to describe something small in size, amount, or importance (e.g., una piccola sorpresa, una piccola somma, una piccola busta). With some nouns it can imply “just a little” in a polite or minimizing way (e.g., asking for a tip: Una piccola mancia?). The masculine form is "un piccolo".
target_language_example: Posso avere una piccola informazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a little bit of information, please?

additional_notes: Means a small town/community. In Italian, "città" can sometimes be used even for places that English would call a “town,” so "una piccola città" often translates naturally as “a small town.” The adjective "piccola" agrees with the feminine noun "città" (una piccola città).
target_language_example: Sono cresciuto in una piccola città sul mare.
native_language_example: I grew up in a small town by the sea.

additional_notes: Literal meaning: a (small) stone you can pick up (raccogliere) or throw (tirare) at something/someone. In comparisons like "come una pietra" it can mean "like a stone" (very hard, heavy, still, or emotionally cold depending on context).
target_language_example: Ho trovato una pietra interessante sulla spiaggia.
native_language_example: I found an interesting stone on the beach.

additional_notes: Means a pistol/handgun (a small gun). The article changes with gender/number: un/una (a), la (the), delle pistole (some pistols). Often used with verbs like comprare (to buy), possedere (to own), dare (to give).
target_language_example: Non voglio avere una pistola in casa.
native_language_example: I don’t want to have a gun at home.

additional_notes: Used to order or choose food. With "andare" (e.g., "A me va una pizza"), it means "A pizza works for me / I'd like a pizza."
target_language_example: Per me, una pizza margherita, grazie.
native_language_example: For me, a margherita pizza, please.

additional_notes: Used when booking or checking in at a restaurant, hotel, or event. "Per" introduces what the reservation is for: a time (per le sei e mezza), a meal (per pranzo/cena), or a name (per Milton Rockwell). You can also add the number of people (e.g., per due/quattro).
target_language_example: Buonasera, ho una prenotazione per due persone alle otto.
native_language_example: Good evening, I have a reservation for two people at eight.

additional_notes: Used for a commitment you make to do (or not do) something. Common collocations: fare una promessa (to make a promise), mantenere una promessa (to keep a promise), infrangere una promessa (to break a promise). Also used in expressions like È una promessa! (“It’s a promise!”).
target_language_example: Te lo prometto: è una promessa.
native_language_example: I promise you: it’s a promise.

meaning: an issue; a matter; a question (topic to discuss).
additional_notes: Used for a topic/problem to discuss or deal with (often something important or serious): una questione importante/seria. Common in meetings and formal conversations. For a question you ask someone directly, you more often use “una domanda.”
target_language_example: C'è una questione che vorrei chiarire prima di iniziare.
native_language_example: There’s an issue I’d like to clear up before we start.

meaning: “a matter of …” / “an issue of …” (it depends on …).
additional_notes: Used to say what something is really about, or what the deciding factor is: *È una questione di + noun* (“It’s a matter of + noun”). Often emphasizes that it’s not about something else: *non è una questione di X, ma di Y* (“it’s not a matter of X, but of Y”). You can also use it for the reason behind something: *per una questione di lavoro* (“for work reasons”).
target_language_example: Non è una questione di soldi, ma di fiducia.
native_language_example: It’s not a matter of money, but of trust.

additional_notes: Most literally means “a girl” (a young female person). In context (especially with verbs like avere: “Ho una ragazza”), it commonly means “a girlfriend.” Use “la mia ragazza” for “my girlfriend.”
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto una ragazza al corso di italiano.
native_language_example: I met a girl at the Italian course.

additional_notes: This is an incomplete phrase on its own: it normally needs an adjective after molto (e.g., una ragazza molto timida/giovane/simpatica). Ragazza means “girl/young woman.” Molto is an intensifier meaning “very.”
target_language_example: Ho conosciuto una ragazza molto simpatica alla festa.
native_language_example: I met a very nice girl at the party.

meaning: a relationship; also a connection (with someone).
additional_notes: Most commonly used for a romantic relationship (“una relazione seria”, “avere una relazione con…”). It can also mean a personal connection/bond that isn’t romantic, including family relationships (“una relazione difficile con suo padre”) or a special bond (“una relazione speciale”). You can add details like “a lunga distanza” (long-distance).
target_language_example: Non voglio una relazione a lunga distanza.
native_language_example: I don’t want a long-distance relationship.

additional_notes: Used to describe a romantic relationship where the partners live far from each other and don’t see each other often. Common with verbs like “avere” (to have) or “stare in” (to be in): “Ho una relazione a distanza” / “Sono in una relazione a distanza”.
target_language_example: Da due anni ho una relazione a distanza, ma ci vediamo ogni mese.
native_language_example: I've been in a long-distance relationship for two years, but we see each other every month.

additional_notes: Used for social networks/messaging apps when someone asks to add you as a friend/connection. Common verbs: mandare/inviare una richiesta di amicizia (to send a friend request), accettare/rifiutare una richiesta di amicizia (to accept/decline).
target_language_example: Ti ho mandato una richiesta di amicizia su Facebook.
native_language_example: I sent you a friend request on Facebook.

meaning: an answer; a reply (to a message/request).
additional_notes: Used for both answering a question and replying to an email/message or giving an official response. Common with verbs like avere (to have): “Hai una risposta?”, dare (to give): “Mi dia una risposta”, mandare (to send): “mandare una risposta”. You can add adjectives to specify the type: “una risposta definitiva” (a final/definitive answer).
target_language_example: Mi può dare una risposta entro domani?
native_language_example: Can you give me an answer by tomorrow?

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person or organization you heard back from. Often followed by a name or role: “una risposta da Maria”, “una risposta da parte del servizio clienti” (a reply from customer service). You can also say “ho ricevuto una risposta da …” (I received a reply from …).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una risposta da Luca ieri sera.
native_language_example: I got a reply from Luca last night.

additional_notes: Used for an appointment where people get together to discuss something (work, school, town hall, etc.). Common with verbs like avere/essere in/andare a/partecipare a: “Ho una riunione” (I have a meeting), “Tom è in una riunione” (Tom is in a meeting), “andare a una riunione” (to go to a meeting).
target_language_example: Scusa, non posso parlare adesso: sono in una riunione.
native_language_example: Sorry, I can’t talk right now: I’m in a meeting.

additional_notes: Used for a container, usually made of cardboard, wood, or plastic. Often followed by “di” to say what’s inside or what it contains: “una scatola di mele” = “a box of apples.” You can also describe it with adjectives like “piena di …” (full of …): “una scatola piena di mele.”
target_language_example: Puoi mettere questi biscotti in una scatola?
native_language_example: Can you put these cookies in a box?

additional_notes: Used to talk about a quantity contained in a box. The noun after di is usually plural (una scatola di fiammiferi, una scatola di cioccolatini). It can also be used more generally for a boxed package, even if it’s not literally a rigid box in English (e.g., a juice box).
target_language_example: Vorrei una scatola di biscotti, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a box of cookies, please.

meaning: a choice; an option; a decision.
additional_notes: Used for choosing between options (“fare una scelta” = to make a choice). You can also “dare una scelta (a qualcuno)” = to give someone a choice. Often paired with adjectives like “una scelta saggia” (a wise choice).
target_language_example: Hai una scelta: restare qui o venire con noi.
native_language_example: You have a choice: stay here or come with us.

additional_notes: Used literally for the animal. It can also be used as an insult or to say someone looks/behaves like a monkey (often childish and can be offensive). Common patterns: "sembra una scimmia" (he/she looks like a monkey), "si comporta come una scimmia" (he/she behaves like a monkey), "imitare una scimmia" (to imitate a monkey).
target_language_example: Lui sembra una scimmia.
native_language_example: He looks like a monkey.

additional_notes: Most often means “an excuse” (a reason you give to explain/justify something), especially with verbs like inventare/si è inventato una scusa (“to make up an excuse”). With verbs like dovere (Gli/Le dovete una scusa), it means “to owe someone an apology.” The plural is scuse (“excuses/apologies”).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace: ti devo una scusa.
native_language_example: I’m sorry: I owe you an apology.

additional_notes: Feminine form of “secondo/a” used with feminine nouns: **una seconda volta** (a second time), **una seconda possibilità** (a second chance), **una seconda opinione** (a second opinion), **una seconda auto** (a second car). The noun can sometimes be understood from context and left out.
target_language_example: Mi puoi dare una seconda possibilità?
native_language_example: Can you give me a second chance?

additional_notes: Used when you want someone to forgive a mistake or allow someone to try again. Often appears with verbs like dare (“to give”) and meritarsi (“to deserve”). It changes with the indirect object pronoun: dagli/dalle/gli dia una seconda occasione = “give him/her a second chance.”
target_language_example: So che ho sbagliato, ma ti chiedo una seconda occasione.
native_language_example: I know I made a mistake, but I’m asking you for a second chance.

additional_notes: Used to ask for, offer, or refer to a single chair. Often appears with verbs like "dare" (to give), "portare" (to bring), and "sedere/siedere" (to sit).
target_language_example: C'è una sedia libera vicino alla finestra.
native_language_example: There’s a free chair near the window.

meaning: a series of; a number of.
additional_notes: Used before a plural noun to mean “a sequence/collection of things,” often translating naturally as “a number of.” Very common with “tutta una serie di” = “a whole series of / all sorts of.”
target_language_example: Devo fare una serie di telefonate prima di partire.
native_language_example: I have to make a series of phone calls before leaving.

additional_notes: Used to talk about a duration (for one week) or a point in time in the future with "fra/tra" (= in a week). Can also mean "per una settimana" (= for a week) depending on context.
target_language_example: Resto a Roma per una settimana.
native_language_example: I’m staying in Rome for a week.

additional_notes: Used to ask for or refer to a single cigarette. With verbs like "fumare" (to smoke), "accendere" (to light), and with items like "un accendino" (a lighter). In requests you’ll often hear: "Posso avere una sigaretta?" (Can I have a cigarette?).
target_language_example: Scusa, hai una sigaretta?
native_language_example: Excuse me, do you have a cigarette?

meaning: a solution; a way to solve a problem.
additional_notes: Used for an answer or practical way to fix/resolve a problem (“trovare una soluzione” = to find a solution). Also used for a possible option/approach (“una soluzione migliore” = a better solution). Feminine noun: la soluzione / una soluzione; plural: le soluzioni.
target_language_example: Cerchiamo una soluzione insieme.
native_language_example: Let’s look for a solution together.

additional_notes: Used to say something unexpected happens or to keep something secret until the moment (e.g., a gift, a party, news). With the verb "essere": "È/È stata una sorpresa" = "It’s/It was a surprise."
target_language_example: Il regalo per tuo padre deve restare una sorpresa.
native_language_example: The gift for your father has to stay a surprise.

additional_notes: Used to introduce the person who will receive the surprise: "una sorpresa per + [person]". You can add a verb like "Ho una sorpresa per te" (I have a surprise for you) or "È una sorpresa per mia sorella" (It’s a surprise for my sister). The article can change (una/un/una grande, etc.) depending on the noun and context.
target_language_example: Ho una sorpresa per te.
native_language_example: I have a surprise for you.

meaning: 'a kind of' / 'sort of' (used to describe something approximately).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to mean something is similar to that thing, but not exactly (or you don’t want to be too precise): "una sorta di celebrità" = "a sort of celebrity." Often used when you’re unsure, simplifying, or being intentionally vague. Can also introduce an approximate explanation/idea ("una sorta di spiegazione").
target_language_example: È una sorta di problema, ma possiamo risolverlo.
native_language_example: It’s kind of a problem, but we can solve it.

additional_notes: Used to describe something approximately or loosely: it’s similar to X, but not exactly X. Very common in spoken Italian. It can also soften what you’re saying (making it less direct). Usually followed by a noun: "una specie di test", "una specie di crisi".
target_language_example: È una specie di scusa, ma non mi convince.
native_language_example: It’s kind of an excuse, but it doesn’t convince me.

additional_notes: "Spia" is a feminine noun; "una spia" refers to a female spy or uses the feminine form as the default. For a male spy you often hear "una spia" as well, but you can also say "una spia (uomo)" or more commonly "un agente segreto". It can also mean an indicator light (e.g., on a car dashboard): "una spia rossa".
target_language_example: In quel film lei è una spia.
native_language_example: In that movie she is a spy.

additional_notes: Used when you want a reason or clarification for something. Often followed by "per" (for) to explain what it’s about: "una spiegazione per ciò" / "una spiegazione per il suo errore". "Hai una spiegazione?" is a common way to ask "Do you have an explanation?"
target_language_example: Puoi darmi una spiegazione, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you give me an explanation, please?

meaning: a room (in a house, building, hotel, etc.).
additional_notes: Commonly used for any kind of room: a bedroom, an office, a waiting room, etc. In hotels, you’ll often hear it with details: "una stanza con doccia" (a room with a shower), "una stanza pulita" (a clean room), "una stanza sul retro" (a room in the back). Don’t confuse with "uno stanzo" (not used) or "la stanza" (the room).
target_language_example: Scusi, vorrei una stanza per due notti.
native_language_example: Excuse me, I’d like a room for two nights.

meaning: “a room for …” (used to say who/what the room is for, or how long you need it).
additional_notes: Common when booking accommodation. After per you can add: (1) the purpose/people: per gli ospiti (“for guests”), per due persone (“for two people”); or (2) the length of stay: per sei notti (“for six nights”). In questions you’ll often hear: Avete/Hai una stanza per …? (“Do you have a room for …?”).
target_language_example: Avete una stanza per due persone per tre notti?
native_language_example: Do you have a room for two people for three nights?

additional_notes: Used when talking about seeing a streak of light in the night sky (a meteor). Often said as an exclamation when you spot one: “Guarda, una stella cadente!” You can use it with “vedere” (to see) and “mai” (ever): “Hai mai visto…?”
target_language_example: Ieri notte abbiamo visto una stella cadente.
native_language_example: Last night we saw a shooting star.

additional_notes: Often means “a story” (a tale someone tells or reads), but it can also mean “history” (the past of a place/people), especially in phrases like “una storia ricca.” Context tells you which meaning is intended.
target_language_example: Mi racconti una storia prima di dormire?
native_language_example: Will you tell me a story before I go to sleep?

additional_notes: Used to describe a story (spoken or written) that is engaging or catches your attention. Common with verbs like raccontare (to tell) and leggere (to read). Agreement: una storia (feminine singular) + interessante (same form for masculine/feminine singular).
target_language_example: Vuoi sentire una storia interessante?
native_language_example: Do you want to hear an interesting story?

additional_notes: "Studentessa" is the feminine form of "studente". Use "una" before a singular feminine noun starting with a consonant sound (e.g., una studentessa). To talk to someone directly: "Sei una studentessa?" = "Are you a student?"
target_language_example: Una studentessa cerca il professore.
native_language_example: A (female) student is looking for the professor.

meaning: “a cup of” (a cupful of a drink or ingredient).
additional_notes: Used to indicate a quantity measured in cups, especially in recipes (“una tazza di riso”) and when ordering drinks (“una tazza di caffè”). With ingredients you can often also say “una tazza *d’*…” before a vowel (e.g., “una tazza d’acqua”).
target_language_example: Vorrei una tazza di tè, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a cup of tea, please.

additional_notes: Common in everyday requests and orders. Use it with verbs like voglio (I want), mi piacerebbe (I’d like), ordinare (to order), and versare (to pour). You can change the article: una tazza di caffè (a cup), due tazze di caffè (two cups), la tazza di caffè (the cup). In many cafés you might also hear just un caffè for an espresso.
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una tazza di caffè, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have a cup of coffee, please?

additional_notes: Used when ordering or offering a drink. Common with polite requests like (Mi) dia / Datemi… per favore (“Please give me…”) and with offers/questions like Vuoi/Volete…? or Vorresti/Vorreste…? (“Would you like…?”).
target_language_example: Potrei avere una tazza di latte caldo, per favore?
native_language_example: Could I have a cup of warm milk, please?

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase for offering or talking about a drink. Often used with verbs like preparare (to prepare), portare (to bring), versarsi (to pour oneself), and with offers/questions like Vuoi una tazza di tè? (Do you want a cup of tea?).
target_language_example: Dopo cena, prendo sempre una tazza di tè.
native_language_example: After dinner, I always have a cup of tea.

additional_notes: Used when offering, ordering, or serving tea for a person. It’s normally followed by a name or pronoun: "Una tazza di tè per me/te/lui/lei" (a cup of tea for me/you/him/her). You may also hear "Una tazza di tè per favore" to mean "A cup of tea, please."
target_language_example: Una tazza di tè per me, per favore.
native_language_example: A cup of tea for me, please.

additional_notes: Used with fare/ricevere: "fare una telefonata" = to make a phone call; "ricevere una telefonata" = to receive a phone call. Can be modified (e.g., "una telefonata urgente" = an urgent phone call).
target_language_example: Scusa, devo fare una telefonata veloce.
native_language_example: Sorry, I have to make a quick phone call.

additional_notes: Used to say who the caller is. "Da" means “from” (the source/origin of the call). Often used with pronouns: "una telefonata da lui/lei" (“a call from him/her”). In speech you may also hear "ho ricevuto una telefonata da…" (“I got a call from…”).
target_language_example: Ho ricevuto una telefonata da mia madre ieri sera.
native_language_example: I got a call from my mother last night.

additional_notes: Noun phrase: the indefinite article "una" (a/an) + feminine singular noun "tigre". Used when talking about a tiger in general or an unknown tiger. In questions like "Ha mai visto..." it often means "Have you ever seen...".
target_language_example: Ho visto una tigre allo zoo.
native_language_example: I saw a tiger at the zoo.

additional_notes: Used for a sweet cake (e.g., banana cake, Christmas cake). Common patterns: "una torta alla ..." (a ...-flavored cake, like banana), "una torta di ..." (a ... cake, often for an occasion or style, like Christmas), and "tagliare una torta in due" (to cut a cake in half).
target_language_example: Per il suo compleanno ho comprato una torta al cioccolato.
native_language_example: For her birthday I bought a chocolate cake.

meaning: a tragedy; (also figuratively) a disaster / a very bad situation.
additional_notes: Used for a real serious tragic event (death, accident, catastrophe): "È avvenuta una tragedia." It’s also common as an exaggerated reaction meaning “it’s awful/terrible”: "No, una tragedia." In the expression "farne una tragedia" it means “to make a big deal out of it / to overreact”: "Perché ne stai facendo una tragedia?"
target_language_example: Ho perso il treno: per me è stata una tragedia!
native_language_example: I missed the train: for me it was a disaster!

additional_notes: Literally a device used to catch animals or pests (e.g., a mousetrap). Figuratively, it means a plan to trick someone or lure them into danger ("It could be a trap"). Often used with "essere" (è/era/sarebbe una trappola) or "tendere una trappola" (to set a trap for someone).
target_language_example: Non fidarti: potrebbe essere una trappola.
native_language_example: Don’t trust it: it could be a trap.

additional_notes: Medical term. Often used with: “fare una trasfusione di sangue (a qualcuno)” = “to give someone a blood transfusion” (passive is very common: “A Tom è stata fatta…”), and “servire/essere necessaria una trasfusione di sangue” = “to need a blood transfusion.”
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente, gli hanno fatto una trasfusione di sangue.
native_language_example: After the accident, they gave him a blood transfusion.

additional_notes: A common noun phrase for time off from work/school for rest or travel. Often used with verbs like fare (to take/go on) and avere bisogno di (to need): fare una vacanza, avere bisogno di una vacanza. Plural: vacanze.
target_language_example: Quest’estate voglio fare una vacanza al mare.
native_language_example: This summer I want to take a vacation at the seaside.

additional_notes: Feminine singular form of *vecchio* (“old”). Often used before a feminine noun: *una vecchia bici* (“an old bike”), *una vecchia storia* (“an old story”). When used on its own as a noun, *una vecchia* usually means “an old woman” (can sound blunt depending on context; *un’anziana* is more neutral/polite).
target_language_example: In autobus c’era una vecchia che chiedeva informazioni.
native_language_example: On the bus there was an old woman asking for information.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun to emphasize that something is genuine or truly has a quality: una vera amica (a true friend), una vera festa (a real party). It’s the feminine form of the adjective vero; compare: un vero amico (masculine), una vera amica (feminine), dei veri amici / delle vere amiche (plural).
target_language_example: Vorrei una vera pizza napoletana.
native_language_example: I’d like a real Neapolitan pizza.

meaning: a visit (an appointment/visitor; or the act of visiting).
additional_notes: Used for both formal and casual visits. Common patterns: "fare una visita a [someone/place]" = to pay a visit to; "passare a fare una visita" = to stop by for a visit; "avere una visita" can mean "to have a visitor" (e.g., at home, at the office, in a hospital). In some contexts (like reception/phone calls), "Ha una visita" means someone is here to see you.
target_language_example: Domani pomeriggio ho una visita, quindi non posso uscire.
native_language_example: Tomorrow afternoon I have a visitor/appointment, so I can’t go out.

additional_notes: Usually refers to someone’s life ("una vita lunga e felice" = “a long and happy life”). In phrases like "sembra/sentirsi come se fosse passata una vita", it’s often used more loosely to mean “a very long time / ages,” even if not literally a whole lifetime. "I risparmi di una vita" means “a lifetime’s savings” (money saved over many years).
target_language_example: Ho aspettato una vita per questo momento.
native_language_example: I’ve waited ages for this moment.

additional_notes: Common phrase meaning a life that is generally happy and satisfying. Used with verbs like vivere (to live), aver(e) avuto (to have had), and condurre (to lead): vivere/condurre una vita felice. In questions, it can ask whether someone’s life overall has been happy.
target_language_example: Spero che tu possa vivere una vita felice.
native_language_example: I hope you can live a happy life.
