additional_notes: Usually means "once" or "one time" when talking about how many times something happened. In other contexts, especially with past descriptions, it can mean "once" in the sense of "formerly" or "used to".
target_language_example: Ci sono andato una volta.
native_language_example: I went there once.

additional_notes: Used to say how often something happens (frequency). It commonly goes after the verb: "Ci vediamo una volta al mese". Related patterns: "una volta alla settimana" (once a week), "due volte al mese" (twice a month).
target_language_example: Faccio la spesa una volta al mese.
native_language_example: I do the grocery shopping once a month.

additional_notes: Used to say something happens with weekly frequency. It often comes at the end of the sentence, but it can also appear earlier for emphasis. You can change the time unit: una volta al giorno (once a day), una volta al mese (once a month), una volta all’anno (once a year).
target_language_example: Vado in piscina una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the pool once a week.

additional_notes: Used to talk about frequency. It can go at the beginning or end of the sentence (often after the verb): “Ci vediamo una volta alla settimana.” Similar patterns: “una volta al giorno” (once a day), “due volte alla settimana” (twice a week).
target_language_example: Vado in palestra una volta alla settimana.
native_language_example: I go to the gym once a week.

additional_notes: Used to introduce a condition in time: after something happens or is completed, then the next thing will happen. Often followed by a verb in the present tense for future meaning (e.g., “Una volta che mi dai…, chiamerò…” = “Once you give me…, I’ll call…”). Similar to “dopo che” (“after”), but “una volta che” emphasizes “as soon as/once it’s done.”
target_language_example: Una volta che finisci il lavoro, possiamo uscire.
native_language_example: Once you finish the work, we can go out.

meaning: once in a while; every now and then.
additional_notes: Used to talk about something that happens occasionally, not regularly. Often placed at the beginning of the sentence for emphasis, but it can also go after the verb (e.g., "Gioco a tennis una volta ogni tanto").
target_language_example: Una volta ogni tanto prendo un caffè al bar.
native_language_example: Once in a while I have a coffee at the café.

meaning: once and for all; for good (finally, permanently).
additional_notes: Used to say you want to end or settle something definitively, so it won’t come back (a problem, argument, situation, or person). Often appears with verbs like finire (to stop), sistemare (to fix), liberare (to free), risolvere (to solve), or in a slightly threatening tone: la pagherai una volta per tutte (“you’ll pay for it once and for all”).
target_language_example: Chiudiamo questa discussione una volta per tutte.
native_language_example: Let’s end this discussion once and for all.

additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something happens (or should happen) a single time. Common in warnings or firm statements ("I’ll say it only once") and to mean you’ve done something only one time in your life ("We went there only once").
target_language_example: Te lo ripeto: lo spiego una volta sola.
native_language_example: I’ll repeat it: I’ll explain it only once.

additional_notes: Used when asking for coffee or tea to specify one cube of sugar. Often said on its own as a polite request (e.g., at a bar/café). Plural: "due zollette di zucchero" (two sugar cubes).
target_language_example: Nel tè vorrei una zolletta di zucchero, grazie.
native_language_example: In my tea I’d like a sugar cube, thanks.

meaning: one by one (one at a time).
additional_notes: Used to say actions happen individually, in sequence. It agrees with the noun’s gender/number: una ad una for feminine plural things (le uova, le auto), uno ad uno for masculine plural (i documenti). You can also hear/see the variant “una per una”.
target_language_example: Ho controllato le risposte una ad una.
native_language_example: I checked the answers one by one.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person out of a group of feminine plural nouns: una delle ragazze (one of the girls), una delle cose (one of the things), una delle spiagge (one of the beaches). For masculine plural, use “uno dei” (uno dei ragazzi = one of the boys). Often followed by a superlative: una delle più belle = one of the most beautiful.
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei miei ristoranti preferiti, ma quella è una delle mie pizzerie preferite.
native_language_example: This is one of my favorite restaurants, but that is one of my favorite pizzerias.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group of feminine plural nouns (e.g., amiche, cose, magliette). It’s the feminine form; compare masculine “uno dei”. Often followed by a superlative: “una delle più + adjective” = “one of the most + adjective”.
target_language_example: Vorrei una delle tue borse, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like one of your bags, please.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group: “una di + plural noun/pronoun.” Common with demonstratives (una di queste/quelle…), numbers (una di queste due…), or pronouns (una di loro/voi). For masculine you usually say “uno di” (one of).
target_language_example: Vorrei una di queste magliette, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like one of these T-shirts, please.

meaning: “one of us” (referring to a female person).
additional_notes: Used to say that a woman/girl belongs to your group (“one of us”). With a male person or a mixed group, you typically use **uno di noi**. You can also specify a smaller group: **una di noi due** = “one of the two of us.”
target_language_example: Giulia è una di noi, quindi può venire alla riunione.
native_language_example: Giulia is one of us, so she can come to the meeting.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a specific item or person belonging to a previously mentioned or implied group of feminine plural things/people (“quelle”). Often followed by a noun (e.g., "una di quelle candele" = “one of those candles”) or used more generally about a type of person (“una di quelle donne” = “one of those women”). For masculine, use "uno di quelli".
target_language_example: Puoi passarmi una di quelle bottiglie, per favore?
native_language_example: Can you pass me one of those bottles, please?

meaning: "one of those" (referring to a feminine noun).
additional_notes: Used to pick out or ask for one item from a group already known/pointed out in context (e.g., items on a shelf). It agrees with the noun: una (feminine singular). Variations: "uno di quelli" (masculine singular), "una di queste" (feminine, "these"), "uno di questi" (masculine, "these"). Often follows verbs like comprare (to buy), prendere (to take), volere (to want), avere (to have).
target_language_example: Scusi, posso avere una di quelle borse, per favore?
native_language_example: Excuse me, can I have one of those bags, please?

meaning: "one of these" (referring to a feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to pick one item from a group indicated by "queste" (“these”, feminine plural). It agrees with the noun: for masculine you say "uno di questi"; for plural “some of these” you can say "alcune di queste" (fem.) / "alcuni di questi" (masc.). Often used in questions like "Hai mai usato una di queste?" (“Have you ever used one of these?”).
target_language_example: Posso provarne una di queste?
native_language_example: Can I try one of these?

meaning: "one of these before" / "one of these earlier".
additional_notes: Used to say or ask whether someone has previously seen/received one item from a group you’re pointing to or talking about (often with "Hai/Ha mai visto...?"). It agrees with the noun: "una di queste" (feminine singular), but you may also hear "uno di questi" (masculine singular) or plural versions ("alcune di queste", etc.). "Prima" here means "before/earlier" (not "first").
target_language_example: Ho già comprato una di queste prima, ma questa è più grande.
native_language_example: I’ve already bought one of these before, but this one is bigger.

additional_notes: Used to invite, ask, or talk about someone becoming part of your group or activity. "Unirsi" is a reflexive verb (unirsi = to join), and it’s often followed by "a" + a person/group: unirsi a noi/voi/loro. You’ll commonly see it after verbs like chiedere (to ask), convincere (to convince), invitare (to invite), or in polite offers like "Può unirsi a noi".
target_language_example: Può unirsi a noi se vuole.
native_language_example: You can join us if you want.

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to become part of your group or to take part in an activity with you. It’s the informal (tu) form: unirti = “to join” + ti (“yourself/you”), a noi = “us”. For the polite form, you’d say: "unirsi a noi" or "vuole unirsi a noi?".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi unirti a noi domani.
native_language_example: If you want, you can join us tomorrow.

additional_notes: “Sbirro” is an informal slang word for a police officer and can sound distrustful or insulting depending on context and tone. In neutral/polite situations, prefer “un poliziotto / una poliziotta” or “un agente (di polizia)”. “Uno” is the masculine indefinite article used before s+consonant (sb-, sp-, st-, etc.), z, gn, ps, x, y: e.g., “uno sbirro”, “uno studente”.
target_language_example: Secondo me è uno sbirro, quindi stai attento a quello che dici.
native_language_example: I think he’s a cop, so be careful what you say.

additional_notes: Used to say something is meant as humor or not serious: "È/era solo uno scherzo" (“It’s/it was just a joke”). Often appears in the negative to stress seriousness: "Non è uno scherzo!" / "Questo non è uno scherzo" (“This is no joke”).
target_language_example: Scusa, era solo uno scherzo.
native_language_example: Sorry, it was just a joke.

additional_notes: Used when talking about buying/getting a gift for someone’s mother. Note that "sua" can mean "his" or "her" (it agrees with the thing owned: "madre"), so the context tells you whose mother. "Uno" is used because "scialle" starts with s + consonant (sc-).
target_language_example: Ho comprato uno scialle per sua madre.
native_language_example: I bought a shawl for his/her mother.

additional_notes: Used for a male person; for a female scientist, say “una scienziata”. “Uno” is used (instead of “un”) because “scienziato” starts with “s” + consonant (sc-). Often used with “diventare” (to become) or “essere” (to be).
target_language_example: Da grande, vuole diventare uno scienziato.
native_language_example: When he grows up, he wants to become a scientist.

additional_notes: "Scoiattolo" is masculine; before most words it takes the article "uno" (e.g., uno scoiattolo, uno studente). The plural is "scoiattoli" ("due scoiattoli"). You’ll often hear it in exclamations when you spot one: "Guarda, uno scoiattolo!"
target_language_example: Nel parco ho visto uno scoiattolo.
native_language_example: In the park I saw a squirrel.

additional_notes: Used when negotiating or asking for a larger reduction in price. It literally means “a greater discount.” You can also hear: “uno sconto più grande” (more common in everyday speech) or “uno sconto più alto” (a higher discount).
target_language_example: Possiamo avere uno sconto maggiore se paghiamo in contanti?
native_language_example: Can we get a bigger discount if we pay in cash?

additional_notes: Used to say someone’s job or identity is “a writer,” often with adjectives (e.g., uno scrittore famoso) or with “di…” to add details (e.g., uno scrittore di grande talento). For a female writer, say “una scrittrice.”
target_language_example: Mio fratello è uno scrittore e lavora da casa.
native_language_example: My brother is a writer and works from home.

additional_notes: Used with verbs in the infinitive (e.g., "fare uno sforzo per + infinitive") to say someone tries hard or makes a special effort. Common with "fare" (to make) and "dovrebbe" (should).
target_language_example: Sto facendo uno sforzo per parlare italiano ogni giorno.
native_language_example: I’m making an effort to speak Italian every day.

additional_notes: Used for looking briefly at something (dare uno sguardo = to take/have a look) or for an exchanged look between people (scambiarsi uno sguardo). It can also mean a meaningful look (a look can “say” something).
target_language_example: Puoi dare uno sguardo a questo documento?
native_language_example: Can you take a look at this document?

meaning: a specialist; an expert (often a doctor or professional).
additional_notes: Used for someone with specialized knowledge in a field. Often followed by **di** (area of expertise) or **in** (field), e.g., *uno specialista di sicurezza / in sicurezza*. In medical contexts it means a specialist doctor (*vedere uno specialista* = to see a specialist). The feminine form is **una specialista**.
target_language_example: Devo prendere un appuntamento con uno specialista.
native_language_example: I need to make an appointment with a specialist.

additional_notes: Used to say that an activity isn’t useful or worth doing. Often appears with extra details like “prezioso” (precious) or “e sforzi” (and effort). You can use it after “è/era/è stato” (it is/was/it was) to judge a situation: “È uno spreco di tempo.”
target_language_example: Aspettare senza informazioni è uno spreco di tempo.
native_language_example: Waiting with no information is a waste of time.

additional_notes: Used for a small bite between meals. Very common with the verb "fare": "fare uno spuntino" = "to have a snack". You can also offer it politely: "Vuole uno spuntino?" (formal) / "Vuoi uno spuntino?" (informal).
target_language_example: Ho fame: facciamo uno spuntino prima di cena.
native_language_example: I’m hungry: let’s have a snack before dinner.

meaning: a state of (a condition or situation).
additional_notes: Used before a noun to describe a condition (emergency, shock, anger, etc.). Often appears in fixed expressions like "uno stato di emergenza" (a state of emergency) or with emotions/mental or physical conditions: "essere in uno stato di..." = "to be in a state of...".
target_language_example: Dopo l’incidente, era in uno stato di confusione.
native_language_example: After the accident, he was in a state of confusion.

meaning: a lifestyle; a way of living.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s habits and daily choices (diet, exercise, work-life balance, etc.). Often followed by an adjective like sano/salutare (healthy), sedentario (sedentary), frenetico (hectic), semplice (simple), or by “da + noun” (e.g., uno stile di vita da atleta = an athlete’s lifestyle).
target_language_example: Da quando lavoro da casa, conduco uno stile di vita più tranquillo.
native_language_example: Since I started working from home, I lead a calmer lifestyle.

additional_notes: Most commonly means “a foreigner” (a person from another country): *Tom è uno straniero.* It can also be used more figuratively as “a stranger/someone unfamiliar” to a situation or idea: *La morte resterà per lui sempre uno straniero* (“death will always remain something unfamiliar to him”). Masculine singular; the feminine is *una straniera*.
target_language_example: Per uno straniero è facile perdersi in questa città.
native_language_example: For a foreigner, it’s easy to get lost in this city.

meaning: a jerk / an asshole (a very offensive insult).
additional_notes: Very vulgar and insulting. Used to call someone a terrible, unpleasant person (usually a man; for a woman you’d say “una stronza”). Commonly used after “Sei…” (“You’re…”) or “Sei stato…” (“You’ve been…”). Avoid in polite situations; use only if you understand the social consequences.
target_language_example: Sei proprio uno stronzo, signor Berg.
native_language_example: You’re really an asshole, Mr. Berg.

meaning: a tool; an instrument (especially a musical instrument).
additional_notes: Used for something you use to do a task (a tool) or to achieve a goal (“a powerful tool”, “a tool for improving…”). With music verbs like "suonare" it usually means a musical instrument: "suonare uno strumento" = "to play an instrument". It can also be used figuratively to mean someone is being used as a means to an end (and can sound insulting, e.g. "uno strumento inutile").
target_language_example: Questo sito è uno strumento utile per imparare l’italiano.
native_language_example: This website is a useful tool for learning Italian.

meaning: "a tool with which" / "a tool to (do something) with".
additional_notes: Used to introduce the tool or instrument needed to perform an action. It’s typically followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., aprire, tagliare, riparare). "Con cui" literally means "with which" and refers back to the tool (strumento).
target_language_example: Mi serve uno strumento con cui tagliare questa corda.
native_language_example: I need a tool to cut this rope with.

additional_notes: Used to refer to any instrument used to make music (e.g., chitarra, pianoforte, violino). Often appears with verbs like suonare (to play) or imparare a suonare (to learn to play). The noun changes with gender/number: uno strumento musicale (sing.), due strumenti musicali (pl.).
target_language_example: Vorrei imparare a suonare uno strumento musicale.
native_language_example: I’d like to learn to play a musical instrument.

additional_notes: "Uno" is the masculine singular indefinite article used before words starting with s + consonant (st-, sp-, sc-, etc.), z, ps, pn, or gn (e.g., "uno studente"). With "a" (to) you often see the combined form "a uno" → "ad uno" in more formal/written Italian, though in everyday speech "a uno studente" is also common.
target_language_example: In casa con me vive uno studente di medicina.
native_language_example: A medical student lives in my house with me.

additional_notes: Used to say what subject/field someone studies, especially at university: “uno studente di medicina / di italiano”. For a female student: “una studentessa di …”. In the plural: “studenti di … / studentesse di …”. The article (uno/una) may be omitted in some contexts (e.g., in lists or titles).
target_language_example: Marco è uno studente di ingegneria.
native_language_example: Marco is an engineering student.

additional_notes: Used when you mention an uncle and then add extra information about him with a relative clause starting with che (= who/that), e.g. where he lives or where he works. It can also be plural: due zii che…
target_language_example: Ho uno zio che parla tre lingue.
native_language_example: I have an uncle who speaks three languages.

meaning: 'one, two!' (counting to start or keep a rhythm).
additional_notes: Used to count off before starting something (e.g., music, dancing, exercise) or to keep a steady rhythm. Often repeated ("uno, due, uno, due") and may be followed by "e tre" ("and three").
target_language_example: Pronti? Uno, due!
native_language_example: Ready? One, two!

meaning: “one, two, three” (counting; often to start an action like “Ready… go!”).
additional_notes: Used to count out loud. In games or playful contexts it can act like a quick countdown before everyone moves (often followed by an instruction, e.g., “Uno, due, tre, tocca la parete!” = “One, two, three, touch the wall!”).
target_language_example: Uno, due, tre… via!
native_language_example: One, two, three… go!

meaning: “one, two, three, four” (counting; also said before starting).
additional_notes: Used to count out loud (e.g., when learning numbers) or as a quick countdown/beat to start an action (like clapping, taking a photo, beginning a song, etc.). Often said with an exclamation mark when used as a cue to begin.
target_language_example: Uno, due, tre, quattro! Andiamo!
native_language_example: One, two, three, four! Let’s go!

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a plural group. It agrees with the noun you’re talking about: uno dei + masculine plural noun (uno dei luoghi, uno dei tori). For feminine nouns use: una delle (una delle cose). Often followed by a superlative or adjective phrase: uno dei più + adjective ("one of the most...").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei ristoranti più buoni della zona.
native_language_example: This is one of the best restaurants in the area.

additional_notes: Used to single out one animal/person/thing from a known group: uno/una dei/delle + plural noun (e.g., uno dei cani, una delle ragazze). Often followed by a verb describing what that one did.
target_language_example: Uno dei cani è scappato dal giardino.
native_language_example: One of the dogs escaped from the yard.

additional_notes: Used to describe a type of person by adding a relative clause with **che**: **uno che + verb** (“someone who…”). It often comments on someone’s character or habits (sometimes with a judgment). It changes with gender/number: **una che** (a woman who), **uno che** (a man who / someone), **quelli che** (those who).
target_language_example: Non sono uno che si arrende facilmente.
native_language_example: I’m not someone who gives up easily.

additional_notes: Used before a plural noun or plural idea to mean a single member of a set: uno dei ristoranti (one of the restaurants), uno dei guanti (one of the gloves). It often takes a possessive: uno dei miei/tuoi/suoi (one of mine/yours/his/hers/theirs). With feminine singular: una delle; plural: alcuni/e dei/delle.
target_language_example: Vorrei uno dei tuoi consigli.
native_language_example: I’d like one of your pieces of advice.

additional_notes: Used to refer to one member of a group that belongs to you or is connected to you. Often the noun is understood from context (e.g., "uno dei miei (amici)" = one of my friends). It’s masculine singular: for feminine use "una delle mie"; for plural you’ll often hear "alcuni dei miei" / "alcune delle mie".
target_language_example: Luca è uno dei miei migliori amici.
native_language_example: Luca is one of my best friends.

meaning: one of his/her friends (also: one of your friends, formal).
additional_notes: "Uno" = "one"; "dei" = "of the/some"; "suoi" is the plural of "suo" and agrees with "amici" (not with the owner). "Suo/sua/suoi/sue" can mean "his", "her", "its", or "your" (formal "Lei"); context tells you which. Feminine: "una delle sue amiche" (one of her/your female friends).
target_language_example: Uno dei suoi amici vive a Roma.
native_language_example: One of his friends lives in Rome.

additional_notes: Used to indicate a single person or thing belonging to a group: "uno" + "dei" (plural "di + i" = "of the"). The noun after it is usually plural: "uno dei suoi figli" = "one of his sons". For feminine/plural forms you’ll also see: "una delle" (one of the [fem. pl.]), "uno/una degli/delle" depending on gender/number.
target_language_example: Marco è uno dei miei migliori amici.
native_language_example: Marco is one of my best friends.

meaning: "one of my" (followed by a plural noun).
additional_notes: Used to say a single person/thing from your group: uno dei miei + plural noun (libri, cani, denti, amici, zii). It agrees with what “one” is: uno (masc. singular); una delle mie (fem. singular). You can also use plural: due dei miei = “two of my.”
target_language_example: Uno dei miei vicini parla inglese.
native_language_example: One of my neighbors speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to praise a person or thing as belonging to the top group. It agrees with gender/number: uno dei migliori (masc. sing. person/thing), una delle migliori (fem. sing.), uno/una dei/delle migliori + plural noun: È uno dei migliori ristoranti della città. You can also add a field like di + place/group (uno dei migliori del mondo) or a relative clause (uno dei migliori che abbia mai visto/mangiato).
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei migliori film che abbia mai visto.
native_language_example: This is one of the best movies I’ve ever seen.

meaning: one of ours; one of our (people/things).
additional_notes: Used to say that someone or something belongs to “us” or is part of our group/category (family, team, club, students, pets, favorite places, etc.). It’s usually followed by a noun ("uno dei nostri bambini") or a plural category ("uno dei nostri testimoni"), and it agrees in gender/number: "una delle nostre" (feminine), "uno dei nostri" (masculine), "una dei nostri" is not used.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è uno dei nostri studenti.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s one of our students.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a person (or sometimes something) that belongs to your group, side, family, team, organization, etc. It often implies loyalty or shared identity ("one of us"). Grammar: masculine singular; for a woman you can say "una delle nostre". In more neutral English, it can be translated as "one of our members".
target_language_example: Non toccare Marco: è uno dei nostri.
native_language_example: Don’t touch Marco: he’s one of ours.

additional_notes: Used to pick one item/person from a group that belongs to someone. The possessive "suoi" agrees with what is owned (masculine plural): "uno dei suoi libri" = one of his/her books. For feminine plural, use "una delle sue" (e.g., "una delle sue amiche"). For masculine singular, "uno dei suoi" often appears as part of a longer phrase (e.g., "uno dei suoi studenti").
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei suoi film preferiti.
native_language_example: This is one of his/her favorite movies.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single artwork within a set owned/created by someone. "suo/sua/suoi/sue" agrees with the thing possessed (here: "dipinti" = masculine plural), not with the owner, so it can mean either “his” or “her” depending on context.
target_language_example: Questo è uno dei suoi dipinti più famosi.
native_language_example: This is one of his/her most famous paintings.

additional_notes: Used to pick a single person or thing from a group: "uno di voi" (one of you), "uno di questi libri" (one of these books). It agrees with gender/number: "uno di" (masc.), "una di" (fem.), and with plurals: "uno/una dei/delle" (e.g., "uno dei miei amici" = one of my friends; "una delle mie amiche" = one of my (female) friends).
target_language_example: Posso prendere uno di questi dolci?
native_language_example: Can I take one of these desserts?

meaning: “one of them” (referring to a group of people).
additional_notes: Used to say someone is one person among a group. It agrees with gender/number: uno di loro (masc.), una di loro (fem.), uno/una di voi (“one of you”), uno/una di noi (“one of us”). Often follows “essere” (to be): essere uno di loro = to be one of them.
target_language_example: Non voglio essere uno di loro.
native_language_example: I don’t want to be one of them.

additional_notes: Used to say someone belongs to a group (often to show solidarity, protection, or shared identity). It can also be used with suspicion/accusation depending on context (e.g., pointing out a traitor or someone who’s secretly part of the group). You can specify the group: "uno di noi due" = "one of the two of us."
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: è uno di noi.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: he’s one of us.

meaning: "one of those" (one item/person from a group already understood).
additional_notes: Used to point to or refer back to a specific thing (or person) among several, usually something visible or already mentioned. Agree it with what you mean: uno di quelli (masc. sg.), una di quelle (fem. sg.), uno di quelle (mixed/unspecified group; often for people), una di quelli (rare).
target_language_example: Non so quale scegliere: prendo uno di quelli in vetrina.
native_language_example: I don’t know which one to choose: I’ll take one of those in the window.

meaning: one of these days; sometime soon.
additional_notes: Used to mean an unspecified day in the near future (often as a friendly suggestion or vague plan). It can also be used as a warning/threat: “One of these days, I’ll…”. As a stand-alone phrase (“Uno di questi giorni.”) it implies “someday soon / I’ll do it soon,” often without committing to a specific date.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo prenderci un caffè uno di questi giorni.
native_language_example: We should grab a coffee one of these days.

additional_notes: Used to refer to a single item within a group of things that are present, shown, or understood from context. It often appears with questions like Avete mai…? (“Have you ever…?”) and with Ti serve… (“You need…”). You can change gender/number depending on what you’re referring to: una di queste (feminine), uno di quelli / una di quelle (“one of those”).
target_language_example: Vuoi provare uno di questi?
native_language_example: Do you want to try one of these?

meaning: “the man who…” (a man + a relative clause).
additional_notes: Used to introduce a relative clause with **che** (“who/that”) describing a man: **L’uomo che…** = “The man who…”. Often appears with the article (**un uomo che…** = “a man who…”, **l’uomo che…** = “the man who…”). You may see **l’uomo** with elision before a vowel.
target_language_example: L’uomo che lavora qui parla inglese.
native_language_example: The man who works here speaks English.

additional_notes: Used to introduce or identify a man by his name. It’s often followed by the name (e.g., “uomo che si chiama Marco”) or by “come” + name (“uomo che si chiama come me”). In everyday Italian, you’ll also commonly hear “un uomo che si chiama…” or “un uomo di nome…”.
target_language_example: C'è un uomo che si chiama Marco che ti sta cercando.
native_language_example: There’s a man named Marco who is looking for you.

additional_notes: Common everyday phrase: "uomo" = man, "ricco" = rich. Adjective agreement: masculine singular "ricco"; plural "uomini ricchi". You can also hear "un ricco" meaning "a rich person/man" (more like a noun).
target_language_example: Vivere da uomo ricco non significa vivere bene.
native_language_example: Living like a rich man doesn’t mean living well.

additional_notes: Used to say that eggs are what you eat at breakfast time. Very common with verbs like mangiare (to eat) and adverbs like di solito/sempre/spesso (usually/always/often). You can also add other foods: pancetta e uova per colazione (“bacon and eggs for breakfast”).
target_language_example: Oggi voglio uova per colazione.
native_language_example: Today I want eggs for breakfast.

additional_notes: Common breakfast dish. Used with the plural noun phrase "le uova strapazzate"; in polite offers/questions you’ll often hear "Vuole/Volete delle uova strapazzate?" (some scrambled eggs?).
target_language_example: Per colazione prendo le uova strapazzate e un caffè.
native_language_example: For breakfast I’ll have scrambled eggs and a coffee.

additional_notes: Used for an egg boiled in its shell until the yolk and white are firm. Contrast: “uovo alla coque” (soft-boiled). Plural: “uova sode”.
target_language_example: Vuoi un uovo sodo per colazione?
native_language_example: Do you want a hard-boiled egg for breakfast?

additional_notes: An instruction using the tu (2nd person singular) imperative: usa = “use (you)”. It’s common in casual speech, manuals, or when talking to someone you’re on familiar terms with. For a more formal request to one person, use: "Usi questa macchina fotografica."
target_language_example: Usa questa macchina fotografica per fare una foto migliore.
native_language_example: Use this camera to take a better photo.

additional_notes: A very literal combination of usare + il, used before a masculine singular noun: usare il dizionario, usare il computer. The article changes with other nouns, for example usare la for many feminine nouns, lo before some masculine nouns, and l' before vowels.
target_language_example: Non so usare il computer.
native_language_example: I don't know how to use the computer.

additional_notes: A common, neutral phrase for talking about being careful and responsible with spending. Often used with dovere (devo/devi/deve/dobbiamo/dovete/devono) to express advice or obligation.
target_language_example: Dobbiamo usare il denaro con saggezza se vogliamo risparmiare.
native_language_example: We have to use money wisely if we want to save.

meaning: to use mine / to use my (one).
additional_notes: Used when you mean you will use your own item instead of someone else’s. Often appears with a noun ("usare il mio telefono" = "use my phone") or on its own when the noun is understood ("Posso usare il mio?" = "Can I use mine?"). "Il mio" is a possessive pronoun meaning "mine" (masculine singular).
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti, posso usare il mio.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I can use mine.

additional_notes: Used to give someone permission to use your dictionary. The polite form is "Può usare il mio dizionario" (formal you), while "Puoi..." is informal (to a friend). You can add "sempre" (always) or "quando vuoi" (whenever you want) to sound more welcoming.
target_language_example: Se ti serve, puoi usare il mio dizionario.
native_language_example: If you need it, you can use my dictionary.

additional_notes: Built with the verb "usare" (to use) + the possessive "il mio" (my) + the noun "yacht". In everyday Italian you’ll more often hear "usare" for using an object (a phone, an app, a tool). For vehicles/boats, Italians may also say "prendere" (to take) or "andare in barca" (to go boating), depending on the context.
target_language_example: Puoi usare il mio yacht questo weekend?
native_language_example: Can you use my yacht this weekend?

additional_notes: “Il suo / la sua / i suoi / le sue” is the possessive pronoun/adjective with the definite article, and it agrees with the thing owned (il suo dizionario, la sua penna, i suoi libri). It can mean “his,” “her,” “its,” and in formal address (Lei) it can also mean “your.” Often followed by a noun (e.g., usare il suo dizionario), but it can also stand alone if the noun is understood (Posso usare il suo? = Can I use yours?).
target_language_example: Posso usare il suo telefono per un minuto?
native_language_example: Can I use your phone for a minute?

additional_notes: Means using someone else’s computer (suo/sua = “his/her” depending on who owns it). Often appears after verbs like lasciare (“to let/allow”) or permettere (“to permit/allow”), e.g., “Mi ha lasciato usare il suo computer” = “He/She let me use his/her computer.” You can swap in other possessives: usare il mio computer (my), usare il tuo computer (your), usare il loro computer (their).
target_language_example: Posso usare il suo computer per cinque minuti?
native_language_example: Can I use his/her computer for five minutes?

meaning: “to use the” (with a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: “Usare” means “to use.” “La” is the definite article “the” for feminine singular nouns (la macchina, la pala, la ragione). You’ll usually see it followed by the thing being used: usare la + noun. The verb changes with the subject/tense (posso usare…, puoi usare…, devi usare…).
target_language_example: Posso usare la tua penna?
native_language_example: Can I use your pen?

additional_notes: Commonly used for going out socially with someone, and often implies dating/romantic interest depending on context. It’s followed by a person: uscire con lui/lei, uscire con i miei amici. In invitations it can mean “go out (together)”: Vuoi uscire con me stasera?
target_language_example: Non voglio uscire con lui perché beve troppo.
native_language_example: I don’t want to go out with him because he drinks too much.

meaning: to get out of here / to leave this place.
additional_notes: Used to say you want (or need) to leave the current place. Often expresses urgency or frustration, especially with adesso (“now”) or with an exclamation. It can be used literally (leaving a room/building) or more generally (leaving a situation).
target_language_example: Dobbiamo uscire da qui prima che sia troppo tardi.
native_language_example: We have to get out of here before it’s too late.

meaning: to get out of here; to leave this place.
additional_notes: Used when you want to leave a place, often urgently or because you feel trapped or unsafe. Common with dovere (Dobbiamo uscire di qui subito. = We have to get out of here right away) and with imperative forms to ask/command someone to let you out: Fammi uscire di qui! (Let me out of here!).
target_language_example: Non mi sento al sicuro: dobbiamo uscire di qui adesso.
native_language_example: I don’t feel safe: we have to get out of here now.

additional_notes: "Utilizzare" means "to use" (a bit more formal than "usare"). "Il suo" is a polite/formal way to say "your" (to one person, Lei), and it can also mean "his" or "her" depending on context. Often used with verbs like "permettere" or "lasciare" to ask/allow someone to use a computer.
target_language_example: Potrei utilizzare il suo computer per un minuto?
native_language_example: Could I use your computer for a minute?

additional_notes: Used when you give someone permission to use something that belongs to you. "La mia" is a possessive pronoun meaning “mine” and usually refers to a feminine noun already mentioned (e.g., "la mia scrivania" = "my desk"). In everyday speech, "usare" is more common than "utilizzare".
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi utilizzare la mia penna.
native_language_example: If you want, you can use my pen.

additional_notes: Form of the verb andare (“to go”): va = “he/she goes” or “you (formal) go.” Use va a + place/destination (va a Boston, va a casa) or va a + activity/event (va a un picnic, va a caccia). Often answers “Where is he/she going?” (Dove va?). In questions, Italian may omit the subject: Va a Londra? = “Is he/she going to London?”
target_language_example: Va a scuola in bici.
native_language_example: He/She goes to school by bike.

meaning: “(He/she) goes to work on foot” / “(He/she) walks to work.”
additional_notes: Used to say someone commutes to their workplace by walking. "Va" is the 3rd person singular of "andare" (to go): lui/lei va. Other forms: io vado, tu vai, noi andiamo, voi andate, loro vanno. "A piedi" means "on foot" (by walking).
target_language_example: Lei va a lavorare a piedi quando fa bel tempo.
native_language_example: She walks to work when the weather is nice.

additional_notes: Formed from andare (to go): va = 'he/she goes' + a scuola = 'to school'. Used to talk about someone attending school or going there regularly (often as part of a routine). You can add how someone goes (in autobus, in bicicletta) or when (il sabato). For 'I go to school' you say: vado a scuola.
target_language_example: Mia sorella va a scuola ogni giorno.
native_language_example: My sister goes to school every day.

meaning: (He/she) goes to school on foot (walks to school).
additional_notes: Common way to say someone goes somewhere walking. Structure: andare + a + place (a scuola) + a piedi (“on foot”). Conjugate "andare" for the subject: vado/va/andiamo/vanno a scuola a piedi.
target_language_example: Mia sorella solitamente va a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: My sister usually walks to school.

meaning: “goes to work by/in (a means of transport)”.
additional_notes: Used to say how someone commutes to work. After "in" you usually add the transport: "in treno" (by train), "in auto / in macchina / in automobile" (by car). With a specific vehicle you often use "con" instead (e.g., "va al lavoro con la mia macchina").
target_language_example: Lei va al lavoro in autobus ogni mattina.
native_language_example: She goes to work by bus every morning.

additional_notes: Very common informal filler in speech. Used to accept something, end a topic, or move on (similar to “anyway”). Often written as “vabbè” or “vabbè,” especially in informal texting.
target_language_example: Va beh, allora ci vediamo domani.
native_language_example: Alright then, I’ll see you tomorrow.

additional_notes: A very common expression used to agree, accept, say something is fine, or ask for confirmation. At the end of a sentence, va bene? often means "okay?" or "is that okay?". Literally it is something like "it goes well," but that is not how it is usually translated.
target_language_example: Ci vediamo alle sette, va bene?
native_language_example: We'll see each other at seven, okay?

additional_notes: Used in conversation to accept what was said (or decide something) and then introduce the next step or consequence. Often said with a pause: “Va bene, allora…” = “Alright, then…” You can also say just “Va bene” (“okay”) or “Allora” (“so/then”).
target_language_example: Va bene, allora ci vediamo domani alle nove.
native_language_example: Okay then, I’ll see you tomorrow at nine.

additional_notes: Used to accept something while adding a limitation, condition, or concern right after. Often followed by a question (Va bene, ma come?) or a restriction (…ma solo lì / …ma dopo / …ma prima). In speech it can sound like “Alright, but…”.
target_language_example: Va bene, ma non oggi: domani.
native_language_example: Okay, but not today: tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to agree/accept (“va bene” = “OK/fine”) and then immediately add a negative instruction/request (often a gentle command: “don’t move/cry”) or acknowledge a negative fact (“you don’t have a boss”). In speech it can sound like “Va bene, non…”.
target_language_example: Va bene, non dire niente a nessuno.
native_language_example: OK, don’t tell anyone anything.

meaning: "Okay, okay" / "Alright, alright" (often to agree or to calm someone down).
additional_notes: Repeating *va bene* adds emphasis. It can signal quick agreement, but very often it’s used to stop an argument or to show reluctant acceptance (like “fine, fine”). Tone matters: it can sound reassuring or slightly annoyed depending on how it’s said.
target_language_example: Va bene, va bene—adesso mi fermo.
native_language_example: Okay, okay—I’ll stop now.

meaning: “Is it okay if…?” / “Is it alright if…?”
additional_notes: Used to ask for permission or check if something is acceptable. Often followed by a verb phrase (usually in the present tense): “Va bene se entro adesso?” = “Is it okay if I come in now?” You can also use it without “se”: “Va bene se…?” is a very common spoken pattern.
target_language_example: Va bene se pago con la carta?
native_language_example: Is it okay if I pay by card?

meaning: (with “non”) “goes nowhere / isn’t going anywhere” (literally or figuratively: isn’t making progress).
additional_notes: Most often used in the negative: “non va da nessuna parte.” It can mean (1) someone is not allowed to leave/go anywhere (“Nessuno va da nessuna parte.” = Nobody’s going anywhere.), or (2) something isn’t getting results / won’t lead to success (“Questo non va da nessuna parte.” = This isn’t going anywhere.).
target_language_example: Se continuiamo a litigare così, questa relazione non va da nessuna parte.
native_language_example: If we keep fighting like this, this relationship isn’t going anywhere.

additional_notes: Used to introduce something considered self-evident or a logical consequence of what was just said. Often follows a condition (e.g., “Se…, va da sé che…”). Common in spoken and written Italian; slightly formal in tone.
target_language_example: Se hai già pagato, va da sé che non devi pagare di nuovo.
native_language_example: If you’ve already paid, it goes without saying that you don’t have to pay again.

meaning: "Do you feel like going to the theater?" / "Would you like to go to the theater?"
additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun to ask if someone is in the mood for doing something: "Ti va di…?" (to you), "Le va di…?" (formal to you), "Vi va di…?" (to you all). Literally it contains "va" (goes), but the meaning is "feel like" rather than physical going.
target_language_example: Ti va di andare a teatro domani sera?
native_language_example: Do you feel like going to the theater tomorrow evening?

meaning: "(he/she/it) goes to" (a place/country) or "goes by" (a means of transport).
additional_notes: “Va” is the 3rd person singular of *andare* (to go). With **in** it’s used for destinations like **countries** (*va in Croazia, va in Francia*) and some **places/buildings** (*va in una moschea*). It’s also used for **how someone goes somewhere** with certain transport words: *va in bicicletta* = “goes by bike.” (For many specific places like cities you often use *a*: *va a Roma*.)
target_language_example: Marta va in Italia a luglio.
native_language_example: Marta goes to Italy in July.

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go). "Va" is the present tense for lui/lei/Lei (he/she/you-formal). Often followed by a purpose: "per + infinitive" (per leggere = to read) or "a + infinitive" (a studiare = to study). You can swap the subject: "Io vado in biblioteca", "Noi andiamo in biblioteca".
target_language_example: Oggi va in biblioteca per studiare.
native_language_example: Today he/she goes to the library to study.

additional_notes: From the verb andare (to go): va = “goes” (also used for “you go” in the formal Lei form). In everyday use it often means attending church services (e.g., on Sundays, at Christmas), not just physically entering the building. For “I go,” say vado in chiesa; for “we go,” andiamo in chiesa.
target_language_example: Mio padre va in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My dad goes to church every Sunday.

meaning: “(he/she) goes to church every …” (followed by a time period, like “Sunday” or “week”).
additional_notes: This is a sentence fragment that normally needs a time expression after ogni (“every”), e.g. ogni domenica (“every Sunday”) or ogni settimana (“every week”). In Italian you often say andare in chiesa (“to go to church”).
target_language_example: Mia nonna va in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My grandma goes to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used to check if a situation is okay (often as a question). Literally it’s like “everything goes well,” but in English you usually say “is everything okay?” You can use it about home, relationships, work, etc. As a reassurance/statement, it’s often said as “va tutto bene.”
target_language_example: Non ti preoccupare, va tutto bene.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, everything’s fine.

additional_notes: Refers to holidays taken in the summer. Often used with possessives: le mie/le tue/le nostre vacanze estive. Common verbs: passare/trascorrere le vacanze estive (to spend your summer vacation).
target_language_example: Quest'anno le nostre vacanze estive saranno in Sicilia.
native_language_example: This year our summer vacation will be in Sicily.

meaning: Go easy / take it easy (with something or someone).
additional_notes: Colloquial imperative (to one person: tu). Often used as a warning to tell someone to slow down, calm down, or not overdo it. Very common with **con/col** + noun/person: **Vacci piano con gli insulti** = “Go easy on the insults,” **Vacci piano con lui** = “Go easy with him.” Can also be used alone: **Vacci piano!** = “Easy!” / “Take it easy!”
target_language_example: Vacci piano con il sale, è già abbastanza salato.
native_language_example: Go easy on the salt, it’s already salty enough.

additional_notes: "Vada" is the polite/formal command (Lei form) of andare (“to go”). With "a" it introduces the destination or purpose: vada a casa (“go home”), vada a parlare (“go and speak”). It can also appear after "Lasci che..." meaning “Let (him/her) go to…”.
target_language_example: Scusi, vada a parlare con il direttore, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please go speak with the manager/director.

additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (Lei form): vada = “(you) go” (from andare). Often said firmly as an instruction: “Vada a parlare con lei.” With lasci/lascia/lasciate che… it means “let him/her go talk to her.” Note: lei (lowercase) can mean “her”; Lei (capitalized) is the polite “you.”
target_language_example: Per favore, vada a parlare con lei adesso.
native_language_example: Please, go talk to her now.

additional_notes: Uses the formal imperative with Lei: vada (from andare, “to go”). It’s used to tell someone politely or formally to go and help a person (Vada ad aiutare sua madre.) or to help with an activity (Vada ad aiutare a lavare i piatti.). In everyday speech, Italians often shorten this to “Vada ad aiutare Tom” = “Go help Tom.”
target_language_example: Vada ad aiutare i suoi colleghi, per favore.
native_language_example: Please go help your colleagues.

meaning: "go away" / "leave" (formal/polite: to someone you address as Lei).
additional_notes: Uses the Lei form (formal/polite) of the verb: "vada" = (that you) go. Often used as a command: "Vada via!" = "Go away!" It can also appear after "che" to express a wish/order: "Voglio/Che vada via" = "I want/Make sure he/she goes away."
target_language_example: Mi scusi, ma deve andare: vada via, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, but you have to go: please leave.

additional_notes: From the verb "andare" (to go): "vado" = "I go" / "I’m going". Common patterns: (1) "vado a" + place = "I go to" (often implies movement): "vado a casa" = "I’m going home". (2) "vado a" + infinitive = "I’m going to" (to do something): "vado a spegnere la radio" = "I’m going to turn off the radio".
target_language_example: Scusa, vado a prendere un caffè.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going to get a coffee.

meaning: I’m going home / I’m going to (my) house.
additional_notes: Used to say you’re leaving and heading home. Often said on its own as a simple statement (like “I’m going home.”). In Italian you usually don’t need a possessive: “a casa” commonly means “home” (your own). You can add details like time or who you’re with: “Vado a casa, è tardi” (I’m going home, it’s late) or “Vado a casa con…” (I’m going home with…).
target_language_example: Scusa, vado a casa: domani lavoro presto.
native_language_example: Sorry, I’m going home: I work early tomorrow.

additional_notes: Used to say you’re going to bed / going to sleep, often with a time (alle dieci = at 10). It’s the 1st-person singular of andare a letto (to go to bed).
target_language_example: Sono stanco: vado a letto.
native_language_example: I’m tired: I’m going to bed.

meaning: I'm going to go get/pick up (something/someone).
additional_notes: Used when you leave to fetch something or pick someone up. It’s the present tense of "andare a" + infinitive: "(io) vado a" = "I’m going to" and "prendere" = "to take/get". Common with objects (le cose, del cibo) and people (i bambini) and often implies you’ll come back soon.
target_language_example: Aspetta qui: vado a prendere un caffè e torno.
native_language_example: Wait here: I'm going to get a coffee and I'll be back.

additional_notes: Used to say you go to school (often as part of your daily routine, or today specifically). Italian often drops the subject, so you can simply say “Vado a scuola.” You can add details like time/frequency (oggi, quasi sempre) or transportation (in macchina, in bici).
target_language_example: Domani vado a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I go to school on foot.

meaning: “I go to school on foot” / “I walk to school.”
additional_notes: Common way to say how you get to school. Uses the present tense of andare (vado = I go). Italians often omit the subject pronoun (Io) because it’s already clear from the verb. You can swap scuola for other places (es. vado al lavoro a piedi = I walk to work).
target_language_example: Quando fa bel tempo, vado a scuola a piedi.
native_language_example: When the weather is nice, I walk to school.

additional_notes: Used to say how you travel to school. In Italian, the transport is often introduced with “in” + vehicle (in autobus, in treno, in macchina). You can swap “a scuola” with another destination: “Vado al lavoro in autobus.”
target_language_example: Di solito vado a scuola in autobus, ma oggi vado a piedi.
native_language_example: I usually go to school by bus, but today I'm walking.

meaning: "I go to work" ("I’m going to work").
additional_notes: Used with the verb andare (to go) in the present tense. It can mean a routine (“I go to work every day”) or something happening soon (“I’m going to work earlier tomorrow”). Often followed by how you travel: a piedi (on foot), in autobus (by bus), in bici (by bike).
target_language_example: Oggi vado al lavoro in metro.
native_language_example: Today I’m going to work by subway.

additional_notes: Usually used with **non**: **Non vado da nessuna parte!** to insist you won’t leave (often in an argument). **Vado** is 1st person singular of *andare* (“I go”); you can change the subject: **Non vai da nessuna parte** (you’re not going anywhere), **Non andiamo da nessuna parte** (we’re not going anywhere).
target_language_example: Tranquillo, non vado da nessuna parte.
native_language_example: Don’t worry, I’m not going anywhere.

meaning: "I go to" / "I’m going to"; also "I go by" (a means of transport) or "I get into" (a state).
additional_notes: From the verb *andare* (to go): *io vado* = “I go”. You use **vado in** with many destinations (especially countries: *vado in America* = “I’m going to America”), with some transport/ways of going (*vado in bicicletta* = “I go by bike”), and with certain conditions/states (*vado in confusione* = “I get confused”).
target_language_example: Domani vado in Italia per lavoro.
native_language_example: Tomorrow I’m going to Italy for work.

meaning: “Go on!” / “Come on!” (urging someone to act or move).
additional_notes: Repeated imperatives like "vai, vai" are common in spoken Italian. Depending on tone and context it can be encouragement ("Come on, keep going!") or a dismissive push to leave ("Go on, go home."). Often used alone as an exclamation, and can be repeated more times for emphasis ("vai, vai, vai...").
target_language_example: Dai, vai, vai: ce la fai!
native_language_example: Come on, go on: you can do it!

additional_notes: "Vai a" is the 2nd-person singular form of "andare" (you go / go!). It can be followed by a place ("Vai a casa" = go home) or by an infinitive to mean "go and + verb" ("Vai a parlare" = go and talk). In questions it can mean "do you go to…?" ("Vai a scuola?" = do you go to school?).
target_language_example: Vai a comprare il pane, per favore.
native_language_example: Go and buy the bread, please.

additional_notes: Imperative form of "andare" (to go), used to tell someone to go home. Often said as an instruction or order. You can add details like "vai a casa da tua moglie" (go home to your wife) or combine it with another command: "vai a casa e cambiati" (go home and change).
target_language_example: È tardi: vai a casa.
native_language_example: It’s late: go home.

additional_notes: From andare (to go) + a + dormire (to sleep). It can be a statement (“you go to bed”) or, very often, an imperative telling someone to go to bed (“Go to sleep!”). For questions you’ll also see: «Quando vai a dormire?» (“When do you go to bed?”).
target_language_example: È tardi: vai a dormire!
native_language_example: It’s late: go to bed!

additional_notes: Extremely offensive and aggressive. Used to tell someone off or dismiss them with contempt. Usually addressed directly to a person (“Vai a farti fottere!”). Avoid in polite or everyday situations; it can easily start a fight.
target_language_example: Se non ti sta bene, vai a farti fottere.
native_language_example: If you don’t like it, go f**k yourself.

additional_notes: Imperative form addressed to one person (tu): a common way to tell someone to go to bed (often a child). Related questions use the same phrase: “A che ora vai a letto?” = “What time do you go to bed?” You can add time words like adesso/ora (now) or in orario (on time).
target_language_example: Dai, è tardi: vai a letto!
native_language_example: Come on, it’s late: go to bed!

additional_notes: Used to tell someone ("tu") to go and talk to a person. Common in suggestions/questions (Perché non vai a parlare con...?) and in direct instructions (Vai a parlare con...). You can also say "vai a parlare con" + a title/role (il mio collega, la mia collega).
target_language_example: Se hai un problema, vai a parlare con la responsabile.
native_language_example: If you have a problem, go talk to the manager.

additional_notes: Common instruction using vai (you go) + a + prendere (to take/get). Used for fetching items (food, drinks, objects) or picking up a person (e.g., by car or to go bring them). In speech it can also be shortened to "vai a prenderlo/la/li/le" (go get him/her/them) or "vai a prenderne" (go get some).
target_language_example: Vai a prendere le chiavi e poi torniamo a casa.
native_language_example: Go get the keys and then we'll go home.

additional_notes: "Vai" is the present tense of "andare" (to go) for "tu". Used to ask or state that someone goes/attends school; you can add days/times like "il sabato" (on Saturdays). For polite/formal "you," use "Va a scuola?" (Lei).
target_language_example: Vai a scuola oggi o resti a casa?
native_language_example: Are you going to school today or are you staying home?

additional_notes: Imperative (tu) form of "andare avanti". Used to tell someone to continue speaking or doing something ("Vai avanti con la tua storia"), to proceed without you ("Vai avanti da solo"), or to encourage someone to do something/confirm permission ("Vai avanti, spara" = "Go ahead, shoot/say it"). Can also mean to move forward physically ("go on ahead").
target_language_example: Se vuoi, vai avanti: io ti ascolto.
native_language_example: If you want, go ahead—I’m listening.

meaning: “go like that / like this” (also: “that’s it, keep going!”).
additional_notes: Literally “you go like this/that.” Used (1) as a question showing surprise/criticism: “You’re leaving like that?” (e.g., without saying goodbye, without getting ready), and (2) as an encouraging exclamation meaning “That’s the way! Keep it up!” Repeating it (“Vai così, vai così!”) can sound like a chant to cheer someone on.
target_language_example: Dai, vai così: stai facendo progressi!
native_language_example: Come on, keep it up: you’re making progress!

meaning: (usually with **non**) “you won’t get anywhere / you won’t make any progress.”
additional_notes: Most commonly used as **non vai da nessuna parte**. It can mean literally “you can’t go anywhere from here,” but very often it’s figurative: “you’ll never succeed / you won’t move forward” (e.g., without effort, without the right resources, etc.). You can also say **non andiamo da nessuna parte** (“we’re not getting anywhere”).
target_language_example: Se continui a rimandare, non vai da nessuna parte.
native_language_example: If you keep putting it off, you won’t get anywhere.

meaning: “you go to / you go into” (vai in + place).
additional_notes: Used with andare (“to go”) + in to talk about going to a place, especially countries/continents (in Europa), and many locations like church/theater (in chiesa, in teatro). With specific places you may also see an article: in questa chiesa (“in this church”). Note: in insults like “Vai in culo” it’s very rude (literally “go in [your] ass,” meaning “fuck off”).
target_language_example: Vai in Italia quest’estate?
native_language_example: Are you going to Italy this summer?

additional_notes: Imperative form of **andare via** (“to go away/leave”). It can be a firm order and may sound rude depending on tone and context (especially when shouted). Often used with **da qui** (“from here”) or **subito** (“right away”): *Vai via da qui!* / *Vai via subito!* You can also use it more neutrally in urgent situations (e.g., “get out/leave now”).
target_language_example: C'è pericolo: vai via subito!
native_language_example: It’s dangerous: leave right away!

additional_notes: Used to say that an action or experience is worth the effort, time, or cost. Often followed by an infinitive: "Vale la pena + verb" (e.g., "Vale la pena vedere..."). In the negative: "non vale la pena" = "it’s not worth it".
target_language_example: Non vale la pena discutere adesso.
native_language_example: It’s not worth arguing right now.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort or time. Most often followed by an infinitive: "Vale la pena di + verbo" (e.g., "vale la pena di provare"). You’ll also see "vale la pena" without "di" when it’s not directly followed by a verb.
target_language_example: Vale la pena di visitare Napoli in primavera.
native_language_example: It’s worth visiting Naples in the spring.

additional_notes: Used to say something is worth doing, especially in passive forms like “vale la pena di essere visitato/tradotto/considerato” = “it’s worth visiting/translating/considering.” The subject is the thing that’s worth it. You’ll often see it with a past participle that agrees in gender/number: visitato/visitata/visitati/visitate.
target_language_example: Quel film vale la pena di essere visto al cinema.
native_language_example: That movie is worth seeing at the cinema.

additional_notes: Used to recommend a place or attraction, meaning the visit is worth the time/effort. Very common pattern: “Vale la pena + infinitive” (e.g., visitare, vedere, provare). You can also use it with a noun: “Vale la pena la visita?” = “Is the visit worth it?”
target_language_example: Se sei in città, vale la pena visitare il centro storico.
native_language_example: If you’re in town, it’s worth visiting the old town.

meaning: to be worth it; to be worth the effort.
additional_notes: Used to say that something is worthwhile. Commonly appears with the particle "ne" ("Ne vale la pena" = "It’s worth it"), but the base multi-word term is "valere la pena". You can also use it with an infinitive: "Vale la pena provare" = "It’s worth trying." In questions/negatives: "Ne vale la pena?" / "Non ne vale la pena."
target_language_example: Visitare questo museo può valere la pena, perché è bellissimo.
native_language_example: Visiting this museum can be worth it, because it’s beautiful.

meaning: “to be worth it” / “to be worth doing.”
additional_notes: Used to say something is worth the effort, time, or cost. Typically appears after expressions that trigger the subjunctive (e.g., *pensi che / credi che / mi chiedo se*), hence *valga la pena*. You can also say *ne valga la pena* (“that it’s worth it”), with *ne* referring back to the thing you’re considering.
target_language_example: Mi chiedo se valga la pena frequentare un corso di lingua.
native_language_example: I wonder if it’s worth taking a language course.

additional_notes: From the verb "andare" (to go): "vanno" = "they go" (also used for "you" plural formal in some contexts). "Andare in chiesa" often means going to church for a service/Mass, and it’s commonly used with time expressions like "ogni domenica" (every Sunday) or "la domenica mattina" (on Sunday morning). You can change the subject: "vado in chiesa" (I go), "vai in chiesa" (you go), "va in chiesa" (he/she goes).
target_language_example: I miei nonni vanno in chiesa ogni domenica.
native_language_example: My grandparents go to church every Sunday.

additional_notes: Used in questions like “Come ti vanno le cose?” to ask how someone is doing or how the situation is going. The indirect object changes with the person: mi (to me), ti (to you), le (to you formal), ci (to us), vi (to you plural), gli (to him). Often followed by a place or context (e.g., “lassù”).
target_language_example: Ciao Marco, come ti vanno le cose al lavoro?
native_language_example: Hi Marco, how are things going at work?

additional_notes: A common household item: the tub you fill with water to take a bath. Often used with verbs like fare il bagno (to take a bath) or pulire (to clean).
target_language_example: C'è una vasca da bagno in questo hotel?
native_language_example: Is there a bathtub in this hotel?

additional_notes: Combination of pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you” (to you all, or formal to one person), **lo** = “it” (masculine singular; often stands for a whole idea). Common with verbs like **dire** (to tell), **chiedere** (to ask), **assicurare** (to assure): *Ve lo dico* = “I’m telling you (it).” If the "it" is feminine, you’ll hear **ve la** instead.
target_language_example: Ve lo spiego domani.
native_language_example: I’ll explain it to you tomorrow.

additional_notes: An emphatic way to insist you’re sure about something or that others should listen to you (“believe me”). Literally it’s “I tell it to you”: **ve** = “to you” (often plural or polite), **lo** = “it/that”, **dico** = “I say/tell”, **io** = “I”. It can stand alone (Ve lo dico io!) or be added at the end of a sentence for emphasis.
target_language_example: Non preoccuparti: andrà tutto bene, ve lo dico io.
native_language_example: Don’t worry: everything will be fine, I’m telling you.

meaning: "to you" + "of it/them" or "from there" (a common pronoun combo).
additional_notes: It’s a combination of two pronouns placed before the verb: **ve** = “to you (plural)” (also used as the polite **you** in some regions), and **ne** = “of it/of them/some” or “from there/away.” Very common with **andarsene** (“to go away/leave”): *Ve ne state andando?* = “Are you leaving?” It’s also used with quantities: *Ve ne posso prendere di più* = “I can take more (of them/it),” and with *una* meaning “one (thing)” in *Ve ne dobbiamo una* = “We owe you one.”
target_language_example: Ve ne posso dare due, se volete.
native_language_example: I can give you two of them, if you want.

additional_notes: Form of the pronominal verb "andarsene" (= to leave, go away). "Ve" refers to "you" (plural) and "ne" adds the idea of leaving from here/from a place. Used in questions like "Ve ne andate?" (= Are you leaving?) and in either/or statements like "O ve ne andate voi o ce ne andiamo noi" (= Either you leave or we leave).
target_language_example: Scusate, ve ne andate già?
native_language_example: Sorry, are you leaving already?

additional_notes: Used to talk about the past in a nostalgic way. Often appears in phrases like "per amore dei vecchi tempi" (for old times’ sake) or "in nome dei vecchi tempi" (in the name of the old times), meaning you do something because of shared history or memories.
target_language_example: Facciamolo per amore dei vecchi tempi.
native_language_example: Let’s do it for old times’ sake.

additional_notes: Usually a respectful/polite way to refer to an older woman (more courteous than just saying "vecchia"). It can be used with "una/quella/la" depending on whether the person is unknown, indicated, or already mentioned.
target_language_example: Ho aiutato la vecchia signora ad attraversare la strada.
native_language_example: I helped the elderly lady cross the street.

meaning: an old friend; a long-time friend.
additional_notes: Used for someone you’ve known for a long time (often from the past, e.g., school/childhood). Here vecchio means “long-standing/previous,” not necessarily “elderly.” Often appears with possessives: il mio/un vecchio amico.
target_language_example: Ho incontrato un vecchio amico al bar dopo tanti anni.
native_language_example: I ran into an old friend at the café after many years.

meaning: “my old friend/buddy” (affectionate way to address someone).
additional_notes: Used as a familiar, often affectionate form of address (usually to a male friend). It can sound warm and friendly, and sometimes mildly ironic depending on tone. Often placed at the end of a sentence (e.g., “Ciao, vecchio mio”) or said on its own.
target_language_example: Come va, vecchio mio? È da tanto che non ci vediamo.
native_language_example: How’s it going, buddy? We haven’t seen each other in a long time.

additional_notes: An infinitive phrase often used after another verb (e.g., voglio/posso/devo) to talk about the plan or ability to visit your parents. You can change the possessive and the people: vedere i tuoi genitori (your parents), vedere i suoi genitori (his/her parents).
target_language_example: Questo weekend voglio vedere i miei genitori.
native_language_example: This weekend I want to see my parents.

additional_notes: A regular, compositional combination of vedere + il. It is not a fixed expression: il is the masculine singular definite article ('the') used before many masculine singular nouns, but it may change to lo or l' depending on the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Voglio vedere il film stasera.
native_language_example: I want to see the movie tonight.

additional_notes: Used when you’re talking about seeing something that belongs to you (or is connected to you), e.g. “vedere il mio ritratto” = “see my portrait.” In practice, what changes is the possessive: il mio (masc. singular), la mia (fem. singular), i miei (masc. plural), le mie (fem. plural), matching the noun that follows.
target_language_example: Vuoi venire a vedere il mio appartamento?
native_language_example: Do you want to come see my apartment?

meaning: “to see the” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used when the direct object is feminine singular (la + noun), e.g., la foto, la luna, la mia famiglia. The verb “vedere” changes with the subject (vedo, vedi, vede, vediamo, vedete, vedono). For “to see her/it” as a pronoun, Italian uses “vederla” (one word) instead of “vedere la”.
target_language_example: Da qui possiamo vedere la città.
native_language_example: From here we can see the city.

meaning: to see the light; to finally understand/realize (also: to be born / to come out).
additional_notes: Often used figuratively to mean someone finally understands the truth or changes their mind after a long time. It can also be used more literally to mean “to be born” (a baby) or “to be released/published” (a project, book, idea) — i.e., to “see the light of day.” Common pattern: "finalmente ha iniziato a vedere la luce".
target_language_example: Dopo tante spiegazioni, finalmente ha iniziato a vedere la luce e ha capito il problema.
native_language_example: After so many explanations, they finally started to see the light and understood the problem.

meaning: "to see his/her new …" (incomplete phrase; needs a noun after nuova).
additional_notes: This is not a complete expression on its own. In Italian, the possessive "sua" agrees with the thing owned (feminine singular here), and "nuova" is an adjective meaning "new" that must describe a following feminine singular noun (e.g., "la sua nuova casa" = "his/her new house"). For masculine nouns you’d use "il suo nuovo …".
target_language_example: Voglio vedere la sua nuova casa.
native_language_example: I want to see his/her new house.

meaning: to see the (feminine plural); also “to watch the …” (shows/performances).
additional_notes: Used with feminine plural nouns after the verb "vedere" (to see): "vedere le balene" (to see the whales), "vedere le differenze" (to see the differences). Depending on context, "vedere" can mean physically see/notice or watch (especially theatre, films, etc.). It’s simply "vedere" + the feminine plural article "le".
target_language_example: Domani andiamo a vedere le montagne.
native_language_example: Tomorrow we’re going to see the mountains.

additional_notes: Used with verbs of movement or purpose (often with "per") to say why you went somewhere: "andiamo a/per vedere le statue" = "we’re going to see the statues." "Vedere" can mean either simply "to see" or "to visit/go see" in a sightseeing context.
target_language_example: Siamo andati in centro per vedere le statue.
native_language_example: We went downtown to see the statues.

additional_notes: Used when asking if someone can make out/spot anything inside a place or container. "lì dentro" means "in there/inside (that place)" and often points to something at a distance or not easily visible. Often used with "puoi/potete" (can you) or "riuscire a" (manage to).
target_language_example: Riesci a vedere qualcosa lì dentro, con tutta questa oscurità?
native_language_example: Can you see anything in there, with all this darkness?

additional_notes: Used when pointing out a specific light source (often at a distance) that is visibly unsteady or blinking. You’ll often hear it in questions with "può/puoi" (can you) or "riesce/riuscite" (are you able to), e.g., asking if someone can make it out or spot it.
target_language_example: Riesci a vedere quella luce tremolante in fondo alla strada?
native_language_example: Can you see that flickering light at the end of the street?

additional_notes: Used to check a condition or find out information: "Vado a vedere se..." (I’ll go check if...). Often follows verbs of going/trying ("vai a vedere se..." = go and see if), or expresses curiosity/verification ("volevo vedere se..." = I wanted to see if). Takes a clause with the verb in the appropriate tense (e.g., "se è...", "se dormivi").
target_language_example: Vado a vedere se il negozio è ancora aperto.
native_language_example: I’m going to see if the shop is still open.

meaning: to see a doctor (to go for medical help).
additional_notes: Common way to say you should go to a doctor for advice or treatment. "Vedere" here means "to consult/visit" (not just "to look at"). Often used with "dovresti/dovrebbe" (you should/he should).
target_language_example: Se hai la febbre da due giorni, devi vedere un dottore.
native_language_example: If you’ve had a fever for two days, you need to see a doctor.

additional_notes: Uses vedere (“to see”) to mean “to watch.” Common with TV/cinema plans: andare a vedere un film = “to go watch a movie” (often at the cinema).
target_language_example: Domani sera andiamo a vedere un film al cinema.
native_language_example: Tomorrow evening we’re going to watch a movie at the cinema.

additional_notes: Used to suggest trying something, checking what happens, or testing whether something works. It’s the 1st-person plural of *vedere* (“to see”), often used inclusively like English “let’s…”. Common before a verb: *Vediamo se funziona* (“Let’s see if it works”).
target_language_example: Vediamo se domani hai tempo per un caffè.
native_language_example: Let’s see if you have time for a coffee tomorrow.

additional_notes: Usually used in the expression "essere di vedute ristrette" to describe a person who is not open to new ideas, different lifestyles, or other opinions. Often has a negative, critical tone.
target_language_example: Non voglio lavorare con persone di vedute ristrette.
native_language_example: I don’t want to work with narrow-minded people.

additional_notes: Used before a feminine singular noun with the definite article “la” (e.g., “vendere la macchina” = “to sell the car”). It’s the verb “vendere” (to sell) + “la” (the). If the noun is masculine, use “vendere il/lo”; if plural, “vendere i/gli/le.”
target_language_example: Non voglio vendere la macchina.
native_language_example: I don’t want to sell the car.

additional_notes: This isn’t a fixed idiom—it's the verb phrase **vendere** (“to sell”) + **la sua** (“his/her” referring to a feminine singular noun). You normally expect a noun right after it (e.g., **la sua casa**, **la sua macchina**). For masculine/feminine and singular/plural you change it: **il suo** (masc. sing.), **la sua** (fem. sing.), **i suoi** (masc. pl.), **le sue** (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: Vuole vendere la sua macchina.
native_language_example: He/She wants to sell his/her car.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "vendere" (to sell) + the possessive "la sua" (his/her/its, feminine singular) + "auto" (car). "Sua" agrees with the noun owned (auto is feminine), not with the owner, so it can mean either "his" or "her" depending on context. In real life you might also hear "macchina" instead of "auto".
target_language_example: Non vuole vendere la sua auto perché gli serve per andare al lavoro.
native_language_example: He doesn't want to sell his car because he needs it to go to work.

additional_notes: "Vendere" means "to sell". "La sua" means "his/her" (and can also mean formal "your" in contexts like "la Sua"). "Automobile" is understood, but in everyday Italian people often say "macchina" or "auto". Whose car it is (his vs. her) is usually clear from context.
target_language_example: Mary sta provando a vendere la sua automobile.
native_language_example: Mary is trying to sell her car.

additional_notes: Common with verbs like decidere di (to decide to), cercare di (to try to), provare a (to try to), volere (to want to), and expressions like non avere fretta di (to not be in a hurry to). Note: sua can mean “his,” “her,” or “its” depending on context. Also, macchina often means “car” in everyday Italian, not just “machine.”
target_language_example: Non voglio vendere la sua macchina senza parlarne con lei.
native_language_example: I don’t want to sell his/her car without talking to her about it.

additional_notes: "Vendere" means "to sell." "Le loro" is "their" (plural), and "case" is "houses/homes." Used when talking about people putting their property up for sale or trying/planning to sell it.
target_language_example: Quest'anno vogliono vendere le loro case e trasferirsi in città.
native_language_example: This year they want to sell their houses and move to the city.

additional_notes: “Vendette” is the passato remoto (simple past) of *vendere* (“to sell”), common in written stories and in some regions; in everyday speech you’ll often hear *ha venduto*. “La sua” means “his/her/its” referring to a feminine singular thing (e.g., *la macchina, la casa, l’azienda*). The owner’s gender is not shown here—*sua* can mean “his” or “her.”
target_language_example: Ieri vendette la sua macchina e comprò una bicicletta.
native_language_example: Yesterday he/she sold his/her car and bought a bike.

additional_notes: Used when talking about selling something feminine singular (la macchina, la casa, la mucca). It commonly appears in the passato prossimo with avere (ho/abbiamo/hai venduto...). With avere, the past participle venduto usually does not change to match gender/number in normal sentences.
target_language_example: Abbiamo venduto la casa la settimana scorsa.
native_language_example: We sold the house last week.

additional_notes: Usually used with an auxiliary verb, especially in the passato prossimo: **Ho venduto la mia...** = “I sold my...”. **La mia** refers to a feminine noun understood from context (e.g., *la macchina* = “the car”, *la bici* = “the bike”).
target_language_example: Ho venduto la mia macchina ieri.
native_language_example: I sold my car yesterday.

additional_notes: "Venga" is the formal (Lei) command form of "venire" (to come). It’s often followed by an infinitive to say what you want the person to come and do: "venga a vedere" (come and see), "venga a parlare" (come and speak). Use with people you address as "Lei" (e.g., strangers, customers, officials).
target_language_example: Signora, venga a sedersi qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Ma’am, please come sit here.

additional_notes: From *venire a casa* (“to come home”). **Venga** is the present subjunctive (used after phrases like *voglio che…*, *è probabile che…*, *spero che…*) and it’s also the **formal command** (imperative) for *Lei*: *Venga a casa immediatamente.* For an informal command to one person you’d say *Vieni a casa!*.
target_language_example: Spero che venga a casa per cena.
native_language_example: I hope you come home for dinner.
