additional_notes: Uses the formal command form (imperative with "Lei"): "venga" from "venire". It’s used when speaking politely to one person (a stranger, customer, older person, etc.), often with "Prego". Informal version to a friend: "Vieni con me".
target_language_example: Mi scusi, venga con me, per favore.
native_language_example: Excuse me, please come with me.

additional_notes: "Venga" is the formal (Lei) imperative of "venire" (to come). It’s used to address someone politely (e.g., a customer, a stranger, an older person) or in formal situations; it can also sound firm/authoritative depending on tone. "Qui" means “here,” and you can add adverbs like "immediatamente" (immediately) or "lentamente" (slowly), or "per favore" (please).
target_language_example: Dottore, venga qui un momento, per favore.
native_language_example: Doctor, come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Used to say where you are from (a city/country), or your origin/background. With places: "Vengo da Roma" = I’m from Rome. With distance: "Vengo da lontano" = I’ve come from far away. With family/background: "Vengo da una famiglia..." = I come from a ... family. From the verb "venire" (to come) + "da" (from).
target_language_example: Ciao! Vengo da New York, ma vivo a Milano.
native_language_example: Hi! I’m from New York, but I live in Milan.

additional_notes: Used with the verb **venire** (“to come”) to express that something happens to someone: **A/mi/ti/le/vi vengono gli incubi?** = “Do you get nightmares?” The person is shown with an indirect object (a + name, or mi/ti/le/ci/vi/gli). Often said at night or when talking about scary dreams.
target_language_example: Dopo quel film mi vengono gli incubi.
native_language_example: After that movie, I get nightmares.

meaning: to come to; to come and
additional_notes: Often followed by an infinitive: "venire a vivere" = "to come to live" / "to come and live." With a noun, it can mean coming to a place or event: "venire a una festa" = "to come to a party."
target_language_example: Io voglio venire a vivere qui.
native_language_example: I want to come and live here.

additional_notes: Used when the movement is toward the speaker’s home or the place thought of as “home.” Italian often uses the preposition "a" (“to”) with "casa" in this expression (literally “to come to home”), where English typically just says “come home.”
target_language_example: Puoi venire a casa stasera?
native_language_example: Can you come home tonight?

meaning: to be born; to come into the world.
additional_notes: Used to talk about someone’s birth (often in a slightly poetic or formal tone). Common in the past tense: "è venuto/a al mondo" (he/she was born). You can add a place or date: "è venuto/a al mondo a Roma" (was born in Rome).
target_language_example: Mia nonna è venuta al mondo nel 1945: in un'Italia che stava cambiando.
native_language_example: My grandmother was born in 1945, in an Italy that was changing.

additional_notes: Used for accompanying someone or joining them. It is usually followed by a person or pronoun: con me, con te, con noi, con voi. In context, English may sometimes translate it as "go with" depending on perspective.
target_language_example: Vuoi venire con noi al cinema?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with us to the movies?

additional_notes: Used to invite someone to accompany you. Often appears after verbs like chiedere (to ask) or volere (to want): "Ti va di venire con me?" = "Do you want to come with me?" You can add a destination with "a" (to): "venire con me a un concerto". In polite/formal situations, use "Lei": "Le dispiacerebbe venire con me?"
target_language_example: Ti va di venire con me al mercato?
native_language_example: Do you want to come with me to the market?

meaning: to come with us / to join us.
additional_notes: Used to invite someone to accompany your group. Often appears as a question ("Vuoi/Vorresti venire con noi?") or with plans/intentions ("voglio venire con voi/voi"). Note: the object changes with the group: con me (with me), con te (with you), con voi (with you all).
target_language_example: Se vuoi, puoi venire con noi a cena stasera.
native_language_example: If you want, you can come with us to dinner tonight.

additional_notes: Used to say you will accompany someone (the person addressed: "te" = "you" singular/informal). With verbs like "devo" (I have to), "voglio" (I want), or "potremmo" (we could) to express obligation, desire, or possibility.
target_language_example: Posso venire con te al supermercato?
native_language_example: Can I come with you to the supermarket?

meaning: 'to come out' / 'to come outside'; also 'to come up' or 'to turn out (to be revealed)'.
additional_notes: Used literally for leaving a place (Venire fuori di casa = to come out of the house). Very common figuratively to mean something appears, emerges, or is discovered (È venuto fuori un problema = a problem came up; La verità è venuta fuori = the truth came out). In the past, it often uses essere: è venuto/venuta fuori, sono venuti/venute fuori.
target_language_example: Può venire fuori la verità, prima o poi.
native_language_example: The truth can come out, sooner or later.

additional_notes: A straightforward phrase meaning movement toward the speaker's location. In the examples it appears after dire + di, as in dire a qualcuno di venire qui ('to tell someone to come here'). For a direct command to one person, Italian usually says vieni qui.
target_language_example: Puoi venire qui un momento?
native_language_example: Can you come here a moment?

meaning: to come up; to rise; (people/children) to grow up.
additional_notes: Common uses: (1) something physically rises/appears: “Mi viene su un nodo in gola” (a lump comes up in my throat), “Mi viene su un bernoccolo” (a bump comes up). (2) children growing up: “È venuto su in campagna” (he grew up in the countryside). (3) cooking/food: “La torta viene su” (the cake rises). Also in “venire su bene/male” = to turn out well/badly (especially about how someone grows up).
target_language_example: La torta non riesce a venire su bene.
native_language_example: The cake can’t manage to rise well.

meaning: to come off / come away; (also) to leave (with someone).
additional_notes: Often used when something detaches or comes loose: "La macchia non viene via" = "The stain won’t come out"; "Il tappo viene via" = "The cap comes off". With a person (often with "con me/te/lui...") it can mean to go away/leave together: "Vieni via con me" = "Come away/come with me".
target_language_example: Devo far venire via questa etichetta.
native_language_example: I have to get this label to come off.

meaning: "come to" / "come and" (you all), before an infinitive.
additional_notes: Used with the plural imperative of "venire" ("venite") followed by "a" + infinitive to invite or tell a group of people to come and do something: "Venite a fare festa!" It can also be used in a reproachful way like English "don’t come telling me...": "Non venite a dirmi...". For one person you’d say "vieni a".
target_language_example: Venite a cena da noi stasera!
native_language_example: Come over for dinner at our place tonight!

meaning: "Come and see" (addressed to more than one person).
additional_notes: Imperative of venire ("to come") in the voi form, used to call/invite a group to come and look at something. Often said as an excited invitation or to get people’s attention: "Venite a vedere!" You can add what you want them to see: "Venite a vedere la camera."
target_language_example: Venite a vedere cosa ho trovato!
native_language_example: Come and see what I found!

additional_notes: Used to invite or tell more than one person to accompany you. It’s also the polite/formal form when speaking to one person (Lei): “Lei viene con me?”. For one friend (tu): “Vieni con me.”
target_language_example: Scusate, venite con me un momento.
native_language_example: Excuse me, come with me for a moment.

meaning: “came to” (went/arrived at a place), in the simple past.
additional_notes: “Venne” is the passato remoto (simple past) of “venire” (to come). It’s common in stories, history, and written narration; in everyday conversation many speakers prefer “è venuto/a” (passato prossimo). Use “venne a + place” (venne a Roma) or “venne a + infinitive” to mean “came to (do something)” (venne a visitare...).
target_language_example: L’anno scorso venne a Milano per lavoro.
native_language_example: Last year he came to Milan for work.

additional_notes: "Venne" is the passato remoto (literary/historical past) of "venire". In everyday spoken Italian you usually hear "è venuto/a a casa" instead. "A casa" can mean either 'home' or 'to someone’s house' depending on context (e.g., "a casa mia" = 'to my house').
target_language_example: Dopo il lavoro, venne a casa tardi.
native_language_example: After work, he came home late.

additional_notes:
Feminine past participle of "venire" used with "essere" (e.g., "è venuta"). Often followed by:
- a place: "è venuta a Parigi" = "she came to Paris".
- an infinitive: "è venuta a chiedermi..." = "she came to ask me..." (often implies purpose).
Common fixed expression: "venire a sapere" = "to find out / to learn" ("Come sei venuta a saperlo?" = "How did you find out?").
target_language_example: È venuta a parlarmi dopo la lezione.
native_language_example: She came to talk to me after the lesson.

additional_notes: Past participle of **venire** (“to come”) + **qui** (“here”). It’s used with **essere** in compound tenses, and it agrees with the subject: **venuta** (female singular), **venuto** (male singular), **venuti/venute** (plural). Often appears in questions like **Perché è venuta qui?** (“Why did you come here?”) or in regrets like **non essere mai venuta qui** (“to have never come here”).
target_language_example: Non so perché sono venuta qui.
native_language_example: I don’t know why I came here.

meaning: came to; have come to (a place).
additional_notes: Past participle of venire (“to come”), used with essere to indicate arrival at a destination: sono/è venuto a + city/place. It agrees with the subject: venuto (m. sg.), venuta (f. sg.), venuti (m. pl./mixed), venute (f. pl.). Often followed by a purpose or circumstance, e.g., per + infinitive (per partecipare…), per + noun (per affari), or per caso (“by chance”).
target_language_example: Io sono venuto a Tokyo per partecipare a una conferenza.
native_language_example: I came to Tokyo to attend a conference.

meaning: came to / have come to (a place introduced by “in”)
additional_notes: Past participle of "venire" used with "essere" in compound tenses (e.g., passato prossimo): "sono venuto/a in ..." = "I came to / I have come to ...". Common with countries/regions (and some places) that take "in" (e.g., in Australia, in Giappone). Agreement changes by gender/number: "venuto" (m. sg.), "venuta" (f. sg.), "venuti" (m. pl.), "venute" (f. pl.). In polite questions you may see "è venuto in ...?" (formal "Lei").
target_language_example: Io sono venuto in Giappone per vedere Kyoto.
native_language_example: I came to Japan to see Kyoto.

additional_notes: Past participle of venire ('to come') + qui ('here'). In the passato prossimo, venire uses essere: sono/sei/è venuto/a qui, siamo/siete/sono venuti/e qui. The past participle agrees with the subject (venuto = masculine singular, venuta = feminine singular, venuti/venute = plural). Often used in questions with perché/per cosa to ask someone's reason for coming.
target_language_example: Sono venuto qui per parlare con te.
native_language_example: I came here to talk to you.

meaning: "(have) come here to / for" (to explain your purpose).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *venire* (to come) in the past: *sono venuto qui per...* = “I came / I have come here to...”. It agrees with the subject: *venuto* (male), *venuta* (female), *venuti/venute* (plural). You can also use other tenses: *ero venuto qui per...* (I had come here to...), *è venuto qui per...* (he came here to...). The *per* is followed by an infinitive (*per imparare*, *per salvarti*) or a noun (*per gli archivi*).
target_language_example: Sono venuto qui per parlare con te.
native_language_example: I came here to talk to you.

additional_notes: Used to describe the stage of ripeness, especially for fruit (e.g., bananas, tomatoes). It can refer to color (“green”) and/or not being fully ripe yet. You may also see the masculine plural form “verdi o maturi” depending on the noun being described.
target_language_example: Preferisci le banane verdi o mature?
native_language_example: Do you prefer bananas green or ripe?

additional_notes: Used to introduce an honest explanation, correction, or important point. It’s usually preceded by the article: **La verità è che…** (most common). Often followed by a full clause in the indicative: *La verità è che non ho tempo.*
target_language_example: La verità è che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: The truth is that I can’t come today.

additional_notes: Used with (essere) to check or state whether a claim is true: “È vero che…?” = “Is it true that…?” and “È vero che…” = “It’s true that…”. In negative: “Non è vero che…” = “It’s not true that…”. You can also see it in hypothetical forms: “Se fosse vero che…” = “If it were true that…”.
target_language_example: È vero che oggi il museo è chiuso?
native_language_example: Is it true that the museum is closed today?

meaning: real; proper; genuine; the actual/true one (often: “a real/proper …”, “the actual …”, “downright …”).
additional_notes: Used to emphasize that something is the genuine, full, or “proper” version of something (not partial, not just in name). It agrees in gender/number with the noun: vero e proprio (m. sing.), vera e propria (f. sing.), veri e propri (m. pl.), vere e proprie (f. pl.). Note: the fixed multi-word term is the same, but in many sentences it appears inflected (e.g., vera e propria).
target_language_example: Galinette, è un vero e proprio sciocco.
native_language_example: Galinette, he’s a real idiot.

additional_notes: Used to contrast a person’s legal or actual name with a nickname, stage name, or a name they use publicly. Often appears with verbs like "rivelare" (reveal) or with "il mio/il suo vero nome" (my/his/her real name).
target_language_example: Il suo vero nome è diverso da quello che usa online.
native_language_example: His real name is different from the one he uses online.

additional_notes: Usually used with a reflexive pronoun (mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si) to mean you pour yourself a drink: "Mi sono versato un bicchiere di vino". Because it’s reflexive, it commonly uses "essere" in the passato prossimo (mi sono versato/a…). The past participle can agree in gender/number in reflexive forms (e.g., "Mi sono versata…" if the speaker is female).
target_language_example: Dopo cena mi sono versato un bicchiere di acqua.
native_language_example: After dinner I poured myself a glass of water.

additional_notes: Used with stressed pronouns to say movement/direction toward a person: verso di me/te/lui/lei/noi/voi/loro. With nouns you usually just use verso (verso casa, verso Roma). Often interchangeable with "verso" in casual speech, but "verso di + pronoun" is very common and clear.
target_language_example: Vieni verso di me, per favore.
native_language_example: Come toward me, please.

additional_notes: Used to indicate movement or orientation in the direction of the speaker. Common with verbs like girarsi/girare (to turn), venire (to come), correre (to run), dirigersi (to head). Often appears in requests: “Girati/Giratevi verso di me” = “Turn toward me.”
target_language_example: Vieni verso di me, così ti faccio vedere meglio.
native_language_example: Come toward me, so I can show you better.

additional_notes: Used with the preposition **verso** + the masculine singular article **il**. It can express physical direction (**verso il tetto** = toward the roof) or figurative orientation/attitude (**interesse verso il golf** = interest toward/in golf). Changes with the article: **verso l’** (before a vowel), **verso lo** (e.g., *verso lo stadio*), **verso la** (feminine).
target_language_example: Andiamo verso il centro.
native_language_example: We’re going toward the city center.

additional_notes: Uses verso + a place to show direction (“toward”). Often answers “Where is it going?” or “Which way?” You can also say “in direzione del mare” with a similar meaning. Note: al mare means “to/at the seaside,” while verso il mare emphasizes direction (not necessarily arriving).
target_language_example: Camminiamo verso il mare prima che faccia buio.
native_language_example: Let’s walk toward the sea before it gets dark.

meaning: 'toward the' / 'in the direction of' (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate direction or movement toward a place or thing: verso la stazione, verso la città. It can also be figurative, meaning “toward” in the sense of attitude or relationship: un atteggiamento verso la vita. Grammar note: it’s verso + la (feminine singular). For masculine singular use verso il/lo; for plural verso i/gli/le.
target_language_example: Camminiamo verso la stazione, poi prendiamo il treno.
native_language_example: We’re walking toward the station, then we’ll take the train.

meaning: “get dressed so quickly” / “dress yourself so fast.”
additional_notes: Uses the imperative (command) of the reflexive verb *vestirsi* (“to get dressed”). *Vestiti* is the **informal singular** command addressed to one person (“you”). *Così* means “so/like this,” and *velocemente* means “quickly.” Often used to express urgency, surprise, or mild criticism depending on tone and context. Not to be confused with *i vestiti* = “clothes.”
target_language_example: Non vestirti così velocemente: fa ancora freddo fuori.
native_language_example: Don’t get dressed so quickly: it’s still cold outside.

meaning: I wish you (all) / I wish you (formal/plural).
additional_notes: Used to give good wishes to more than one person, or to one person using the formal "voi". It’s commonly followed by a noun phrase ("vi auguro buona fortuna", "vi auguro felicità") or by "di" + infinitive to wish someone something happens ("vi auguro di avere successo", "vi auguro di riuscirci"). For one person informal you’ll often hear "ti auguro"; for one person formal "Le auguro".
target_language_example: Vi auguro un buon viaggio!
native_language_example: I wish you a good trip!

additional_notes: Polite way to ask permission or check if something bothers someone. "Vi" is used for speaking to more than one person or in very formal situations (more commonly, you’ll hear "Le dispiace se…?" for one person formal, and "Ti dispiace se…?" informal singular). Often followed by a verb in the present tense: "Vi dispiace se fumo?"
target_language_example: Vi dispiace se apro la finestra?
native_language_example: Do you mind if I open the window?

additional_notes: Used with the pronoun "vi" (= you all / yourselves) plus "dovere" to express obligation. Common in reflexive/pronominal verbs where "vi" is required: "vi dovete scusare" (you must apologize), "vi dovete sbrigare" (you need to hurry up), "vi dovete prendere cura" (you must take care). Often sounds like a firm instruction, especially in negatives like "non vi dovete..." (= you must not / don’t you dare).
target_language_example: Ragazzi, vi dovete calmare subito.
native_language_example: Guys, you need to calm down right now.

meaning: “you should apologize to (someone).” (addressed to more than one person)
additional_notes: Used to tell a group of people that apologizing is the right thing to do. Structure: vi (to you / you all) + dovreste (you should) + scusarvi (to apologize) + con + person (Tom, lei/him/her). With a specific person you usually say “scusarsi con qualcuno” (apologize to someone).
target_language_example: Vi dovreste scusare con la professoressa per il ritardo.
native_language_example: You should apologize to the teacher for being late.

additional_notes: Used to ask or state what leads someone to a conclusion. "Vi" is "you" (plural) or polite/formal "you"; in informal singular you’d usually say "ti fa pensare che". Often appears in questions like "Cosa vi fa pensare che...?" (= "What makes you think that...?").
target_language_example: Cosa vi fa pensare che sia una buona idea?
native_language_example: What makes you think it’s a good idea?

meaning: “you trust” / “do you trust?” (plural, informal or formal).
additional_notes: Form of the verb "fidarsi" (to trust), used with "di": "vi fidate di me" = "you trust me". It’s reflexive: "voi vi fidate" (you trust). In questions, intonation or "o no?" can make it explicit: "Vi fidate di me o no?" = "Do you trust me or not?".
target_language_example: Non vi fidate di lui: non dice la verità.
native_language_example: Don’t trust him: he’s not telling the truth.

meaning: “has … to you” / “has … you” (addressing you plural or formal).
additional_notes: “Vi” is an object pronoun meaning “to you” (plural) or “to you” (formal, addressing more than one person). It usually comes before the verb. “Ha” is the 3rd person singular of avere (“has”) and is often used as the auxiliary in the passato prossimo (e.g., vi ha detto = “has told you”). With direct-object “vi” (meaning “you”), the past participle can agree in gender/number (vi ha trovati/trovate).
target_language_example: Il professore vi ha mandato un’email ieri.
native_language_example: The professor sent you an email yesterday.

meaning: 'has given you' (to you all / to you, formal).
additional_notes: Used with the verb "dare" in the passato prossimo. "Vi" is the object pronoun meaning "to you" (plural) or "to you" in the formal address (instead of "ti"). It’s often followed by what was given: "vi ha dato un regalo" = "has given you a gift".
target_language_example: Il direttore vi ha dato i documenti ieri.
native_language_example: The manager gave you the documents yesterday.

meaning: "(he/she) told you" (to you all / to you, formal).
additional_notes: "Vi" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (plural) or "to you" in formal address; "ha detto" is the past tense of "dire" ("to say/tell"). Used to report what someone said to the listener(s).
target_language_example: Chi vi ha detto questa storia?
native_language_example: Who told you this story?

additional_notes: 'vi' means 'you' (plural, or sometimes formal singular) and comes before 'ho' ('I have'). This combination is common in the passato prossimo, where English usually puts 'you' after the verb: e.g. vi ho chiamate = 'I called you'. 'Vi' can be a direct object ('you') or an indirect object ('to you'). When it is direct, the past participle may agree in gender and number.
target_language_example: Vi ho mandato un messaggio ieri.
native_language_example: I sent you a message yesterday.

meaning: "I told you" (to you all / to you formal).
additional_notes:
"Vi" means "to you" (plural "you all" or formal "you"), and "ho detto" is the past tense (passato prossimo) of "dire" = "to say/tell": "I have said/told" → natural English: "I told you." Often followed by:
- "che" + a full sentence: "Vi ho detto che..." (I told you that...)
- "di" + infinitive: "Vi ho detto di..." (I told you to...)
target_language_example: Vi ho detto di non preoccuparvi.
native_language_example: I told you not to worry.

meaning: "I told you (all) that…" / "I have told you that…"
additional_notes: "Vi" means "to you" (plural), and it’s also used as a formal "to you" (singular) in some contexts. "Ho detto" is the passato prossimo of "dire" (to say/tell), so it refers to something you said earlier. It’s usually followed by "che" + a full clause.
target_language_example: Vi ho detto che oggi non posso venire.
native_language_example: I told you (all) that I can’t come today.

meaning: “I told you (all) to …” / “I told you (formal ‘you’) to …”
additional_notes: Used to report a past instruction or order. "Vi" means "you" (plural) or "you" (formal, addressing one person politely). It’s in the passato prossimo: "ho detto" = "I said / I told." It’s normally followed by "di" + infinitive (e.g., "di aspettare", "di partire").
target_language_example: Vi ho detto di non entrare senza bussare.
native_language_example: I told you not to come in without knocking.

meaning: "I told you (all) not to…" / "I told you not to…" (to you plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used to report a past instruction or warning addressed to more than one person ("you all") or to a group formally ("you" polite). It is followed by an infinitive: "vi ho detto di non + VERB" (e.g., "vi ho detto di non entrare"). Literally it’s "I have told you not to", often translated as simple past in English.
target_language_example: Vi ho detto di non lasciare la porta aperta.
native_language_example: I told you not to leave the door open.

meaning: "I saw you" / "I've seen you" (addressing more than one person, feminine).
additional_notes: Used with the direct object pronoun **vi** (= you plural) and the passato prossimo of **vedere** (**ho visto**). When a direct object pronoun comes before the verb, the past participle often agrees in gender/number: **viste** = feminine plural. If the group is masculine or mixed, you’ll usually hear **vi ho visti**. Often followed by an infinitive to mean “I saw you do …”: **vi ho viste sorridere** = “I saw you smile.”
target_language_example: Vi ho viste uscire dal cinema.
native_language_example: I saw you (all) leave the movie theater.

additional_notes: Past tense of vedere (“to see”) in the passato prossimo: ho visto/a/i/e. Vi = “you” (plural, object). Visti is masculine plural; use viste for a group of all women. In everyday English it’s often translated as “I saw you” even though it literally means “I have seen you.”
target_language_example: Vi ho visti uscire dal cinema.
native_language_example: I saw you coming out of the cinema.

meaning: 'do you (plural/formal) like ...?' / '... are liked by you (plural/formal)'.
additional_notes: "Vi" is an object pronoun meaning "to you" (to you all / to you, formal), and "piacciono" is used with plural things that are liked. With piacere, the thing you like is the grammatical subject: "Vi piacciono le mele" literally "Apples are pleasing to you" = "You like apples." For singular things, use "vi piace" (e.g., "Vi piace questo film?").
target_language_example: Vi piacciono questi ristoranti?
native_language_example: Do you like these restaurants?

meaning: "Do you like the ...?" (addressing you all / formal you).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone likes something plural (or one thing in plural form). Italian uses piacere with the structure "to someone + be pleasing": vi (to you) + piacciono (are pleasing) + i + plural noun. For a singular noun, use "vi piace il/la...".
target_language_example: Vi piacciono i film italiani?
native_language_example: Do you like Italian movies?

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone likes certain things/people. "vi" = "to you" (you all / you formal), "piacciono" agrees with what is liked (here feminine plural), and "le" is the feminine plural article "the". Use it before a feminine plural noun (e.g., le banane, le chitarre) or a feminine plural adjective/noun used as a group (e.g., le asiatiche = Asian women). For masculine plural, use "vi piacciono i/gli"; for singular feminine/masculine: "vi piace la/il/lo".
target_language_example: Vi piacciono le paste alla crema?
native_language_example: Do you like custard pastries?

meaning: do you like (you all / formal you)
additional_notes: Used with the verb piacere, which works like “to be pleasing to”: the thing you like is the grammatical subject. So “Vi piace il vino bianco?” is literally “Does white wine please you?” but means “Do you like white wine?” Used for “you” plural (voi).
target_language_example: Vi piace questa pizza?
native_language_example: Do you like this pizza?

meaning: "do you like more?" / "which do you prefer?" (addressing you all or using polite 'you')
additional_notes: Used in comparisons to ask which person/thing/activity someone likes more. "Vi" is (1) plural "you" (you all) or (2) formal "you" in some regions (instead of "Le"). Often follows a question word: "Che/Cosa/Quale/Chi ... vi piace di più?"
target_language_example: Tra questi due ristoranti, quale vi piace di più?
native_language_example: Between these two restaurants, which one do you like more?

meaning: “Do you like the …?” (to you all / to you, formal).
additional_notes: Used to ask if someone likes something. Grammatically it literally means “the … is pleasing to you,” so the thing liked is the subject (e.g., *il tofu piace a voi*). **vi** = “to you (plural)” or polite “to you” (formal). **il** is the masculine singular “the”; for feminine use **la** (e.g., *Vi piace la pizza?*) and for plural use **i / le** (e.g., *Vi piacciono i libri?*).
target_language_example: Vi piace il caffè?
native_language_example: Do you like coffee?

meaning: "Do you (all) like the …?" (talking about one feminine thing).
additional_notes: Used to ask if a group of people likes something. Italian literally says “it is pleasing to you”: *piace* is used with singular things. *la* introduces a singular feminine noun (e.g., *la Cina, la Francia, la pizza*). For masculine singular, use *vi piace il…*. For plural things, use *vi piacciono i/le…* (e.g., *Vi piacciono le patatine?*).
target_language_example: Vi piace la musica italiana?
native_language_example: Do you all like Italian music?

meaning: I can teach you (plural/formal) how to…
additional_notes: Used when offering instruction: "vi" = "to you" (plural or polite), "posso" = "I can", "insegnare" = "to teach", "come" = "how". Often followed by an infinitive verb (e.g., guidare, vendere, sparare). You can also say "ti posso insegnare come" (to one friend) or "le/Le posso insegnare come" (very formal, to one person).
target_language_example: Vi posso insegnare come cucinare la pasta.
native_language_example: I can teach you how to cook pasta.

additional_notes: Used to make a strong, polite request or plea. "Vi" addresses more than one person, or one person formally (like "you" in a formal situation). Often used with the imperative: "Vi prego, aiutatemi" = "Please, help me." Can also be said alone ("Vi prego!") to emphasize urgency.
target_language_example: Vi prego, non ditelo a nessuno.
native_language_example: Please, don’t tell anyone.

additional_notes: Used to make a polite request or instruction, often in formal situations (announcements, apologies, addressing a group). It literally means “I beg you to…”. "Vi" is the formal/plural “you” (to you all / to you formally), and it’s followed by an infinitive: "vi prego di" + verb (e.g., mantenere, perdonare).
target_language_example: Vi prego di aspettare qui un momento.
native_language_example: Please wait here for a moment.

meaning: “do you remember?” (to a group, or formal “you”).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **ricordarsi** (“to remember”), in the **2nd person plural**. It’s often used in questions: **Vi ricordate…?** = “Do you remember…?” It can address multiple people (**you all**) or one person in very formal/old-fashioned speech (like addressing someone as “you” formally). Often followed by **di** before a person/thing: **Vi ricordate di me?** = “Do you remember me?”
target_language_example: Vi ricordate di questo posto?
native_language_example: Do you remember this place?

additional_notes: From the verb "ricordarsi di" (to remember). "Vi" is used for "you" plural (or formal "you"), and "ricordate" can be a question (with rising intonation or a question mark) or a statement. It’s followed by a noun ("Vi ricordate di Guo Jing?") or by an infinitive in the past: "di avermi visto" = "of having seen me".
target_language_example: Vi ricordate di dove abbiamo parcheggiato?
native_language_example: Do you remember where we parked?

additional_notes: Used when speaking politely to more than one person, or formally to one person (as “Lei”/“voi” form in some contexts). Often followed by molto (“very much”), per + noun/infinitive (“for …”), or di + infinitive (“for …”): vi ringrazio per il vostro aiuto; vi ringrazio di essere venuti.
target_language_example: Vi ringrazio per la vostra disponibilità.
native_language_example: Thank you for your availability/helpfulness.

meaning: “you’re wrong / you’re mistaken” (to more than one person, or formal “you”).
additional_notes: From the verb "sbagliarsi" (to be mistaken). "Vi" can mean (1) you-plural (you all), or (2) formal "you" (Lei) in some contexts. Often used to disagree or correct someone: "Secondo me vi sbagliate" (I think you’re wrong), "Temo che vi sbagliate" (I’m afraid you’re mistaken).
target_language_example: Mi dispiace, ma vi sbagliate: la riunione è domani.
native_language_example: I’m sorry, but you’re mistaken: the meeting is tomorrow.

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb **sentirsi** (“to feel”), used to talk about physical or emotional states. **Vi** = “yourselves/you (plural)”, so it’s addressed to more than one person (or as a polite/formal plural). It’s often followed by an adjective: **Vi sentite stanchi/stanche?** (“Do you feel tired?”).
target_language_example: Come vi sentite oggi?
native_language_example: How do you all feel today?

meaning: "How do you feel about ...?" (asking a group or using polite/formal "you").
additional_notes: Uses the reflexive verb "sentirsi" (to feel). "Vi" = "you" (plural, or formal). Common in questions: "Come vi sentite riguardo a ...?" / "Come vi sentite riguardo alla proposta?" You can also hear the singular versions: "ti senti riguardo a" (informal singular) and "si sente riguardo a" (formal singular).
target_language_example: Come vi sentite riguardo a questa decisione?
native_language_example: How do you feel about this decision?

meaning: "Do you need...?" / "Do you need (anything else)?" (addressing 'you' plural or formal).
additional_notes: From the verb "servire" used in the sense of "to need." "Vi" means "to you" (either to more than one person, or polite/formal 'you'). Common in shops, restaurants, and service situations: "Cosa vi serve?" = "What do you need?" / "What can I get you?"
target_language_example: Vi serve aiuto con le valigie?
native_language_example: Do you need help with the bags?

additional_notes: Combination of the pronoun "vi" (you all / yourselves) + "siete" (you are), used with verbs in the passato prossimo. Very common with reflexive verbs (e.g., "vi siete alzati" = you got up) and with some verbs that take "essere" (e.g., "vi siete incontrate" = you met). With reflexive verbs, English often uses the simple past ("you washed") rather than "have" ("you have washed"). Agreement: the past participle matches the gender/number of the group (e.g., "vi siete lavati" mixed/masc. plural, "vi siete lavate" fem. plural).
target_language_example: Vi siete già svegliati?
native_language_example: Have you (all) woken up already?

meaning: “you met (each other)” / “you got to know each other” (past).
additional_notes: From the reflexive verb conoscersi (“to meet/get to know each other”). It’s passato prossimo with essere, used when talking to two or more people ("you" plural) about when/how they first met. Often appears in questions like: Quando vi siete conosciuti? (“When did you meet?”).
target_language_example: Dove vi siete conosciuti?
native_language_example: Where did you meet?

meaning: "have you (all) ever …?" (used with reflexive verbs in the past).
additional_notes: Used mainly in questions with the passato prossimo of reflexive verbs: vi (to yourselves) + siete (auxiliary 'to be', 2nd person plural) + mai (ever). With non-reflexive verbs you typically use "avete mai" instead (e.g., "Avete mai visitato Roma?"). With negation it often means "never": "Non vi siete mai lasciati" = "You never broke up."
target_language_example: Vi siete mai svegliati troppo tardi per andare al lavoro?
native_language_example: Have you ever woken up too late to go to work?

additional_notes: From the reflexive verb "ricordarsi di" (to remember to). It’s used with "essere" in the passato prossimo: "vi siete ricordati" = "you (all) remembered". It’s typically followed by "di + infinitive" (an action you were supposed to do): "Vi siete ricordati di comprare…?" You can use it when speaking to more than one person ("voi"); it can also sound polite/formal in some contexts.
target_language_example: Vi siete ricordati di chiamare il medico?
native_language_example: Did you (all) remember to call the doctor?

meaning: “is waiting for you” (you = plural or formal).
additional_notes: Used with the present progressive: "sta" + gerund ("aspettando") = “is waiting.” "Vi" means “you” (plural) or “you” formal (used instead of "ti"). Note that Italian "aspettare" takes a direct object ("aspettare qualcuno"), but in English you usually say “wait for someone,” so it’s not a word-for-word literal translation. Also, "aspettare" can look like English “expect,” but it usually means “to wait for.”
target_language_example: Il direttore vi sta aspettando in ufficio.
native_language_example: The manager is waiting for you in the office.

additional_notes: "Vi" is the pronoun for "you" plural (or formal "you" in some contexts) and is also used with reflexive verbs (meaning "yourselves / each other"). "State" is the "voi" form of "essere". Together, "vi state" commonly appears before a gerund to form the present continuous with reflexive verbs: "vi state + verbo-ando/-endo" (e.g., "vi state scusando" = "you are apologizing").
target_language_example: Perché vi state preoccupando così tanto?
native_language_example: Why are you worrying so much?

meaning: "I suggest you (plural/formal) to… / I recommend that you…"
additional_notes: Used to give advice or a recommendation. "Vi" means "to you" (addressing more than one person, or used as a formal "you" in some contexts). It’s normally followed by "di" + infinitive: "vi suggerisco di + verb" (e.g., andare, parlare, studiare). For one person (formal), you often hear "Le suggerisco di…"; for one person (informal), "ti suggerisco di…".
target_language_example: Vi suggerisco di prenotare in anticipo.
native_language_example: I suggest you book in advance.

meaning: “Did you like the…?” (asking a group politely).
additional_notes: Used to ask more than one person if they liked something feminine singular (la foto, la partita, la pasta, la spiaggia). It’s the polite/plural form: vi = “to you (plural)”. With "è piaciuta" the thing liked is the subject, so the verb agrees with it: è piaciuta (fem. sing.); è piaciuto (masc. sing.); vi sono piaciute (fem. plural); vi sono piaciuti (masc. plural).
target_language_example: Vi è piaciuta la cena di ieri?
native_language_example: Did you like yesterday’s dinner?

via fax a questo numero a

target_language_multi_word_term: via fax a questo numero a
meaning: “by fax to this number to …” (as written; the final “a” is likely a typo or an unfinished template).
additional_notes: Seen in instructions on forms or notices indicating where to send something by fax. In idiomatic Italian you would normally see “via fax a questo numero:” (with a colon) or “via fax al numero …”. The trailing “a” is not standard on its own; it often introduces what comes next (e.g., a department/name) or is simply an error left in the text.
target_language_example: Invii il modulo via fax a questo numero a Ufficio Reclami: 02 1234 5678.
native_language_example: Send the form by fax to this number to the Complaints Office: 02 1234 5678.

additional_notes: Used after verbs like andare (go), portare (take/bring), or in commands to tell someone/something to leave this place. Common in urgent or angry imperatives: "Vattene via da qui!" (= Get out of here!). "Via" adds the idea of moving away; "da qui" specifies the starting point (from here).
target_language_example: Per favore, togli queste scatole via da qui.
native_language_example: Please, move these boxes out of here.

meaning: out of here; away from here.
additional_notes: Used with verbs like andare (to go), portare (to take), and mandare (to send) to mean leaving this place. Often in urgent commands: “Andate via di qui!” = “Get out of here!” Similar to “via da qui”.
target_language_example: Andiamo via di qui prima che inizi a piovere.
native_language_example: Let’s get out of here before it starts raining.

additional_notes: Used with verbs like "lavare" / "lavarsi" to express removing something by washing: "lavarsi via X" = “to wash X off.” "Dalle mani" means “from/off the hands” (da + le = dalle). Often appears with a reflexive pronoun (mi/ti/si/ci/vi/si): "Mi sono lavato/a via il sangue dalle mani."
target_language_example: Mi sono lavato via il sangue dalle mani.
native_language_example: I washed the blood off my hands.

meaning: “Come on!” / “Let’s go!” (urging someone to move or leave).
additional_notes: Used as an interjection, often repeated (via! via!) to hurry someone along or to shoo them away. You can add a verb like “andiamo” (“let’s go”): “Via, via, andiamo!”. Tone depends on context: it can sound impatient or playful.
target_language_example: Via, via, siamo in ritardo!
native_language_example: Come on, come on, we’re late!

meaning: “Go on!” / “Move!” / “Come on, get going!” (an urgent way to hurry people along).
additional_notes: Repeated *via* is used as a strong prompt to get someone to move, leave, or start doing something immediately. It’s common in spoken Italian (often with an impatient/urgent tone), and can also be used to shoo people away: *Via!* = “Off you go!” / “Get out!” depending on context.
target_language_example: Via, via, via, che siamo in ritardo!
native_language_example: Come on, come on, let’s go—we’re late!

meaning: "away from" (to move/go away from a place or person).
additional_notes: Used after verbs of movement (like andare, correre, scappare, stare lontano) to express getting away from someone/something or leaving a place. Example patterns: "Vai via da qui" = "Go away from here"; "Stai via da me" = "Stay away from me." Note: Italian "via" here means "away" and is not the same as English "via" (= "by way of").
target_language_example: Vai via da qui, per favore.
native_language_example: Go away from here, please.

additional_notes: Used with a following noun to mean a literal route (a road/path) or a figurative path/process (e.g., “on the way to recovery”). It’s the feminine singular form: la via + del (= di + il). Often appears in set phrases like "sulla via del..." (“on the road to...”).
target_language_example: Dopo l’operazione, è sulla via del recupero.
native_language_example: After the operation, he’s on the road to recovery.

additional_notes: Used especially for animal or plant species whose numbers are declining and could disappear. Often follows a noun: “una specie via di estinzione” or “specie in via di estinzione” (very common variant). Literally “on the way to extinction.”
target_language_example: Il rinoceronte è una specie in via di estinzione.
native_language_example: The rhinoceros is an endangered species.

meaning: the green light; authorization/approval (to go ahead).
additional_notes: Used as a noun phrase meaning official permission/approval (often with verbs like dare/concedere: “dare il via libera” = “to give the go-ahead”). It can also be used alone as a short announcement or question (“Via libera!” / “Via libera?”) meaning “All clear!” / “Are we cleared to go ahead?”. Common in news, bureaucracy, and projects (e.g., “Via libera per il lancio”).
target_language_example: Il direttore ha dato il via libera al progetto.
native_language_example: The director gave the green light to the project.

additional_notes: "Da sola" agrees with the speaker: a woman says "da sola"; a man says "da solo". You can use it with many verbs to mean "alone/by yourself": e.g., "andare da sola" (go alone), "vivere da sola" (live alone).
target_language_example: Preferisco viaggiare da sola, ma a volte vado con un'amica.
native_language_example: I prefer to travel alone, but sometimes I go with a friend.

meaning: to travel alone; to travel by yourself.
additional_notes: "Da solo" means "alone / by yourself" (for a male speaker). For a female speaker, say "viaggiare da sola". Often used with "essere" + adjective: "Sono felice di viaggiare da solo/a" (I’m happy to travel alone).
target_language_example: Preferisco viaggiare da solo quando devo lavorare.
native_language_example: I prefer to travel alone when I have to work.

additional_notes: Used to say you are making a journey using a bus as your means of transport. Very often appears with "dovere" (e.g., "ho dovuto...") to express that you had to travel by bus. You may also hear "viaggiare in autobus" with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Oggi devo viaggiare su un autobus perché la metro è chiusa.
native_language_example: Today I have to travel by bus because the subway is closed.

meaning: near (to) / close to (a masculine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to indicate physical or figurative closeness. It’s the masculine-singular form: vicino + a + il → vicino al. For feminine singular: vicino alla; masculine plural: vicino ai; feminine plural: vicino alle. Often used for locations: vicino al mare (near the sea), vicino al ponte (near the bridge), vicino al sole (closest to the sun).
target_language_example: C'è una farmacia vicino al supermercato.
native_language_example: There’s a pharmacy near the supermarket.

additional_notes: Used to say someone/something is at a short distance from a place or person. It usually comes before a noun or pronoun: vicino a casa, vicino a te, vicino a lui. You can also use it with an infinitive in phrases like: vicino a cadere (“close to falling”), meaning ‘almost’.
target_language_example: La farmacia è vicino a casa mia.
native_language_example: The pharmacy is near my house.

additional_notes: Used to say something is located close to a specific masculine singular place/thing: vicino + a + il → vicino al. For feminine singular use vicino alla (e.g., vicino alla stazione).
target_language_example: C'è un bar vicino al museo.
native_language_example: There’s a café near the museum.

additional_notes: Used to indicate location close to something. It’s the preposition "vicino a" + the definite article "la" (feminine singular): vicino alla spiaggia, vicino alla finestra. With other articles: vicino al (masc. sing.), vicino ai/agli (masc. pl.), vicino alle (fem. pl.).
target_language_example: C'è un bar vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There’s a bar near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say something is physically close to a place. It’s made of vicino + a + the definite article: alla = a + la (feminine singular). With other nouns you’ll see different forms: vicino al (a+il), vicino allo (a+lo), vicino ai (a+i), vicino agli (a+gli), vicino alle (a+le).
target_language_example: C’è una farmacia vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: There’s a pharmacy near the station.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something is located. It often follows verbs like "abitare" or "vivere" (to live), or it can be added to other location statements. "Vicino a" = "near"; "alla" is the contraction of "a + la"; "diga" means "dam".
target_language_example: C'è un parcheggio vicino alla diga.
native_language_example: There’s a parking lot near the dam.

additional_notes: Used to say that something (a home, hotel, restaurant, etc.) is located close to the beach. Often follows verbs like abitare/vivere (to live) or essere/trovarsi (to be / to be located): “L’hotel è vicino alla spiaggia.”
target_language_example: Il nostro hotel è vicino alla spiaggia.
native_language_example: Our hotel is near the beach.

meaning: a dead end (literally: a blind alley); a situation with no way forward.
additional_notes: Used both literally (a street/alley that doesn’t continue) and figuratively to mean you’ve reached a point where there are no good options or progress (“we’re stuck”). Often used with “essere in un vicolo cieco” = “to be at a dead end.”
target_language_example: Con questa trattativa siamo in un vicolo cieco.
native_language_example: With these negotiations we’re at a dead end.

meaning: “video to declare/file the …” (introduces what you’re declaring).
additional_notes: This phrase is incomplete on its own: after **dichiarare il** you normally need a masculine noun (e.g., **reddito** = income, **furto** = theft, **sinistro** = accident/claim). You’ll often see it as a title for an instructional video: **video per dichiarare il reddito** (“video to file your income/tax return”).
target_language_example: Guarda questo video per dichiarare il reddito.
native_language_example: Watch this video to file your income tax return.

additional_notes: Mostly used in formal, literary, or old-fashioned Italian (often written as one word: "vieppiù"). It intensifies a comparison or a change over time: something becomes progressively more true/strong (similar to "sempre più").
target_language_example: Con il tempo, mi sento vie più sicuro di questa scelta.
native_language_example: With time, I feel more and more confident about this choice.

additional_notes: Form of **venire** (to come) in the present tense: **lui/lei viene**. Used with **a + place** (destination) or **a + infinitive** to mean “comes to + verb” (often with the sense of coming in order to do something). In questions, intonation or a question mark makes it “Is he/she coming to…?”
target_language_example: Marco viene a prenderti alle otto.
native_language_example: Marco is coming to pick you up at eight.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone/something originates. Literally "(he/she/it) comes from" (3rd person singular of venire + da). Can be used for people (nationality/city), things (a train/letter), and figuratively ("comes from another world" = seems very strange/unreal).
target_language_example: Questa pizza viene da un ristorante napoletano.
native_language_example: This pizza comes from a Neapolitan restaurant.

additional_notes: Used with places, people’s origin, or the source of something (like a word, an idea, a feeling). It’s the 3rd-person singular of "venire" + "da" + "il" (dal). You can also use it with other people: "vengo dal" (I’m from), "vieni dal" (you’re from), "vengono dal" (they’re from).
target_language_example: Questo formaggio viene dal nord Italia.
native_language_example: This cheese comes from northern Italy.

additional_notes: Used with an indirect object pronoun: mi viene in mente (it comes to my mind), ti viene in mente, gli/le viene in mente, ci/vi viene in mente. Common in questions like “Che cosa ti viene in mente?” (“What comes to mind?”) and negatives like “Non mi viene in mente niente” (“Nothing comes to mind”). “Come ti viene in mente?” often means “How could you even think of that?” (a reproachful tone).
target_language_example: Non mi viene in mente nessuna soluzione adesso.
native_language_example: I can’t think of any solution right now.

meaning: “come to …” / “come and …” (inviting someone to do something).
additional_notes: Used with an infinitive to invite or tell someone to come and do an action: "Vieni a + infinitive" (e.g., "vieni a giocare", "vieni a prendermi"). It can sound like an invitation (“Come play…”) or a request/order (“Come pick me up”). The subject “tu” (you) is implied.
target_language_example: Vieni a mangiare con noi stasera?
native_language_example: Do you want to come eat with us tonight?

additional_notes: Imperative (informal singular) used to call someone’s attention and invite them to look at something happening now or to show them something (“Vieni a vedere!”). You can add what you want them to see: “Vieni a vedere questo/qui/il mio giardino…”. For formal or plural use: “Venga a vedere” (formal singular), “Venite a vedere” (plural).
target_language_example: Vieni a vedere, c’è qualcosa di strano fuori.
native_language_example: Come and see, there’s something strange outside.

additional_notes: An invitation or request for someone to accompany you. It’s the informal singular imperative of "venire" (you say it to one person you address as "tu"). You can add a destination: "Vieni con me al/in..."
target_language_example: Dai, vieni con me al mercato!
native_language_example: Come on, come with me to the market!

additional_notes: An invitation (or sometimes a firm instruction) to join the speaker and their group. Uses the informal singular imperative of "venire" (vieni), so it’s said to one person; for more than one person you’d say "venite con noi". You can add time words like "adesso/ora" (now) or a destination: "vieni con noi al cinema" (come with us to the movies).
target_language_example: Dai, vieni con noi al bar dopo lavoro!
native_language_example: Come on, come with us to the café/bar after work!

additional_notes: Imperative (tu) of **venire** + **fuori**. Used to call someone to come out from a place (a room, hiding spot, etc.), often when you can’t see them. You can add a name after it (e.g., *Vieni fuori, Marco!*).
target_language_example: Dai, vieni fuori! Non ti arrabbio mica.
native_language_example: Come on, come out! I’m not going to get mad at you.

additional_notes: Direct way to call someone to come closer to you. Common in speech; can sound like an order depending on tone (soften with “per favore” or use “vieni qui” which is very similar). Used to get someone’s attention or to check/see something up close: “vieni qua, che vediamo…”.
target_language_example: Vieni qua un attimo, per favore.
native_language_example: Come here a moment, please.

additional_notes: Commonly used as an imperative (command) to one person you address with "tu". For a more formal/polite command ("Lei"), use "venga qui". You can add details like time/place: "Vieni qui alle sei" = "Come here at six."
target_language_example: Vieni qui un attimo, per favore.
native_language_example: Come here for a moment, please.

additional_notes: Often used in the plural as a collective: i vigili del fuoco (“the firefighters” / “the fire brigade”). Singular: un vigile del fuoco (male or generic), una vigile del fuoco (female). In Italian it can refer both to an individual firefighter and (in plural) to the service.
target_language_example: Ho chiamato un vigile del fuoco perché c’era fumo in cucina.
native_language_example: I called a firefighter because there was smoke in the kitchen.

additional_notes: Used to refer to December 24th and especially the evening/night before Christmas Day. Often appears with "la" (la vigilia di Natale) and with prepositions like "a" or "alla" to mean "on/at Christmas Eve" (e.g., "alla vigilia di Natale").
target_language_example: Alla vigilia di Natale ceniamo tutti insieme.
native_language_example: On Christmas Eve we all have dinner together.

villaggio ha bisogno di una moschea

target_language_multi_word_term: villaggio ha bisogno di una moschea
additional_notes: Compositional sentence: *il villaggio* = “the village”, *ha bisogno di* = “needs” / “is in need of”, *una moschea* = “a mosque”. In natural Italian you’d usually include the article: **Il villaggio ha bisogno di una moschea.**
target_language_example: Il villaggio ha bisogno di una moschea.
native_language_example: The village needs a mosque.

additional_notes: Common in restaurants or at the table to order or request wine. You’ll often hear it with quantities or containers: "Un bicchiere di vino, per favore" (a glass), "Una bottiglia di vino, per favore" (a bottle), or "Altro vino, per favore" (more wine). With "del vino" it means “some wine.”
target_language_example: Un bicchiere di vino, per favore.
native_language_example: A glass of wine, please.

additional_notes: Used to order or talk about wine in restaurants/at home. Often appears with partitives like "del vino bianco" (some white wine) or in comparisons: "vino bianco o vino rosso?" (white or red?).
target_language_example: Per me un bicchiere di vino bianco, grazie.
native_language_example: For me, a glass of white wine, please.

additional_notes: Common restaurant/host question to ask what kind of wine someone wants. You can include the article (il vino) or omit it (vino) in this question. Used with formal (preferisce/Lei), informal (preferisci/tu), and plural (preferite/voi) forms.
target_language_example: Per cena prendiamo vino bianco o rosso?
native_language_example: For dinner, should we have white wine or red?

meaning: “wine in his/her/its …” (an incomplete phrase; “sua” needs a feminine noun after it).
additional_notes: This looks like a fragment rather than a fixed expression. In Italian, the possessive “sua” means “his/her/its” and must match the gender/number of the noun that follows (feminine singular), e.g. “la sua bottiglia” = “his/her/its bottle”. “Nella” = “in the” (in + la). So you’ll normally see something like “vino nella sua bottiglia” (wine in his/her bottle) or “vino nella sua borsa” (wine in his/her bag).
target_language_example: Ho messo il vino nella sua bottiglia.
native_language_example: I put the wine in his/her bottle.

additional_notes: Common in restaurants and shops. You can order it as a full request ("Un vino rosso, per favore") or very briefly ("Vino rosso, per favore"). Often contrasted with "vino bianco" (white wine).
target_language_example: Vorrei un bicchiere di vino rosso, per favore.
native_language_example: I’d like a glass of red wine, please.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase used to say someone has won the top prize in a contest/competition/raffle. It often appears after the auxiliary verb (usually "ha/hanno"): "ha vinto il primo premio" = "(he/she) won first prize."
target_language_example: Mia sorella ha vinto il primo premio al concorso di fotografia.
native_language_example: My sister won first prize in the photography contest.

additional_notes: Used to say you won something with a feminine singular noun (la gara, la causa, la scommessa, la battaglia, la partita). It typically appears after the auxiliary verb in the passato prossimo (e.g., ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno vinto la...).
target_language_example: Abbiamo vinto la partita.
native_language_example: We won the match.

additional_notes: Used with the auxiliary verb (usually avere) in the passato prossimo: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno vinto la corsa. Often used literally for a competition, and also figuratively to mean someone is celebrating or acting like they achieved a big win. Note: corsa means 'race' or 'run' (not the same as English 'course').
target_language_example: Finalmente abbiamo vinto la corsa!
native_language_example: We finally won the race!

additional_notes: Used with the verb "vincere" (to win). In the examples it appears as the past participle "vinto" with an auxiliary verb: "ho/ha/hanno vinto la lotteria" = "I/you/he-she/they won the lottery" (passato prossimo). Often used literally, but it can also be used figuratively to mean someone got extremely lucky.
target_language_example: Sei pazzo? Hai vinto la lotteria!
native_language_example: Are you crazy? You won the lottery!

meaning: “won the genetic lottery” (born with especially lucky genes/advantages).
additional_notes: Used figuratively to say someone is naturally lucky in traits like looks, height, health, or athletic ability, as if they “won” at birth. Often used with avere: “ha vinto la lotteria genetica” = “he/she won the genetic lottery.” Common in casual speech and online.
target_language_example: Con quei lineamenti e quella salute, ha proprio vinto la lotteria genetica.
native_language_example: With those features and that health, he really won the genetic lottery.

additional_notes: Past tense with the verb "vincere" (to win). You normally use it with an auxiliary: "ho vinto la partita" (I won the match), "hai vinto la partita?" (Did you win?). "Partita" means "game/match" (sports, cards, etc.) and is a false friend with English "party".
target_language_example: Abbiamo vinto la partita 2 a 1.
native_language_example: We won the match 2–1.

visitate da quando ci siamo trasferite

target_language_multi_word_term: visitate da quando ci siamo trasferite
additional_notes: Used when asking or talking about how many times someone has visited you from the time you moved up to now. **Da quando** = “since / ever since (the moment when)”. **Ci** means “us” (direct object here). **Visitate** is feminine plural to match **noi** (a group of women) in **ci siamo trasferite**; if the group includes men or is mixed, you’d usually say **ci siamo trasferiti** and **ci avete visitati**.
target_language_example: Non ci avete visitate da quando ci siamo trasferite a Milano.
native_language_example: You haven’t visited us since we moved to Milan.

additional_notes: Used to ask if someone has been to a zoo in a certain place, often followed by a location phrase like “nel tuo/vostro/suo paese” (“in your country”). Commonly appears with the present perfect: “Hai/Avete/Ha già visitato…?” = “Have you already visited…?”
target_language_example: Hai già visitato uno zoo nel tuo paese?
native_language_example: Have you already visited a zoo in your country?

meaning: (has/have) lived here for a long time.
additional_notes: Uses the past participle of **vivere** (“to live”) with **essere**: *ho/è/hanno vissuto…* In sentences like the examples, it’s in the **passato prossimo**, often meaning someone lived here for a long time (and may or may not still live here—context decides). *Qui* = “here”; *per molto tempo* = “for a long time.”
target_language_example: Abbiamo vissuto qui per molto tempo, ma ora ci siamo trasferiti.
native_language_example: We lived here for a long time, but now we’ve moved.

meaning: (we/you/they) saw each other last night / seen last night.
additional_notes: Literally “seen last night.” It’s the past participle of vedere (“to see”) + a time expression. Often used with ci + essere to mean “to see each other”: “Ci siamo visti la scorsa notte.” Note agreement: visto (m. sg.), vista (f. sg.), visti (m. pl. or mixed), viste (f. pl.).
target_language_example: Ci siamo visti la scorsa notte al bar.
native_language_example: We saw each other last night at the bar.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "vedere" (to see/watch) in the past: "ho/ha/hai visto..." = "I/you/he/she have seen" (often meaning "watched"). "dei" is a partitive meaning "some/any," so questions like "Hai visto dei film nuovi (ultimamente)?" mean "Have you seen/watched any new movies (lately)?" You can add time expressions like "di recente / recentemente / ultimamente" to mean "recently/lately."
target_language_example: Hai visto dei film nuovi ultimamente?
native_language_example: Have you seen any new movies lately?

additional_notes: Used with the verb "vedere" (to see). In the passato prossimo, it appears after forms of "avere": "ho visto il..." (I saw / I have seen the...), "hai visto il...?" (Have you seen the...?). "Il" is the masculine singular definite article; use "visto lo" before s+consonant/z/gn/ps (e.g., "ho visto lo zaino"), and "visto l'" before a vowel (e.g., "ho visto l'aula").
target_language_example: Hai visto il mio telefono?
native_language_example: Have you seen my phone?

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of vedere (to see/watch). Most often it appears with the auxiliary avere to form the past tense: ho visto il film = I watched the film / I’ve seen the film. It can also be used after words like dopo/avendo to mean “after/having watched the film.”
target_language_example: Ho visto il film ieri sera.
native_language_example: I watched the movie last night.

meaning: “seen my phone” (usually part of “Hai visto il mio telefono?” = “Have you seen my phone?”).
additional_notes: This is the past participle phrase “visto” (seen) + “il mio telefono” (my phone). In normal Italian you’ll typically include an auxiliary verb: “Hai visto il mio telefono?” In casual speech/text, “Hai” may be dropped, especially in a quick question.
target_language_example: Hai visto il mio telefono? Non lo trovo più.
native_language_example: Have you seen my phone? I can’t find it anymore.

meaning: “seen the” (past of “see” + “the” for a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used with the verb *vedere* (“to see”). In the *passato prossimo* (present perfect), you say *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno visto* + *la* + noun: *Ho visto la collina* (“I saw the hill / I’ve seen the hill”). Common in questions with *mai* (“ever”): *Hai mai visto la…?*
target_language_example: Hai mai visto la mia nuova casa?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen my new house?

meaning: "(have) seen something …" (usually before an adjective, like "strange").
additional_notes: This is a common pattern in questions/negative sentences: «Hai visto qualcosa di + aggettivo?» = “Did you see anything + adjective?” The «di» introduces what comes next (typically an adjective): «qualcosa di strano» = “something strange.” «Visto» is the past participle of «vedere» and is usually used with «avere» (e.g., «hai visto…», «ho visto…»).
target_language_example: Hai visto qualcosa di strano qui vicino?
native_language_example: Did you see anything strange nearby?

additional_notes:
Used with the verb vedere in the past: 
- Ho visto qualcosa di strano. = “I saw something strange.”
In reported speech you’ll often hear:
- Dicono che hanno visto qualcosa di strano. (“They say they saw…”) 
- Dicono di aver visto / di avere visto qualcosa di strano. (“They say they have seen/saw…”) 
In the last two, di + infinitive (aver/avere visto) is a common way to report what someone says without using che.
target_language_example: Ho visto qualcosa di strano vicino alla porta.
native_language_example: I saw something strange near the door.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle visto (“seen”) with avere to talk about having seen a particular movie: (ho/hai/ha) visto quel film. Common in questions with già (“already”) or mai (“ever”): Hai già visto quel film? / Hai mai visto quel film? With non...mai it means “never”: Non ho mai visto quel film.
target_language_example: Hai già visto quel film o lo guardiamo stasera?
native_language_example: Have you already seen that movie, or shall we watch it tonight?

additional_notes: Used with the verb vedere (“to see/watch”) in the present perfect: ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno visto questo film (“I/you/he… have seen this movie”). Very common in questions with già (“already”) or mai (“ever”): Hai già visto questo film? / Hai mai visto questo film?
target_language_example: Non ho mai visto questo film.
native_language_example: I’ve never seen this movie.

additional_notes: Used with the verb vedere (“to see”) in the past participle visto, often with avere (ho/hai/ha…): ho visto un… = “I saw / I have seen a…”. “Un” is the masculine singular indefinite article; for feminine use: ho visto una… (“seen a…”).
target_language_example: Hai visto un gatto nero vicino alla porta?
native_language_example: Did you see a black cat near the door?

additional_notes: Past participle of *vedere* (“to see”) used with an object. Very common in questions with **mai** (“ever”): *Hai/Avete mai visto un elefante?* = “Have you ever seen an elephant?” You may also see it with *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno visto* (“I/you/he… have seen”).
target_language_example: Hai mai visto un elefante allo zoo?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen an elephant at the zoo?

additional_notes: Literally means someone has seen a ghost (from the verb *vedere*). It’s often used with *avere* in the past tense: *ho/hai/ha visto un fantasma*. In phrases like *sembra che abbia visto un fantasma*, it can also mean someone looks very shocked, scared, or pale—as if they’d seen a ghost.
target_language_example: Quando mi hai chiamato, sembravi che avessi visto un fantasma.
native_language_example: When you called me, you looked like you had seen a ghost.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "avere" to form the passato prossimo of "vedere" (to see): "ho/hai/ha visto" = "I/you/he/she have seen" (often just "saw" in English). Very common in questions with "mai" to mean "ever": "Hai mai visto un leone?" = "Have you ever seen a lion?"
target_language_example: Hai mai visto un leone allo zoo?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a lion at the zoo?

additional_notes: This is a regular (non-idiomatic) phrase built around the past participle **visto** from **vedere** (“to see”). It commonly appears with **avere** in the **passato prossimo**: **ho/ha/hanno visto** = “I/he/they saw” or “have seen.” **Ieri** means “yesterday” and can go at the end (as here) or earlier in the sentence.
target_language_example: Abbiamo visto un leone ieri allo zoo.
native_language_example: We saw a lion yesterday at the zoo.

additional_notes: Uses the past participle of *vedere* (to see) in the *passato prossimo* with *avere*: *ho/hai/ha/abbiamo/avete/hanno visto un lupo* = 'I/you/he… have seen a wolf' / '… saw a wolf'. In questions you often see *Hai mai visto un lupo?* = 'Have you ever seen a wolf?'
target_language_example: Non ho mai visto un lupo dal vivo.
native_language_example: I've never seen a wolf in real life.

additional_notes: Past participle phrase from the verb "vedere" (to see), used with the auxiliary "avere": "ho/hai/ha/avete mai visto un panda?" = "have I/you/he ever seen a panda?". Without "mai", it often means you saw one at a specific time: "Ho visto un panda una volta" = "I saw a panda once."
target_language_example: Hai mai visto un panda dal vivo?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a panda in real life?

additional_notes: Commonly used with the passato prossimo to say someone saw a mouse (often suddenly or unexpectedly). The full form is usually a subject + avere in the present + visto: "Ho visto un topo" (I saw a mouse / I’ve seen a mouse), "Hai visto un topo?" (Did you see a mouse?). "Un" is the masculine singular article (“a”).
target_language_example: Ho visto un topo in cucina!
native_language_example: I saw a mouse in the kitchen!

additional_notes: Not a fixed expression. visto is the past participle of vedere ('to see'), and una means 'a/an' before a feminine singular noun. It commonly appears with forms of avere, as in ho visto una... or avete visto una....
target_language_example: Hai mai visto una stella cadente?
native_language_example: Have you ever seen a shooting star?

additional_notes: Introduces a reason or situation that explains what follows. Very common in spoken and written Italian; often at the start of a sentence, but can also appear in the middle. Similar in meaning to "siccome" or "dato che".
target_language_example: Visto che piove, restiamo a casa.
native_language_example: Since it's raining, let's stay home.

additional_notes: "vita" = "life" + "è" = "is" (3rd person singular of "essere"). Very common pattern in sentences like "La sua vita è in pericolo" (His/Her life is in danger) or "La sua vita è nelle tue mani" (His/Her life is in your hands). Often used with possessives: "la mia/tua/sua vita è…".
target_language_example: La mia vita è cambiata dopo quel viaggio.
native_language_example: My life changed after that trip.

additional_notes: Used to say that life contains many examples of something (good or bad). In full form you’ll often see the article: “La vita è piena di …”. After “piena di” you typically use a plural noun (“sorprese”, “opportunità”) or an uncountable noun (“gioia”, “problemi”).
target_language_example: La vita è piena di sorprese.
native_language_example: Life is full of surprises.

additional_notes: Means “(he/she) lives in/at” and is used to say where someone lives, typically with cities (vive a Roma, vive a Tokyo). With countries you usually use "vive in" (vive in Italia). You can also use it in general statements like "come si vive a Boston" = "what it’s like to live in Boston".
target_language_example: Mio fratello vive a Milano.
native_language_example: My brother lives in Milan.

additional_notes: Used with a person/people you share a home with. The verb is "vivere" (to live). In these examples it’s in the 3rd person singular present tense: "lei/lui vive" = "she/he lives". Use "vive con" + a person or family member: "vive con i genitori", "vive con suo padre", "vive con sua mamma".
target_language_example: Marco vive con sua sorella in centro.
native_language_example: Marco lives with his sister downtown.

additional_notes: Used to say that a woman lives on her own (not with family/roommates). For a man, you say “vive da solo”. Often followed by a place: “vive da sola a/in…”. Can also be a yes/no question: “Vive da sola?”
target_language_example: Anna vive da sola in centro.
native_language_example: Anna lives alone downtown.

additional_notes: “Da solo” means “alone / on one’s own.” With “vivere” it usually means living without other people in the home (no roommates/partner). Sometimes it’s used more loosely to mean “without a partner,” so you may see it even if someone lives with family (e.g., “vive da solo con i suoi genitori,” meaning he’s single even though he lives with his parents). Feminine: “vive da sola.” Other persons: “vivo da solo” (I), “viviamo da soli” (we), etc.
target_language_example: Tom vive da solo in un appartamento.
native_language_example: Tom lives alone in an apartment.

meaning: “lives in” (lives in a place / lives in).
additional_notes: “Vive” is the 3rd person singular of *vivere* (“to live”). Use **vive in + place** to say where someone lives: *Vive in Francia / in questo quartiere*. It can also be used figuratively with abstract places: *vive in un mondo di fantasia* (“he lives in a fantasy world”). For cities, countries, and neighborhoods you often use **in**; with specific addresses you typically use **a** (e.g., *vive a Roma*).
target_language_example: Mia sorella vive in Canada.
native_language_example: My sister lives in Canada.

additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives: **vivere** (to live) + **in** + an indefinite article. It’s followed by a place noun (e.g., *quartiere, palazzo, villaggio*). The article changes with gender/number: **vive in un** (masc.), **vive in una** (fem.), **vive in uno** (before *s+consonant, z, ps, gn*), **vive in un’** (before a vowel).
target_language_example: Mio fratello vive in un appartamento vicino al centro.
native_language_example: My brother lives in an apartment near the city center.

additional_notes: "Vive" is the present tense of "vivere" (to live) for he/she/you-form (Lei). Often Italian drops the subject pronoun: "Vive in un appartamento" can mean "He/She lives in an apartment" (from context) or "You live in an apartment" (formal). You can add details after "appartamento": "di tre camere" (three-bedroom), "al centro" (downtown/in the center), "non lontano da..." (not far from...).
target_language_example: Mia sorella vive in un appartamento vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: My sister lives in an apartment near the station.

meaning: “(he/she) lives in a …” (before a feminine singular noun).
additional_notes: Used to say where someone lives, followed by a feminine singular noun (e.g., una casa, una città, una zona, una comunità, una villa). For a masculine singular noun, use “vive in un …” (e.g., vive in un appartamento). You may also hear “abita in una …” with the same meaning.
target_language_example: Mia sorella vive in una casa piccola vicino al mare.
native_language_example: My sister lives in a small house near the sea.

additional_notes: Used with a place or person to say where someone lives: **vive vicino a + noun/pronoun** (e.g., *vive vicino a me*, *vive vicino alla biblioteca*). In Italian you usually add **a** before the person/place you’re near.
target_language_example: Mia sorella vive vicino alla stazione.
native_language_example: My sister lives near the station.

additional_notes: Used with a person or group after "con" to say you share a home with them (cohabit). It can be neutral (roommates/family) or imply living together as a couple, depending on context.
target_language_example: Non voglio più vivere con i miei genitori: voglio un appartamento mio.
native_language_example: I don’t want to live with my parents anymore: I want my own apartment.

additional_notes: Uses the feminine form "sola" and is used when the subject is a woman (e.g., "io" referring to a woman, or talking about "lei"). For a man, say "vivere da solo". Here "da" has the sense of "on one’s own / by oneself".
target_language_example: Preferisco vivere da sola.
native_language_example: I prefer to live alone.

meaning: to live alone; to live by yourself.
additional_notes: Used to say that someone lives without roommates/housemates (and often without family). You can change the gender/number: "vivere da sola" (a woman), "vivere da soli" (we/they or mixed group). Common with verbs like "odiare" (to hate), "volere" (to want), and expressions like "essere abituato/a" (to be used to).
target_language_example: Sono abituato a vivere da solo.
native_language_example: I’m used to living alone.

additional_notes: Used for living or being based in a place, such as a city, country, or neighborhood. It often appears in expressions like andare a vivere in, meaning "to go live in" or "to move to" a place.
target_language_example: Vorrei vivere in campagna.
native_language_example: I'd like to live in the countryside.

additional_notes: Uses the verb vivere (to live) + in (in) + questa città (this city). Often appears with conditional forms to talk about a wish or possibility: mi piacerebbe vivere... ('I’d like to live...'), potrei/potresti/potrebbe vivere... ('could I/you/he-she live...').
target_language_example: Non potrei mai vivere in questa città: è troppo rumorosa.
native_language_example: I could never live in this city: it’s too noisy.

additional_notes: Used with the verb "vivere" (to live). For where you live in a city, Italians typically use "a" (e.g., "Vivo a Roma"). For countries you usually use "in" ("Vivo in Italia").
target_language_example: Vivo a Milano, ma lavoro a Monza.
native_language_example: I live in Milan, but I work in Monza.

additional_notes: Uses the verb "vivere" (to live). "con" means "with." "mio" (my) agrees with the noun: "zio" (uncle) → "mio zio". Word order is flexible; "ora/adesso" (“now”) can go at the beginning or end: "Ora/Adesso vivo con mio zio."
target_language_example: Da due mesi vivo con mio zio.
native_language_example: I’ve been living with my uncle for two months.

additional_notes: Used to say where you live. "Vivo" is the 1st person singular of "vivere" (to live), and "in" is used before many places (countries, continents, and also things like "in un appartamento").
target_language_example: Vivo in Italia da due anni.
native_language_example: I’ve been living in Italy for two years.

meaning: “they live in” (they reside in a place).
additional_notes: "Vivono" is the 3rd person plural of "vivere" (to live). Use "vivono in" before a place (city/country/house/area): "Vivono in Italia", "Vivono in questa casa". For questions, intonation or a question mark is enough: "Vivono in Algeria?"
target_language_example: I miei nonni vivono in Canada.
native_language_example: My grandparents live in Canada.

additional_notes: Often used in the phrase **a voce alta**, meaning **“out loud / aloud”** (speaking so others can hear). On its own, **voce alta** literally means “loud/high voice” and can describe someone’s speaking voice.
target_language_example: Puoi leggere questo testo a voce alta?
native_language_example: Can you read this text out loud?

additional_notes: Used to express a desire/urge.
